units.la: INTER cætera quæ ad studium assiduæ lectionis sacrarum literarum inflammandum, à piis & eruditis Theologis, afferuntur argumenta, mirificè me affecit & altius pectori insedit meo, comparatio illa, quam à Iuris & Medicinæ consultorum diligentiâ indefessâ in suæ professionis vastissimis voluminibus legendis memoriâque reponédis,affert & inculcat D. Andreas Hyperius, lib. 1. de S. Scripturæ lectione quotidiana. pag. 138. hisce [?] proditam verbis: Iurisconsulti, quò in suo studiorum genere laudem promerean-tur, totos viginti annos dant legum Imperatoriarum immensis & spinosis voluminibus: Medicos non piget, in Hippocrate, & Galeni prolixis commentariis bonam ætatis partem terere. Quòd si suæ professionis placita omnia tam exiguo libro haberent comprehensa, quàm sunt sacra Biblia, credo equidem universa ad verbum memoriter ediscerent: ac videremus, illos quidem leges tam veteres quàm novas, hos vero aphorismos & præcepta rationalia seu dogmatica de unaquaque re propositá, sta-tim & celeriter, & quasi uno spiritu recitare. Eos qui Ciceroniani haberi affectant, audi-mus dies noctesque in sisicere [?] libris Ciceronis: & sæpius universos non cursim & obiter, sed tanta contentione & attentione perlegere, ut non modo res, verum etiam singula verba, atque horum tum significationem, tum collocationem observent. Quam operam verè laboriosissimam, & ad Ecclesiæ vel Reipub. ordinationem non valde necessariam, doctissimis quibusque aduertimus oppido probari. Quin igitur, qui Christianarum Ecclesiarum doctores esse debent, ac magistri, parem adhibent diligentiam in ediscendo paruo, imo facili ac peruio opere sacrorum Bibliorum, quorum, explicatione quam plurimum non modò Eccle-siæ, verum etiam Respub. iuuari queant? Magnum admittunt dedecus ministri Ecclesiarum, si superari se lectionis diligentia à Iurisconsultis, Medicis, Oratoribus patiuntur. Hactenus ille. Et sanè ex conuictu atque consuetudine, quæ mihi in Germaniæ Academiis cum Iuris & Medicinæ peritis intercessit, tanquam αὐτόπτης[?], de veritate præconij huius ipsorum diligentiæ edoctus, pudibundus ingemui, meque ipsum, & alios S. Theologiæ candidatos, in S. Scripturæ lectione remissiores, negligentiæ crimine tantum non in-expiabili obnoxium reputas, æmulandam hanc ipsam industriam, inE-loquiis Dei omni exceptione maioribus, Justitiam æternam, & Jus beatæ immortalitatis, nec non animarum ex peccato sauciarū[?] cer-tissimamMedicinam pandentibus,
units.tr: Among the other arguments that pious and learned theologians put forward to kindle the zeal for constant reading of Holy Scripture, I was greatly moved by, and it lodged deeply in my heart, the comparison which D. Andreas Hyperius draws and presses home from the tireless diligence of lawyers and physicians in reading the vast volumes of their profession and committing them to memory, in book 1 of On the Daily Reading of Holy Scripture, p. 138, where he sets it out in these words: Lawyers, so that they may earn praise in their field of study, spend whole twenty-year periods on the immense and thorny volumes of the imperial laws; physicians do not mind spending a good part of their lives on the lengthy commentaries of Hippocrates and Galen. But if the decrees of their profession were all contained in a book as small as the Holy Bible, I believe they would learn everything by heart word for word, and we would see them recite at once and quickly, as if in one breath, the laws both old and new, and those physicians the aphorisms and rational or dogmatic precepts on any subject proposed. We hear of those who aim to be thought Ciceronians, that they spend days and nights in the books of Cicero, and often read through them entire, not hastily and in passing, but with such strain and attention that they observe not only the matter but each single word, both its meaning and its arrangement. We note that this work, truly very laborious and not very necessary for the ordering of the Church or the commonwealth, is greatly approved by all the most learned men. Why then do the teachers and masters of the Christian churches not apply an equal diligence to learning by heart the small, nay easy and plain, work of the sacred Bible, by whose exposition not only the Church but also the commonwealth could be greatly helped? The ministers of the churches incur great disgrace if they allow themselves to be surpassed in diligence of reading by lawyers, physicians and orators. So far he. And indeed, from the close company and acquaintance I had with lawyers and physicians in the German universities, I learned, as an eyewitness [αὐτόπτης], the truth of this praise of their diligence, and I groaned in shame, reckoning myself and other candidates for theology too slack in reading Holy Scripture, guilty of a fault almost beyond atonement of negligence; and I resolved to imitate this same industry, in the words of God, which are greater than any exception, which lay open the eternal justice and the law of blessed immortality, and the most certain medicine for souls wounded by sin,

units.la: [illegible, ~20 letters] altissimâ intimâque memoriâ re- condendis, persæpe mihi propo- sui. De huius propositi mei effectu quod prædicem ferè nihil, de asse- ctu quod pollicear, nonihil habeo. Nam conatus iste meus, quantum- uis variis directè & transuersim in- currentibus impedimentis variè retardatus & læsus, numquam ta- men adeò est elisus, vt d[?] esuccesu ipso, Deo vitam virésque largien- te, animum abiecerim, aut studiù hoc depositerim; donec superiori- bus annis mihi ex impositi ratione muneris, maiore quodam nisu ad idipsum persequendum & oc- casio oblata, & necessitas impo- sita fuit. Cùm enim ex veteri con- suetudine & sanctione legum Col- legij nostri, (cuius me indignum In- spectotem & moderatorem volue- runt & vocauerunt illi, penes quos vocandi resìdet potestas) lectio S. Scripturæ horis matutinis & vespertinis, nec non ante, & interdū etiam post sumptionem cibi, instituēda sit; in id pro tenui virili mea semper incubui, vt illa lectio κατὰ παιδείας τρόπον instituueretur, & certis strictæ & generalis Analyseos includeretur limitibus, ne scilicet perfunctoria solùmodo, fluxa, vaga, & proinde ἄκαρπος, hoc est omnis intelligentiæ, vtilitatis & ædificationis expers esset, qualis est indoctorum Monachorum & Monialium ad pensum absoluendum & Horas suas complendas, ex opere operato, Psalterij, Euangeliorum & Epistolarum suscepta lectio. Præclarè & grauiter D. Benedictus Aretius, lectionē Sacræ Scripturæ definit, quod sit diligens & cum iudicio suscepta sacrarum literarū meditatio, mádata divinitus omnibus vitæ humanæ ordinibus, inprimis verò his qui alios cum fructu docere volunt. Meditationem definit lectionem, quia sensum & succum Scripturæ non tam oculari inspectione, quam præsentis animi attetione & solerti indagine venamur & assequimur:(Psal.1.v.2.) Hac Meditationem in medio quasi locat inter duo extrema, negligentiam & sophisticen, negligentiæ tanquam defectui opponens diligentiam, sophisticæ autem (quâ alius Scripturæ præter genuinū, sensus affingitur) velut excessui, iudicium sanū. Ad huiusmodi diligentem cum sano iudicio & euidenti utilitate coniū-ctam Verbi divini lectionem seu meditationem, hac meâ apellâ viâ sternere conatus, ea quæ à doctissi-mis quibusvis Theologis recentio• ribus στροφάδιω[?] ad rerum & argume-torum τάξιν τῆς συνάφειαν[?]. i. seriem & coherentiam ostendendam scripta sunt, quasi in vnum corpus colli-go, & connexione congrua & me-thodica copulo, publicique iuris in gratiam S. Theologiæ Tyronū, haud grauatim operam suam loca-te Typographo, facio.
units.tr: [illegible, about 20 letters] to commit to the deepest and most inward memory, which I have often proposed to myself. Of the effect of this my purpose I can hardly foretell anything, but of its result I have something to promise. For this my endeavour, although it has been variously hindered and harmed by various obstacles that have met it head-on and from the side, has never been so beaten down that I gave up hope of success, or abandoned this pursuit, God granting me life and strength. Until, in recent years, by reason of the office laid upon me, an opportunity for pursuing this very thing with greater effort was offered to me and a necessity was imposed. For since, by the old custom and the statutes of our College (whose inspector and moderator, though I am unworthy, those to whom the power of appointing resides have wished and appointed me), the reading of Holy Scripture is to be carried out in the morning and evening hours, and also before and sometimes after taking food, I have always laboured, as far as my modest strength allows, that this reading should be conducted [κατὰ παιδείας τρόπον] in a manner of instruction, and be contained within certain limits of a strict and general analysis; lest it be merely perfunctory, flowing, wandering, and therefore unfruitful, that is, empty of all understanding, usefulness and edification, such as is the reading of the Psalter, the Gospels and the Epistles undertaken by ignorant monks and nuns to finish their daily task and to complete their Hours, by the work done. The blessed D. Benedict Aretius defines the reading of Holy Scripture admirably and weightily: it is a diligent meditation on the sacred letters, undertaken with judgment, commanded by God to all orders of human life, but especially to those who wish to teach others with profit. He defines meditation as reading, because we hunt out and grasp the sense and juice of Scripture not so much by outward inspection as by the attention of a present mind and clever inquiry (Ps. 1.v.2). He places meditation as it were in the middle between two extremes, negligence and sophistry, setting diligence against negligence as its defect, and sound judgment against sophistry (by which some sense other than the genuine one is attached to Scripture) as against its excess. Aiming to pave a way to this diligent reading or meditation of the divine Word, joined with sound judgment and evident usefulness, I gather together, as if into one body, those things which the most learned recent theologians have written to show the order [τάξιν] and connection [συνάφειαν] of things and arguments, linking them in a fitting and methodical arrangement, and I have gladly given my work to a printer, for public use, for the benefit of the beginners in holy theology.

units.la: Sub vestri autem nominis au-spicio, Reuerendi & doctissimi viri, hæc in apertum referre mihi visum, vt hoc tenui munusculo significa-tionem gratianimi vobis exhibe-rem, quando quidem nulla alia via mihi patefacta est. Te enim, Reue-rende Domine Flückingere, vsus sum præceptore ante annos plus minus viginti, in schola patria, Zof-fingæ nimirum, oppido florentis-simo; vbi ex fidelissima institutio-ne tua Græcarum & Hebraicarum literarum fui imbutus primordiis. Ex eo etiam tempore, perpetuum singularis benevolentiae tuae vigorem multis magnisque apud animum meum obsignasti beneficiis, quibus tum parentem meum Gualtherum Herlinum beatae recordationis, tum meipsum ad hunc usque diem φιλοφρόνως, ornavisti. Tuum autem clarissime & doctissime Domine praeceptor CHIORE, quo me complexus es, favorem & gratiam; mei constans patrocinium tuum, tuamque in adolescentiæ meæ studiis informandis fidem, nisi agnoscerem, nisi memore animo recolerem & praedicarem, scelerate ingratus essem. Enimuero non solus ego, velut ex multis unus, sed insuper Antistitum Ecclesiarū & Scholarum in amplissimo illustrissimi Magi-
units.tr: Under the auspices of your name, Reverend and most learned men, I have thought fit to bring these matters into the open, so that I might offer a sign of my gratitude to you with this small gift, since no other way has been opened to me. For you, Reverend Lord Flückiger, I had as my teacher about twenty years ago, in the school of my homeland, namely at Zofingen, a very flourishing town, where, through your most faithful instruction, I was steeped in the first principles of Greek and Hebrew letters. From that time on, you have also, by many great benefits, sealed in my mind the lasting vigour of your singular goodwill, with which you have treated both my late father, Walther Herlin, of blessed memory, and myself, kindly [φιλοφρόνως], down to this day. Your favour and grace, most illustrious and learned Lord teacher, with which you embraced me; your constant patronage of me, and your faithfulness in forming me in the studies of my youth, I would be shamefully ungrateful if I did not acknowledge, did not recall with a grateful mind and proclaim. And indeed I am not alone, one among many; but moreover the greatest part of the church leaders and schoolmasters in the most ample territory of our most illustrious magis-

units.la: Magistatus nostri territorio, pars multo-maxima, te suum fidelissi-mum agnoscit, salutat & veneratur praeceptorem: Tibi fere omnes in vrbe & agro Bernensi docentes,ingeniorum culturam referunt acceptam. Hinc etiam alia huius meae ad vos, Reuerendi Dd. praeceptores, institutae προσφωνήσεως[?] promanat ratio: siquidem ex nominis vestri honoratissimi inscri-ptione & ex praesidio authoriratis vestrae, non leue commendationis momentum apud studiosam iu-uentutem nostram,cui hunc labo-rem praecipuè desudamus & desti-namus,huic meo opusculo acces-surum confido. Hanc igitur gra-titudinis meae testificationem pu-blicam, & hos qualescunque conatus meos, rogo, benigna mente & manu accipientes, me studiaque mea vobis, ut hactenus, de meliore nota commendata esse patiamini. DEUS Opt. Max. cui per Seruatorem Iesum Christum, vota nostra nuncupamus, vos ani-mo & corpore valentes & incolu-mes ad ædificationem Scholæ & Ecclesiæ, sustentet quàm diutis-simé. Bernæ ex musæo nostro, An-no salutis restauratæ M. D. C. V. mense Iulio.
units.tr: trates acknowledges you as its most faithful teacher, greets you and reveres you as such. Almost all who teach in the city and countryside of Bern trace the cultivation of their minds to you. Hence also comes the reason for this other address [προσφωνήσεως] to you, Reverend teachers, which I have composed: for I confidently hope that, from the inscription of your most honoured names and the protection of your authority, my little work will gain no small weight of recommendation among our studious youth, for whom above all I toil and labour at this task. Therefore, I ask you to receive this public testimony of my gratitude, and these my attempts, whatever their worth, with a kind mind and hand, and to allow me and my studies, as hitherto, to be commended to you in a good light. May God, the best and greatest, to whom we offer our prayers through our Saviour Jesus Christ, keep you healthy and safe in body and soul for as long as possible, for the building up of the school and the Church. At Bern, from our Muses' house, in the year of restored salvation 1605, in the month of July.

units.la: ORDO SEV METHODVS QVAE SERVATVR INLECTIONE CA-pitum Biblicorum in collegio Bernensi, ma-tutinis & vespertinis horis, &c.
units.tr: THE ORDER OR METHOD FOLLOWED IN READING THE BIBLICAL CHAPTERS IN THE COLLEGE AT BERN, IN MORNING AND EVENING HOURS, ETC.

units.la: 1. Coherentiæ & series omnium librorum, tum totius corporis Biblici, tum singularum eius classium ostenditur, vna cum prolegomenis generalibus.
units.tr: 1. The coherence and sequence of all the books are shown, both of the whole biblical corpus and of its individual classes, together with general prolegomena.

units.la: 2. Singulorum librorum prolegomena necessaria, hoc est isagogica, præmittuntur analysi generali.
units.tr: 2. The necessary prolegomena of each single book, that is, its introductory matters, are placed before its general analysis.

units.la: 3. Synopses singulorum librorum, in quibus series & connexio omnium capitum, ob oculos ponitur.
units.tr: 3. Synopses of the individual books are given, in which the sequence and connection of all the chapters is set before the eyes.

units.la: 4. Summa uniuscuiusque capitis seu primaria eius propositio ostenditur.
units.tr: 4. The summary of each chapter, or its main proposition, is shown.

units.la: 5. Summa capitis si prolixior fit & multi-plex, tum partes eius singulæ indicantur, & cu-jusque partis propositio.
units.tr: 5. If the summary of a chapter is rather long and complex, its individual parts are indicated, together with the proposition of each part.

units.la: 6. Partium item ex toto distributarum subdiuisiones non omittuntur.
units.tr: 6. The subdivisions of the parts, distributed from the whole, are not omitted either.

units.la: 7. Loca quædam obscuriora explicantur, in elucidatione Hebraismi vel Hellenismi alicuius, siue in Tropi & Figuræ insignioris enucleatione.
units.tr: 7. Certain more obscure passages are explained, either by elucidating some Hebraism or Hellenism, or by unfolding a notable trope or figure.

units.la: 8. Αντ[?]λογιῶν φαινομένων[?], hoc est, Apparentium contradictionum conciliatio instituitur.
units.tr: 8. The reconciliation of apparent contradictions [ἀντιλογιῶν φαινομένων] is undertaken.

units.la: 9. Testimonia quædam illustria Orthodoxam fidem demonstrantia notantur & applicantur.
units.tr: 9. Certain notable testimonies demonstrating the Orthodox faith are noted and applied.

units.la: 10. Abusus testimoniorum S. Scripturæ in
units.tr: 10. The abuses of the testimonies of Holy Scripture in the objections of opponents against the Helvetic Confession are shown and refuted.

units.la: obiectionibus aduersariorum contra confessio-nem Helueticam, ostenduntur & refutantur.
II. Doctrinæ principales Capitis, vel par-tium illius, delibantur.
units.tr: 11. The principal doctrines of the chapter, or of its parts, are touched upon.

units.la: 12. Dicta insigniora quædam memoriæ præcipue mandanda monstrantur.
units.tr: 12. Certain more notable sayings are pointed out, which should be especially committed to memory.

units.la: HAEC (inquam) vel omnia, vel pleraque, vel aliqua, pro re natâ, occasione oblatâ, & temporis ratione, in singulorum lectione capitum observantur: sicuti γ[?]ύμαςτως ἐνίαχα[?] specimen exhibitum est in Analysi Epi-stolæ S. Pauli ad Philemonem. In hac autem Meditatione, isagogica ad lectionis intelligentiam, diligentiam, & memoriam adiuvandam, sex solummodo priora exhibentur adminicula; Quibus adiunxi versus μνημονευτικὰ seu memoriales triplices: priores & prolixiores, capitum singulorum argumenta insinuantes, à Dn. Rodolpho Gualthero Tigurino editos: medios & strictiores ex Gemâ Fabri transscriptos & ordine alphabetico ita concinnatos, ut capitum sententias insigniores seu gemmæs[?] sic delibent, ut eos cum versione D. Bezæ conferre, eorumque sensum ex eadem supplere sit necessarium. Tertiò adieci versus συνο[?]μ[?]τικὸς, hoc est , breuissimo compendio singulorum capitum selectas Notas memoriales, nunquam per omnes S S. Bibliorum libros in hisce versibus repetitas, ita subministrantes, vt singulis versibus hexametris quina capita, numeris suis signata includantur: subiuncta horum versuum & Notarum ex texu D. Beza declaratione.
units.tr: These (I say) all, or most, or some, as the occasion, the opportunity offered and the time allow, are observed in the reading of the individual chapters, just as a specimen was given in the analysis of Paul's Epistle to Philemon [ἐνίαχα]. In this meditation, intended as an introduction to aiding understanding, diligence and memory in reading, only the first six aids are set forth. To these I have added memorial verses in three kinds: the first and longer ones, hinting at the arguments of the individual chapters, were published by Mr. Rudolf Gwalther of Zurich; the middle and shorter ones are transcribed from Fabri's Gemma and arranged in alphabetical order so as to touch upon the more notable sentiments or gems of the chapters, so that it is necessary to compare them with Beza's version and supply their sense from it. Thirdly I have added synoptic verses [συνοπτικὸς], that is, in a very brief compendium, selected memorial notes on each single chapter, never repeated through all the books of the Holy Scriptures in these verses, supplied in such a way that five chapters, marked with their numbers, are enclosed in each hexameter line; with an explanation of these verses and notes from Beza's text added.

units.la: IN BIBLIA SACROSANCTA.
units.tr: ON THE HOLY BIBLE.

units.la: D. NATHAN CHYTRAEUS.
units.tr: MR. NATHAN CHYTRAEUS.

units.la: IN tam rixosis qui nostri erroribus ævi Non terit inuicta Biblia sacra manu, Is nihil ignavo differt a milite, bellum Absque ense & clypeo qui male sanus init: Nil etiam a cæco aut lusco, funalibus absque Aut duce qui ignotas ausit inire vias. Hic ille est anceps gladius, qui viscera transit Intima, & a falsis vera resecta probat. Hic ille est clypeus patulo qui vmbone sagittas Reiicit, igni vomus quas iacit ore Draco. Hæc est norma boni, & recti certissima amisis, Cui quod non penitus congruit omne, malum est. Hæc illa errorum in tenebris lux pravia, fax ha[?] Vnica, quæ recto ducit ad astra gradu. Sed tibi nil prodest clypeus, nihil ensis hic,hosti Si vis nudum amens opponuisse latus.
units.tr: Whoever in this age of ours, so full of quarrels and errors, does not wear out the Holy Bible with an unconquered hand, differs in nothing from a lazy soldier who joins battle badly armed, without sword or shield. Nor is he any better than one blind or one-eyed, without torches or guide, who dares to enter unknown ways. This is the two-edged sword that passes through the innermost parts and, cutting away falsehoods, proves what is true. This is the shield that with its broad boss throws back the arrows which the dragon hurls from its fiery mouth. This is the surest rule of good and right, lost to the blind; whatever does not wholly agree with it is evil. This is the one guiding light and torch in the darkness of errors, which leads by a straight course to the stars. But the shield avails you nothing, nor the sword here, if you foolishly wish to expose your bare side to the enemy.

units.la: Nil etiam hac prodest adamantina regula veri, Si arbitrio fiat Les bia[?] norma tuo. Nil facula, nil crystalli, nil lumina possunt, Compressis si nil cernere vis oculis.
units.tr: Nor does this adamantine rule of truth avail anything if the norm is made to bend to your own will. Torches, lamps and lights can do nothing if you wish to see nothing with your eyes shut.

units.la: APHORISMI VITÆ SALVTARIS.
units.tr: APHORISMS OF A WHOLESOME LIFE.

units.la: 1. Verâ fide, assiduâ invocatione, & legiti-mâ obedientiâ Deum in sacrificio & obedietiâ Christi nobis per fidem imputatis, rite colimus.
units.tr: 1. By true faith, constant invocation and lawful obedience, we duly worship God, through the sacrifice and obedience of Christ imputed to us by faith.

units.la: 2. Eruditâ pietate & virtutum exercitio animam exhilaramus, & vitam honorificè tradu-cimus,
units.tr: 2. By learned piety and the exercise of virtues we cheer the soul and lead a life of honour.

units.la: 3. Curarum evacuatione, moderato labore, & sobriâ temperantiâ, animi angustiis, & dubiæ valetudini corporis medemur.
units.tr: 3. By the removal of cares, moderate labour and sober temperance, we remedy the straits of the mind and uncertain bodily health.

units.la: 4. Honestâ diligentiâ, servatâ fide, & libe-rali parsimoniâ rem familiarem augemus & conservamus.
units.tr: 4. By honest diligence, kept faith and generous thrift, we increase and preserve our household property.

units.la: 5. Sapienti & conditâ lingua, inculpatâ vitâ & comprobatis moribus pium favorem ho-minum nobis conciliamus.
units.tr: 5. By a wise and seasoned tongue, a blameless life and approved morals, we win for ourselves the kindly favour of men.

units.la: 6. Fideli benevolentiâ & mutuis officiis amicitiam comprobamus.
units.tr: 6. By faithful goodwill and mutual services, we confirm friendship.

units.la: 7. Iustâ tolerantiâ, pacificis verbis, & spe-ctatis officiis etiam inimicos lucramur.
units.tr: 7. By just forbearance, peaceable words and well-regarded duties, we win even our enemies.

units.la: 8. Deo hoc genus vitæ gratissimum est, be-nefacere omnibus & tamen sustinere invidiam, odium & iniurias Diaboli & hominum.
units.tr: 8. This kind of life is most pleasing to God: to do good to all, and yet to bear envy, hatred and the injuries of the Devil and of men.

units.la: ISAGOGE AD LECTIONEM LIBRORUM NOUI TE-STAMENTI OMNIUM, PER ANA-LYSIN EORUM PRIMARIAM SEU GE-neralem, ad rerum & argumentorum sum-mam seriemque facilius intelligen-tia ac memoria com-plectendam.
units.tr: ISAGOGE TO READING ALL THE BOOKS OF THE NEW TESTAMENT, THROUGH THEIR PRIMARY OR GENERAL ANALYSIS, TO GRASP AND REMEMBER MORE EASILY THE SUM AND SEQUENCE OF THEIR THINGS AND ARGUMENTS.

units.la: DE TITULO SEU INSCRIPTIONE TOTIUS VOLUMINIS, deque libris Noui Testamenti ingenere.
units.tr: ON THE TITLE OR INSCRIPTION OF THE WHOLE VOLUME, AND ON THE BOOKS OF THE NEW TESTAMENT IN GENERAL.

units.la: INSCRIPTIO generalis arcano & singulari Dei consilio à Veteribus toti codici præfixa hæc est: τῆς καινῆς διαθήκης ἅπαντα. In qua tria distinctè notanda veniunt. 1, quid sit διαθήκη?, hoc est Testamentum seu fedus 2 qua ratione appelletur καινὴ? .i. nouū, scil: testamentum :3. vox ἅπαντα cuius nos ad-moneat.
units.tr: The general inscription, which the Ancients prefixed to the whole codex by the hidden and singular counsel of God, is this: All of the New Testament [τῆς καινῆς διαθήκης ἅπαντα]. Three things need to be noted here, distinctly: (1) what is meant by διαθήκη, that is, testament or covenant; (2) for what reason it is called καινή, that is, new, namely a testament; (3) what the word ἅπαντα reminds us of.

units.la: De primo.
units.tr: On the first.

units.la: Quod Hebræi voce Berith, significante pactionem seu fedus, à barath .i. fedus inire, denotant, id Græci διαθηκην .i. dispositio-nem, Latini vero Testamentum appellant. Sed vox Testamenti ambigua est, & hinc non tam vo-luntatem morientis, quam appellant ultimam, quam viventium pacta declarat. Hac signifi-catione dicimus, Testamentum Dei; id est fedus seu pactum, & ordinationem, quam Deus ra-tam haberi voluit: prorsus uti cōditiones & pa-cta percutientium federa, aut quæ morientium extrema voluntate sunt constituta violare ne-phas est.
units.tr: What the Hebrews express by the word berith, meaning a compact or covenant, derived from barath, to make a covenant, the Greeks call διαθήκη, that is, an arrangement, and the Latins call testamentum. But the word "testament" is ambiguous. Here it does not so much mean the last will of a dying man as the compact that the will of the living declares. In this sense we speak of the Testament of God, that is, the covenant or agreement, and the ordinance which God willed to be held firm, just as it is wrong to violate the covenants of those who strike agreements, or the terms set down by the final will of the dying.

units.la: Cùm autem passim in libris sacris potissi-mum doceatur, quomodo Deus humanum ge-nus promiserit se seruaturum, atque ad id perfi-ciendum missurum etiam semen benedictum, id est proprium & vnigenitum filium IESVM CHRISTVM: rursus vero, quomodo homines qui huius beneficentiæ Dei futuri sunt partici-pes, vicissim obstringantur ad præstandum cer-ta fidei & charitatis officia ad Dei gloriam: ap-positè sanè omnes libri, in quibus his de rebus disseritur, Testamenti appellatione honestan-tur.
units.tr: Since the books of Scripture teach chiefly, everywhere, how God promised that he would preserve the human race, and would also send, to accomplish this, the blessed Seed, that is, his own and only-begotten Son Jesus Christ; and again, how the men who are to share in this beneficence of God are in turn bound to render certain duties of faith and love to the glory of God: all the books in which these matters are treated are rightly honoured with the name of Testament.

units.la: De secundo.
units.tr: On the second.

units.la: EST autem vnicum tantum Dei Testamen-tum, immutabile, æternum, sicut ipse quoque immutabilis atque æternus existit: verùm Testamentum Vetus nominatur pars illa, cui libri accensentur, in quibus modò apertis verbis{a}
units.tr: There is only one covenant of God, unchangeable and eternal, just as he himself is unchangeable and eternal. But the part of Scripture to which the books belong in which, sometimes in plain words and sometimes through types and figures, discourses are set forth concerning the promised salvation, that is, the sending of Christ, is called the Old Testament.{a}

units.la: modò typis & figuris, de salute promissa, siue de Christo mittendo sermones instituuntur. Testamentum autem Nouum libros habet, in quibus de salute exhibita, deque Christo iam misso agitur. Hoc igitur loco Nouum Testamentum est systema seu corpus librorum Canonicorum, quibus fedus Dei gratuitum & æternum cum populo electo initum & in Christo iam exhibito sanctitum, panditur. Fedus hoc appellatur gratuitum seu gratiæ fedus: quia Deus id ex mera misericordia cum peccatoribus, nempe omnibus electis pepigit: in quo promittit iis remissionem peccatorum, & inscriptionem legis suæ in mentibus & cordibus eorum: Ierem: cap. 13.v.33.34. Hinc patet, federatos, (id est electos) repromittere quidem fidem & pietatem, quod crediturí sint remissionem peccatorum, & Spiritui sancto legem inscripturo mentibus ipsorum obedituri: verùm non ex propriis viribus, quæ nullæ sunt, sed ex Dei gratia præstandam. Hoc fedus fundatum est in manuChristi mediatoris, vnici nostri ad salutem verè magnifici rectoris, qui pro nostris peccatis morte sua satisfecit, & eorum remissionem sua passione, atque perfecta diuinæ legis impletione, seu obedientia sua actiuâ, per fidem nobis imputata, veram iustitiam, indeq; fauorem Dei, & à fauente Deo Spiritus sancti gratiam nobis impetrauit. Ideoque ratum est in æternum. Vnde Ierem: 30.v.21. magnificus appellatur. Nam ille merito & efficacia eorum est seruator. vide ad Hebr. 8. v. 6. vbi Apostolus hæc verba explicat. Propterea Christus foederis angelus dicitur, Malach. 3. v. 1. vide etiam 2. Cor 5.v.19. Hinc patet,hoc fedus solum proprie dici , percuti & feriri,quia victi-mâ intercedente Filio Dei,in carne patefacto confirmatum est:item hoc solum appellari pos-se Testamentum, quia non nisi in tercedente morte Mediatoris ratum esse potuit. Deus enim veritatem & iustitiam suam mutare non po-terat.
units.tr: The New Testament, on the other hand, contains books in which the salvation already bestowed is treated, and Christ already sent. Here, therefore, "New Testament" means the system or body of canonical books which sets forth the gratuitous and eternal covenant of God, made with the chosen people and now confirmed in Christ, who has been revealed. This covenant is called gratuitous, or the covenant of grace, because God made it out of pure mercy with sinners, namely with all the elect. In it he promises them forgiveness of sins and the writing of his law upon their minds and hearts (Jer. 13.33, 34). From this it is clear that those in the covenant (that is, the elect) promise faith and godliness, that they will believe in the forgiveness of sins and will obey the Holy Spirit, who will write the law on their minds. Yet this is to be performed not by their own powers, which are nothing, but by the grace of God. This covenant is founded on the hand of Christ the mediator, our only truly glorious ruler for salvation, who by his death satisfied for our sins and by his passion obtained for us their forgiveness, and, by the complete fulfilment of the divine law, that is, by his active obedience, which is imputed to us through faith, obtained for us true righteousness, and from that, the favour of God, and from the God who favours us, the grace of the Holy Spirit. Therefore it is established for ever. Hence he is called "magnificent" in Jer. 30.21, for he is the Saviour by his merit and efficacy. See on Heb. 8.6, where the Apostle explains these words. For this reason Christ is called the angel of the covenant (Mal. 3.1); see also 2 Cor. 5.19. From this it is clear that this covenant can properly be said to be struck and smitten, because it was confirmed by the interceding of a victim, the Son of God, revealed in the flesh. Likewise it can be called a Testament only, because it could not be ratified except by the interposed death of the Mediator. For God could not change his truth and justice.

units.la: Hoc fedus,licet quoad substantiam non mu-tetur,aliter tamen administratum fuit veteri po-pulo ante Christi aduentum, aliter nouo,id est post Christum in carne exhibitum ; unde con-uenientia & discrimen Veteris & Noui Testa-menti sunt notanda,quatenus nempe per vtrun-que , fedus gratiae intelligitur. Est autem con-uenientia inter utrunque Testamentum in sub-stantia hactenus dicta. Eadem enim salus ab eodem Deo per eundem Mediatorem , aeque preciosa fide accipenda , & studio pietatis testi-ficanda, promittitur & praestatur omnibus hic sederatis,& vtrobique verbo & sacramentis, vt gratiae suae signis , Deus declarauit suam volun-tatem. Differentia autem est primo in sederatis, deinde in federalibus ( vt ita loquar) bonis & fe-deralibus signis. In Veteri Testameuto fuerunt posteri Abrahae federati,neglectis vel parce ad-modum accersitis gentibus. In Nouo Testa-mento est Ecclesia Catholica , etiam gentibus aduocatis,Ierem : cap.30.v.12.cap.3 .v.10. inter federalia bona veteribus aliquandiu fuit terra Chananaea, vt typus patriae caelestis. Signa fue-runt alia, atque hodie sunt. Nam licet verbum & sacramenta vtrobique,vt iam diximus,confi-derenderentur : veteribus tamen illa obscuriora erant in prophetiis & umbris ceremoniarum, & sacramenta erant difficilioris usus, in quibus erat sanguinis effusio, ut in circumcisione & agno paschali. Erant etiam sumtuosa valde sacrificia.
units.tr: Although this covenant is not changed in substance, it was administered differently to the old people before the coming of Christ, and differently to the new, that is, after Christ was revealed in the flesh. Therefore the agreement and the difference between the Old and New Testaments must be noted, insofar as through both the covenant of grace is understood. The agreement between the two Testaments lies in the substance already mentioned. For the same salvation, from the same God, through the same Mediator, is promised and bestowed on all who are here in the covenant, to be received with equal faith and attested by a zeal for godliness; and in both, God has declared his will through the word and the sacraments, as signs of his grace. The difference lies first in those in the covenant, and then in the covenant's goods and signs (so to speak). In the Old Testament the descendants of Abraham were in the covenant, the Gentiles being neglected or called in only sparingly. In the New Testament there is the Catholic Church, with the Gentiles also called (Jer. 30.12; 3.10). Among the covenant's goods, for the ancients the land of Canaan was for a time a type of the heavenly fatherland. The signs were different from what they are today. For although the word and the sacraments were in both, as we have already said, they were more obscure to the ancients, in the prophecies and in the shadows of the ceremonies; and the sacraments were of more difficult use, involving the shedding of blood, as in circumcision and the Passover lamb. The sacrifices were also very costly.

units.la: In Nouo Testamento verba & sacramenta sunt clarissima, utpote Christum exhibitum & exaltatum testantia, ceremoniarum omnium Leviticarum umbris antiquatis & ablatis: quibus jam, ipsa luce & corporeChristo exhibito, æque non est opus, atque sole clarè orto supra nostrum horizontem, non est opus, quæ atræ noctis caliginem fugabant, candelis. Et sacramenta præterea incruenta & facillimi usus nunc habemus. Sanguis enim Christi effusus sistit omnem sanguinem. Breuiter: Foederis gratiæ bona dispensantur in N. Testamento uberius seu plus & pluribus; in V. T. minus & paucioribus sunt dispensata.
units.tr: In the New Testament the words and the sacraments are most clear, since they bear witness that Christ has been revealed and exalted, the shadows of all the Levitical ceremonies having been abolished and taken away. Now that Christ himself has been revealed in the light and in bodily form, these are no more needed than lamps are needed when the sun has risen clearly above our horizon, or than candles were needed to chase away the darkness of black night. Moreover, we now have sacraments that are bloodless and very easy to use. For the blood of Christ, once shed, puts an end to all blood. In short: the goods of the covenant of grace are dispensed more abundantly, or more and to more people, in the New Testament; in the Old they were dispensed in smaller measure and to fewer.

units.la: De tertio.
units.tr: On the third point

units.la: SUperest[?] tertia vox inscriptionis: ἅπαντα[?] .i. omnia scil. γεγραμμένα .i. scripta, seu βιβλία i. libri. Hinc antiquiores patres, qui magno & arcano Dei consilio titulum hunc, hisce libris in ordinem collectis, præfixerunt, admonere atque testari voluerunt; & omnes qui in hoc codice continentur libros esse Canonicos; & præter hos, nullos alios Novi Testamenti libros authenticos esse. Facessant igitur libri Ecclesiæ olim obtrusi sub Apostolorum nomine, sed adulterini: Ut sunt Euangelium secundum Hebræos vel Nazarenorum, liber pastoris seu Hermæ, Acta Panli, Apocalypsis Petri, & alij his absurdiores.
units.tr: There remains the third word of the title, hapanta [ἅπαντα], that is, "all things," namely the things written [γεγραμμένα], or biblia [βιβλία], that is, books. Hence the earlier Fathers, who by the great and hidden counsel of God prefixed this title when these books were gathered into order, wished to admonish and bear witness that all the books contained in this codex are canonical, and that besides these there are no other authentic books of the New Testament. Away, then, with the books that were once thrust upon the Church under the names of the apostles but are spurious, such as the Gospel according to the Hebrews or of the Nazarenes, the Shepherd of Hermas, the Acts of Paul, the Apocalypse of Peter, and others more absurd than these.

units.la: Maclenus de Titulo seu Inscriptione atque adeo Descriptione N. Testamenti: consequens esset, vt ad eius Distributionem accederemus: verum hic
units.tr: Maclenus, on the title or inscription and therefore on the description of the New Testament: it would follow that we proceed to its distribution; but here

units.la: QVAERITVR:
units.tr: THE QUESTION:

units.la: AN N. Testamentum literis mandari potuerit, & debuerit: & cur, seu quo fine?
units.tr: Whether the New Testament could and should be committed to writing; and why, or to what end?

units.la: Iesuitæ dicunt, naturam Noui Testamenti non ferre, vt chartis inscribatur, sed spiritualiter esse propagandum, cum sit spirituale; Ierem: 13. 2. Cor. 3. Vos estis Epistola Christi, scripta non atramento, sed spiritu Dei viuentis. RESPON: Non modò potuit, sed etiam debuit literis consignari. Probamus potuisse ex euentu, nam Apostoli omnia ad salutem necessaria consignarunt diuinissimè, & fidelissimè nobis reliquerunt. Debuit etiam, quia voluit. Voluit & debuit; quia Deus hac in parte agit cum noua Ecclesia, vt cum veteri illa Mosaica. Nam illam non solum voluit instruere viua voce per Mosem, & Prophetas, sed voluit, vt vera doctrina literis quoque ad posteros propagaretur. Sic in noua Christi Ecclesia veram doctrinā, & memoriam suorum beneficiorū & miraculorū scripto conseruauit. Deinde cum Apostoli debuerint esse testes Christi, Luc: 24. & quidem [Greek], vt est Act. 1. par fuit vt ea oretenus & scripto docerent. Tertiò curandum randum erat ipsis, vt post mortem ipsorum pu-ra extaret doctrina Euangelij: ad vtrunq; com-modissime beneficio scriptionis & librorum poterant peruenire.
units.tr: The Jesuits say that the nature of the New Testament does not allow it to be inscribed on paper, but that it must be propagated spiritually, since it is spiritual: Jeremiah 13; 2 Corinthians 3: "You are the letter of Christ, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God." ANSWER: It was not only able to be committed to writing, but it ought to have been. We prove that it could be from the outcome, for the Apostles most divinely committed to writing everything necessary for salvation and most faithfully left it to us. It also ought to have been, because God willed it. He willed and ought to have done so, because in this matter God deals with the new Church as with the old Mosaic one. For to that one he willed to teach not only by the living voice of Moses and the Prophets, but also willed that the true doctrine be propagated to posterity in writing. So too in the new Church of Christ he has preserved true doctrine and the memory of his benefits and miracles in writing. Next, since the Apostles were to be witnesses of Christ (Luke 24; and indeed, as in Acts 1), it was fitting that they should teach both by word of mouth and in writing. Thirdly, they had to take care that after their death the pure doctrine of the Gospel would remain, and to attain both ends most conveniently they could use the benefit of writing and books.

units.la: OBIECTIO: Ierem:31. dicitur: Non tale fedus faciam,vt cum patribus eorū,ego legem meam ponam in cor eorum,verf.31. &c. RESP: A positione finis ad sublationem mediorum non valet consequentia. Nam vt Deus indat legem suam in corda nostra, adhibet media ἐξωθεν, per quae Spiritus S. efficax est ἔσωθεν, nimirum lectione nostra, meditatione, oratione, scriptione: Deinde hoc modo totū ministerium euertetur. Tertiò Decalogus etiam fuerat inscriptus cordibus, & nihilominus in duabus quoque tabulis exaratus. Quarto resp: quod est scriptum in cordibus, videlicet immediatè, specialiter, & perfectè, id non necesse est chartis inscribi, in N. Testamento mentes nostras non perfectè, in hac vitâ illustrat, etiamsi perfectius quàm sub lege. Significat autem seu vaticinatur loco citato propheta, in N.T. maiorem fore patefactionem, quàm in V.T. fuit.
units.tr: OBJECTION: Jeremiah 31 says: "I will not make a covenant like the one with their fathers; I will put my law in their heart," verse 31, etc. ANSWER: The inference from the positing of an end to the removal of the means is not valid. For although God puts his law into our hearts, he employs external means (ἐξωθεν), through which the Holy Spirit works effectively from within (ἔσωθεν): namely our reading, meditation, prayer and writing. Next, in this way the whole ministry would be overturned. Thirdly, the Decalogue too was inscribed on hearts, and nevertheless was also engraved on two tablets. Fourthly, the answer is this: what is written in hearts, that is, immediately, specially and perfectly, does not need to be inscribed on paper; in the New Testament he illuminates our minds not perfectly, in this life, even though more perfectly than under the law. Moreover, the prophet in the cited place foretells or prophesies that in the New Testament there will be a greater revelation than there was in the Old.

units.la: Pontificij negant libros N.T. ideò scriptos esse vt sint mensura & regula fidei, sed occasionaliter duntaxat, propter particulares quasdam Ecclesias. Resp: Duplex scriptorum N.T. est vsus.1. privatus seu practicus: sic Apostoli & Euangelistae scripserunt hos libros, in singulorum doctrinam, consolationem, & hortationem. Rom.15. 2.Tim.3. Omnis scriptura diuinitus inspirata vtilis est ad doctrinam, &c. haec exhortatio, doctrina, consolatio, reprehensio etiam publicè fieri potest: de hoc fine non est controuersia. 2. publicus seu theoricus, vt sit norma fidei & omnis doctrinæ mensura in Ecclesia :Galat.1.v.8. Anathema denunciatur corruptoribus huius doctri næ. Philip: 3. Eadem me non piget scribere quia tutū est vobis,ne circumueniamini falsis doctrinis. Irenæus lib. 3.cap.1. Ideò scripserunt libros N. Testamenti vt essent columna & fundamentum fidei. Ob: At causæ scribendi fuerunt particulares.Resp. Occasiones fuerunt particulares,respectu humano, sed finis Apostolorum erat vniuersalis, videlicet instruere non tantum illos,quibus tum scribebant,sed etiam alios. & quidem omnes. Obiect: scriptura est quidem norma dogmatum fidei,sed partialis: quia & Traditiones sunt norma, pari cum verbo Dei scripto, pietatis affectu ac reuerentia, suscipiendæ. Concil: Trid: Sess: 8: Resp.: præcisè negamus;scriptura enim perfecta est, secundum illud: Scriptura est vtilis ad institutionem, vt sit homo Dei perfectus.perfecti effecti causa est perfecta. Traditiones vero,quia sunt mutabiles,vanæ,infinitæ, sibi ipsis & scripturæ sunt contrariæ, non possunt esse norma fidei.
units.tr: The Papists deny that the books of the New Testament were written so as to be the measure and rule of faith, but only occasionally, on account of certain particular churches. Answer: The writings of the New Testament have a twofold use. 1. Private or practical: in this way the Apostles and Evangelists wrote these books for the instruction, consolation and exhortation of individuals (Romans 15; 2 Timothy 3: "All Scripture inspired by God is profitable for teaching," etc.). This exhortation, teaching, consolation and also reproof can be done publicly; there is no controversy about this purpose. 2. Public or theoretical, that it might be the norm of faith and the measure of all doctrine in the Church (Galatians 1:8: anathema is pronounced on the corrupters of this doctrine; Philippians 3: "It is no trouble to me to write the same things, and it is safe for you, lest you be deceived by false doctrines"). Irenaeus, book 3, chapter 1: "They therefore wrote the books of the New Testament that they might be the pillar and foundation of faith." Objection: But the causes of writing were particular. Answer: The occasions were particular, from a human point of view, but the purpose of the Apostles was universal, namely to instruct not only those to whom they were then writing but also others, and indeed all. Objection: Scripture is indeed a norm of the doctrines of faith, but a partial one, because traditions too are a norm, to be received with the same affection of piety and reverence as the written Word of God. Council of Trent, session 8. Answer: We flatly deny this; for Scripture is perfect, according to that saying: "Scripture is profitable for instruction, that the man of God may be perfect" (2 Timothy 3); and the cause of perfection is perfect. Traditions, however, since they are changeable, vain and countless, and are contrary both to themselves and to Scripture, cannot be a norm of faith.

units.la: Vtilissimum itaque nobis & tutissimum suit,literis mandari doctrinam N. Testamenti: quia aliter scire non poteramus, quæ doctrina,verè esset Apostolica, quod fundamentum esset salutis nostræ, quid docuisset & fecisset Christus, hæc omnia sine libris certò constare non poterant posteritati. Nam Cabalistica illa ratio, quæ traditionibus constat per manus acceptis,admodum est in certa & dubia: Cum in illa sinla singulis licuisset sua insomnia & deliria tradere, sub fuco & specie veræ doctrinæ, quasi hæc à maioribus sic essent tradita. Nam cum illa fiant libris conscriptis & consignatis, quid futurum credendum est, si libri nulli extarent? Fuit igitur & nobis admodum utile, & Apostolis necessarium in explendo munere suo, scripto conservari & propagari veritatis historiam in Ecclesia.
units.tr: It was therefore most useful and most safe for us that the doctrine of the New Testament be committed to writing; for otherwise we could not know with certainty which doctrine was truly apostolic, what foundation there was for our salvation, and what Christ had taught and done. None of these things could be certainly handed down to posterity without books. For that Cabbalistic method, which consists in traditions received by hand, is very uncertain and doubtful, since in it each person would have been free to hand on his own dreams and delusions under the disguise and appearance of true doctrine, as if they had been so handed down by our forefathers. For since these things are done in written and sealed books, what would be believed if no books existed at all? It was therefore both very useful for us and necessary for the Apostles in discharging their office that the history of the truth should be preserved and propagated in writing in the Church.

units.la: Hactenus ea quæ ad Definitionem, seu Descriptionem librorum N. T. spectabant, sequitur
units.tr: So far, what pertained to the definition or description of the books of the New Testament. There follows

units.la: DISTRIBUTIO LIBRO-RUM. N. TESTAMENTI.
units.tr: DISTRIBUTION OF THE BOOKS OF THE NEW TESTAMENT.

units.la: Librorum N. Testamenti alii sunt Histori-ci, alii Didactici seu doctrinales.
units.tr: Some books of the New Testament are historical, others didactic or doctrinal.

units.la: HISTORICOS vocamus in quibus rerum gestarum continetur quædam narratio historica: & quanquam in his quoque sunt multa didactica, tamen præcipuus scopus, & orationis filum narrationem habet historiæ gestæ, hinc libet historicos appellare.
units.tr: We call books HISTORICAL when they contain a certain historical narrative of things done. Although these also contain much that is didactic, their chief aim and the thread of their discourse is the narration of the history that was enacted, and so it is fitting to call them historical.

units.la: Porrò ea narratio instituitur, vel de ipso Mes-sia exhibito; vel de ipsius Discipulis, & doctri-nae eius testibus.
units.tr: Moreover, this narrative is set out either about the Messiah himself who was revealed, or about his Disciples, the witnesses of his teaching.

units.la: Prioris generis sunt quatuor Evangelistae. Habent enim historiam de incarnatione, vitâ, do-ctrinâ, miraculis, ac moribus Filii Dei, mortem etiam & quæ mortem sint consecuta studiosè describunt.
units.tr: Of the former kind are the four Evangelists. For they contain the history of the incarnation, life, teaching, miracles and conduct of the Son of God, and they also diligently describe his death and what followed upon it.

units.la: Posterioris sunt Acta Apostolorum, nam hæc describunt doctrinæ Christi per Apostolos pro-pagationem.
units.tr: Of the latter kind is the Acts of the Apostles, for these describe the spread of Christ's doctrine through the Apostles.

units.la: Didactici seu doctrinales nos instruunt & edocent de rebus vel præsentibus, vel futuris.
units.tr: Didactic or doctrinal books instruct and teach us about things either present or future.

units.la: De præsentibus quidem Epistolæ Apostolorum: quæ definiendo, confirmando, refu-tando, &c: tractari solent. In iis præcipue do-cetur ratio iustificationis, & doctrina Christi illustratur; de corruptione naturæ humanæ, de gravitate peccati, de merito Christi, donatione iustitiæ, vita æterna, malorum pœnis, aliisque locis.
units.tr: Concerning present things, there are the Epistles of the Apostles, which are usually handled in defining, confirming, refuting, and so on. In them the way of justification is taught above all, and the doctrine of Christ is illustrated: concerning the corruption of human nature, the gravity of sin, the merit of Christ, the imputation of righteousness, eternal life, the punishments of the wicked, and other topics.

units.la: De futuris autem, est unicus liber propheti-cus, in Apocalipsi Johannis.
units.tr: Concerning future things, however, there is a single prophetic book, the Apocalypse of John.

units.la: ORDO ET SERIES, OMNIVM librorum N.T. quæ in editionibus hodie observantur.
units.tr: THE ORDER AND SEQUENCE OF ALL THE BOOKS OF THE N.T. as they are observed in editions today.

units.la: LIBRI N.T. sunt vel: Historici: Historia. Christi descripta à Matthæo. Marco. Luca. Iohanne. Discipulorum Christi, à S.Luca exarata in Actis Apost. Doctrinales instruentes nos de rebus Præsen-tibus: ut sunt Epistolæ tum Pauli, numero·quarum [?] quædam sunt de quarum auctore & auctoritate nunquam fuit dubitatum: scripte ad particulares Ecclesias ad: Romanos. Corinthios duas. Galatas. Ephesios. Philippenses. Colossenses. Thesalonicenses duas. certas personas: Timotheum. Titum. Philemonem. una est de qua olim fuit dubitatum, ad Hebræos: Reliquorum Apostolorum Iacobi. Petri duas. Iohannis tres. Iudæ. Futuris, unicus est liber propheticus, Apocalipsis S.Iohannis.
units.tr: The books of the N.T. are either: Historical: the history of Christ described by Matthew, Mark, Luke and John; the history of the disciples of Christ, written by St Luke in the Acts of the Apostles. Doctrinal, instructing us about present things: such as the Epistles of Paul, of which some, whose author and authority were never doubted, were written to particular churches: to the Romans, two to the Corinthians, to the Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, two to the Thessalonians; and to certain persons: to Timothy, Titus, Philemon. One, about which there was once doubt, is to the Hebrews. Of the remaining Apostles: of James, two of Peter, three of John, and of Jude. Concerning future things there is a single prophetic book, the Apocalypse of St John.

units.la: TETRASTICHON ORDINEM librorum N.T. exhibens.
units.tr: A FOUR-LINE VERSE showing the ORDER of the books of the N.T.

units.la: Matthæus, Marcus, Lucas, Iohannes, & Acta. Roma: Corin: Galat: Ephes, Philip: Colosenses, Thessal: & Timotheus, Titus, Philemon, Hebr. Iacobi, Petri, Iohannis, & Iudas, Apoc. (raus[?]
units.tr: Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, and Acts. Romans, Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, Thessalonians, and Timothy, Titus, Philemon, Hebrews, James, Peter, John, and Jude, Apocalypse.

units.la: NUMERUS CAPITUM SEU membrorum in libris N. T.
units.tr: THE NUMBER OF CHAPTERS OR SECTIONS in the books of the N.T.

units.la: Matthæus septena quater, Marcusq; bis octo, Lucas sena quater: tot, tribus absq; Iohan. Actus dant septena quater, sed Roma bis octo, Prima, tot, urbs bimaris: posterior tredecim, Sex Galatis, Epheso totidem: sed deinde Philippis Quatuor, & totidem scripta Colossiacis. Thessalonica prius quinque, & tria postea coepit, Bis tria Timotheus, bis duo deinde simul, Sunt tria scripta Tito, Philemon legerat unum, Quinque Iacob, unum Iuda fidelis habet. Undecies binis Iohannes ultima scribit Tempore, sic sedus clauditur omne Novum.
units.tr: Matthew has four times seven, and Mark twice eight; Luke four times six, so many, and three without John. Acts has four times seven, but Romans twice eight. The first (to the Corinthians) has so many, the city of two seas; the second thirteen. Galatians has six, and Ephesians as many. Then Philippians four, and as many writings go to the Colossians. Thessalonians first five, and afterwards three. Timothy twice three, then twice two together. Three writings go to Titus; Philemon has read one. James has five, and faithful Jude has one. John writes his last in eleven times two; so the whole New Testament is closed.

units.la: IDEM MAIORIS PERSPICUITATIS gratia germanice.
units.tr: THE SAME, IN GERMAN, FOR THE SAKE OF GREATER CLARITY.

units.la: Mattheus der hat viermal siben/ Marcus demnach sechzehen gschribe. In Luca vier vnd zwenzig sind/ In Johan dreyer minder sind. Die Gschichten acht vnd zwenzig hand Vnd Römer sind sechzehen gstandt. In eiden Brieffen gan Corinth Man sechzehen dreyzehen findt.
units.tr: Matthew has four times seven, Mark then sixteen written. In Luke there are twenty-four, in John three fewer. The stories are twenty-eight, and Romans stands at sixteen. In the two letters to Corinth one finds sixteen and thirteen.

units.la: Sechs d' Epistel und' Galater/ Dergleichen sechs an d' Ephefer. Die zu philipp hand vier empfangen So vil auch an d' Colosser glangen. Beid so an Thessalonich geschriben/ Bey fünff vnd dreyen sind geblíben. ◆ Die zwen Sendbriess Thimothei Sechs vnd vier/ drey d' greifft des Tit. Philemonis eins/ an d' Hebreer Dreyzehne/ fünff Sanct Jacobs Lehr Sanct Peter zwo Epistel gmacht/ Fünffer vnd dreyer hab gut acht. Bey Sanct Johanse.1 findst du drey/ Fünff Capitel der ersten sey/ Der andren jede mit eim verfaß/ Alu 9 schreibt vns nur eins Sanct Judas Zwenzig zwey d' Offenbarung g rempt. Ist d' sum Im Neuwen Testament.
units.tr: Six is the Epistle to the Galatians, likewise six to the Ephesians. Those to Philippi have four, and as many come to the Colossians. Both written to Thessalonica remain at five and three. The two letters of Timothy, six and four; three to Titus, one to Philemon; thirteen to the Hebrews, five of St James's teaching. St Peter has made two epistles, five and three; mark them well. In St John's first epistle you find three, five chapters in the first, and in each of the others one. Jude alone writes one; the Revelation touches twenty-two. That is the sum in the New Testament.

units.la: Hactenus de omnibus libris N. Testamenti in genere: sequitur
units.tr: So far concerning all the books of the New Testament in general. Follows

units.la: DE SCRIPTIS EVANGELI-starum.
units.tr: CONCERNING THE WRITINGS OF THE EVANGELISTS.

units.la: EVANGELII vox ob εὐ[?] & ἀγγέλλω, I. felicia annuncio, Græcis quemuis bonum & optatum nuncium declarans, hoc in loco, pro læta & felici exhibi-ti Messiæ dudum promissi, tamdiu à populo Dei expeti & expectati, annunciatione seu revela-tione accipitur.
units.tr: The word EVANGELIUM comes from εὐ and ἀγγέλλω, that is, I announce good things [εὐαγγέλλω]. Among the Greeks it denotes any good and welcome message; here it is taken for the joyful and happy announcement or revelation of the Messiah now displayed, long promised and so long sought and awaited by the people of God.

units.la: Est igitur Evangelium solenne Christi Gratiæ à seculo abscondita, præconium seu revelatio, facta primum voce ipsius Christi & apostolorum, & miraculis confirmata: deinde verò vt continuo progressu eius veritas seculis omnibus superstes esset in mundo, ab Evangelistis & Apostolis diuinitus inspiratis, mandata literis, & publicis quasi tabulis consignata, ad perfectam Ecclesiæ in doctrina salutis institutionem.
units.tr: The Gospel is therefore the solemn proclamation or revelation of Christ's grace, hidden from the ages, made first by the voice of Christ himself and of the apostles, and confirmed by miracles. Then, so that its truth might survive in the world through all ages, it was entrusted to writing by the Evangelists and Apostles, inspired by God, and sealed as it were in public tablets, for the complete instruction of the Church in the doctrine of salvation.

units.la: Proprium igitur Euangelicæ historiæ subiectum est, Christus θεάνθρωπος, diuinæ in nos misericordiæ ac fauoris pignus; cuius incarnationem, doctrinam & gesta, mortem & resurrectionem, & in cœlos ascensum, & horum omnium fructum & finem, hoc est personam & officium, meritum & efficaciam Christi, θεόπνευστοι Amanuenses, hoc est quatuor illi Evangelistæ, magno consensu exponunt.
units.tr: The proper subject of the Gospel history is therefore Christ, the God-man, the pledge of divine mercy and favour toward us. The Evangelists, those four God-breathed amanuenses [θεόπνευστοι], set out with great agreement his incarnation, teaching and deeds, his death and resurrection, and his ascent into heaven, and the fruit and end of all these: that is, the person and office, the merit and efficacy of Christ.

units.la: Evangelistas igitur hoc loco vocamus, non in genere omnes eos qui tradiderunt doctrinam de Messia, in qua significatione vox illa accipitur Eph. 4. & 2. Sed in specie authenticos scriptores historiæ de persona & officio Christi in carnati: Historici certissimi, verissimi. Vide Luc. 1. v. 2. & 4. & Ioh. 21. v. 24. licet inter eos emineat propter argumenti sublimitatem de Christi diuinitate Iohannes.
units.tr: Here we call the Evangelists not all those in general who handed down doctrine about the Messiah, which is the sense in which the word is taken at Eph. 4 and 2. Rather, we mean in particular the authentic writers of the history of the person and office of Christ incarnate: the most certain and most truthful historians. See Luke 1 vv. 2 and 4, and John 21 v. 24, although John stands out among them because of the sublimity of his subject, the divinity of Christ.

units.la: Scopus seu finis huius historiæ proximus est, demonstrare, Quod hic Iesus Nazarenus Mariæ filius, sit Christus ille Dei filius, ac Saluator Mundi. Scopus principalis, cui proximus ille subordinatus est atque inseruit, est: electos qui hanc historiam cognituri erant, ad fidem in Christum, atque ita ad vitam æternam per illam fidem, vt nominatim indicatur Ioh. 20. v. 31. Hæc scripta sunt vt credatis Iesum esse Filium illum Dei, & vt credentes vitam habeatis per nomen eius. Confer. 1. Ioh. 5. v. 1. Sed interim aliæ inferiores quæstiones, de Christi doctrinæ & ceremoniarum, quibus in salutis instauratione vtitur, capitibus, passim incidunt.
units.tr: The immediate aim or end of this history is to demonstrate that this Jesus of Nazareth, son of Mary, is that Christ, the Son of God and Saviour of the world. The principal aim, to which that immediate one is subordinate and serves, is that the elect, who were to come to know this history, should be brought to faith in Christ, and so to eternal life through that faith, as is expressly indicated in John 20 v. 31: These things are written that you may believe that Jesus is that Son of God, and that believing you may have life through his name. Compare 1 John 5 v. 1. Meanwhile, other lesser questions, about the heads of Christ's doctrine and of the ceremonies he uses in restoring salvation, occur here and there.

units.la: Porrò Scopus ille seu finis vniuersæ historiæ Euangelicæ propositus constituitur & demonstratur Veteris Testamenti iudicio diuinitus patefacto, in Nouo ad IESVM Mariæ filium applicando. Etenim sic eius generatio, vita, doctrina, miracula, afflictiones, mors, resurrectio, & ad cœlos ascensio, additis certis locis, temporibus, aliisque rebus circumstantibus, ad Vetus Testamentum accommodatè describitur, vt cùm in eo sunt iacta fundamenta & Propositiones syllogismorum enunciatæ; in Nouo tum eæ ipsæ sæpè attingantur, tum præcipuè Assumptiones, de IESV Mariæ filio copiosè explicentur, & Complexiones seu Conclusiones partim ab eo ipso, & fidelibus hominibus, partim ab hostibus etiam inuitis inferantur.
units.tr: Moreover, that aim or end of the whole Gospel history is established and demonstrated by the judgment of the Old Testament, divinely revealed, when it is applied in the New to Jesus, son of Mary. For thus his generation, life, teaching, miracles, afflictions, death, resurrection and ascension into heaven are described in a way suited to the Old Testament, with certain places, times and other surrounding circumstances added. So, whereas in the Old Testament the foundations are laid and the premises of the syllogisms stated, in the New these same premises are often touched on again, and above all the minor premises concerning Jesus, son of Mary, are fully explained. Conclusions are drawn partly by himself and by faithful men, and partly even by unwilling enemies.

units.la: Itaque perpetua illa & principalis per totam historiam demonstratio, non tam perspicua breuiqúe[?] forma conclusa, quàm historicè explicata, ideoque in toto eius progressu spectanda est. Cæteræ verò in concionibus & contentionibus Conclusiones minùs principales magis perspicuæ, & ad communem formam accommodatæ sunt.
units.tr: Therefore that continuous and principal demonstration, running through the whole history, is to be looked for in its whole course, not so much as a clear form briefly concluded, but as historically unfolded. The other conclusions, less principal, which occur in sermons and disputations, are more evident and are adapted to the common form.

units.la: Ad uniuersæ igitur historiæ à singulis quatuor Euangelistis descriptæ Analysin paulò post commodiùs instituendam; summatim præcipua de Messia argumenta, uno syllogismo concludemus.
units.tr: Therefore, for the analysis of the whole history as described by the four Evangelists individually, which we shall set out more conveniently a little later, we will sum up the chief arguments about the Messiah in a single syllogism.

units.la: EXEMPLVM PRINCIPALIS SYLLO-gismi ex multis argumentis coacervati, & ad Euang: Matthæi accommodati, hoc est.
units.tr: EXAMPLE OF THE PRINCIPAL SYLLOGISM, gathered from many arguments and adapted to the Gospel of Matthew, that is:

units.la: PROPOSITIO Ex V. Test. Is qui oriturus fuit ex Abrahamo (Gen. 22.18.) & Davide, (2. Sam. 7.12.) nasciturus ex Virgine, (Esa.7.14.) in oppidulo Bethleem, (Mich.5.2.) vocandus ex Ægypto, (Osææ.11.1.) educandus in urbe Galilææ Nazareth: (Esa. 11.1.) qui ad officium propheticum in populo Dei administrandum habiturus fuit præcursorem Eliam (Malach. 3.) seu vocem clamantis in deserto, (Esa:40.3.) qui Euangelium fuit prædicaturus in Galilæa (Esa: 9.1.) & prædicationem suâ multis ac variis atq; stupendis miraculis confirmaturus (Esa: 35. 5.) sanando scil: morbos incurabiles solo verbo seu imperio: qui Hierosolymam fuit ingressurus insidens asino, (Zach. 9. 9.) acclamante populo, Hosanna filio David, (Psal: 118. 25.) qui prodendus fuit Iudæis per unum ex domesticis, (Psal. 14. 10.) pro tribus argenteis, pro quibus postea emendus fuit ager figuli, (Zach. 11.13.) qui reputandus fuit inter facinorosos:(Esa.53.12) flagellandus, (Esa.53.5.) crucifigendus, (Psal.22. 17.) in cruce pendens ab inimicis suis irridendus: (Psal. 22. 8.) item,cui in cruce pendenti in potum præbendum fuit acetum felle mistum, (Psal:69.22.)cuius partienda vestimenta, & sors super tunicam iacienda: (Psal. 22. 19.)cuius corpus à diuite ad sepulchrum fuit impetrandum, (Esa : 53.9.)qui tertio die (Ioæ.2.1.) é sepulchro fuit resurrecturus,(Esa : 53.11.) & postea in cœlũ ascensurus : (Psal.68.19.) is,in quam,in quo cõ-memorata omnia fuerunt euentura,est CHRI-STVS,seu seruator mundi.
units.tr: PROPOSITION: From the Old Testament. He who was to arise from Abraham (Gen. 22.18) and David (2 Sam. 7.12), to be born of a Virgin (Isa. 7.14) in the little town of Bethlehem (Mic. 5.2), to be called out of Egypt (Hos. 11.1), and to be brought up in the city of Nazareth in Galilee (Isa. 11.1); who was to have Elijah as his forerunner (Mal. 3), or the voice of one crying in the wilderness (Isa. 40.3), in exercising the prophetic office among the people of God; who was to preach the gospel in Galilee (Isa. 9.1) and to confirm his preaching by many varied and wonderful miracles (Isa. 35.5), namely by healing incurable diseases by a word or command alone; who was to enter Jerusalem riding on an ass (Zech. 9.9), with the people crying out "Hosanna to the son of David" (Ps. 118.25); who was to be betrayed to the Jews by one of his household (Ps. 14.10), for three pieces of silver, with which the potter's field was afterwards bought (Zech. 11.13); who was to be counted among malefactors (Isa. 53.12); who was to be scourged (Isa. 53.5), crucified (Ps. 22.17), and hanging on the cross to be mocked by his enemies (Ps. 22.8); likewise, to whom, while he hung on the cross, vinegar mixed with gall was to be given to drink (Ps. 69.22); whose garments were to be divided, and lots cast upon his tunic (Ps. 22.19); whose body was to be begged from the rich man for burial (Isa. 53.9); who was to rise from the tomb on the third day (Joel 2.1), and afterwards to ascend into heaven (Isa. 53.11; Ps. 68.19). He in whom and through whom all these things mentioned were to come about is CHRIST, or the Saviour of the world.

units.la: ASSVMTIO : Atqui Iesus ille Nazarenus,est in quo commemorata omnia fuerunt euentura, & impleta sunt.Etenim ortus est ex Abrahamo, (Matth.1.1.) & Dauide : (ibidem:)natus ex Virgine,(ibid.v.18.)in oppidulo Bethleë[?]: (cap. 2.1.) vocatus ex Ægypto ( v. 15. educatus in urbe Galilæae Nazareth :(v. 23.) præcursorem Eliam, (cap. 3.v.14.) seu vocem clamantis in deserto, (cap. 3.v.3.)videlicet Iohannem Baptistam:prædicauit Euangelium in Galilæa : (4. v.12.)suamque prædicatione miraculis confirmauit, (ibid. v. 23. 24. Item à cap. 8. deinceps vsq; ad cap.21.) Hierosolymam ingressus est insidens asino, (cap. 21. 7.) acclamante populo , Hosanna filio Dauid, (ibid.v. 9.). proditus fuit Iudæis per unū ex domesticis, ( cap. 26. v. 49.) videlicet per Iudam Ischariotem,pro triginta argeteis,pro quibus postea emtus fuit ager figuli : ( cap.27. v.7.) prætera reputatus fuit inter facinorosos, (ibid. 17. 38.)flagellatus fuit,(ibid.v.26.)crucifixus, (v. 35.) in cruce irrisus (v.39.) potus aceti & fellis eì præbitus(v. 34.48.)vestimenta eius partita sunt, &sors supra tunicam iacta : (v.35.) corpus eius à diuite ad sepulturam impetratum:(cap. 27.v.58) tertia die è sepulchro resurrexit ( v. 6.)& postea in cœlum ascendit ( v. 16. & seq.)
units.tr: ASSUMPTION: But that Jesus of Nazareth is the one in whom all the things mentioned were to happen, and they have been fulfilled. For he was descended from Abraham (Matt. 1.1) and David (ibid.); born of a Virgin (ibid. v.18) in the little town of Bethlehem (ch. 2.1); called out of Egypt (v.15) and brought up in the city of Nazareth in Galilee (v.23); with Elijah as his forerunner (ch. 3 v.14), or the voice of one crying in the wilderness (ch. 3 v.3), namely John the Baptist; he preached the gospel in Galilee (ch. 4 v.12) and confirmed his preaching by miracles (ibid. vv.23-24; likewise from ch. 8 onwards to ch. 21); he entered Jerusalem riding on an ass (ch. 21.7), with the people crying out "Hosanna to the son of David" (ibid. v.9); he was betrayed to the Jews by one of his household (ch. 26 v.49), namely by Judas Iscariot, for thirty pieces of silver, with which the potter's field was afterwards bought (ch. 27 v.7); moreover he was counted among malefactors (ibid. v.38); he was scourged (ibid. v.26), crucified (v.35), mocked on the cross (v.39), and given vinegar and gall to drink (vv.34, 48); his garments were divided and lots cast upon his tunic (v.35); his body was begged from the rich man for burial (ch. 27 v.58); on the third day he rose from the tomb (v.6), and afterwards ascended into heaven (v.16 and following).

units.la: Conclusio: Ergo Iesus Nazarenus Mariæ Filius est Christus seu seruator mundi.
units.tr: Conclusion: Therefore Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Mary, is the Christ, or the Saviour of the world.

units.la: Huius syllogismi Propositio Messiæ quandam descriptionem continens, confirmatur testimoniis Prophetarum, quæ passim in hac historia allegantur.
units.tr: The proposition of this syllogism, which contains a certain description of the Messiah, is confirmed by the testimonies of the Prophets, which are cited throughout this history.

units.la: Assumptio confirmatur testimonio huius narrationis: quæ fidem meretur apud omnes bonos: cum scripta sit ab iis qui fuerunt αὐτόπται,& historiam suam ediderint, cùm res illæ recens gestæ essent; idque apud eos, apud quos fuerant gestæ: nec tamen mendacij ab illis fuerunt in simulati, aut conuicti.
units.tr: The assumption is confirmed by the testimony of this narrative, which deserves credit with all good people, since it was written by those who were eyewitnesses [αὐτόπται] and published their history while those events were still recent, and among the very people among whom they had taken place; nor were they ever convicted of having invented or feigned any falsehood.

units.la: Conclusionem in historia sæpe tum Iesus infert, & fideles colligunt, tum hostes etiam diaboliq ue nonnullibi confitentur. Vide Parallela D. Iunij, hoc est comparatione Locorum Scripturæ sacræ, qui ex Veteri Testamento in Nouo adducuntur.
units.tr: The conclusion is often drawn within the history, both by Jesus himself and by the faithful, and sometimes even enemies and the devil confess it. See the Parallela of D. Junius, that is, the comparison of passages of holy Scripture which are adduced from the Old Testament in the New.

units.la: DE CONSENSV EVANGELISTARUM.
units.tr: ON THE AGREEMENT OF THE EVANGELISTS.

units.la: INTER divinas authoritates, quæ sacris literis continentur, (vt rectè scribit Augustinus lib. 1. de consensu Euangelistarum)Euangelium merito excellit, quod cùm sit fidei nostræ fundamentum & columna, (vt loquitur Irenæus lib. 3 cap. 1.) non per quosuis homines, sed per eos qui à Deo ad id munus præordinati erant, (inquit S. Petrus Act. 10. & qui vel αὐ-τόπται[?] fuerunt, & quidem Apostoli Christi, vel eorum auditores fidissimi, (Luc. 1. v. 1. 2.) historiam Ecclesiasticam scribere oportuit. Cæteri omnes, qui talia scribere conati sunt (inquit Augustinus) non tales extiterunt, ut eis fidem haberet Ecclesia, atque in authoritatem canonicam eorum scripta acciperet: non solùm quia illi tales non erant quibus narrantibus credi oporteret, sed etiam quia scriptis suis quædam fallaciter indiderunt, quæ Catholica & Apostolica regula, & sana doctrina condemnat. Hos vero quatuor Euangelistas, quemadmodum uno ore agnoscunt vetusti Patres, tanquam sanctas quadrigas deberi Domino, quibus vectus subigeret populos, & per quos Christiana Religio per quatuor mundi plagas disseminaretur: contra quos ipsi infideles vix jam suas calumnias mussitare audent. Nec defuerunt tamen inter Ethnicos, ut Celsus & Prophyrius, tum inter eos qui Christiani haberi volebant, ut Marcionitæ & Manichæi, qui authoritate Euangelistarum eleuare conati sunt. Atque illos quidem qui sibi plus quàm luci Ecclesiæ fidem adhiberi volebant, refutauit Irenæus lib. 1. & 3. Tertull: lib. 4. contra Marcionem, August. lib. 32. & 33. contra Faustum Manichæum.
units.tr: Among the divine authorities contained in the sacred writings (as Augustine rightly writes, book 1 of On the Consensus of the Evangelists), the Gospel deservedly excels, since it is the foundation and pillar of our faith (as Irenaeus says, book 3 ch. 1). The ecclesiastical history had to be written not by just any men, but by those who had been predestined by God to that office (as St Peter says, Acts 10), and who were either eyewitnesses [αὐτόπται] and indeed apostles of Christ, or the most faithful hearers of them (Luke 1.1-2). All the others who tried to write such things (says Augustine) were not such that the Church would trust them and receive their writings as canonical authority; not only because they were not such men as one ought to believe when they narrate, but also because they falsely inserted certain things into their writings, which the Catholic and Apostolic rule and sound doctrine condemn. But these four Evangelists, as the ancient Fathers acknowledge with one voice, are to be regarded as the holy four-horse chariots owed to the Lord, on which he rides forth to subdue the peoples, and through which the Christian religion is spread through the four quarters of the world. Against them the unbelievers themselves now hardly dare to mutter their calumnies. Yet there were not lacking opponents: among the Gentiles, such as Celsus and Porphyry; and among those who wished to be considered Christians, such as the Marcionites and Manichaeans, who tried to undermine the authority of the Evangelists. Irenaeus refuted those who wished faith to be placed in themselves rather than in the light of the Church, in books 1 and 3; Tertullian in book 4 against Marcion; and Augustine in books 32 and 33 against the Manichaean Faustus.

units.la: Ac varia illi quidem contra Euangelistas obiiciebant, sed hæc tria erant omnium speciosissima: 1. quòd exemplaria & versiones Ecclesiasticæ historiæ variæ & corruptæ essent: 2. quòd magna Euangelistarum esset dissonantia. 3. quòd scripta hæc viderentur scopæ dissolutæ & sine ordine. Ad primam obiectionem respondebant Patres, partim per negationem, partim per distinctionem: negantes videlicet corruptam esse Euangelicam Historiam quantumuis variae eius essent versiones, si capita & Articulos fidei spectent. Nam illa omnia, vt de Christi natiuitate, passione, morte, resurrectione &c. in omnibus exemplaribus reperiuntur. Deinde per distin-ctionem, non quidem ita puras esse, & textui Graeco respondentes omnes versiones, sed remedium facile huic incommodo reperiri, si ad Graeci textus originem recurratur. Sic Hieronymus in praefatione in Euangelistas ad Dardanum: Varia sunt quidem (inquit) & innumera latina exemplaria, sed si veritas quaerenda est, cur non ad Graecam recurrentes, ea quae vel a vitiosis interpretibus male reddita, vel a resumptoribus imperitis peruersa, vel a librariis dormitantibus mutata obseruamus?
units.tr: They raised many objections against the Evangelists, but these three were by far the most specious: (1) that the copies and versions of the ecclesiastical history were varied and corrupt; (2) that there was great discord among the Evangelists; (3) that these writings seemed to be a loose heap, without order. To the first objection the Fathers replied partly by denial and partly by distinction. By denial, namely, they held that the Evangelical history is not corrupted, however varied its versions may be, if one looks to the heads and articles of faith: for all those things, such as the birth, passion, death and resurrection of Christ, and so on, are found in all copies. Then by distinction: that not all versions are indeed so pure, or so exactly corresponding to the Greek text; but an easy remedy for this inconvenience is found if we have recourse to the origin of the Greek text. Thus Jerome in his preface on the Evangelists to Dardanus: "There are indeed (he says) various and countless Latin copies. But if the truth is to be sought, why do we not have recourse to the Greek, and observe those things which were either badly rendered by faulty translators, or perverted by unskilled correctors, or changed by sleepy scribes?"

units.la: Eorum calumniam, qui magnam aliquam διαφωνίαν inter Euangelistas esse sibi imaginantur, ac inde concludunt, non posse eis haberi fidem, cum in testibus idoneis oporteat esse consen-sum, abunde & euidenter refutarunt illi qui Harmoniam quatuor Euangelistarum editis voluminibus demonstrarunt, vt sunt S. Augustinus de consensu Euangelistarum: Harmonia Iohannis Caluini, Osiandri, Gerardi Mercato-ris, Danielis Toffani, &c: ex quibus regulas quasdam & certas obseruationes, de locorum in spe-ciem pugnantium conciliatione, trademus. [illegible, ~20 letters] [illegible, ~20 letters] [illegible, ~20 letters]
units.tr: As for the calumny of those who imagine some great discord (διαφωνία) among the Evangelists, and conclude from this that they cannot be believed, since agreement ought to exist among reliable witnesses: those who demonstrated the harmony of the four Evangelists in published volumes refuted it fully and clearly. Among them are St Augustine in On the Consensus of the Evangelists, the Harmony of John Calvin, Osiander, Gerard Mercator, Daniel Toffanus, and others. From these we shall set out certain rules and sure observations for reconciling passages that seem to conflict. [illegible, ~20 letters] [illegible, ~20 letters] [illegible, ~20 letters]

units.la: Si Euangelistæ, qui easdem res referunt, alicubi in circumstantiarum explicatione videntur sic dissidere, ut conciliationem excogitare haud possimus: non tamen propterea censebi-mus, eorum dignitati quicquam derogatum, multò minus de veritate ac certitudine eorum dubitabimus. Hic igitur tenenda est obseruatio Chrysostomi, in 1 Homilia in Matthæum, hisce prodita verbis: Non sufficiebat unus Euangelista cuncta memorare? Sufficiebat quidem, sed cùm quatuor sunt, qui Euangelia conscribant, nec iisdem temporibus, nec in eisdem locis, neque pariter congregati, & inter se conferentes, & tamen quasi uno ore pronunciant: sit hoc sine dubio veritatis grande iudicium. Verum é[?] contrario, (inquis,) ista res accidit: in multis enim dissidere redarguuntur. Immo hoc ipsum maximum est testimonium veritatis.
