Si enim ad unguem in omnibus consonarent, etiam usque ad tempora ac loca, ipsaque adeò verba: nemo inimicus credidisset unquam, eos non communi ad decipiendum consilio congregatos, quasi ex humana quadam conspiratione Euangelium condidisse. Non enim simplicitatis fuisse tam solicitam consonantiam iudicarent. Nunc verò quæ videtur in rebus exiguis dissonantia, ab omni illos suspicione defendit, & satis clarè scribentium existimationem tuetur. Si verò aliquid de temporibus ac locis varie dixerunt, nihil quidem dictorum obest veritati. Sed tamen & hæc prout donauerit Deus, progredientes declarare tentabimus : illud post hæc quæ dixi-mus, postulantes, ut diligenter notetis, quod in illis principalibus caussis ; in quibus & vita no-stra, & prædicationis summa consistit, consen-tiunt, neque quisquam illorum vspiam vel tan-tillum discrepare inuenitur. Quæ vero ista sunt? Nempe, quòd Deus homo factus sit, quòd mirabilia operatus, quòd crucifixus, quòd sepultus sit, quòd resurrexerit ; quòd ascenderit in cœ-lum, quòd iudicaturus sit; quòd salutaria præcepta dederit, quòd non contrariam legem intulerit priori, quòd filius, quòd vnigenitus, quòd germanus & verus, quòd eiusdem cum patre substantiæ, & quæcunque sunt talia. In his quippe omnibus maximam illorum inueniemus esse concordiam. Si vero in miraculis non omnes omnia dixerunt, si hic quidem illa, alter vero alia narrauit, nihil te omnino conturbet. Nam si vnus vniuersa dixisset, superfluus iam fuisset numerus cæterorum : sin varia omnes inter se scripsissent, ac noua omnia, nullum potuisset conuenientiæ apparere documentum. Hac-tenus ille. Vide insuper nobile illud opus Augustini de Consensu Euangelistarum lib. 2.
units.tr: If Evangelists who relate the same things seem to disagree in the explanation of circumstances in such a way that we cannot devise a reconciliation, we shall not on that account judge that anything has been taken from their dignity, much less shall we doubt their truth and certainty. Here, then, the observation of Chrysostom must be kept, in his first Homily on Matthew, given in these words: "Was it not enough for one Evangelist to relate everything? It was enough indeed; but since there are four who write the Gospels, not at the same times, nor in the same places, nor gathered together and conferring with one another, yet they pronounce as if with one mouth, this is without doubt a great proof of the truth. But, you will say, the contrary happens, for they are shown to disagree in many things. Indeed this very thing is the greatest testimony to the truth. For if they agreed exactly in all things, even as to times and places and the very words, no enemy would ever have believed that they had not gathered together with a common plan to deceive, as if they had composed the Gospel by some human conspiracy. For they would judge that such a careful agreement was not of simplicity. But now the apparent discord in small matters defends them from every suspicion, and sufficiently protects the reputation of the writers. If indeed they have spoken variously about times and places, nothing they said is harmful to the truth. Yet we shall try to declare these things too, as God grants, as we proceed. But after what we have said, we ask that you note carefully that in those principal matters, in which both our life and the sum of our preaching consist, they agree, and none of them is found to differ even a little anywhere. What are these? Namely, that God was made man, that he worked wonders, that he was crucified, that he was buried, that he rose again, that he ascended into heaven, that he will judge, that he gave saving precepts, that he did not introduce a law contrary to the former, that he is the Son, the only-begotten, genuine and true, of the same substance as the Father, and whatever else is of this kind. For in all these things we shall find their greatest concord. But if in the miracles they did not all tell everything, if one related these things and another others, let nothing at all trouble you. For if one had related everything, the number of the others would already have been superfluous; but if all had written variously and everything new, no proof of agreement could have appeared." Thus far he. See also that noble work of Augustine, On the Consensus of the Evangelists, book 2.

units.la: SECUNDA REGULA
units.tr: SECOND RULE

units.la: QUi Euangelistam aliquem legit, caute con-feret quæ de adem re, quæ in manibus est, cæteri quoque Euangelistæ memorant. Siquidem fit nonnunquam, ut vnus Euangelista ali-quid præteremittere, veluti circumstantiam aut simile quippiam, alius vero aliquid superaddere videatur. Exempli causa: Historiam transformationis Christi describunt Lucas cap. 9. & Marcus cap. 9. & Matth: 17. Lucas autem ait: & facta est, dum oraret, species vultus eius alia. Marcus vero de immutatione vultus Christi mentionem non facit: sed satis habet simpli-citer dixisse, Christum in conspectu discipulo-rum transformatum. Cæterum cum Lucas non exprimat, quomodo mutata sit Christi facies: discendum id est ex Matthaeo, qui ait: splenduit facies eius sicut sol. De vestimentis autem Christi scribit idem: Vestimenta illius facta sunt candida sicut lumen. Marcus vero: Vestimenta illius facta sunt splendida, candida valde veluti nix, quam candida non potest facere fullo super terram. Lucas denique comprehendit utrunque; Vestitus eius candidus, (inquit) ac re-fulgens.
units.tr: Whoever reads one of the Evangelists should carefully compare what the others also record about the same matter that is before him. For it sometimes happens that one Evangelist omits something, such as a circumstance or something similar, while another seems to add something. For example, the account of the transfiguration of Christ is described by Luke chapter 9, Mark chapter 9, and Matthew 17. Luke says: "And as he prayed, the appearance of his face was altered." Mark makes no mention of a change in the face of Christ, but is content to have said simply that Christ was transfigured in the sight of his disciples. Since Luke does not explain how the face of Christ was changed, we must learn this from Matthew, who says: "His face shone as the sun." Matthew also writes about the garments of Christ: "His garments became white as light." Mark says: "His garments became glistening, exceedingly white, like snow, such as no fuller on earth can make white." Finally, Luke comprehends both: "His raiment was white and glistening."

units.la: Tertia Regula.
units.tr: Third Rule.

units.la: Porrò vnus quispiam Euangelistarum quan-doque refert historiam, quam nemo attingit alius: aut si quis præterea alius, non tamen conscribunt eam omnes. Iohannes illam de transf-formatione præteriuit: similiter nonnulla à tempore coenæ ad ingressum vsque in hortum trans torrentem Kedron: At idem Iohannes solus prolixam atque admirabilem illam concio-nem Christi à coenâ habitam, diffusè describit: solus recitat historiam de eo qui 28. annos mor-bo affectus, ad Probaticam piscinam decubuit.
units.tr: Furthermore, one of the Evangelists sometimes relates a story that no other touches, or, if another does touch on it, not all of them record it. John passed over the transfiguration; similarly he omitted some things from the time of the supper up to his entering the garden across the brook Kidron. But John alone describes at length that long and admirable sermon of Christ delivered after the supper; he alone recounts the story of the man who had been ill for 38 years and lay by the pool of Bethesda.

units.la: QVARTA REGVLA.
units.tr: FOURTH RULE.

units.la: Interdum unus sine additione, vel detractio-ne, plane idem narrat quod alius: alter tamen altero loquitur evidentius, ac verba magis ido-nea usurpat. Exempla sunt passim in conspectu posita.
units.tr: Sometimes one Evangelist, without addition or omission, relates exactly the same thing as another, yet one expresses it more clearly than the other and uses more suitable words. Examples are set out everywhere.

units.la: QVINTA REGVLA.
units.tr: FIFTH RULE.

units.la: Discrepant igitur Euangelistae quandoque in circumstantiis, quae rei summam non variant. hic astrictius rem narrat, ille fusius: hic perhibet sanatos duos, alter tres: unus in egressu portae, alius in ingressu. quod illa de causa saepe evenit, quod est tanta miraculorum Christi multitudo, ut quae sunt diversa, nos tamen propter aliquam inter se similitudinem eadem esse existimemus. Eundem in modum usuenit in dictis & sententiis doctrinae. eadem dixit Dominus variis locis, variis verbis: hic refert quae dixit hoc modo, ille quae illo in loco paulum diversè: colligunt videlicet summas concionum & verborum Christi, quae ad institutionem & salutem nostram facerent &c. Lud Vines[?], lib. 2. de veritate fidei Christi.
units.tr: The Evangelists therefore sometimes differ in circumstances that do not alter the substance of the matter: one relates the matter more briefly, another more fully; one reports two men healed, another three; one at the going out of the gate, another at the coming in. This often happens for the following reason: the miracles of Christ were so many that, since some of them are different, we nevertheless think them to be the same on account of some resemblance between them. In the same way it happens with the sayings and teachings. The Lord said the same things on various occasions, in various words: one reports what he said in this way, another what he said in that place in a slightly different way. For they gather, of course, the sum of the sermons and words of Christ that serve for our instruction and salvation, and so forth. Lud. Vives[?], book 2, On the Truth of the Christian Faith.

units.la: SEXTA REGVLA.
units.tr: SIXTH RULE.

units.la: Contra obiectum de ordine confuso Euangelistarum, tenendae sunt hae observationes: Primum Euangelistas non ubique exactum temporis ordinem secutos: siquidem non Chronographos agere, aut Ephemerides scribere voluerunt. Annorum quidem habita fuit ab illis ratio, vt conspicuum esset lectoribus quomodo defunctus sit Christus quadriennij cursu abini-tio praedicationis vsque ad mortem: sed quae in idem fere tempus inciderunt miracula, liberè permiscent, quia non certa distinctaque temporum serie Annales componere, sed ex rebus gestis Christi praecipuas quasdam summatim colligere propositum fuit. Calvinus in Harm. Evan.
units.tr: Against the objection concerning the confused order of the Evangelists, the following observations must be held. First, the Evangelists did not everywhere follow an exact order of time, since they did not wish to write chronicles or diaries. Indeed, they did take account of years, so that it would be evident to readers how Christ, from the beginning of his preaching until his death, passed through the course of four years. But miracles that fell about the same time they mix together freely, since their purpose was not to compose annals in a fixed and distinct series of times, but to gather briefly certain principal matters from the deeds of Christ. Calvin, in the Harmony of the Evangelists.

units.la: Deinde obseruandum nonnulla re & tempore esse eadem, vt miraculum de quinque panibus, quod Matth. 14. & Ioh. 6. recitatur: alia re sed non tempore, vt admonitio de primatu vitando, bis facta, Matth. 20. & Luc. 22. & iuxta multorum sententiam recitatio Orationis Dominicae, Matthaei 6. Luc. 11. Sic & similia gesta (vti supra ex Viuete adductum,) recitantur, diuersa tamen, & diuersis gesta temporibus, vt irrigatio & vnctio pedum Iesu, Luc. 7. & Matth. 26. rursum. Item de duobus caecis, Matt: 9. & rursus, 20.
units.tr: Second, it must be observed that some things are the same both in substance and in time, as the miracle of the five loaves, which is recounted in Matthew 14 and John 6. Other things are the same in substance but not in time, as the warning about avoiding the primacy, given twice, in Matthew 20 and Luke 22; and, according to the opinion of many, the recitation of the Lord's Prayer in Matthew 6 and Luke 11. Thus similar deeds too are recounted (as adduced above from Vives), yet they are different and were done at different times, such as the anointing and washing of Jesus' feet in Luke 7 and again in Matthew 26; likewise the two blind men in Matthew 9 and again in Matthew 20.

units.la: Tertiò: Euangelistae saepe aut compendij, aut expositionis gratia, quasi per digressionem aliquid narrant, quod non (vt etiam supra admonitum,) ad temporis seriem quadrat: nonnulla quoque per anticipationem recensent, vt mortem Iohannis Baptistae Luc. cap. 3. annotare videtur, circa tempus quo Christus fuit baptizatus, cùm constet id diu post Baptismum Christi esse factum.
units.tr: Third: the Evangelists often, for the sake of brevity or explanation, relate something as if by digression, which (as also noted above) does not fit the sequence of time. They also sometimes record some things by anticipation, as Luke chapter 3 seems to note the death of John the Baptist at the time when Christ was baptized, although it is certain that this happened long after the baptism of Christ.

units.la: Quarto Multa etiam, quantum ad circumstantiam temporis, per Synecdochen intelligenda sunt, vt ex ex parte totum vel contra: Vt cùm dicitur Christus tribus diebus, & tribus noctibus in vtero terræ concludendus fuisse, Matth. 12. vbi pars aliqua tantum, & quidem breuissima primi diei, & quotacunque pars tertiæ, pro tribus noctibus accipitur. Item cùm Christus Matthæi 17. post 6. dies transformatus dicitur; apud Lucam verò cap. 8. post dies octo. Qui octo dicit, (vt monet Augustinus) comprehendit aliquam partem diei quo se Christus ad id præparauit; & partem diei aliquam quo id completum fuit: qui dixit 6. solos medios & integros nominat. Sic quoque Chrysostomus. Sic cum alius ex Euangelistis dicit, vt Luc. 9. accubuisse, 5000. Marcus quinquagenos & centenos, ille partem dixit, hic totum.
units.tr: Fourth, many things, as regards the circumstance of time, must also be understood by synecdoche, that is, a part for the whole or the reverse. For example, when it is said that Christ was to be confined in the womb of the earth for three days and three nights (Matthew 12), where some part only, and indeed the very briefest part of the first day, and however much of the third, is taken for three nights. Likewise, when Christ is said in Matthew 17 to have been transfigured after six days, but in Luke chapter 8 after eight days: he who says eight includes some part of the day on which Christ prepared himself for it, and some part of the day on which it was completed; he who says six names only the whole, middle days. So also Chrysostom. Thus when one of the Evangelists says, as in Luke 9, that there reclined 5,000 men, while Mark says by hundreds and fifties, the one spoke of a part, the other of the whole.

units.la: Septima Regula.
units.tr: The Seventh Rule.

units.la: Quoad nomina Personarum vel locorum propria obseruandum, vni diuersa nomina tribui: sic Iudas ille, & Thaddæus & Lebbæus cognominabatur: Simon & Cephas Syriaco idiomate, &, quod idem est apud Græcos, Petrus.i. Rupes siue saxum. Ioh. 1. In personis etiá numerandis obseruandum, alios Euangelistas plures nonnunquam nominare, alios præcipuû aliquem & maximè insignem, vt Matth. 8. duo dicuntur fuisse qui legionem dæmonum habebant quæ in porcos irruebant: Lucas commemorat. Ita Lucas Cap. 18. vnum cæcum nominat, quem & Marcus cap. 10. Bartholomæum vocat: Matthæus cap. 20.[?] duorum facit mentionem: & sic intelligendus est locus Luc. 22. de vno latrone, scilicet præcipuè blasphemante Christum, cùm Matthæus plurium meminerit. Idem intelligendum est de angelis qui post resurrectionem ad sepulcrum apparuerunt.
units.tr: As to the proper names of persons or places, one should observe that one person may be given different names. Thus that Judas was also called Thaddaeus and Lebbaeus; and Simon is called Cephas in the Syriac idiom, which among the Greeks is the same as Peter, that is, a rock or stone (John 1). Regarding the numbering of persons, one should also observe that some Evangelists sometimes name several, while others name only one, and that the most prominent. Thus Matthew 8 says there were two men who had a legion of demons which rushed into the swine, whereas Luke mentions only one. Likewise Luke 18 names one blind man, whom Mark 10 calls Bartimaeus, while Matthew 20 mentions two. In this way the passage in Luke 22 about one thief must be understood as referring chiefly to the one who blasphemed Christ, though Matthew speaks of several. The same is to be understood of the angels who appeared at the tomb after the resurrection.

units.la: Octava Regula.
units.tr: The Eighth Rule.

units.la: DE aliis & rerum & circumstantiam, causarum & casuum requisitis, hæc quoque ab eruditis observantur
units.tr: Concerning the other requirements of things, circumstances, causes and cases, learned writers also observe the following.

units.la: Primo : Diversas poni nonnunquam circumstantias loci, temporis, &c. quando aliquid bis, vel sæpius gestum & repetitum fuit: Ut eiectio ementium & venditium ex templo, initio prae-dicationis Christi Ioh. 2. & postea rursus paulò ante mortem, Matth. 21.
units.tr: First: Different circumstances of place, time and so on are sometimes given when something was done and repeated twice or more often. Thus the driving out of the buyers and sellers from the temple is placed at the beginning of Christ's preaching (John 2), and again shortly before his death (Matthew 21).

units.la: Secundo : Eundem in modum circumstantiæ loci non pugnant, quando initium sermonis alicuius, vel facti potuit fieri in uno loco, & continuo in altero : Ut, Sermo ille Christi, qui dicitur Matthæi 5.[?] cap. habitus in monte:Lucæ 6. in loco campestri; quo relicto, procul dubio ascendit montem, videns magnam turbam, ut commodius docere posset.
units.tr: Second: In the same way, circumstances of place do not conflict when the beginning of a discourse or deed could have taken place in one place and been continued in another. Thus that sermon of Christ which is said in Matthew 5 to have been delivered on the mountain, and in Luke 6 on a level place, was undoubtedly, after leaving that place, taken up onto the mountain, seeing the great crowd, so that he could teach more conveniently.

units.la: Tertio: Nec semper interest, (inquit Augustinus lib. 2. de consensu Euangel: cap. 21.) quid quis aliquo ponat, dum id non adversetur aliis narrationibus, ubi ordo temporum non apparet, nihil (inquit) nostra interesse debet, quem narrandi ordinem quilibet tenuerit, ut de sanatione socrus Petri, Matt: 8. cap. & Lucæ 4. Vide Regulas Gerhardi Mercatoris Iuliacensis Chronographi & Cosmographi, in Euangelicæ historiæ quadripartitæ Monadis demonstratione.
units.tr: Third: Nor does it always matter, says Augustine (De consensu Evangelistarum, bk. 2, ch. 21), what order someone adopts in setting things down, provided it does not conflict with other narratives where the order of times does not appear. Nothing of ours, he says, should depend on which order of narration anyone has followed, as in the healing of Peter's mother-in-law, Matt. 8 and Luke 4. See the rules of Gerhard Mercator of Jülich, chronographer and cosmographer, in his demonstration of the fourfold Gospel history, Monas.

units.la: Quarto : Sæpe quæ diversa videntur, eodem redeunt, si momenta distinguantur, ut quod Marci 5. Luc. 8. filiam Archisynagogæ fuisse in extremis scribunt, cum ille venisset ad Iesum: Matthæus 9. mortuam fuisse. Illi enim recitant in quo statu silam reliquerit discedens domo, videlicet agentem animam: Matthæus, quo in statu fuerit tunc cum alloqueretur Christum, videlicet mortua, sicut ei renunciatum fuit.
units.tr: Fourth: Often things that seem different come to the same point, if the moments are distinguished. For example, Mark 5 and Luke 8 write that the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue was at the point of death when he came to Jesus, while Matthew 9 says she had already died. The former report the state in which he left her when he went away from home, namely that she was still breathing; Matthew reports her state when he addressed Christ, namely that she was dead, as he had been told.

units.la: Sic non pugnat, quòd ficus illicò arefacta dicitur, Matth. 21. Marcus verò cap. 11. secundâ demum die visam arefactam. Ille enim narrat, quid statim sit factum ex Christi imprecatione: hic quid postridie demum animadversum ab Apostolis. Nec pugnat, sed dòdem[?] redit quod Matth : 28. scribitur extremo sabbatho, vel ad verbum, vespere sabbathi, mulieres ad monumentum venisse: & Marc. 16. valdè manè dicuntur venisse. Nam Romanorum more qui diem naturalem ab ortu solis numerarunt, erat diluculum. Hebræorum more erat vespera sab-bathi quæ illucescebat in diem sequentem: ideo Matthæus dicit; cùm illucesceret in primum diem hebdomadis.
units.tr: So it is no contradiction that Matthew 21 says the fig tree withered at once, while Mark 11 says it was seen withered only on the second day. The one tells what immediately followed Christ's curse; the other tells what the apostles noticed only the next day. Nor does it conflict that Matthew 28 says that at the end of the Sabbath, that is, literally, in the evening of the Sabbath, the women came to the tomb, while Mark 16 says they came very early in the morning. For by the Romans' reckoning, which counted the natural day from sunrise, it was dawn. By the Hebrews' manner, the evening of the Sabbath was the start of the following day, which was dawning; therefore Matthew says, "when it began to dawn on the first day of the week." ## NINTH RULE.

units.la: NONA REGULA.

Phrases etiam considerandæ sunt, & quo sensu aliquod vocabulum usurpetur: Eadem enim vox diversis locis posita, diverso modò sæ-pe intelligenda: ut Iudicij vox, quæ aliquando condemnationem, aliquando iustam admini-strationem significat. Sic conciliantur illa duo loca Ioh. 3. ver. 17. Non enim misit Deus fi-lium suum in mundum, ut damnet (ἵνα κρίνῃ[?]) mun[?]undum,&c. Et Ioh. 9. v. 39. Ad iudicium (εἰς κρίμα) exercendum ego in hunc mundum veni. Sic & illud Ioh. 4 Christus dicitur baptizasse, & non baptizasse; Baptizasse quatenus autor baptismi & per ministerium Apostolorum baptizauit: Non baptizasse. i. sua persona signum non administrasse.
units.tr: Phrases too must be considered, and in what sense a word is used. The same word, placed in different passages, is often to be understood in different ways: for example, the word judgment, which sometimes means condemnation and sometimes the just administration of justice. In this way those two passages, John 3:17, "For God did not send his Son into the world to condemn [ἵνα κρίνῃ] the world," and John 9:39, "I came into this world for judgment [εἰς κρίμα]," are reconciled. So too John 4 says that Christ baptized and that he did not baptize: he baptized inasmuch as he is the author of baptism and baptized through the ministry of the apostles; he did not baptize, that is, he did not administer the sign in his own person. ## TENTH RULE.

units.la: DECIMA REGULA.

Obseruandum est Christum partim proprie, partim figuratè, & saepe in eodem sermone locutum esse. Augustinus 2. lib. de consensu E-vangelistarum, cap. 30. Quisquis putat Dominum in uno sermone non potuisse quaedam figuratè, quaedam proprie ponere, certa eius dicta inspiciat, & videbit quàm hoc temere & in crudite arbitretur. Et rem, (inquit idem) vtilissimam discimus, si statuimus, in verbis semper voluntatem & intentionem loquentis respiciendum, cui verba seruire debent. Exempli gratia: Quod Matth: 19. de castratione propter regnum coelorum, & aliquid de amputatione manuum scribit, non de facto externo, sed quomodo animus comparatus esse debeat, est intelligendum. Item quando Christus Matthaei 10. cap. noluit aurum, argentum, virgam, peram à discipulis portari; non fuit perpetuum praeceptum, sed admonitio potius consolatoria, ipsis nihil defuturum; Item operarium suo dignum esse alimento. Sic Ioh. 15. quando Christus se vitem veram appellat, postea, v. 4. sine tropo id explicat: Item videre est in verbis S. coenae: hoc facite in mei recordationem.
units.tr: It must be observed that Christ spoke partly literally and partly figuratively, and often within the same discourse. Augustine, De consensu Evangelistarum, bk. 2, ch. 30: "Whoever thinks that the Lord could not in one discourse use some things figuratively and some literally, let him examine certain of his sayings, and he will see how rashly and unlearnedly he judges. (So he says.) We learn a most useful principle, if we establish that in words one must always look to the will and intention of the speaker, to which the words ought to be subordinate." For example, what Matthew 19 writes about making oneself eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven, and something about cutting off hands, is to be understood not of an outward act but of how the mind ought to be disposed. Likewise, when Christ in Matthew 10 would not have his disciples carry gold, silver, a staff, or a bag, this was not a perpetual precept but rather a consoling admonition that they would lack nothing; and likewise that the worker is worthy of his food. So in John 15, when Christ calls himself the true vine, he afterwards, in verse 4, explains this without a figure. The same can be seen in the words of the Lord's Supper: "Do this in remembrance of me."

units.la: QVO ORDINE SCRIPSERINT quatuor Euangelistæ.
units.tr: In what order the four Evangelists wrote

units.la: Recte monet Irenæus lib. 3. aduersus hæreses,cap. 1. Nos Euangelium & dispensationem salutis accepisse non ab hominibus ignotis,sed ab iis qui primò annunciarunt,deinde per Dei voluntatem in scripturis nobis tradiderunt, nec fas esse dicere, vt quidam hæritici ausi sunt,nos esse emendatores Apostolorum, & eos docuisse antequam perfectam haberent cognitionem: Illi enim post acceptum Spiritum sanctum missi sunt in omnes fines terræ,& licet humana eloquentia & potentia non essent instructi, ( vt fatetur Paulus 1. Cor 2. ) Dei tamen virtus mirabiliter se in eis exeruit, vt radij solaris instar (inquit Eusebius lib. 2. hist.) doctrina Euangelij,vniuersum orbem compleuit.
units.tr: Irenaeus rightly admonishes in book 3 against heresies, chapter 1: "We have received the Gospel and the dispensation of salvation not from unknown men, but from those who first announced it and then, by the will of God, handed it down to us in the Scriptures; nor is it lawful to say, as some heretics have dared to say, that we are the correctors of the Apostles, and that they taught before they had perfect knowledge. For those men, after receiving the Holy Spirit, were sent into all the ends of the earth; and although they were not furnished with human eloquence or power (as Paul confesses, 1 Cor. 2), the power of God was wonderfully displayed in them, so that the doctrine of the Gospel, like the rays of the sun (as Eusebius says, book 2 of the History), filled the whole world."

units.la: Recepta est autem sententia(idque iuxta Irenæi testimonium loco citato, & Eusebium lib. 1. historiæ, & Augustinum lib. 1. de consensu Euangelistarum ) Matthæum primum Euangelij historiam Hebraeis in ipsorum lingua obtulisse, idque iuxta supputationem Eusebij anno .8. post ascensum Christi. Postea Marcum quæ à Petro audierat conscripsisse, vt vult Irenæus. Tertius in ordine Lucas ponitur S. Pauli sectatur. S. Iohannem postremò Epehesi scripsisse historiam Euangelicam contra glisccentes hæreses, apud omnes est extra controuersiam. Sunt qui existimant Lucam ante Matthæum & Marcum scripsisse Historiam Euangelicam; proinde quod eius seriem attinet, Lucam proregula ponendum , ad cuius historiae ductum reliqui reuocandi.Nituntur vero illi hac coniectura: Si Matthaeus ante Lucam scripsisset,tunc Lucas in Exordio libri sui honorifica Matthaei mentionem facere debuisset, cum videatur potius eleuare autoritatem eorum, qui ante ipsum Euangelicam historiam contexere sunt conati. Resp. 1. S. Lucas eos solummodo perstringit, qui conabantur,sed non perfecerant: 2. qui de rebus non certo compertis scribere nitebantur: 3. Vero consentaneum est, Euangelicae scriptores historiae,se inuicem commendare aut laudare non voluisse, ne suspectum foret eorum praeconium. Hinc S. Matthaeum primum scripsisse probabile est.Interea & hoc concedo,eos qui posteriores scripserunt, vt Lucas & Iohannes, in annorum & festorum annotatione fuisse accuratiores.
units.tr: The opinion, moreover, has been received (and this according to the testimony of Irenaeus in the place cited, and of Eusebius in book 1 of the History, and of Augustine in book 1 of On the Harmony of the Evangelists), that Matthew first offered the history of the Gospel to the Hebrews in their own language, and this, according to Eusebius's reckoning, in the eighth year after the ascension of Christ. Afterwards Mark wrote down what he had heard from Peter, as Irenaeus holds. Luke is placed third in order, as the follower of St. Paul. That St. John wrote the Gospel history last, at Ephesus, against the heresies that were growing up, is beyond all controversy among everyone. There are some who think that Luke wrote the Gospel history before Matthew and Mark; therefore, as far as the order is concerned, Luke should be placed first as the rule, by whose course of history the others are to be brought back. But they rest on this conjecture: if Matthew had written before Luke, then Luke ought to have made honourable mention of Matthew in the preface of his book, since it would seem rather to lessen the authority of those who had tried to compose the Gospel history before him. Answer: (1) St. Luke only glances at those who attempted but did not accomplish it; (2) at those who strove to write about matters not known for certain; (3) indeed it is consistent that the writers of the Gospel history did not wish to commend or praise one another, lest their testimony be regarded with suspicion. Hence it is probable that St. Matthew wrote first. Meanwhile I also grant this, that those who wrote later, such as Luke and John, were more accurate in noting the years and festivals.

units.la: ANALYSIS EVANGELII secundum Matthaeum.
units.tr: ANALYSIS OF THE GOSPEL according to Matthew.

units.la: INSCRIPTIO libri est: εὐαγγέλιον κατὰ[?] Ματ-θαῖον : i. Euangelium secundum Matthaeum. De prima huius tituli voce, Euangelio nimirum iam diximus: de qua tamen & illud libet adiicere, diligenter notandum esse quod Paulus ad Gal. 1. v. 8. dicit: Si nos, aut Angelus e coelo euangelizet vobis praetes ID[?] quod vobis euangelizauimus, anathema esto, non dicit, praeter ea, ne quis existimet totidem Euangelia esse, quot sunt Euangelicae historiae scriptores.Licet igitur Euangelium dicatur secundum Matthaeū, secundum Marcum, &c. vnum tamen est Euan-gelium, siue vna & eadem doctrina de Christo; & est proprie Euangelium Christi.Phil.1. quod ab effectu vocatur Euangelium salutis nostrae, Ephes. 1. Sed potest dici Euangelium Matthaei, vel Pauli, (inquit Augustinus lib. 3. contra lite-ras P.) propter munus dispensationis: aeternum vero ratione diuini consilij dici potest, Apocal. cap. 14.
units.tr: The title of the book is: εὐαγγέλιον κατὰ Ματθαῖον [Euangelion kata Matthaion], that is, The Gospel according to Matthew. We have already spoken of the first word of this title, "Gospel." It is worth adding here that one must carefully note what Paul says in Gal. 1.8: "If we, or an angel from heaven, preach to you anything beside that which we have preached to you, let him be accursed." He does not say "beside these," lest anyone think there are as many Gospels as there are writers of gospel history. Therefore, although it is called "according to Matthew," "according to Mark," and so on, there is one Gospel, that is, one and the same doctrine about Christ, and it is properly the Gospel of Christ (Phil. 1), which from its effect is called the Gospel of our salvation (Eph. 1). Yet it can be called the Gospel of Matthew or of Paul (as Augustine says in book 3 against the letters of Petilianus) by reason of the office of dispensing it; but it can be called eternal by reason of the divine counsel (Apoc. 14).

units.la: Autor igitur Euangelij secundum Matthaeū est Spiritus S. quo inspirante & dictante illud à Matthaeo scriptum nobisque quasi Epistola Dei de coelo missum est, vt Augustinus libro 1. de consensu Euangelistarum cap. vltimo testa-tur,dum dicit , Christum scripsisse ea omnia, quæ Apostoli & Euangelistæ: quia Apostoli manus fuerunt tantum : Christus vero caput: manus vero nihil scribunt nisi cogitante & di-ctante capite, ergo eodem in precio habendi ac si Christus propria manu scripsisset.
units.tr: The author of the Gospel according to Matthew, therefore, is the Holy Spirit, by whose inspiration and dictation it was written by Matthew and sent to us as a letter of God from heaven. Augustine bears witness to this in the last chapter of book 1 of On the Harmony of the Evangelists, where he says that Christ wrote all those things which the Apostles and Evangelists wrote, because the Apostles were only the hands, but Christ the head; and the hands write nothing except while the head thinks and dictates. Therefore it is to be held in the same esteem as if Christ had written it with his own hand.

units.la: Porro qui artiū præcepta sequūtur in explicā-dis authoribus,tria fermè in generali seu primaria analysi obseruant.Primum enim quis scribat expendunt, deinde quibus scribat, tertio etiam quid. De primo,hoc est de Matthaeo,qui dictante Spiritu S. hunc librum scripsit,vide Prolegomaena B. Aretij in Matthaeū, quis scilicet fuerit, & qualis ante conuersionē,de vita post conuersionem,hoc est vbi docuerit,quos, quid, scripta etiam, miracula & genus mortis. Item de secundo quibus scribat : Iudaeis nimirum Hebraicè scripsit suum Euangelium , iam ad Gentes abi-turus. Quæ quidem sic accipienda sunt, vt etiam ad totam postoritatem spectent credentium in Christum. Quare & nobis scripta putemus ut his fidem confirmemus & alamus, in quos fines sæculorum inciderunt.
units.tr: Moreover, those who follow the precepts of the arts in explaining authors observe roughly three things in a general or primary analysis. First they consider who writes; then to whom he writes; and third what he writes. Concerning the first, that is, Matthew, who wrote this book under the dictation of the Holy Spirit, see the Prolegomena of B. Aretius on Matthew: who he was, and what kind of man he was before his conversion; his life after conversion, that is, where and to whom he taught and what he taught; also his writings, his miracles, and the manner of his death. Likewise, concerning the second, to whom he writes: he wrote his Gospel in Hebrew for the Jews, since he was about to go on to the Gentiles. These things are to be understood in such a way that they also concern the whole posterity of those who believe in Christ. Hence we may think they were written for us too, so that we may confirm and nourish our faith in them, we upon whom the ends of the ages have come.

units.la: De tertio, hoc est quid scribat, licèt id iam sit expilcatum in genere, ratio tamen propositi nostri postulat, ut argumentum explicetur operis speciatim & per partes. Dicemus igitur de occasione scripti, de argumento, idea orationis, propositione & partibus historiæ præsentis.
units.tr: Concerning the third, that is, what he writes: although this has already been explained in general, the plan of our undertaking requires that the subject of the work be explained in particular and part by part. We shall therefore speak of the occasion of the writing, of the subject matter, of the design of the discourse, of the proposition, and of the parts of the present history.

units.la: Occasio scripti. Sunt quædam communia omnibus sacris scriptoribus, quæ scribendi dedere occasionem, quædam singulis propria: nam quod rerum gestarum fidem indubitatâ posteris voluerunt relinquere: quòd veram invocationem, rationem salutis, iustificationis, & meriti Christi authoritatem conservare voluerunt, non solùm apud homines sui sæculi, sed etiam apud posteritatem omnem; communia omnibus fuerunt in N. Testamento. Cæterùm Matthæo priuata etiâ fuit scribendi ratio, nimirum ut Judæi certam haberent fidei, & religionis Christianæ historiam: abituro ipso ad gentes, voluit apud suam gentem Messiæ iam præstiti historiam extare; de vita, moribus, miraculis, morte, resurrectione, reditu ad cælos, datâque potestate docendi discipulis.
units.tr: The occasion of the writing. Some causes that gave occasion for writing were common to all the sacred writers, and some were peculiar to individuals. Common to all in the New Testament was the wish to leave to posterity an indubitable faith in the events that happened; the wish to preserve the true invocation, the reason of salvation, justification, and the authority of Christ's merit, not only among the men of their own age but also among all posterity. Matthew, however, had a private reason for writing as well, namely, that the Jews should have a certain history of the Christian faith and religion. Since he was about to depart to the Gentiles, he wished there to exist among his own nation a history of the Messiah now already given: of his life, manners, miracles, death, resurrection, return to the heavens, and of the power of teaching given to the disciples.

units.la: Argumentum: Humanitatis historiam præci- puè persequitur; quare genus ab Abrahamo ad Josephum putatitium patrem deducit: hinc nativitatem, & primum in hoc mundo [illegible, ~1 letter][?]atum[?] salvatoris describit, vitam privatam, inde publicam, ut ascitis discipulis cœperit docere turbâ, postea etiam authoritatem docendi dederit dis-cipulis, & quo fructu illa omnia successerint. Postea conuersus ad historiam passionis, repe-tit omnia illa, quæ Christus ab interiori Gali-læa Ierosolymam ascendendo & docuerit & fecerit, diuersis oblatis occasionibus. In histo-riam Passionis perductus, diligenter circunstan-tias omnes describit, causas adiuuantes & orga-nicas, mortem, & quæ mortem sunt consecuta, vt est resurrectio & apparitiones diuersas, & de-nique eius ad cælos ascensum.
units.tr: Subject matter: He pursues chiefly the history of the humanity of Christ. Therefore he traces the lineage from Abraham to Joseph, the supposed father. Hence he describes the birth and first [...] of the Saviour in this world, his private life, then his public life: how, once disciples had been taken on, he began to teach the crowd, and afterwards gave the disciples the authority to teach, and with what fruit all those things turned out. Then, turning to the history of the passion, he repeats all those things which Christ taught and did as he went up from inner Galilee to Jerusalem, on the various occasions that offered themselves. Brought to the history of the passion, he describes carefully all the circumstances, both the contributing and the principal causes, the death and what followed death, such as the resurrection and the various appearances, and finally his ascent to heaven.

units.la: Idea orationis in his à plerisque censetur hu-milis: sed cum in idea constituenda duo sint cri-teria, ex quibus nobis argumentum est sumen-dum, res scilicet & phrasis; res extra controuer-siam sublimes sunt, diuinæ & augustæ. Quid e-nim maius Filio Dei?quid augustius vita & mi-raculis eius? quid diuinius doctrina eius? quid admirabilius morte, resurrectione, ascensuque ad cœlos? hæ res tantæ fide historica bona & integra, vt gestæ erant, stylo explicandæ erant. Deinde phrasis genus dicendi Hebræum resi-pit, in qua lingua suam habet maiestatem, pudi-cum ornatum & matronalem, grauitate & ma-iestate plenum. Idea igitur grauis hic agnosca-tur.
units.tr: The style of the work is considered by most to be humble. But since two criteria must be used in determining the style, from which we must take our argument, namely the matter and the phrasing, the matters are beyond controversy sublime, divine, and august. For what is greater than the Son of God? What more august than his life and miracles? What more divine than his teaching? What more admirable than his death, resurrection, and ascent to heaven? Such great matters had to be set forth in a style that was historically faithful, sound and whole, as they actually happened. Then the phrasing has a Hebrew character in its manner of speaking; in that language it has its own majesty, a modest and matronly ornament, full of gravity and dignity. The style here is therefore to be recognized as grave.

units.la: Propositio est, Messiæ iam tandem exhibiti vitam in terris actam describere: hoc est, perso-nam, doctrinam, miracula, veros in eo humanæ naturæ affectus sine peccati labe, mortem, resur-rectionem, in cœlos ascensum, & authoritatem docendi Apostolis traditam, vt Ecclesia in his terris vsque ad finem mundi ad vitam æternam per ministerium illud calligatur.
units.tr: The proposition is to describe the life on earth of the Messiah now at last revealed: that is, his person, his teaching, his miracles, the true human affections in him without any stain of sin, his death, resurrection, ascent into heaven, and the authority of teaching handed down to the Apostles, so that the Church on this earth, until the end of the world, may be gathered to eternal life through that ministry.

units.la: Hieronymus Euangelistas ab exordiis distinguit. Matthæum similem dicit esse homini, quòd ab humanitate Christi orditur: Marcum leoni, quòd à prædicatione Iohanuis, quæ fuit quasi tugitus leonis: Lucam boui, quòd à Zacharia sacerdote sacri ficante: Iohannem aquilæ, quòd quasi altè volans à Deitate Christi incipit.
units.tr: Jerome distinguishes the Evangelists by their beginnings. He says Matthew is like a man, because he begins from the humanity of Christ; Mark like a lion, because he begins from the preaching of John, which was like the roar of a lion; Luke like an ox, because he begins from Zechariah the priest offering sacrifice; John like an eagle, because, as if flying high, he begins from the Deity of Christ.

units.la: DISTRIBVTIO SEV PARTES.
units.tr: DISTRIBUTION, OR DIVISION INTO PARTS.

units.la: PARTES Euangelij secundum Matthæum duæ sunt: Prima de Christi persona & vita priuata. Secunda de officio & vita publica eius.
units.tr: The parts of the Gospel according to Matthew are two: the first concerns the person and private life of Christ; the second concerns his office and public life.

units.la: PRIMA PARS.
units.tr: THE FIRST PART.

units.la: Prima pars ab initio capitis primi, vsque ad ver. 12. quarti capitis extensa de persona & vita priuata Christi, continet eius. 1. Natales. cap. 1. 11. Educationem, cap. 2 .111. Præpara-tionem ad officium,cap. 3. & parte. 4. cap.
units.tr: The first part, extending from the beginning of chapter 1 to verse 12 of chapter 4, concerns the person and private life of Christ. It contains: (1) his birth, chap. 1; (2) his upbringing, chap. 2; (3) his preparation for the office, chap. 3 and the first part of chap. 4.

units.la: Capitis primi de ortu seu natalibus Christi membra duo sunt: in primo recensentur illius maiores in Genealogia Christi secundum carnem: in secundo modus conceptionis & natiuitatis describitur. v. 18.
units.tr: The members of chapter 1, concerning the origin or birth of Christ, are two. In the first, his ancestors are listed in the genealogy of Christ according to the flesh; in the second, the manner of his conception and birth is described, v. 18.

units.la: Secundi capitis partes sunt tres,iuxta triplicem Christi educationem, nimirum Bethlehemiticam, Ægyptiacam, & Nazarethanam.
units.tr: The parts of chapter 2 are three, corresponding to the threefold upbringing of Christ, namely at Bethlehem, in Egypt, and at Nazareth.

units.la: I. Christus natus in Bethlehem, à magis orientalibus gentium primitiis, duce stella, vt Rex qua-vitur[?],inuenitur,salutatur atque honoratur. II. Monitu Dei, ad cauendas Herodis insidias, transfer-mur in Ægyptum. v. 1ı. 14. 15. his attexitur narratio cædis infantum Bethlehemiticorum, quæ iis propter Christum accidit. ver. 16. 17. 18. III. Dei monitu Christus rursum ex Ægypto, in terra Israël, & nominatim Nazaretham transfertur. v. 19. vsque ad finem capitis.
units.tr: I. Christ, born in Bethlehem, is sought as king by the eastern magi, the first-fruits of the Gentiles, guided by a star; he is found, greeted and honoured. II. At God's warning, to avoid Herod's plots, Christ is carried into Egypt, v. 13, 14, 15; to this is joined the account of the slaughter of the infants of Bethlehem, which befell them on Christ's account, v. 16, 17, 18. III. By God's warning Christ is again brought from Egypt into the land of Israel, and specifically to Nazareth, v. 19 to the end of the chapter.

units.la: De infantia igitur Christi & pueritia hactenus.
units.tr: So much, then, concerning Christ's infancy and boyhood.

units.la: Tertium membrum in vita Christi priuata est eius ad officium redemtorium peragendum Præparatio. Hic primo narratur quomodo auditores Christo præparati sint per Iohannem Baptistam : cap.3. vsque ad ver.13. Deinde quomodo præparatus & ad officium sit inauguratus ipse Christus: idque partim per solennem seu publicam consecrationem, in altera huius capitis parte : partim per priuatam & arcanam tentationem, in prima parte capitis quarti,
units.tr: The third member of Christ's private life is his preparation for carrying out the redemptive office. Here it is first narrated how the hearers were prepared for Christ through John the Baptist, chap. 3 to v. 13. Then how Christ himself was prepared and inaugurated into the office: partly through the solemn or public consecration, in the latter part of this chapter; partly through the private and secret temptation, in the first part of chapter 4.

units.la: Capitis igitur tertiū duo sunt membra. I. De prædicatione Iohannis Baptistæ II. De Baptizatione Christi: quæ peractâ, consecratus fuit voce patris & infessione Spiritus sancti ad muneris sui functionem.
units.tr: The third chapter therefore has two members. I. The preaching of John the Baptist. II. The baptism of Christ, which having been done, he was consecrated by the voice of the Father and the descent of the Holy Spirit for the performance of his office.

units.la: Capitis quarti parte prima, ad uersum vsque 12. habetur præparatio Christi per tentationem à Diabolo: vbi specimen præbuit in nobili illa palæstra, quid facturus aliquando hic Christus esset, quantam cladem regno diaboli allaturus.
units.tr: The first part of chapter 4, up to verse 12, contains Christ's preparation through temptation by the Devil. There he gave a sample, in that noble contest, of what this Christ would one day do and how great a defeat he would bring upon the kingdom of the devil.

units.la: Et hæc quidem initia erant: sed rudimenta maiorum. Ex priuata iam vita descendit Christus in cætus hominum, doctoris munere functurus.
units.tr: These were indeed beginnings, but the rudiments of greater things. From his private life Christ now came down into gatherings of men, about to discharge the office of teacher.

units.la: DE SECVNDA PARTE SECVNDA PARTE docetur quomodo do Chri-
units.tr: CONCERNING THE SECOND PART. The second part teaches how Christ

units.la: stus officio suo sit perfunctus.
units.tr: performed his office.

units.la: Idque tum in statu Humiliationis, in quo Pro-phetico & Sacerdotali munere functus est: tum in Exaltationis statu, in quo Regium munus in-choavit.
units.tr: This is done both in the state of humiliation, in which he discharged the prophetic and priestly office, and in the state of exaltation, in which he began the kingly office.

units.la: DE PROPHETICO CHRIsti officio.
units.tr: CONCERNING THE PROPHETIC OFFICE OF CHRIST.

units.la: Quicquid de munere Christi Prophetico tradidere Evangelici scriptores, ad duo summa capita revocat, & vocabulis διδάσκειν, ποιεῖν[?] i. docere & facere, complectitur S. Lucas Act. 1. v. 1. quorum utrumque copiosè & mixtim persequitur Matthæus à v. 12. capitis quarti, usque ad finem 25. capitis.
units.tr: Whatever the evangelists have handed down concerning the prophetic office of Christ, Luke reduces to two chief heads and embraces in the words "to teach" and "to do" [διδάσκειν, ποιεῖν], Acts 1:1. Matthew pursues both of these fully and intermingled, from chap. 4 v. 12 to the end of chap. 25.

units.la: Nos autem docendi & memorandi causa di-cta & gesta Christi bipartitò distinguemus.
units.tr: We, however, for the sake of teaching and remembering, will divide the sayings and deeds of Christ into two parts.

units.la: 1. In ea quæ dixit fecitque ante postremam eius Hierosolymam perfectionem à capitis quarti v. 12. usque ad cap. 16. versum 21.
units.tr: 1. Those things he said and did before his last journey to Jerusalem, from chap. 4 v. 12 to chap. 16 v. 21.

units.la: II. In ea quæ docuit & operatus est in postrema illa Hierosolymam ad paschatis festum profectione, inde usque ad initium capitis 26.
units.tr: II. Those things he taught and did on that final journey to Jerusalem for the feast of the Passover, from there to the beginning of chap. 26.

units.la: Prioris membri subdivisio hæc est:
units.tr: The subdivision of the former member is this:

units.la: Christus officio prædicandi & miracula edendi functus est primò Solus, à capite quarto usque ad finem noni capitis: Deinde collegis seu sociis adscitis, abinitio capitis decimi, usque ad cap. 16. v. 21.
units.tr: Christ discharged the office of preaching and working miracles first alone, from the beginning of chap. 4 to the end of chap. 9; then, with companions or colleagues taken on, from the beginning of chap. 10 to chap. 16 v. 21.

units.la: EX HIS TALIS DISPOSITIO generalis Euangelij secundum Matthæum emergit.
units.tr: FROM THESE THINGS A GENERAL OUTLINE OF THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MATTHEW EMERGES.

units.la: S. Matthæus scr. de Christo [?] Persona & vita priuata. Hic considerari debent Christi natales, cap. 1. Educatio, cap. 2. præparatio ad officiū cap. 3. 4. officio triplici quo perfunctus est in munu. [?] Humiliationis officium Propheticum, quo functus est docendo & operando tum Ante postremam eius Hierosolymā profectionē idque vel Solus Hic doctrina & miracula cum 1. Breuiter perstringitur, reliquo cap. 4. 2. Copiosius enarratur, usque ad cap. 10. Sociis adscitis cap. 10-16. In postrema illa profectione Christi ad vltimum pascha Hierosol: in quo incidit mors Christi. cap. 16-25. Sacerdotale vbi pe passione & mort{c} Christi: cap. 26. & 27. Exaltationis officium Regium. De resurrectione & in cœlum ascensione cap. vltimo.
units.tr: St Matthew writes of (1) the person and private life of Christ. Here one must consider Christ's birth, chap. 1; his upbringing, chap. 2; his preparation for the office, chap. 3–4. (2) The threefold office he discharged in his ministry. In the state of humiliation, the prophetic office, which he discharged by teaching and working, both before his last journey to Jerusalem, either alone, where his teaching and miracles are briefly touched on in the rest of chap. 4, or more fully narrated up to chap. 10; then with companions taken on, chap. 10–16; and on that final journey to the last Passover at Jerusalem, in which the death of Christ fell, chap. 16–25. The priestly office, where his passion and death are set out: chap. 26 and 27. The kingly office of exaltation: concerning his resurrection and ascension into heaven, in the last chapter.

units.la: DE EXECVTIONE PROPHETICI muneris Christi in dictis & factis ante vltimam eius Hierosol: profectionem.
units.tr: ON THE EXECUTION OF CHRIST'S PROPHETIC OFFICE IN WORD AND DEED BEFORE HIS LAST JOURNEY TO JERUSALEM.

units.la: POSTEAQUAM Matthæus primo breuiter perstrinxit in secunda parte capitis quarti, doctrinam & miracula Christi, quod nimirum Iohanne praecursore ipsius jam incarcerato, munus suum publice administrare inceperit in Galilæa, vocando primum quatuor discipulos, Petrũ, Andream, Iacobum & Iohannem: usque ad v. 21: Deinde caeptam illam administrationem continuando, & miraculis confirmando, usque ad finem capitis quarti: Deinceps doctrinae eius plenos sermones, & miraculorum narrationes integras pertexit. Christus igitur officio prophetico perfunctus est Solus.
units.tr: AFTER Matthew first briefly set out, in the second part of the fourth chapter, the teaching and miracles of Christ: namely that, with John the forerunner already imprisoned, he began to exercise his office publicly in Galilee, first calling four disciples, Peter, Andrew, James and John, up to v. 21; then continuing and confirming by miracles the work he had begun, up to the end of the fourth chapter; after that he goes on to give full discourses of his teaching and complete accounts of his miracles. Christ therefore discharged the prophetic office alone.

units.la: 1. Docendo: Sermo Chirsti in monte habitus, de vera pietate hominis Christiani, cap. 5. 6. 7. Edendo miracula quibus doctrinam suam confir-mauit, in urbe Caper-naitica, idque. Ante traiectum lacum Geneza-reth, cap. 8. Post reditum per eundem lacum &[?] finibus Geneza-reth, cap. 9.
units.tr: 1. By teaching: the sermon Christ delivered on the mount concerning the true piety of a Christian, ch. 5, 6, 7. By performing miracles by which he confirmed his teaching, in the city of Capernaum, and that before crossing the lake of Gennesaret, ch. 8. After his return across the same lake and into the region of Gennesaret, ch. 9.

units.la: In prolixa illa concione quam Christus coram Discipulis ad populum habuit in monte, multa & varia agit. Atque ea quidem parte quæ continetur in quinto capite, agit ista quatuor. 1. Indicat causas procreantes beatitudinis. 11. Discipulos hortatur ad studium bonorum operum. v. 13. 111. Præfatur in expositione legis, v. 17. 1v. Exponit aliquot legis præcepta: v. 21. videlicet sextum usque ad v. 27. deinde septimum, usque ad v. 33. tum tertium, usque ad v. 38. postea legem de diligendo proximo, usque ad finem capitis.
units.tr: In that lengthy address which Christ gave to the people on the mount, before his disciples, he deals with many and varied matters. In the part contained in the fifth chapter, he deals with these four things. 1. He states the causes that produce blessedness. 2. He exhorts the disciples to zeal for good works, v. 13. 3. He introduces his exposition of the law, v. 17. 4. He expounds several precepts of the law: v. 21, namely the sixth, up to v. 27; then the seventh, up to v. 33; then the third, up to v. 38; afterwards the law about loving one's neighbour, to the end of the chapter.

units.la: Vindicata Lege Dei à variis corruptelis Scribarum & Pharisæorum, transit Christus ad va-rias admonitiones ad veram[?] pietatem pertinentes : & in capite sexto primum monet de cauendis vitiis Pharisaorum in faciendis rebus quibusdam per se bonis : vt 1 in danda Elemosyna, vsque ad v. 5. 11 in modo precandi, vsque ad verf: 16.111 in modo ieiunandi, vsque ad v. 19. Deinde vero de cauendis affectibus quibusdam per se malis ac vitiosis, vt 1. studio opum & auaritia, vsque ad v.24. 11 De cauenda sollicitudine victus atque amictus, ad finem capitis.
units.tr: Having vindicated God's law from the various corruptions of the scribes and Pharisees, Christ passes to various admonitions pertaining to true piety. And in chapter six he first warns against the faults of the Pharisees in doing certain things that are good in themselves: (1) in giving alms, up to v. 5; (2) in the manner of praying, up to v. 16; (3) in the manner of fasting, up to v. 19. Then, indeed, concerning the avoidance of certain affections that are evil and vicious in themselves: (1) the zeal for wealth and avarice, up to v. 24; (2) concerning the avoidance of anxiety about food and clothing, to the end of the chapter.

units.la: Capite septimo varias alias admonitiones ad iustitiam & prudentiam Christianam pertinentes proponit: 1. De cauendis peruersis reprehensionibus, & de omittendis sanctis monitis apud contemptores: vsque ad v. 7. 11. De petendis a Deo bonis necessariis, & de regula iustitia generali, vsque ad v. 13. 111. cauendis exemplis mundi, (v. 13. & 14.) & Pseudoprophetis, vsque ad v. 21. 1111. De studio pietatis cum professione nominis Christiani coniungendo, & de studio praestandi hos sermones vsque ad v. 28. Sub finem duobus versibus vltimis narrat Euangelista illius sermonis effectum in turba quae illum audierat.
units.tr: In chapter seven he sets out various other admonitions pertaining to Christian righteousness and prudence: 1. concerning the avoidance of perverse censures, and concerning not offering holy admonitions to scorners, up to v. 7; 2. concerning asking God for the goods we need, and concerning the general rule of righteousness, up to v. 13; 3. concerning avoiding the examples of the world (v. 13 and 14) and false prophets, up to v. 21; 4. concerning joining zeal for piety with the profession of the Christian name, and concerning zeal for practising these sermons, up to v. 28. At the end, in the last two verses, the evangelist relates the effect of that sermon on the crowd that had heard it.

units.la: Hactenus Enangelista per tria capita narrauit doctrinam Christi,sequentibus duobus narrat varia illius miracula,quibus doctrinam suam confirmauit.
units.tr: Thus far the evangelist has related Christ's teaching over three chapters; in the following two he relates various miracles by which he confirmed that teaching.

units.la: Capite octauo narrat miracula quinque, videl: 1. sanationem leprosi, vsque ad verf: 5. 11. sanationem paralytici, vsque ad v.14. 111. Sanationem socrus Petri, vsque ad v. 18. Hic inseritur narratio de Scriba quodam (Christum sequi volente reiecto, & de discipulo quodam sine mora sequi iusso: vsque ad verf: 23. 1111. Miraculum seda-ta temta tempestatis in mari vsque ad v. 28. v. Miracu-lum eiectorum daemoniorum.
units.tr: In chapter eight he relates five miracles, namely: 1. the healing of the leper, up to v. 5; 2. the healing of the paralytic, up to v. 14; 3. the healing of Peter's mother-in-law, up to v. 18. Here is inserted the account of a certain scribe, who was rebuffed when he wished to follow Christ, and of a certain disciple who was told to follow without delay, up to v. 23; 4. the miracle of the calming of the storm at sea, up to v. 28; 5. the miracle of the expelled demons.

units.la: Capite nono similiter quinque miracula narrantur, cum nonnullis aliis. 1. Miraculum in sanatione paralytici: vsque ad v. 9. Inde interiicitur vocatio Matthaei in numerum discipulorum Christi: & refutatio discipulorum Iohannis in quæstione de ieiunio, vsque ad v. 18. 11. Miraculum sanatæ hæmorrhoissæ: vsque ad v. 23. 111. Excitatio puellæ mortuæ, vsque ad v. 27. 1 v. Sanatio duorum cæcorum, vsque ad vers. 32. v. Eiectio dæmonij muti, vsque ad v. 35. Hinc conclusionis loco additur narratio generalis de prædicatione & miraculis Christi, deque affectu eius erga turbam.
units.tr: In chapter nine likewise five miracles are related, along with some other matters. 1. The miracle of the healing of the paralytic, up to v. 9. Inserted here are the calling of Matthew into the number of Christ's disciples, and the refutation of John's disciples in the question about fasting, up to v. 18. 2. The miracle of the woman with the issue of blood healed, up to v. 23. 3. The raising of the dead girl, up to v. 27. 4. The healing of two blind men, up to v. 32. 5. The expelling of a dumb demon, up to v. 35. Here, by way of conclusion, is added a general account of Christ's preaching and miracles, and of his feeling towards the crowd.

units.la: Ad Maiora progreditur Historia. Nam hactenus Christus solus docuit tum discipulos priuatim, tum Scribas etiam & alios publicè: so-lus etiam doctrinam veram confirmauit mira-culis. Nunc Filius Dei adhibet huic negotio plures symmystas, nempe 12. Apostolos, quos binos & binos mittit ad docendum, & edenda miracula. Ac de ipsorum doctrina parcius agit. Christi doctoris enim cursum sibi proposuit, tantum quod missi sint ad certum ministerium narrrat, & quod vtiliter docuerint, ac magna cum felicitate, sine omni etiam rerum penuria, paucis infra perstringit.
units.tr: The history now proceeds to greater matters. For hitherto Christ alone taught, both the disciples in private and the scribes and others in public; he alone also confirmed his true doctrine by miracles. Now the Son of God brings in several fellow-workers for this business, namely the twelve apostles, whom he sends out two by two to teach and to perform miracles. And he deals more sparingly with their teaching. For he has set before himself the course of Christ's teaching as the pattern; he merely relates that they were sent on a definite ministry and that they taught profitably and with great success, without any lack of necessities, and these things he briefly touches on below.

units.la: Capite igitur decimo narrat, primum qua potestate ac virtute Christus instruxerit Apostolos, quorum nomina recenset. Deinde quibus mandatis eos instruxerit: v. 5. & seqq: Tum docet quomodo se in periculis variis, & erga hostes gerere debeant. v. 16. Quo quidem loco delabitur vltra ptæsens[?] tempus, quippe loquens de periculis quæ demum post ipsius in cœlos ascensionem eis erant eventura: nam præsens hæc legatio periculorum expers & multa cum commoditate coniuncta fuit, vt pater ex Luc. 22. v. 35. Postremo perget eos hortari ad constantiam, in confitendo Evangelio, & contra dehortatur ab eiusdem abnegatione repetita consolatione contra odia & contemptum mundi. à v. 32. vsque ad finem capitis I.
units.tr: In chapter ten, then, he relates first with what power and virtue Christ equipped the apostles, whose names he recounts. Then with what instructions he equipped them, v. 5 and following. Then he teaches how they ought to conduct themselves in various dangers and towards their enemies, v. 16. In this passage he indeed slips beyond the present time, since he speaks of dangers that were to befall them only after his ascension into heaven; for this present mission was free of danger and attended by much convenience, as appears from Luke 22, v. 35. Lastly he goes on to exhort them to steadfastness in confessing the Gospel, and on the contrary dissuades them from denying it, with a repeated consolation against hatred and the world's contempt, from v. 32 to the end of the tenth chapter.

units.la: Post missionem Apostolorum redit ad narrationem eorum quæ Christus dixit & fecit.
units.tr: After the sending out of the Apostles, he returns to the narrative of what Christ said and did.

units.la: Dicta & facta Christi alternis capitibus distinctè vel coniunctim deinceps narrantur Dicta: cap. II. Facta & dicta, cap. 12. Dicta, cap. 13. Facta, cap. 14. Dicta & facta, cap. 15. Dicta. cap. 16.
units.tr: The sayings and deeds of Christ are then narrated in turn, in alternate chapters, either separately or together. Sayings: chapter 11. Deeds and sayings: chapter 12. Sayings: chapter 13. Deeds: chapter 14. Deeds and sayings: chapter 15. Sayings: chapter 16.

units.la: Sermonum Christi in cap. vndecimo obiecta sunt. I. Baptista quem Christus laudat ex occasione missæ ad ipsum legationis. II. Judæi, in quorum pertinaciam vehementissime inuehitur. v. 16. & sequ.: III. Pater cœlestis, quem alloquendo seipsum consolatur Christus, v. 25. IIII. Consternati peccatores quos inuitat. v. 28.
units.tr: The sayings of Christ in chapter 11 have these objects: I. the Baptist, whom Christ praises on the occasion of the mission of his messengers to him. II. the Jews, against whose obstinacy he inveighs most vehemently, v. 16 and following. III. the heavenly Father, addressing whom Christ comforts himself, v. 25. IV. the distressed sinners whom he invites, v. 28.

units.la: Caput duodecimum est ἀγωνιστικὸν, controuersias enim aduersus Pharisæos complectitur. Prima pars habet excusationem discipulorum spicas sabbatho vellentium. Altera defensionem humanitatis; quæ Deo longè sit gratior, quam rigida ceremoniarum legis obseruantia; vtraque autem ad quæstionem de Sabbathi culmi[?] spectat. à v. 9. vsque ad 14. Tertia pars demonstrationem complectitur diuinitatis Christi, & indurata pertinacia Pharisæorum: vsque ad v. 38. Quarta hypocrisin detegit signum petentium, cum graui comminatione poenarum, v. 38. Vltima Doctrinam habet, quo loco amici carnales habendi sint in causa religionis, à v. 46. vsque ad finem cap.
units.tr: Chapter 12 is agonistic (ἀγωνιστικόν), for it contains controversies against the Pharisees. The first part contains the excuse of the disciples who plucked ears of grain on the Sabbath. The second is a defence of humanity, which is far more pleasing to God than the rigid observance of the ceremonies of the law; both, however, pertain to the question of the Sabbath's observance, from v. 9 to 14. The third part contains a demonstration of the divinity of Christ and the hardened obstinacy of the Pharisees, up to v. 38. The fourth lays bare the hypocrisy of those seeking a sign, with a grave threat of punishments, v. 38. The last contains a teaching on where carnal friends are to be had in matters of religion, from v. 46 to the end of the chapter.

units.la: Cap. xiii. recitantur septem parabolæ quas Christus de natura & conditione Euangelij atque Ecclesiæ apud turbam proposuit, & nonnullas earum discipulis suis priuatim explicauit: exponit etiam causas cur hoc dicendi genere sit vsus. In fine addit historiam de scandalo Nazarethanorum, quod acceperunt ex doctrina & miraculis Christi.
units.tr: Chapter 13 recounts seven parables which Christ proposed to the crowd concerning the nature and condition of the Gospel and the Church, and he explained some of them privately to his disciples. It also sets out the causes why he used this kind of speech. At the end it adds the story of the offence taken by the Nazarenes at the teaching and miracles of Christ.

units.la: Cap. xiiii. Fama Christi doctrinam cœlestem stupendis miraculis confirmantis in aulam Herodis peruenit, & ipsum Herodem excitat in eius admirationem: quare de Christo nō obscurē suum fert iudicium, hac occasione 1. prolixior texitur narratio de Iohanne Baptista occiso à Nerone. 1 1. Redit ad θαυμασιουργίαν[?] Christi, cuius tria miracula commemorantur. 1 Cibatio quinquies mille & amplius hominum é quinque panibus. v. 13. 2 de ambulatione Christi & Petri super mare, v. 22. 3 sanatio ægrotorum in terra Genezareth. v. 34.
units.tr: Chapter 14. The fame of Christ, who confirmed his heavenly doctrine with astonishing miracles, reaches the court of Herod and stirs Herod himself to wonder; so he gives no obscure judgment about Christ. On this occasion (1) a fuller narrative is woven concerning John the Baptist, killed by Herod. (1.1) He returns to the wonder-working of Christ, of which three miracles are recorded. (1) The feeding of more than five thousand men from five loaves, v. 13. (2) the walking of Christ and Peter on the sea, v. 22. (3) the healing of the sick in the land of Gennesaret, v. 34.

units.la: Cap. xv. narrantur quatuor. 1 Disceptatio Christi cum scribis & pharisæis Hierosolymitanis, vsque ad v. 21. Deinde sanatio puellæ dæmoniacæ Chananææ, vsque ad v.29. Tertiò sanatio multorum ac variorum ægrotorum, vsque ad v.32. Postremò cibatio quater mille virorum per septem panes vsque ad finem capitis.
units.tr: Chapter 15 recounts four things. (1) The dispute of Christ with the scribes and the Pharisees of Jerusalem, up to v. 21. Then the healing of the demon-possessed daughter of the Canaanite woman, up to v. 29. Thirdly, the healing of many and various sick, up to v. 32. Lastly, the feeding of four thousand men with seven loaves, to the end of the chapter.

units.la: Christus aut docet, aut edit miracula, otiosus nunquam legitur. doctrina & miracula sunt muneris publici,& veriMessiæ:præcipuum tamen doctrina & principale. miracula doctri-nam comitantur vt testes, qui fidem faciunt, confirmant auditores, conuincunt aduersarios.
units.tr: Christ either teaches or performs miracles; he is never read of as idle. Doctrine and miracles belong to his public office and to his character as the true Messiah, but the principal thing is doctrine. Miracles accompany doctrine as witnesses: they give assurance, confirm the hearers, and convict the adversaries.

units.la: Et quanquam Christus hæc coniuncta tracta-rit, h. e, simul cum miraculis docuerit: tamen historiæ euangelicæ non vtrunque simul descri-bunt: aliàs enim sola miracula recensent, aliàs solam doctrinam,aliàs vtrunque simul.Sic præ-cedenti capite prosecutus est miracula Christi in monte,quæ sanando & cibando patrauit: sic iam ad doctrinam Christi redit. Ac vti audito-rum est diuersitas,ita doctor Christus genus di-cendi variat. Cum aduersariis est acer, cum di-scipulis patiens,cum turbis misericors,cum pri-uatis mitis,& clemens: & cùm omnia norit,ta-men suos certo fine ad certam vtilitatem explo-rat, cuius rei sequens caput specimen nobis ex-hibet.
units.tr: And although Christ handled these things together, that is, he taught together with the miracles, the gospel histories do not always describe both at once. At times they recount only the miracles, at times only the doctrine, and at times both together. Thus in the preceding chapter he pursued the miracles of Christ on the mount, which he performed by healing and feeding; now he returns to the doctrine of Christ. And as his hearers differ, so Christ the teacher varies his manner of speaking. With adversaries he is sharp; with disciples, patient; with crowds, merciful; with private persons, mild and gentle. And although he knows all things, he still tests his own, to a definite end and for a definite benefit, and the following chapter gives us an example of this.

units.la: Partes cap. xvi. sunt quatuor. 1 De signis quæ tentando petunt Pharisæi & Sadducæi, quibus nullum datur præter Ionæ Prophetæ. 11 Admonitio Christi ad discipulos de cauendo fermento. i.doctrina Pharisæorum versu.5. 111 Explorat Christus quæ sint populi de se iudicia, quid item discipuli de seipso sentiant: quo loco habetur splendida Petri confessio, nec non elegans Christi commendatio & promissio verf. 13.[?] iv. Vaticinium suæ mortis, & admonitio de officio suorum sectatorum in tolerandâ eruce & persecutione.versu.21.
units.tr: The parts of chapter 16 are four. (1) The signs which the Pharisees and Sadducees seek by testing, to which none is given except that of the prophet Jonah. (2) Christ's admonition to the disciples to beware of the leaven, that is, the doctrine of the Pharisees, v. 5. (3) Christ tests what the people's judgments about him are, and what the disciples too think of him. Here is the splendid confession of Peter, and also Christ's elegant commendation and promise, v. 13. (4) The prophecy of his death, and the admonition about the duty of his followers in bearing the cross and persecution, v. 21.

units.la: Priora tria membra adhuc ad antecedentem partem Muneris prophetici spectant: ultimum ad sequentem refertur.
units.tr: The first three parts still pertain to the preceding part, concerning the prophetic office; the last is referred to the part that follows.

units.la: Hactenus igitur fuit historia de Christo docente publicè, & faciente miracula liberè, & sine mortis vel mentione vel anxietate.
units.tr: Thus far, then, has been the history of Christ teaching publicly and performing miracles freely, and without any mention or anxiety of death.

units.la: IN GEMMA FABRI CONNE-xio capitum de ministerio Christi huc usque descripto talis est.
units.tr: ACCORDING TO FABER'S GEMMA, the connection of the chapters describing the ministry of Christ up to this point is as follows.

units.la: Ministerii Christus obiit Solum: eius praedicatio in mõte, de piorum Beatitudine. c.5. Exercitiis.c.6. Impedimentis. cap. 7. Operatio in Caper-naum ante traiectum Genezareth. c. 8. post reditum ad locum. cap. 9. Cum a-liis Discipulis Suis cap. 10. Iohannis cap. II. Alie-nis Adversantibus pharisaeis.c.12. Addiscentibus c. 13. Insidian-tibus per Vim.Herode.c.14. Pharisaeis tentanti-bus eum in Doctrina, cap. 15. signis. cap. 16.
units.tr: Christ engaged in the ministry alone. His preaching, on the mount, on the blessedness of the pious: chapter 5. Exercises: chapter 6. Hindrances: chapter 7. His working in Capernaum before crossing to Gennesaret: chapter 8; after his return to that place: chapter 9. With his disciples: chapter 10. With John: chapter 11. With the alien adversaries, the Pharisees: chapter 12. With those who learn: chapter 13. With those who plot by force, Herod: chapter 14. The Pharisees tempting him in doctrine: chapter 15. Signs: chapter 16.

units.la: Verum ex antegressa Analysi generali seu dispositione & argumentis capitum patet 1. prædi-cationem & operationem ita coniungi vt in tali synopsi tanquam partes sibi invicem op-positas statui non possunt.2 hisce capitum sin-gulorum notis tantum particulam eius capitis aliquam sæpe designare: cum præstet omnes totius capitis partes in conspectu positas habere.
units.tr: But from the preceding general analysis, or arrangement and arguments, of the chapters, it is clear: first, that preaching and working are so joined that in such a synopsis they cannot be set down as parts opposed to one another; second, that these marks of the individual chapters often designate only some part of a chapter, whereas it is better to have all the parts of the whole chapter set out in view.

units.la: HACTENUS fuit historia de Christo docente publicè, & faciente miracula liberè, & sine mortis vel mentione vel anxietate: sequitur
units.tr: Thus far has been the history of Christ teaching publicly and performing miracles freely, and without any mention or anxiety of death. What follows is

units.la: DE PROFECTIONE CHRISTI Hierosolymam ultima, ad festum paschatis.
units.tr: ON CHRIST'S JOURNEY TO JERUSALEM The last, for the feast of the Passover.

units.la: CHRISTUS vitæ cursum inter mortales iam fere peregit: appropinquante igitur actu ultimo, & festo paschatis, in quo hostiam puram & perfectam Deo patri offerre & debuit & voluit, ad istud certamen maturè discipulos suos instruxit cohortatione & miraculo. Hinc mox iter arripit Hierosolymam versus, & quicquid in hac via memorabile fecit aut dixit, Evangelista studiosè recensent. Hinc occasiones Hierosolymis quæsitas & oblatas indicat, quibus Christus tandem ad mortè traditus est.
units.tr: Christ had now nearly finished the course of his life among mortals. As the final act drew near, and with it the feast of the Passover, at which he both ought and wished to offer the pure and perfect sacrifice to God the Father, he promptly prepared his disciples for that contest by exhortation and by a miracle. Then he at once set out on the road to Jerusalem, and the Evangelist carefully records whatever memorable things he did or said on this road. He then points out the occasions, sought out and offered in Jerusalem, by which Christ was at last handed over to death.

units.la: Versus 21.capitis xvi. habet propositionem generalem seu summam consequentium omnium tripartitam.
units.tr: Verse 21 of chapter 16 contains a general proposition, or a summary of all that follows, in three parts.

units.la: Ex eo tempore cœpit Iesus indicare discipulis suis, 1 quod oporteret illum abire Hierosolymam: 2 & multa pati a senioribus. &c. 3. & tertio die resuscitari.
units.tr: From that time Jesus began to show his disciples, 1 that he must go to Jerusalem; 2 and suffer many things from the elders, etc.; 3 and on the third day be raised again.

units.la: Ea autem omnia quæ à Christo Servatore in eo itinere usque ad S. cœnæ institutionem dicta gestaque sunt, sic connecti possunt. Nota Lucae processionis [?] à quo: è superio-Galilaeæ: Christi Dicta ad discipulos quibus morte suam praedicit, eosque aduersus crucis scandalum confirmat. cap. 16. v. 21. Facta: Transfiguratio gloriosa, & quae eam consecuta. cap. 17. Dicta: in ambitiosorum discipulorum correptione. cap. 18. per quem: itineris per Iudaeam continuatio: Christi Dicta sermo Didascalicus, de vita oeconomica. cap. 19. Reprehensorius: contra ambitionem discipulorum. cap. 20. Facta: Ierechunte egressus sanat duos caecos. Ad quem Hierosolymam: Christi in Vrbem ingressus. cap. 21. Commoratio in urbe & quid illic dixerit: ubi eius sermonum obiectum sunt. Aduersarii quos disputando conuincit. cap. 22. incusat & condemnat. cap. 23. Discipuli quos docet Prophetice vaticinando de destructione templi & mundi. c. 24. Hortando ad vigilantiam. cap. 25.
units.tr: All the things that Christ our Saviour said and did on that journey, up to the institution of the Holy Supper, can be arranged as follows. From which place: from Upper Galilee: of Christ. Words addressed to the disciples, in which he foretells his death and strengthens them against the scandal of the cross, chapter 16, verse 21. Deeds: the glorious Transfiguration and what followed it, chapter 17. Words: in rebuking the ambitious disciples, chapter 18. By which route: the continuation of the journey through Judaea: of Christ. Words: a teaching discourse on domestic life, chapter 19. Reproving words against the ambition of the disciples, chapter 20. Deeds: leaving Jericho he heals two blind men. To which place: Jerusalem: Christ's entry into the city, chapter 21. His stay in the city and what he said there, where his words were objected to. The adversaries whom he convicts in argument, chapter 22. He accuses and condemns them, chapter 23. The disciples whom he teaches prophetically by prophesying about the destruction of the temple and the world, chapter 24. Exhorting them to watchfulness, chapter 25.

units.la: Capitis igitur decimi septimi propositio est: Christus Iesus, quanquam Dei sit verus filius, tamen non erubuit, ut homo, sese submittere magistratibus, cum id sine peccato fieri potuit. Quod Dei sit Filius verusque Deus confirmat historia montis,miraculum quod in Lunatico edidit, quod mortem sua iterum, & praecise praedicit. Quod autem fe magistratui submiserit, cum id fine peccato fieri potuerit, testatur historia dati tributi. Partes insigniores sunt tres Prima habet narrationem de transfiguratione in monte, vsque ad v. 14. Altera historiam de lunatico: cui annectimus repetitam eommonefactionem de morte sua, v. 24. Tertia est de tributo postulato, & dato, cuius rationes reddit Christus: v. 24, &c.
units.tr: The proposition of chapter 17 is therefore this: Christ Jesus, although he is the true Son of God, nevertheless did not disdain, as a man, to submit himself to the magistrates, although this could be done without sin. That he is the Son of God and true God is confirmed by the story of the mountain, and by the miracle he performed on the lunatic boy, in which he again foretells his death, and does so plainly. That he submitted himself to the magistrate, although this could be done without sin, is attested by the story of the tax demanded and paid. There are three more notable parts. The first contains the narrative of the transfiguration on the mountain, down to verse 14. The second is the story of the lunatic boy, to which we join the repeated reminder of his death, verse 24. The third concerns the tax demanded and paid, whose grounds Christ gives, verse 24, etc.

units.la: Capitis xviii Argumentum: Discipuli de primatu altercantur: Quaestionem ad se delatam Christus explicat, & extendit non ipsorum esse quaerere quis sit futurus maximus in regno coelorum: sed quomodo ipsi possint in illud ingredi. Propositio igitur est; Sine vera humilitate & condonatione offensarum fratris, non esse nobis sperandam vitam aeternam. Quatuor insunt huic argumento insignes loci. Primus est de maximo in regno coelorum: Alter de scandalo non necessario vitando pius v. 5. Tertius de admonitione fraterna in offensa: v. 15. Quartus de remittenda eisdem offensa: v. 21.
