Postremò ab apparitione facta discipulis compluribus congregatis, usque ad v. 5o-[?]
units.tr: Now in this twenty-fourth and last chapter, those things are described which concern the beginning or first stages of the kingly office. The chapter has two main parts: the first concerns the Resurrection, the second the Ascension. As for the Resurrection of Christ, it is shown first by the testimony of two angels to the women who wished to complete the burial more fittingly. It therefore shows how eagerly and anxiously they hastened to the tomb, what state of affairs they found there, and with what mind they received the report given to them, up to verse 13. Secondly, the Resurrection is shown from the appearance of the Lord himself, made to two disciples who were going to Emmaus, up to verse 36. Lastly, from the appearance made to several disciples gathered together, up to verse 50.

units.la: Ascensionis Christi in coelum historia describitur reliquis versibus.
units.tr: The history of Christ's Ascension into heaven is described in the remaining verses.

units.la: ARGVMENTVM CAPITVM ex versibus. D. R. G. CAPVT I.
units.tr: ARGUMENT OF THE CHAPTERS, from the verses. D. R. G. CHAPTER I.

units.la: Decrepito natus patri promittitur: inde Virgineas ades angelus alter adit. Cagnatam visens decantat numen Olympi. Baptistam sterilis mater at inde parit. Cùm pater exiliens linguæ compage soluta Supremum sancto concinit ore Deum.
units.tr: Born to a decrepit father, he is promised; then another angel comes to the Virgin's house. Seeing his kinswoman, he sings of the God of Olympus. The barren mother then bears the Baptist. When the father, his tongue loosed, leaps up and sings God Most High with holy mouth.

units.la: Virgo parit CHRISTVM: pastores nuncia læta Accipiunt, sanctis vocibus aura sonat. Hunc tenet in templo Simeon ac Anna pudica. Amissus doctos erudit atque puer.
units.tr: The Virgin bears Christ. The shepherds receive the joyful news, and the air resounds with holy voices. Simeon and chaste Anna hold him in the temple. Lost, the boy instructs the learned.

units.la: Baptista altisoni iam proseri iussa minasque, Et capitur summum dum notat ille ducem. Ante tamen tingit sacrato in flumine CHRISTVM Cuius dinumerat pagina sacra patres.
units.tr: Now the commands and threats of the loud-voiced Baptist are proclaimed, and he is seized while he points out the supreme leader. Yet first he baptises Christ in the sacred river, whose sacred page enumerates the fathers.

units.la: Tenatur CHRISTVS, exponit verba prophetæ, Cui parat immeritam patria dura necem. Liberat à Satana, febris depellitur ardens. Hinc plures morbis liberat atque docet.
units.tr: Christ is seized; he expounds the words of the prophet, for whom his hard fatherland prepares an undeserved death. He frees from Satan, and the burning fever is driven out. Hence he frees many from diseases and teaches.

units.la: Hic docet ingressus navim, sunt retia plena Piscibus, à fœdo corpore lepra fugit. Exurgit sanus, qui languidus ante iacebat. Matthæum recipit: convocat inde malos.
units.tr: Here he teaches, entering the boat; the nets are full of fish; leprosy flees from the foul body. He who lay sick before rises whole. He receives Matthew; then he calls the sinners.

units.la: Religione docet quà Sabbata sancta colenda. Discipulosque legit, & bona summa docet. Sit syncerus amor, qui se nec deneget hosti. Non satis audire est, sed mea iussa sequi.
units.tr: He teaches by what religion the holy Sabbaths are to be observed. He chooses his disciples and teaches the highest good. Let there be sincere love, which does not deny itself even to an enemy. It is not enough to hear; one must follow my commands.

units.la: Centurio fidei virtute excelluit omnes. Restituit vitæ mortua membra nouæ. Mittit Iohanuet[?]: Iudæis pectora dura Obiicit: extergit[?] fœmina mæsta pedes.
units.tr: The centurion excels all in the virtue of faith. He restores dead limbs to new life. He sends [John?]; he sets before the Jews their hard hearts; a sorrowful woman wipes his feet.

units.la: 8 Fœmineis opibus alitur, quæ semina Verbi, Et quis nam fratres sit[?] suus inde docet. Compescit fluctus, porcos fert dæmonis æstus. Sistitur & sanguis: mortua virgo valet.
units.tr: 8 He is sustained by the resources of women, who [minister] the seed of the Word, and from this he teaches who his brethren are. He calms the waves; the frenzy of the demon drives the swine away. The flow of blood is stayed, and the dead maiden revives.

units.la: 9 Discipulos mittit, pascuntur millia multa. Agnoscit CHRISTVM pectore & ore Petrus, Præmia sanctorum: transformat: dæmona pellit. Quis sit sanctorum maximus inde docet. Vltrices inhibet dextras mala sæva precantium, Ac animo intento se iubet usque sequi.
units.tr: 9 He sends out the disciples; many thousands are fed. Peter acknowledges Christ with heart and mouth. He sets forth the rewards of the saints; he is transfigured; he drives out the demon. From this he teaches who is greatest among the saints. He restrains the avenging hands of those who pray for evil, and bids them follow him with an attentive mind.

units.la: 10 Emittit plures, qui dogmata sancta docerent. Ingratis mores exprobrat atque suos. Indicat & quis sit tibi proximus, maxima pars est Quam Maria elegit, dogmata sancta petens.
units.tr: 10 He sends out several who were to teach holy doctrines. He rebukes the ungrateful for their conduct, and their own. He shows who your neighbour is; the greater part is that which Mary chose, seeking holy doctrine.

units.la: 11 Hic orare docet, depellit dæmona mutum, Et virtute Dei se facere illa docet. Fœlices, quotquot læti mea iussa sequuntur: Signa negat: vitæ facta decora petit. Extrema mundos specie reprendere pergit. Devouet hic scribas sanguineumque genus.
units.tr: 11 Here he teaches to pray; he casts out the dumb demon, and teaches that he does these things by the power of God. Happy are all who gladly follow my commands. He refuses signs; he seeks the honourable deeds of life. Finally he goes on to rebuke the world for its outward show. Here he curses the scribes and the bloody generation.

units.la: 12 Fermentum caveas: mortem contemnite opesque. Thesaurum vigili quærite mente bonum. Verbera plura feret, qui cognita iura fefellit. Dissidium gignunt dogmata nostra graue.
units.tr: 12 Beware the leaven; despise death and riches. Seek the good treasure with a watchful mind. He who has deceived known law will bear many stripes. Our doctrines beget a grievous division.

units.la: 13 Gens Galilæa perit sterilisque excinditur arbor. Quæque prius fuerat fœmina curva valet. Est Verbum Sinapi, fermentum angustaque porta Est vitæ: in Solymis sæpe propheta perit.
units.tr: 13 The Galilean race perishes, and the barren tree is cut down. The woman who was bent over before is made well. The Word is like mustard seed, leaven, and the narrow gate of life. In Jerusalem a prophet often perishes.

units.la: 14 Hydrops sanatur, ventosa superbia fallit. Ad mensam veniat indiga turba tuam. Abstrahit affectus multos ne fercula gustent Dulcia, res omnes deservisse decet.
units.tr: 14 The dropsy is healed; windy pride deceives. Let the needy crowd come to your table. He draws many affections away, so that they do not taste the sweet dishes; it is fitting that all possessions be given up.

units.la: 15 Vt saluet miseros à diro crimine CHRISTVS Venit, id amissus nummus onisque[?] docent. Filius acceptis opibus postquam omnia perdit. Clementi patrem corde reversus habet.
units.tr: 15 That Christ came to save the wretched from dire guilt, the lost coin and the sheep teach. The son, after he has squandered all the wealth he received, returns and finds his father merciful at heart.

units.la: 61 Oeconomus raptis opibus sibi quærit amicos. Turpis opum toto pectore cedat amor. Coniugii[?] leges: lautus conviuia dies Aspicit, ægrotus Lazarus inde perit.
units.tr: 61 The steward, by plundering wealth, seeks friends for himself. Let base love of riches yield with the whole heart. The laws of marriage [...]: the rich man sees the days of feasting, and sick Lazarus then perishes.

units.la: 17 Scandala fac caveas, fratrique remittere sæpe Convenit: haud factis est tribuenda salus. Bis quinque à lepra mundantur, at unus eidem est gratus: quàm sit dura suprema dies,
units.tr: 17 Take care to avoid offences, and it is fitting often to forgive a brother; salvation is not to be ascribed to deeds. Ten are cleansed from leprosy, but only one is grateful to him: how hard the last day is,

units.la: 18 Sæpius orandum est: duo sunt, qui limina templi Intrant: & pueros dextera sancta tegit. Dimittibus gravis est via vitæ, præmia sanctis Magna jacent: sano lumine cæcus abit.
units.tr: 18 One must pray more often. There are two who enter the threshold of the temple, and the holy right hand covers the boys. For those who dismiss, the way of life is hard; great rewards lie for the saints; the blind man departs with his sight restored.

units.la: 19 Excipit unigenam dives Zachæus Jesum, Distribuit servis multa talenta suis. Conscendens asinam Solymarum tristia fata Flet: sancta merces ejicit atque domo.
units.tr: 19 Rich Zacchaeus receives Jesus, the only-begotten; he distributes many talents to his servants. Mounting the ass, he weeps for the sad fate of Jerusalem; holy reward casts out and drives from the house.

units.la: 20 Quislicita, inquirunt, dederit sibi iura docendi, Agricolæ domino debita vina negant. Reddatis censum: defuncti à morte resurgunt. CHRISTUS Davidi sit filius & Dominus.
units.tr: 20 They ask who gave him the right to teach, and they deny the vineyard's owed wines to the farmer. Render the tribute; the dead rise from death. Christ is David's son and David's Lord.

units.la: 21 Parvula laudantur vidua munuscula grata, Excidium templi duraque fata canit. Sint vigiles animi: fortis patientia servat. Hæc etenim grandis pœna futura brevi[?] est.
units.tr: 21 The small gifts of the poor widow are praised; he sings of the destruction of the temple and its hard fates. Let the mind be watchful; steadfast patience preserves. For this will soon be a great punishment.

units.la: 22 Doctorem turpi precio[?] divendit Judas, Instituit cœnam, corda superba notat. Sit gladius vobis: offerte sua vota parentis: Dum capitur fortis dimicat ense Petrus. Sed negat infelix hunc quem defenderat ante, Illusus CHRISTUS verbera multa tulit.
units.tr: 22 Judas sells the teacher for a base price; he institutes the Supper and marks the proud hearts. Let there be swords for you; offer your parent's vows. While he is seized, Peter fights boldly with the sword. But the unhappy man denies him whom he had defended before; mocked, Christ bore many stripes.

units.la: 23 Pontius Herodi CHRISTUM transmittit iniqua Barrabam immanem vult tenuisse cohors. Sistitur ploratus: ligno dependet ab alto. Latroni sæno[?] gratia læta datur. Multa necem pariter testantur signa nefandam: Et nova defuncti marmora corpus habent.
units.tr: 23 Pontius sends Christ on to Herod; the wicked cohort wishes to hold the savage Barabbas. The weeping is stopped; he hangs from the high wood. To the thief joyful grace is given. Many signs equally bear witness to the unholy death, and new marbles hold the dead body.

units.la: 24 Angelus hic Mariæ enarrat vivere CHRISTUM, Cumque alias vivens urbem Emaunta petit. Apparens rursum, sumto se vivere pisce Approbat & toto in orbe docere jubet. Scripturam enarrans cœlum conscendit in altum, Ad Solymas redit cum pia turba domus.
units.tr: 24 This angel tells Mary that Christ lives, and that, living, he goes to Emmaus. Appearing again, having taken fish, he proves that he lives and bids him teach throughout the whole world. Expounding Scripture, he ascends into high heaven; the pious crowd returns with joy to the household in Jerusalem.

units.la: ARGUMENTA CAPITUM exG. F.
units.tr: ARGUMENTS OF THE CHAPTERS, from G. F.

units.la: CAP. I.
units.tr: CHAP. I.

units.la: Angelus en his adest, innisens cantat, idemque Nato vate, patris lingua soluta, facit.
units.tr: Here the angel stands by, singing as he leans in, and with the prophet born, his father's tongue is loosed, and he does so.

units.la: 2 Bethlemica cunæ, pastores, virgo piata. Anna, Simon, doctos pulso multa rogat.
units.tr: 2 The Bethlehem cradle, the shepherds, the purified virgin. Anna and Simeon; he asks the learned many questions.

units.la: 3 Clamor, baptismus, pia verba, catena prophetæ, Visa columba sonus desuper, ordo patrum.
units.tr: 3 The cry, the baptism, the holy words, the prophet's chain (genealogy), the dove seen, a sound from above, the order of the fathers.

units.la: 4 Detentante Deum, recitato vate, paratis Insidiis, pulso Damone, febre socrus,
units.tr: 4 God holding back, the prophet recited, snares laid, the demon driven out, the mother-in-law's fever.

units.la: 5 En Petrus & fratres alii, lectica, telones. Sponsi habitus, vestis rupta, cadique novi.
units.tr: 5 Behold Peter and the other brothers, the litter, the tax collectors. The bridegroom's guests, the torn garment, the new wineskins.

units.la: 6 Factum Davidis, manus arida nomina, fausti. Quid facias, quid non, stripsque domusque bona.
units.tr: 6 The deed of David, the withered hand, the names, the fortunate ones. What to do and what not to do; the stripped man and the house's goods.

units.la: 7 Gaudet Centurio, & Naim, veniunt duo, vatem Laudat, cui similes? pes lachrymisque madet.
units.tr: 7 The centurion rejoices, and Nain; two come. He praises the prophet: "to whom are they like?" The foot is wet with tears.

units.la: 8 Iactatur semen, cessat mare, grex perit undis. Gaudet Iairus, desinit ire cruor.
units.tr: 8 The seed is scattered, the sea is calm, the flock perishes in the waves. Jairus rejoices; the bleeding stops.

units.la: 9 Legati Herodis, pisces, confessio, vultus Splendor, luna, puer, flamma, caverna vale.
units.tr: 9 Herod's envoys, the fishes, the confession, the countenance, the splendour, the moon, the boy, the flame, the cave, farewell.

units.la: 10 Missi vae ter, quae bona gaudia, parvule nosti. Hoc fac, pene neci dat latro, Martha tace.
units.tr: 10 Woe, woe, woe to those sent; what goods, what joys; you know the little one. Do this. He nearly gives the robber to death. Martha, be silent.

units.la: 11 Norma precum, divisa domus, fausta ubera, Ionas. Lux, oculos, patinae lotio, vaque frequens.
units.tr: 11 The rule of prayer, the divided house, the blessed breasts, Jonah. Light, eyes, the washing of the dish, and the frequent emptiness.

units.la: 12 Occultum, passer, fassus meditatio, quis me? Horrea, aues, grex, lux, fur, famulus, pyra, lig[?]
units.tr: 12 The hidden thing, the sparrow, the confessing meditation: "who am I?" Granaries, birds, flock, light, thief, servant, pyre, wood.

units.la: 13 Post turrim, ficus contracta, sinape, farina. Arcta via, ignoro, vade relicta domus.
units.tr: 13 After the tower, the withered fig, the mustard, the flour. The narrow way; I do not know; leave the house.

units.la: 14 Quid sanatur Hydrops? sedans ita coena parata est. Non peragens Turrim, bellaue, salque malus.
units.tr: 14 Why is the dropsy healed? The supper is thus prepared. Not finishing the tower, war, and bad salt.

units.la: 15 Reddit ouis laetum, scrutatur foemina drachmam Et siliquis vesci cogit amara fames.
units.tr: 15 The sheep is returned rejoicing; the woman searches for the drachma; bitter hunger forces one to eat the husks.

units.la: 16 Subdolus oeconomus, mammon, servusque duorum, Lex vata, missa vxor, purpureusque miser.
units.tr: 16 The dishonest steward, Mammon, the servant of two masters; the prophesied law, the sent wife, the purple-clad wretch.

units.la: 17 Tolle, remitte, auge, nihili tua pendito facta. Cerne decem leprās, iudiciisque diem.
units.tr: 17 Take up, forgive, increase; count your deeds as nothing. Behold the ten lepers and the day of judgement.

units.la: 18 Vis viduæ orantis. fastus. tactisque puelli. Dives abit, linquunt omnia. cæce vides.
units.tr: 18 The widow's importunity, pride, the touched girl. The rich man departs; they leave everything. Blind, you see.

units.la: 19 Ascendit nanus. rex it sibi regna paratum. Abducunt asinum, fletque fugatque lucrum.
units.tr: 19 Zacchaeus climbs, the nobleman goes to receive the kingdom prepared for him. They lead away the ass; gain flees and weeps.

units.la: 20 Baptisma unde? fata est vitæ, petra. pensio. septem Ben David. sedes. fraus precis, atque stolæ.
units.tr: 20 Whence the baptism? The fate of life, the rock, the payment, the seven, the son of David, the seat, the deceit of prayer, and the stole.

units.la: 21 Collaudat viduam. ruet ædes. signa dei. Cura mala. excidium. sobrius esto. vigil.
units.tr: 21 He praises the widow. The house will fall. The signs of God. Evil care, destruction. Be sober, be watchful.

units.la: 22 Dat corpus. certant spondet Petrus. ecce duo enses. Dum rogat, en capitur. flet Petre. dant alapas
units.tr: 22 He gives up his body. They strive; Peter promises; behold two swords. While he asks, behold, he is seized. Peter weeps; they give blows.

units.la: 23 Eludit clamant. homicida. Simon lachrymantes, En latro. Centurio. membra sepulta. quies.
units.tr: 23 They mock and cry out. Murderer! Simon weeping. Behold the robber. The centurion. The buried limbs. Rest.

units.la: 24 Fulgura. vestitus. bona nuntia. sermo duorum. Fit comedendo palam Christus & astra petit.
units.tr: 24 Lightnings, garments, good tidings, the speech of two. Christ eats openly with them and goes up to the stars.

units.la: PENTASTICHON EX SINGV-LIS CAPITIBVS VOCEM ALI-quam præcipuam, argumenti capi-tis nos admonentem com-plectens.
units.tr: PENTASTICH, EMBRACING A SINGLE PRINCIPAL WORD FROM EACH CHAPTER, WHICH REMINDS US OF THE CHAPTER'S SUBJECT.

units.la: 1 2 3 4 5 Conceptus, Puer, Unda, Socrus, Piscatio felix 6 7 8 9 10 Dextra, Naitana, Rector, Pastusque, Latrones. 11 12 13 14 15 Tu Digito, Fermetu, Incuruaq., Hydrops, Siliquisq. 16 17 18 19 20 Purpura, Scandala, Pectus Zacheus, atque Coloni, 21 22 23 24 Prælia, & ad Prunas, Crux, Emaunta petunt.
units.tr: 1 2 3 4 5 Conception, Boy, Wave, Mother-in-law, Lucky catch 6 7 8 9 10 Right hand, of Nain, Ruler, and the feeding, Robbers. 11 12 13 14 15 By the finger, Leaven, and the bent woman, Dropsy, and the husks. 16 17 18 19 20 Purple, Stumbling-blocks, Breast, Zacchaeus, and the Tenants, 21 22 23 24 Battles, and by the coals, Cross, they make for Emmaus.

units.la: [?] Conceptus Iohannis & Christi. Puer Christus duodecim annorum disputat. v. 42. 46. Vnda in qua Iohannes Christum baptizauit. v.7. Socrus Petri sanatur à Christo. v. 38. Piscatio felix v. 1. Dextra arida sanatur à Christo, v. 6. 10. Naïnæ[?] viduæ filius exitatur à morte. v. 12. Rector synagogæ accidit ad pedes Iesu. v. 41. Passusque miraculosus τῶν 5000. Latrones sauciant & spoliant viatorem. v. 30. Tum Digito Dei eiicit Christus Dæmonia v. 20. Fermentum pharisæorum cauendum. v. 1. Incurvaque mulier sanatur à Christo v. 11. Hydrops sanatur 2. Siliquisque vescitur filius prodigus. v. 16. Purpura qua indutus diues. v. 19. Scandala væ danti homini. v. 1. Petrus percutit publicanus. v. 13. Zachæus ascendit arborem. v. 4. atque Coloni ingrati in vinea. verf: 1. Pralia prædicuntur. v. 9. & ad prunas se calefacit Petrus v. 55. Crux de qua Iosephus Christum aufert. v. 53. Emaunta petunt, duo discipuli cum Christo. v. 13. & seqq.
units.tr: [?] Conception: of John and of Christ. Boy: Christ, aged twelve, disputes. vv. 42, 46. Wave: the water in which John baptized Christ. v. 7. Mother-in-law: Peter's mother-in-law is healed by Christ. v. 38. Lucky catch: v. 1. Right hand: the withered hand is healed by Christ. vv. 6, 10. Of Nain: the son of the widow of Nain is raised from the dead. v. 12. Ruler: the ruler of the synagogue falls at Jesus' feet. v. 41. And the feeding: the miraculous feeding of the five thousand. Robbers: they wound and despoil the traveller. v. 30. By the finger: by the finger of God Christ casts out demons. v. 20. Leaven: the leaven of the Pharisees is to be guarded against. v. 1. And the bent woman: the woman is healed by Christ. v. 11. Dropsy: is healed. v. 2. And the husks: the prodigal son feeds on husks. v. 16. Purple: in which the rich man was clothed. v. 19. Stumbling-blocks: woe to the man who gives offence. v. 1. Breast: the publican beats his breast. v. 13. Zacchaeus: climbs the tree. v. 4. And the Tenants: the ungrateful tenants in the vineyard. verse 1. Battles: are foretold. v. 9. And by the coals: Peter warms himself. v. 55. Cross: from which Joseph takes Christ down. v. 53. They make for Emmaus: two disciples with Christ. v. 13 and following.

units.la: ANALYSIS EVANGELII SECUNDUM IO-hannem.
units.tr: ANALYSIS OF THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO JOHN.

units.la: PRIMO de autore, deinde de ipso opere, quædam προγινωσκομένων loco, nostro more, præmittemus.
units.tr: First, in our customary manner, I shall set out a few preliminary matters, as things already known (προγινωσκομένων), about the author and then about the work itself.

units.la: Quæcunquæ à Prophetis & Apostolis vel viva voce tradita, vel postmodum literis consignata sunt, ea omnia ad primum autorem Spiritum sanctum sunt referenda. Spiritus igitur sanctus verissimus est libri huius autor & dictator: Amanuensis autem siue Notarius Spiritus sancti est Iohannes & Euangelista & Apostolus: idque luculenter apparet tum ex inscriptione, quæ habet: Euangelium secundum Iohannem, tum ex fine huius libri, cap. 21 v. 24. Hic est discipulus ille qui de his testatur, & hæc scripsit: & scimus verum esse testimonium eius: vbi simul & certitudo huius narrationis historicæ, & do-ctrinæ in ea comprehensæ indubia veritas ex-primitur: quam certitudinis πληροφορίαν etiam capite 19. v. 35. ostendit, dicens: Et qui vidit, te-statur;& verum est testimonium eius:ille (inquam) scit se vera dicere,vt & vos credatis.
units.tr: Whatever the Prophets and Apostles delivered, whether by living voice or afterwards committed to writing, must all be referred to the first author, the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit is therefore the most true author and dictator of this book, and John the Evangelist and Apostle is his amanuensis or scribe. This is clear from the title, which reads The Gospel according to John, and from the end of this book, chapter 21, verse 24: This is the disciple who testifies of these things and wrote these things, and we know that his testimony is true. Here the certainty of this historical narrative and the indubitable truth of the teaching contained in it are both expressed together. He shows the same full assurance (πληροφορίαν) of certainty in chapter 19, verse 35, saying: And he who saw it bears witness, and his testimony is true; he (I say) knows that he speaks true things, so that you also may believe.

units.la: De ipsius igitur Autoris nomine, patria, pa-rentibus, Vita, & scriptis quædam delibanda.
units.tr: Let us therefore touch briefly on the name, country, parents, life and writings of this author.

units.la: 1. Nomen Iohannes origine hebraicum est, Io-chanan, & significat χαριέντα[?], i. gratiosum, qualem solemus apud nos appellare Huldrichum, Latini Gratianum. ( Palæoterici nostri Ianum dicunt.) Huic nomini fata & facta in Euangeli-sta nostro responderunt. Primum enim gratia Domini Christi illum perfudit, vt illi etiam quodammodo fuerit charior reliquis. Hinc in sinu illius recumbit, in Cœna, infrà cap. 13. 25. Ex eadem gratiæ vbertate refluxit amor & studium erga Dominum suum, quem videtur enixius etiam amasse, suspexisse, paratioreque coluisse obsequio. Quòd vel inde patet, quòd solus Iohannes ingredi audet atrium summi sacerdotis, eiusque opera admittitur Petrus etiam, reliquis præ metu dilapsis. Sed etiam crucem accessit, & spectauit rei euentum: Ioh. 19. 3. Accedit quòd donum Spiritus sancti in eo fuit, vberrimum. Nam cùm reliqui Euangelistæ humanitatis historiam præcipuè persequantur: so-lus Iohannes clarius diuinam originem proferre, & de λόγῳ æterno, humanis verbis potuit disse-rere. Hinc Aquilæ ille volatus, & in intelligen-do, percipiendo, eloquedoque maiestas diuina. Facit huc etiam nominis mutatio. Nam ex circircumcisione indubie dictus est Iohannes. Christus vero ex vocatione etiam alterum ei largitus est nomen, ut cum fratre Iacobo diceretur Boaner-ges, hoc est, filius tonitrui, Matth. 3. 17. Nam buccina Domini fuit, penetrans totum mundum, cui nec ulla potentia, nec ulla sapientia potuit resistere.
units.tr: 1. The name John is Hebrew in origin, Jochanan, and means gracious [χαριέντα], that is, full of grace, such as we among ourselves are accustomed to call Huldrich, and in Latin Gratian. (Our forefathers call him Ian.) The facts of his life and deeds answered to this name in our Evangelist. For first, the grace of the Lord Christ flooded him, so that he was in some way dearer to him than the rest. Hence he lay in Christ's bosom at the supper (John 13:25). From the same abundance of grace there flowed back love and devotion towards his Lord, whom he seems to have loved more eagerly, revered, and served with more ready obedience. This is clear from the fact that John alone dared to enter the courtyard of the high priest, and through his help Peter too was admitted, when the others had fled in fear. He also drew near to the cross and watched the outcome of the event (John 19:3). Moreover, the gift of the Holy Spirit was in him in the greatest abundance. For while the other Evangelists chiefly pursue the history of Christ's humanity, John alone could set forth more clearly the divine origin, and speak in human words of the eternal Word (λόγος). Hence came that eagle-like flight, and the divine majesty in his understanding, perception and speech. The change of his name also contributes to this. For John was surely so named from his circumcision. But Christ, from his calling, gave him another name as well, so that together with his brother James he was called Boanerges, that is, sons of thunder (Mark 3:17). For he was the trumpet of the Lord, penetrating the whole world, which no power and no wisdom could resist.

units.la: II. Patria illi fuit Betzaida supra Capernaū ad ripas Iordanis, quæ postea Iulias dicta est à Iulia Augusti filia. Hinc oriundus etiam fuit Iacobus maior, Andreas, Petrus, Philipus: illustris igitur fuit hic locus ex prouentu tantorum Apostolorum, nisi sua ingratitudine promeritam audiat maledictionem, Væ tibi Betzaida. Luc. 10. Matth. 11.
units.tr: II. His country was Bethsaida, above Capernaum on the banks of the Jordan, which was later called Julias after Julia, the daughter of Augustus. From there also came James the Greater, Andrew, Peter and Philip. This place was therefore famous from the produce of so great Apostles, unless by its ingratitude it has deserved to hear the curse: Woe to you, Bethsaida (Luke 10; Matthew 11).

units.la: III. Parentes habuit honestos & mediocris fortis, Zebedæum patrem piscatorem, Salomen matrem. Quam Salomen Theophylactus scribit esse filiam Iosephi ex priore uxore defuncta, unde soror Domini Christi habita est, & Iohannes ex sorore putatiua Christi nepos.
units.tr: III. He had honest parents of middling fortune: Zebedee his father, a fisherman, and Salome his mother. Theophylact writes that this Salome was the daughter of Joseph by his first wife, now dead, and for this reason she was regarded as the sister of the Lord Christ, and John was Christ's nephew through his putative sister.

units.la: IIII. Genus vitæ simplex & honestum fuisse constat ex vocatione eius, & fratris Iacobi, Matth. 4. v. 21. ubi piscatores sunt, & farciunt retia sua. Piscator igitur fuit ante vocationem, e piscatore natus. Erant de familia Dauid & quamquam res ad labores deuenerint: tamen mediocres opes habuisse est credibile, quia non errant hinc inde, sed fixam habent patriam, domum & familiam. Et Nicephorus lib. 2: cap. 3. autor est, Zebedæum duobus filiis suis Iacobo & Ioanni, tolerabiles opes reliquisse, ac Ioannem sua portione diuendita in Galilæa, Hierosolymi[?] emisse propriam domum ad Sionem montem sitam, in qua virginem Mariam receperit. Infra cap. 19. v. 27. Post vocationem igitur Christo magno ardore adhaesit, & unus ex praecipuis & primariis Apostolis fuit. Unde princeps Apostolorum Paulus, Gal. 2. v. 9. ipsum columnam Ecclesiae nominat. Deinde hoc etiam nomine maximè fuit conspicuus, quòd haec ipsius quasi paraphrastica notatio est, qua discipulus Domino charus ἀγαπητὸς appellatur, Iohannis 13. & 21. Quem etiam Dominus praecipuis suis & gravissimis negotiis testem semper asciuit, sicut ex historia resuscitationis filiae Iairi, clarificationis item Christi in monte, & agonis illius ac luctae, cum mortis terroribus in horto manifestum est, ubi tantummodo Petrum, Ioannem & Iacobum tanquam intimos suos ac secretissimos amicos assumpsit. Idem sub cruce matrem à Christo sibi commendari audit: cap. 19. v. 26. Vita diuturna illi fuit, ut merito inter μαρτύρους recenseri possit. Attigit enim annū 99. Fuit is annus Traiani 4. à nato Christo 102. Hieronymus ait fuisse annum à passione Christi 68. Ephesi ubi plurimum vixerat mortuus quoque est, propriis manibus sibi parato sepulcro, ut Dorotheus autor est, & Niceph. lib. 2. cap. 42. Discipulos plurimos reliquit, inter quos postea excelluerunt Papias Hieropolitanus Episcopus, Polycarpus Smyrnaeus, & Ignatius Antiochenus, qui viva voce veram de Christo doctrinam ab eo didicerunt.
units.tr: IV. His way of life was plain and honest, as is clear from his calling and that of his brother James (Matthew 4:21), where they are fishermen and mend their nets. He was therefore a fisherman before his calling, born of a fisherman's family. They were of the house of David, and although their circumstances had come down to labour, it is still credible that they had moderate means, since they did not wander here and there but had a settled country, home and family. Nicephorus (book 2, chapter 3) also states that Zebedee left his two sons, James and John, tolerable means, and that John, after selling his share in Galilee, bought at Jerusalem a house of his own on Mount Zion, in which he received the Virgin Mary (John 19:27). After his calling, then, he clung to Christ with great ardour and became one of the chief and foremost Apostles. Hence Paul, the prince of the Apostles, calls him a pillar of the Church (Galatians 2:9). Moreover, he was especially distinguished by this name as well, that the disciple beloved of the Lord is called, in a kind of paraphrase of his name, the beloved [ἀγαπητὸς], as in John 13 and 21. The Lord also always took him as a witness in his chief and most weighty affairs, as is clear from the history of the raising of Jairus's daughter, likewise from Christ's transfiguration on the mountain, and from his agony and struggle with the terrors of death in the garden, where he took with him only Peter, John and James as his most intimate and most secret friends. Under the cross he also heard Christ commend his mother to him (John 19:26). He had a long life, so that he may rightly be counted among the martyrs [μαρτύρους]. For he reached the ninety-ninth year. That was the fourth year of Trajan, 102 years after the birth of Christ. Jerome says that it was the sixty-eighth year after the passion of Christ. He died at Ephesus, where he had lived for most of his life, and, as Dorotheus and Nicephorus (book 2, chapter 42) report, he prepared his own grave with his own hands. He left very many disciples, among whom later excelled Papias, bishop of Hierapolis, Polycarp of Smyrna, and Ignatius of Antioch, who learned the true doctrine of Christ from him by living voice.

units.la: v. Scripta. Sed non contentus fuit sui seculi docere homines veram religionem, scriptis quoque eandem ad posteros transmisit. Scripsit igitur 1. Evangelium hoc praesens sub finem vitae: quamuis Theophylactus in Pathmo scriptum ab eo dicat anno, 32. post ascensionem. 2 Scripsit etiam tres Epistolas Canonicas, & 3 Apocalypsin, de quibus suo loco. Ex his intelligi potest plurima ipsum & vidisse & effecisse. Etenim annis illis 100. plurima contigere quae doctrinam Christi confirmabant, ut Judaicae Gentis interitus, praedicatio Evangelij per universum terrarum orbem: martyres omnes ante se Apostolos audivit, &c. Haec lectionem scriptorum huius autoris nobis commendare, & attentionem animi magnam excitare debent, ut eo studiosius observemus praevolantem divinam hanc Aquilam.
units.tr: V. Writings. But he was not content to teach the true religion to the men of his own age; he also handed it on to posterity in writing. He therefore wrote: (1) this present Gospel, towards the end of his life, although Theophylact says that he wrote it on Patmos in the thirty-second year after the ascension; (2) also three Epistles, the Catholic letters, and (3) the Apocalypse, of which in their proper place. From this it can be understood that he had seen and done very much. For in those hundred years very many things happened which confirmed the doctrine of Christ, such as the destruction of the Jewish nation and the preaching of the Gospel throughout the whole orb of the earth; he heard of all the martyrs before him, the Apostles, and so on. These things ought to commend the reading of this author's writings to us and arouse great attention in our minds, so that we may observe more eagerly this divine eagle soaring before us.

units.la: Hac de Autore.
units.tr: Concerning the Author.

units.la: Ad ipsius operis considerationem pertinet Occasio scripti, Argumentum, Propositio summa, orationis Idea, & Partitio.
units.tr: To the consideration of the work itself belong the occasion of the writing, the argument, the chief proposition, the character of the discourse, and its division.

units.la: 1. Occasio seu causa, qua impulsus hanc de Jesu Christo historiam texeret, & literis mandatam posteritati transmitteret, duplex a scriptoribus Ecclesiasticis commemoratur. Quarum una fuit furor & rabies haereticorum, quales fuerunt Ebion, Cerinthus, Marcion, Carpocras, &c: qui vivente adhuc Joanne horrendis blasphemiis aeternam Christi deitatem convellere & evertere conati sunt. Hos Johannis Apostoli fuisse συγχρόνους, praeter scriptores Ecclesiasticos testatur Danaeus libro de Haeresibus, cap. 8. 10. sol. 25. & 30. Unde illud 1 Joh. 2. v. 19: Exierunt à nobis, quia non erant ex nobis. & 1. Joh. 4. v. 3. Quorum errorem etiam Paulus cauere iubet, Rom. 15. v. 17. Hodie hanc hæresin retinent Mahometistæ, & ex Anabapti-stis quidam Huteriani, & Sociniani. Cùm igitur cæteris Apostolis omnibus iam defunctis, solus Johannes adhuc superstes esset, exoratus ab Asiæ Episcopis fuit, ut ipse tanquam Apostolica auctoritate pollens, contra istam Hæreticorum intemperiem publico scripto promulgato, suam de hoc Articulo sententiam Ecclesiæ testatam faceret. Quod Euangelio hoc in lucem edito præstitit, cuius principalem scopum fuisse cernimus, ut Christi Deitatem illustraret. Unde propter Argumenti, quod tractat, sublimitatem, à Domini Spiritu per prophetam Ezechielem Aquilæ comparatus censetur, eo quòd omnium altissimè inter Euangelistas ad summum Divinitatis Christi arcanum describendum subvolârit. Altera causa fuit, ut plenior extaret historia cursus Ministerij Christi. Cæteri enim Euangelistæ fere tantum unius anni præcipuè texerunt historiam, ultimi scilicet, quo & passus est Dominus, commemorantes ea, quæ posteaquam Johannes iam in carcerem coniectus fuerat, à Christo gesta sunt. Johannes igitur omissis fere iis, quæ à cæteris Euangelistis exposita erant, commemorat Acta Christi præcedentium temporum, antequam scilicet Johannes coniiceretur in vincula. Inde à primis illis ad postrema descendit, omissis fere intermediis, in quorum descriptione cæteri laborârant. Digreditur enim ad historiam resuscita-tionis Lazari, quæ proximè passionem Domi-nicam antecessit, & describenda Passione ipsa, gloriosaque Christi resurrectione,& subsecutis patefactionibus, libro suo ultimam manum imponit.
units.tr: 1. The occasion or cause, which moved him to write this history of Jesus Christ and commit it to writing for posterity, is recorded by ecclesiastical writers in two forms. The first was the fury and rage of heretics, such as Ebion, Cerinthus, Marcion, Carpocrates and others, who, while John was still alive, tried with horrible blasphemies to overthrow and subvert the eternal deity of Christ. That these were contemporaries [συγχρόνους] of the Apostle John is attested by Danaeus in his book on heresies, ch. 8, 10, pp. 25 and 30, as well as by other ecclesiastical writers. Hence the words of 1 John 2:19: "They went out from us, because they were not of us," and 1 John 4:3. Paul too bids us beware of their error, Rom. 15:17. Today the Mahometans hold this heresy, and among the Anabaptists some Hutterites and Socinians. Since all the other Apostles had now died, and John alone was still living, he was entreated by the bishops of Asia to publish a written work against this lawlessness of the heretics, lending his authority as an Apostle and making his opinion on this article known to the Church. He did this by bringing out this Gospel, whose principal aim, we see, was to illuminate the deity of Christ. For this reason, because of the sublimity of the subject he treats, he is compared by the Spirit of the Lord, through the prophet Ezekiel, to an eagle, since he soared higher than all the other Evangelists to describe the supreme mystery of the divinity of Christ. The second cause was that a fuller history of the course of Christ's ministry might exist. For the other Evangelists had chiefly covered the history of only one year, namely the last, in which the Lord also suffered, recording what was done by Christ after John had already been thrown into prison. John, therefore, leaving aside almost everything that had been set out by the other Evangelists, records the acts of Christ from earlier times, that is, before John was cast into chains. He passes from those first events to the last, leaving out almost all the intervening matters on which the others had laboured. For he turns to the history of the raising of Lazarus, which came just before the Lord's passion, and, after describing the Passion itself and Christ's glorious resurrection and the appearances that followed, he puts the final touch to his book.

units.la: I I Argumentum ex jam dictis concipere li-cet. Exorsus à demonstratione æternæ Christi diuinitatis, ostendit quomodo idem mundo sit patefactus: mox quorundam discipulorum m[?] vocationem attingit. Dehinc vitam Christi in terris actam persequitur. Et cum reliqui Euan-gelistæ miracula copiosè retulerint, ille magis doctrinam, & orationes Christi grauissimas, à reliquis intermissas, accuratè commemorat: nec non miracula nonnulla, de quibus reliqui prorsus tacent. Ac sermones quidem à solo Ioanne descripti, hi sunt: cap.3. sermo cum Nicodemo de regeneratione: cap. 4. sermo cum Samaritana de aqua viua: cap. 5. sermo cum Iudæis de miraculosè sanato eo,qui 38.annos decubuerat: cap. 6. sermo cum turba de pane vitæ: cap. 8. sermo cum Pharisæis in templo, vbi eis ex probrat cæcitatem & malitiam: cap. 10. sermo de bono pastore, item de ouibus suis: cap. 11. sermo cum Martha de resurrectione: cap.14.15.16. sermo cum discipulis, peractâ vltimâ cœna, de Spiritu sancto paracleto: cap. 17. preces ad Patrem pro Ecclesia: cap. 20. sermo cum Thoma de fide: cap. 21. sermo cum Petro de sui delectione. Miracula verò quæ apud solum Ioannem reperiuntur, sunt ista: cap. 2. miracu-lum aquæ in vinum versæ: cap. 5.[?] miraculum sanati eius qui decubuerat annos 38. cap. 9. miraculi sanati cæci à natiuitate : cap. 11. miraculi excitati é morte Lazari.
units.tr: I. The argument may be grasped from what has already been said. Beginning with a demonstration of the eternal deity of Christ, he shows how the same was made manifest to the world; then he touches on the calling of some of the disciples. Next he follows the life Christ lived on earth. And whereas the other Evangelists related the miracles at length, John more carefully records the teaching and the most weighty discourses of Christ, which the others passed over, as well as some miracles of which the others say nothing at all. The discourses described by John alone are these: ch. 3, the discourse with Nicodemus on regeneration; ch. 4, the discourse with the Samaritan woman on living water; ch. 5, the discourse with the Jews about the man healed miraculously after lying sick for thirty-eight years; ch. 6, the discourse with the crowd on the bread of life; ch. 8, the discourse with the Pharisees in the temple, where he rebukes them for their blindness and malice; ch. 10, the discourse on the good shepherd and on his sheep; ch. 11, the discourse with Martha on the resurrection; chs. 14, 15 and 16, the discourse with the disciples, after the last supper was finished, on the Holy Spirit the Paraclete; ch. 17, the prayers to the Father for the Church; ch. 20, the discourse with Thomas on faith; ch. 21, the discourse with Peter on his love for him. The miracles found in John alone are these: ch. 2, the miracle of water turned into wine; ch. 5, the healing of the man who had lain sick for thirty-eight years; ch. 9, the healing of the man blind from birth; ch. 11, the raising of Lazarus from the dead.

units.la: III Propositio principalis, & summarius status est, Christum Iesum verum esse Dei Filium mundo in redemptionem propositum, vt in eum credentes vitam habeamus æternam : vt constat ex cap. 20. v. 31. Hæc scripta sunt,vt credatis Iesum esse Christum Filium Dei: & vt credentes vitam æternam habeatis in nomine ipsius. Vnde etiam insignem ac prorsus incomparabilem vtilitatem fructumque ex hoc libro credentibus efflorescentem æstimare licet. Proponit enim eum , qui omnis salutis nostræ principium & finis est,Christum scilicet,in cuius cognitione cardo æternæ felicitatis vertitur, dicente ipso Christo : Hæc est vita æterna, vt cognoscant te solum verum Deum,& quem misisti Iesum Christum cap. 17. v. 3.
units.tr: III. The principal proposition and summary of the whole is that Jesus Christ is the true Son of God, set forth to the world for redemption, so that believing in him we may have eternal life. This is clear from ch. 20:31: "These things are written that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have eternal life in his name." From this we may also judge the remarkable and utterly incomparable usefulness and fruit that flourish from this book for believers. For it sets before us him who is the beginning and end of all our salvation, namely Christ, in whose knowledge the hinge of eternal happiness turns, Christ himself saying: "This is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent," ch. 17:3.

units.la: IV Idea orationis grauis est , tum propter materia quæ explicanda est , tum propter phrasin,quæ concinnitatem habet ; breuitatem perspicuam,amplitudinem, & cælestem indubitatamque veritatem. Nam res diuinas ante Ioannem nemo mortalium sic ausus est explicare. Nemo generationem Filij Dei sic exposuit. Iesaias exclamat,& stupens hæret: Generationem eius quis enarrabit ? Iesa : 53. 8. quasi verbis & oratione idonea destituetur. Ioannes autem magna grauitate tantam rem breui commate explicat : In principio erat Sermo ille , & Sermo ille erat apud Deum : eratque ille Sermo Deus cap.1. v. 1.
units.tr: IV. The character of the discourse is weighty, both because of the matter to be explained and because of the phrasing, which has a fine balance, a clear brevity, a largeness, and a heavenly and undoubted truth. For before John no mortal dared to explain divine things in this way. No one set out the generation of the Son of God so. Isaiah cries out and stands amazed: "Who shall declare his generation?" Isa. 53:8, as if he were left without words and a fitting discourse. But John, with great gravity, explains so great a matter in a brief clause: "In the beginning was that Word, and that Word was with God, and that Word was God," ch. 1:1.

units.la: DISTRIBVTIO.
units.tr: DISTRIBUTION.

units.la: Iuvat & lubet hic praemittere Methodum Euangelij S. Ioannis a D. Friderico Beurhusio, Scholae Tremoniane quondam Rectore, magno iudicio delineatam & a nobis maioris perspicuitatis causa interpolatam; cuius manuductione universam Scripti praesentis œconomiam, uno brevique obtutu intueri, & in antecedentium Euangelistarum lectione felicius versari liceat.
units.tr: It is a pleasure and a delight to set down here in advance the Method of the Gospel of St John, outlined with great judgment by Dr Friedrich Beurhus, once Rector of the school at Tremonia, and by us improved for the sake of greater clarity; with its guidance the reader may take in at a single brief glance the whole plan of the present writing, and may more profitably engage in reading the Evangelists who went before.

units.la: METHODUS EVANGELII S. Ioannis.
units.tr: THE METHOD OF THE GOSPEL OF ST JOHN.

units.la: I. Occasio & summa.
units.tr: I. Occasion and summary.

units.la: CUM pestilentissimae, & de Christi divini-tate, & de salute obtinenda, haereses dissemina-rentur, S. Iohannes divini Spiritus instinctu ac piorum fratrum rogatu, ita post caeteros Euan-gelistas suum hoc de Iesu Christo Euangelium descripsit, ut singulari diligentia per totam hi-storiam, tum Christi personam, ac praecipuè divinitatem asserendo, & officium ; tum saluber-rimas de salute obtinenda conciones doctrinas-que explicarit.
units.tr: WHEN the most pestilential heresies, concerning both the divinity of Christ and the obtaining of salvation, were spreading, St John, moved by the divine Spirit and at the request of pious brothers, wrote this Gospel concerning Jesus Christ after the other Evangelists. He wrote it so that, throughout the whole history, he might with singular diligence both assert the person of Christ, especially his divinity, and set out his office, and explain the most wholesome sermons and teachings on obtaining salvation.

units.la: 2. Propositum seu Quaestio principalis.
units.tr: 2. Purpose, or the principal question.

units.la: Etsi historica est explicatio, cui una quaedam quaestio non videatur esse proposita: tamen hic omnia ad unum certum scopum referuntur, qui & initio proponitur & passim saepe infertur, si-cut etiam capite 20.v.30.& 31. apertissimè com-monstratur,nempe haec quaestio:
units.tr: Although the explanation is historical, and no single question seems to be proposed in it, yet here everything is referred to one certain aim. This aim is stated at the beginning, is often repeated throughout, and is most plainly shown in chapter 20, verses 30 and 31. The question is this:

units.la: AN IESUS NAZARETHANUS, Mariae filius, sit verus Deus & homo, ideoque promissus Messias, cuius fide homines, serventur?
units.tr: WHETHER JESUS OF NAZARETH, the son of Mary, is true God and man, and therefore the promised Messiah, by whose faith men are saved?

units.la: Constituitur & disseritur affirmatè argumētis praecipuè consentaneis, quæ sæpius quidem ut in historia fieri solet, axiomatico iudicio enunciantur; aliquando etiam syllogismo con-cluduntur: tota autem explicatio in verae me-thodi ordinem redacta est.
units.tr: This is set up and argued affirmatively, chiefly by arguments that fit the matter. As is usual in history, these are stated by way of axiomatic judgment, though sometimes they are also concluded in syllogisms. The whole explanation, however, is arranged in the order of a true method.

units.la: PARTES VNIVERSÆ METHODI duæ principales non obscurè distingui possunt:
units.tr: THE TWO MAIN PARTS OF THE WHOLE METHOD can be clearly distinguished:

units.la: PRIOR est generalis comprehensio, tum quaestionis de Persona & officio Christi, tum praecipuorum argumentorum, quibus ea de-monstratur, ab initio capitis primi, ad eiusdem versum 19. ALTERA est totius particularis vitae ac rerum gestarum Christi explicatio.
units.tr: The FIRST is a general survey, both of the question concerning the person and office of Christ and of the chief arguments by which it is proved, from the beginning of chapter 1 to verse 19 of the same chapter. The SECOND is an explanation of the whole particular life and deeds of Christ.

units.la: De Prima.
units.tr: Concerning the First.

units.la: In prima parte tanquam Exordio omnia definiente, PRIMO Natura divina tum essentialibus suis proprietatibus (liceat nobis hic ra-tionionis argumentis balbutire, & de Deo, augustissimâ maiestate omnia longissimè superante, cùm melius non possimus, humanarum artium terminis agere) per adiunctam æternitatem, relatum Patrem,coæternum, & propriam ipsius naturalem lucem vitamq; vivificantem: tum effectis, scil: creatione, illuminatione,& adoptione iustificationeque hominum demon-stratur,vbi sic officium etiam continetur: v. 1. vsque ad 6. Interponitur & testimonium Baptistæ eiusque a d sparato differentia: itemque ad-iuncta dissimilia, tum spernentium, tum recipientium. pientium oblatam lucem, usque ad v. 14. DEINDE Natura humana & maiestatis patefactio (quae frequens per miracula in historia deinceps) attingitur, & experientia arguitur, v. 14. inde repetitur testimonium Iohannis, tum de divina, tum de humana natura. v. 15.
units.tr: In the first part, as a prologue that defines everything, FIRST, the divine nature is shown, both by its essential properties (let me here stammer with the arguments of reason, and, since we cannot do better, speak of God, who far surpasses all things in his most august majesty, in the terms of human arts), through its attached eternity, the Father who is related to the Son, the co-eternal Son, and his own natural light and life-giving life. Then it is shown by its effects, namely creation, illumination, and the adoption and justification of men. Here the office too is contained, from verse 1 to verse 6. The testimony of the Baptist is interposed, and the difference between him and Christ, as well as the accompanying circumstances, both of those who spurn and of those who receive the light offered, up to verse 14. THEN the human nature and the manifestation of his majesty (which later becomes frequent through miracles in the history) is touched on and proved by experience, verse 14. From there the testimony of John is repeated, both concerning the divine and concerning the human nature, verse 15.

units.la: Tum officium rursum explicatur, & quidè per dissimilitudinem Mosis, v. 16. 17. & 19.
units.tr: Then the office is explained again, and indeed by way of contrast with Moses, verses 16, 17 and 19.

units.la: Atque ita in hoc quasi ingressu summa argumenta & semina universae deinceps explicationis continentur: sequitur
units.tr: And so in this, as it were, entrance the main arguments and the seeds of the whole explanation that follows are contained. There follows

units.la: DE ALTERA PARTE IN EXplicatione particulari.
units.tr: CONCERNING THE SECOND PART, IN THE PARTICULAR EXPLANATION.

units.la: Altera deinceps est tota Christi vitae ac rerum gestarum explicatio: qua plurima deinceps, & de persona, & de officio Christi, atque ita de doctrinae sacrae capitibus, argumenta, tum simpliciter explicantur, (unde pij syllogisticas conclusiones extruere possunt) tum syllogismis etiam concluduntur.
units.tr: The second part is then the whole explanation of the life and deeds of Christ. In it very many things, both concerning the person and concerning the office of Christ, and so concerning the heads of sacred doctrine, are explained as arguments (from which the godly can build syllogistic conclusions), and are also concluded in syllogisms.

units.la: HÆC AVTEM RVRSVS PER-spicuæ explicationis & memoriæ causa in duas partes distingui queat.
units.tr: THESE PARTS, AGAIN, can be distinguished into two, for the sake of a clear explanation and of memory.

units.la: Prior est, de publica Christi vita & functione, qua se docendo & miracula edendo patefecit.
units.tr: The first is concerning the public life and office of Christ, by which he revealed himself through teaching and working miracles.

units.la: Secunda est in acerbissima passione, & gloriosissimo triumpho.
units.tr: The second is concerning his most bitter passion and his most glorious triumph.

units.la: Prior specialis pars.
units.tr: The First Particular Part.

units.la: Hic tria sunt praecipua argumentorum genera, quae non ita praecisè ordine distinguuntur. sed opportunè passim miscentur. 1. A coelesti Dei Patris & angelorum testimonio, quod ab aliis apertius explicatur: itemque praecursoris, ac discipulorum adiuncto comitatu testimo-nioque. 11 Ab effecto, scilicet, doctrina Euan-gelij tum in concionibus, tum in disputationi-bus & confessionibus privatim & publicè. 111 Etiam ab effecto proprio, scilicet in miraculis edendis: quo etiam illa Dei propria pertinent, Scrutari corda, omnia scire, &c.
units.tr: Here there are three chief kinds of arguments, which are not distinguished in such a precise order but are opportunely mixed together throughout. (1) From the heavenly testimony of God the Father and of the angels, which is explained more openly by others; likewise from the testimony and accompanying company of the forerunner and of the disciples. (2) From the effect, namely the teaching of the Gospel, both in sermons and in disputations and confessions, privately and publicly. (3) Also from a proper effect, namely in the working of miracles, to which belong also those things that are proper to God: to search the hearts, to know all things, and so on.

units.la: Ac de his in vetere foedere erant oracula edi-ta: quae sunt fundamenta & propositiones syllo-gisticae: Euangelica historia, vspiam aliquando illa fundamenta attingens, assumtiones explicat, & aliquando complexiones, vel ab ipso Christo, vel ab aliis, imò aliquando etiam à Sa-thana inuito & fraudulento, expressas addit. In aliis Euangelistis praecipuè Baptismus, Transf-figuratio & apertius Patris testimonium acce-dunt, vt in altera etiam parte institutio Baptismi & Coenae.
units.tr: And concerning these, oracles had been given in the Old Covenant. These are the foundations and the syllogistic propositions. The Gospel history, wherever it at some point touches on those foundations, explains the assumptions, and sometimes adds the complete syllogisms, expressed either by Christ himself or by others, or even sometimes by Satan, unwilling and deceitful. In the other Evangelists, chiefly the Baptism, the Transfiguration and the more open testimony of the Father are added, as in the second part also the institution of Baptism and of the Supper.

units.la: Hæc igitur particularis explicatio, v.19 cap.I. à praecursoris Baptistæ testimonio palam edito in-choatur, vbi etiam Dei testimonium singulariter[?] Baptistæ patefactum continetur, & de Baptismo attin-gitur. Vbi tum Baptistæ interrogati confessio, suique à Christo distinctio, tum apertior etiam ad suos discipulos Christo adiungendos concio. Hinc est discipulorum vocatio & comitatus. Atque ita paulatim doctrina & miracula miscentur, ordineque exponuntur, continuata hac explicatione ad caput. 12. A, xii[?] deinceps capite ad 18. est transitus & praeparatio ad secundam explicationis specialis partem. partem in CHRISTI tum vnctione, tum regio in vrbem ingressu, & hominum approbatione, tum saluberrimis precationibus & concionibus, tum cœna (quæ attingitur) ac pedum lotione, tum admonitione prædictioneque de proditore, cap. 13. A capite vero 14. ad 18. saluberrimæ illæ conciones & precationes præcipuè ad discipulos confirmandos continuantur. Atque ita hæc partim ad primam partem, vt conciones: partim ad secundam pertinent.
units.tr: This particular explanation therefore begins at chapter 1, verse 19, with the openly given testimony of the forerunner, the Baptist, where also the testimony of God, singularly revealed to the Baptist, is contained, and Baptism is touched on. There is the confession of the Baptist when questioned, and his distinction from Christ, and then a more open sermon to bring his disciples to Christ. Hence comes the calling and company of the disciples. And so gradually teaching and miracles are mixed together and set out in order, and, this explanation continuing to chapter 12, from chapter 12 on to chapter 18 there is a transition and preparation for the second part of the particular explanation. CHRIST's anointing, his royal entry into the city, and the approval of the people, the most wholesome prayers and sermons, the supper (which is touched on) and the washing of feet, and the warning and prediction concerning the traitor, chapter 13. From chapter 14 to chapter 18 those most wholesome sermons and prayers are continued, chiefly to strengthen the disciples. And so these things pertain partly to the first part, as the sermons, and partly to the second.

units.la: Secunda, specialis explicationis pars est, tum in acerbissima, ad hominum redemptionem Passione, tum in gloriosissimo, ad eorundem iustitiam, victoriæ triumpho.
units.tr: The second, particular part of the explanation is both in the most bitter Passion, for the redemption of men, and in the most glorious triumph of victory, for their righteousness.

units.la: 1. Passio est, tum in comprehensione & iudiciali actione: tum in eductione, & crucifixione: vbi passim quæ tam interne, quam externe perpessus sit, spectanda. Variè autem ista causis, effectis subiectisque & adiunctis explicantur à cap. 18. ad v. 38. capitis 19.
units.tr: 1. The Passion is both in the arrest and the judicial action, and in the leading out and the crucifixion, where what he suffered, both inwardly and outwardly, is to be observed throughout. These things are explained in various ways, with their causes, effects, subjects and circumstances, from chapter 18 to verse 38 of chapter 19.

units.la: 2. Gloriosissimus triumphus est in aperta augustissimæ maiestatis vsurpatione, vt tum in honorifica Sepultura, ac à morte Resurrectione, tum in magnifica ad cœlos Ascensione, ac ad dextram Sessione: quæ ab aliis plenè exponuntur. Sepultura capite 19. extremo efficientibus magnis viris, subiecto loco & adiunctis exponitur. Resurrectio tum adiunctis, vt tempore & testibus reipsa experientibus, tum effectis Christi sæpius apparentis, colloquentis, rursum instituentis, Spiritum sanctum dantis, Apostolosque mittentis, atque ita certissima Thomæ cæterorumque experientia explicatur, clauditurque apertissimè indicato historiæ scopo, id est principali quæstione cap. 20. & cap. 21. alia etiam miraculi & doctrinæ consolationisque singularis experientia additur, historiaque testimonio Apostoli & significatione plurium rerum à Christo gestarum claudiuntur. Ascensio quod à cæteris perspicuè explicata esset, à S. Ioanne tantum vspiam attingitur.
units.tr: 2. The most glorious triumph consists in the open assumption of his most august majesty, both in the honourable burial and in resurrection from death, and in the magnificent ascension to heaven and sitting at the right hand. These are fully expounded by others. The burial is set out at the end of chapter 19, with the great men as agents, and the place and circumstances as the subject. The resurrection is explained both by its circumstances, such as the time and the witnesses who actually experienced it, and by the effects of Christ, who often appeared, talked, instituted again, gave the Holy Spirit, and sent out the Apostles, and so the most certain experience of Thomas and the others is explained and most plainly concluded, with the stated aim of the history, that is, the principal question, in chapter 20 and chapter 21. Another experience of a singular miracle, teaching and consolation is added, and the history is closed by the testimony of the Apostle and by the indication of many things done by Christ. The ascension, which the others had explained plainly, is touched on only here and there by St John.

units.la: Hæc igitur rudior quædam & scholastica Euangelicæ huius Methodi, à generalibus, per media, ad postrema progredientis adumbratio fuerit, ad Christi personam & officium patefaciendum accommodata: in qua doctrinæ Christianæ capita passim in Christi disputationibus, sermonibus & concionibus speciatim distinguuntur.
units.tr: This, then, is a rather rough and schoolish outline of this Gospel method, which proceeds from the general, through the middle, to the last things. It is adapted to disclosing the person and office of Christ, and in it the heads of Christian doctrine are distinguished, in particular, throughout Christ's disputations, discourses and sermons.

units.la: Hactenus Analysis Beurhusiana: sequitur
units.tr: Thus far the analysis of Beurhusius. There follows

units.la: PLENIOR HVIVS LIBRI ANALYSIS, in capitum, tum omnium coherentia, tum singulorum distributione.
units.tr: A FULLER ANALYSIS OF THIS BOOK, covering both the coherence of the chapters with one another and the division of each chapter.

units.la: PARTES EVANGELII secundum Iohannem duæ sunt principales. PRIMA est Exordium per prolepsin seu anticipationem quandam, summam eorum quæ toto hoc libro tractantur, complexum. ALTERA habet pleniorem vitæ Christi descriptionem, in historia ipsius doctrinæ, miraculorum, mortis & resurrectionis.
units.tr: The Gospel according to John has two main parts. The FIRST is an Exordium, a kind of anticipation or prolepsis that gathers up in summary form the matters treated throughout the whole book. The SECOND gives a fuller account of Christ's life, in the story of his teaching, his miracles, his death and his resurrection.

units.la: DE PRIMA PARTE.
units.tr: ON THE FIRST PART.

units.la: PRIMA pars est quoddam velut Exordium, summa definitione, omnia quæ sigillatim deinceps exponuntur comprehendens, de Chri-sti persti persona & officio, deque vita ipsius priva- ta, nec non de primitiis ministerij ipsius & vocatione quorundam discipulorum:cap primo.
units.tr: The first part is, as it were, a certain Exordium, which, in a summary definition, comprehends everything that is afterwards set out one by one. It concerns the person and office of Christ, his private life, and the first beginnings of his ministry and the calling of certain disciples: chapter 1.

units.la: CAPITIS primi partes tres sunt: Prima agit de Christi potissimum Personam, usque ad v.15. Secunda, de Officio praecipue ex variis Baptistae testimoniis, usque ad v.35. Tertia, quomodo in Christi cognitionem discipuli quidam peruenerint, usque ad finem capitis.
units.tr: The first chapter has three parts. The first deals chiefly with the person of Christ, to verse 15. The second, concerning his office, principally from the various testimonies of the Baptist, to verse 35. The third, how certain disciples came to the knowledge of Christ, to the end of the chapter.

units.la: Prima pars. Iohannes alius cæteris Euangelistis suum librum exorsus, recta principalem Euangelij sui statum & scopum aggreditur, dum Christi, cuius historiam scripturus est, personam & officium respectu diuinitatis describit, parique officij eius praecipuum scopum indicat, ut quo dirigendus sit sequentis historiae intellectus, & quis inde ad nos redeat fructus intelligamus, adeoque auide legamus, & diligenter omnia perdendamus. Christi autem aeternam Deitatem astruit, dum ipsum & aeternum, & Dei nomine insignem, & rerum omnium conditorem, viuificatorem, & vnicum humani generis illuminatorem introducit, atque ita ab aeternitate eius, operibus, officiis, ac beneficiis Diuinitatem ipsius euincit.
units.tr: The first part. John, unlike the other evangelists, begins his book and at once takes up the principal state and purpose of his Gospel. He describes the person and office of Christ, whose history he is going to write, with respect to his divinity, and so indicates the chief aim of his office, so that we may understand by what direction the meaning of the following history is to be guided, and what fruit comes back to us from it, and so that we may read it eagerly and ponder everything carefully. He asserts the eternal Deity of Christ, presenting him as eternal, marked with the name of God, the creator and quickener of all things, and the one enlightener of the human race. Thus from his eternity, his works, offices and benefits he proves his divinity.

units.la: Secunda parte tradit doctrinam praecipue de Christi Officio, testimonio Iohannis praecursoris comprobatam, qui cum in summa esset apud Iudaeos auctoritate, utpote non solum vitae sanctimonia insignis, sed propheticis insuper elogiis ac vaticiniis commendatus tanquam πρόδρομος Messiae: Ideo cursum ministerij eius copiosius describit, & testimonia ipsius de Christo diligenter annotat. Recitantur autem tria Iohannis de Christo testimonia; primum est generale ex illius diuersis concionibus de-sumtum; ubi etiam varia recenset Christi benefi-cia, quæ hominibus contulit, qua item fortuna veni-ens in hunc mundum fit exceptus. a v. 15. usque ad v. 19. Secundum speciale est, quod Iohannes de-dit Christo in celebri illa legatione, ad ipsum missa ex Metropoli sciscitatum an ipse esset Messias, aut quisnam tandem ei docendi & baptizandi autori-tatem dedisset. Scopus legationis est, Ioanni Ba-ptistæ titulum Messiæ obliquè attribuere; sed ipse magna gratuitate hunc & alios ipsi oblatos titulos constanter respuit, ac Messiæ titulum Christo conseruat in turba adhuc latenti: usque ad v. 29. Tertium testimonium itidem speciale est, quia præsente Christo est exhibitum turbis. Scopus & summa testimonij huius est: Christum ve-rum mundi redemptorem esse: patefactum Io-hanni vero & infallibili signo cælitus, in testi-monium, quod verus sit Dei Filius: usq; ad v. 35.
units.tr: The second part sets out the teaching chiefly concerning the office of Christ, confirmed by the testimony of John the forerunner. Since John held great authority among the Jews, being not only remarkable for the holiness of his life but also commended by prophetic praises and prophecies as the forerunner of the Messiah, John describes at some length the course of his ministry and carefully records his testimonies about Christ. Three testimonies of John about Christ are recounted. The first is a general one, drawn from his various sermons; there he also lists the various benefits of Christ that he bestowed on men, and how he was received when he came into this world: from verse 15 to verse 19. The second is special, which John gave concerning Christ on the famous occasion of the embassy sent to him from the capital, asking whether he himself was the Messiah, or who then had given him the authority to teach and baptize. The purpose of the embassy was to attribute indirectly to John the Baptist the title of Messiah; but with great candour he constantly rejects this title and the others offered to him, and in the crowd, where Christ is still hidden, he reserves the title of Messiah for Christ: to verse 29. The third testimony is likewise special, because it was given to the crowds in the presence of Christ. The purpose and substance of this testimony is that Christ is the true redeemer of the world, made known to John by an infallible sign from heaven, as a witness that he is the true Son of God: to verse 35.

units.la: Tertia pars, habet Quartum Iohannis de Chri-sto testimonium, quo exponit eadem coram discipu-lis, quæ prius aliquoties coram turbis est testatus. Quo permouentur duo discipuli, vt relicto Iohanne Christum sequantur, manentque eadem die apud ipsum: & Simonem Petrum mox eidem Christo ad-ducunt, qui benigne (vt illi prius) ab eo excipitur: usque ad v. 44. Vocati igitur iam sunt tres, An-dreas, Ioannes, & Simon, illi duo inuitati ab ipso Baptista, Simon autem à fratre Andrea excitatus est. His tribus adhuc duo iam adduntur, Philip-pus & Nathanael. Ille à Christo immediatè vo-catus: hic autem à Philippo adductus ad Chri-stum, usq; ad v. 48. quem vt receperat Christus, & in fide fide confirmarit bene proficientem, declaratur a v. 48.usque ad finem cap.
units.tr: The third part contains the fourth testimony of John about Christ, in which he sets out before his disciples the same things he had already several times testified before the crowds. By this, two disciples are moved to leave John and follow Christ, and they remain with him that same day; and they soon bring Simon Peter to the same Christ, who receives him kindly, as he had received the others: to verse 44. Three are now called: Andrew, John and Simon; the two were invited by the Baptist himself, while Simon was roused by his brother Andrew. To these three two more are now added, Philip and Nathanael. Philip was called immediately by Christ; Nathanael was brought to Christ by Philip: to verse 48. Since Christ received him, and confirmed him in faith as he was making good progress, this is declared from verse 48 to the end of the chapter.

units.la: PARS SECVNDA.
units.tr: PART TWO.

units.la: CHRISTVM esse verum Deum & hominem, hoc est Messiam, qui Messias Filius Dei, Deus de Deo, & homo verus, Redemtor humani generis sit, primo capite est ostensum.
units.tr: It has been shown in the first chapter that Christ is true God and man, that is, the Messiah, who as the Messiah is the Son of God, God of God and true man, the Redeemer of the human race.

units.la: IAM ad res Christi gestas propius accedit. Nam Christum Baptismi sacro quasi inauguratum, cum comitatu discipulorum quatuor in Christi cognitionem deductorum, in publicum producit, & qualiter haec Persona, Filius Dei θεάνθρωπος[?], Officio suo sit perfuncta distincte explicat: Nam officia personas determinant, sicut propria & accidentia individua describunt. Proprium autem Christi officium est, destruere opera Diaboli. Haec destruxit, primum doctrina & miraculis, tum passione, tandem etiam Resurrectione.
units.tr: Now he comes closer to the deeds of Christ. For he brings Christ forward in public, as one just installed by Baptism, with a company of four disciples led into the knowledge of Christ, and he sets out clearly how this Person, the Son of God, God-man [θεάνθρωπος], has carried out his office. For offices define persons, just as proper and accidental qualities describe individuals. Now the proper office of Christ is to destroy the works of the Devil. He destroyed them first by teaching and miracles, then by his passion, and finally also by his resurrection.

units.la: Has officij partes S. Iohannes secundum Quatuor Christi profectiones Hierosolymam susceptas distinxit. Hinc huius
units.tr: St John distinguished these parts of his office according to the four journeys of Christ to Jerusalem, which he undertook. Hence this

units.la: SECVNDÆ PARTIS MEMBRA sunt quatuor.
units.tr: THE MEMBERS OF THIS SECOND PART are four.

units.la: Primum continet narrationem profectionis Christi Hierosolymam susceptae, ad festum Paschatis: cap. 2. 3. & 4.
units.tr: The first contains the account of the journey of Christ to Jerusalem for the feast of the Passover: chapters 2, 3 and 4.

units.la: Secundum est de profectione ad eandem Metropolin, ad festum pentecostes: cap. 5 & 6.
units.tr: The second concerns the journey to the same metropolis for the feast of Pentecost: chapters 5 and 6.

units.la: Tertium, ad festum tabernaculorum usque ad cap. 12.
units.tr: The third runs to the feast of Tabernacles, up to chapter 12.

units.la: Quartum habet profectionem Christi vltimam ad Pascha-tis solennitatem institutam, in quam incidit Passio & mors eius, à cap. 12. vsque ad libri huius finem.
units.tr: The fourth has the last journey of Christ to the solemnity of the Passover, the one in which his passion and death fell, from chapter 12 to the end of this book.

units.la: PRIMVM MEMBRVM DE PRI-ma Christi Hierosolymam profectione ad festum Paschatis.
units.tr: THE FIRST MEMBER, CONCERNING THE FIRST JOURNEY OF CHRIST TO JERUSALEM FOR THE FEAST OF THE PASSOVER.

units.la: Huius itineris notantur partes tres: Profectio è Cana Galilææ, ( vbi ex a-qua vinum fecerat ) ad vrbem Hie-rosolymorum, & Templum Domini,quod repurgat & reformat:cap.2. Commoratio, durante illo festo Pa-schatis: Disputatio Christi cum Ni-codemo de Regeneratione: Item quæstio de Purificatione seu Baptif-mo agitata, in egressu ex vrbe, in agrum Iordani vicinum : cap. 3. Reuersio per Samariam, vbi collo-quium cum Samaritana, de vera re-ligione: postea in Galilæam dela-tus, Reguli filium pristinæ valetu-dini restituit : cap. 4.
units.tr: Three parts of this journey are noted: the departure from Cana of Galilee, where he had made wine from water, to the city of Jerusalem and the Temple of the Lord, which he cleanses and restores (chapter 2); the stay during that Passover feast, with Christ's disputation with Nicodemus about regeneration, and also the question of purification or baptism, debated as they went out of the city into the country near the Jordan (chapter 3); and the return through Samaria, where there is a conversation with the Samaritan woman about true religion, after which he was brought into Galilee and restored to health the son of a royal official (chapter 4).

units.la: Capite igitur secundo duæ historiæ propo-nuntur : prior de nuptiis in Cana celebratis, in quibus Christus aquam in vinum conuertens edidit primum miraculum: vsque ad v. 12. posterior de reformatione templi Hierosolymitani, quam Christus aggressurus suum officium,suscipit, atque ita locum suis concionibus ac ministerio destinatum,à nummulariorum profanis vsibus repurgat.
units.tr: In chapter 2, therefore, two stories are set forth: the first, about the wedding celebrated at Cana, in which Christ, by turning water into wine, performed his first miracle, up to verse 12; the second, about the reform of the Temple of Jerusalem, which Christ, about to undertake his office, takes in hand, and thus cleanses the place destined for his sermons and ministry from the profane uses of the money-changers.

units.la: III Capite partes principales duæ sunt: Prior est colloquium Christi cum Nicodemo, cuius principrincipalis quæstio vel propositio est, de via consequendi salutem æternam. Vbi Christus ostendit opus esse quandam Regenerationē, quæ hactenus mundo fuit incognita, ideoque docet unde nobis expectanda sit, per quid nobis conferatur, quomodo a nobis percipi possit, quis eam nobis det, quod sit illius organum, hoc est causa media, quid nobis detur: usque ad v.22. Posterior pars est quæstio de Purificatione & Baptismo inter Iudæos & discipulos Ioannis primum agitari cœpta, deinde vero Ioanni a discipulis excutienda proposita, una cum responso Ioannis sese excusantis, ac ostendentis ita fieri oportere. Hinc in laudes Christi plenius descendit, seque iterum plane illius pedibus subiicit.
units.tr: In chapter 3 there are two main parts. The first is the conversation of Christ with Nicodemus, whose chief question or proposition concerns the way to obtain eternal salvation. Here Christ shows that a certain regeneration is necessary, which until now was unknown to the world; therefore he teaches whence we are to expect it, through what it is conferred on us, how it can be received by us, who gives it to us, what is its instrument, that is, its means of cause, and what is given to us: up to verse 22. The second part is the question about purification and baptism, which first began to be debated between the Jews and the disciples of John, and then was put to John by his disciples to be resolved, together with John's answer, excusing himself and showing that it must be done so. From this he descends more fully into praise of Christ, and once again plainly submits himself at his feet.

units.la: Caput quartum in duas partes principales distingui potest: In prima commemorat quid Christus ex Iudæa per Samariam transiens in civitate Sichar egerit, & quomodo a Samaritanis eius loci sit exceptus: ubi colloquium eius cum Samaritana de aqua saliente ad vitam æternam: usque ad v.43. Posteriore parte describit Ioannes, quomodo Christus in patria sua Nazareth reliquisque Galilæa locis acceptus fuerit, & quomodo Regulí cuiusdam filium febricitantem sanarit.
units.tr: The fourth chapter can be divided into two main parts. In the first, he recounts what Christ did as he passed through Judea and Samaria into the city of Sychar, and how he was received there by the Samaritans; here is his conversation with the Samaritan woman about the living water springing up to eternal life, up to verse 43. In the latter part John describes how Christ was received in his homeland of Nazareth and in the other places of Galilee, and how he healed the feverish son of a certain royal official.

units.la: SECUNDUM HISTORIÆ VITÆ Christi membrum: qua continetur altera peregrinatio Hierosolymam, ad festum Pentecostes, & quid illic, ac alibi memorabile gesserit.
units.tr: THE SECOND PART OF THE HISTORY OF CHRIST'S LIFE: which contains the second journey to Jerusalem, for the feast of Pentecost, and what he did there and elsewhere that is worth remembering.

units.la: Prima Christi peregrinatio Hierosolymam admodum fuit fructuosa: Nam & templum repurgavit: & Nicodemum convertit ex Pharisæis. In reditu quoque mulierem cum ciuibus in Sichar ad poenitentiam adduxit. Demum reguli filium Capernaumi ipse absens curauit. Nunc altera describitur peregrinatio in urbem primariam, continens tria miracula, quibus ubique sua illustris adducitur doctrina.
units.tr: Christ's first journey to Jerusalem was very fruitful. For he cleansed the temple and converted Nicodemus, a Pharisee. On his return he also brought a woman of Sychar, along with her fellow citizens, to repentance. Lastly, though absent, he healed the official's son at Capernaum. Now the second journey is described, to the chief city, containing three miracles by which his remarkable teaching is recommended everywhere.

units.la: Capitis v. partes duae sunt. 1. Christus e Galilaea, in quam relictis Iudææ finibus illum descendisse superiore capite Evangelista dixerat, nunc denuo festi celebrandi causa Hierosolymam ascendit. Vbi ad piscinam quandam Probaticae vicinam, hominem ab inueterato morbo liberat: usque ad v.17.
units.tr: Chapter 5 has two parts. (1) Christ, who had gone down from Galilee, having left the borders of Judea (as the Evangelist said in the previous chapter), now goes up to Jerusalem again to keep a feast. There, near a certain pool close to the Probatica, he frees a man from a long-standing disease: as far as verse 17.

units.la: 11 Continet apologiam Christi, qua factum illud suum aduersus Iudaeos defendens, & auctoritatem suam plenissime asserit, & Iudaeorum incredulitatem reprehendit.
units.tr: (2) It contains Christ's defence, in which he defends that deed of his against the Jews, asserts his authority most fully, and rebukes the unbelief of the Jews: verse 18 onward.

units.la: Sexti capitis partes sunt tres: 1 Descriptio miraculi in deserto editi, quo Dominus populi eum sequentis diligentiam pensaturus, quinque panibus & duobus piscibus ipsorum quinque millia sic pascit, ut plus tolleretur quam initio fuerat appositum,
units.tr: Chapter 6 has three parts. (1) A description of the miracle performed in the desert, in which the Lord, wishing to test the diligence of the people who followed him, feeds five thousand of them with five loaves and two fish, so that more was taken up than had been set out at the start,

units.la: usque ad v.16. II. Navigatio discipulorum noctura & periculosa, & eorundem per Christum miraculosè super mare ambulantem liberatio: usque ad v.22. III. Iudæi desiderio bonorum corporalium, quæ apud Christum, occasione præcedentis miraculi moti, quærebant, navali simul pedestrique itinere ad ipsum contendunt Capernaumum. Quod illorum peruersum studium reprehendens Dominus, ad spiritualem potius animæ cibum quærendum hortatur: vbi disputatio de carne Christi mystica fide manducanda describitur, & euentus disputationis sequitur, defectio nimirum Iudæorum, solis verè discipulis perseuerantibus.
