units.la: Capite duodecimo describitur primo martyrium Iacobi,fratris Iohannis. v.1. 2. Deinde liberatio Petri è carcere, vsque ad v.20. Tertio Exitus vitæ Herodis tragicus: vsque ad v. 24. quo versu de statu Ecclesiæ Hierosolymitanæ mentio fit. Quartò, reditus Pauli & Barnabæ Antiochiam, versu vltimo.
units.tr: In chapter 12 there is described, first, the martyrdom of James, brother of John, verses 1 and 2. Then the deliverance of Peter from prison, to verse 20. Third, the tragic end of Herod's life, to verse 24, in which verse mention is made of the state of the church at Jerusalem. Fourth, the return of Paul and Barnabas to Antioch, in the last verse.

units.la: HACTENUS de Apostolis communiter & in genere quædam scripsit Lucas: de nonnullis etiam quædam priuata, vt de Stephano, de Philippo, de Petro, de Pauli conuersione & fuga, de Iacobi maioris morte: iam narrabit.
units.tr: Hitherto Luke has written certain things about the Apostles in general and as a whole, and also certain private matters concerning some of them, such as Stephen, Philip, Peter, the conversion and flight of Paul, and the death of James the Elder; now he will relate...

units.la: DE DUOBUS APOSTOLIS adscititiis, Paulo & Barnaba, inprimis autem de Paulo, usque ad finem huius libri.
units.tr: Concerning the two apostles added by choice, Paul and Barnabas, and especially concerning Paul, to the end of this book.

units.la: SUPRA, cap. decimo, initium fecit Petrus recipiendi Gentes incircumcisas in Ecclesiam Dei: nunc vero iisdem solenniter duo Apostoli, Paulus & Barnabas destinantur: qui ipsis Euangelium Christi annuncient, atque in communionem bonorum caelestium recipiant. Hic igitur describitur Pauli, qui nondum habuit certum mandatum docendi gentes, nova vocatio & confirmatio & missio ad eas docendas; quas quanto cum fructu docuerit, quanto vitae periculo, quas molestias sustinuerit, quanta itinera sit emensus, quoties [?]captus, caesus, lapidatus, causam tamen Christi semper & ubique intrepide defenderit, luculenter docebit haec consequens historia, quae in quatuor peregrinationes Pauli distincta est.
units.tr: ABOVE, in chapter ten, Peter made a beginning of receiving the uncircumcised Gentiles into the Church of God. Now two apostles, Paul and Barnabas, are solemnly appointed for them: they are to announce the Gospel of Christ to them and receive them into fellowship in the heavenly goods. Here, then, is described Paul's new calling, confirmation and sending to teach the Gentles, though he did not yet have a definite commission to teach them. The following history, which is divided into Paul's four journeys, will clearly show with what fruit he taught them, at what peril to his life, what hardships he endured, how great the distances he travelled, how often he was seized, beaten and stoned, and yet how fearlessly he always and everywhere defended the cause of Christ.

units.la: DE PRIMA PAULI PERE-grinatione cum Barnaba.
units.tr: Concerning Paul's first journey, with Barnabas.

units.la: IN OMNI peregrinatione Pauli respiciendum est ad certas quasdam metas: sic enim negotium rectius intelligetur: ut: 1 quos habuerit comites peregrinationum: 2 unde peregrinetur: 3 per quae loca: 4 quid memorabile hinc inde effecerit, aut quid passus sit pro nomine Christi. Haec si requiras in prima peregrinatione, (quae describitur capite decimo tertio, decimo quarto & parte decimi quinti) 1 Comitem habuit iubente Spiritu S. Barnabam, qui qua occasione ab eo sit in altera separatus, cap.15. v. 35. ex sequentibus docetur. 11 Peregrinatio autem initium habuit ab Antiochena Ecclesia. Eadem meta est in secunda & tertia peregrinatione. Quarta in eo ab aliis variat, non ab Antiochia, sed ex Caesarea Romam usque supputatur. 3 Loca, & 4 gesta praecipua peregrinationis: Ab Antiochia pergunt in Seleuciam: hinc in Cyprum navigant, quam totam perambulant ab Oriente, initio facto à Salamine, ad Occasum usque in Paphos, ubi Paulus proconsulem Sergium Paulum conuertit. Refutatur hic Elymas Bariesus Magus. Antiochiam Pisidiae deveniunt: ubi per duo Sabbatha docet: cap. 14. Iconij docet, Lystris claudum curat, tandem redit Antiochiam: cap.15. quaestio de Circumcisione & Iustificatione oritur, propter quam Hierosolymam mittitur Paulus ad Apostolos.
units.tr: IN EVERY journey of Paul we must look to certain fixed goals, for in this way the matter will be understood more correctly: (1) who his companions on the journeys were; (2) from where he travelled; (3) through what places; (4) what memorable things he did there, or what he suffered for the name of Christ. If you ask these questions about the first journey (which is described in chapter thirteen, chapter fourteen and part of chapter fifteen): (1) he had as companion Barnabas, by the command of the Holy Spirit, and the occasion on which he was separated from him in the second journey is taught from what follows, in chapter 15, verse 35. (2) The journey had its beginning at the Church of Antioch. The same goal applies to the second and third journeys. The fourth differs from the others in that it is reckoned not from Antioch but from Caesarea to Rome. (3) and (4) The places and the chief deeds of the journey: from Antioch they go to Seleucia, and from there they sail to Cyprus, which they traverse entirely from east to west, beginning at Salamis and ending at Paphos, where Paul converts the proconsul Sergius Paulus. Here Elymas Bar-Jesus the magician is refuted. They come to Antioch in Pisidia, where for two Sabbaths he teaches. In Iconium he teaches; in Lystra he heals a lame man; at last he returns to Antioch. Chapter 15: a question arises about circumcision and justification, on account of which Paul is sent to the apostles at Jerusalem.

units.la: Cap. xiii. quatuor narrantur. Primum, profectio Pauli & Barnabae ad Gentes: usque ad v.5. Deinde quid egerint Salamine: v.5. Tertió, quid egerint Paphi: usque ad v, 13. Postremò, quid egerint Antiochiae in urbe Pisidiae.
units.tr: In chapter 13 four things are related. First, the departure of Paul and Barnabas to the Gentiles, down to verse 5. Next, what they did at Salamis: verse 5. Third, what they did at Paphos, down to verse 13. Last, what they did at Antioch in the city of Pisidia.

units.la: Cap. xiv. Continuatur historia legationis Pauli & Barnabae ad gentes: & narrantur quinque. Primum quid egerint ac perpessi sint Iconij: usque ad v.7. Deinde quid egerint & perpessi sint Lystris, usque ad v.21. Tertió, quid egerint Derbae, & iterum Lystris &c. usque ad v.24. Quartò, quid egerint Perga. v.24. & 25. Postremò, quid egerint Antiochiae Syriae, cum eo essent reversi.
units.tr: In chapter 14 the history of the mission of Paul and Barnabas to the Gentiles continues, and five things are related. First, what they did and suffered at Iconium, down to verse 7. Next, what they did and suffered at Lystra, down to verse 21. Third, what they did at Derbe, and again at Lystra, etc., down to verse 24. Fourth, what they did at Perga, verses 24 and 25. Last, what they did at Antioch in Syria, when they had returned to it.

units.la: Hactenus Satan Ecclesiam Dei perse-cutionibus im-pugnauerat: nunc eam alio modo deriuare co-natur, dum ipsam doctrinam corrumpere, & in ipsis visceribus Eccl.siæ bellum intestinum, hoc est dissensiones & hæreses excitare studuit: hinc docemur qua ratione ista controuersia in primi-tiua Ecclesia sit sopita & sublata.
units.tr: Until now Satan had assailed the Church of God with persecutions; now he tries to attack it in another way, seeking to corrupt the doctrine itself and to stir up internal war within the very bowels of the Church, that is, dissensions and heresies. Hence we are taught by what means this controversy was quieted and removed in the primitive Church.

units.la: Capite x v. duo narrantur. Primum, quomodo Concilium Hierosolymis celebratum sit per Apostolos propter Controuersiam Antiochiæ exortam de Circumcisione Gentium fidem Christianam amplexarum, & de Iustificatione, usque ad v. 35. Deinde, quomodo Paulus & Barnabas in dissidium sive discordiam inciderint propter Iohannem Marcum. Prior pars capitis ad primam adhuc profectionem pertinet, posterior vero ad secundam.
units.tr: In chapter 15 two things are related. First, how the Council was held at Jerusalem by the apostles on account of the controversy that arose at Antioch concerning the circumcision of Gentiles who had embraced the Christian faith, and concerning justification, down to verse 35. Then, how Paul and Barnabas fell into dissension or discord because of John Mark. The first part of the chapter still belongs to the first journey, but the latter part to the second.

units.la: DE SECUNDA PEREGRINA-tione Pauli cum Sila.
units.tr: Concerning Paul's second journey, with Silas.

units.la: QUID interiecto tempore à primæ peregrinationis fine usque ad initium secundæ actum sit, superior docuit historia de Concilio Apostolico. Hinc iam redit ad peregrinationes, quarum secunda quam cum Sila suscepit describitur à v. 36. capitis decimi quinti, usque ad caput decimum nonum. Nam dissidio inter Paulum & Barnabam orto, Barnabas Cyprum petit, assumto Marco. Paulus vero cum Sila in Syriam pergit, &c. Et sic Deus pro immensa sua sapientia & bonitate dissidium à Satana inter synceros Ecclesiæ ministros excitatum, in bonum finem convertit; hoc enim modo breui tempore per distractionem illam Apostolorū, plures Ecclesiæ visitatæ, confirmatæ & constitutæ sunt, quàm si coniuncti mansissent.
units.tr: WHAT was done in the interval between the end of the first journey and the beginning of the second, the earlier history of the Apostolic Council has taught. Now it returns to the journeys, of which the second, which he undertook with Silas, is described from verse 36 of chapter 15 to chapter 19. For after the dissension between Paul and Barnabas arose, Barnabas sought Cyprus, taking Mark with him, while Paul set out with Silas for Syria, and so on. And thus God, in his immense wisdom and goodness, turned to a good end the dissension that Satan had stirred up among the sincere ministers of the Church; for in this way, in a short time, through that separation of the apostles, more congregations were visited, strengthened and established than if they had remained together.

units.la: Ut igitur hactenus in historia peregrinationis prima narratum fuit, quid Paulus & Barnabas coniunctim effecerint: sic deinceps quid Paulus solus egerit, describitur. Pauli in secunda ipsius Peregrinatione cū Sila: eius Abitus ex Antiochia in Syriam ac Ciliciam, cap.15.v.36. & seqq: Commora-tio in Asia, in urbe Lystra & Troade: quibus etiam accedit profectio & statio Philippensis.cap.16. Græcia, in urbe Thessalo-nicensi, Beroeensi, & Athe-niensi.cap.17. Reditus, pręmissis duabus stationibus, Corinthiaca, & Ephesina: cap.18.
units.tr: Therefore, just as up to this point the history has related what Paul and Barnabas accomplished together in the first journey, so now what Paul alone did is described. In Paul's second journey with Silas: his departure from Antioch into Syria and Cilicia, chapter 15, verse 36 and following; his stay in Asia, in the cities of Lystra and Troas, to which is added also the journey and stay at Philippi, chapter 16; Greece, in the cities of Thessalonica, Berea and Athens, chapter 17; the return, with two stops, at Corinth and Ephesus, chapter 18.

units.la: Cap: XVI. Narratur primùm, quid egerit Paulus tum Lystris tum in cæteris urbibus illius regionis, in quibus antea cum Barnaba Ecclesias plan-tauerat, usque ad v. 6. Deinde quid Paulo acci-derit volenti Euangelium prædicare in Asia & Bi-thynia. v. 6. & 7. Tertiò quid ei acciderit Troa-de, à v. 8. usque ad duodecimi medium. Postremò quid egerit ac perpessus sit Philippis: à v. 11. usque ad finem.
units.tr: Chapter 16. It is related, first, what Paul did both at Lystra and in the other cities of that region, in which earlier with Barnabas he had planted churches, down to verse 6. Next, what happened to Paul when he wished to preach the Gospel in Asia and Bithynia, verses 6 and 7. Third, what happened to him at Troas, from verse 8 to the middle of verse 12. Last, what he did and suffered at Philippi, from verse 11 to the end.

units.la: Cap: XVII. Narratur quid Paulus egerit ac perpessus sit primùm Thessalonicæ, vbi Euangelium annunciat, sed diuerso apud diuersos auditores effectu: nam Iudæi infideles seditionem excitant in Paulum: eum Iason excipit, & pro eo fide inbet[?] non sine periculo: usque ad v. 10. Deinde Beroeae, quo Paulus noctu emittitur, usque ad v. 16. Postremo, Athenis: Athenienses ad ignoti Dei notitiam adducit: Dionysius Areopagita, Damaris mulier, & alii plures ad Christum convertuntur.
units.tr: Chapter 17. It is related what Paul did and suffered, first, at Thessalonica, where he announces the Gospel, but with different effects among different hearers: for the unbelieving Jews stir up sedition against Paul; Jason receives him, and stands surety for him, not without danger, down to verse 10. Then at Berea, from where Paul is sent away by night, down to verse 16. Last, at Athens: he leads the Athenians to the knowledge of the unknown God; Dionysius the Areopagite, the woman Damaris, and many others are converted to Christ.

units.la: Cum videret Paulus, se Athenis praedicando Evangelium Christi non ita multum proficere, alio migrandum iudicavit, ne multum temporis insumeret apud eos, qui doctrinam salutis fere tantum irridebant.
units.tr: When Paul saw that, by preaching the Gospel of Christ at Athens, he was not making much progress, he judged that he must move elsewhere, lest he spend much time among those who almost only mocked the doctrine of salvation.

units.la: Tria narrantur in XVIII capite. Primum, quid Paulus egerit ac perpessus sit Corinthi, ubi apud Aquilam & Priscillam diuertens Euangelium docet, docentem Dominum in visione solatur, & Corinthi sesquiennium moratus, coram Gallione, Romano Procunsule, frustra accusatur: usque ad v. 18. Deinde, quid idem egerit rediens Antiochiam Syriae, atque illinc rursum abiens, a v. 18. usque ad 23. Postremo, inseritur historiae Pauli narratio de quodam Apollo, quid ille vir potens in Scripturis, magno cum successu Ephesi docueris. Postrema haec pars huius capitis pertinet ad tertiae peregrinationis Paulinae initium.
units.tr: Three things are related in the eighteenth chapter. First, what Paul did and suffered at Corinth, where, staying with Aquila and Priscilla, he teaches the Gospel; the Lord, teaching him in a vision, comforts him; and after staying in Corinth a year and a half, he is falsely accused before Gallio, the Roman proconsul; down to verse 18. Then, what the same man did on returning to Antioch in Syria, and on leaving it again from there, from verse 18 to verse 23. Last, into the history of Paul is inserted the account of a certain Apollos, a man powerful in the Scriptures, who taught at Ephesus with great success. This last part of the chapter belongs to the beginning of Paul's third journey.

units.la: DE TERTIA S. PAVLI PEREGRINATIONE, propter Ephesios potissimum instituta.
units.tr: On the Third Journey of St Paul, undertaken chiefly on account of the Ephesians.

units.la: Huius peregrinationis notæ [?] A quo initium factum est, cap.18. v. 23. Per quem, seu loca per quæ iter fecit, & in quibus commoratus est in Abeundo: Statio Ephesina biennalis. cap.19. Redeundo: Statio Miletana præcipua est. cap.20. Adque, nempe Hierosolymam: ubi tri- plex conatus placādi Iudæos Facta, seu voti specie, c.21. Verbis, sive oratione habita ad Populum Iudaicū. cap.22. Magistratus & Iudices. cap.23. Cæsaream: occurrit hic Actio Paulus [?] Præside Felice. c.24. Festo. c.25. Rege Agrippa. c.26.
units.tr: The marks of this journey: it begins from where it was started, Acts 18:23. As to the places through which he travelled and where he stayed: on the outward way, the stay at Ephesus, lasting two years, Acts 19. On the return way, the stop at Miletus is the chief one, Acts 20. Then to Jerusalem, where there was a threefold attempt to placate the Jews: by a deed done in the form of a vow, Acts 21; by a speech delivered to the Jewish people, Acts 22; before the magistrates and judges, Acts 23. Then to Caesarea, where Paul is brought before Governor Felix, Acts 24; before Festus, Acts 25; before King Agrippa, Acts 26.

units.la: Cap. xix. narratur, quid Paulus egerit ac perpessus sit Ephesi, cùm eò è Syria esset reversus. Sunt autem septem principales istius narrationis partes. 1 Quid egerit Paulus cum duodecim quibusdam rudibus discipulis, usque ad v. 8. II Quomodo docuerit in schola Tyranni: usque ad v. 11. III Quomodo doctrinam suam confirmarit miraculis: v. 11. & 12. IV Quomodo doctrina & miracula ipsius asserta sint contra septem exorcistas, usque ad v. 18. V Efficacia ipsius doctrinae in multis auditorum. v. 18.19. & 20. VI Propositum Pauli proficiscendi Hierosolymam & Romam: Romam: v. 21. & 22. VII Tumultus contra Paulum & discipulos excitatus per Demetrium quendam aur fabrum.
units.tr: Chapter 19 relates what Paul did and suffered at Ephesus after he had returned there from Syria. There are seven principal parts to this narrative. I. What Paul did with twelve rough disciples, to verse 8. II. How he taught in the school of Tyrannus, to verse 11. III. How he confirmed his teaching with miracles, verses 11 and 12. IV. How his teaching and miracles were defended against seven exorcists, to verse 18. V. The effectiveness of his teaching in many of the hearers, verses 18, 19 and 20. VI. Paul's purpose of travelling to Jerusalem and Rome, verses 21 and 22. VII. The tumult raised against Paul and his disciples by a certain Demetrius, a silversmith.

units.la: Capite xx: Narrantur quatuor. Primùm, quibus itineribus Paulus Ephesò venerit Troadem, usque ad v. 7. Deinde, quid Troade egerit: quomodo nimirum sermonem in mediam noctem protendens, Eutychum quendam, ex tertia contignatione delapsum, & ex lapsu mortuum resuscitarit: usque ad v. 13. Tertiò, quibus itineribus venerit Miletum, usque ad v. 17. Postremò, quomodo Mileti Ephesinos Presbyteros officii sui admonuerit, ac quid sibi illisque expectandum sit, exposuerit: hinc fletus inter fideles ob discessum Pauli ortus.
units.tr: Chapter 20 relates four things. First, by what journeys Paul came from Ephesus to Troas, to verse 7. Then, what he did at Troas: namely, how, prolonging his preaching into the middle of the night, he raised to life Eutychus, a young man who had fallen from the third storey and died of the fall, to verse 13. Third, by what journeys he came to Miletus, to verse 17. Last, how at Miletus he admonished the Ephesian elders about their duty, and set out what awaited them and himself; hence the weeping among the faithful at Paul's departure.

units.la: Cap. xxi. Describitur primò quibus itineribus Paulus Mileto peruenerit Hierosolymam, & quomodo in illo itinere Philippum Evangelistam Cæsareæ accesserit: ubi etiam Paulum in vincula coniiciendum prædicit Agabus: usque ad v. 17. Deinde quid egerit atque perpessus sit Hierosolymis, ubi templum ingressus comprehenditur à Judæis, & per Lysiam Tribunum eisdem eripitur, ac duabus vincitur[?] catenis.
units.tr: Chapter 21. It first describes by what journeys Paul came from Miletus to Jerusalem, and how on that journey he visited Philip the evangelist at Caesarea, where Agabus also foretold that Paul would be bound with chains, to verse 17. Then it describes what he did and suffered at Jerusalem, where, having entered the temple, he is seized by the Jews, is snatched from them by Lysias the tribune, and is bound with two chains.

units.la: Voti species ad placundum Judæos Hierosolymis frustra suscepta esi[?] antecedente capite: alter nunc conatus describitur, etiam fruftraneus, nam oratione quantumuis longa & erudita nihil profecit: sed magis ea irritantur adversarii.
units.tr: The show of a vow, undertaken at Jerusalem in vain to placate the Jews, was described in the previous chapter. Now another attempt is described, equally fruitless: for however long and learned the speech, it achieved nothing, but rather the adversaries were roused the more.

units.la: Duo narrantur cap. xxii. 1. Sermo Pauli ad populum Hierosolymitanum, in quo voluit docere, se neque ex imprudentia in Christianismum incidisse, neque animi quadam leuitate impulsum fuisse, vt Religionem Christianam tam Gentibus, quam Iudæis prædicaret: sed miraculo diuino at-que cœlestibus reuelationibus eo perductum, & ne-cessario docere Euangelium de Christo, nisi Deo re-sistere velit: vsque ad v. 22. 11 Euenta sermonis Pauli nec dum ad finem perducti.
units.tr: Two things are related in chapter 22. 1. Paul's speech to the people of Jerusalem, in which he wished to show that he had fallen into Christianity neither through thoughtlessness, nor impelled by any levity of mind, so as to preach the Christian religion to Gentiles and Jews alike; but that he had been led to it by a divine miracle and heavenly revelations, and that he must necessarily teach the Gospel about Christ, unless he wished to resist God, to verse 22. II. The outcome of Paul's speech, which has not yet been brought to an end.

units.la: Cap. xxiii Trium dierum historia continetur. 1 Die coram Synedrio apologiam instituit, at colaphos recipit. Obiecta autem Assessoribus contentionis occasione, ipse elabitur, & in castra redu-citur. Secunda die noua fit coniuratio aduersus Paulum: at patescit hostium Pauli coniuratio, & effectu caret. Ea ipsa etiam nocte monitor & consolator Paulo Dominus astat: a v. 11. vsque ad v.32. Tertia die Paulus Cæsaream ad Felicem transf-mittitur.
units.tr: Chapter 23 contains the history of three days. On the first day he makes his defence before the Sanhedrin, but receives blows. Then, the assessors having been set against him by the occasion of the dispute, he himself slips away and is led back into the camp. On the second day a new plot is made against Paul; but the conspiracy of Paul's enemies is revealed and comes to nothing. In that same night the Lord stands by Paul as his admonisher and comforter, verses 11 to 32. On the third day Paul is sent on to Caesarea, to Felix.

units.la: Cap. xxiiii: Narratur quid cum Paulo actum sit Cæsareæ apud præsidem Felicem. Sunt autem duæ principales capitis partes. In priore narratur processus iuridicialis cum Paulo institus coram Felice: vbi Tertullus nomine Sacerdotum Iudaicorum aduersus Paulum perorat: Paulus causam suam, vel Christi potius, defendit; vsque ad v. 23. In posteriore narrantur actiones quædam Felicis erga Paulum: nam Felici eiusque coniugi Drusillæ verbum Dei annunciat: & felix ab officio decedens & successori locum præbens, Paulum in gratiam Iudæorum captiuum relinquit.
units.tr: Chapter 24 relates what was done with Paul at Caesarea before the governor Felix. There are two principal parts to the chapter. In the first, the legal process begun against Paul before Felix is narrated: where Tertullus, speaking on behalf of the Jewish priests, pleads against Paul; Paul defends his cause, or rather the cause of Christ; to verse 23. In the second, certain actions of Felix towards Paul are narrated: for Paul announces the word of God to Felix and his wife Drusilla; and Felix, on leaving office and giving place to his successor, leaves Paul in prison to please the Jews.

units.la: Cap. xxv Continuatur narratio quid cum Paulo Cæsareæ actum sit, primùm coram Præside Festo, qui Paulum à Iudæis accusatum adduci iubet: is post solidam defensionem appellat ad Cæsarem, vsque ad v. 13. Deinde coram rege Agrippa pas[?] pa,cui Festus controuersiam Paulinam exponit, & eidem Paulum sistit.
units.tr: Chapter 25 continues the narrative of what was done with Paul at Caesarea. First, before the governor Festus, who orders Paul, accused by the Jews, to be brought forward; after a solid defence, Paul appeals to Caesar, to verse 13. Then, before King Agrippa, to whom Festus sets out the dispute concerning Paul, and to whom he presents Paul.

units.la: Cap. xxvi. Continuatur narratio superiore capite coepta, de actis Pauli coram rege Agrippa: ac duo in summa narrantur, primum, Sermo Pauli ad illum caeterosque auditores, usque adv. 24. Deinde sermonis illius eventa.
units.tr: Chapter 26 continues the narrative begun in the previous chapter, concerning Paul's acts before King Agrippa. Two things are related in summary. First, Paul's speech to the king and the other hearers, to verse 24. Then, the outcome of that speech.

units.la: Cap. xxvii Narratur quibus itineribus Paulus Romam deducendus, vna cum sociis seu vectoribus reliquis venerit in insulam Melitam: & quomodo ipse vna cum illis ex naufragio salvus euaserit. Itinera quae in autumnali navigatione narrantur, sunt ista. 1. Caesarea venerunt Sidonem. v. 3. 11 Sublegerunt Cyprum, v 4. 111 Emensi pelagus quod est secundum Ciliciam & Pamphiliam, deuenerunt Mira urbem Lyciae, v. 5. 1111 Navigantes secundum Cnidum, sublegerunt Cretam secundum Salmonem, v. 7. v Peruenerunt ad pulchros portus, v. 8. praeterlegerunt Cretam, v. 13. v1 Delati sunt infra insulam Claudam, v. 16. v11 Naufragio facto euaserunt in insulam Melitam. v. vlt. Nafragium quod attinet, quatuor principaliter narrantur. 1. Praemonitio Pauli, v. 9. & 10. 11. 11 periculum naufragy, a v. 14. vsque ad 41. quod illustratur ex effectis variis, videlicet tum factis destinatis ad consolationem atque recreationem ex metu. 111 Naufragium ipsum describitur, v. 41. 1 v Euasio naufragorum, vestibus reliquis.
units.tr: Chapter 27 relates by what journeys Paul was to be taken to Rome, and how, together with his companions and the other passengers, he came to the island of Melita; and how he himself, along with them, escaped safe from the shipwreck. The voyages narrated in the autumn navigation are these. 1. From Caesarea they came to Sidon, verse 3. 2. They sailed under the lee of Cyprus, verse 4. 3. Having crossed the sea which is along Cilicia and Pamphylia, they came to Myra, a city of Lycia, verse 5. 4. Sailing by Cnidus, they passed under the lee of Crete off Salmone, verse 7. 5. They came to a place called Fair Havens, verse 8. 6. They passed by Crete, verse 13. 7. They were driven under the island Clauda, verse 16. 8. After the shipwreck they escaped to the island of Melita, verse last. As for the shipwreck, four things are related principally. 1. Paul's forewarning, verses 9 and 10. 2. The danger of the wreck, from verse 14 to 41, which is illustrated by its various effects, namely the things done to console and refresh them from fear. 3. The shipwreck itself is described, verse 41. 4. The escape of the shipwrecked, with the remaining clothing.

units.la: Cap. xxviii tria narrantur. Primum, quid memorabile Paulus egerit in insula Melite, vsque ad v. 11. Deinde quibus itineribus in verna navigatione venerit Romam, vsque ad ver-
units.tr: Chapter 28 relates three things. First, what memorable things Paul did on the island of Melita, to verse 11. Then, by what journeys in the spring navigation he came to Rome, to the verse-

units.la: SVMMÆ CAPITVM ex R. G. CAP. I.
units.tr: SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTERS from R. G. CHAP. I.

units.la: A Solymis prohibet discedere mœnibus illos. Omnibus instructis cœlica regna subit. Angelicæ voces solantur, & inde reversi Alterum in amissi substituere locum.
units.tr: He forbids them to leave the walls of Jerusalem. When all were equipped, he ascends to the heavenly kingdom. Angelic voices comfort them, and having returned from there, they put another in place of the one who was lost.

units.la: Pneuma sacrum sumunt, vario sermone loquuntur. Et CHRISTVM fortis prædicat ore Petrus. Pectora compuncti tria millia credere CHRISTO Incipiunt, precibus se pia turba juvat.
units.tr: They receive the holy Spirit and speak in various tongues. And Peter boldly proclaims Christ with his mouth. Three thousand, pierced in heart, begin to believe in Christ; the pious crowd helps them with prayers.

units.la: Languidus exiliit cœlestis nomine CHRISTI. Factum miratur nescia turba novum. Hosce monet Petrus, quod CHRISTO gloria danda Ac illi attento credere corde, jubet.
units.tr: The lame man leaps up at the name of heavenly Christ. The ignorant crowd marvels at the new deed. Peter admonishes these people that glory must be given to Christ, and bids them believe with an attentive heart.

units.la: Pontifices capiunt, sed cum pia causa valeret. Dimittunt, duras incutiuntque minas. Orant unanimes, motu mox terra movetur. Qui status illorum conditione docet.
units.tr: They seize the high priests, but since the pious cause prevails, they let them go and hurl harsh threats. United in prayer, the earth is soon moved by a tremor, which teaches the state of those people by their condition.

units.la: Morte cadit subita coniux tristisque maritus. Signa ædunt, captos carcer inanis habet. Angelus educit, stant coram judice iniquo. Cæsi discedunt Gamalielis ope.
units.tr: By sudden death the wife falls, and the sad husband too. They perform signs; the empty prison holds the captives. An angel leads them out; they stand before the unjust judge. Those who were beaten depart by the help of Gamaliel.

units.la: Murmura iniqua movent præfecto pectore Græci. Oeconomos septem cætera turba legit. Sed capitur Stephanus, cui falsis testibus instant, Angelico vultu splenduit ille tamen.
units.tr: The Greeks stir unjust murmurs with a prefect's heart. The rest of the crowd chooses seven stewards. But Stephen is seized, against whom they press with false witnesses; yet he shone with an angelic face.

units.la: Quæsit vera fides, qua posset quisque placere Altisono, forti disserit ore Stephan. Obturant aures: lapidoso grandine pressus. Proque suis moriens hostibus ille rogat.
units.tr: He sought true faith, by which each might please the Most High; Stephen speaks with a strong voice. They stop their ears, and he is pressed by a stony hail. And dying, he prays for his enemies.

units.la: Persequitur sanctos crudeli pectore Saulus. Samariæ Verbum suscipit ora Dei. Inde patent falsi fallacia corda Simonis. Æthiopem, doctum magne Philippe, lauat [?].
units.tr: Saul persecutes the saints with a cruel heart. Samaria receives the Word of God. Then the deceit of Simon's false heart is revealed. Great Philip, you wash the Ethiopian, a learned man [?].

units.la: Conuersus Christi Paulus iam verba docebat; Cum raptum insidiis pendula sporta tulit.
units.tr: Converted, Paul was already teaching the words of Christ, when a hanging basket, by plots, carried him off.

units.la: Pax floret sanctis, Aeneae corpora sanat. Restituit vitae funera mœsta Petrus.
units.tr: Peace flowers for the saints; he heals Aeneas' body. Peter restores the sad funeral of life.

units.la: Centurio Petrum Domino mandante vocauit. Paruit hic, Domini mystica signa videns.
units.tr: At the Lord's command, the centurion called Peter. He obeyed, seeing the mystic signs of the Lord.

units.la: Ethnica gens CHRISTVM recipit cum munere sanctis Pneumatis, & Christi symbola sancta simul.
units.tr: The Gentile nation receives Christ, with the gift of the holy Spirit and the holy symbols of Christ at the same time.

units.la: Se Petrus excusat, quod in Ethnica tecta subiuit. Incipiunt gentes nomen habere Dei.
units.tr: Peter excuses himself, because he entered Gentile houses. The nations begin to have the name of God.

units.la: Et primum CHRISTI dicuntur nomine in urbe Antiochi: surgunt tempora dura fames.
units.tr: And first they are called by the name of Christ in the city of Antioch; hard times arise, with famine.

units.la: Impius Herodes Iacobum perdidit ense, Iniicit & forti vincula dura Petro.
units.tr: Impious Herod destroyed James with the sword, and cast hard chains on brave Peter.

units.la: Liberat hunc Dominus, cui dum scelerate resistit Herodes, factus vermibus esca, peris.
units.tr: The Lord frees him; while Herod impiously resists, he is made food for worms and perishes.

units.la: Barnaban & Saulum Domini sors eligit, hisce Sergius vt credit, tam Mage cacus abis.
units.tr: The lot of the Lord chooses Barnabas and Saul; Sergius believes them, while you, blind magician, depart.

units.la: Paulus & Antiochi verbum denarrat in urbe. Hinc tamen excusso puluere lentus abit.
units.tr: Paul and Barnabas proclaim the word in the city of Antioch. Hence, however, having shaken off the dust, he departs slowly.

units.la: Iconio fugiunt, aedant miracula Lystris. Aduenisse Deos barbara turba putat.
units.tr: They flee to Iconium and do miracles at Lystra. The barbarian crowd thinks the gods have come down.

units.la: Obruitur saxis Paulus, mox inde resurgit, Hinc varias numerat pagina sacra vias.
units.tr: Paul is stoned, but soon rises again; hence the sacred page counts his various journeys.

units.la: Antiochensis habet tristes Ecclesia turbas, Dum circuncidi pars quota saepe monet.
units.tr: The Antiochene church has sad troubles, while a part of it often warns that they must be circumcised.

units.la: Conueniunt fratres Solymis, sua dogmata tribunt. Cumque tuo comiti iurgia, Paule, mouet.
units.tr: The brethren gather at Jerusalem and bring their doctrines. And he stirs quarrels with your companion, Paul.

units.la: Timotheum assumit Paulus, Macedum arua peregrans, Et sanam discit Lydia casta fidem.
units.tr: Paul takes Timothy, wandering through the fields of Macedonia, and chaste Lydia learns sound faith.

units.la: Eiicitur Python, caeduntur corpora sancta. Carceris, & fidei dona, magister habet.
units.tr: The Python is cast out, and holy bodies are beaten. The jailer receives the gifts of prison and of faith.

units.la: Thessalonican adit Paulus, suscepit Iason Cogitur hinc tacita rursus abire fuga.
units.tr: Paul goes to Thessalonica; Jason receives him; hence he is compelled to depart again in silent flight.

units.la: Denuo Berrhaeam linquens contendit Athenas, Queis prius ignotum praedicat ille Deum.
units.tr: Leaving Berea again, he hastens to Athens, where he preaches the God previously unknown to them.

units.la: In bimari Paulus contexit vela Corintho. Crimina & illius Gallio nulla putat.
units.tr: Paul sets sail from Corinth, which lies between two seas. Gallio thinks his offences are nothing.

units.la: Inde comis rasis Ephesum devenit: Apollos Dogmata constanti pectore sancta docet.
units.tr: Then, with his hair shaven, he came to Ephesus; Apollos teaches holy doctrines with a steadfast heart.

units.la: 19 Bis senos Ephesi Baptizat, signaque multa Aedit, Sceuidas daemonis ira rapit. Infames rutilo conflagrant igne libelli: Hinc faber insidias disidiumque monet.
units.tr: 19 He baptizes about twelve at Ephesus and does many signs; the anger of the demon seizes the sons of Sceva. Infamous books burn in red fire; hence the craftsman warns of plot and discord.

units.la: 20 Discedens Epheso peruenit Troada Paulus. Decidis ex alto, somniculose, loco. Et Solymos repetens clara inter tecta Mileti Chara Epheso dicit, tristia verba, Vale.
units.tr: 20 Departing from Ephesus, Paul reaches Troas. You fall from a high place, drowsy one. And returning to Jerusalem, among the bright houses of Miletus, he speaks sad words to Ephesus: farewell.

units.la: 21 Paulus multum errans contingit Caesaris urbem. Hic vates Pauli vincula dura canit. Verberatin Solymis hunc impia turba, tribunus Liberat, & vincit dupla catena virum.
units.tr: 21 Paul, wandering far, reaches the city of Caesar. Here the prophet sings of Paul's harsh chains. The impious crowd beats him in Jerusalem; the tribune frees him and binds the man with a double chain.

units.la: 22 Exponit Paulus qua fit ratione vocatus. Gentibus auditis impia turba furit. Dumque volunt vinctum prolatis cadere virgis, Romanum redimit patria terra virum.
units.tr: 22 Paul explains how he was called. When they hear about the Gentiles, the impious crowd rages. And while they want the bound man to be struck with the rods that have been brought forth, his native land redeems the Roman man.

units.la: 23 Denuo productus Paulus se a crimine purgat. Iudicium turbant litibus inde nomis. Insidia Paulo devota mente struuntur. Caesaream multo milite tutus abit.
units.tr: 23 Brought forward again, Paul clears himself of the charge. They disturb the judgment there with quarrels. A plot is devised against Paul with a devoted mind. Safe under a large guard of soldiers, he departs for Caesarea.

units.la: 24 Intendit rursum Tertullus crimina falsa. Indesuam Paulus purgat vt ante fidem. Saepius hunc audit Felix praefectus auarus, Sperans a capto turpia lucra viro.
units.tr: 24 Tertullus again levels false charges. Paul then defends his faith, as before. The greedy prefect Felix hears him often, hoping for shameful gain from the captive man.

units.la: 25 Rursus vt accusant appellat Caesara Paulus. Sed non certa satis crimina Festus habet. Aduenit ad Festum chara cum coniuge Agrippa, Festus ab hoc causas consiliumque petit.
units.tr: 25 When they accuse him again, Paul appeals to Caesar. But Festus does not find the charges certain enough. Agrippa arrives with his dear wife; Festus seeks from him the grounds of the case and his counsel.

units.la: 26 Paulus agit CHRISTI conflanti pectore causam. Et repetit primi pristina facta status. Rex quoque deuicto tantum non pectore credit Et Paulum insontem praedicat esse virum.
units.tr: 26 Paul pleads Christ's cause with a blazing heart, and recounts the earlier deeds of the former state. The king too, almost overcome in heart, believes, and declares Paul an innocent man.

units.la: 27 Italiam versus Syrio de litore soluunt, Et Creta aduerso flamine regna tenent. Non parent Paulo, venti furiis aira procella. Mergitur insana naufraga puppis aqua.
units.tr: 27 They set sail from the Syrian shore toward Italy, and against an adverse wind hold to Crete. They do not obey Paul; the winds, with furies, raise a storm. The shipwrecked stern sinks in the mad water.

units.la: 28 In Melitem veniunt, prendit fera vipera dextram, Et multi, Paulo sic operante, valent. Delatus Romam Iudaeos conuocat omneis. Et verum sancto praedicat ore Deum.
units.tr: 28 They come to Melita; a fierce viper seizes his hand, and many are made well, Paul working thus. Brought to Rome, he calls together all the Jews and preaches the true God with a holy mouth.

units.la: ARGVMENTA CAPITVM ex G. F. CAP. I.
units.tr: ARGUMENTS OF THE CHAPTERS from G. F., Chapter 1.

units.la: Apparet crebro, spondet noua tempora celat. Scandit turba rogat. fors quoque bina cadit.
units.tr: He appears often, promises new times, and hides them. The crowd climbs up and asks; perhaps two also fall.

units.la: 2 Barbara quæque suam nunc audit natio linguam. Ioël & Dauid. corpora multa lauant.
units.tr: 2 Each foreign nation now hears its own language. Joel and David wash many bodies.

units.la: 3 Claudipedem sanat prædulcis nomen Iesu. Hortaturque reos ad meliora Petrus.
units.tr: 3 The sweetest name of Jesus heals the lame man, and Peter exhorts the accused to better things.

units.la: 4 Declaras Petre vim Iesu, spernisque minantes. Cumque tuis oras. propria nullaquibus.
units.tr: 4 You declare the power of Jesus, Peter, and you scorn threatening men. And as you pray for yours, nothing is your own.

units.la: 5 Expirant duo mendaces. iuuat umbra reclusi Quæruntur loqueris non male Gamaliel.
units.tr: 5 Two liars expire. The shadow of the released man helps. They ask you to speak, and Gamaliel does not speak badly.

units.la: 6 Fit grave pro viduis murmur, septemque ministrans. Testes in Stephanum quæ didicere citant.
units.tr: 6 A heavy murmur arises over the widows, and the seven who minister. They cite the witnesses whom they had instructed against Stephen.

units.la: 7 Grandia perstringit Stephanus mysteria paucis; Quem ceu blasphemum perfida turba necat.
units.tr: 7 Stephen touches on great mysteries in few words, and the faithless crowd kills him as a blasphemer.

units.la: 8 Infestat Saulus. credit Simon, arguiturque. Labilis Eunuchum dum legit, unda beat.
units.tr: 8 Saul attacks; Simon believes and is refuted. While the eunuch reads, the sliding water blesses him.

units.la: 9 Lux tibi Saule datur periturum sportula seruas. Saluus es Aenea, functa puella redit.
units.tr: 9 Light is given to you, Saul. The basket saves you from perishing. You are saved, Aeneas; the dead girl returns to life.

units.la: 10 Monstrat Corneli tibi Petrus quid sit agendum. Et monitus visis, teque, tuosque lauat.
units.tr: 10 Peter shows you, Cornelius, what must be done, and warned by visions he washes you and yours.

units.la: 11 Narrat facta Petrus culpantibus Antiochem[?] Credunt, atque Agabo est mox fore visa fames.
units.tr: 11 Peter relates the deeds to those who blame him. The Antiochenes believe, and soon famine is foretold by Agabus.

units.la: 12 Occlusus rediit, mirantur, res male vexas Custodes, sæda morte Tyrannus obit.
units.tr: 12 Shut up, he returned; they wonder. You treat the matter badly, guards; the tyrant dies a foul death.

units.la: 13 Paulus seligitur. Bariesum corripit, idem Multa docet gentes inde repulsus abit.
units.tr: 13 Paul is chosen. He rebukes Bar-Jesus, and likewise teaches the nations, then departs when driven out.

units.la: 14 Quæstus in Iconio. Lystrensis claudus, honores Exhibiti lapides, presbyterique dati.
units.tr: 14 Gained at Iconium. The Lystran lame man; honours are shown with stones, and elders are appointed.

units.la: 15 Religio Mosi, Petro suadente, vexatur. Disiungit Marcus, lite calente, duos.
units.tr: 15 The religion of Moses, at Peter's urging, is vexed. Mark separates two men while the quarrel is hot.

units.la: 16 Spiritus ire vetat. Macedo astat. Lydia credit. Pytho fugit, rupti carceris ima tremunt.
units.tr: 16 The Spirit forbids going. The Macedonian stands by. Lydia believes. Python flees; the depths of the broken prison tremble.

units.la: 17 Thessalonica fidem recipit. Berrhæaque fœlix. Cecropiis monstras Paule salutis iter.
units.tr: 17 Thessalonica receives the faith, and fortunate Berea. Paul, you show the Athenians the way of salvation.

units.la: 18 Vera Corinthe probas. Paulum tibi Gallio sistunt, Quem Priscilla docet, victor ubique volat.
units.tr: 18 You prove true at Corinth. Gallio brings Paul before you; Priscilla teaches him; the victor flies everywhere.

units.la: 19 Abluti rursum. dissertio, signaque Pauli. Ardentes libri magna Diana sonant.
units.tr: 19 Washed again, the disputation and the signs of Paul. The burning books sound out great Diana.

units.la: 20 Blandè sopitus moritur. Paulusque vocatos Bellè facta viros, moxque futura docet.
units.tr: 20 Gently lulled, he dies; and Paul teaches the summoned men deeds well done and things soon to come.

units.la: 21 Constrictæ palmæ, uti simulatio duplex Compes. Tarsensem Græca loquela probat.
units.tr: 21 Hands bound, a double pretence, a fetter. The Greek speech proves Paul of Tarsus.

units.la: 22 Denarrat Paulus, quo verterit ordine sectam Dic mihi, Romanus sisne, Tribunus ait.
units.tr: 22 Paul recounts in what order he turned the sect. "Tell me, are you a Roman?" the tribune says.

units.la: 23 Eriperis pervim, tua cædes, Paule, vouetur. Et per te mitti Dux sua scripta Duci.
units.tr: 23 You are snatched away by force, Paul; your slaughter is vowed; and through you the commander sends his writings to the governor.

units.la: 24 Facundi Paulus Tertulli verba refutat. Fœlix rem differt, munus habere volens.
units.tr: 24 Paul refutes the eloquent words of Tertullus. Felix postpones the matter, wishing to have a favour.

units.la: 25 Gratificaturus Paulum vult mittere Festus, Gnarus at [?]is dixit, Cæsarem adire volo.
units.tr: 25 Festus, wishing to do Paul a favour, wants to send him; but Paul, knowing this, says he wants to go to Caesar.

units.la: 26 Illicet Agrippam narrans quæcunque patrasset, Insanis, inquit præses: at ille negat.
units.tr: 26 Straightway, Paul narrates whatever he had done before Agrippa. The governor says he is mad; but Paul denies it.

units.la: 27 Longa maris patimur discrimina, denique nantes Luctantesque diu, proxima terra capit.
units.tr: 27 We suffer long dangers at sea; at last, swimming and struggling for a long time, the nearby land receives us.

units.la: 28 Morderis, pellis febrem. Romamque profectus, Mordes iure tuos Paule, diuque doces.
units.tr: 28 You are bitten, but the viper shakes off the fever. Having set out for Rome, you, Paul, bite and teach for a long time.

units.la: SYMBOLA MONITORIA Capitum.
units.tr: SYMBOLS FOR REMEMBERING THE CHAPTERS.

units.la: 1 2 3 4 5 Supplet, Flatinges, Claudus salit, Actio, Frausque; 6 7 8 9 Murmura, post Saxis, Eunuchus, Paulus, & 10 en Vas: 11 12 13 14 15 Gentibus, Herodes, Elymas, Tauros, Synodusque; 16 17 18 19 20 Lydia, Athenarum, Gallion, Magica, Vinit:
units.tr: 1 2 3 4 5 They fill up, the blowing, the lame man leaps, Action, Fraud; 6 7 8 9 Murmurs, after Stones, Eunuch, Paul, and 10 the Vessel: 11 12 13 14 15 Gentiles, Herod, Elymas, Bulls, and Synod; 16 17 18 19 20 Lydia, of the Athenians, Gallio, Magic, lives:

units.la: 21 22 23 24 25 Zona, Flagellatur, Iudex, Feliceque, Festus: 26 27 28 Agrippam alloquitur, Naufraga, Roma potens
units.tr: 21 22 23 24 25 Girdle, is scourged, Judge, and Felix, Festus: 26 27 28 Addresses Agrippa, Shipwrecked, Rome powerful

units.la: Declaratio.
units.tr: Declaration.

units.la: Supplent numerum duodebim Apostolorum: v.26. Flat ingens ventus domum concutiens. v.2 Claudus salis sanatus à Petro. v.8. Actio primorum contra Petrum: v.5. Frausque Ananiæ & Sapphiræ, v 2.
units.tr: They fill up the number of the twelve apostles: v.26. A violent wind shaking the house: v.2. The lame man leaps, healed by Peter: v.8. Action of the first men against Peter: v.5. And fraud of Ananias and Sapphira: v.2.

units.la: Murmura Græcorum, quod ipsorum viduæ despi-cerentur, v.1. Post Saxis obruitur Stephanus: v. 58. Eunuchus Reginæ Candaces conuertitur à Philippo, v.27. Paulus conuertitur: v.1. & en Vas de cœlo de-missum: v. 11.
units.tr: Murmurs of the Greeks, because their widows were despised: v.1. After stones Stephen is overwhelmed: v.58. The eunuch of Queen Candace is converted by Philip: v.27. Paul is converted: v.1. And the vessel let down from heaven: v.11.

units.la: Gentibus cur annunciatum sit Euangelium, v.1. Herodes erosus à vermibus: v.23. Elymas excæcatur. v.10. Tauros vittatos adducunt: v. 13. Sinodusque Apostolorum: v.6.
units.tr: Gentiles, why the Gospel was announced: v.1. Herod eaten by worms: v.23. Elymas is struck blind: v.10. Bulls with fillets are brought: v.13. And the synod of the apostles: v.6.

units.la: Lydia purpurarea conuertitur. v.14. Athenarum populo ostendit Paulus ignotum Deum: v. 23. Gallion abigit Iudæos à tribunali: v. 16. Magica scripta exu-runtur: v.18. Viuit denuò adolescens supra quam se Paulus extendit: v.10.
units.tr: Lydia, the seller of purple, is converted: v.14. Paul shows the unknown God to the people of the Athenians: v.23. Gallio drives the Jews from the judgment seat: v.16. Magic books are burned: v.18. He lives again, the young man, beyond what Paul stretched himself to: v.10.

units.la: Zona qua ligatur Paulus: v.11. Flagellatur Paulus: v.25. Iudex Ananias sedens in tribunali: v.3. Feliceque decedente de prouincia: v.23 26. Festus succedit: v.1.
units.tr: Girdle with which Paul is bound: v.11. Paul is scourged: v.25. Judge, Ananias sitting on the judgment seat: v.3. And Felix, departing from the province: v.23, 26. Festus succeeds: v.1.

units.la: Agrippam alloquitur Paulus: v. 2. Naufraga tur-ba enatat: v. 41. Roma potens excipit Paulum: v.16.
units.tr: Paul addresses Agrippa: v.2. The shipwrecked crowd swims ashore: v.41. Rome, powerful, receives Paul: v.16.

units.la: Finis Analyseos Librorum N. T. Historicorum.
units.tr: End of the Analysis of the Historical Books of the New Testament.

units.la: ISAGOGE
units.tr: ISAGOGE

units.la: AD LECTIONEM ET MEDITATIONEM LIBRORVM N. TESTAMENTI Didascalicorum seu doctrinalium, per Analysin eorum summariam.
units.tr: AN INTRODUCTION TO READING AND MEDITATING ON THE BOOKS OF THE NEW TESTAMENT that teach and instruct, by a summary analysis of each.

units.la: TRIA SVNT SCRIPTORVM (ratione temporis)genera inNo-vo Testamento: Historicum, didascalicum, & propheticum. Historicum dico, quod res gestas continet, vel ipsius Salvatoris, vel etiam Apostolorum eius, ac habet praeteriti temporis seriem: quo pertinent Evangelica scripta, de Christo, & liber Actorum Apostolicorum. Didascalicum genus scripti est, quod ad doctrinam magis est accommodatum, fidem & vitam fidelium instituit, ac praesentis temporis habet formam, quo pertinent Epistolae Paulinae & Canonicae reliquae septem. Propheticum vero, statum & mores futurae Ecclesiae adumbrat, iudicium infidelium & praemia sanctorum exprimit, qualis est liber Apocalypseos Iohannis, quem in primaria Scriptorum N.T. distributione ad secundum membrum librorum scil: doctrinalium referimus, quia rerum futurarum complectitur doctrinam.
units.tr: There are three kinds of writing in the New Testament, classed according to time: historical, didactic, and prophetic. By historical I mean that which contains the deeds done, either of the Saviour himself or of his Apostles, and which has the sequence of past time; to this kind belong the Gospel writings about Christ and the Acts of the Apostles. The didactic kind of writing is that which is better suited to teaching, establishes the faith and life of believers, and has the form of the present time; to this kind belong the Epistles of Paul and the remaining seven Catholic Epistles. The prophetic kind, however, sketches the condition and manners of the future Church and sets forth the judgment of unbelievers and the rewards of the saints; such is the Book of the Revelation of John, which in the primary division of the New Testament writings we refer to the second member, that is, the doctrinal books, because it embraces the teaching about things to come.

units.la: Ac primum quidem genus, nempe libros histohistoricos hactenus resoluendo percurrimus: sequuntur libri Didasticieu doctrinales. EPISTO-LÆ nimirum APOSTOLICÆ, quæ vel Pauli sunt, vel reliquorum Apostolorum.
units.tr: Now the first kind, namely the historical books, we have so far gone through by analysis; there follow the didactic or doctrinal books, namely the APOSTOLIC EPISTLES, which are either of Paul or of the other Apostles.

units.la: Ut igitur doctrina de Christi potissimum Persona & Merito in libris Euangelistarum enoluta continentur: sic in libro Actorum, & Epistolis Apostolicis, de Christi Efficacia, hoc est, de propagatione atque applicatione meriti Christi tractatur. Ac in Actis quidem quid Apostoli, & quos, uiua voce docuerint, est traditum: deinceps quid & quos iidem Scripto docuerint, in Epistolis ipsorum panditur.
units.tr: Just as the doctrine of the Person and Merit of Christ is chiefly contained in the books of the Evangelists, so in the Acts and in the Apostolic Epistles the efficacy of Christ is treated, that is, the propagation and application of the merit of Christ. In the Acts, indeed, it is handed down what the Apostles taught by the living voice, and to whom; afterwards, in their Epistles, is set out what and to whom the same Apostles taught in writing.

units.la: Quæritur hic: quorsum scripserint Apostoli Epistolas, nec prædicatione contenti fuerint, de qua mandatum acceperant: Ite, prædicate, &c: Respondeo: Scripserunt ideò, non ut aliam doctrinam, aut aliud Euangelium traderent, sed ut quæ coram docuerunt, inculcarent, & suam absentiam ita sarcirent, nascentibus controuersiis & scandalis obuiam irent: Vide Rom. 1. v. 13. & 15. Item cap. 15. v. 15. Phil. 3. v. 1. 2. Pet. 3. v. 1. Item ut ad quæstiones nonnunquam sibi propositas responderent. 1. Cor. 7. v. 1. Epistolæ Pauli (inquit Ambrosius epistolâ ad Sabinum) effigies fuere eius præsentiæ. Nec aliud vocant Apostoli traditiones suas quam doctrinam a se traditam: 1. Cor. 15. v. 3. 2. Thessal. 2. v. 15. State igitur fratres, (inquit) & eas tenete traditiones, quas docti estis vel sermone, vel Epistolis nostris. Quæ causa est, quod adiurat illos ibidem, ut Epistolam suam recitent cunctis. Unde Tertullianus contra Hæreticos ait; Apostolos condidisse Ecclesias tum prædicando voce, tum per Epistolas. Et Irenæus lib. 3. cap. 4 & 5. eos refutat qui prætexebant Apostolos non omnia scriptis mandasse qui docuerant.
units.tr: Here the question is asked: why did the Apostles write Epistles, and not rest content with preaching, which was the commission they had received: "Go, preach," etc.? I answer: they wrote not to hand down another doctrine or another gospel, but to impress upon people what they had taught in person, and in this way to make up for their absence, meeting controversies and scandals as they arose. See Rom. 1 v. 13 and 15; likewise ch. 15 v. 15; Phil. 3 v. 1, 2; 2 Pet. 3 v. 1. Also so that they might answer questions sometimes put to them: 1 Cor. 7 v. 1. Paul's Epistles (says Ambrose in his letter to Sabinus) were the images of his presence. Nor do the Apostles call their traditions anything other than the doctrine handed down by them: 1 Cor. 15 v. 3; 2 Thess. 2 v. 15: "Stand firm, therefore, brothers," he says, "and hold the traditions which you were taught, whether by word or by our Epistle." This is why he there charges them to read his Epistle to all. Hence Tertullian says against the heretics that the Apostles founded churches both by preaching with the voice and by Epistles. And Irenaeus, book 3, chapters 4 and 5, refutes those who pretended that the Apostles had not committed to writing everything they had taught.

units.la: Hactenus de Epistolis omnium Apostolorum in genere sequitur.
units.tr: So much for the Epistles of all the Apostles in general; what follows.

units.la: DE EPISTOLIS S. APOSTOLI Pauli.
units.tr: ON THE EPISTLES OF THE HOLY APOSTLE PAUL.

units.la: Ad fructuosam Epistolarum S. Pauli lectionem ea sunt προπαρασκευῆς[?]. i. generalis præparationis ergò notanda, quæ in Euangelistarum scriptis obseruanda monuimus: nimirum I Quis scripserit: II Quibus: III Quid: IV Quomodo.
units.tr: For a fruitful reading of the Epistles of St. Paul, these things are to be noted as a general preparation, in the same way as we pointed out what should be observed in the writings of the Evangelists, namely: I. Who wrote them; II. To whom; III. What; IV. How.

units.la: De Primo.
units.tr: On the First.

units.la: Quis scripserit: PAVLVS APOSTOLVS, cuius conuersionem miraculosam & vocationem immediatam habuimus in Actis Apost: cap. 9. item ad Apostolatum inter Gentes functionem, Act. 13. deque ipsius ministerij cursu, inde ad libri vsque finem. De nomine Pauli, Patria, præceptoribus, vitæ genere, eruditione[?], scriptis, matrimonio, &c: vide Isagogen B. Arctij ad lectionem Epist: paulin. & eiusdem in Epistolam ad Romanos prolegomena: & nostra in Exordium eiusdem Epistolæ annotata.
units.tr: Who wrote them: the Apostle Paul, whose miraculous conversion and immediate calling we have in Acts 9, and whose appointment to the apostolate among the Gentiles we have in Acts 13, and the course of his ministry from there to the end of the book. For his name, country, teachers, way of life, learning, writings, marriage, etc., see the Isagoge of B. Arctius to the reading of the Pauline Epistles, his prolegomena to the Epistle to the Romans, and our notes on the introduction to that Epistle. ## Concerning the Second.

units.la: De Secundo.

Quibus scripserit: Primò in genere, omnibus Christianis: Ideò Apostolus omnibus se debitorem perfitetur: Rom: i. v, 14. Et Augusti-nus lib. i. contra Cresconium Grammaticum, cap. 8. Memento (inquit) Apostolicas Episto-las non iis tantum scriptas, qui tempore illo quo scribebantur vixerant; sed etiam nobis: atque ideo in Ecclesia recitantur, &c: Deinde nominatim & inspecie, iis ad quos mittuntur. Ubi observandum qui & quales isti populi seu per-sonæ tum temporis fuerint: quod modo ex ipsis epistolis, modo ex geographis cognosci potest. Nonnunquam vero ad hominum, ad quos scribit, ingenia, attemperata videtur Apo-stoli oratio. Hinc ad Romanos rerum domi-nos, cernimus grauiter & cum maiestate qua-dam tractata universa: ad Galatas vero, tan-quam ad leues & inconstantes, alius est sermo-nis habitus, nempe acris & mordens, alicubi et-iam perturbatior. Ad hanc considerationem pertinet etiam occasio scriptionis, seu quare una-quæque Epistola sit scripta. Ubi disquiren-dum, quis tum fuerit Ecclesiæ, ad quam episto-la datur, status: num quæ controversiæ de dog-matibus ibi exortæ: num à Pseudo Apostolis sollicitatæ fuerint ad defectionem; num con-stantes in doctrina accepta perseveraverint: cæ-teraque his similia, quæ non aliunde certius, quam ex iis quæ in Epistola ipsa continentur, possunt colligi.
units.tr: To whom he wrote: first, in general, to all Christians. Therefore the Apostle declares that he is a debtor to all: Rom. 1.14. And Augustine, book 1 against Cresconius the Grammarian, chapter 8: "Remember," he says, "that the Apostolic Epistles were written not only for those who lived at the time when they were written, but for us also; and therefore they are read in the Church," etc. Then, by name and in particular, to those to whom they are sent. Here we must observe who these peoples or persons were at that time, and what they were like; this can be learned partly from the epistles themselves and partly from the geographers. Sometimes, indeed, the Apostle's speech seems adapted to the natures of the people he is writing to. Thus to the Romans, lords of the world, he treats everything gravely and with a certain majesty; but to the Galatians, as to light and inconstant people, his manner of speaking is different, namely sharp and biting, and in places even more agitated. To this consideration belongs also the occasion of writing, that is, why each Epistle was written. Here we must inquire what the state of the Church was to which the epistle is addressed: whether controversies about doctrine had arisen there; whether they had been pressed by false apostles towards defection; whether they had persevered steadfastly in the doctrine received; and other things like these, which cannot be gathered more certainly from anywhere else than from the contents of the Epistle itself. ## Concerning the Third.

units.la: De Tertio.

Quid scripserit: seu quid epistola conti-neat, siue quot sint præcipuæ eius partes. Cùm autem appellentur Epistolæ & sint; nemo non intelligit, Epistolarum decorum in iis spectan-dum esse. Omnis quidem generis materia re-cte epistolis committitur: at interim retineri observarique semper decet praecipuas scribendarum epistolarum leges. Itaque in epistolis Paulinis in-scriptiones seu salutationes in initio, & comprecationes in fine, interdum cum adiunctis mandatis de rebus familiaribus, & aliae partes crypticae seu accessoriae, ab essentialibus membris diligenter sunt distinguendae. Essentialia membra dico graves illas quae fere singulis epistolis comprehenduntur disputationes, & eos etiam, qui tractantur, locos, quos Ecclesiarum status poscebat explicari. Quamobrem operae est pre-cium, summa animi contentione in id adniti, quo prudenter distinguas vbi disputationis sit initium, vbi eiusdem finis. Deinde, vtrum hanc sequatur disputatio alia, & quousque haec protrahatur: qui praeterea loci subiiciantur. Nam incidunt redargutiones falsorum dogmatum, reprehensiones errorum in ritibus, obiurgationes aduersus vitia & corruptos mores, &c: Ex his ita pensitatis, facile erit colligere totius epistolae, aut vniuscuiusque nouae disputationis sta-tum,seu propositionem generalem: qui omnino ab incidentibus disputationibus distingui debet, & in quem praecipue est respiciendum: item ad quod genus causae,siue potius concionis Theologicae (etenim causae aguntur in foro, at in Ecclesia proprie habentur conciones de rebus coelestibus) epistola vnaquaeque referatur.
units.tr: What he wrote, that is, what the epistle contains, or what its principal parts are. Since they are called epistles and are epistles, no one fails to understand that the proper form of epistles must be observed in them. Indeed, material of every kind may rightly be committed to epistles; yet meanwhile it is always fitting to keep and observe the chief rules of writing letters. Accordingly, in the Pauline epistles the greetings or salutations at the beginning, and the prayers at the end, sometimes with added instructions about private affairs, and other incidental or accessory parts, must be carefully distinguished from the essential members. By essential members I mean those weighty discussions that are contained in nearly every epistle, and also those topics which were treated and which the condition of the Churches demanded be explained. Therefore it is worth the effort to strive with the greatest concentration of mind to distinguish wisely where a discussion begins and where it ends; then whether another discussion follows it, and how far it is extended; and what topics are added besides. For refutations of false doctrines, rebukes of errors in rites, reproofs against vices and corrupt morals, etc., intrude. When these have been weighed in this way, it will be easy to gather the state of the whole epistle, or of each new discussion, that is, the general proposition, which must indeed be distinguished from the intervening discussions, and to which attention must chiefly be paid; likewise to which kind of case, or rather of theological sermon, each epistle is to be referred (for cases are argued in the forum, but in the Church sermons are properly delivered on heavenly matters). ## Concerning the Fourth.

units.la: DE QVARTO.

Quomodo scripserit. Huc incidit disquisitio generalis de Idea orationis, & de epistolarum atque rerum in iis contentarum ordine. Orationem quod attinet, ea adsurgit nonnunquam paulò altius, atque supra epistolarem mediocritatem attollitur. Etenim dicendi figuras atque schemata, graui generi orationis apta, subinde adhibet Apostolus: interdum quoque affectus vehementiores mouet, atque animos nititur ad res maximas inflammare. Sed & illud tenendum, Paulum Apostolum primum natura, fuisse vehementem, & deinde ex Spiritus diuini instinctu valde serio ardenterque omnibus in negotiis agere solitum: quod sicut ex Actis Apostolorum, ita ex ipsius quoque scriptis licet cognoscere: aliquando vero & genus negotij in quo versabatur, aliquam postulasse vehementiam & comitationem. Hinc igitur fit, quod vbi tempestiuum iudicabat, maximeque in disputationum confirmationibus & confutationibus, itemque redargutionibus, acer, instans, premens, vrgens conspiciatur. Quapropter quod Græci de Pericle dicere solent, eum fulminare, tonare, & totam commouere Græciam: id nos multo iustius de nostro dicemus Paulo, qui verè fulmina & tonitrua sua oratione ciebat, quæ in vniuersa Asia atque Europa, imò in toto quàm late patet orbe, exaudita sunt: & hodie quoque per Dei gratiam audiuntur. Hæc idcirco annotantur, vt sciant omnes, se tunc quoque multa longè clarius intellecturos, cum acres intentique erunt ad omnia: & modò tanquam si inter hostium vibrata tela periclitarentur, animo strenui, erectique: modò tanquam si in dulcissimorum amicorum considerent coetu, blandi & suaves. In summa, vis ad intelligenda scripta Paulina certam tenere viam: pro negotiorum quae in illis explicantur qualitate, affectus Paulinos induè, adeoque studio ac voluntate animi in Paulum transformeris, & opinione omnium maius experieris adiumentum.
units.tr: How he wrote. Here falls the general inquiry into the character of the discourse, and into the order of the epistles and of the matters contained in them. As for the style, it sometimes rises rather high and is lifted above epistolary moderation. For the Apostle from time to time employs figures and forms of speech suited to the grave style, and at times he also stirs more vehement emotions and strives to inflame minds to the greatest matters. But we must also keep in mind that the Apostle Paul was by nature vehement, and then, moved by the impulse of the divine Spirit, was accustomed to act in all matters very earnestly and ardently; this can be known from the Acts of the Apostles and equally from his own writings; and sometimes the kind of business in which he was engaged demanded a certain vehemence and urgency. Hence it comes about that where he judged it timely, and especially in the confirmations and refutations of arguments, as well as in rebukes, he is seen to be sharp, insistent, pressing, urgent. Therefore what the Greeks are accustomed to say of Pericles, that he thundered and lightened and stirred all Greece, we may say with much more justice of our Paul, who truly launched lightnings and thunderbolts with his speech, which were heard throughout all Asia and Europe, indeed throughout the whole wide world, and are heard today also by the grace of God. These things are noted for this reason, so that everyone may know that they too will understand many things far more clearly when they are keen and attentive to everything: sometimes as if they were in peril amid the hurled weapons of enemies, with spirit brave and alert; sometimes as if they were sitting in the company of their dearest friends, gentle and sweet. In short, if you wish to understand the Pauline writings, keep a sure path: according to the quality of the matters explained in them, put on the Pauline affections, and so, by the zeal and will of your mind, be transformed into Paul, and you will experience, beyond everyone's expectation, a greater help.

units.la: Ordinem rerum quod attinet, in singulis sive disputationibus, sive locis gravioribus, inuestigandum est, ubi sit propositio, ubi confirmatio, ubi confutatio, ubi conclusio. Frequenter namque videas capita quaedam doctrinae Christianae hac methodo per Apostolum explicata. Dialectici artificij peritus hac in parte multum, prae eiusdem imperitis, assequetur & praestabit. Non abs re Sedulius in Collectaneis ad secundum caput epistolae ad Rom. pronunciat, Paulina scripta syllogismis & schematibus abundare: Idcoque si quis diligentius scrutetur, sicut vina in vitibus, messes in semine, frondes in radicibus; sic de profundissima abysso exceptari delicatum piscem, qui ante humanis oculis minime apparebat. Est autem Apostolo nostro familiare, epistolas secare in duas partes principales, quarum priore ea tradit quae pertinent ad doctrinam, id est, dogmata fidei: ut de lege, de peccato, de gratia, de hominis iustificatione, de vocatione gentium ad Euangelium, de abdicatione Iudaeorum, de Ecclesia, de praestantia Euangelij prae Philosophia humana, de sacramentis, de resurrectione mortuorum: Posteriore verò exponit, quæ referenda sunt ad institutionem, hoc est, præcepta morum, & vitæ in vera sanctimonia confirmationem: vt de obedientia erga magistratus, de charitate ac fide coniugali, de officio dominorum ac seruorum, de hospitalitate, de eleemosyna, &c: Breuiter, in priore parte monstrat Apostolus, quæ sunt fidei; in posteriore, quæ operum: in priore docet, quomodo homo iustificetur, in posteriore, qualis esse debeat hominis iam iustificati vita: in priore erudit hominem internum, in posteriore externum, vt totus homo integer atque perfectus, tam apud Deum, quàm apud homines, & sit & habeatur. De hoc nonnihil S. Augustinus lib. de fide & operibus, cap. 7. Et cur Apostoli eum retinuerint in docendo ordinem, hanc redit rationem. Nisi (inquit) in homine præcedat fides, vita bona sequi non poterit: quicquid enim homo veluti rectè fecerit, nisi ad pietatem quæ secundum Deum est referatur, rectum dici non oportet.
units.tr: As for the order of matters, in each discussion or weightier topic, one must investigate where the proposition is, where the confirmation, where the refutation, where the conclusion. For you will often see certain heads of Christian doctrine explained by the Apostle in this method. One skilled in the art of dialectic will in this respect grasp and achieve much more than those inexpert in it. Not without reason Sedulius, in his Collectanea on the second chapter of the Epistle to the Romans, declares that the Pauline writings abound in syllogisms and figures; therefore, if anyone examines them more diligently, just as wine is found in vines, harvests in seed, and leaves in roots, so a delicate fish is drawn up from the deepest abyss, which before was scarcely visible to human eyes. Now it is customary for our Apostle to divide the epistles into two principal parts, of which the former sets out those things which pertain to doctrine, that is, the dogmas of faith: such as the law, sin, grace, the justification of man, the calling of the Gentiles to the Gospel, the rejection of the Jews, the Church, the superiority of the Gospel over human philosophy, the sacraments, the resurrection of the dead. The latter sets out those things which are referred to instruction, that is, precepts of morals and the confirmation of life in true holiness: such as obedience towards the magistrates, conjugal love and fidelity, the duty of masters and servants, hospitality, almsgiving, etc. In brief, in the first part the Apostle shows what belongs to faith; in the second, what belongs to works: in the first he teaches how a man is justified; in the second, what sort of life a man already justified ought to lead; in the first he instructs the inner man, in the second the outer, so that the whole man may be and be held whole and perfect, both before God and before men. St Augustine says something about this in his book on faith and works, chapter 7. And why the Apostles kept this order in teaching, he gives this reason: unless faith (he says) precedes in a man, a good life cannot follow; for whatever a man does, as if rightly, ought not to be called right unless it is referred to piety, which is according to God.

units.la: Quantum ordinem Epistolarum inter se concernit, is duplex est: 1 ordo temporis, quo scriptæ sunt, 11 editionis, quo ordine hodie leguntur in Canone. Quod ordinem scriptionis seu temporis attinet, scriptæ sunt alia ante captiuitatem, aliæ post eam. Ante captiuitatem scriptæ sunt (vt eruditi colligunt) primò, duæ ad Thessalonicenses, Athenis datæ. Secundò ordine videtur succedere, prior ad Timotheum, Laodiceæ Phrygiæ Pacatianæ scripta. Tertiò, prior ad Corinthios, ex Ephesο data quò iam venerat sccundò Act. 19. Nam in hac colligi iubet Elee-mosynam, quam secum deferat in Iudæam. Græca quidem subscriptio habet, ex Philippis Macedoniæ, verum inde missam, vix fit probabile: nam cap. 16. salutationes habet nomine Ecclesiarum Asiæ, quod non videtur commodè facere potuisse in Macedonia, in qua Philippi sunt. Præterea significat, quamdiu sit adhuc mansurus Ephesi eodem capite, notans haud dubiè, tempore scriptionis se ibidem fuisse. Quarto, Epistola ad Titum, ex Nicopoli Macedoniæ, quod subscriptio etiam habet. Quinto, posterior ad Corinthios ex Philippis scripta censetur. Demum nobilis illa epistola ad Romanos Corinthi scripta est, ex itinere, quum vltimò iam ascenderet Hierosolymam, anno 25 suæ conuersionis, anno natiuitatis Christi 55. Post captiuitatem Romæ in illo biennio liberæ custodiæ has scripsit: Primò illam ad Philippenses: Nam subscriptio habet, Romæ scriptam esse: & cap. 1. meminit suorum vinculorum, tanquam rei nouæ, & cap. 4. familiæ Cæsaris: prima igitur videtur. Secundò, Epistola ad Colossenses, ex subscriptione. Tertiò, ad Philemonem, in qua nomina salutantium eadem fere sunt, quæ in Epistola ad Colossenses, vt videri possint eodem tempore datæ. Quarto, ad Ephesios, in qua magna est argumenti similitudo, cum illa ad Colossenses. Quinto, secunda ad Timotheum, in qua conqueritur se ab omnibus desertum. Demas quoque, qui dum scriberetur illa ad Colossenses adhuc constans permanserat, iam illum quoque deseruit, vt vel hoc nomine posterior sit. Sexto, ad Galatas, in qua grauissimè in ceremonias inuehitur, adeò vt non dubitet dicere: Si quis aliud Euangelium annunciet, siue Angelus etiam de cœlo, anathema sit: cap. 1. & de Circūcisione cap. 5. simpliciter pronunciat: Si circumcidamini, Christus vobis nihil prodest. Non itâ vehementer causam hanc in aliis epistolis agit: hinc cap. 6. v. 14. tanquam ad metam properans ait, ne quis illi deinceps molestus sit, se enim mundo crucifigi. Sé-ptimò, Epistolam ad Hebræos, siue Romæ, siue alibi agens in Italia, Paulus exarauit; nam habet Salutationem nomine Italicorum. De eius authore dubitatum est olim: Tertullianus enim eam Barnabæ tribuit: alij S. Lucæ, tanquam discipulo & comiti Pauli, alij Clementi Romano, de quo vide Eufeb. lib. 4. cap. 18. Sunt qui putent Hebraicè scriptam à Paulo: à Clemente verò, vel Luca, aut ab alio Græcè versam, unde quoque varitas aliqua sit enata, vt à Paulino stylo doctis videatur remotior.
units.tr: As far as the order of the Epistles among themselves is concerned, it is twofold: (1) the order of time, in which they were written, and (2) the order of edition, in which they are read today in the Canon. As regards the order of writing or of time, some were written before the imprisonment, others after it. Before the imprisonment were written, as learned men gather, first, the two to the Thessalonians, given at Athens. Secondly, in order the letter to Timothy seems to follow, written at Laodicea in Pacatian Phrygia. Thirdly, the earlier letter to the Corinthians, given from Ephesus, where he had already come a second time (Acts 19). For in it he bids them collect alms, which he would carry with him into Judea. The Greek subscription indeed says it was sent from Philippi in Macedonia, but that it was sent from there is scarcely probable: for in chapter 16 he sends greetings in the name of the churches of Asia, which he would hardly have been able to do from Macedonia, where Philippi lies. Besides, in the same chapter he says how long he will still remain at Ephesus, undoubtedly indicating that he was there at the time of writing. Fourthly, the Epistle to Titus, from Nicopolis in Macedonia, as the subscription also says. Fifthly, the later letter to the Corinthians is thought to have been written from Philippi. Lastly, that noble epistle to the Romans was written at Corinth, on his journey, when he was about to go up to Jerusalem for the last time, in the twenty-fifth year of his conversion, in the year 55 after the birth of Christ. After the imprisonment at Rome, during those two years of open custody, he wrote these. First, the letter to the Philippians: for the subscription says it was written at Rome, and in chapter 1 he mentions his bonds as a new matter, and in chapter 4 the household of Caesar; so it seems to be the first. Secondly, the Epistle to the Colossians, according to the subscription. Thirdly, to Philemon, in which the names of those sending greetings are almost the same as in the Epistle to the Colossians, so that they may seem to have been given at the same time. Fourthly, to the Ephesians, in which there is great similarity of subject with that to the Colossians. Fifthly, the second letter to Timothy, in which he complains that he has been deserted by all. Demas also, who had still remained steadfast when the Epistle to the Colossians was written, had now deserted him too, so that on this ground alone it is later. Sixthly, to the Galatians, in which he attacks the ceremonies most severely, so much so that he does not hesitate to say: "If anyone preaches another gospel, even an angel from heaven, let him be accursed" (chap. 1); and concerning circumcision he states plainly: "If you are circumcised, Christ profits you nothing" (chap. 5). He does not press this cause so vehemently in other epistles; hence in chapter 6, verse 14, as one hastening to the goal, he says that no one is henceforth to trouble him, for he bears in his body the marks of Christ... for he is crucified to the world. Seventhly, the Epistle to the Hebrews, which Paul wrote either at Rome or elsewhere while staying in Italy, for it has a greeting in the name of the Italians. Its author was doubted in former times: Tertullian indeed attributes it to Barnabas, others to St Luke as a disciple and companion of Paul, others to Clement of Rome, on whom see Eusebius, book 4, chapter 18. Some think it was written by Paul in Hebrew, but that it was translated into Greek by Clement, or Luke, or another, whence also some variation has arisen, so that to learned men it seems more remote from Paul's style.

units.la: Hic est ordo scriptionis. In ordine editionis seu collocationis obseruandum est, eos qui epistolas Pauli collegerunt, non habuisse rationem temporis, sed vel dignitatis argumenti, vel copiae: vberiores enim epistolae primo loco collocatae sunt.
units.tr: This is the order of writing. As to the order of edition, or arrangement, it must be observed that those who gathered the Epistles of Paul did not take account of time, but of either the dignity of the subject or the length of the letters: for the fuller epistles were placed first.

units.la: Nos in praesenti seriem epistolarum sequemur eam, quae in hodiernis editionibus obseruatur, & quae à nobis supra, pagina vndecimâ, in tabellâ ordinis omnium librorum N. T. delineata est.
units.tr: In the present work we shall follow the sequence of the Epistles that is observed in today's editions, and which was set out by us above, on page eleven, in the table of the order of all the books of the New Testament.

units.la: M. j.
units.tr: M. j.

units.la: DE EPISTOLA S. PAVLI ad Romanos.
units.tr: ON THE EPISTLE OF ST PAUL TO THE ROMANS.

units.la: PRIMVM hæc in editionibus sortita locum videtur, quòd primaria quæstio salutis nostræ diserte, & copiosius etiam, in ea, quàm aliis in epistolis, explicetur: illa autem est: per quid iustificemur, fidéne, an operibus: remouet autem opera; quia nec Ethnicus suis moralibus, nec Iudæus suis legalibus iustificari potest. Itaque fide necesse est nos iustificari. Deinde ad sedem Imperij & tanquam arcem scribitur, qualis tum Roma erat, gentium Domina: in qua vrbe cum Iudæi & Gentiles promiscuè ad fidem Christi conuersi essent, ideoque Gentium vocationem hic diligentius explicat, vt & Iudæorum reiectionem: in Christo tamen vtrunque populum studiosè coniungit & conciliat.
units.tr: This epistle seems to have been placed first among the others for this reason: the chief question of our salvation is explained plainly, and at greater length, in it than in the other epistles. That question is whether we are justified by faith or by works. It rejects works, because neither the Gentile can be justified by his moral conduct nor the Jew by his observance of the law. Therefore we must necessarily be justified by faith. Next, it is addressed to the seat of empire, as it were its citadel, Rome as it then was, mistress of the nations. In that city Jews and Gentiles had been converted to the faith of Christ side by side, and so Paul explains more carefully here the calling of the Gentiles, and also the rejection of the Jews. Yet in Christ he earnestly joins and reconciles the two peoples.

units.la: Occasio huius epistolæ respectu Apostoli fuit, vrgens ipsum indesinenter sollicitudo de omnibus Ecclesiis, cuius meminit 2. Cor. 11. verf. 28. & muneris Apostolici ratio, sicut ait Rom. 15. v. 15.
