Audacius scripsi vobis, commonefaciens vos per gratiam quæ data est mihi à Deo, ad hoc vt sim minister Christi apud Gentes, &c: Occasio respectu eorum ad quos scribebat fuit conditio & status illius Ecclesiæ, quæ in illa celeberrima vrbe variis ex populis collecta erat: quorum alij, vt Iudæi, lege Mosis & suis prærogatiuis adhuc superbiebant, & iustitiæ laudem cum obseruatione legis & Euangelio diuidere volebant: alij, vt Ethnici, vel Philosophiæ nimis tribuebant, vel Iudæos tanquam quam Christi homicidas & populum à Deo abiectum auersabantur: Nonnulli etiam doctrinâ Euangelij ad libertatem carnis, petulantiam, Magistratus & legum ciuilium contemtum abutebantur: Quibus omnibus grauiter & appositè in hac epistola occurrit Paulus, reuocans eos ad rectam definitionem tum Euangelij,tum eius iustitiæ quæ verè talis censeri debet, ac salutaris est ac viuifica.
units.tr: The occasion of this epistle, with respect to the Apostle, was his own constant anxiety for all the churches, which he mentions in 2 Cor. 11:28, and the nature of his apostolic office, as he says in Rom. 15:15: "I have written to you more boldly, reminding you by the grace given me by God, that I should be a minister of Christ to the Gentiles," etc. With respect to those to whom he was writing, the occasion was the condition and state of that church, gathered from various peoples in that most famous city. Some of them, such as the Jews, still prided themselves on the law of Moses and their own privileges, and wished to divide the praise of righteousness between the observance of the law and the gospel. Others, such as the Gentiles, either attributed too much to philosophy, or shrank from the Jews as the murderers of Christ and a people cast off by God. Some also misused the teaching of the gospel as a licence for the freedom of the flesh, wantonness, and contempt for the magistrate and civil laws. Paul meets all these problems in this epistle, gravely and to the point, recalling them to the right definition both of the gospel and of that righteousness which must truly be considered such, and which is saving and life-giving.

units.la: Porrò cùm ea quæ προλεγομένων loco, Analysi, vt aliorum scriptorum, ita & Epistolarum Paulinarum præmitti solent, nimirum de Persona & officio scribentis, de Scripti summa, & scopo, de persona vel populo ad quem scribitur, &c: hæc (inquam) cùm ex ipsa ἐπιγραφῇ & exordio huius epistolæ simul & semel liquidò colligi & deduci possint; ideò ad eius considerationem accessuri, proponemus
units.tr: Moreover, since those matters which are customarily placed before the other writings, and likewise before the Pauline epistles, in the position of a prologue (an analysis), namely the person and office of the writer, the summary and aim of the writing, and the person or people to whom it is addressed, can (I say) all be clearly gathered and deduced at once from the very superscription and opening of this epistle, therefore, about to take up its consideration, we shall set out:

units.la: PARTES EPISTOLÆ praesentis.
units.tr: THE PARTS OF THE PRESENT EPISTLE.

units.la: Sunt ex vel cryptica seu accessoria, vel essentiales.
units.tr: They are either incidental or accessory, or essential.

units.la: Accessoria sunt tum in principio, tum in fine epistolæ.
units.tr: The accessory parts are both at the beginning and at the end of the epistle.

units.la: In principio quidem est Epigraphe seu inscriptio, & Exordium: in fine verò Epilogus seu peroratio, à v. 14. capitis 15. vsque ad epistolæ finem.
units.tr: At the beginning there is the epigraph or inscription, and the exordium; at the end, the epilogue or peroration, from verse 14 of chapter 15 to the end of the epistle.

units.la: DE INSCRIPTIONE ET EXORDIO cui & summa Propositio huius scripti annexa.
units.tr: ON THE INSCRIPTION AND EXORDIUM, with the summary proposition of this writing attached.

units.la: EPIGRAPHE seu inscriptio qualis nulla tam insignis tamque conserta sententiis in sequentibus epistolis reperitur, quatuor comple-ctitur: 1 Nomen & vocationem autoris. 11 Sub-iectum huius epistolae nobilissimum. 111 Nomen eo-rum ad quos scribit, eorundemque pulcerrima elo-gia. 1 v Salutationem sive votum.
units.tr: The epigraph or inscription, which no other epistle contains so remarkable and so closely packed with ideas, comprises four things: (1) the name and calling of the author; (2) the most noble subject of this epistle; (3) the names of those to whom he writes, with their most beautiful commendations; (4) the greeting or wish.

units.la: 1. Nomen Pauli de tota eius historia nos admonet iam antea in Actorum Apost: libro descripta. Is vero etiamsi initio iam Saulus, iam Paulus nominabatur, vt videre est Act. 13. postea tamen, cum Gentium potissimum Apostolus esset, Pauli nomen Gentibus familiare reti-nuit. Verum quia non cuiuis spiritui credendum est, & magnum erat discrimen inter priorem Paulum Pharisaeum, & Paulum conversum Christique Apostolum, statim suae ad minifte-rium Christi in Apostolatu vocationis singula-ris, & diuinae ad id officium segregationis meminit: ne eodem modo Christi seruus esse videatur, quo in genere sunt omnes Christiani vel alij ministri, Episcopi & Doctores in Ecclesia, qui & mediate vocantur, & certis in locis subsistunt, & errare possunt: cum Apostolicae doctrinae non minus quam Christi ipsius verbis fides sit adhibenda, & superstructa sit Ecclesia super fundamentum Apostolorum & Prophetarum, apud quos scilicet deposita fuit infallibilis veritas doctrinae salutis; cuius tamen aedificij basis & caput est ipse Christus. Inter omnes igitur functiones nulla sublimior fuit vnquam Apostolorum, qui & Christum viderunt, & retecta facie gloriam eius in Euangelio aspexerunt, & aliis per totum mundum notam fecerunt.
units.tr: (1) The name "Paul" reminds us of his whole history, already described in the book of the Acts of the Apostles. He was indeed at first called now Saul, now Paul, as may be seen in Acts 13; but afterwards, since he was chiefly the Apostle of the Gentiles, he kept the name Paul, familiar to the Gentiles. But since one must not believe every spirit, and since there was a great difference between the former Paul the Pharisee and Paul converted and made an apostle of Christ, he at once mentions his own special calling to the ministry of Christ in the apostolate, and his separation by God to that office. This is so that he may not seem to be a servant of Christ in the same way as all Christians are, or other ministers, bishops and teachers in the Church, who are called mediately, remain in certain places, and can err. For apostolic teaching is to be believed no less than the words of Christ himself, and the Church is built upon the foundation of the Apostles and Prophets, in whom, that is, the infallible truth of the doctrine of salvation was deposited. Yet the basis and head of this building is Christ himself. Among all functions, therefore, none has ever been more lofty than that of the Apostles, who both saw Christ and beheld his glory in the gospel with unveiled face, and made it known to others throughout the whole world.

units.la: II Subiectæ materiæ meminit videlicet Euangelij, quod magnificis elogiis describit, vt attentionem statim initio sibi conciliet & eis occurrat, qui Euangelij doctrinam vel propter nouitatem, vel propter statum humiliationis Christi fastidiebant. Primum elogium est ab antiquitate: quod ante promiserat per prophe-tas suos in scripturis. Secundum est à dignitate obiecti: quandoquidem continet magnum illud mysterium pietatis de Filio Dei missō in carne, siue Θεανθρώπῳ[?], vnitis duabus naturis in vnam hypostasin, & tamen inconfusis: Ideò S. Paulus ait illum natum & factum ex semine Dauidis, siue ex muliere, vt idem scribit Gal.4.quæ videlicet fuit ex prosapia Dauidis. Est ergo Christus factus secundum humanam naturam, genitus, non factus secundum diuinam, vt habet Symbolum Nicenum. Et notum quidem erat Iudæis Messiam fore filium Dauidis: sed mysterium illud vnionis personalis non intel-ligebant; quapropter naturam diuinam lucu-lenter exprimit Apostolus, dicens illu ἐρισθένλα[?], & vt Chrysostomus interpretatur ἀποδεικνύσα[?]... i. euidentissimis argumentis demonstratum, vt postea ait Paulus, ἐν δυνάμει[?], exertis testimoniis variis potentiæ diuinæ, de quibus Act. 2. v. 22. & 1. Cor. 1. Documentum autem maximè il-lustre potentiæ Christi recensèt Apostolus, Re-surrectionem ex mortuis, in qua, vt idem ait ad Ephes:1. exertum fuit efficax robur potentiæ Dei, quò respicere videtur etiam 1 Tim.3. cùm ait, iustificatum Spiritu, quo etiam hæc verba respiciunt, κατὰ πνεῦμα ἁγιωσύνης[?]: i. secundum Spiritum sanctificationis, describens Spiritum ab effectu maximè noto in Ecclesia: [Hæc de persona Christi.] Tertium elogium à fine & usu ministerij Evangelici. Gratiam, i. gratiosa dona requisita ad Apostolatum, & ipsum Apostolatum à Christo se accepisse profitetur ad obedientiam fidei, scilicet suadendam non inter Judæos solum, sed omnes gentes, ut quæ antea per inobedientiam coram Deo rei erant, Rom. 5. nunc abnegata omni sapientia carnali propriaque voluntate, se se totos Christo dedant. Addit Apostolus: pro ipsius nomine, i. ut innotescat nomen Jesu Christi, eum scil. esse Mediatorem & Redemtorem mundi, ut Act. 9. dicitur Paulus nomen Christi, id est, eius notiam prolaturus ad Gentes.
units.tr: (2) He names the subject matter, namely the gospel, which he describes with magnificent commendations, so as to win attention from the outset and to meet those who scorned the doctrine of the gospel either because of its novelty or because of the humble state of Christ. The first commendation is from its antiquity: it was promised beforehand through his prophets in the Scriptures. The second is from the dignity of its object: for it contains that great mystery of godliness concerning the Son of God sent in the flesh, or the God-man [Θεάνθρωπος], the two natures united in one hypostasis yet unconfused. Therefore St Paul says that he was born and made from the seed of David, or from a woman, as he also writes in Gal. 4, that is, from the stock of David. Christ therefore was made according to his human nature, begotten, not made, according to his divine nature, as the Nicene Creed has it. And it was indeed known to the Jews that the Messiah would be a son of David; but they did not understand that mystery of personal union. Therefore the Apostle expresses the divine nature clearly, saying that he was declared [ὁρισθέντος] the Son of God, and, as Chrysostom interprets it, shown [ἀποδεικνύσα], that is, demonstrated by the most evident arguments. Then, as Paul says afterwards, it was shown "in power" [ἐν δυνάμει], by the manifest testimonies of divine power of various kinds, of which we read in Acts 2:22 and 1 Cor. 1. The most illustrious proof of the power of Christ, however, the Apostle counts as his resurrection from the dead, in which, as he says in Eph. 1, the effective strength of God's power was displayed. He seems also to have this in view in 1 Tim. 3, where he says that he was justified in the Spirit, and these words too refer to it: "according to the Spirit of holiness" [κατὰ πνεῦμα ἁγιωσύνης], that is, according to the Spirit of sanctification, describing the Spirit by the effect most well known in the Church. [This is said of the person of Christ.] The third commendation is from the end and use of the evangelical ministry. He professes that he has received from Christ grace, that is, the gracious gifts required for the apostolate, and the apostolate itself, to bring about the obedience of faith, namely by persuading not only Jews but all nations, so that those who before were guilty before God through disobedience (Rom. 5) might now, having renounced all carnal wisdom and their own will, give themselves wholly to Christ. The Apostle adds: "for his name", that is, so that the name of Jesus Christ may be made known, namely that he is the Mediator and Redeemer of the world, just as in Acts 9 Paul is said to carry the name of Christ, that is, to bring the knowledge of him to the Gentiles.

units.la: 111 Membrum τῆς ἐπιγραφῆς[?] habet eorum ad quos scribit descriptionem, scil: Romanorum: scribit autem non ad omnes, verùm ad Ecclesiam quæ Romæ tum colligebatur, quam appellat cœtum vocatorum à Christo, qui nimirum prior dilexit nos, 1. Joh. 4. & cœtum dilectorum Dei, qui nos diligit in Christo, licet multæ in nobis supersint infirmitates. Unde definitio Ecclesiæ extrui potest, quòd sit cœtus dilectorum Dei sive electorum in Christo & vocatorum ad eius communionem, & purificantium se indies, sicut ille purus est, 1 Joh. 3. v. 3. & Coloss: 3. v. 12.
units.tr: (3) The member of the inscription contains the description of those to whom he writes, namely the Romans. He writes not to everyone, but to the Church which was then gathering at Rome. He calls it the assembly of those called by Christ, who of course loved us first (1 John 4), and the assembly of the beloved of God, who loves us in Christ, although many weaknesses remain in us. Whence a definition of the Church may be framed: that it is the assembly of the beloved or elect of God in Christ, and of those called to his communion, who purify themselves daily, as he is pure (1 John 3:3; and Col. 3:12).

units.la: 1v Membrum est Salutatio Apostolica, quæ etiam in aliis epistolis occurrit: χάρις[?] hoc loco Dei favorem significat, non autem τὰ χαρίσματα, sed fontem τῶν χαρισμάτων, Dei erga nos benigninignitatem. Per pacem intelligitur praecipuè tranquillitas conscientiarum de qua Rom. 5. & simul prosperitas omnis: & quia omne praeclarum donum à Deo proficiscitur, ideò omnia illa precatur à Deo Patre, & Domino nostro Iesu Christo: nam quorum est natura vna, & eadem operatio, licet peculiariter à Christo etiam vt mediatore bona dona nobis communicantur.
units.tr: (4) The member is the apostolic greeting, which also occurs in the other epistles. Here "grace" [χάρις] signifies the favour of God, not the gifts [τὰ χαρίσματα], but the fountain of the gifts [τῶν χαρισμάτων], the kindness of God towards us. By "peace" is understood chiefly the tranquillity of conscience, of which Rom. 5 speaks, and at the same time every prosperity. And because every excellent gift proceeds from God, he therefore prays for all these things from God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ; for those whose nature is one and whose operation is the same, yet good gifts are communicated to us particularly through Christ also as Mediator.

units.la: Inscriptioni subiungitur
units.tr: Appended to the inscription

units.la: EXORDIUM
units.tr: EXORDIUM

units.la: Flagrantissimis affectibus plenum, in quo pri-mò benevolentiam auditorum (sine tamen assenta-tione 1.Thess. 2.) captat, profitendo summum suum erga Ecclesiam Romanam studium: deinde attentionem conciliat à rerum de quibus scripturus est maiestate & amplitudine.
units.tr: A most ardent exordium, in which he first wins the goodwill of his hearers (yet without flattery, 1 Thess. 2) by professing his great zeal for the Roman Church; then he secures their attention by the majesty and weight of the matters he is about to write about.

units.la: Studium erga Ecclesiam Romæ ex Iudæis & Gentibus collectam probat tribus argumentis.
units.tr: He proves his zeal for the Church at Rome, gathered from Jews and Gentiles, by three arguments.

units.la: 1. quòd de eorum fide & laudibus laetetur, & Deo gratias agat. v. 8. 11, quòd indesinenter pro ipsis oret, v. 9. 10. 111 quòd eos invisere & coram videre cupiat, v. 10. rationem huius sui desiderij duplicem affert, primò, mutuam in fide & consolatione confirmationem. v. 11. 12. 13. deinde muneris sui rationem, quo tenetur omnibus sine discrimine Evangeliz̄are; ne quis enim obiiceret, eum inepte agere, qui velit docere Romanos, homines scilicet sapientia & peritia rerum excellentes: demonstrat, se recte agere: quia agat ex officio: quippe qui tam sapientes quàm insipientes docere debeat. v.41.15.
units.tr: 1. He rejoices in their faith and praise and gives thanks to God (vv. 8, 11); he prays for them without ceasing (vv. 9, 10, 11); and he desires to visit them and see them face to face (v. 10). He gives a twofold reason for this desire: first, mutual strengthening in faith and comfort (vv. 11, 12, 13); then the reason for his office, by which he is bound to preach the Gospel to all without distinction. For lest anyone object that he acts foolishly in wanting to teach the Romans, people excellent in wisdom and skill, he shows that he acts rightly, because he acts from duty, since he ought to teach the wise as well as the foolish (vv. 14, 15).

units.la: Attentionem conciliat, à rei de qua di[?] est, praestantia, v. 16. & 17. ubi simul est
units.tr: He wins attention from the excellence of the subject of which he is about to speak (vv. 16, 17), where at the same time there is

units.la: SVMMA PRINCIPALIS TRACTATIONIS Propositio.
units.tr: THE MAIN SUBSTANCE OF THE PRINCIPAL TREATMENT: The Proposition

units.la: Paratum se, dixit modò Apostolus, ad prædicandum omnibus, & proin Romanis quoque, Euangelium; quod nunc describit à principali effectu & fructu, quòd in eo communicetur vera iustitia & salus, & sic viam sibi sternit[?] ad præcipuam tractationem huius epistolæ, quæ est de iustificatione hominis peccatoris coram Deo, quod S. Augustinus in Psal. iii magnificentissimum Dei opus appellat. Summa propositionis hoc syllogismo includi potest:
units.tr: The Apostle has just said that he is ready to preach the Gospel to all, and so to the Romans too. Now he describes it by its chief effect and fruit: that in it true righteousness and salvation are imparted. In this way he prepares the way for the principal treatment of this epistle, which concerns the justification of sinful man before God, which St Augustine, in Psalm 3, calls the most magnificent work of God. The substance of the proposition can be contained in this syllogism:

units.la: Nec me pudet docere, nec vos tædere debet audire eam doctrinam quæ sola expeditissimam, & certissimam rationem ostendit salutis consequenda.
units.tr: I am not ashamed to teach, and you ought not to be weary of hearing, that doctrine which alone shows the most expedient and most certain way of obtaining salvation.

units.la: Euangelium est talis doctrina, efficax scilicet & potens Dei organon ad seruandū omnes credentes.
units.tr: The Gospel is such a doctrine: namely, an effective and powerful instrument of God for saving all who believe.

units.la: Ergo licet totus mundus contra fremat, promptus sum etiam vobis qui Romæ estis euangelizare, & vos quoque talem doctrinam promtis animis excipere decet.
units.tr: Therefore, though the whole world rage against it, I am ready to preach the Gospel to you also who are at Rome, and you too ought to receive such a doctrine with eager minds.

units.la: Probatio Assumtionis talis est.
units.tr: The proof of the assumption is as follows.

units.la: Illa demum doctrina certam rationem salutis & certitudinis nostræ monstrat, quæ veram iustitiam, quæ coram Deo consistere potest, affert & communicat,
units.tr: That doctrine alone shows the certain way of salvation and of our certainty which brings and imparts the true righteousness that can stand before God.

units.la: Euangelium solum, siue doctrina de fide in Christum ostendit nobis talem iustitiam:
units.tr: The Gospel alone, or the doctrine of faith in Christ, shows us such righteousness.

units.la: Ergo recte dicitur potentia Dei ad salutem, & in ea recte quaritur omnis ratio salutis.
units.tr: Therefore it is rightly called the power of God unto salvation, and in it rightly is sought every reason for salvation.

units.la: Huius Syllogismi Propositio etiam apud Ethnicos confessa; omnibus enim natura notum est iustos esse Dei amicos, & proinde beatos hinc Plato & Aristoteles beatitudinem dixe-runt esse ὁμοίωμα θεῦ.i. similem esse Deo, & Arist:io. Ethic.c.7. non hoc ipso (inquit) quo homo est, ita viuit, sed quo est quid in ipso diui-num, &c: Sed illud diuinum quod in nobis esse debet, fidem nimirum apprehendentem iustitiam quae Deo probatur, quam Paulus vocat δικαιοσύνην θεοῦ, ignorauerunt: in cuius iustitiae definitione est tota vis argumenti Paulini, quia opponitur illa iustitia laruatae iustitiae, in qua Ethnici & Iudaei acquieuerunt, quae tamen co-ram Deo consistere nequit.
units.tr: The major premise of this syllogism was also acknowledged among the heathen, for it is known to all by nature that the righteous are God's friends and therefore blessed. Hence Plato and Aristotle said that happiness is ὁμοίωμα θεοῦ [a likeness to God], that is, to be like God. Aristotle, Ethics c. 7: "man does not live by that by which he is a man, but by that in him which is divine," and so on. But that divine element which ought to be in us, namely faith laying hold of the righteousness that is acceptable to God, which Paul calls δικαιοσύνη θεοῦ [the righteousness of God], they did not know. The whole force of Paul's argument lies in the definition of this righteousness, because it is set against a masked righteousness, in which Gentiles and Jews rested, and which nonetheless cannot stand before God.

units.la: Assumtio autem illius Syllogismi erat ὁ [illegible, ~7 letters]: An Euangelium seu doctrina in Christum ostenderet veram iustitiam iustificantem & Deo gratam. Hanc confirmat Primo summatim & concisè idque tum ab effectis, vbi metonymi-cam illam locutionem, Euangelium est potentia Dei ad salutem, ipse explicat & resoluit, dicens, in eo reuelari iustitiam & vitam; tum testimonio prophetae Habacuc; cap. 2. v. 4. Iustus fide viuet: quasi dicat Propheta quicunque vere iusti sunt, & tales habentur à Domino, fide viuunt, id est, sustentantur ad spem vitae, & sunt certi, se Deo acceptos esse, & haeredes vitae.
units.tr: The assumption of that syllogism, however, was ὁ [illegible, about seven letters]: whether the Gospel, or doctrine concerning Christ, shows the true justifying righteousness that is pleasing to God. He confirms this first briefly and concisely, and that both from its effects, where he himself explains and unfolds that metonymical expression, "the Gospel is the power of God unto salvation," saying that in it righteousness and life are revealed; and then by the testimony of the prophet Habakkuk, chap. 2, v. 4: "The just shall live by faith." As if the prophet said: whoever are truly righteous and are so regarded by the Lord live by faith, that is, are sustained in hope of life, and are certain that they are accepted by God and are heirs of life.

units.la: Secundò eadem Assumptio disputatur & demonstratur copiosè in principalis, huius Epistolae, tractationis parte prima. Nam
units.tr: Secondly, the same assumption is argued and demonstrated at length in the first part of the principal treatment of this epistle. For

units.la: PRINCIPALIS TRACTATIO huius epistolæ, id est:
units.tr: THE MAIN TREATMENT of this epistle, that is:

units.la: Institutio Christianæ Religionis, seu explicatio salutaris ac coelestis sapientiæ duabus partibus absoluitur, quarum prima est doctrina de iustitia fidei, seu de fide iustificante: altera est doctrina de fidei operibus, seu de pia iustificatorum vita.
units.tr: The Institution of the Christian Religion, or an explanation of saving and heavenly wisdom, is set out in two parts. The first is the doctrine of the righteousness of faith, or of justifying faith; the second is the doctrine of the works of faith, or of the godly life of the justified.

units.la: Doctrinae fidei, quae usque ad capitis duodecimi initium explicatur, haec summa & hic scopus est: Nos coram Deo iustificari sola fide in Iesum Christum, per eandem nos regenerari, per eandem consolationem nos accipere, in omnibus tentationibus: veram illam & salutificam fidem non omnibus hominibus communem, sed electorum Dei propriam esse, proindeque offendi debere neminem, quod non omnes Iudaei, (sicut nec inter cateras gentes omnes & singuli) in Christum credant.
units.tr: The summary and aim of the doctrine of faith, which is explained up to the beginning of the twelfth chapter, is this: We are justified before God by faith alone in Jesus Christ, are regenerated through the same faith, and receive through it comfort in all temptations. That true and saving faith is not common to all men but belongs to the elect of God. Therefore no one should be offended that not all Jews (just as not all and each of the other nations) believe in Christ.

units.la: In doctrina vitae Christianae, quodnam eorum qui per fidem in Christum iustificati sunt, officium sit, edocet.
units.tr: In the doctrine of the Christian life, he teaches what duty belongs to those who have been justified through faith in Christ.

units.la: PRIMÆ PARTIS
units.tr: OF THE FIRST PART

units.la: σνωψις[?] Agitur hic de nostræ iustificationis causis Propinqua: quæ est Fides in Christum: quod demonstratur per Remotionem causæ falsæ, i. bonorum operum: peccati cœuncit Gentes c.1 v.18 & reliquis. Iudæos potissimùm: cap.2. & 3. usque ad v.9. Gentes & Iudæos, cap.3. à v.9 usque ad v.21. Confirmatione causæ veræ: Fide iustificamur: c.3. v.21. demonstratur Fidei ipsius Fidelis Abrahæ exemplo, c.4. Obiecto Christo, qui opponitur Adamo. cap.5. Adiuncto duplici Sanctificatione, quæ docet esse Necessaria. cap.6. Imperfectam. c.7 Fiduciâ, ex Spiritu iustificante, sanctificante, consolante, cap.8. Remota: prædestinatio: ubi de Iudæorum Reiectione, & eius Causa, Dei voluntate, cap.9. Signis & effectis, ipsorum ignorantia supina. cap.10. Restauratione & reliquiis. cap.11.
units.tr: Synopsis [σύνοψις]. The subject here is the nearer cause of our justification, which is faith in Christ. This is shown by removing a false cause, namely good works. Sin has bound all: the Gentiles (chapter 1, verse 18 and following), and especially the Jews (chapters 2 and 3 to verse 9); both Gentiles and Jews (chapter 3, from verse 9 to verse 21). The true cause is confirmed: we are justified by faith (chapter 3, verse 21). It is shown by the example of Abraham, the faithful man of faith (chapter 4). Christ is set forth as the object of faith, opposed to Adam (chapter 5). Two kinds of sanctification are added, which teach that it is necessary (chapter 6), and that it is imperfect (chapter 7). Trust is shown, arising from the Spirit who justifies, sanctifies and comforts (chapter 8). The remote cause, predestination, is treated where the rejection of the Jews and its cause, the will of God, are discussed (chapter 9). Its signs and effects, their supine ignorance, are treated (chapter 10). The restoration and the remnant are treated (chapter 11).

units.la: Prima igitur parte huius epistolæ naturam Iustificationis declarat Apostolus ex causis, effectis, adiunctis & contrariis. Causas tractat partim efficientes, easque tum principales, tum instrumentales:partim formale. Primo omnium agit de instrumentali in homine, nimirum fide: docens hominem iustificari fide, vsque ad caput quintum : in quo deinde iustificationis effecta exponit, ibidemq; de causa instrumentali extra hominem, videlicet obedientia mortis Christi tractat: simulque de causa formali: quæ est obedientiæ huius imputatio. Tertio illustrat iu-stificationem à contrario, videlicet condemna-tione nostri per inobedientiam Adæ : à v. 12. capitis quinti vsq; ad finem illius capitis. Quarto agit de necessario quodam iustificationis adiuncto, videlicet sanctificatione: de qua agit toto capite sexto & parte septimi. Quinto, agit de causis efficientibus principalibus: quas proponit duas: videlicet Deum Patrem qui misit Filium, & Filium qui Legi pronobis satisfecit, capite octauo : iisque explicatis redit ad adiunctum, videlicet sanctificationem iustificatorum,vsque ad finem capitis.
units.tr: In the first part of this epistle, therefore, the Apostle sets out the nature of justification from its causes, effects, accompaniments and contraries. He treats of the causes, partly the efficient causes, both principal and instrumental, and partly the formal cause. First of all he deals with the instrumental cause in man, namely faith, teaching that man is justified by faith, up to the fifth chapter. There he then sets out the effects of justification, and in the same place he treats of the instrumental cause outside man, namely the obedience of Christ's death, and at the same time of the formal cause, which is the imputation of this obedience. Third, he illustrates justification by its contrary, namely our condemnation through the disobedience of Adam, from verse 12 of the fifth chapter to the end of that chapter. Fourth, he deals with a certain necessary accompaniment of justification, namely sanctification, which he treats in the whole of the sixth chapter and part of the seventh. Fifth, he deals with the principal efficient causes, which he sets out as two: namely God the Father, who sent the Son, and the Son, who satisfied the Law on our behalf (chapter 8). When these have been explained, he returns to the accompaniment, namely the sanctification of the justified, up to the end of the chapter.

units.la: Primo igitur omnium (vt dixi) agit Apostolus de iustificationis causa instrumentali in homine, videlicet fide: docens hominem iustificari fide,hoc est, coram tribunali Dei à peccatis absolui, & innocentem iustumque pronunciari,quatenus credit in Christum,hoc est,quatenus credit promissioni Euangelij de remissione peccatorum propter Christum: quòd scilicet Deus sibi peccata sua condonauerit atque ignouerit propter Christum, qui pro illis sua morte satisfecit. Hanc iustificationis causam concludit Apostolus argumento diuisionis in hanc sententiam:
units.tr: First of all (as I said) the Apostle deals with the instrumental cause of justification in man, namely faith. He teaches that man is justified by faith, that is, that he is absolved from sins before the judgement seat of God and pronounced innocent and righteous, insofar as he believes in Christ, that is, insofar as he believes the promise of the gospel concerning the forgiveness of sins for Christ's sake: that God has indeed pardoned and forgiven him his sins for Christ's sake, who by his death made satisfaction for them. The Apostle concludes this cause of justification by an argument from division, in this sense:

units.la: Homo iustificatur vel ex suis operibus, seu ex Lege: vel Christi obedientia, seu fide.
units.tr: Man is justified either by his own works, that is, by the Law, or by the obedience of Christ, that is, by faith.

units.la: Non iustificatur ex operibus.
units.tr: He is not justified by works.

units.la: Ergo ex fide.
units.tr: Therefore he is justified by faith.

units.la: Huius Syllogismi Propositionem (hoc est sententiam primam, qua continetur diuisio) Apostolus tanquam per se manifestam certamque omittit ac praesupponit: nam cum constet dis-iunctione aduersorum immediatorum, illustris est & plane necessaria: necessitas enim disiun-ctionis, pendet ex necessaria partium oppositione. Certum autem est, hominem iusti-sicari aut iustitia sua, id est, ex Lege suis viribus praestita, aut aliena iustitia, id est, ex fide apprehendente sibique applicante iustitiam alienam. Nam si quis legem suis viribus implerei, is iusti-ficaretur sua iustitia: sicut is qui credit, Christum pro se Legi satisfecisse, iustificatur iustitia alienâ, nempe Christi, sibi per fidem imputata ac donata.
units.tr: The Apostle passes over the major premise of this syllogism (that is, the first statement, which contains the division) as evident in itself and certain, and presupposes it. For since it rests on the disjunction of immediate opposites, it is clear and plainly necessary: the necessity of the disjunction depends on the necessary opposition of the parts. It is certain that a man is justified either by his own righteousness, that is, by the Law performed by his own strength, or by another's righteousness, that is, by faith which lays hold of and applies to himself the righteousness of another. For if someone fulfilled the Law by his own powers, he would be justified by his own righteousness; and in the same way, he who believes that Christ satisfied the Law on his behalf is justified by another's righteousness, namely Christ's, imputed and given to him through faith.

units.la: Assumtionem vero, hoc est, secundam sententiam, qua negatur hominem iustificare ex operibus, probat tali syllogismo:
units.tr: The minor premise, that is, the second statement, which denies that man is justified by works, he proves by the following syllogism:

units.la: Nullus transgressor Legis ex operibus Legis iustificatur.
units.tr: No transgressor of the Law is justified by the works of the Law.

units.la: At omnis homo transgressor Legis est.
units.tr: But every man is a transgressor of the Law.

units.la: Nullus igitur homo ex operibus Legis iustificatur.
units.tr: Therefore no man is justified by the works of the Law.

units.la: Huius Syllogismi Propositio extra controversiam est. Assumtionem approbat Apostolus primum de gentibus incircumcisis, (quae tamen demonstratio pertinet etiam ad Iudæos) à v. 18. cap. 1. Deinde de Iudæis cap. 2. & in genere de omnibus hominibus,cap. 3. Summa est: Neque Gentes, neque Iudæi ex operibus iustificari possunt, cum illi ex Lege Naturæ impietatis in Deum & iniustitiæ in proximum conuincantur. Hi ex Lege scripta Mosis, concinentibus etiam Prophetis, interpretibus ipsius Legis, peccati itidem conuincantur: imo adeo, ut per eos sanctum Dei nomen male audiat etiam apud Gentes. Atqui iustitia ex Lege perfectam Legis impletionem in omni opere, ne uno quidem excepto, requirit. Maledictus qui non manserit in omnibus,&c.
units.tr: The major premise of this syllogism is beyond dispute. The Apostle proves the minor premise first concerning the uncircumcised Gentiles (though this demonstration also applies to the Jews), from verse 18 of chapter 1; then concerning the Jews in chapter 2; and in general concerning all men in chapter 3. The sum is this: neither Gentiles nor Jews can be justified by works, since the former are convicted by the Law of nature of impiety towards God and injustice towards their neighbour. The latter are likewise convicted of sin by the written Law of Moses, with the agreement of the Prophets, the interpreters of the Law itself; indeed to such an extent that through them the holy name of God is badly spoken of even among the Gentiles. But righteousness by the Law demands the perfect fulfilment of the Law in every work, not even one excepted: Cursed is everyone who does not continue in all things, etc.

units.la: Hæc est prima ἀπόδειξις[?] sententia seu summa: nunc ad specialem capitum œconomiam descendemus.
units.tr: This is the first demonstration, or summary of the argument; now we shall descend to the particular arrangement of the chapters.

units.la: POSTQUAM Apostolus summatim, tum ab effectis manifestis prædicationis Euangelicæ in credentibus (v.16.) tum ex Scripturis (v.17.) ostendit, Euangelium esse organon salutaris Dei potentiæ, & in eo revelari iustitiam Deo acceptam quam per fidem percipimus: nunc illius iustitiæ fidei necessitatem demonstrat, & eorum præsumptionibus occurrit, qui vel sapientia sua humana, vel aliis virtutibus nituntur; quos solidis argumentis refellit, ut intelligant iustitiam illam Euangelicam necessario sibi quærendam & amplectendam, si salui esse velint. Ac primum quidem venusta anthitesi revelationem irae Dei, id est, ultionis & pœnarum diuinarum, quæ conspicitur erga infideles, opponit revelationi iustitiæ, salutis & vitæ, quæ cernitur in Euangelio & fidelibus: v. i8. ubi notanda est ellipsis seu omissio assumptionis principalis Syllogismi: quam hic probare instituit nempe, neminem iustificari ex operibus Legis: cum qua proprie cohaeret coniunctio rationalis γαρ[?] .i. enim. Quum enim dixisset, hominem iustificari & saluari ex fide: promptum erat quaerere, Et cur non ex operibus Legis? quae tum apud maximam hominum partem recepta erat (sicut etiamnum hodie est) opinio. Haec igitur interrogatio omissa est: & tanquam esset posita, ita nunc ratio subiungitur, Palam est enim ira Dei &c: Sententia est: Ideo non ex operibus Legis iustificatur homo, quia homo opera Legis non facit. Id primum probat de lege naturae & de gentibus incircumcisis. Lex autem naturae complectitur duas partes: videlicet cultum Dei, & amorem proximi. Apostolus primum agit de cultu Dei, ostendens primo, notitiam Dei hominibus esse insitam: v. 19. 20. deinde Gentes legem naturae de Deo vere colendo violasse: id quod probat ex idololatria: vsque ad v. 24. Deinde hoc ipsum confirmat ex effectis, videlicet ex poenis gravissimis, nempe detestandis flagitiis & sceleribus quae commiserunt, in reprobum sensum iusto Dei iudicio traditi: quorum scelerum prolixum catalogum in fine capitis recenset;quo ipso etiam demonstrat, Gentes violasse legem naturae de dilectione proximi.
units.tr: AFTER the Apostle has shown briefly, both from the manifest effects of the Gospel preaching in believers (verse 16) and from the Scriptures (verse 17), that the Gospel is the instrument of God's saving power, and that in it is revealed the righteousness acceptable to God which we receive through faith, he now demonstrates the necessity of that righteousness of faith and meets the presumptions of those who rely either on their human wisdom or on other virtues. He refutes them with solid arguments, so that they may understand that they must seek and embrace that Gospel righteousness if they wish to be saved. First, with a striking antithesis, he sets the revelation of God's wrath, that is, his vengeance and divine punishments, which is seen against unbelievers, over against the revelation of righteousness, salvation and life, which is seen in the Gospel and in believers (verse 18). Here one should note the ellipsis, or omission, of the assumption of the principal syllogism, which he now undertakes to prove, namely that no one is justified by the works of the Law. With it is properly joined the causal conjunction for [γάρ]. For having said that man is justified and saved by faith, it was natural to ask: and why not by the works of the Law? That was the opinion widely held among most men at that time, as it still is today. This question, then, is left out, and the reasoning is added as though it had been put: For the wrath of God is plainly revealed, etc. The sense is: Therefore man is not justified by the works of the Law, because man does not do the works of the Law. He proves this first from the law of nature and concerning the uncircumcised Gentiles. The law of nature comprises two parts: namely the worship of God and the love of one's neighbour. The Apostle first deals with the worship of God, showing first that the knowledge of God is implanted in men (verses 19 and 20), and then that the Gentiles violated the law of nature concerning the true worship of God. He proves this from idolatry, up to verse 24. Then he confirms this same point from its effects, namely from the most grievous punishments: those detestable vices and crimes which they committed, being given over by the just judgement of God to a reprobate mind. He recounts a long catalogue of these crimes at the end of the chapter, by which he also demonstrates that the Gentiles violated the law of nature concerning love of neighbour.

units.la: Summa analytica, seu analysis summaria capitis secundi, hoc est eius cum antecedente connexio, summa, partes, & partium œconomia seu dispositio haec est:
units.tr: The analytical summary, or summary analysis, of the second chapter: its connection with the preceding chapter, its main points, its parts, and the order and arrangement of those parts, is as follows:

units.la: Posteaquam in antecedente capite sententiam illam peccatorum in utramq; tabulam,& sum-[?] [?]mam hominis non regeniti vel à Deo deserti miseriam nobis proposuit Apostolus : iam hoc capite per prolepfin occurrit exceptionibus hy-pocrytarum,& confirmat principalem propo-fitionem , omnibus tum sapientibus inter Gentes, tum ipsis Iudaeis quærendam esse iustitiam extra se & sua opera, videlicet per fidem in Christum, cum omnes peccarint, aly quidem contra legem non in tabulis lapideis ; sed in cordibus scriptam. i. naturalem ; aly vero contra legem datam & promulgatam. Sunt autem huius capitis partes duae: prior respondet ad exceptiones hypocrytarum, vsque ad v. 12. Altera nominatim ad Iudaeos dirigitur, qui de lege & circumcisione gloriantes, Euangelium siue doctrinam gratuitae redemptionis aspernabantur. Postquam enim pronunciauit Apostolus, sine respectu gentis & personarum, omnibus peccatoribus iratus Deum, nunc causam exponit, cur ne ij quidem qui legem Mosis habebant & quotidie euoluebant, iusti coram Deo censeri potuerint. Ratio sumta est à definitione iustitiae legalis, non in auditione sed in-tegra præstatione consistentis. Nullus autem Iudaeus præstat illam obedientiam. Ergo per legem non possunt iustificari Iudaei. Assumtionem probat ex multiplici transgressione legis & scandalo dato a Iudaeis, idque a v. 17. ad 24. Inde vero ad finem vsque capitis, refutat falsam opinionem eorum qui existimant sacramenta conferre iustitiam ex opere operato.
units.tr: Having set before us, in the preceding chapter, the statement about sins against both tables of the law and the sum of the misery of a man who is unregenerate or forsaken by God, the Apostle now meets the objections of hypocrites by way of prolepsis, and confirms his main proposition: that all men, both the wise among the Gentiles and the Jews themselves, must seek righteousness outside themselves and their own works, namely through faith in Christ, since all have sinned: some indeed against the law not written on tablets of stone but written in the heart, that is, the natural law; others against the law given and promulgated. The chapter has two parts. The first answers the objections of hypocrites, up to verse 12. The second is addressed by name to the Jews, who, boasting of the law and of circumcision, despised the Gospel, or the doctrine of free redemption. For after the Apostle has declared, without regard to nation or person, that God is angry with all sinners, he now explains why not even those who had the law of Moses and read it every day could be counted righteous before God. The reasoning is taken from the definition of legal righteousness, which consists not in hearing the law but in fully performing it. But no Jew performs that obedience. Therefore Jews cannot be justified by the law. He proves this minor premise from the many transgressions of the law and the scandal given by the Jews, from verse 17 to verse 24. From there to the end of the chapter he refutes the false opinion of those who think that the sacraments confer righteousness by the work done (ex opere operato).

units.la: Cap. tertio pergit Apostolus in eius parte prima, vsque ad v. 9. protensa, Iudaeos peccati reos peragere, praeoccupando & confutando eorum quasdam obiectiones: quarum prima est: An igi-turtur Iudæi nullo præ reliquis gentibus propter circum-cisionem polleant priuilegio? Respondet Paulus concedendo eos quidem Gentes antecellere propter ipsis concredita eloquia Dei, hoc ipsum vero non ad ipsorum dignitatem, sed ad Dei erga ipsos singularem gratiam demonstrandam facere, quam ipsi quidem per incredulitatem reiiciunt, Dei tamen veritatem non tollant. Secunda obiectio est v.5. Cùm nostra iniustitia Dei commendet iustitiam, annon hinc sequitur securè peccandum? Negat Paulus: quia Deus iustus sit mundi iudex, & iustus voluntariè peccantium vltor & vindex. Secunda parte huius capitis, testimoniis Scripturæ omnes homines, hoc est, tam Iudæos quam Gentes probat esse peccatores: à v. 9. vsque ad 20. quo continetur conclusio syllogismi primary primi.
units.tr: In the first part of the third chapter, which runs to verse 9, the Apostle goes on to show that the Jews are guilty of sin, anticipating and refuting some of their objections. The first objection is: Do the Jews then have no advantage over the other nations because of circumcision? Paul answers by conceding that they do excel the Gentiles, because the oracles of God were entrusted to them; but this does not serve their dignity, rather it serves to show God's singular grace toward them, which they reject through unbelief, though they do not thereby nullify the truth of God. The second objection is (verse 5): Since our unrighteousness commends the righteousness of God, does it not follow that we may sin with impunity? Paul denies it, because God is a just judge of the world, and a just avenger and punisher of those who sin willingly. In the second part of this chapter, by the testimonies of Scripture, he proves that all men, that is, both Jews and Gentiles, are sinners, from verse 9 to verse 20, where is contained the conclusion of the first syllogism of the principal argument.

units.la: Posteaquam Apostolus negatiuam thesin expediuit, gentibus scilicet & Iudæis iustitiam illam deesse quam Deus requirit, & legem tum naturalem tum scriptam nihil aliud quam summam impietatem & iniustitiam hominum detegere, redit ad principalem suam propositionem affirmatiuam, siue statum huius controuersiæ, Ex Euangelio solo de fide in fidem reuelari illam Dei iustitiam, sicut cap. 1. v. 17. asseruit, in qua probanda deinceps insistit, vsque ad cap. 9. A versu igitur 21. vsque ad finem capitis, veram iustificationis rationem, quæ per fidem fit, dilucidè proponit.
units.tr: Having set out the negative thesis, that both Gentiles and Jews lack that righteousness which God requires, and that both the natural law and the written law reveal nothing but the utmost impiety and unrighteousness of men, the Apostle returns to his principal affirmative proposition, or the state of this controversy: that this righteousness of God is revealed from the Gospel alone, from faith to faith, as he asserted in chapter 1, verse 17. He sets out to prove this from here on, up to chapter 9. From verse 21 to the end of the chapter, he clearly sets out the true reason for justification, which comes through faith.

units.la: Cap. 1 v. Ad stabiliendam doctrinam de iustificatione superioris capitis versiculo 28. conclusam, plura argumenta ab Apostolo afferuntur: quorum primum ac præcipuum est ab exemplo Abrahæ, hoc est, à pari collatione Abra-hæ tanquam patris, cum reliquis benedicendis seu saluandis, tanquam filiis: quippe quum unâ eâdemque ratione iustificentur pater & filij: at Pa-ter Abraham fide iustificatus fuit. Ergo pari ratio-ne & filios Abrahæ, hoc est, cæteros benedicendos Abrahamum sequutos, iustificari oportet. Et sic de-clarat, quod superiore capite v. 21. dixit: iustitiam Dei, id est, iustitiam fidei, quam Deus per fidem im-putat, comprobatam esse testimonio Legis & Pro-phetarum. exemplum enim Abrahæ petitum est ex Lege, videlicet libro primo Mosis, cui adiungit te-stimonium prophetæ Dauid, ad eandem doctrinam confirmandam, v. 6. 7. 8. Simul autem docet, iu-stitiam fidei non ad solos Iudæos sed etiam ad Gen-tes pertinere: ibidemque Circumcisionis vsum de-clarat: v. 9. & deinceps. 1 1. Aliud argumen-tum pro iustitia fidei affert, ex natura promissæ heredi-tatis, v. 13. & deinceps. 111 Fidem Abrahæ commendat, v. 18. & deinceps. Postremò exem-plum Abrahæ ad se & Romanos accommodat: & fidem iustificantem e subiectis occupantibus decla-rat: v. 23. vsque ad finem capitis.
units.tr: Chapter 4. To establish the doctrine of justification, which was concluded in the previous chapter at verse 28, the Apostle brings forward several arguments. The first and chief of these is taken from the example of Abraham, that is, from a parallel comparison of Abraham as father with the rest who are to be blessed or saved as sons, since father and sons are justified by one and the same method; but Father Abraham was justified by faith. Therefore the sons of Abraham, that is, the others who follow Abraham and are to be blessed, must likewise be justified. In this way he explains what he said in chapter 3, verse 21: that the righteousness of God, that is, the righteousness of faith, which God imputes through faith, is confirmed by the testimony of the Law and the Prophets. For the example of Abraham is taken from the Law, namely from the first book of Moses, and to it he adds the testimony of the prophet David, to confirm the same doctrine, verses 6, 7 and 8. At the same time he teaches that the righteousness of faith pertains not only to the Jews but also to the Gentiles, and there he explains the use of circumcision, verse 9 and following. Second, he brings another argument for the righteousness of faith, from the nature of the promised inheritance, verse 13 and following. Third, he commends Abraham's faith, verse 18 and following. Finally, he applies Abraham's example to himself and the Romans, and declares justifying faith to be distinct from the things that occupy the subjects, verse 23 to the end of the chapter.

units.la: Hactenus Apostolus demonstrauit, homi-nem iustificari fide: deinceps capite v iustifi-cationem fidei amplius declarat & illustrat: par-tim ex effectis, partim ex oppositis. Effecta iu-stificationis exponit duo: primum pacem erga Deum, id est, reconciliationem cum Deo, vel etiam inde ortam tranquillitatem conscientiæ, v. 1. Dein-de spem gloriæ Dei, hoc est, gloriæ cælestis, qua Deus in vita æterna iustificatos ornaturus est, v. 2. & de-inceps. Collatio oppositorum ( v. 12. & deinceps ) partim similium est, partim dissimilium. Comparat enim autorem iustitiae & vitae, videlicet Christum, cum autore peccati & mortis, videlicet Adamo, primo nostro parente: partim ut similem: quia sicut per Adamum peccatum in omnes homines introiit, & per peccatum mors: ita per Christum iustitiam in omnes credentes intrat, & per iustitiam vita. Partim ut dissimilem: quia sicut per Adamum peccatum in omnes homines introiit, fuit unum tantum: at iustitia Christi ( id est, parta morte & obedientia Christi ) quae credentibus imputatur, delet non solum peccatum illud unum, sed etiam alia plura, videlicet peccata credentium omnia
units.tr: So far the Apostle has shown that man is justified by faith. In chapter 5 he explains and illustrates the justification by faith more fully, partly from its effects and partly from its opposites. He sets out two effects of justification: first, peace toward God, that is, reconciliation with God, or also the tranquillity of conscience arising from it, verse 1. Then the hope of God's glory, that is, of heavenly glory, with which God will adorn the justified in eternal life, verse 2 and following. The comparison of opposites (verse 12 and following) is partly of similar things and partly of dissimilar ones. For he compares the author of righteousness and life, namely Christ, with the author of sin and death, namely Adam, our first parent. He does so partly as similar: just as through Adam sin entered into all men, and through sin death, so through Christ righteousness enters into all believers, and through righteousness life. And partly as dissimilar: for through Adam sin entered into all men, but it was only one sin; whereas the righteousness of Christ (that is, obtained by the death and obedience of Christ), which is imputed to believers, blots out not only that one sin but also many others, namely all the sins of believers.

units.la: Postquam Apostolus totam rationem nostrae iustificationis coram Deo accurate exposuit, evidentissimisque argumentis ostendit eam a mera Dei gratia pendere, & sola fide a nobis apprehendi & applicari: iam transit ad explicationem aliquot quaestionum quas supra obiter attigerat, plenam earum tractationem reliciens in hunc locum & capita aliquot sequentia. Quaestiones autem potissimum tres aspersae fuerant cap. 3. Prima: An gratia Dei excludat bona opera: &, an sint mala facienda ut eveniant bona: haec pertractat capite sexto, ubi de fructibus fidei & de vita nova sive iustitia operum continuata cum gratuita iustificatione disserit Apostolus. Altera fuit de lege: An per fidem inanis reddatur, de qua re plenissime capite 7. & initio 8. Tertia erat de populo Iudaico: An Deus illum plane abiecisset, foederis sui immemor, ad quam quaestionem luculenter respondet capite 9. 10. & 11. ac simul varios terminos ipsi usitatos explicat: videlicet quid sit, esse sub lege, & esse sub gratia, &c:
units.tr: Having set out accurately the whole account of our justification before God, and having shown by the clearest arguments that it depends on the mere grace of God and is apprehended and applied by us through faith alone, the Apostle now passes to explain some questions which he had touched on in passing above, reserving their full treatment for this place and for some of the following chapters. Three questions had been raised chiefly in chapter 3. The first: whether grace of God excludes good works, and whether evil is to be done so that good may come. He treats this in chapter 6, where the Apostle discourses on the fruits of faith and on the new life, or the righteousness of works that continues alongside gratuitous justification. The second concerned the law: whether it is made void through faith. He treats this most fully in chapter 7 and the beginning of chapter 8. The third concerned the Jewish people: whether God had utterly cast them off, forgetful of his covenant. To this question he answers clearly in chapters 9, 10 and 11, and at the same time explains the various terms customarily used for them: namely, what it is to be under the law, and to be under grace, and so on.

units.la: Capitis VI duae sunt partes: prior est refutatio per praeoccupationem eorum qui ex abundantia gratia existimant inuehi licentiam peccandi, vel perseuerantiam in peccatis: quos refutat partim ex natura contrariorum: partim ex causa finali nostræ iustificationis cuius in Baptismo admonemur. Altera pars à v.12. usque ad finem est παραινετικη, habens adhortationes ad vitæ nouitatem & puritatem: Nam licet peccatum in altera scilicet æterna demum vita radicem amissurum sit: regnum tamen amittit in terra, in credentibus.
units.tr: Chapter 6 has two parts. The first is a refutation, by anticipation, of those who, from the abundance of grace, conclude that license to sin is introduced, or that one may persevere in sins. He refutes them partly from the nature of contraries, and partly from the final cause of our justification, of which we are reminded in Baptism. The second part, from verse 12 to the end, is exhortatory [παραινετικη], containing exhortations to newness and purity of life. For although sin will lose its root only in the other life, namely eternal life, yet it loses its kingdom on earth, among believers.

units.la: Potest autē hæc pars subdiuidi in tria membra: 1. in ipsam adhortationem, v. 12. 13. 11 In duas prolepses, v.14. & 15. 111 in gratiarum actionem, à v. 17. ad finem, quæ eucharistia continet ευχαριστιαν adhortationis, & amplificationem per αντιθετον gratiæ quæ contingit iis, qui à legis maledictione & seruitute peccati liberati sunt.
units.tr: This part can be subdivided into three sections: (1) the exhortation itself, vv. 12–13; (2) two prolepses, vv. 14 and 15; (3) the thanksgiving, from v. 17 to the end, which contains the thanksgiving [εὐχαριστίαν] of the exhortation and an amplification by antithesis [ἀντίθετον] of the grace that comes to those who have been freed from the curse of the law and from the slavery of sin.

units.la: Cap. v 11 cohæret cum antecedente, & est magna ex parte exegesis eius quod supra dixit: nos non esse sub lege, sed sub gratia: & quomodo fit intelligendum, quòd à legis subiectione traducti sumus ad seruitium Christi. Partes capitis sunt tres præcipuè: prima est explicatio illustrata exemplo coniugij, quare non simus amplius sub lege, id est, cur abrogatum sit rigidium eius in nos imperium. Secunda pars v. 7. est excusatio legis per præoccupationem, vbi lex omni suspicione liberatur, & culpa omnis in hominem transfertur: Tertia est φιλαγιαςμος, à v.14. usque ad finem, continens tristem querelam de Sanctificationis imperfectione, de dissidio corrupte natura cum lege Dei, & de perpetua luctu Spiritus & carnis in ipsis renatis. Vnde rursum concludit: In solo Christo, & liberatione per eum parta acquiescendū esse.
units.tr: Chapter 5, verse 11 coheres with what precedes it and is for the most part an exposition of what he said above: that we are not under the law but under grace, and of how it is to be understood that we have been transferred from subjection to the law into the service of Christ. The chapter has three main parts. The first is an explanation, illustrated by the example of marriage, of why we are no longer under the law, that is, why its rigorous rule over us has been abrogated. The second part, v. 7, is a defence of the law by way of anticipation, in which the law is cleared of every suspicion and all the blame is laid upon the human being. The third is a philallagismos, from v. 14 to the end, containing a sorrowful complaint about the imperfection of sanctification, about the discord of corrupt nature with the law of God, and about the perpetual struggle of spirit and flesh in the regenerate themselves. From this he again concludes that one must rest in Christ alone and in the deliverance obtained through him. ## Chapter

units.la: Caput

Caput VIII: in duas partes principales distingui potest. in quorum prima Apostolus permixtim agit de iustificatione & sanctificatione, usq; ad v. 17. In altera parte agit de cruce seu afflictionibus credentium, usque ad finem capitis. Ac de iustificatione quidem paucis hic agit, v. 1. 3. & 4. concludens doctrinam supra copiosius expositam & demonstratam. Summa est: Qui credunt in Christum, ij sunt iustificati: quia Deus peccatum eorum in carne Christi condemnavit. De Sanctificatione autem pluribus disputat: partim docens, credentes sanctitati vitae studere; quia donati sunt spiritu Christi, v. 1. 2. 3. 4. 5. 9. 10. 11. Partim vero illos ad vitae sanctitatem exhortans exponendo effectus: videlicet tum bonum, & expetendum effectum vitae sanctae, qui est vita aeterna: tum e contrario malum effectum vitae peccatricis, qui est mors: v. 6. 7. 8. 12. 14. 15. 16. 17. Altera pars capitis incipit in medio versus decimiseptimi, Si modo simul &c: ubi agit de cruce seu afflictionibus credentium. Hortatur autem ad crucem patienter cum Christo toleran-dam: argumentum affert ab effectu utili, videlicet glorificatione seu gloria coelesti: quod argumentum copiose & varie tractat. Porro cum exhortatione coniungit consolationem, docens fore ut credentes tandem ex cruce eluctentur, non autem sub illius mole succumbant: id quod probat tribus argumentis: quorum primum sumtum est à certitudine spei credentium, v. 24. & 25. alterum ab ope Spiritus S. v. 26. & 27. tertium vero à caritate Dei, qua credentes complectitur in Christo, v. 28. & inde usque ad finem capitis.
units.tr: Chapter 8 can be distinguished into two principal parts. In the first of these the Apostle deals in a mixed way with justification and sanctification, down to v. 17. In the second part he deals with the cross, or the afflictions of believers, to the end of the chapter. He treats justification here only briefly, at vv. 1, 3 and 4, concluding the doctrine set out and demonstrated more fully above. The summary is: those who believe in Christ are justified, because God condemned their sin in the flesh of Christ. He discusses sanctification at greater length, partly teaching that believers should strive for holiness of life, since they have been given the Spirit of Christ (vv. 1–5, 9–11), and partly exhorting them to holiness of life by setting out its effects: on the one hand the good and desirable effect of a holy life, which is eternal life, and on the other the evil effect of a sinful life, which is death (vv. 6–8, 12, 14–17). The second part of the chapter begins in the middle of the seventeenth verse, "If indeed we suffer together," etc., where he deals with the cross, or the afflictions of believers. He exhorts them to endure the cross patiently with Christ, and he brings forward as an argument its useful effect, namely glorification, or heavenly glory, which argument he treats fully and in various ways. Further, he joins consolation to the exhortation, teaching that believers will at last struggle free of the cross and will not sink under its weight. He proves this by three arguments: the first is taken from the certainty of the believers' hope (vv. 24–25); the second from the help of the Holy Spirit (vv. 26–27); the third from the love of God, by which he embraces believers in Christ (v. 28 and onwards to the end of the chapter).

units.la: Hactenus disputauit Apostolus de causa salutis nostra proxima, hoc est, de iustificatione fidei, seu de fide iustificante, deque eius effectis & adiunctis, vt sunt sanctificatio, spes, tolerantia crucis, &c. Deinceps per tria capita vsque ad caput duodecimum, disputaturus est de Praedestinatione. Accidit autem ad hanc doctrinam per tacitam prolepsin. Nam contra doctrinam de iustificatione traditam obiici poterat incredulitas gentis Iudaicae, hoc syllogismo: Si doctrina illa de iustificatione per fidem in Christum, esset vera: approbaretur quoque & reciperetur a gente Iudaica: quippe quae tunc erat populus Dei. At Iudaei, saltem maxima ex parte, doctrinam illam improbabant ac damnabant. Non ergo videtur doctrina illa esse vera. Apostolus negat propositionem, & respondet ad rationem: docens, non omnes Iudaeos pertinere ad populum illum Dei, ad quem proprie pertinet promissio gratiae Dei, sed tantum eos qui promissioni gratiae credunt. Quod autem pauci credunt, plerique non credunt, id pendere ab arcano voluntate & praedestinatione Dei: vt qui alios pro sua misericordia elegerit ad vitam aeternam, alios vero pro sua inscrutabili iustitia reprobarit: ex qua quidem reprobatione pendeat maximae partis Iudaeorum illius temporis reiectio, & contra Gentium in illorum locum vocatio.
units.tr: Thus far the Apostle has disputed about the nearer cause of our salvation, that is, about justification by faith, or faith that justifies, and about its effects and attendants, such as sanctification, hope, endurance of the cross, etc. Next, over three chapters, to the twelfth chapter, he is going to dispute about predestination. He comes to this doctrine by a tacit prolepsis. For against the doctrine of justification as delivered, the unbelief of the Jewish people could be raised by this syllogism: If that doctrine of justification through faith in Christ were true, it would also be approved and received by the Jewish people, since they were then the people of God. But the Jews, at least for the most part, disapproved and condemned that doctrine. Therefore that doctrine does not seem to be true. The Apostle denies the proposition and replies to the argument, teaching that not all Jews belong to that people of God to whom the promise of God's grace properly belongs, but only those who believe the promise of grace. That few believe and most do not believe depends on the hidden will and predestination of God: he who in his mercy has chosen some to eternal life, and in his inscrutable justice has rejected others. From this rejection depends the rejection of the greater part of the Jews of that time, and, on the contrary, the calling of the Gentiles into their place.

units.la: Itaque capite ix[?]: redit Apostolus ad illam quaestionem, quam attigerat capite tertio de praerogatiuis Iudaeorum: &, an illi sua incredulitate Dei fedus cum Abrahamo irritum reddiderint. Quaestio igitur capitis est: Quinam sint veri Israelita & filij Abrahami. Conclusio subiicietur initio capitis undecimi: Deum non reiecisse populum suum quem praecognouit, iuxta id quod supra cap. 8. [illegible, ~5 letters] docuit, Nihil condemnationis metuendum electis Dei: & ab hac thesi ad hypothesin hoc quoque capite descendit Apostolus. Partes capitis sunt quatuor. 1. Exordium continens insinuationem valde patheticam qua mollit ea quae de reiectione magna partis Iudaeorum dicturus est: & partim de suo summo studio erga suam gentem testificatur: partim priuilegia & praerogatiuas illius gentis prolixe commemorat. II pars est propositio, habens praeoccupationem: Obiici enim poterat: Fac fide iustificari homines, sed si id fit, quomodo constabit fedus cum Israelitis, cum plerique nolint credere Christo? & quomodo constabunt illorum priuilegia, si gentes in eundem gratiam societatem veniunt? Respondet v. 6. Non excidere sermonem Dei, reiectis multis Iudaeis & vocatis Gentibus, quod confirmat distinctione filiorum Abrahami, & verorum Israelitarum a Pseudo-Israelitis; quod discrimen in duabus illis illustribus familiis Abrahami & Isaaci maturè praesignificatum ostendit, a v. ad 14. III pars continet solutionem duarum obiectionum: Annon videatur Deus iniustus dum hos eligit, illos reiicit? & de eius Voluntate cui nemo resistere potest; in quibus soluendis ab hypothesi ad thesin descendit, & ex ipsis Scripturarum fontibus doctrinam de electione gratuita ad vitam, & reprobatione confirmat, illiusque doctrina vsum indicat. v. 22. & 23. Vltima parte agit de vocatione Gentium, quam alienam non videri debere testimoniis prophetarum probat a v. 24. ad finem.
units.tr: Therefore, in chapter 9, the Apostle returns to that question which he had touched on in chapter 3, concerning the privileges of the Jews: whether by their unbelief they have made the covenant of God with Abraham void. The question of the chapter, then, is: who are the true Israelites and the children of Abraham? The conclusion is set out at the beginning of chapter 11: that God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew, in accordance with what he taught above in chapter 8 [illegible], namely that the elect of God have nothing to fear from condemnation; and from this thesis the Apostle, in this chapter too, descends to the hypothesis. The chapter has four parts. 1. The introduction contains a very emotional insinuation by which he softens what he is about to say concerning the rejection of the greater part of the Jews; partly he bears witness to his own great zeal for his nation, partly he recounts at length the privileges and prerogatives of that nation. 2. The second part is a proposition with an anticipation. For it could be objected: granted that men are justified by faith, yet if this is so, how will the covenant with the Israelites stand, since most of them are unwilling to believe in Christ? And how will their privileges stand, if the Gentiles come into the same grace and fellowship? He replies in v. 6 that the word of God has not failed, though many Jews are rejected and the Gentiles are called. He confirms this by the distinction between the children of Abraham and true Israelites on the one hand and pseudo-Israelites on the other, which distinction he shows was signified in advance in the two famous families of Abraham and Isaac, from v. 7 to v. 14. 3. The third part contains the solution of two objections: Does God not seem unjust when he chooses these and rejects those? And what of his will, which no one can resist? In resolving these, he descends from the hypothesis to the thesis, and from the very sources of the Scriptures he confirms the doctrine of gratuitous election to life and of reprobation, and he indicates the use of that doctrine (vv. 22–23). 4. In the last part he deals with the calling of the Gentiles, and proves from the testimonies of the prophets that it should not seem strange, from v. 24 to the end.

units.la: Caput x. cohaeret cum fine praecedentis: continet enim partim mitigationem eorum quae ibi dixerat de Iudaeis impingentibus in lapidem offensionis: partim causam cur a Iudaeis inventa non fuerit iustitia quam tam laboriosè sectabantur: & confirmationem utriusque propositionis de vocatione Gentium & reiectione Iudæorum. Partes capitis, post insinuationem duobus primis versibus, duæ sunt: Prima est tota doc-trinalis, usque ad v.16. explicans quænam sit iu-stitia euangelica, quomodo a legali discernenda, quodnam eius proprium sit obiectum, quod primarium effectum, quænam causæ instrumentales & media per quæ fides in adultis excitatur. II pars est ἐλεγκτικὴ[?], a v.16. ad finem: confirmans superio-rem censuram incredulitatis & contumaciæ Iudæo-rum, quam Paulus prudenter non tam suis, quam Mosis & Isaiæ verbis perstringere voluit.
units.tr: Chapter 10 coheres with the end of the preceding one. For it contains partly a softening of what had been said there about the Jews stumbling at the stone of offence, and partly the reason why the righteousness which they so laboriously pursued was not found by the Jews; and a confirmation of both propositions concerning the calling of the Gentiles and the rejection of the Jews. The parts of the chapter, after the insinuation in the first two verses, are two. The first is wholly doctrinal, down to v. 16, explaining what the evangelical righteousness is, how it is to be distinguished from the legal, what its proper object is, what its primary effect is, and what the instrumental causes and means are through which faith is awakened in adults. The second part is elenctic [ἐλεγκτικὴ], from v. 16 to the end, confirming the earlier censure of the unbelief and obstinacy of the Jews, which Paul prudently chose to rebuke not so much in his own words as in the words of Moses and Isaiah.

units.la: Cap. x 1. est mitigatio & correctio quædam eorum quæ cap. 9. & 10. de Israelitis secundum carnem, de plerorum-que cœcitate, contumacia & reiectione, ex ipsorum prophetarum oraculis allata fuerunt, & simul conclusio & decisio quæstionis iam ante motæ: An Deus vocando Gentes populum suum abiecerit, quem tot signis & memorabilibus liberationibus olim vindicaut[?], & in quo tot magni prophetæ & patriarchæ exstiterunt.
units.tr: Chapter 11 is a certain softening and correction of what was brought forward in chapters 9 and 10 concerning the Israelites according to the flesh, concerning the blindness, obstinacy and rejection of most of them, drawn from the very oracles of their prophets. It is at the same time the conclusion and decision of the question raised earlier: whether God, by calling the Gentiles, has cast off his people, whom he once vindicated with so many signs and memorable deliverances, and among whom so many great prophets and patriarchs arose.

units.la: Summa & propositio est: Ecclesiam proprie sic dictam .i. cœtum electorum non posse perire, nec unquam deseri a Domino. Partes sunt quatuor:
units.tr: The summary and proposition is this: that the Church, properly so called, that is, the assembly of the elect, cannot perish, nor ever be forsaken by the Lord. There are four parts.

units.la: 1 est responsio negativa ad illam quæstionem de populo Dei: non abiectum esse Dei populum, quem-admodum illum initio capitis noni definiuit, quem Deus præcognouit, & secundum propositum elegit: Absit (inquit) ut id inferatur ex mea doctrina: Nam si omnes Israelitæ reiecti essent, nullam ego spem haberem vitæ æternæ. Atqui certus sum me esse esse ex numero electorum & filiorum Dei, & tamen sum Israelita. Ergo non eo spectat mea oratio[?]. Deinde ex paucitate credentium non esse concludendum nullam superesse Ecclesiam inter Israelitas, vel omnes reiectos esse; probat exemplo illustri du-ctu ex temporibus Eliae celeberrimi illius Prophetae, qui cum se solum ex veris Dei cultoribus superesse putaret, grassante tyrannide Achabi & Iezabelis, responsum accepit a Deo 1 Reg. 19. reservata adhuc ad 7000 virorum, id est, mediocrem adhuc coetum hominum, qui non defecerunt a vero Dei cultu: ita Deum adhuc in illa gente proculdubio habere non contemnendum numerum electorum. II pars capitis v.5. medio. est repetitio illius primariae doctrinae huius epistolae, de gratuita electione & iustificatione, cum ἀντιθέσει[?] electorum & reproborum, quorum posteriorum induratio ex prophetis describitur. III pars, a v. 11. ad 22. est explicatio & mitigatio eorum quae de lapsu & ruina Iudaeorum ante dixerat, ubi exponit ad quem finem Deus illum lapsum direxerit, & quas habeat conditiones: praedicit etiam multos Iudaeos suo tempore rursus colligendos in Ecclesiam: & graviter Gentes monet, ne propter suam vocationem insolescant. Quarta pars, a v. 23. ad finem est conclusio epiphonematica, in qua Dei sapientiam & iudicia admirari & adorare, omnesque curiosas speculationes cohibere iubemur, ne in hac doctrina evagemur extra metas, sed in terminis voluntatis divinae & verbi eius nos contineamus.
units.tr: (1) It is a negative answer to that question about the people of God: that God's people, whom he defined at the beginning of chapter nine as those he foreknew and elected according to his purpose, has not been cast off. "Far be it," he says, "that this should be inferred from my teaching. For if all Israelites were rejected, I would have no hope of eternal life. Yet I am certain that I am among the number of the elect and sons of God, and yet I am an Israelite. Therefore my argument does not aim at this." Next, he shows that from the small number of believers one should not conclude that no Church remains among the Israelites, or that they have all been rejected. He proves this by an illustrious example from the time of Elijah, that most famous prophet, who thought he alone was left of the true worshippers of God while the tyranny of Ahab and Jezebel was raging. He received an answer from God (1 Kings 19) that 7000 men had been reserved, that is, a moderate company of people who had not fallen away from the true worship of God. So God, without doubt, still has in that nation a number of the elect that is not to be despised. (2) The second part, from chapter 5, verse 5 onward, is a repetition of the chief doctrine of this letter, concerning gratuitous election and justification, set in antithesis [ἀντιθέσει] to the elect and the reprobate; the hardening of the latter is described from the prophets. (3) The third part, from verse 11 to verse 22, is an explanation and softening of what he had said earlier about the fall and ruin of the Jews. There he sets out to what end God directed that fall and on what conditions it rests. He also foretells that many Jews will in his own time be gathered again into the Church, and he gravely warns the Gentiles not to grow proud because of their calling. (4) The fourth part, from verse 23 to the end, is an epiphonematic conclusion, in which we are commanded to admire and adore the wisdom and judgments of God, and to restrain all curious speculations, so that we do not wander beyond the bounds in this doctrine, but keep ourselves within the limits of the divine will and his Word.

units.la: ALTERA PARS PRINCIPALIS Epistolae, quae est Paraenetica.
units.tr: THE SECOND MAIN PART of the Epistle, which is hortatory.

units.la: Tradidit hactenus Apostolus doctrinam fidei, & explicauit illam suam propositionem, Evangelium esse potentiam Dei ad salutem omni credenti: disseruit etiam de causis tum remotis tum propinquis fidei & iustificationis, acde eiusdem signis & variis effectis. Verum quia fides iustificans non est fides otiosa & mortua, sed ἐνεργουμένη[?] ut loquitur Paulus ad Gal. 5. & habens secum Spiritum sanctificationis, de quo cap. 6. & 7 huius epistolae; sequentibus his capitibus varia ἔργα τῆς πίστεως[?] & officia hominis Christiani, partim Ethica, partim politica, partim etiam οἰκονομικὰ[?] describit, tum erga fratres, tum erga infirmos, imò erga ipsos hostes, tum etiam erga Magistratus. Unde apparet, Euangelium non tollere politias, nec invehere ἀναρχίαν; imò nullam doctrinam accuratius ea tradere quae ad felicem gubernationem & societatem huius vitae pertinent: ut inter alios Tertullianus in Apologetico demonstravit.
units.tr: Hitherto the Apostle has set forth the doctrine of faith and explained his proposition that the Gospel is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes. He has also discussed the causes, both remote and proximate, of faith and justification, and their signs and various effects. But since justifying faith is not idle and dead, but is [energoumenē] "active," as Paul says in Gal. 5, and has with it the Spirit of sanctification, of which he speaks in chapters 6 and 7 of this Epistle, in the following chapters he describes the various [erga tēs pisteōs] "works of faith" and the duties of the Christian man, some ethical, some political, and some even [oikonomika] "domestic." He describes them toward the brethren, toward the weak, even toward enemies themselves, and also toward the magistrates. From this it is evident that the Gospel does not abolish civil order nor introduce anarchy. Rather, no teaching sets forth more carefully those things that pertain to the happy governance and fellowship of this life, as Tertullian, among others, showed in his Apologeticus.

units.la: Huius igitur partis ab initio capitis duodecimi usque ad decimiquinti versum 14. protensa, scopus est: hominem Christianum professionem suam fidei, & vita & moribus, omni studio, ornare debere citra arrogantiam.
units.tr: The aim of this part, which runs from the beginning of chapter 12 to verse 14 of chapter 15, is that the Christian man should adorn his profession of faith, both in life and in morals, with every effort, yet without arrogance.

units.la: Partes hoc ordine cohærent:
units.tr: The parts hold together in this order:

units.la: Generatim : ut singuli digne ambulent sua vocatione, cap.12. v. 1. 2. distinctè: ubi præcepta tradit de rebus Necessariis bonis vel malis: potissimum [illegible, ~9 letters]: contra abusum donorum spiritualium, & de fungendis officiis Ecclesiasticis. cap.12. à v. 3. usque ad 9. Ethica: ad varias virtutes in quotidiana vita hortatur, usque ad finem capitis. Politica: officia erga superiores.c.13. Adiaphoris seu in differentibus:cap.14. Speciatim:idque tū promiscuè: hoc est de rebus communibus quibuscunque sive necessariis, sive in differentibus, usque ad v.14.capitis 15.
units.tr: In general: that each may walk worthily in his calling, chapter 12, verses 1 and 2. In particular, where he gives precepts on things necessary, good or bad, and above all [illegible], against the abuse of spiritual gifts, and on performing ecclesiastical offices: chapter 12, from verse 3 to 9. Ethical: he exhorts to various virtues in daily life, to the end of the chapter. Political: duties toward superiors, chapter 13. Adiaphora, or things indifferent: chapter 14. Specifically, and this both in common, that is, concerning common matters of any kind, whether necessary or indifferent, down to verse 14 of chapter 15.

units.la: Capite duodecimo duobus generalibus præceptis præmissis, v. 1. & 2. deinceps specialiter omnibus ordinibus in Ecclesia commendat modestiam, & dehortatur ab arrogantia donorum spiritualium, eaque occasione admonet, quomodo in fungendis officiis Ecclesiasticis Christiani se gerere debeant: a v. 3. usque ad 9. Inde ad varias virtutes & officia Christiana ad quotidianum convictum pertinentia, & tam doctores quàm auditores concernentia, exhortatur, usque ad finem capitis.
units.tr: In chapter 12, after two general precepts (verses 1 and 2), he then commends modesty specifically to all orders in the Church and warns against arrogance in spiritual gifts. On that occasion he advises how Christians ought to conduct themselves in performing ecclesiastical offices, from verse 3 to 9. Then he exhorts to various Christian virtues and duties pertaining to daily living together, and concerning both teachers and hearers, to the end of the chapter.

units.la: Superiore capite Apostolus docuit, quomodo Christiani se gerere debeant in quotidiana conversatione inter ipsos: nunc docet quomodo se gerere debeant erga magistratus. Itaque praecedens caput fuit ethicum, hoc autem est politicum; quanquam in hoc quoque capite ad [illegible, ~6 letters] praeceptionem vedit.
units.tr: In the preceding chapter the Apostle taught how Christians ought to conduct themselves in daily dealings among one another.
