Now he teaches how they ought to conduct themselves toward the magistrates. So the previous chapter was ethical, while this one is political; although in this chapter too [illegible] he gives instruction.

units.la: Cum epistola haec sit absolutissimum compendium locorum S. Theologiae, non potuit praetermitti locus de Magistratu & eius officio: & vicissim atque ἀναλόγως de subditorum officiis erga Magistratum, qua de re etiam ad Titum 3. & 1. Pet. 2. Nam ut recte monet Ambrosius in hoc praesens caput, Nisi bene constituantur politiae, difficulter ordo in Ecclesia retinetur. Huc igitur spectat Apostoli oratio, ut ordinem à Deo institutum & Magistratus officium & necessitatem describat, quod facit hoc cap. XIII. usque ad v. 8. Deinde redit ad doctrinam de charitate erga proximum & ad praecepta secundae tabulae tanquam ad sedem & fundamentum huius loci, usque ad v. 11. Tertiò concludit doctrinam de officiis Christianorum generali adhortatione ad vitae εὐχρηστῶν [?] pulcherrimis argumentis, ab adiunctis, &c.
units.tr: Since this Epistle is the most complete summary of the topics of holy theology, the topic of the magistrate and his office could not be passed over, and likewise, in turn and by analogy, the duties of subjects toward the magistrate. On this matter see also Titus 3 and 1 Pet. 2. For, as Ambrose rightly observes on this present chapter, unless civil governments are well established, order in the Church is with difficulty maintained. The Apostle's discourse therefore aims at this: to describe the order instituted by God, and the office and necessity of the magistrate, which he does in this chapter 13 down to verse 8. Then he returns to the doctrine of love toward one's neighbour and to the precepts of the second table, as to the seat and foundation of this passage, down to verse 11. Thirdly he concludes the doctrine of Christian duties with a general exhortation to a [euchrēstōn] "useful" life, by most beautiful arguments drawn from circumstances, etc.

units.la: Cum in Ecclesia duo sint semper fidelium genera, quorum alij maiores progressus in religione fecerunt, & sunt in fide robustiores, δυνατοί [?]: quos Apostolus 1. Cor. 3. & Gal. 6. spirituales vocat, propter maiora dona Spiritus S. quibus praediti sunt: Alij sunt infirmiores, & quasi nouitij, qui comparatiue, id est spiritualium respectu, carnales adhuc nominantur, & infantibus comparantur: quomodo erga hos posteriores nos gerere debeamus, hoc capite 14. praescribit Apostolus: Occasio huius admonitionis erant controuersiae quae illis temporibus mouebantur de adiaphoris, hoc est rebus indifferentibus seu mediis, ut de certis ritibus, bus, de cibis, & de feriis: quorum vtrumq; obser-uationem sibi cum Euangelio retinendam putabant nonnulli Iudaei: Ethnici vero conuersi libertatem Christianam vrgentes, subinde de his cum Iudaeis contendebant: utrosque corrigere & ad Christianum [illegible, ~8 letters] renocare conatur Apostolus. Nam
units.tr: Since there are always two kinds of believers in the Church, of whom some have made greater progress in religion and are stronger in faith, [dynatoi] "the strong," whom the Apostle in 1 Cor. 3 and Gal. 6 calls spiritual because of the greater gifts of the Holy Spirit with which they are endowed; others are weaker and, as it were, novices, who by comparison, that is, in relation to the spiritual, are still called carnal and are compared to infants. How we ought to behave toward these latter the Apostle prescribes in this chapter 14. The occasion of this admonition was the controversies that were stirred up in those times about adiaphora, that is, things indifferent or neutral, such as certain rites, foods, and festival days. Some Jews thought both of these observances were to be retained alongside the Gospel. The Gentiles who had been converted, urging Christian liberty, from time to time contended with the Jews about these matters. The Apostle seeks to correct both sides and to call them back to the Christian [illegible]. For

units.la: Capite xiv, hortatur firmos id est eos qui libertatem Christianam intelligebant, ac proinde firmiter persuasi erant se ceremonias Mosaicas bona conscientia omittere posse, ne contemnant aut offendat infirmos, qui quanquam in Christum tanquam seruatorem suum credebant; tamen ignorabant, se per illum liberatos esse ab obseruatione ceremoniarum Legis Mosaicae. Hos autem vicissim monet, ne firmos condemnent, neue exemplo firmorum moti, rebus quas illicitas iudicent, vtantur. Sunt igitur duae principales quaestiones huius capitis: vna, eaque praecipua, quomodo firmi se gerere debeant erga infirmos in vsu adiaphororum: altera, quomodo infirmi se gerere debeant erga firmos. Haec duae quaestiones promiscue ac permixtim ab Apostolo tractantur.
units.tr: In chapter 14 he exhorts the strong, that is, those who understood Christian liberty and were therefore firmly persuaded that they could omit the Mosaic ceremonies with a good conscience, not to despise or offend the weak. The weak, although they believed in Christ as their Saviour, nevertheless did not know that through him they had been freed from observing the ceremonies of the Mosaic Law. In turn he warns these weak ones not to condemn the strong, nor, moved by the example of the strong, to use things which they judge unlawful. There are therefore two principal questions in this chapter: one, and the chief one, is how the strong ought to behave toward the weak in the use of adiaphora; the other is how the weak ought to behave toward the strong. These two questions are handled by the Apostle together and intermingled.

units.la: Cap. xv. Post praecepta de rebus necessariis, cap. 12. & 13. & de rebus indifferentibus, cap. 14. subiicitur praeceptio communiter de rebus quibuscunque siue necessariis, siue indifferentibus. Hoc igitur capite primum in genere firmis praecipit, vt infirmos quocunque modo, non in Adiaphoris tantum tolerent, vsque ad v. 14. Pendet & hoc praeceptum ex praecepto illo charitatis generali, supra cap. 13. v. 8.
units.tr: Chapter 15. After the precepts concerning necessary things (chapters 12 and 13) and concerning things indifferent (chapter 14), a precept is added in common concerning all things, whether necessary or indifferent. In this chapter, therefore, he first instructs the strong in general to bear with the weak in every way, not only in matters indifferent, down to verse 14. This precept also depends on that general precept of love above, in chapter 13, verse 8.

units.la: Hactenus principalis Epistolae tractatio sequitur
units.tr: So far the treatment of the principal part of the Epistle follows.

units.la: DE EPILOGO SEV CONCLV-sione Epistolæ.
units.tr: On the Epilogue, or Conclusion, of the Epistle.

units.la: Ad perorationem seu epilogum epistolæ pertinent eæ, quas subiungit, sui scripti excusa-tiones, salutationes, & commendationes fideliū.
units.tr: To the peroration or epilogue of the epistle belong the things he adds at the end: the apologies for his writing, the greetings, and the commendations of the faithful.

units.la: Loci autem perorationis in hoc capite sunt quatuor, primùm se excusat, quod pluribus ad eos scripserit, usque ad v. 17. deinde Apostolatum suum magnificè commendat ab effectis: usque ad v. 22. tertiò Romanis spem facit sui ad ipsos aduentus, usque ad v. 30. Postremò petit ab eis, ut Deum pro se orent; & hunc locum concludit voto seu optatione.
units.tr: The places of the peroration in this chapter are four. First, he excuses himself for having written to them so boldly in several places, up to v. 17. Then he magnificently commends his apostleship from its effects, up to v. 22. Third, he holds out to the Romans the hope of his coming to them, up to v. 30. Finally, he asks them to pray to God for him, and he concludes this passage with a wish or prayer.

units.la: Caput XVI est appendix perorationis quæ incipit præcedente capite, complectens partim commendationes & salutationes, partim ad-monitionem necessariam de vitandis schisma-ticis, partim votum pro ipsis, quo concluditur epistola cum breui eulogio doctrinæ euangeli-cæ, & δοξολογία ad Deum. Membra sunt quatuor: 1. Est commendatio Phœbes: adv. 3. 1 1 Sunt salutationes, ut ita dicam, rogata ad alteram partem, usque ad v. 16. quo loco, altera nimirum parte, v. 16. incipiunt salutationes, ut sic dicam, mis-sæ, à quibus inceptis statim 1 1 1 digreditur in ad-monitionem ad declinandum à falsis fratribus, à v. 17. ad v. 21. quo versu redit ad salutationes mis-sas, in usque pergit, ad v. 24. Hinc Postremò con-cipit preces, concludens epistolam gratiarum actione erga Deum: cuius potentiam & sapientiam ad ipsius laudem & gloriam commemorat.
units.tr: Chapter 16 is an appendix to the peroration, which begins in the preceding chapter. It contains partly commendations and greetings, partly a necessary warning to avoid schismatics, and partly a prayer for them, with which the epistle is concluded, together with a brief eulogy of evangelical doctrine and a doxology to God. It has four parts: (1) the commendation of Phoebe, at v. 1 to v. 3; (2) greetings, as it were, requested from the other party, up to v. 16, where, namely at v. 16, the greetings sent by the author, as it were, begin; from these greetings, once begun, he at once digresses into an admonition to avoid false brothers, from v. 17 to v. 21, where he returns to the greetings sent, and continues them up to v. 24; (3) and finally he composes prayers, concluding the epistle with thanksgiving to God, whose power and wisdom he recalls for his praise and glory.

units.la: ARGUMENTA CAPITUM
units.tr: THE ARGUMENTS OF THE CHAPTERS

units.la: CAP. I.
units.tr: CHAP. I.

units.la: Saepe quidem volui Romanos visere fratres, Impediit fortis sed mea vota Deus. Inde docet quanam vitii sit turpis origo, Si summi ignores numina sancta Dei.
units.tr: I have often wished to visit the brethren at Rome, but mighty God has hindered my desires. Hence he teaches the shameful origin of vice, if you do not know the holy divinity of the highest God.

units.la: Peccarunt omnes humano semine nati, Omnes iratum commeruere Deum. Et ne se immunem Iudaeus diceret esse, Vere Iudaeus quis fiet inde docet.
units.tr: All who are born of human seed have sinned; all have deserved the wrath of God. And lest the Jew should say he is exempt, he teaches who will truly become a Jew.

units.la: Inclyta Iudaeae quamuis sit gloria gentis, Criminibus poenas commeruere tamen. Non enim prosunt divinae dogmata legis, Sola iuvat miseros gratia laeta Dei.
units.tr: Though the glory of the Jewish nation is renowned, they have nonetheless deserved punishment for their crimes. For the doctrines of the divine law do not profit; the joyful grace of God alone helps wretched people.

units.la: Veraci Domino divinus credidit Abram. Illa Deo placuit non dubitata fide. Sic omnis credens dicetur filius Abrae, Sola fides Domino conciliare potest.
units.tr: Abraham believed the truthful Lord, as God ordained. That faith, undoubted, pleased God. So every believer will be called a son of Abraham; faith alone can win the favour of the Lord.

units.la: Principio fidei describit numera sanctae, Ostendens Domini gratia quanta fiet. Hinc quibus emanet peccati fontibus error, Unde fluat fidei gratia grata docet.
units.tr: At the beginning he describes the number of holy faith, showing how great the grace of the Lord will be. Hence he teaches from what springs of sin error flows, and whence the pleasing grace of faith flows.

units.la: Ne vitiis posset nunc ianua aperta videri. Officium fidei factaque sancta docet. Polluti nuper peccati sordibus almo Pergite nunc sancta mente studere Deo.
units.tr: Lest the door should now seem open to vices, he teaches the duty of faith and holy deeds. You who were lately polluted by the filth of sin, now strive with a holy mind for God.

units.la: Edocet aetherea quanam sint munera legis, Et quam nos tristi deprimat illa iugo. Indicat haec etenim quae crimina tecta latebant, Sed nos in CHRISTVM liberat alma fide.
units.tr: He sets forth from heaven what the gifts of the law are, and how it presses us down with its sad yoke. For it points out the sins that lay hidden, but by gracious faith it frees us in Christ.

units.la: Nulla nocere potest damnatio maesta fidenti, Nempe Deum patrem Spiritus esse facis. Quantaque sit summi, scribit, dilectio Patris, Quam nec crux, nec mors tollere sæua potest.
units.tr: Condemnation cannot harm the one who believes; indeed you show God to be Father and Spirit. He writes how great is the love of the highest Father, which neither cross nor cruel death can take away.

units.la: Haec fuit aeterni constans sententia patris, Esset ut afflicto CHRISTVS in orbe salus. Agnoscunt Gentes credenti corde salutem: Iudaeus Christum respuit atque fidem.
units.tr: This was the constant purpose of the eternal Father, that Christ should be salvation for the afflicted world. The Gentiles acknowledge salvation with a believing heart; the Jew rejects Christ and faith.

units.la: 10 Quæ reprobis Christum Iudæis causa negarit, Iustitia & legis quæ stet illa docet. Sancta fides nullum cœlo secludit ab alto: Iudæus proprij nam sibi causa mali est.
units.tr: 10 He teaches what cause the reprobate Jews had for denying Christ, and what righteousness of the law stands. Holy faith shuts no one out from high heaven; for the Jew is the cause of his own evil.

units.la: 11 Fallere non possunt summi promissa Tonantis, Siquis promissis possit habere fidem. Nec tamen elatos animos exsollite Gentes, Quippe fidem amissam mœsta ruina manet.
units.tr: 11 The promises of the highest Thunderer cannot deceive, if anyone can place faith in his promises. Nor, Gentiles, lift up your minds in pride, for faith once lost remains in sad ruin.

units.la: 12 Victima quæ verè cœlesti grata parenti, Quæ fidei virtus officiumque docet. Vivite concordes, fucatum pellite amorem, Nec vos vindictæ cæca cupido trahat.
units.tr: 12 He teaches the victim that is truly pleasing to the heavenly Parent, and the virtue of faith and its duty. Live in harmony, drive out feigned love, and let not blind desire for vengeance draw you on.

units.la: 13 Fac sanctum vigili venereris mente Senatum, Nec cedat sancto pectore fratris amor. Tempus abit, celeri fallax pede labitur ætas, Nunc igitur vitæ sit pia cura piæ.
units.tr: 13 Make yourselves revere the holy Senate with a watchful mind, and let not love of the brethren leave the holy breast. Time passes; deceitful age slips away on swift feet; therefore now let there be pious care for a pious life.

units.la: 14 Multa dapum fuerant discrimina, multa dierum, Equeis[?] surgebant iurgia multa nimis. Admonet hos igitur nimium ne affectibus illis Permittant curæ sit magis almus amor.
units.tr: 14 There were many distinctions of foods and many of days, and quarrels arose exceedingly. He therefore warns them not to give too much rein to those passions, but to let kindly love be their greater concern.

units.la: 15 Ferte ergo infirmos patienti pectore fratres, Nec moveant duri scripta severa styli. Offendit causam, cur non conuenerit illos. Illorum sancto postulat ore preces.
units.tr: 15 Bear, therefore, the weak brethren with a patient heart, and let not the harsh writings of a severe pen move you. He points out the cause why he had not come to them, and asks for their prayers with holy mouth.

units.la: 16 Ultima commendat venientem littera Phæben. Dicatur sanctis fratribus alma salus. Discordes (moneo) doctores pellite semper, Ne veniant lites dissidiumque graue.
units.tr: 16 He commends the last letter, which bears Phoebe. Let saving health be spoken to the holy brethren. I warn you, always drive away discordant teachers, lest quarrels and grievous dissension come.

units.la: ALITER.
units.tr: ANOTHER.

units.la: CAP. I.
units.tr: CHAPTER I.

units.la: AD vos ire iuvat, sum debitor haud pudeso. Notum haud agnoscit reproba turba Deum.
units.tr: I am glad to come to you, and I am no debtor to shame. The reprobate crowd does not acknowledge God.

units.la: 2 Bis malus est damnans quod agit, distinctio nulla. Intus non foris est lex tua, doctor iners.
units.tr: Doubly evil is the one who condemns what he does, and there is no distinction. Your law is within, not without, O idle teacher.

units.la: 3 Conditio Iudæ præstat, peccauimus omnes. Restituitque Deo nos sine lege fides.
units.tr: The condition of Judah is better: we have all sinned. Faith restores us to God without the law.

units.la: 4 Datque fides vitam, quam circumcisio signat. Hæc facis heredes, hac nitet ille Pater.
units.tr: Faith gives life, which circumcision signifies. By this you make heirs, and by this that Father shines.

units.la: Ergo dat haec pacem. Christi mors liberat hostes. Noxa minor dono, mors quoque morte fuit.
units.tr: Therefore this gives peace. Christ's death frees enemies. The offence is less than the gift; death too was overcome by death.

units.la: Fons sacer assimilat Christo ne crimina regnent. Membra vices mutent, mors malefacta manet.
units.tr: The holy fountain makes us like Christ, so that sins may not reign. Let the members change their roles; death remains for evil deeds.

units.la: Grande iugum excussum est. Christo nunc liber obedi. Quod iubet altera lex, altera saepe vetat.
units.tr: The great yoke has been shaken off. Now be free and obey Christ. What one law commands, the other often forbids.

units.la: Insertos vegetat, sonat Abba, flebilis orat. Spiritus, abiungit nil ab amore Dei.
units.tr: It quickens those who are grafted in; Abba sounds, and the weeping one prays. The Spirit separates nothing from the love of God.

units.la: Lugeo cognatos, Iacob non natus amatur. Vasa facit figulus qualiacunque libet.
units.tr: I mourn my kinsfolk; Jacob, not yet born, is loved. The potter makes vessels of whatever kind he pleases.

units.la: Mire caecus amor, Christus perfectio legis. Voxque fidem gignit missa per omne genus.
units.tr: Wonderfully blind is love; Christ is the perfection of the law. And the voice sent through every nation begets faith.

units.la: Non omnes repulit, prodest reiectio pulsis. Spes reditus superest, o via mira Dei.
units.tr: He has not rejected all; the rejection of the rejected profits. The hope of return remains; O wondrous way of God.

units.la: Obsecro quisque suum tueatur munus, amorque sit verus, benedic. & mala vince bona.
units.tr: I beg that each keep his own duty, and that love be true; bless, and overcome evil with good.

units.la: Principibus pare, summa est dilectio legis. Nunc ubi nox pulsa est, arma diurna cape.
units.tr: Obey the rulers; love is the sum of the law. Now that the night is driven away, take up the arms of day.

units.la: Quid spernis fratrem comedens? sunt omnia pura. Sed quod non purum creditur esse, nocet.
units.tr: Why do you despise your brother by eating? All things are pure. But what is believed not to be pure does harm.

units.la: Robusti cedant, Gentes gaudete, ministro Gentibus haec feci, haec porto, redibo breui.
units.tr: Let the strong give way; Gentiles, rejoice. I have done these things for the Gentiles, I bear them, and I shall return soon.

units.la: Scriptis commendat Phoeben, multosque salutat, Vitandosque monet qui mala blanda serunt.
units.tr: He commends Phoebe in writing, greets many, and warns to avoid those who bring smooth evils.

units.la: NOTAE SELECTAE EX SINGVLIS capitibus μνημονευλικῶς[?].
units.tr: SELECTED NOTES FROM EACH CHAPTER, MNEMONICALLY [μνημονευτικῶς].

units.la: 1 2 3 4 5 Gentes, Iudaos, Utrosque, Patrem, Domini mors: 6 7 8 9 Armaque, Luctaque, Maclamur, Miserebor, ad 10 Orbis: 11 12 13 14 15 Parcat, Membra, Minister, Olus, Virtute, 16 Salutem. Q. j.[?]
units.tr: 1 2 3 4 5 Gentiles, Jews, Both, Father, Death of the Lord; 6 7 8 9 Arms, Struggles, We are stained, I will have mercy, to; 10 Ends of the world; 11 12 13 14 15 Spare, Members, Minister, Vegetables, Virtue; 16 Salvation. Q. j.

units.la: Declaratio.
units.tr: Explanation.

units.la: Gentes conuincit peccati, à v. 18. Iudæos conuincit, Vtrosque id est, tam Iudæos quam Gentes. Patrem multarum gentium constituam &c. v. 17. Domini mors quam obiit pro impiis. v. 6.
units.tr: Gentiles he convicts of sin, from v. 18. Jews he convicts; Both, that is, both Jews as well as Gentiles. Father: I will make you the father of many nations, etc., v. 17. Death of the Lord, which he suffered for the ungodly, v. 6.

units.la: Armaque iniustitiæ non offenda[?] sunt membra nostra: v. 13. Luciaque carnis & spiritus. v. 21. Maculamur vt oues: v. 36. Miserebor cuius misertus fuero. v. 15. ad Orbis fines verba eorum: v. 18.
units.tr: Arms of unrighteousness: our members are not to be offered, v. 13. Struggles of flesh and spirit, v. 21. We are stained as sheep, v. 36. I will have mercy on whom I shall have mercy, v. 15. To the ends of the world their words, v. 18.

units.la: Parcat ne non tibi quoque: v. 21. Membra non omnia eandem habent actionem: v. 4. Minister Dei etiam Magistratus: v. 4. Olus comedit infirmus. v. 2. Virtute signorum ac prodigiorum: v. 19. Salutem variam dici iubet: v. 3.
units.tr: Spare: lest he also spare not you, v. 21. Members: not all members have the same action, v. 4. Minister of God, also the magistrate, v. 4. Vegetables: the weak eats vegetables, v. 2. Virtue of signs and wonders, v. 19. Salvation: he bids various greetings be given, v. 3.

units.la: ANALYSIS EPISTOLAE S. PAVLI AD CORINTHIOS prioris.
units.tr: ANALYSIS OF THE FIRST EPISTLE OF ST PAUL TO THE CORINTHIANS

units.la: INlimine huius Analyseos hæc quinque considerabimus. 1 Qui fuerint Corinthij. 2 Occasionem Scriptionis. 3 Statum & argumentum. 4 Vsum. 5 Partes.
units.tr: At the outset of this Analysis we will consider five things: (1) who the Corinthians were; (2) the occasion of the writing; (3) the state and argument; (4) the use; (5) the parts.

units.la: De primo. Corinthus olim Achaiæ fuit metropolis, & vt Cicero inquit, lumen totius Græciæ, adeòque in ea æstimatione, vt Imperij auctoritatem & nomen sustinere posset, quales Veteres Romani tres solum vrbes computabant, Carthaginem, Corinthum, & Capuâ. Ad quam sanè rem magna erat commoditas ex loci opportunitate, cùm inter duo maria Ægeum & Ionium posita esset, vnde quamuis de Imperio certare non potuerit, celeberrimum tamen emporium exhibuit Asiæ & Europæ, & simul vt fit in maritimis emporiis, singularem admisit morum corruptelam. Hinc indubie fluxit, vt iusto Dei iudicio postea fit deleta, quod primùm legimus in historiis factum à Romanis, per L. Mummium Cos. ante bellum Numantinum. Occasio euertendi vrbem illa erat, quod legatos populi Romani stercoribus foedassent. Postea tamen restituta est per Augustum Caesarem, & iterum studiis humanitatis, mercimoniis, operibus ac morum corruptelâ nobilitata. Ibi etiam habitasse multos Iudaeos, & habuisse Synagogam testantur, Act. 18. Vbi verò tot capita & diuersae in vnum locu nationes coeunt, diuersi quoque sensus, discordiae & simultates facile glisc unt. Hinc igitur
units.tr: On the first. Corinth was once the metropolis of Achaia, and, as Cicero says, the light of all Greece. It was held in such esteem that it could support the authority and name of the empire; the ancient Romans reckoned only three cities of this kind, Carthage, Corinth and Capua. Its location gave it great advantage for this, since it lay between two seas, the Aegean and the Ionian. Although it could not contend for empire from there, it nonetheless became a most famous trading centre for Asia and Europe and, as usually happens in maritime trading centres, it admitted a singular corruption of morals. From this, without doubt, came its later destruction by the just judgment of God. The first record of this is in the histories, when the Romans, under Lucius Mummius, consul, before the Numantine war, did it. The pretext for overthrowing the city was that the Corinthians had defiled Roman envoys with dung. Afterwards, however, it was restored by the emperor Augustus, and again made famous by the pursuit of humane learning, by commerce, by public works, and by a corruption of morals. Many Jews also lived there, and the presence of a synagogue is attested, Acts 18. Where so many heads and so many nations come together in one place, diverse opinions, discords and quarrels readily flourish. Hence then

units.la: II. Occasio hanc scribendi epistolam nata est Apostolo Paulo, qui prius Corinthiacam Ecclesiam plantauerat & docendo Euangelium per sesquiannum irrigauerat Act. 18. Ideo, vt inquit Ambrosius, maiore cum fiducia cum iis agit: aliquando blandiens ipsis paternè, tanquam liberis: aliquando obiurgans, arguens; & de variis rebus eos commonefaciens. Vidit enim post suum discessum, idem fere eis accidisse, quod olim Israelitis absente Mose Exodi 22. vt lasciuirent & à puritate Euangelica degenerarent, & Diabolus sua Zizania sereret, quod ei difficile non fuit in vrbe Graeca, populosa, deuitiis & delitiis affluente. Geminam autem habuit Apostolus scribendae huius epistolae occasionem. 1 Dissidia & ἀλαζονίαν [?] quae ab hominibus vanis & ambitiosis excitari videbat. 2 Epistolam Ecclesiae, quae suum Apostolum & doctorem de aliquot quaestionibus consuluerat, vt videre est initio capitis septimi.
units.tr: II. The occasion of writing this letter arose for the Apostle Paul, who had earlier planted the Corinthian Church and watered it by teaching the gospel for a year and a half, Acts 18. Therefore, as Ambrose says, he deals with them with greater confidence: sometimes flattering them fatherly, as children; sometimes rebuking and reproving them; and reminding them of various matters. For he saw that after his departure the same thing had nearly happened to them as once to the Israelites when Moses was absent, Exodus 22, that they grew wanton and fell away from evangelical purity, and that the Devil sowed his tares, which was not hard to do in a Greek city, populous and overflowing with luxuries and pleasures. The Apostle had a twofold occasion for writing this letter: (1) the dissensions and arrogance [ἀλαζονίαν] which he saw being stirred up by vain and ambitious men; (2) a letter from the Church, which had consulted its Apostle and teacher on several questions, as is seen at the beginning of chapter seven.

units.la: III. Status, etsi propter varietatem rerum & quaestionum vix definiri potest: recte tamen refertur haec epistola ad genus partim suaso-rium, partim didascalicum. Ad Suasorium sive de-liberativum: cum eos dehortatur a contentionibus, schismatibus, & a nimia admiratione sapientiae & eloquentiae humanae: a communione mensae daemoniorum & aliis huiusmodi. Ad Didascalicum: Cum quaestiones aliquot explicat, ut de coniugio, virginitate & coelibatu, quem tunc nonnulli nimis extollebant: de Coena Domini: de Resurrectione mortuorum. Tandem in fine concludens epistolam, hortatur ut fratrum Hierosolymitanorum inopiae succurratur per collectam & subventionem aliquam: & quemadmodum ab amica gratulatione & exhortatione Epistolam erat exorsus, eodem modo eam claudit. Habent singulae quaestiones, quammultae sunt, suas peculiares propositiones, ut est videre cap. 7. & consequentibus: tamen tota Epistola revocanda est ad unam generalem sententiam, tanquam ad scopum. Sit igitur haec propositio: Corinthiis omnibus modis curandum esse, ut dissidiis & morum corruptela sublatis, consensum in doctrina sibi tradita, & in moribus innocentiam colant omni virtutum genere, ut imago Dei in ipsis restauretur & perficiatur ad adventum Domini nostri Iesu Christi.
units.tr: III. The state of the letter, though it can hardly be defined because of the variety of matters and questions, is nonetheless rightly referred partly to the persuasive kind and partly to the didactic. To the persuasive or deliberative kind: where he dissuades them from quarrels, schisms, and from excessive admiration of human wisdom and eloquence, and from communion at the table of demons and other such things. To the didactic: where he explains several questions, such as those concerning marriage, virginity and celibacy, which some at that time praised excessively; concerning the Lord's Supper; concerning the resurrection of the dead. Finally, concluding the letter at the end, he urges that aid be given to the poverty of the Jerusalem brethren through a collection and some support; and just as he began the letter with friendly congratulation and exhortation, so he closes it in the same way. Each of the questions, however many there are, has its own particular propositions, as may be seen in chapter 7 and those following. Nevertheless the whole letter is to be traced back to one general sentiment, as to its aim. Let this, then, be the proposition: that the Corinthians must by all means take care, with divisions and corruption of morals removed, to hold to consensus in the doctrine delivered to them and to innocence in their conduct, in every kind of virtue, so that the image of God may be restored in them and brought to perfection at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.

units.la: IV. Vtilitas seu vsus huius epistolae multiplex est: admonet nos de variis Stratagematibus Diaboli, quibus Ecclesiam adoriri solet, videlicet per schismata, haereses, scandala, ἀ[?]λ[?]ξιαν[?]. Quae omnia tum Pastores tum auditores expergefacere debent, ne minor fit in eis vigilantia, & promptitudo ad resistendum Diabolo, quàm in eo ad Ecclesiam adoriendam. Docet nos etiam hæc Epistola, quàm malè conveniat simplicitati & puritati Euangelicæ cum luxu & superbia filiorum huius seculi, & quàm sit difficile in splendidis, opulentis & populosis civitatibus retinere τῶ πίστιν [?] καὶ τάξιν Ecclesiæ. Admonet Pastores Ecclesiæ, quam debeant esse exercitati in Scripturis, & rerum variarum cognitione, ut de variis, quæ subinde oriuntur, controversiis, ut erant illæ de divortiis, de libertate Christiana, de velandis mulieribus, respondere possint. Explicantur denique in hac Epistola præclari multi loci, ut de coniugio, de Cœna Domini, de ordine & Politia Ecclesiæ, & conventibus Ecclesiasticis, de variis Dei donis erga Ecclesiam, de resurrectione & similibus.
units.tr: IV. The usefulness or use of this letter is manifold. It warns us of the various stratagems of the Devil, by which he is accustomed to assail the Church, namely through schisms, heresies, scandals, arrogance [ἀλαζονίαν]. All of these ministers and hearers alike ought to wake up to, lest in them there be less watchfulness and readiness to resist the Devil than there is in him to assail the Church. This letter also teaches us how ill the simplicity and purity of the gospel agree with the luxury and pride of the children of this age, and how difficult it is to keep the faith and order [τὴν πίστιν καὶ τάξιν] of the Church in splendid, wealthy and populous cities. It admonishes the ministers of the Church how practised they ought to be in the Scriptures and in knowledge of various things, so that they may be able to answer the various controversies that arise from time to time, such as those about divorce, Christian liberty, and the veiling of women. Finally, many notable passages are explained in this letter: concerning marriage, the Lord's Supper, the order and polity of the Church, ecclesiastical assemblies, the various gifts of God to the Church, the resurrection, and similar matters.

units.la: PARTES EPISTOLÆ
units.tr: THE PARTS OF THE EPISTLE

units.la: Sunt tres, Exordium, Tractatio principalis, & Conclusio.
units.tr: There are three: the Introduction, the principal Treatment, and the Conclusion.

units.la: De Prima.
units.tr: On the First Part.

units.la: Exordium est ab initio capitis primi usque ad v.10. complectens subscriptionem, (v.1.) inscri-ptionem, (v.2.) salutationem, (v.3.) & testificationem suæ erga Corinthios benevolentiæ quam arguit tum gratiarum actione pro uberrima Dei erga ipsos be-nedictione in præsens, (à v.4. usque ad 8.) tum confirmatione fiduciæ ipsorum de incremento gra-tiæ Dei in posterum, v. 8 & 9.
units.tr: The Introduction runs from the beginning of chapter 1 to v. 10. It comprises the subscription (v. 1), the inscription (v. 2), the salutation (v. 3), and the testimony of his goodwill towards the Corinthians. He shows this goodwill both by a thanksgiving for the most abundant blessing God has so far bestowed on them (from v. 4 to 8), and by a confirmation of his confidence that the grace of God will increase in them in future (vv. 8 and 9).

units.la: DE SECUNDA PARTE QUÆ est Tractatio principalis.
units.tr: CONCERNING THE SECOND PART, WHICH IS THE PRINCIPAL TREATMENT.

units.la: PRINCIPALIS Tractatio,à v.10. capi-tis primi, usque ad ultimi capitis initium pro-currens, habet doctrinam Vitæ & Fidei Chri-stianæ.
units.tr: The PRINCIPAL Treatment, running from v. 10 of chapter 1 to the beginning of the last chapter, contains the doctrine of Christian Life and Faith.

units.la: Doctrina Vitæ in ἐπανορθώσει[?] seu correctione vitæ ac nævorum seu defectuū qui irrepserant, emendatione versatur: usque ad cap.15. in quo tractatur doctrina Fidei.
units.tr: The doctrine of Life is concerned with correction [ἐπανορθώσει], that is, the amendment of life and of the blemishes or defects that had crept in, up to chapter 15, where the doctrine of Faith is treated.

units.la: Correctio Vitæ rursum bipartita est: prima par-te corrigit in eis vitia quæ Apostolus auditione perceperat, & quæ Corinthij minùs grauia iu-dicabant, & ob id eius iudicium non requisie-rant, cum interim essent grauissima: qualia sunt studium sectarum, dissidia publica in dogmati-bus religionis, ambitio eloquentiæ, & sapientiæ persuasio, quasi sine his non posset recte doceri Euangelium. Item scortatio, incestus, litigan-di mos coram infidelibus.
units.tr: The correction of life is again in two parts. The first part corrects those vices which the Apostle had learned of by report, and which the Corinthians judged less serious, so that they had not asked his judgment on them, although they were in fact most grievous. Such are the pursuit of factions, public quarrels over matters of religious doctrine, the ambition for eloquence, and the belief that wisdom is needed, as if the Gospel could not be taught rightly without it. Likewise fornication, incest, and the custom of going to law before unbelievers.

units.la: Secunda parte demum cap. 7. & deinceps, re-prehendit nævos & vitia de quibus scripto erat edoctus, & respondet ad illorum quæstiones ab ipsis propositas, quales erant multæ de matrimonio, de ciborum delectu, de Idolothytis[?], de cœtibus ecclesiasticis, & an liceret mulieribus docere, & movere quæstiones in cœtibus publicis. De cœna Domini, & de eius vero usu;de donis spiritualibus & illorum præstantia, nominatim de prophetandi munere. Hæc omnia pertinent ad Epistolam Corinthiorum.
units.tr: In the second part, finally, from chapter 7 onwards, he rebukes the blemishes and vices of which he had been informed in writing, and answers the questions they had put to him. These included questions about marriage, the choice of foods, meats offered to idols, the assemblies of the Church, and whether women may teach and raise questions in public assemblies. He also treats of the Lord's Supper and its right use, and of spiritual gifts and their excellence, particularly the office of prophesying. All these things pertain to the Epistle to the Corinthians.

units.la: PARTES EPISTOLÆ sic coherent.
units.tr: THE PARTS OF THE EPISTLE HANG TOGETHER AS FOLLOWS.

units.la: Exordium, cap. 1. vsque ad versum. 10. Tractatio principalis, in qua agitur de Philippenses ad Corinthios habet Vsque hic notanda [?] Redargutio criminum, quae auditu praecepera: quod sit fidelium officium 1. In vitandis dissidiis & schismatibus, à v. 10. cap. 1. vsque ad initium capitis 5. II. In conseruanda disciplina ecclesiastica, cap. 5. III In virandis litibus forensibus & scortatione, cap. 6. Responsio didascalica ad eorum epistolam: de rebus Adiaphoris vbi de Coniugio & coelibatu, cap. 7. Idolothytis, cap. 8. 9. 10. Necessariis, vbi de obseruanda & decoro in coetibus ecclesiasticis, potissimum quoad vestitu, coenam Domini, & dona spiritualia, cap. 11. 12. 13. 14. Doctrina, vbi de Resurrectione: cap. 15. Conclusionem, cap. 16. agit de priuatis rebus quae per appendicem, quae ex animo Apostoli fluebant, publico aut priuato bono.
units.tr: The Introduction is chapter 1 to verse 10. The principal Treatment deals with the rebuke of the faults he had heard of by report, and shows what the duty of the faithful is: I. In avoiding dissensions and schisms, from v. 10 of chapter 1 to the beginning of chapter 5. II. In maintaining church discipline, chapter 5. III. In avoiding lawsuits and fornication, chapter 6. It then gives a didactic response to their letter on indifferent matters: marriage and celibacy, chapter 7; meats offered to idols, chapters 8, 9 and 10. Next come the necessary matters, where he treats of observing decorum in church assemblies, chiefly as to dress, the Lord's Supper, and spiritual gifts, chapters 11 to 14. The doctrine follows, on the Resurrection, chapter 15. The Conclusion, chapter 16, deals with private matters, which flowed from the Apostle's heart as an appendix, for public or private good.

units.la: PRIMA PARS OFFICII CHRISTIANI est de vitandis dissidiis & schismatibus. cap. 1. 2. 3. 4.
units.tr: THE FIRST PART OF THE CHRISTIAN DUTY is concerning the avoiding of dissensions and schisms. Chapters 1, 2, 3, 4.

units.la: Capite igitur primo, à v. 10. vsque ad finem Concordiam hortatur tum Auditores seu ipsam Ecclesiam, tum Antistites Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: In the first chapter, from verse 10 to the end, he urges concord both on the hearers, or the Church itself, and on the leaders of the Church.

units.la: Ecclesiam monet ne propter ministros seu antistites schismata moueant: (v.10.11.12.) cum omnes inter se sint ratione officij æquales, vt qui habeant, 1 vnum idemque caput Christum qui diuidi nequit, 2 vnam per eundem Christum redemptionem, 3 idem Baptisma in Christum, à v.13. vsque ad 17. Antistites laude eloquentiæ & sapientiæ humanæ tumidos ad concordiam & in docendo simplicitatem hortatur duobus argumentis: primùm à suo ipsius exemplo, v.17. Deinde à consideratione diuinæ, 1 gloriæ, cuius interest ei conuersionem hominum insolidum transscribi. (v.18.) 2 voluntatis, sapientiam mundi huius reiicientis, (v.19.20.) 3 iustitiæ, thesauros cœlestis sapientiæ ingratis & inflatis tum Iudæis tum Gentibus occultantis, (v.21.22.23.) 4 bonitatis, cum simplicibus agentis simpliciter, (v.24.) 5 potentiæ, magis in simplicitate doctrinæ, quàm in affectata eloquetia elucescentis. v.25. Hæc amplificat & confirmat exemplo ipsorum Corinthiorum per antithesin contrariorum, (v.26.27.28.) illustratam finibus: Deus abiectissimos homines elegit & vocauit, 1 vt hominum arrogantiam retundat, (v.29.) 2 vt suam illustrem gloriam in Christo, v.30.
units.tr: He warns the Church not to stir up schisms on account of the ministers or leaders (vv. 10, 11, 12), since all are equal among themselves in office, as those who have 1 one and the same head, Christ, who cannot be divided; 2 one redemption through the same Christ; 3 the same baptism into Christ, from verse 13 to 17. He urges the leaders, who are puffed up with the praise of eloquence and human wisdom, to concord and to simplicity in teaching, by two arguments. First, from his own example, v. 17. Then from the consideration of the divine: 1 glory, to which it belongs that the conversion of men be wholly ascribed to him (v. 18); 2 will, which rejects the wisdom of this world (vv. 19, 20); 3 justice, which hides the treasures of heavenly wisdom from Jews and Gentiles alike, who are ungrateful and puffed up (vv. 21, 22, 23); 4 goodness, which deals simply with the simple (v. 24); 5 power, which shines more in the simplicity of the teaching than in affected eloquence, v. 25. He enlarges on and confirms these points by the example of the Corinthians themselves, through the contrast of opposites (vv. 26, 27, 28), illustrated by its ends: God chose and called the most abject men, 1 so that he might crush human arrogance (v. 29); 2 so that his own illustrious glory in Christ might appear, v. 30.

units.la: Capitis secundi partes duæ sunt. 1 Repetitio primi argumenti capitis antecedentis v.17. ab exemplo ipsius Pauli petiti, & eiusdem plena declaratio. Vbi docet Paulus se simplici & humili dicendi genere in docendo vsum, (v.1. vsque ad 5.) quo omnis efficacia doctrinæ Spiritui S. adscribatur, & fides nostra inconcussa perstiat. v.5. 11. Discrimen inter Euangelium & cætera genera doctrinarum. Euangelium est cœlestis sapientia principibus & sapien-tibus huius mundi abscondita, adeoque omni naturali homini, i. per Spiritum S. nondum regenito & sanctificato incomprehensibilis, patefacta vero à Deo rudibus Apostolis, & cuilibet homini spirituali, hoc est per Dei Spiritum renouato, non in grandiloquentia humana, si eloquio spirituali prodita & renouelata &c: à versu 6. vsque ad finem capitis. Huius posterioris partis membra tria sunt. 1 indicatur qualem sapientiam doctrina Euangelij contineat, vsque ad v. 10. 2 quomodo sapientia illa à nobis percipiatur, v. 10.11.12. 3 rediens ad suam docendi rationem, causam exponit cur doctrina Euangelij à paucis intelligatur, à v.13. vsq; ad finem capitis.
units.tr: The second chapter has two parts. 1 A repetition of the first argument of the preceding chapter, v. 17, taken from the example of Paul himself, and its full explanation. Here Paul teaches that he used a plain and humble manner of speaking in teaching (vv. 1 to 5), by which all the efficacy of the teaching is ascribed to the Holy Spirit, and our faith remains unshaken, v. 5. II. The difference between the Gospel and other kinds of teaching. The Gospel is heavenly wisdom, hidden from the rulers and wise men of this world, and so incomprehensible to every natural man, that is, to one not yet regenerated and sanctified by the Holy Spirit; but it was revealed by God to the unlearned Apostles, and to every spiritual man, that is, to one renewed by the Spirit of God, not in human eloquence but when it is set forth and renewed in spiritual speech, etc., from verse 6 to the end of the chapter. This latter part has three members. 1 It shows what kind of wisdom the teaching of the Gospel contains, up to v. 10. 2 It shows how that wisdom is perceived by us, vv. 10, 11, 12. 3 Returning to his manner of teaching, he explains why the teaching of the Gospel is understood by few, from v. 13 to the end of the chapter.

units.la: Cap. iii. quatuor habet membra. 1 Causam ostendit, cur simplex Apostoli praedicatio, quae, ( vt cap.2. ostendit )non fuit in sermonibus calamistratis sapientia humana, delicatulis & morosulis apud Corinthios displicuerit: quod eorum vitio factum dicit, non culpa praedicationis: & simul eorum arrogantiam seria reprehensione, sed quam emollit dulcè appellatione fratrum, deiicit. ii Parte, v.5. agit de efficacia ministerij, quam totam à Deo non à personis Ministrorum pendere, & vnum ac idem omnium esse ministerium ideò demonstrat, vt à factionibus illis, quibus Corinthij turbabantur, eos abducat. iii Pars incipit versu vndecimo, vbi ad vnicum fundamentum, super quo tamen diuerso modo aedificatur, nos reuocat. iv Pars à v. 17. continet adhortationem grauem, vt cum templum Dei facti simus, non sinamus illud templum profanari per stultam mundi sapientiam aut mores vitiosos, sed in sola Domino gloriemur.
units.tr: Chapter 3 has four members. 1 He shows the cause why the plain preaching of the Apostle, which (as chapter 2 shows) was not human wisdom in polished speeches, displeased the Corinthians, who were fastidious and captious. He says this happened through their fault, not through any fault in the preaching; and at the same time he casts down their arrogance with serious rebuke, which he softens with the gentle address of brethren. ii In the second part, v. 5, he treats of the efficacy of the ministry, which he shows depends wholly on God and not on the persons of the ministers, and that the ministry is one and the same for all, so that he may draw them away from those factions by which the Corinthians were troubled. iii The third part begins at verse 11, where he recalls us to the one foundation, upon which, nevertheless, people build in different ways. iv The fourth part, from v. 17, contains a grave exhortation: since we have become the temple of God, we must not allow that temple to be profaned by foolish worldly wisdom or by vicious conduct, but must glory only in the Lord.

units.la: Postquam Apostolus schismata Ecclesiae Corinthiacae reprehendit, & eorum fontem ostendit, sapientiae nimirū carnalis & eloquentiae humanae nimiam admirationem: quâ taxatâ ad Christum Ecclesiae fundamentum & caput eos reuocauit: Nunc hoc capite IV, instituit ἀπολογίαν [?] sui Apostolatus contra eos qui ministerium suum extenuabant. Duo quippe hæc incommoda afferebat illa Corinthiorum sapientia,1 nimirum Schismata,2 contemptum doctrinæ & simplicitatis Apostolicæ. Partes sunt tres: I est recusatio temerarij iudicij aliquot Corinthiorum de Paulo, & provocatio ad iudicium verum, usque ad v.9. II pars habet quidem aliquid falsæ Ironiæ, quâ fastum Corinthiorum notat: certis vero & manifestis signis, suam humilitatem, patientiam, fidem in docendo Euangelio probat, & ad tale exemplum imitandum eos hortatur, usque ad v.17. III Timothei facit mentionem, quo loco eum habeat, cur eum ad Corinthios miserit, & denique seipsum breui venturum confirmat: usque ad v. 21. qui est ultimus, in quo transit ad reprehensionem grauissimi sceleris, nempe incesti in Ecclesia Corinthiorum admissi: qua de re agit toto capite sequente.
units.tr: After the Apostle has rebuked the schisms of the Corinthian Church and shown their source, namely an excessive admiration for carnal wisdom and human eloquence, and having censured this, he recalls them to Christ, the foundation and head of the Church. Now in this fourth chapter he sets out an apology [ἀπολογία] for his Apostleship against those who belittled his ministry. Indeed that Corinthian wisdom brought two evils: namely, 1 schisms, and 2 contempt for the doctrine and the simplicity of the Apostle. There are three parts. I is the refusal of the rash judgement of some Corinthians about Paul, and an appeal to the true judgement, up to v. 9. II contains indeed something of a false irony, by which he marks the pride of the Corinthians; but by certain and clear signs he proves his own humility, patience and faithfulness in preaching the Gospel, and urges them to imitate such an example, up to v. 17. III he makes mention of Timothy: where he places him, why he sent him to the Corinthians, and finally he assures them that he himself will come shortly, up to v. 21. This is the last part, in which he passes on to the rebuke of a most grave wickedness, namely the incest committed in the Corinthian Church; he treats of this matter through the whole following chapter.

units.la: Caput quintum coheret quidem cum praecedentibus hoc nomine, quòd euidentibus signis ostendit inanem esse praesumtionem & gloriationem Corinthiorum, qui se iam regnare & ad summam perfectionem peruenisse putabant, cùm tamen mores eorum & scandala, quæ ibi conspiciebantur, clamarent, illos admodum esse carnales: sed tamen secundus huius epistolae locus hic tractatur, qui continet seuerissimam reprehensionem incestuosi coniugij, nimirum priuigni cum nouerca: hinc satis causae esse admonet cur pudore deiici potius quam super-bire debeant.
units.tr: The fifth chapter certainly coheres with the preceding ones in this respect, that it shows by evident signs that the presumption and boasting of the Corinthians is empty; they thought they already reigned and had attained to the highest perfection, when nevertheless their conduct and the scandals visible among them cried out that they were very carnal. Yet this passage is the second place of this letter, treated here, which contains the most severe rebuke of an incestuous marriage, namely of a stepson with his stepmother. Hence he shows that they have sufficient cause to be cast down with shame rather than to be proud.

units.la: Partes v. cap. sunt tres: I Obiurgatio, quod incestuosum tamdiu toleraverint, nec excommunicarint. Propositio igitur est v.2. & ultimo: Submovendum esse ab Ecclesia illum sceleratum: II Agit de modo tollendi eum, nimirum per excommunicationem, cuius formam & finem praescribit. III Necessitatem excommunicationis in Ecclesia exponit, allusione ad Paschatis ceremonias facta, & simul ad vitae innocentiam, & vitandam familiaritatem cum flagitiosis, hortatur.
units.tr: The fifth chapter has three parts: I Reproof, because they had tolerated the incestuous man for so long and had not excommunicated him. The proposition, therefore, is in v. 2 and at the end: that that wicked man must be removed from the Church; II He treats of the manner of removing him, namely by excommunication, whose form and purpose he prescribes; III He sets out the necessity of excommunication in the Church, with an allusion to the ceremonies of the Passover, and at the same time exhorts them to innocence of life and to avoiding familiarity with the wicked.

units.la: Cap. VI. tractatur tertius primae partis huius epistolae locus. Nam ut capite superiori conquestus est iudicia & censuras ecclesiasticas iacere apud Corinthios, & de illis restituendis admonuit: sic initio huius capitis, quod totum est ἐγκλημον[?], & ad fastum Corinthiorum magis ac magis reprimendum faciens, litigandi studium in foro Ethnicorum, & scortationem reprehen-dit. Partes igitur duae sunt: I invehitur in-fo-renses contentiones, quibus se mutuo vexabant sub infidelibus, cum magno Euangelij dedecore, quod hoc pacto ludibrio exponatur; deinde quod illae lites arguant animum charitatis expertem, & odio atque avaritia delibutum. II. Reprehendit abusum libertatis Christianae in rebus mediis, in quo duo reprehendit: primum, quod illi libertate non uterentur, cum temperamento charitatis Christianae: deinde quod inter res medias flagitia numerarent: & nominatim taxat scortationem, quam multi tunc excusabant, ipse autem gravissimis rationibus ad-ductus damnat.
units.tr: Chapter 6 treats the third passage of the first part of this letter. For as in the previous chapter he complained that judgements and ecclesiastical censures were lying neglected among the Corinthians, and admonished them to restore them, so at the beginning of this chapter, which is wholly a complaint [ἔγκλημα], and which serves to check more and more the pride of the Corinthians, he rebukes the eagerness for litigation in the court of the heathen and fornication. There are therefore two parts. I He inveighs against the troublesome disputes by which they harassed one another before unbelievers, with great dishonour to the Gospel, since in this way it was exposed to mockery; and further, that those lawsuits show a mind without charity, steeped in hatred and greed. II. He rebukes the abuse of Christian liberty in matters indifferent, in which he rebukes two things: first, that they did not use liberty with the moderation of Christian charity; then that they counted vices among indifferent things; and he names fornication in particular, which many at that time excused, but which he, moved by the gravest reasons, condemns.

units.la: Hactenus prima epistolae pars principalis sequitur secunda, cap.7. & seqq: generis didascalici: Explicat enim aliquot quaestiones, de quibus per literas eum consuluerant Corinthij: unde colligimus in illa Ecclesia semper fuisse aliquem coetum, qui ministerium Apostoli venerabatur.
units.tr: So far the first, principal part of the letter. There follows the second part, chapter 7 and following, of a didactic kind: for he explains several questions about which the Corinthians had consulted him by letter. From this we gather that in that Church there was always some group which revered the ministry of the Apostle.

units.la: Capita sic connecti possunt.
units.tr: How the chapters may be connected.

units.la: In responsione didascalica ad Corinthios epistolam agit Apostolus de rebus Adiaphoris in coetu Primato: vbi de coniugio & coelibatu, cap.7. publico: vbi ab idolothytis abstinendum docet ab Effectu, fratrum scandalo, cap.8. Exemplo suo, de iure suo cedentis, cap.9. Israelitarum & eorum poena, cap.10. Necessariis, quae erant facienda quoad Coetus spirituales in precibus & prophetia; cap.11. Coena dominica, ibid. dona spiritualia: quorum ostendit Abusum, ut caveatur, cap.12. Usum: si referantur ad Charitatem, quae effert & praefert. cap.13. Prophetiam potius quam linguam peregrinam. cap.14.
units.tr: In his didactic reply to the Corinthians, the Apostle treats of matters indifferent in the public assembly, in the first place. Concerning marriage and celibacy, chapter 7. Where he teaches that abstinence from idol-meats must be observed because of the effect on the brethren's offence, chapter 8. By his own example, of one who yields his right, chapter 9. The Israelites and their punishment, chapter 10. The necessary things which had to be done for the spiritual assemblies in prayers and prophecy, chapter 11. The Lord's Supper, ibid. The spiritual gifts, of which he shows the abuse, that it may be guarded against, chapter 12. The use, if they are referred to charity, which carries and surpasses all, chapter 13. Prophecy rather than the foreign tongue, chapter 14.

units.la: Capite VII. De rebus matrimonialibus:
units.tr: Chapter 7. On matrimonial matters:

units.la: quaestiones solvuntur sex. 1. Annon praestaret hominem vitam agere coelibem? Resp: Praestaret quidem; sed ad vitandam fornicationem, Coniugium à Deo institutum est, (v.1.2.) in quo fides coniugalis utrinque seruanda: (v.3.4.5.) & licet matrimonium non sit praecisè imperatum omnibus, non tamen omnes dono continentiae, sicuti Paulus, ornati sint: hinc patet votum perpetui coelibatus improbandum esse, à v.6. usque ad 10. II quaestio, de coniugibus: respondet, vel diuortium esse cauendum, vel à secundis abstinendum nuptiis. v. 10. 11. III. Ad interrogatum de imparibus coniugibus ratione religionis, respondet quo pacto fidelis cum infideli conuersari debeat: (v.12. usque ad 16.) Jv.17[?]. admonet cuique in eo statu externo seu conditione vitae, in qua sit vocatus, esse manendum, usque ad v.25. IV Quaestium de virginitate, quae licet imperata non sit, tamen ab Apostolo approbatur propter praesentem necessitatem: (v.25.26.27.) non tamen peccare eos qui matrimonium contrahant; (v.28.) in quo ita ipsis viuendum, vt nullis rebus terrenis se mancipent, cum omnia huius vitae sint transitoria: (v.29.30.) vitam vero coelibum potiorem esse, quia persecutionum tempore omnia facilius, propter Christum, deserent, nec de congerendis diuitiis anxy erunt, Deoque longe expeditius inseruient, v.31. usque ad v.36. V Quaestionis solutio: parentes liberos nec à matrimonio arcere, nec ad idipsum cogere debent, sed secundum circumstantiarum requisita hic procedendum, v.36.37. VI Quaestio, de secundis nuptiis; respondet, eas quidem esse concessas: sed in viduitate perseuerare esse beatius, hoc est paucioribus molestiis, & in cultu diuino impedimentis obnoxium. v.39.40.
units.tr: The questions are resolved in six parts. 1. Would it be better for a man to live a single life? Answer: indeed it would be better, but marriage was instituted by God to avoid fornication (v.1.2.), and in it conjugal faithfulness must be kept on both sides (v.3.4.5.). Although marriage is not commanded absolutely to all, not all are endowed with the gift of continence, as Paul was. Hence it is clear that the vow of perpetual celibacy is to be disapproved, from v.6 to 10. II. A question about spouses: he answers that either divorce must be avoided or second marriages must be abstained from. v.10.11. III. To the question about unequal spouses in respect of religion, he answers how a believer ought to live with an unbeliever (v.12 to 16). IV. (v.17.) He admonishes each person to remain in the external state or condition of life in which he has been called, up to v.25. IV. A question about virginity: although virginity is not commanded, the Apostle approves it on account of the present necessity (v.25.26.27.). Yet those who contract marriage do not sin (v.28.). In either state they ought so to live as not to give themselves over to earthly things, since all the things of this life are transitory (v.29.30.). The life of the unmarried is preferable, because in times of persecution they will more easily abandon everything for Christ, will not be anxious about heaping up riches, and will serve God far more freely (v.31 to v.36.). V. Solution of a question: parents ought neither to keep their children from marriage nor compel them to it, but one must proceed here according to the requirements of the circumstances (v.36.37.). VI. A question about second marriages: he answers that these are indeed permitted, but that to persevere in widowhood is more blessed, that is, with fewer troubles and fewer hindrances to divine worship (v.39.40.).

units.la: Cap. 8. 9. 10. disputat de esu Idolothytorum, hoc est, carnium idolis immolatarum. Consuetudo erat, vt in sacrificiis, diebus praesertim festis, quando pars
units.tr: Chapters 8, 9 and 10 discuss the eating of idol-offerings, that is, meats sacrificed to idols. It was the custom that in sacrifices, especially on festival days, when

units.la: animalium immolatorum patrifamilias cedebat, conuiuium celebraretur, ad quod cognati & amici vocabantur in ipsa Idolea, vt apparet ex v.10. cap.8. Quaerebatur igitur, an non liceret Christianis ad fouendam societatem ciuilem huiusmodi conuiuiis interesse, & carnibus illis vesci? Apostolus negatiuam ponit & defendit.
units.tr: a portion of the sacrificed animals went to the head of the household, a feast was held, to which relatives and friends were invited in the very temple of the idol, as appears from v.10 of chapter 8. The question therefore was whether Christians might not, in order to foster civil fellowship, take part in such feasts and eat those meats? The Apostle takes the negative and defends it.

units.la: Capite VIII primo refellit per praeoccupationem rationes eorum, qui Idolothytis licenter vescebantur: dictitantes se scire, idolum nihil esse, ac proinde carnes idolis immolatas non esse idolorum cultu pollutas, ut homo Christianus illis bona conscientia vesci non possit. Hoc autem istorum facto offendebantur alij infirmiores seu rudiores, non intelligentes carnes istiusmodi suâ naturâ puras, ac proinde eorum esum Christiano homini licitum atque concessum esse: sed iudicanabt esse immundas, eo quod idolis immolatae essent. Interim tamen cum viderunt, scientiores illos & in doctrina Christiana eruditiores liberè eiusmodi carnibus vesci, idque in ipso idolorum templo: mouebantur istorum exemplo, ut auderent & ipsi carnes istas edere: qua quidem in re graviter peccabant, facientes nimirum id, quod, an Deo placeret, dubitabant. Apostolus ergo intempestiuum illum & cum scandalo infirmorum coniunctum Idolothytorum esum reprehendit: & istorum argumenta, quibus factum hoc suum defendebant, refellit: vsque ad v. 9. Altera pars capitis, à v. 9. vsque ad finem, affert rationes cur id consultum non esset.
units.tr: Chapter VIII first refutes, by anticipation, the arguments of those who ate freely of idol-meats. They kept saying that they knew an idol is nothing, and therefore that meats offered to idols are not polluted by the worship of idols, so that a Christian man could eat them with a good conscience. But by this conduct of theirs other, weaker or more ignorant, brothers were offended. They did not understand that such meats are by their nature pure, and that their eating is therefore lawful and permitted to a Christian; they judged them to be unclean because they had been offered to idols. Yet when they saw the more knowledgeable, and those more learned in Christian doctrine, eating such meats freely, and that in the very temple of the idols, they were moved by their example to dare to eat these meats too. In this they sinned gravely, doing, of course, what they doubted whether it pleased God. The Apostle therefore rebukes that untimely eating of idol-meats, which was joined with the offence of the weak, and refutes the arguments by which they defended this deed of theirs, down to v. 9. The second part of the chapter, from v. 9 to the end, gives the reasons why this was not advisable.

units.la: Cap. IX. Quoniam superiore capite reprehenderat eos qui Idolothytis cum offendiculo infirmorum fratrum vescebantur: concluseratque se ita animo affectum esse, vt in gratiam il-lorum, hoc est, ne illis sit offendiculo, vel in perpetuum à carnibus abstinere velit: nunc suum ipsius exemplū intempestiuis illis suæ libertatis ac iuris vsurpatoribus imitandum proponit. Partes capitis sunt tres. 1 Apostolus de suo iure docet, quod habeat in res medias, ac specia-tim fruendi stipendio, vsque ad v. 15. 11 ostendit quod non vtatur suo iure, vsque ad v. 24. 111 Hortatur Corinthios vt suum exemplum hac in parte imitentur.
units.tr: Chapter IX. Since in the previous chapter he had rebuked those who ate idol-meats to the offence of weak brothers, and had concluded that he himself was so disposed that, for their sake, that is, lest they be offended, he would abstain from meat forever, he now sets forth his own example to be imitated by those untimely usurpers of their liberty and right. The chapter has three parts. (1) The Apostle teaches about his own right, which he has over indifferent things, and especially about being supported by wages, down to v. 15. (2) He shows that he does not use his right, down to v. 24. (3) He exhorts the Corinthians to imitate his example in this respect.

units.la: Cap. x. partes sunt tres: 1. Confutatio est Corinthiorum, opinantium, se quia baptizati essent & coenæ dominicæ participarent, impunè idolothytis vesci posse. Hoc ita confutat: Si Deus non pepercit Israëlitis, idololatriam exercentibus, & iisdem fere quibus vos, argumentis eam excusantibus, etiam vobis non parcet: Atqui Deus non pepercit illis; Ergo neque vobis: ac proinde vestrum est fugere idololatriam, ne eadem vobis attrahatis poenas: à v. 1. vsque ad v. 7. vbi dehortatio ab idololatria, fornicatione & aliis sceleribus subiicitur, (vsque ad v. 12.) addita consolatione, (v.13.) & conclusione (v. 14.) 11 Subiiciuntur alia argumenta contra vsum & esum idolothytorum: 1 quia cum Christo communionem habemus, quod nobis coena dominica confirmat; ij vero qui idolothytis vescuntur, cum idolis participant, quod vtrunque confirmat exemplo populi Israëlitici, à v.15. vsque ad 19. 2 quia nemo simul & Deo vero, & idolis seruire potest: à v. 19. vsque ad 23. 111 Respondet ad quæstiones duas: prior; Annon liceat Christianis vti cibis quibuslibet? Resp: Licentia hæc ex charitatis lege limitanda, & ad infir-morum ædificationem temperanda est. v. 23.24. po-sterior; liceat ne carnes idolis immolatas in foro emere? vel, virum inuitati ad conuiuia Ethnico-rum in ædibus ipsorum, illis vesci liceat? Resp: Li-cet; sed hac restrictione, vt id fiat sine scandalo infir-morum, & vt in omnibus disp iciamus, quid gloria Dei & ædificatio proximi requirat. v. 25. &c.
units.tr: Chapter 10 has three parts. (1) There is a refutation of the Corinthians, who thought that, because they had been baptized and took part in the Lord's Supper, they could eat idol-meats with impunity. He refutes this as follows: If God did not spare the Israelites, who practised idolatry, and who excused it by nearly the same arguments as you, then he will not spare you either. But God did not spare them; therefore neither will he spare you. And so it is your duty to flee idolatry, lest you draw the same punishments upon yourselves. This runs from v. 1 to v. 7, where dissuasion from idolatry, fornication and other crimes is added (down to v. 12), with consolation (v. 13) and conclusion (v. 14). (2) Other arguments are added against the use and eating of idol-meats: first, because we have communion with Christ, which the Lord's Supper confirms for us; but those who eat idol-meats participate with idols, which both are confirmed by the example of the people of Israel (vv. 15 to 19). Second, because no one can serve both the true God and idols at once (vv. 19 to 23). (3) He answers two questions. The first: may Christians use any kind of food whatever? Answer: this liberty must be limited by the law of love and tempered for the building up of the weak (vv. 23, 24). The second: may they buy meats offered to idols in the market, or, when invited to the feasts of the Gentiles in their houses, may they eat those meats? Answer: they may, but with this restriction, that it be done without offence to the weak, and that in all things we consider what the glory of God and the edification of our neighbour require (v. 25 and following).

units.la: Cum in Ecclesia non puritatem solum doctrinæ & vitæ retinere, verum etiam decenter & ordine omnia facere conueniat, vt monet Apostolus cap. 14. 40. sequentibus quatuor capitibus nonnullos abusus notat, qui in cœtibus ecclesiasticis apud Corinthios committebantur, & ad hæc tria capita revocari possunt, ad decentem nimirum virorum & fœminarum habitum in cœtibus publicis, ad legitimam ritus Cœnæ Domini administrationem, quam nonnulli admissis prophanis conuiuiis profanabant, denique ad certum & decentem vocationum & donorum spiritualium vsum.
units.tr: Since it is fitting in the Church not only to keep the purity of doctrine and life, but also to do all things decently and in order, as the Apostle admonishes in chapter 14, verse 40, in the following four chapters he notes some abuses which were being committed among the Corinthians in the ecclesiastical assemblies. These can be referred to three heads: namely, the decent dress of men and women in public assemblies; the lawful administration of the rite of the Lord's Supper, which some were profaning by admitting profane feasts; and finally the fitting use of callings and spiritual gifts.

units.la: Capite x 1 de duobus primis, habitu nimi-rum decenti, & de Cœna Domini disserit. Partes igitur capitis duæ sunt. 1. Post prouocationem ad imitationem sui (v. 1.) & commendationem obedientiæ ipsorum (v. 2.) reprehendit [?]ἀλα-ξίαν, quod viri operto, mulieres vero aperto capite in cœtu publico compareant. Monet igitur ne viri velatis sint capitibus, quia apud Græcos retecto capite in cœtibus comparere, infame fuerit libertatis & dominij, (v. 3. 4.) 2 & quia velamen testimonium sit subiectionis: hinc velamen capitis potestas appellatur per metonymiam subiecti, i. significati pro signo; ad denotandum, mulierem sub potestate viri esse, (v. 7.8. 9.) 3 propter angelorum in sacris coetibus præsentiam, qui non sunt fugandi per ἀτα-ξίαν[?]. v. 10. usque ad 17. 1 pars reprehensio est ἀταξίας[?] in usu cœnæ dominicæ, quam non unanimiter & communiter celebrabant, (v. 17.18.19.) sed in publicum conuiuium conuertebant, cum magna pauperum confusione, (v. 20 21.) quare primam eius institutionem & legitimam administrationem repetit, v. 23: usque ad 28. monens ut ante eius usum semetipsos probent & decenter præparent, ne indignè ea participantes, sibi iudicium manducent. (v. 28.29.) quod ipsum multis iam usuenisse ad ipsorum necessariam emendationem ostendit: (v. 30. 31.32.) Deinde ut simul seu coniunctim cœnam celebrent, hortatur. v. 33. 34.
units.tr: In chapter 11 he discusses the first two, namely decent dress, and the Lord's Supper. The parts of the chapter are therefore two. (1) After appealing to his own imitation (v. 1) and commending their obedience (v. 2), he rebukes disorder [ἀταξίαν], namely that men appear with covered heads and women with uncovered heads in the public assembly. He therefore admonishes that men should not be veiled on the head, because among the Greeks to appear in public with a bare head was a mark of freedom and lordship, and to be disgraceful (vv. 3, 4). (2) And because the veil is a testimony of subjection, the veil of the head is called power by metonymy of the subject, that is, the sign is put for the thing signified, to denote that the woman is under the power of the man (vv. 7, 8, 9). (3) On account of the presence of angels in the sacred assemblies, who are not to be driven away by disorder [ἀταξίαν] (vv. 10 to 17). The first part of the rebuke is of disorder [ἀταξίας] in the use of the Lord's Supper, which they did not celebrate unanimously and in common, but turned into a public feast, with great confusion for the poor (vv. 17, 18, 19, 20, 21). Wherefore he repeats its first institution and lawful administration (v. 23 to 28), admonishing them to prove themselves before its use and to prepare themselves decently, lest, partaking of it unworthily, they eat judgement to themselves (vv. 28, 29). He shows that this had already happened to many, for their necessary amendment (vv. 30, 31, 32). Then he exhorts them to celebrate the supper together, that is, in common (vv. 33, 34).

units.la: Sequitur deinceps de recto donorum spiritualium usu quam quæstionem tractat Apostolus per tria sequentia capita.
units.tr: Next follows the right use of spiritual gifts, a question the Apostle treats in the three following chapters.

units.la: Cap. xii. Quia Corinthij, atque inter eos inprimis ipsi doctores linguarum & aliis Spiritus S. donis ad superbam ostentationem abutebantur: hortatur eos Apostolus ut ad ædificationem Ecclesiæ ea conuertant: 1 quia ipsi prius infideles Ethnici existentes, hæc charismata a Spiritu sancto acceperint, quia omnia ad Christi honorem referat: (v. 1. 2.3.) 2 quia hæc dona Corinthios ad mutuam vnionem impellere debent, vtpote ab vno eodemque Spiritu & Domino profecta, (v. 4.5. 6.) 3 quia ad communem effusa vtilitatem (usque ad v. 12.) quia Christus & ipsius Ecclesia variis licet constans membris, vnum est corpus. Hæc ratio insigni similitudine membrorum corporis humani inter se ad vtilitatem corporis conspirantium illustratur, vsque ad v. 27. inde vsque ad finem capitis est accommodatio illius similitudinis ad Ecclesiam, quae est corpus Christi, & illorum donorum mater.
units.tr: Chapter 12. Because the Corinthians, and above all their teachers of tongues and others with the gifts of the Holy Spirit, abused them for proud display, the Apostle urges them to turn these gifts to the edification of the Church: 1 because they themselves were formerly unbelieving Gentiles and received these charismata from the Holy Spirit, and he refers all things to the honour of Christ: (v. 1. 2. 3.) 2 because these gifts ought to move the Corinthians to mutual union, as coming from one and the same Spirit and Lord, (v. 4. 5. 6.) 3 because they are poured out for the common benefit (to v. 12) because Christ and his Church, though consisting of many members, is one body. This truth is illustrated by a striking likeness: the members of the human body, working together for the benefit of the body, up to v. 27. From there to the end of the chapter the likeness is applied to the Church, which is the body of Christ and the mother of those gifts.

units.la: Occasione disputationis institutae de recto donorum spiritualium vsu, Apostolus hoc xiii capite digreditur in disputationem de charitate Christiana & fraterna, qua scilicet Christiani sese mutuo vt fratres complecti debent. Hor-tatur itaque credentes omnes, imprimisque Antistites Ecclesiae Dei, vt charitati mutuae in-ter se studeant, omniaq; ad eam dirigant; 1 quia omnia quantumuis excellentia dona, exclusa charitate sint inutilia: (v. 1. 2. 3.) 2 ab eius praeclaris adiunctis & effectis, non quidem ad iustificationem hominis peccatoris coram Deo sed ad societatem & pacem Ecclesiae (vsque ad v. 8.) 3 ab eius duratione & collatione cum summis virtutibus, fide & spe: quae tamen collatio non simpliciter sed secundum quid instituitur.
units.tr: Prompted by the dispute about the right use of spiritual gifts, the Apostle in this thirteenth chapter digresses into a discussion of Christian and brotherly love, by which Christians ought to embrace one another as brothers. He therefore urges all believers, and especially the leaders of God's Church, to strive for mutual love among themselves and to direct everything to it: 1 because all gifts, however excellent, are useless without love: (v. 1. 2. 3.) 2 from its excellent attendants and effects, not indeed toward the justification of sinful man before God, but toward the fellowship and peace of the Church (up to v. 8.) 3 from its duration and its comparison with the highest virtues, faith and hope; yet this comparison is made not absolutely but in a certain respect.

units.la: Cap. xiv. Redit ad quaestionem de recto donorum spiritualium vsu : partes sunt tres. 1 Illatio ex superioribus, de perseguenda charitate, licet perfectio nobis non contigat, & adhortatio ad prophetiae studium, quae est instar propositionis. v. 1. 11 Confirmatio propositionis, prophetiam scilicet linguis anteponendam esse, quod probat variis argumentis, inprimis collatione vsus, qui redit ad Ecclesiam, statuens hanc supremam legem: Ecclesiae aedificationem[?]; vsque ad v. 26. 111: A versu 26. ad finem vsque habet hanc propositionem, quae versus vltimo exprimitur: omnia in Ecclesia decenter & ordine facienda: ideo reprehendit confusionem, quae tunc in coetibus Corinthiorum conspiciebatur, & quod & quòd confusè docebant & loquebantur in cœtu publico: Deinde quòd mulieribus etiam in tali cœtu potestatem loquendi faciebant.
units.tr: Chapter 14. He returns to the question of the right use of spiritual gifts. There are three parts. 1 An inference from what has gone before, that we should pursue love, although we do not attain perfection, and an exhortation to the study of prophecy, which stands as the proposition. v. 1. 2 Confirmation of the proposition, namely that prophecy is to be preferred to tongues, which he proves by various arguments, especially by the comparison of use, which returns to the Church, laying down this supreme rule: the edification of the Church; up to v. 26. 3 From v. 26 to the end he holds to this proposition, which is stated in the last verse: all things in the Church are to be done decently and in order. Therefore he rebukes the confusion then seen in the assemblies of the Corinthians, namely that they taught and spoke confusedly in the public gathering; and then that they also gave women the power to speak in such a gathering.

units.la: Emendatis in vitâ & rebus Ecclesiasticis apud Corinthios emendandis, ad doctrinam fidei accedit, multisque & solidissimis argumentis confutatis horribilem errorem, quo quidam asserebant, non esse expectandam carnis resurrectionem: & dicta Scripturæ interpretabantur tantum de spirituali resurrectione, quâ à peccatis resurgimus.
units.tr: Having set right the life and church affairs of the Corinthians that needed correcting, he turns to the doctrine of faith. With many very solid arguments he refutes a horrible error, by which some asserted that the resurrection of the flesh was not to be expected, and interpreted the words of Scripture as referring only to the spiritual resurrection by which we rise from sins.

units.la: Cap. xv. post succinctam de visu & summâ totius Euangelij de Christo repetitionem (v. 1. 2. 3.) copiosè disserit de resurrectione mortuorum: de qua tres quæstiones explicat: quarum prima est, an sit resurrectio mortuorum: huius affirmationem demonstrat sex argumentis. 1 ab exemplo Christi, tanquam à pari, (à v. 3. usque ad 19.) 2 ab effectu contrary seu à consequente absurdo sententiæ contrariæ, (v. 19.) 3 à genere, (v. 25.26.) 4 à testimonio, videlicet iudicio eorum qui baptizantur supra mortuos (v. 29.) 5 etiam à testimonio, videlicet iudicio confessorum Christi, & nominatim suo: (v. 30. 31. 32.) 6 rursum ab effectu contrary seu consequente absurdo sententiæ contrariæ, (v. 32.) Secunda quæstio, quali corpore mortui resurrecturi sint: respondet, eos resurrecturos corpore spirituali, à v. 35. usque ad 51. Tertia, quid futurum sit iis quos dies Domini vivos deprehendet; respondet, eos mutatum iri, hoc est, indutum iri incorruptibilitate atque immortalitate, à v. 51. usque ad v. ultimum: ubi disputationem hanc exhortatione inde deducta concludit.
units.tr: Chapter 15. After a brief repetition of the account and summary of the whole gospel concerning Christ (v. 1. 2. 3.), he discourses at length on the resurrection of the dead, explaining three questions. The first is whether there is a resurrection of the dead; he demonstrates the affirmation by six arguments. 1 From the example of Christ, as from a like case (from v. 3 to 19). 2 From the effect of the contrary, or the absurd consequence of the contrary opinion (v. 19). 3 From the genus (v. 25. 26). 4 From testimony, namely the judgment of those who are baptized over the dead (v. 29). 5 Also from testimony, namely the judgment of the confessors of Christ, and by name his own (v. 30. 31. 32). 6 Again from the effect of the contrary, or the absurd consequence of the contrary opinion (v. 32). The second question is with what body the dead will rise; he answers that they will rise with a spiritual body, from v. 35 to 51. The third is what will become of those whom the day of the Lord finds alive; he answers that they will be changed, that is, clothed with incorruptibility and immortality, from v. 51 to the last verse, where he concludes this disputation with an exhortation drawn from it.

units.la: ULTIMA PARS EPISTOLÆ, Epilogus seu Conclusio.
units.tr: The Last Part of the Epistle: the Epilogue or Conclusion.

units.la: Cap. xvi partes sunt tres. 1 Est admonitio de collectis in vsum pauperum instituendis, & quidem certo ordine & certis diebus, usque ad v. 5. 11 pars est de variis rebus familiaribus, de suo ad Corinthios aduentu, commendatio Timothei, Apollos, & familiæ Stephanæ de ministerio bene merita, &c. 111 amicæ & syncerae salutationes, à v.19. usque ad finem capitis.
units.tr: Chapter xvi has three parts. (1) The first is an admonition about the collections to be made for the relief of the poor, to be done in a fixed order and on fixed days, up to v. 5. (2) The second part concerns various domestic matters: Paul's coming to the Corinthians, the commendation of Timothy, Apollos, and the household of Stephanas, who have deserved well of the ministry, and so on. (3) The third part consists of friendly and sincere greetings, from v. 19 to the end of the chapter.

units.la: ARGVMENTA CAPITVM. CAP. I
units.tr: ARGUMENTS OF THE CHAPTERS. CHAPTER I

units.la: Displicet infamis vestra, ô discordia, fratres, Doctores varios quæ putat esse suos. Non humili moueat quod sim sermone locutus, Nempe solent magno parua placere Deo.
units.tr: It displeases me, O discord, that your fellow believers say they belong to various teachers. Let it not trouble you that I have spoken in a plain style; for God is wont to be pleased by small things.

units.la: 2 Non ego iactabam doctæ præconia linguæ, Sed solum CHRISTVM me docuisse, scio. Sed quæ stultitia est vobis, sapientia summa est, Quam nequit infirmus discedere quæ sit homo.
units.tr: 2 I did not boast of the praises of learned speech, but I know that I taught only Christ. But what is folly to you is the highest wisdom, which feeble man cannot grasp.

units.la: 3 Mollia nutrimi[?] candenti pectora lacte Non quicquam docta voce minister aget. Spiritus ipse Dei est, qui nutrit semina verbi. Ego omnis soli gloria danda Deo est.
units.tr: 3 A learned minister will not accomplish anything with a learned voice on tender breasts nourished with shining milk. It is the Spirit of God himself who nourishes the seeds of the word. All glory is to be given to God alone.

units.la: 4 Præcones verbi quales sint esse putandi: Hinc male sanctorum corda superba notat. Hypocrisin damnat, fratrem commendat amicum, Et se promittit velle venire brevi.
