units.tr: 4 We must consider what kind of heralds of the word they ought to be. Here he marks out the proud hearts of the saints as bad. He condemns hypocrisy, commends a friendly brother, and promises that he himself wishes to come soon.

units.la: 5 Num iuuat elatas tantum vos tollere mentes, Cum tantum impingant turpia stupra notam[?]. Quin potius tantum pœnis suffollite crimen. Et nunc sit vitæ cura pudica piæ.
units.tr: 5 Does it help you only to lift up your proud minds, when shameful fornications stain you? Rather, cut off the crime with punishments. And now let the care of life be chaste and pious.

units.la: 6 Fraternum multis Paulus commendat amorem, Illiciti culpans iurgia fœda furi[?]. Pellite luxuriam, cedat scortatio longè, Ne sanctam CHRISTI polluat illa domum?
units.tr: 6 Paul commends brotherly love to many, blaming the foul quarrels of unlawful [?]. Drive out lust; let fornication depart far away, lest it defile the holy house of Christ.

units.la: Coniugii leges tractat causasque modumque Quamuis virginei sitque pudoris honor. Quid deceat viduas: prohibet divortia: cælebs Commodius Domino quippe studere potest.
units.tr: He treats the laws of marriage, its causes and manner, though virginal modesty is an honour. He says what is fitting for widows and forbids divorces; the unmarried man can indeed devote himself more suitably to the Lord.

units.la: Si quæ forte fuit simulachris victima cæsa, Cuius quis iubeat participare cibis. Scandala fac caveas: fraterni munus amoris Sectare, in vera te regat ille via.
units.tr: If by chance any meat was slaughtered as a sacrifice to idols, and someone bids you share in that food, take care to avoid scandals. Pursue the gift of brotherly love; may that guide you in the true way.

units.la: Hoc ego iam feci, ne quos offendere posset Libertas, multis me caruisse iuvat. Non etenim precium pro nostro posco labore: Nec mihi, quae poterat, nupta pudica comes.
units.tr: This I have now done, so that liberty might not offend anyone; I am glad to have gone without for the sake of many. For I do not demand payment for our labour, nor a married woman as a companion, though I could have had one.

units.la: Seducat ne vos libertas caeca cavete Nec curæ vobis mensa prophana fiet. Tristia quin moveant Iudæ crimina gentis: Sit libertatis regula sanctius amor.
units.tr: Beware lest blind liberty seduce you, and the profane table not become a concern for you. Let the sad crimes of the Jewish people move you; let love be a holier rule than liberty.

units.la: Quo ritu deceat sacros invisere coetus, Et quem vir seruet, fœmina quemque modum. Perdita restituis sacra convivia Caenae, Ad CHRISTI hancvitum[?] restituisse docens.
units.tr: In what manner it is fitting to visit the holy assemblies, and what measure each man and each woman should keep. You restore the sacred banquets of the Supper that had been lost, teaching that they were restored to the institution of Christ.

units.la: Discite doctorum varias discernere mentes, Ne sint hi rixæ causa parata novis Quin potius variis crescat concordia donis. Unum etenim corpus membraque multa sumus.
units.tr: Learn to discern the various minds of teachers, lest these become a ready cause of strife among new converts; rather, let concord grow with its various gifts. For we are one body, yet many members.

units.la: Murmura quo possit querulis compescere vulgi, Divitiis nimis corda superba simul, Inclyta fraterni præconia scribit amoris, Quo sine non virtus ulla juvare potest.
units.tr: By what means the murmurs of the common crowd may be restrained, and the proud hearts of the rich likewise. He writes the glorious praises of brotherly love, without which no virtue can help.

units.la: Quænam doctiloqui sint munera sancta prophetæ, Et quonam fuerint hæc obeunda modo. Linguarum quod sit fluidum, quæ forma docendi, Ut fructus habeant hinc pia turba suos.
units.tr: What the holy offices of the teaching prophets are, and in what manner these are to be performed. What the flow of tongues is, and what the form of teaching, so that the pious crowd may have its fruits from them.

units.la: Mortua cum multi consurgere membra negarent, Hoc Paulus multa cum ratione probat. Hæc etenim nostræ fidei spes[?] vnica restat. Et quæ corporibus forma futura docet.
units.tr: When many denied that dead limbs would rise again, Paul proves this with much reasoning. For this is the sole remaining hope of our faith, and it teaches what form bodies will have in the future.

units.la: Munera quisque, precor, miseris seponat egenis, Repperiam ut veniens ista[?] parata simul.
units.tr: Let each one, I pray, set aside gifts for the needy poor, so that when I come I may find them made ready all at once.

units.la: Commendat fratrem, qui illius haec scripta ferebat;Adeat in sancto pectore sanctus amor. ALITER.
units.tr: He commends the brother who carried this writing; may holy love enter the holy breast. OTHERWISE.

units.la: CAP. I.
units.tr: CHAPTER I.

units.la: Audio propter vos lites sapientia mundiStulta est.infirmis fortia facta vivunt.
units.tr: I hear that there are quarrels among you. The wisdom of the world is foolishness. The weak things of the world achieve strong deeds.

units.la: 2 Blandis non utar, mysterio condita pando,Quæ neque scit mundus neue animalis homo.
units.tr: 2 I will not use enticing words; I set out things hidden in a mystery, which neither the world nor the natural man knows.

units.la: 3 Carnales estis.planto fundamina ieci.Arguet ignis opus.stultus es o sapiens.
units.tr: 3 You are still carnal. I have planted, I have laid the foundation. The fire will test the work. You are a fool, O wise man.

units.la: 4 Dispensatores. patefient.tot mala passus.Ut pater admoneo. quomodo vultis agam?
units.tr: 4 Stewards, let them be made manifest. I have suffered so many evils. As a father I admonish you. What do you want me to do?

units.la: 5 Expelli talem iubeo, purgetis amarumPanem.cumque malis nemo vel esse velit.
units.tr: 5 I order that such a man be cast out. Purge out the old leaven, and let no one want to be with such evil men.

units.la: 6 Fiunt cur lites? regnum non cedit iniquis?Cuncta licent.fluprum quale sit ecce nefas.
units.tr: 6 Why do quarrels arise? Does the kingdom not pass to the unrighteous? All things are lawful. Behold what fornication is, and how wicked it is.

units.la: 7 Gratis hic Paulus verbis de coniugis usus,Mox de virginibus,de viduisque monet.
units.tr: 7 Here Paul, speaking gladly of marriage, then gives counsel concerning virgins and widows.

units.la: 8 Idolum scis esse nihil.Sed ne sua fratremPerdat cognitio,dum male cautus edis.
units.tr: 8 You know that an idol is nothing. But lest your knowledge destroy your brother, do not eat carelessly.

units.la: 9 Liber non posco mea iura sed omnia fio.In stadio curro,membraque subiicio.
units.tr: 9 I am free and do not claim my rights, but I become all things. I run in the race and bring my body into subjection.

units.la: 10 Mystica designant patres.idola cauete.Qui bibitis calicem. vendita cuncta licent.
units.tr: 10 The Fathers designate these things as mystical figures. Beware of idols. You who drink the cup: all things sold in the market are lawful.

units.la: 11 Nudet vir caput, at mulier velata precetur.O quales mores mensa sacrata petis [?].
units.tr: 11 Let a man pray with his head uncovered, but a woman veiled. What manner of conduct do you seek at the holy table [?]?

units.la: 12 Omnia dat flamen, sicut vult, & facit unumEx multis corpus,sit tamen ordo decens.
units.tr: 12 The Spirit gives all things as he wills, and makes one body out of many members; yet let there be a seemly order.

units.la: 13 Pluribus,vt sine quo nil prosit,laudat amorem.Quodque sit hoc monstras spesque fidesque minor.
units.tr: 13 He praises love above many things, without which nothing profits. He shows what this is, and that hope and faith are lesser.

units.la: 14 Qui loquitur linguis,minor est interprete sacro.Sed quem præscribo servet uterque modum.
units.tr: 14 He who speaks in tongues is less than the one who interprets the sacred word. But let each keep the measure I prescribe.

units.la: 15 Reddidus [?] est vita Christus,vivemus & ipsiDenuo,victores mors tua Christe facit.
units.tr: 15 Christ has restored life, and we too shall live again. Your death, Christ, makes us victors.

units.la: 16 Sepositis donis veniam ipse recusat Apollo.Nomiñis [?] Stephanum scriptor ego ipse fui.
units.tr: 16 Setting aside the gifts, Apollos himself refuses to come. I myself, the writer, was of the household of Stephanas [?].

units.la: Notæ Memoriales.
units.tr: Memorial Notes.

units.la: 1 2 3 4 5 Schismata, Perfectos, Laclis, Purgamina, Massam: 6 7 8 9 10 Rapax, Quisque suam, Idolü, Stadioque, Typique: 11 12 13 14 15 16 Nudus, Corporis, Aes, Lingua, Vivemus, Apollo.
units.tr: 1 2 3 4 5: Schisms, Perfect, Milk, Purgings, Lump; 6 7 8 9 10: Rapacious, Each his own, Idol, Race, Types; 11 12 13 14 15 16: Bare, Body, Brass, Tongue, We shall live, Apollos.

units.la: Declaratio.
units.tr: Explanation.

units.la: Schismata ne sint inter vos: v.10. Perfectos inter loquimur sapientiam: v.6. Laclis potu[?] alui vos: v.2. Purgamina mundi facti sumus; v.13. Massam paulum fermenti infermentat. v.6.
units.tr: Let there be no schisms among you: v.10. We speak wisdom among the perfect: v.6. I fed you with milk: v.2. We have become as the filth of the world: v.13. A little leaven leavens the whole lump: v.6.

units.la: Rapax non possid b tregni[?] Dei hereditatem: v.10. Quisque suam uxorem habeto: v.2. Idolum nihil est in mundo: v.4. Stadioque qui currunt, ex iis unus accipit præmium: v.24. Typique ut hæc sint, acciderunt. v.6.
units.tr: The covetous shall not possess the inheritance of the kingdom of God: v.10. Let each man have his own wife: v.2. An idol is nothing in the world: v.4. Of those who run in the race, one receives the prize: v.24. That these things are types, they came to pass: v.6.

units.la: Nudus capite sit vir: v.7. Corporis & membrorum similitudo, v.12. Aes resonans est Ministerexpers charitatis. v.1. Lingua qui loquitur, Deo loquitur. v.2. Vivemus denuò in resurrectione. Apollo recusat adire Corinthios. v.12.
units.tr: Let the man be bare-headed: v.7. The likeness of the body and its members: v.12. A sounding brass is a minister without love: v.1. He who speaks in a tongue speaks to God: v.2. We shall live again in the resurrection. Apollos refuses to go to the Corinthians: v.12.

units.la: ANALYSIS EPISTO-LÆ II. AD CORIN-thios.
units.tr: ANALYSIS OF THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORINthians.

units.la: HÆc Epistola cum præcedenti rectè coniungitur. Nam etsi diversis tempori-bus & per diversas personas scriptæ & missæ sunt, prior per Fortunatum & Timotheum, po-sterior per Titum & Lucam, colligitur tamen ex hac Epistola fructus prioris Epistolæ, quæ inanis non fuit apud Corinthios, à quibus Ti-motheus benignè exceptus, excommunicatio moechri & collecta pro fratribus in Iudæa im-petrata fuerat. Ideo quantum ad Ecclesiam at-tinet, maiore lenitate utitur, quàm in priori, & ἐπιείκειαν[?] quandam adhibet rigoris illius quem in priori exercuerat. Quantum verò Pseudoapo-stolos attinet & obtrectatores, vehementer eos perstringit, & primis atque extremis capitibus ministerij sui dignitatem contra eos tuetur.
units.tr: This Epistle is rightly joined to the preceding one. For although they were written and sent at different times and by different persons (the former through Fortunatus and Timothy, the latter through Titus and Luke), the fruit of the former Epistle is nonetheless gathered from this one. That Epistle was not in vain among the Corinthians: Timothy was kindly received by them, the excommunication of the adulterer was carried out, and the collection for the brothers in Judea had been secured. Therefore, as far as the Church is concerned, he uses greater gentleness than in the former, and applies a certain clemency [ἐπιείκειαν] to that severity which he had exercised in the former. But as far as the pseudo-apostles and detractors are concerned, he attacks them vehemently, and in the first and last chapters he defends the dignity of his ministry against them.

units.la: Occasio nata est ex malevolentia adversario-rum Pauli, qui more suo omnia dicta & facta Apostoli rapiebant in deterius, inprimis ea quæ in priore Epistola pie ipse monuerat, & candi-dè promiserat, ut quod cap. 5. severiter iusserat illum incestu pollutum tradi Satanæ, id adversarij mirificè exagitabant, quasi dictum homi-nis ambitiosi, & censoris nimium severi. Sic quod ultimo capite promiserat suum adven-tum, quem impeditus variis persecutionibus non potuit præstare: hoc rapiunt adversarij in calumniam & argumentum levitatis. Eodem pacto alia multa rapiebant in contumeliam, quasi Apostolus dominationem quæreret, & autoritatem nimiam peteret, legem everteret, homines carnales & dissolutos efficeret, impe-riosus nimium inscribendo esset, cum interea persona esset abiecta & contemptibilis. His & similibus calumniis diligenter in-hac epistola occurrit, & apud eosdem causam disceptat, apud quos hostes inprimis illum laedebant.
units.tr: The occasion arose from the malice of Paul's adversaries, who, as is their habit, twisted everything the Apostle said and did for the worse, especially what he had piously admonished in the earlier Epistle and frankly promised. For example, when in chapter 5 he sternly ordered that the man polluted by incest be handed over to Satan, the adversaries savagely harried this, as if it were the word of an ambitious man and an overly severe censor. Likewise, what he had promised in the last chapter, his coming, which he could not fulfil because various persecutions hindered him, they seized upon as a slander and a proof of fickleness. In the same way they twisted many other things into insults, as if the Apostle sought dominion, claimed excessive authority, subverted the law, made men carnal and dissolute, and wrote in an overbearing manner, when in fact he was a humble and despised person. This Epistle carefully meets these and similar slanders, and argues the case before the same people among whom the enemies had especially harmed him.

units.la: Genus scripti ex occasione facilè diiudicari potest. Quanquam enim mixtum sit genus scribendi:tamen principale est Apologeticum, quod constat excusatione & calumniarum depulsione. Purgat autem se inprimis contra crimen leuitatis, asperitatis, ambitionis, inconstantiae & cauponationis doctrinae, qui affectus erat carnalis, doctrinam accommodandi ad priuatum quaestum: quae omnia ita diluit, vt ostendat dilucidè, haec omnia multò magis aduersariis competere.
units.tr: The kind of writing can easily be judged from the occasion. For although the genre is mixed, the principal kind is apologetic, which consists in excuse and the rebuttal of slanders. He clears himself chiefly of the charges of levity, harshness, ambition, inconstancy, and of peddling doctrine, which was a carnal disposition, adapting teaching to private gain. He refutes all of these in such a way as to show clearly that they apply far more to his adversaries.

units.la: Propositio & scopus principalis est: Cùm Apostolus Paulus nulla leuitate in promissis, aut dominandi studio quicquam scripserit, nulla etiam ambitione quicquam docuerit, sed singulari erga Corinthios amore & beneficiendi studio, omnia & scripserit & docuerit: ideò Corinthij eius Euangelium aspernari, aut Pseudo-apostolis aures praebere non debent, sed potius in doctrina ab ipso tradita constanter perseue-rare, & eum tanquam syncerum Apostolum Christi agnoscere. Istam propositionem tractat praecipuè cum refutatione calumniarum. Habet etiam digressiones quasdam haec propositio; vt cap. 2. de recipiendo incestuoso qui poenitentiam egerat: cap. 6. de fugienda idololatria, cap. 7. de agenda poenitentia: cap. 8. & 9. de liberalitate in pauperes. In sequentibus redit ad primariam propositionem apologeticam: est multus in commendatione sui Apostolatus, subinde praedicat suas laudes & labores, & gloriatur de afflictionibus, donis & reuelationibus suis: id autem facit non studio & cupiditate inanis gloriae consequendae, sed potius in defensionem sui Apostolatus contra calumnia-tores. Intererat autem ipsius autoritatem esse integram apud Ecclesiam & intemeratam, par-
units.tr: Proposition and principal aim: since the Apostle Paul wrote nothing out of levity in his promises, nor out of a desire to dominate, and taught nothing out of ambition, but wrote and taught everything out of singular love for the Corinthians and zeal to do them good, therefore the Corinthians ought not to spurn his Gospel or lend their ears to pseudo-apostles, but should rather persevere steadfastly in the doctrine delivered by him and acknowledge him as the sincere Apostle of Christ. He treats this proposition chiefly together with the refutation of the slanders. The proposition also has certain digressions: in chapter 2, on receiving back the incestuous man who had repented; in chapter 6, on fleeing idolatry; in chapter 7, on carrying out repentance; in chapters 8 and 9, on liberality towards the poor. In what follows he returns to the primary apologetic proposition. He is lavish in commending his apostleship, repeatedly recounts his own praises and labours, and boasts of his afflictions, gifts and revelations. He does this not from a zeal to win empty glory, but in defence of his apostleship against the slanderers. Moreover, it was important that his authority remain whole and unblemished in the Church, partly

units.la: [illegible, ~20 letters] tim vt auerteretur scandalum infirmorum, par-tim vt omnibus, etiam nobis, constaret de au-toritate & certitudine vocationis Apostoli & ipsius doctrinæ. Ergo non agitur de Paulo & eius gloria, sed de certitudine fidei nostræ, de-pendente ex doctrinæ huius Apostoli indubita-ta autoritate. Pulcrè Augustinus in Psalmū 144.
units.tr: [illegible, ~20 letters] so that the scandal to the weak might be averted, partly so that it might be clear to all, including us, concerning the authority and certainty of the Apostle's calling and of his doctrine. Therefore the matter concerns not Paul and his glory, but the certainty of our faith, which depends on the indubitable authority of this Apostle's doctrine. Augustine well says on Psalm 144:

units.la: Te laudare potes sine arrogantia, si Deum in te laudes, non te: non quod tu sis talis & talis, sed quia te Deus talem fecit, non quodtu aliquid possis, sed ille in te & per te.
units.tr: You can praise yourself without arrogance, if you praise God in you and not yourself: not because you are such and such, but because God made you such; not that you can do anything, but that he does it in you and through you.

units.la: Vsus epistolæ duplex est: Generalis & specialis. Generalis, vt in doctrina Euangelij, quam magnificis eulogiis commendat, siue vt in doctrina fidei & vitæ novæ magis ac magis confirmemur. Specialis, vt intelligamus 1[?] nunquam plane inanes esse labores piorum Pastorum, quandoquidem Apostolus priore ad Corinthios non parum apud eos profecerat. 2 Fidos ministros multis calamitatibus & obtrectatio-nibus esse obnoxios. 3 Non ideò desponden-dum animum vel deserendum ministerium, quandoquidem crescente pugna crescit pugnan-tium gloria, & eò maiore animo propugnanda est veritas, quo maiore furore eam Diabolus oppugnat.
units.tr: The use of the Epistle is twofold: general and special. General, as in the doctrine of the Gospel, which he commends with magnificent eulogies, or so that we may be confirmed more and more in the doctrine of faith and of the new life. Special, so that we understand: (1) that the labours of pious ministers are never altogether in vain, since the Apostle had accomplished no little good among the Corinthians through the earlier Epistle; (2) that faithful ministers are liable to many calamities and detractions; (3) that the spirit should not therefore be cast down or the ministry abandoned, since as the struggle grows, the glory of those who fight grows with it, and the truth must be defended with all the greater courage the more furiously the Devil assails it.

units.la: PARTES EPISTOLÆ
units.tr: THE PARTS OF THE EPISTLE

units.la: Sunt Exordium, PRINCIPALIS TRACTA-TIO, & Conclusio.
units.tr: There are the Introduction, the Principal Treatment, and the Conclusion.

units.la: Exordium habet 1. Subscriptionem, continen-tem nomen eius qui scribit, sic dictam, quòd hodie ferè subscribere suum nomen soleant: Inscriptio-
units.tr: The Introduction has (1) the Subscription, containing the name of the one who writes, so called because people today generally sign their own name; (2) the Inscrip-

units.la: Inscriptione continentem nomen eius ad quem scribitur, ut hanc epistolam inscribit Paulus partim Ecclesiae Corinthiacae, partim caeteris Ecclesiis Achaicis: (v. 1.) 3. Salutationem, quae duplicem optationem continet, videlicet gratiam Dei Patris, quae omnium bonorum & totius beatitatis fons est: & pacis per Christum partae, cuius interventu gratia nos sua Deus dignatur.
units.tr: tion, containing the name of the one to whom it is written. Paul inscribes this letter partly to the Church of Corinth and partly to the other churches of Achaia (v. 1.); (3) the Salutation, which contains a twofold wish: the grace of God the Father, which is the source of all good things and of all blessedness, and the peace obtained through Christ, by whose intercession God deigns to bestow his grace upon us.

units.la: TRACTATIO PRINCIPALIS
units.tr: MAIN TREATMENT

units.la: Agit partim de ipsius Apostoli Pauli persona, partim de Corinthiis,
units.tr: It deals partly with the person of the Apostle Paul himself, partly with the Corinthians.

units.la: PRIMÆ PARTIS SYNOPSIS.
units.tr: Synopsis of the First Part.

units.la: [label along the left edge, rotated, illegible, ~20 letters] Vitam, quod non sit Seditiosus: cap.1. vsque ad v.10. Mendax: cap.1. à v.10. vsque ad finem cap. Apostolatum, demonstraas se non esse Crudelem: cap.2, vsque ad v.12. Falsarium verbi Dei & inanem iactatore, à v.12.c.2. vsque ad finé quinti c. Hic igitur instituit Evangelii sui Laudationem ex effectis & comparatis: cap.3. Excusatione ob adiutam[?] Obscuritatem, cap.4. Crucem.cap.5.
units.tr: [Label along the left edge, rotated, illegible, about 20 letters] His life, that he is not seditious: chap. 1 to v. 10. That he is not a liar: chap. 1 from v. 10 to the end of the chapter. Demonstrating that in his apostleship he is not cruel: chap. 2 to v. 12. That he is a falsifier of God's word and an empty boaster: from chap. 2 v. 12 to the end of chap. 5. Here he therefore sets out the praise of his Gospel from its effects and comparisons: chap. 3. An excuse for the obscurity (?): chap. 4. The cross: chap. 5.

units.la: Reliquo igitur capite primo, duplicem ha-bet[?] excusationem sui, quarum prima est: se minime seditiosum esse, quantumuis nulla[?] aduersa perpetiatur, 1 quia Deus ipsum in afflictionibus consoletur: 2 quia eas propter Euangelium Christi sustineat; 3 quia ipsarum scopus sit fidelium consolatio & salus, & Dei gloria, à v. 3. vsque ad v.8. Secunda, se neutiquam mendacem & inconstantem, licet ad ipsos, vti promiserat, non venerit: 1 quia in Asia ab aduersantibus sit impeditus (v.8. vsque ad 12.) 2 quia semper & in omnibus veritati stiduerit[?], vt testetur, 1 sua ipsius conscientia: (v.12.13.) 2 Corinthy ipsi: v.1. vsque ad 18.) 3 Constans ipsius de Christo doctrina, v.18 & seqq:
units.tr: In the rest of the first chapter, then, he offers a twofold defence of himself. The first is that he is by no means seditious, however many adversities he endures; (1) because God comforts him in his afflictions; (2) because he bears them for the sake of the Gospel of Christ; (3) because their aim is the comfort and salvation of the faithful and the glory of God, from v. 3 to v. 8. The second is that he is by no means a liar or inconstant, although he has not come to them as he had promised: (1) because in Asia he was hindered by his opponents (v. 8 to 12); (2) because he has always and in everything held to the truth, as he testifies: (1) by his own conscience (v. 12, 13); (2) by the Corinthians themselves (v. 1 to 18); (3) by the consistency of his own doctrine concerning Christ, v. 18 and following.

units.la: Cap. II. Pergit in defensione sui, & post repetitam mutati consilij ad ipsos veniendi causam, penultimo versu superioris capitis expositam, (scilicet ideo non venisse, ne apud eos qui ipsum exhilarare deberent, afficeretur tristitia, v.1,2.3.) deinceps Apostolatum suum defendit contra crimen nimiae seueritatis, & affectati domini quod ipsi impingebatur, quia superiore epistola, c. 5. Apostolica gravitate iusserat excommunicare incestuosum, quem nunc publica autoritate recipi iubet quia poenitentiam egerit: à v. 4. vsque ad v.12.
units.tr: Chap. II. He goes on in his defence of himself. Having repeated the reason for changing his plan of coming to them, which he set out in the penultimate verse of the previous chapter (namely, that he did not come so that he would not be grieved by those who ought to cheer him, v. 1, 2, 3), he then defends his apostleship against the charge of excessive severity and affected lordship that was being laid against him, because in his earlier letter, chap. 5, he had ordered the incestuous man to be excommunicated with apostolic gravity, and now orders him to be received back with public authority because he has repented: from v. 4 to v. 12.

units.la: In altera parte capitis, nouus apologiae locus incipit, in quo crimen ostentationis & falsae doctrinae amolitur: vbi primum narrat, quo consilio profectus sit Troadem, & quid sibi eo loci euenerit, & cur inde mox discesserit in Macedoniam: (v.12.13.) dein sua praedicationis felicem successum exponit & pro illo in gratiarum actionem erga Deum resoluitur: à v.14. vsque ad finem capitis.
units.tr: In the second part of the chapter a new section of the apology begins, in which he rebuts the charge of ostentation and false doctrine. First he tells what his purpose was in setting out for Troas, what happened to him there, and why he soon left from there for Macedonia (v. 12, 13). Then he sets out the happy success of his preaching and breaks into thanksgiving to God for it: from v. 14 to the end of the chapter.

units.la: Cap. III. Persequitur argumentum quod tractare coeperat initio praecedentis capitis, vi-delicet delicet de efficacia sui ministerij; hinc suum Apostolatum defendit, 1 à connersione seu efficaci vocatione Corinthiorum, qui ipsi sint instar epistolæ commendatoriæ seu encomiasticæ:(v.1.2.3.) 2 à cau-sis efficientibus sui ministerij : (v.4.& 5.) 3 à discri-mine inter ministerium Euangelij & Legis: vbi ministerium legis considerat in Mosis persona, per quem videlicet Lex tradita est:cui opponitur Chri-stus, Euangelij autor. partes huius ἀντιθέσεως sunt hæc octo: Ministerium Euangeli-cum est | Contrà,ministerium Le-gale est 1 Noui Testamenti | 1 Veteris Testamenti 2 Spiritus | 2 Litera 3 Vitæ | 3 Mortis 4 Inscriptum cordibus | 4 Inscriptum lapidibus 5 Semper durans | 5 Abolendum {†} 6 Iustitiæ | 6 Damnationis 7 Excellenter gloriosum | 7 Illius respectu ἀδόξου[?] 8 Perspicuum. | 8 Obscurum.
units.tr: Chap. III. He pursues the subject he had begun to treat at the start of the previous chapter, namely the effectiveness of his ministry. Hence he defends his apostleship: (1) from the conversion, or effective calling, of the Corinthians, who are themselves like a letter of commendation or of praise (v. 1, 2, 3); (2) from the efficient causes of his ministry (v. 4, 5); (3) from the distinction between the ministry of the Gospel and that of the Law, where he considers the ministry of the Law in the person of Moses, through whom the Law was given, and sets against it Christ, the author of the Gospel. The parts of this antithesis are these eight: The Gospel ministry is | on the other hand, the legal ministry is (1) of the New Testament | (1) of the Old Testament (2) of the Spirit | (2) of the letter (3) of life | (3) of death (4) written on hearts | (4) written on stones (5) lasting for ever | (5) to be abolished (6) of righteousness | (6) of condemnation (7) excellently glorious | (7) in comparison with it, without glory (8) clear | (8) obscure

units.la: Cap. IV. Pergit in defensione sui Apostolatus, & primùm gloriatur de sua sedulitate & syn-ceritate in prædicando Euangelio,v.1.2. Secundò, occurrit obiectioni contra doctrinæ suæ claritatem motæ: & causam exponit, qui fiat quòd nonnulli lumen Euangelij non possint cernere, v.3. & 4. Tertiò, occurrit suspicioni arrogan-tiæ,ne putetur sibi & collegis suis arrogare vim illam per Euangelium corda illustrandi. Prosi-tetur igitur, se tantùm esse seruos: vim autem illam omnem, qua corda auditorum illustran-tur, à solo Deo manare, v. 5. & 6. Quartò occurrit offendiculo crucis: exponens causas, cu[?] Dominus excellentissimos seruos suos ita velit affligi: ut scilicet omnibus constet, eos non humanâ, si diuinâ virtute consistere: & efficaciam Euangelij non ab ipsis pendere, sed à Deo, à v.7. usque ad 13. Postremò exponit argumenta consolationis, quibus seipsè sub cruce in constantiâ officij sustentet: à v. 13. usque ad finem.
units.tr: Chap. IV. He continues the defence of his apostleship. First he boasts of his earnestness and sincerity in preaching the Gospel (v. 1, 2). Secondly, he meets an objection raised against the clarity of his teaching, and explains why it is that some cannot see the light of the Gospel (v. 3, 4). Thirdly, he meets the suspicion of arrogance, lest he and his colleagues be thought to claim for themselves the power of enlightening hearts through the Gospel. He therefore confesses that they are only servants, and that all that power by which the hearts of the hearers are enlightened flows from God alone (v. 5, 6). Fourthly, he meets the stumbling-block of the cross, setting out the reasons why the Lord wills his most excellent servants to be so afflicted: namely, so that it may be plain to all that they stand not by human but by divine strength, and that the efficacy of the Gospel depends not on them but on God (v. 7 to 13). Last, he sets out the arguments of consolation by which he himself is sustained under the cross, keeping steady in his office (v. 13 to the end).

units.la: Cap: v. pergit Apostolus confirmare Chri-stianos aduersus omnis generis afflictiones; primùm exponens suam cœterorumque sanctorum spem ac desiderium gloriæ cœlestis, usque ad v. 9. Deinde ad defensionem Apostolatus sui reuersus, commemorat suum studium ac synceritatem in fungendo munere Apostoli; à v.9. usque ad 18. Postremò, commendat ministerium Euangelicum, eâque occasione summam Euangelij de officio Christi & ratione nostræ salutis exponit.
units.tr: Chap. V. The Apostle goes on to strengthen Christians against every kind of affliction. First he sets out his own hope and that of the other saints, and their longing for heavenly glory, down to v. 9. Then, returning to the defence of his apostleship, he recalls his diligence and sincerity in discharging the apostolic office (v. 9 to 18). Last, he commends the Gospel ministry, and on that occasion sets out the sum of the Gospel concerning the office of Christ and the manner of our salvation.

units.la: SECUNDA EPISTOLÆ SEU Principalis tractationis pars.
units.tr: THE SECOND EPISTLE, OR THE MAIN PART OF THE TREATISE.

units.la: CORINTHIOS ipsos propiùs concernens: Nam superioribus capitibus Paulus, suam & collegarum suorum personas à calumniis vindicauit, & Ministerium Euangelicum magnis & veris laudibus ornauit: utrumque enim (propter Pseudapostolos) necessarium erat apud Corinthios. Nunc verò eos exhortatur grauissimè, ut oblatam in Euangelio gratiam Dei apprehendant, & gratitudinem suam piâ obedientiâ Deo declarent, non modò piè viuendo, verùm etiam aduersa (propter Christum) patienter ferendo, &c: Quæ Pauli exhortationes ad omnes quidem Christianos, præcipuè autem ad Eccle-siæ ministros spectant.
units.tr: Concerning the Corinthians themselves more closely. In the earlier chapters Paul vindicated from calumnies both his own person and those of his colleagues, and adorned the ministry of the Gospel with great and true praises. Both were necessary among the Corinthians because of the false apostles. Now, however, he most earnestly exhorts them to lay hold of the grace of God offered in the Gospel and to declare their gratitude to God by pious obedience: not only by living piously but also by patiently bearing adversities for Christ's sake, etc. These exhortations of Paul apply to all Christians, but especially to the ministers of the Church.

units.la: HVIVS SECVNDÆ PAR-tis Synopsis:
units.tr: Synopsis OF THIS SECOND PART:

units.la: Corinthios prima[?] Hortatur: Hortatio concernit partim Propriam cuiusque conscientiam, ut quisque exhibitam sibi Dei gratiam magni æstimet, & à peccatis, præsertim idololatrarum commercio caveat: cap. 6. Proximum: nimirum Fideles verbi ministros, qui debita gratitudine recipiendi, vbi simul de fructibus conuersionis disserit. c.7. Pauperes: vbi de Electemosynæ Collectione: cap.8. Collectoribus. cap.9. Reprehendit: expostulans quod Pseudapostolos tam facile reciperent, tantique facerent, se verè contenderent; Purgat igitur se itemrum, excusans suam Abiectionem & humilitatem, cap.10. Gloriationem de rebus Ordinariis, cap:II. Extraordinariis, nimirum revelationibus. cap.12. Variis sese peccatis polluerent: cap.13. usque ad v.11. vbi est Conclusio.
units.tr: He first exhorts the Corinthians. The exhortation concerns partly each person's own conscience, that each should value the grace of God shown to him and beware of sins, especially of association with idolaters: chap. 6. Next, it concerns the faithful ministers of the Word, who should be received with due gratitude, and where he speaks at the same time about the fruits of conversion: chap. 7. Then the poor, where he speaks of the collection of alms: chap. 8, to the collectors. Chap. 9 rebukes them, complaining that they so readily received the false apostles and thought so highly of them, and he strives to clear himself again, excusing his lowliness and humility. Chap. 10 concerns boasting about ordinary matters; chap. 11, extraordinary matters, namely revelations; chap. 12, that they should not defile themselves with various sins; chap. 13 to v. 11, where the conclusion is.

units.la: Capitis v 1. partes principales duæ sunt: In priore pergit declarare rationem sui ministerij, &c. ea occasione suas virtutes & miserias commemorat, usque ad v. 11. In posteriore Corinthios dehortatur a societate infidelium in cultu idolorum.
units.tr: The two main parts of chapter 5, verse 1 are these. In the first he goes on to declare the reason for his ministry, etc. On that occasion he recalls his virtues and miseries, down to v. 11. In the second he dissuades the Corinthians from fellowship with unbelievers in the worship of idols.

units.la: Cap. VII. primus versus coheret cum capite praecedente. Repetit enim in eo conclusionem superioris cohortationis deductam ex postremo argumento. In reliquo capite ad suam personam redit, exponens tum fidelitatis suae, tum perpetuae in eos benevolentiae argumenta. Quae omnia eo pertinent, ut superior exhortatio, itemque quae post sequuntur, locum apud eos inveniant.
units.tr: Chap. VII. The first verse coheres with the preceding chapter. For in it he repeats the conclusion of the earlier exhortation, drawn from the last argument. In the rest of the chapter he returns to his own person, setting out the proofs both of his faithfulness and of his constant goodwill towards them. All of these serve the purpose that the earlier exhortation, and also what follows, may find a place among them.

units.la: Cap. VIII, primum hortatur Corinthios ad collectam quam superiore anno inchoarant, absolvendam, usque ad v. 16. Deinde commendat eis Titum, & alios duos fratres, quos ad collectam illam ab ipsis accipiendam mittebat.
units.tr: Chap. VIII: first he exhorts the Corinthians to complete the collection which they had begun the previous year, down to v. 16. Then he commends to them Titus and two other brothers, whom he was sending to receive that collection from them.

units.la: Cap. IX. Pergit in eadem quaestione, nempe de collecta: ac primum causam exponit, cur tres illos fratres collectae absolvendae gratia ad eos misit: usque ad v. 6. Deinde elemosynas sementi comparans, eos hortatur, ut liberaliter conferant.
units.tr: Chap. IX. He continues on the same question, namely the collection. First he sets out the reason why he sent those three brothers to them to complete the collection, down to v. 6. Then, comparing alms to seed-sowing, he exhorts them to contribute generously.

units.la: Cap. 10. 11. & 12. se iterum purgat a certis calumniis, graviter monens Corinthios, ne a Pseudoapostolis & falsis Doctoribus seduci se patiantur: docetque quanto posset iure superior esse suis adversariis, quia nulla ratione donorum, laborum revelatio numquam suarum magnitudinem attingere possunt.
units.tr: Chaps. 10, 11 and 12. He again clears himself of certain calumnies, earnestly warning the Corinthians not to allow themselves to be led astray by false apostles and false teachers. He also teaches how far he may rightly be superior to his adversaries, since in no way can their gifts, labours and revelations ever reach his greatness.

units.la: Cap. X. Refellit Paulus calumniam quandam Pseudoapostolorum, eorumque vanam gloriationem oblique reprehendit. Calumniam illam arripuerant ex obiurgationibus superioris epistolae, dicentes: Paulum absentem in epistolis affectare aliquam gravitatem, qui tamen coràm[?] sit humilis & abiectus. Apostolus primùm negat, se ambulare secundum carnem, hoc est, se in ministerio suo affectare eloquentiam & eiusmodi res externas: & quanquam soleat se gerere humiliter, praeditum tamen esse potestate & efficacia spirituali, quà & docilcs[?] ad obediendum Christo adducat, & refractariorum contumaciam vindicet. Haec agit usque ad v. 12. Deinde ministerij sui efficaciam ita asserit, ut obliquè perstingat Pseudoapostolorum vanam gloriationem & iactantiam.
units.tr: Chap. X. Paul refutes a certain calumny of the false apostles and obliquely rebukes their vain boasting. They had seized on that calumny from the reproofs of the earlier epistle, saying that Paul, absent, affects a certain severity in his letters, yet when present is humble and lowly. The Apostle first denies that he walks according to the flesh, that is, that in his ministry he affects eloquence and such external things; and although he is accustomed to conduct himself humbly, he nevertheless is endowed with power and spiritual efficacy, by which he brings the teachable to obey Christ and avenges the obstinacy of the refractory. He does this down to v. 12. Then he asserts the efficacy of his ministry in such a way that he obliquely strikes at the vain boasting and bragging of the false apostles.

units.la: Cap. x i. pergit in eadem quaestione: 1. reprehendens Corinthiorum prauum iudicium in honorandis Pseudoapostolis, ambitiosè gloriantibus, & contemnendo ipso, sese modestè demittente: usque ad v. 13. 11 describit Pseudoapostolorum hypocrisin & auaritiam: usque ad v. 22. 111 Comparans se cum Pseudoapostolis, seque illis gloriando partim aequiparans, partim anteponens, multas & varias suas calamitates & pericula & molestias atque curas commemorat.
units.tr: Chap. XI. He continues on the same question: 1. rebuking the Corinthians' perverse judgement in honouring the false apostles, who boast ambitiously, and in despising himself, who humbles himself modestly, down to v. 13. 2. He describes the hypocrisy and greed of the false apostles, down to v. 22. 3. Comparing himself with the false apostles, and boasting partly that he is their equal and partly that he is above them, he recalls his many and various calamities, dangers, troubles and anxieties.

units.la: Cap. xii. In proposito persistens, primùm exponit eximiam quandam visionem, quondam à Domino sibi oblatam: usque ad v. 7. Deinde commemorat singularem quandam tentationem qua subinde à Satana vexetur: usque ad v. 11. Tertiò gloriationem antegressam excusat, eaque occasione Corinthiis ingratitudinem exprobrat, ac rursum de sua erga eos liberalitate & amore ardentissimo gloriatur: usque ad v. 16. Quartò refellit calumniam auaritiæ occultæ & astutæ: usque ad v. 20. Postremò obiurgat eos propter quandam peccata: minaturque eis præsentia suæ seueritatem, nisi ante aduentum eius resipuerint.
units.tr: Chap. XII. Persisting in his purpose, he first sets out a remarkable vision once granted to him by the Lord, down to v. 7. Then he recalls a singular temptation by which he was from time to time troubled by Satan, down to v. 11. Thirdly, he excuses the boasting that had gone before, and on that occasion reproaches the Corinthians for ingratitude, and again boasts of his most ardent liberality and love towards them, down to v. 16. Fourthly, he refutes the calumny of a hidden and cunning greed, down to v. 20. Lastly, he rebukes them for certain sins, and threatens them with the severity of his presence unless they repent before his coming.

units.la: Cap. xiii. Primùm repetit comminationem suæ seueritatis, eiusque rationem exponit, contrariamque obiectionem refutat, usque ad v. 7. Deinde comminationem istam mitigat optatione & propositi conatusque sui expositione, usq; ad v. 11. Postremò
units.tr: Chap. XIII. First he repeats the threat of his severity, and sets out its reason, and refutes the opposing objection, down to v. 7. Then he softens that threat with a wish, and with a statement of his purpose and effort, down to v. 11. Lastly

units.la: CONCLUDIT EPISTOLAM
units.tr: HE CONCLUDES THE EPISTLE

units.la: Partim cohortatione ad virtutes Christianas, partim salutatione.
units.tr: Partly with an exhortation to Christian virtues, partly with a greeting.

units.la: ARGUMENTA CAPITUM ἀμμέλρα[?] CAP. I
units.tr: ARGUMENTS OF THE CHAPTERS, CHAP. I

units.la: NOn moueat tristi seruens afflictio turba, Protegit hanc proprio nempe fauore Deus. Quod nondum veni, non fraudis nostra nosetis Verba, mea iusta est nam mihi causa mora.
units.tr: Let not the troubled crowd be moved by sorrowful affliction; God indeed protects it with his own favour. That I have not yet come, do not blame on any fault of ours; my delay has a just cause.

units.la: Non me crudeli dicatis mente tyrannum, Consilij ratio nam mihi certa mei est. Impostor non sum: diuina dogmata legis, Et vos & reliquos me decuisse scio.
units.tr: Do not call me a tyrant of cruel mind, for my plan of counsel is sure to me. I am no impostor: I know that I have taught you and the rest the divine doctrines of the law.

units.la: Vestra fidem ostendit crescens Ecclesia nostram, Quam docui mitis mitia verba Dei. Cur miscere iuuat fidei legalia sancta? Cum Christus legis Spiritus ipse sit?
units.tr: Your faith is shown by our growing Church, which I taught with the gentle words of God. Why is it pleasing to mix the legal observances with holy faith, since Christ himself is the Spirit of the law?

units.la: Pura fidem docui sanctam per dogmata, si quis Hanc negat, a proprij[?] tunc sibi causa mali est. Nec mea crux moueat, quae tanto fanore CHRISTUM Per mare, per terram & summa pericla ducat.
units.tr: I taught holy faith purely through its doctrines; if anyone denies this, the cause of evil is his own. Let not my cross move you, which with such great love leads Christ through sea, land and the greatest dangers.

units.la: Qua spe tanta ferat patienti in carne pericla, Edocet, officium tradit & inde suum. Non tamen affectio vana praeconia laudis, Sed pura Christi pradico[?] mente fidem.
units.tr: With what great hope he bears dangers in the suffering flesh, he teaches, and from this he hands on his own duty. Yet it is not vain affection for the praises of glory, but the pure faith of Christ that I preach with a pure mind.

units.la: Cura fit innocuæ nunquam non maxima vitæ, Et cura impositam fit tolerare crucem. Impia vitentur turpis consortia turbæ: Nè templum sancti polluat illa Dei.
units.tr: Care for an innocent life is never anything but the greatest, and it is care to bear the cross laid upon us. Let the impious and shameful company of the crowd be avoided, lest it pollute the temple of holy God.

units.la: Non ego vos unquam terrente tyrannide pre[?]si, Quin potius vestræ cura salutis erat. Hinc etiam erga illos quanto teneatur amore, Exemplo & varia cum ratione probat.
units.tr: I never oppressed you with terrifying tyranny; rather, care for your salvation was my concern. Hence, with what great love he is held toward them, he proves by example and by various reasoning.

units.la: Munera non pigeat contemtis tradere egenis. Quin Macedum mores vos iuvet usque sequi. Quod bene cœpistis, nunc tandem absolvite, Tito Fratrib. & reliquis cura placere fiet.
units.tr: Let it not grieve you to hand gifts to needy poor people. Indeed, let the manners of the Macedonians please you enough to follow them still. What you have begun well, now at last finish; care to please Titus and the brothers and the rest will be done.

units.la: Ipse licet vestræ cognoscam mentis amorem, Attamen & Titum mittere cura fuit. Gloria quo maior per munera vestra veniret, Et vester fructus maximus inde foret.
units.tr: Although I know the love of your mind, yet it was also a concern to send Titus. So that greater glory might come through your gifts, and your fruit thence might be greatest.

units.la: Officij proprij dignissima iura tuetur, Virtutis narrans munera sancta suæ. Hac licet ipse usus sim vitæ per omnia semper, Non mihi sed soli gloria danda Deo est.
units.tr: He defends the most worthy rights of his own office, relating the holy gifts of his own virtue. Although he himself has always used this in all things throughout his life, glory is to be given not to him but to God alone.

units.la: Ambitione pia laudat sua munera Paulus, Huc etenim invitum turba coegit iners. Non ego ventoso nimium nunc gloriar ore, In cruce nam sola gloria nostra sita est.
units.tr: Paul praises his gifts with holy ambition, for an idle crowd has compelled him, though unwilling, to this. I do not now boast too much with a windy mouth, for in the cross alone our glory lies.

units.la: Quæ Deus exhibuit Paulo sacra visa recenses. Vsus & hac cur sit postmodo laude docet. Inde suum erga illos sanctum testatur[?] amorem, Se quoque promittit velle venire breui.
units.tr: You recount the holy things that God showed to Paul. He also teaches why he afterwards uses this praise. Thence he testifies his holy love toward them, and promises that he himself wishes to come soon.

units.la: Adveniam certè, ne falso mentiar ore, Nec fidei ostendam robora parua mea. Vos tamen ah potius pura respicite mente: Defendat fortis gratia læta Dei!
units.tr: I will certainly come, lest I lie with a false mouth, nor will I display the small strengths of my faith. Yet, ah, rather look upon me with a pure mind: may the glad, strong grace of God defend you!

units.la: ALITER.
units.tr: ANOTHER VERSION.

units.la: CAP. I
units.tr: CHAPTER I

units.la: Afflicti varie recreamur, mors prope vicit. Nam istis[?] me non est non, etiamque mihi. Bis nolo veniens lugere, sit hoc satis illi, Quæro Titum: Christus nos bene olere facit.
units.tr: Afflicted in various ways, we are refreshed; death has almost conquered. For I was not, and it is not, for these things, even for me. Twice, coming, I did not wish to grieve; let this be enough for him. I seek Titus; Christ makes us smell sweet.

units.la: Commendamus nos? Deus est qui nos facit aptos. Mosis quàm Christi est gloria iure minor.
units.tr: Do we commend ourselves? God is the one who makes us fit. The glory of Moses is rightly less than that of Christ.

units.la: Dicta obscura quibus.gazam vas fictile portat. Exercent vires vitaque morsque suas.
units.tr: Obscure sayings by which we carry the treasure in an earthen vessel. Life and death exercise their own powers.

units.la: Est domus ecce duplex.quod ficit quisque reportat. Mors est pro cunctis.sunt quoque cuncta noua.
units.tr: Behold, there is a double house; each one brings back what he has done. Death is for all; all things are also made new.

units.la: Fortiter enumeras tolerauda [?].Deus male quadras Cum Belial.Christus nos sua templa facit.
units.tr: You bear bravely... God does not agree ill with Belial. Christ makes us his temple.

units.la: Gaudeo quod rectè vos fecit epistola tristes. Exhibitusque Tito me recreauit bonos.
units.tr: I rejoice that the letter made you rightly sorrowful. And Titus, when he came, refreshed me, good men.

units.la: Insignis Macedo,pauperque noscitur Iesus. Perfectè.ecce Titus frater adestque meus.
units.tr: Macedonia is notable, and Jesus is known as poor. Perfectly; behold, Titus my brother is here.

units.la: Laetor vos adeò propensos esse datores. Multiplicetque precor semina vestra Deus.
units.tr: I rejoice that you are so inclined to be givers. I pray that God multiply your seed.

units.la: Milito non carni.at Domino vindicta parata est. Nec superat fines gloria nostra suos.
units.tr: I do not fight according to the flesh; vengeance is ready for the Lord. Nor does our glory exceed its own bounds.

units.la: Non cedo summis. Zelo vos.non sum onerosus. Gloriòr insipiens,& mea facta cano.
units.tr: I do not yield to the highest. I am zealous for you; I am not burdensome. I boast, being foolish, and I sing of my deeds.

units.la: Ob conspecta datur stimulus.tot dicere cogor. Non gravo vos.quales inueniam timeo.
units.tr: Because of what is seen, a goad is given; I am compelled to say so much. I do not burden you; I fear what sort I shall find.

units.la: Praedictum repeto.non parcam vestra probate. Nam mihi pro vobis qualiacunque placent.
units.tr: I repeat what I said before: I will not spare you; test yourselves. For whatever pleases me on your behalf is pleasing.

units.la: NOTÆ MEMORIALES
units.tr: MNEMONIC NOTES

units.la: Declaratio.
units.tr: Explanation.

units.la: Gloria Pauli sunt Corinthij : v.14.suavis Odor Christi sumus: v.15, Tabulis in carneis cordis:v.3.non Fraudibus incedentes : v.2. Arrha quam nobis dedit Deus est Spiritus:v.5.
units.tr: Glory of Paul are the Corinthians: v. 14. Sweet Odour: we are Christ's: v. 15. Tables: in the fleshy tables of the heart: v. 3. Not Frauds, walking: v. 2. The Pledge which God has given us is the Spirit: v. 5.

units.la: Carcer in quo Paulus captiuus: v.5. Gaudio vehementer exundo: v. 4. Prompta mens seu voluntas accepta est: v. 12. Metet parcè qui parcè seuit: v. 6. Vindicta parata est inobedientiæ:v.6. Per Corbem demissus Paulus: v. 33. Colaphis cædi-tur Paulus ab angelo Satanæ: v.7. Robora magna feram veniens ad vos:v. 4.
units.tr: Prison, in which Paul was a captive: v. 5. I rejoice, exulting greatly: v. 4. Ready: the mind or will has been received: v. 12. He reaps, who sowed sparingly, sparingly: v. 6. Vengeance is ready for disobedience: v. 6. Through the basket Paul was let down: v. 33. Blows: Paul is struck by the angel of Satan: v. 7. I shall bear great strength, coming to you: v. 4.

units.la: ANALYSIS EPISTOLAE S. PAULI AD GALATAS
units.tr: Analysis of the Epistle of St. Paul to the Galatians

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: FUIT GALATIA regio Minoris Asiæ, sita inter Bithyniam & Cappadociam; dicta etiam Gallo-græcia. Huic imperavit quondam Deiotarus, quem Cicero defendit accusatum, quod Iulio Cæsari insidias struxisset. Incolæ huius regionis primi fuerunt Germani, qui, relicta Brabantia & ducatu Cleuensi in hanc Græciæ plagam se contulerunt, Gallorum nomen quod Germanum fuit, retinentes. Fuisse autem Germanos Gallorum nomine appellatos testis est Diodorus Siculus lib. 6. qui magnos fluvios per Galatiam, i.l[?] est, Galliam labentes, enumerans, nominatim Danubium & Rhenum vocat. Herodotus propterea Danubium in Celtis oriri scribit, quem tamen ex supremis Herciniæ silvæ montibus deriuari constat. Fuerunt autem eiusdem populi nomina Galatæ, & per syncopen, Celtæ & Galli. Sed de hisce vocibus lege Ph:l:[?] Mel. lib. 2. rerum Germanicarum, Casparum Peucerum in principio libri quarti, Tacitum de Germania.
units.tr: GALATIA was a region of Asia Minor, lying between Bithynia and Cappadocia, also called Gallograecia. Deiotarus once ruled it; Cicero defended him when he was accused of plotting against Julius Caesar. The first inhabitants of this region were Germans, who left Brabant and the duchy of Cleves and moved into this part of Greece, keeping the name of Gauls, which was originally a German name. That the Germans were called by the name of Gauls is attested by Diodorus Siculus, book 6, who, listing the great rivers that flow through Galatia, that is, Gaul, names the Danube and the Rhine. For this reason Herodotus writes that the Danube rises among the Celts, though it is well established that it descends from the highest mountains of the Hercynian forest. The same people were called Galatae, and by contraction Celtae and Galli. On these names, see Philip Melanchthon, book 2 of the Rerum Germanicarum; Caspar Peucer at the beginning of book 4; and Tacitus on Germany.

units.la: Occasio & argumentum. Docuerat Apostololus viua voce Galatas, vt videre est ex Actis Apoft: cap. 18. v. 23. post Pauli discessum irre-pferunt in Galaticam Ecclesiam falsi doctores, aliam à Doctrina Pauli docendi rationem fe-cuti;contendentes legem moralem & ceremo-nialem ad salutem esse necessariam. Quoniam vero Pauli autoritas illis obstabat, opprimere & extenuare eam nitebantur.Cùm igitur Apo-ftolus Galatas, quos prædicatione Euangelij ad fidem Christi adduxerat, seductos videret: ne officio suo deesset, eas hac Epistolâ in viam veritatis reducere conatur: ac proinde post asser-tam autoritatem suam Apostolicam, doctri-nam de iustitia fidei multis argumentis confir-mat, eâdemque operâ iustitiam operum refu-tat: deinde ad pietatis seu bonorum operum studium exhortatur. Idem igitur in hac epistolâ argumentum,quod in ea ad Romanos, si propositio-nem principalem de iustificatione per fidem in Chri-stum speciales,tractatur.
units.tr: Occasion and argument. The Apostle had taught the Galatians by word of mouth, as may be seen from Acts 18:23. After Paul's departure, false teachers crept into the Galatian Church, following a method of teaching different from Paul's doctrine and contending that the moral and ceremonial law is necessary for salvation. Since Paul's authority stood in their way, they strove to suppress and diminish it. Therefore, when the Apostle saw that the Galatians, whom he had brought to faith in Christ by the preaching of the Gospel, had been led astray, lest he fail in his duty, he attempts by this epistle to lead them back to the way of truth. Accordingly, after asserting his apostolic authority, he confirms with many arguments the doctrine of the righteousness of faith, and at the same time refutes the righteousness of works; then he exhorts them to the pursuit of piety and good works. Thus the argument of this epistle is the same as that of the epistle to the Romans, namely, the principal proposition concerning justification through faith in Christ, which is treated specifically.

units.la: PARTITIO.
units.tr: Division.

units.la: Post Inscriptionem seu proœmium; in qua est, 1 subscriptio ( v. 1 & 2. ) 2 inscriptio specialiter dicta ( v. 2. ) 3. salutatio, ( v. 3. ) cui annectitur summa Euangelii, ( v. 4. ) & δοξολογία,id est celebratio nominis Dei, ( v. 5. ) & Conclusionem, à v. 11. capitis sexti usque ad finem; PARTES huius epistolæ principales duæ sunt.
units.tr: After the inscription, or proem, which contains (1) the subscription (vv. 1 and 2), (2) the so-called inscription in particular (v. 2), (3) the salutation (v. 3), to which is joined the sum of the Gospel (v. 4), and the doxology, that is, the celebration of the name of God (v. 5), and the conclusion from verse 11 of chapter six to the end; the principal parts of this epistle are two.

units.la: In prima agit Apostolus de se, seu de sua persona & officio Apostolico, à v. 6. capitis primi, usque ad v. 15. capitis secundi.
units.tr: In the first, the Apostle speaks about himself, that is, about his person and apostolic office, from verse 6 of chapter one to verse 15 of chapter two.

units.la: In secunda agit de Re ipsa: hoc est, doctrinam fidei & vitæ explicat: à v. 15.cap.2.usque ad v.11. capitis sexti.
units.tr: In the second, he speaks about the matter itself: that is, he explains the doctrine of faith and of life, from verse 15 of chapter two to verse 11 of chapter six.

units.la: Prima Pars.
units.tr: First Part.

units.la: Primâ parte acriter reprehenduntur Galatæ, quòd à Doctrina Euangelij per Paulum tradita defecissent, nullam iustam causam defectionis habentes. Huius igitur partis, quæ personalis dici potest, propositio est: Galatas non debuisse deficere ab eo genere doctrinæ, quod à Paulo acceperant. Ad huius probationem subnectitur Narratio, in qua agit de rebus suis, hoc est, de sua vocatione, doctrina, peregrinationibus, congressu cum reliquis Apostolis, conuersatione cum Petro, ciusque lapsu, & reprehensione sua, qua simulantem & dissimulantē castigauit.
units.tr: In this first part the Galatians are sharply rebuked for having abandoned the doctrine of the gospel delivered by Paul, though they had no just cause for their defection. The proposition of this part, which may be called personal, is therefore: the Galatians ought not to have departed from that kind of doctrine which they had received from Paul. To prove this, a narration is added, in which he speaks of his own affairs: of his calling, his teaching, his journeys, his meeting with the other apostles, his dealings with Peter, Peter's fall, and his own rebuke, by which he censured Peter both for dissimulating and for pretending.

units.la: Capitis igitur primi, post Epigraphen, partes sunt tres: Primò enim Apostolatus sui apologiam orditur à reprehensione inconstantiæ & vanitatis Galatarum, & execratione Pseudoapostolorum, qui defectionis illius & inconstantiæ erant autores, à v. 6. usque ad 13.
units.tr: The parts of the first chapter, after the epigraph, are three. First, he opens his defence of his apostleship with a rebuke of the inconstancy and folly of the Galatians and a curse upon the false apostles who were the authors of that defection and inconstancy, verses 6 to 13.

units.la: Deinde ad Apostolatum suum asserendum & vindicandum à calumniis aduersariorum, qui ipsum in dubium vocarunt; & vt clarè constet, se hominum ministerio non vocatum, nec ab homine edoctum esse, sed per reuelationem Iesu Christi, historiam contexit vitæ suæ ante-actæ, primùm in Iudaismo, vsque ad v. 15. huius capitis: posteà in Christianismo: à v. 15. vsque ad capitis finem. Secunda igitur pars capitis habet hi-storiam vitæ Paulinæ in Iudaismo: Tertia vita in Christianismo exacta[?] partem.
units.tr: Next, to assert and vindicate his apostleship against the slanders of opponents who called it into question, and to make it clear that he was not called through human ministry nor taught by man but through a revelation of Jesus Christ, he sets out the history of his earlier life: first in Judaism, to verse 15 of this chapter; afterwards in Christianity, from verse 15 to the end of the chapter. The second part of the chapter therefore contains the history of Paul's life in Judaism; the third, his life in Christianity.

units.la: Cap. 11. partes duæ sunt : 1 perfistit in histo-ria illa vitæ suæ in Christianismo transactæ, ad v. vsque 15. Hic autem primum narrat,quomodo Euangelium suum approbarit reliquis Apostolis, v. 1. & 2. deinde quomodo iis consentientibus non sit coactus circumcidi Titus, quum id vrgerent falsi fratres:v. 3. 4. 5. Tertiò, quomodo præcipui inter Apostolos, apostolatu ipsius approbato, dextras so-cietatis sibi & Barnabæ dederint, & cura pauperũ suorum ipsis mandauerint,vt nimirum pro illis eleemosynam colligerent apud Gentes:v. 6. 7. 8. 9. & 10. Quartò narrat actionem cum Petro,& quibus verbis eum palàm reprehenderit Antiochiæ, cùm is in gratiam Iudæorum quorundam Hierosolymitano-rum Iudaizans, gentes quæ crediderant offendisset, vsque ad v. 15. 11 parte, in illa Pauli cum Petro sermocinatione ( quam probabile est extendi ad finem vsque capitis : quia initio capitis sequentis προσφώνησιν ad Galatas renouat, atque ita nouam orationem orditur ) continetur prima demonstratio quæstionis controuersæ & principalis,de Iustificatio-ne per solam fidem, & refutatio obiectionis contra-riæ. Argumentum primùm, ( v. 15. 16.) quo iu-stificationem fidei confirmat eiusmodi est:
units.tr: Chapter 2 has two parts. (1) He continues the history of his life in Christianity, to verse 15. Here he first tells how he submitted his gospel for approval to the other apostles, vv. 1–2; then how, with their agreement, Titus was not compelled to be circumcised, although the false brothers pressed for it, vv. 3–5. Thirdly, how the leading men among the apostles, once his apostleship had been approved, gave him and Barnabas their right hands of fellowship and entrusted to them the care of their poor, that is, that they should collect alms for them among the Gentiles, vv. 6–10. Fourthly, he relates his dispute with Peter, and with what words he openly rebuked him at Antioch, when Peter, Judaizing out of deference to certain men from Jerusalem, had given offence to the Gentiles who had believed. (2) In that discourse of Paul with Peter (which probably extends to the end of the chapter, since at the beginning of the next chapter he renews his address to the Galatians and so begins a new speech) is contained the first demonstration of the disputed and principal question, concerning justification by faith alone, and the refutation of the opposing objection. The first argument (vv. 15–16), by which he confirms justification by faith, runs as follows:

units.la: In quo Apostoli & reliqui Iudæi Christianam religionem amplexi,iustitiam quæsiuerunt & inuenerunt,in eo etiam Gentes iustificantur: Atqui Apostoli & reliqui Iudæi Christianam religionem amplexi, iustitiam quæsiuerunt & inuenerunt non in operibus legis; sed in Christo fide apprehenso: (probatur hoc testimonio Dauidis,ex Psal.143.v.2.) Ergo etiam gentes iustificantur non ex operibus legis, sed in Christo fide apprehenso.
units.tr: In whom the apostles and the other Jews who embraced the Christian religion sought and found righteousness, in him the Gentiles too are justified. But the apostles and the other Jews who embraced the Christian religion sought and found righteousness not in the works of the law but in Christ, apprehended by faith (this is proved by the testimony of David, Ps. 143:2). Therefore the Gentiles too are justified not by the works of the law but in Christ, apprehended by faith.

units.la: Verf. 17. continetur obiectio Pseudoapostolo-rum, contra assumtionem argumenti superio-ris: cuius sententia est: doctrinam iustificationis per fidem, constituere Christum peccati ministrum: Resp: Paulus negate, & reiicit illationē, quippe plenam blasphemiæ & impietatis! & negationis rationem reddit data instantia adducto suo ipsius exemplo, tam quoad doctrinam, v. 18. quam quoad vitam: v. 19. & 20. Versu 21. est aliud argumentum pro iustificatione fidei in Christum.
units.tr: Verse 17 contains the objection of the false apostles against the assumption of the preceding argument. Its sense is: the doctrine of justification by faith makes Christ a minister of sin. Answer: Paul denies this and rejects the inference as full of blasphemy and impiety, and he gives the reason for his denial by setting forth his own example, as a clear instance, both as to doctrine, v. 18, and as to life, vv. 19–20. Verse 21 contains another argument for justification by faith in Christ.

units.la: Hactenus narravit de suo apostolatu: cuius narratio-nis postrema pars fuit sermocinatio ipsius cum Petro, cuius occasione transiit ad doctrinam de modo quo iustificatur homo coram Deo: nunc ad Galatas redit, ac primum commendat Galatis Euangelij doctrinā, pergit demonstrare, hominem iustificari fide, absque operibus legis, contraviasque obiectiones diluit, ac tandem legem ceremonialem abrogatam esse ostendit: cap. 3 & 4.
units.tr: Hitherto he has told of his apostleship, and the last part of that narration was his discourse with Peter, on whose occasion he passed to the doctrine of how a man is justified before God. Now he returns to the Galatians and first commends to them the doctrine of the gospel. He goes on to show that a man is justified by faith, without the works of the law, and dissolves the objections against this; and finally he shows that the ceremonial law has been abrogated: chapters 3 and 4.

units.la: Cap. 111 partes sunt variæ: primum ex indi-gnatione reprehendit defectionem Galatarum, us-que ad v. 6. Deinde partim confirmat iustificatio-nem per fidem, partim refutat iustificationem per le-gis opera, ad versum usq; 15. Tertiò propositionem quandam affinem illi superiori quam refutauit, pertractat, nempe: Legem non abrogare promissionem, ad v. usque 23. Quartò, ulterius progressus, abrogationem Legis ex parte aliqua ostendit, simul etiam propositionis huius, nos omnes filios Dei esse, vniuer-salitatem obiter quasi confirmans. [ Vide Rob.Rol. loc: &c. ]
units.tr: Chapter 3 has several parts. First, he rebukes the defection of the Galatians with indignation, to verse 6. Then he partly confirms justification by faith and partly refutes justification by the works of the law, to verse 15. Thirdly, he treats a proposition akin to the one he has just refuted, namely that the law does not annul the promise, to verse 23. Fourthly, going further, he shows the abrogation of the law in some respect, while in passing confirming, as it were, the proposition that we are all sons of God, and its universality. [See Rob. Rol. loc. etc.]

units.la: Capitis 1 v.: propositio hæc est: Quemadmo-dum parvulus heres exacto tempore constituto, fit sui iuris & liberatur a custodia curatorum: ita filius Dei exacto tempore constituto & impletis iis, quae impleri prius oportebat, populum Dei liberauit ab illa seruitute Legis, vt iam spontaneo spiritu praedi-tus Deum libere colat, & vt patrem innocet. Partes sunt tres praecipuè. 1 coheret cum praecedenti, & est quasi expositio eius, quod dixerat, Legem fuisse paedagogum nostrum. Per similitudinem infantis explicat, quomodo nunc a seruitute Legis liberati simus per Christum: ideo v. 9. grauiter increpat Galatas, quod ad puerilia elementa & in seruitutem relabi velint: usque ad v. 12. II est testificatio summae suae erga eos benevolentiae, qua asperitatem suarum obiurgationum lenit: usque ad v. 21. III pars est partim allegorica, partim didascalica de veris filiis Abrahae & heredibus vitae aeternae; partim consolatoria contra persecutiones & opprobria, quae filij Dei a falsa Ecclesia patiuntur.
units.tr: Chapter 4, verse 1: the proposition is this: just as a child who is heir, when the appointed time has passed, becomes his own master and is released from the custody of guardians, so the Son of God, when the appointed time had come and those things which had to be fulfilled first had been fulfilled, freed the people of God from that bondage of the law, so that now, endowed with a willing spirit, they may freely worship God and call him Father. There are chiefly three parts. (1) This coheres with what precedes and is in effect an exposition of what he had said, that the law was our tutor. By the likeness of an infant he explains how we have now been freed from the bondage of the law through Christ; therefore in verse 9 he sharply upbraids the Galatians because they wish to return to childish elements and into slavery, as far as verse 12. (2) It is an assurance of his great goodwill towards them, by which he softens the harshness of his rebukes, as far as verse 21. (3) The third part is partly allegorical and partly didactic, concerning the true sons of Abraham and the heirs of eternal life; partly consolatory, against the persecutions and reproaches which the sons of God suffer from the false Church.

units.la: Cap: v. partes duae sunt: Prior habet conclusionem superioris disputationis: eius propositio, ducta a superioribus, talis est: Cum parum sit adipisci aliquod bonum, nisi adeptum tueamur, & nos Christiani non simus filij ancillae, sed liberae, id est, membra eius Ecclesiae, quam Christus morte sua redemit & liberauit, dono Spiritu adoptionis; constanter retineamus illud summum beneficium, nec permitiosa leuitate patiamur nos rursum implicari iugo legalium observationum: usque ad v. 13.
units.tr: Chapter 5 has two parts. The first contains the conclusion of the preceding disputation. Its proposition, drawn from what went before, is this: since it is of little use to obtain some good unless we keep what we have obtained, and since we Christians are not sons of the handmaid but of the free woman, that is, members of that Church which Christ redeemed and set free by his death, with the gift of the Spirit of adoption, let us steadfastly hold fast to that supreme benefit, and not, by pernicious levity, allow ourselves to be entangled again in the yoke of legal observances, as far as verse 13.

units.la: SECUNDÆ PARTIS HUIUS
units.tr: SECUNDÆ PARTIS HUIUS

units.la: Epistolæ initium
units.tr: Epistolæ initium

units.la: Est v. 13. cap. v, ubi ad varia pietatis officia nos exhortatur. Transit autem ad hanc partem perquandam prolepsin: nam cum dixisset, ipsos vocatos esse ad libertatem: ne Galatæ hoc intelligerent de licentia vitæ, quasi Christianis liceret viuere vt liberet: hanc cogitationem anteuertit, & à licentia ista carnali dehortatur: contra, hortatur ad quoddam seruitutis genus, nempe vt alij aliis seruiant ex charitate, quam tanquam fontem & caput officiorum Christianorum proponit, vsque ad v. 16. inde de luctâ carnis & spiritus, vsque ad v. 19. à quo vsque ad finem capitis est Catalogus operum carnis siue naturæ non regenitæ, & fructuum spiritus, i. regeneratorum: inprimis autem enumerat ea vitia, quibus Galatas videbat deditos, vt ostendat, quàm procul abessent à dilectione proximi, atque ita ab observatione Legis.
units.tr: It begins at v. 13 of chapter 5, where he exhorts us to various duties of piety. He passes to this part by a certain prolepsis. For when he had said that they were called to liberty, lest the Galatians should take this to mean licence of life, as if Christians were free to live as they please, he anticipates that thought and dissuades them from that carnal licence. On the contrary, he urges a certain kind of servitude, namely that they serve one another out of love, which he sets forth as the fountain and head of Christian duties, up to v. 16. Then from v. 16 he speaks of the struggle of flesh and spirit, up to v. 19. From there to the end of the chapter is the catalogue of the works of the flesh, or of nature unregenerate, and of the fruits of the Spirit, that is, of the regenerate. He especially lists those vices to which he saw the Galatians given, to show how far they were from love of neighbour, and thus from observance of the Law.

units.la: V. 16: qui est vltimus capitis quinti, ad speciales exhortationes accedit, quas continuat cap. 6. vsque ad v. 11. vbi est Conclusio epistolæ.
units.tr: V. 16: which is the last verse of chapter five, passes to special exhortations, which he continues in chapter 6 up to v. 11, where the conclusion of the letter is.

units.la: Cap. VI. partes duæ sunt: primo enim per-sequitur Apostolus speciales admonitiones, & ea quæ θελικῶς[?] de fructibus spiritualibus dixerat, magis hypotheticè Galatis applicat, eosque hortatur ad quædam officia, quæ sunt effecta partim mansuetudinis & longanimitatis, partim charitatis, vsque ad v. 11. Secunda pars est
units.tr: Chapter VI has two parts. First, the Apostle pursues special admonitions, and applies to the Galatians more hypothetically [θετικῶς] what he had said positively about the fruits of the Spirit, and exhorts them to certain duties, which are effects partly of gentleness and longanimity, partly of charity, up to v. 11. The second part is

units.la: CONCLUSIO
units.tr: CONCLUSIO

units.la: Huius epistolæ, ad quam transit per locum attentionis, quo excitat Galatas ad considerandum laborem suum in scribendo ad ipsos: Deinde ad detegendum Pseudoapostolorum fucū, & Galatarū animos à falsa ipsorum doctrina avocandos, se cum iis comparat, vsque ad v. 18. quem Valedictio occupat.
units.tr: Of this letter, to which he passes by way of a place of attention, by which he rouses the Galatians to consider his labour in writing to them; then, to expose the deceit of the false apostles and to call the Galatians away from their false doctrine, he compares himself with them, up to v. 18, which the Farewell occupies.

units.la: SYNOPSIS EPISTOLÆ AD Galatas.
units.tr: SYNOPSIS OF THE EPISTLE TO THE GALATIANS.

units.la: In Epistolam ad Gal. parte principali agit Paul.[?] Reprehendens primò inconstantiam Galatarum, & Pseudoapostolorum perversitatem: cap. 1. à v. 6. usque ad 13. De sua persona & officio, Exponens vitam suam antea-tam[?] in Iudaismo, usque ad v. 15. Christianismo: à v. 16. capitis primi, usque ad v.15. capitis secundi. De fidei iustificatione, quam Probare instituit cap. 2. v. 15. in illa sua ad Petrum sermocinatione. usque ad finem cap. Persequitur: Ostendens Fide in Christum iustificari electos, & nô bonis operibus Legis cum moralia praecipuè: cap. 3. tum ceremonialis quam docet abrogatam esse: cap.4. Concludit: de libertate, per Christum partâ amplectenda, cap. 5. usque ad v. 13. De bono ope-rib. exhortationes ad officia Christianorum generalia: contra licentiam carnis, &c: c.5. à v.13. usque ad finé. Specialia, tum inferiorum, tum superiorum, c.6. usque ad v.11. ubi conclusio epist. incipit. De reipsa: in doctrinâ
units.tr: In the principal part of the Epistle to the Galatians, Paul first rebukes the inconstancy of the Galatians and the perversity of the false apostles (chap. 1, vv. 6–13). He then sets out his own person and office, describing his former life in Judaism (to v. 15) and his life as a Christian (from chap. 1, v. 16, to chap. 2, v. 15). He begins to prove justification by faith in that speech of his to Peter (chap. 2, v. 15), and pursues the matter to the end of the chapter. He shows that the elect are justified by faith in Christ and not by the works of the Law, both moral and ceremonial, which he teaches has been abrogated (chap. 3; chap. 4). He concludes concerning the liberty won by Christ, which is to be embraced (chap. 5, to v. 13). On good works, he gives exhortations to the general duties of Christians, against the licence of the flesh, etc. (chap. 5, from v. 13, to the end). He gives the special duties, both of inferiors and of superiors (chap. 6, to v. 11), where the conclusion of the epistle begins. Concerning the matter itself, in doctrine

units.la: ARGVMENTA CAPITVM.
units.tr: ARGUMENTS OF THE CHAPTERS.

units.la: Cap. I
units.tr: Chapter I

units.la: Hæc scribo,qui sum cœlesti voce vocatus, Qui veram docui,dogmata sancta,fidem. Miror,quæ levitas animos perturbet inanes, Vt cadat è vano tam cito corde fides. Cum, mea quæ docui,non sint mortalia verba, Qui docuit,Dominus nempe magister erat.
units.tr: I, who was called by a heavenly voice, write these things. I taught the true, holy doctrines of faith. I marvel what levity disturbs empty minds, that faith should fall so quickly from a vain heart. Since the words I taught are not mortal, the one who taught them was surely the Lord, the Master.

units.la: 2 Non me discipuli docuerunt dogmata sancta, Quin potius testor me docuisse Petrum. Namque is sollicito servabat pectore legem, Cum vos sola queat iustificare fides.
units.tr: 2 The disciples did not teach me the holy doctrines; rather, I testify that I taught Peter. For he kept the law with an anxious heart, though faith alone can justify you.

units.la: 3 Quis vos ô[?] stulti Galatæ seduxit in illum Errorem, vt fidei non pia cura siet? Sola fides sanctum Domino coniunxit Abramum. Hinc, cur sit Legis tradita forma, docet.
units.tr: 3 Who, you foolish Galatians, has led you into that error, so that there is no pious care for faith? Faith alone joined holy Abraham to the Lord. Hence it teaches why the form of the Law was handed down.

units.la: 4 Libertas quæ sit fidei, quæ regula legis Edocet, & reprobos increpat inde viros. Indicat illorum quam sit fœdissimus error. Lex nos constringit, liberat alma fides.
units.tr: 4 It teaches what the liberty of faith is and what the rule of the law is, and from this it rebukes the reprobate men. It shows how foul their error is. The law binds us; kindly faith sets us free.

units.la: 5 Libera nunc fidei cœlestis iura tenete: Sin minus: hei vobis Christus inanis erit. Pœna manet falsos, qui vos seducere tentans. Sit pietatis amor, sit superata caro[?].
units.tr: 5 Now hold fast to the free rights of heavenly faith. If not, woe to you: Christ will be in vain. Punishment awaits the false men who try to seduce you. Let there be the love of godliness, and let the flesh be overcome.

units.la: 6 Clementer (moneo) lapsos attollite fratres. Sanctus amor vigeat, gloria vana cadat. Doctores colite, & fidei constantia vobis Adsit: sit Christus gloria vestra simul.
units.tr: 6 Gently (I advise), raise up your fallen brothers. Let holy love flourish and vain glory fall. Honour the teachers, and may steadfastness of faith be with you; may Christ be your glory at the same time.

units.la: ALITER. Cap. I
units.tr: OTHERWISE. Chapter I

units.la: Angelus his dicens contraria sit maledictus. Me docuit Christus, qui populator erat.
units.tr: Let an angel who preaches anything contrary to these be accursed. Christ taught me, who was once a ravager.

units.la: 2 Bis septem exactis repeto Solymos, rogo summos, Qui nihil addebant, corripioque Petrum.
units.tr: 2 After fourteen years had passed, I went back up to Jerusalem, asked the leading men, and rebuked Peter.

units.la: 3 Cæpistis recte; quis vos decepit amici? Sic nos non legem iustificare probo.
units.tr: 3 You began well. Friend, who has deceived you? Thus I prove that we are not justified by the law.

units.la: Dum puer est, heres seruis. quo tempora vobis ? Vos iterum pario libera Sara suis.
units.tr: While the child is an heir, he is no different from a slave. What times are these for you? I bear you again, free Sarah, for her sons.

units.la: Est circumcidi vnum. quis vos ita turbat ? Haec sunt quae pugnant, spiritus atque caro.
units.tr: Circumcision is one thing. Who troubles you in this way? These are the things that fight: spirit and flesh.

units.la: Ferte rogo infirmos, quae seuimus illa metemus. Gloriorin cruce, nam stigmata porto crucis.
units.tr: Carry the weak, I beg you; what we sow, that we shall reap. Shall I glory in the cross? For I bear the marks of the cross.

units.la: SYMBOLA MEMORIALIA.
units.tr: MEMORIAL SYMBOLS.

units.la: {1}Turbat, {2}post Summis, {3}Maledictio, {4}Adoptio, {5}Fructus: {6}Stigmata porto crucis.
units.tr: {1}Troubles {2}after the Summaries, {3}Curse, {4}Adoption, {5}Fruit: {6}I bear the marks of the cross.

units.la: Declaratio.
units.tr: Explanation.

units.la: Turbant vos nonnulli, & volunt inuertere Euangelium Christi, v. 7. post Summis Apostolis exposui Euangelium quod praedico. v. 2. & 6. Maledictio factus est Christus pro nobis, v. 13. Adoptio vt nobis cederet, misit Deus Filium suum: v. 4 5. Fructus Spiritus est charitas, &c: v. 22.
units.tr: Some trouble you and wish to pervert the Gospel of Christ, v. 7. After the Summaries: I have set forth to the Apostles the Gospel which I preach, v. 2 and 6.
