Curse: Christ was made a curse for us, v. 13. Adoption: that we might receive it, God sent his Son, v. 4, 5. Fruit: the fruit of the Spirit is charity, etc., v. 22.

units.la: Stigmata porto crucis Christi in corpore meo: v. 17.
units.tr: I bear the marks of the cross of Christ in my body, v. 17.

units.la: ANALYSIS EPISTO-LÆ AD EPHE-sios.
units.tr: ANALYSIS OF THE EPISTLE TO THE EPHESIANS.

units.la: Ad quos & qua occasione scripta Epistola.
units.tr: To whom and on what occasion the Epistle was written.

units.la: AD QUOS haec epistola missa sit, docetur v.1.cap.1.dicitur enim ibi, scriptam esse sanctis & fidelibus in Christo Iesu, degentibus Ephesi: primum idololatris, Dianae cultoribus, Act: 19. v. 26. 27. & Magiae addictis, Act.19. v. 19. a Deo autem per Paulum conuersis, ibid. & per triennium ab eodem in fide confirmatis, Act.20.v.31. reluctanreluctantibus illi multis hostibus,1.Cor.15. v.31. Fuit autem Ephesus vrbs Ioniæ clarissima, Asiæ minoris Metropolis, condita ab Amazonibus, Dauide in Iudæâ regnante, celeberrima ex templo in honorem Dianæ extructo. Et hæc vrbs nunc sub imperio Turcico, Mahometicæ abominationi mancipata & Euangelio priuata est, iuxta illam Dei comminationem, Apocal:2.v.5. Defracti sunt rami per infidelitatem. Nos per fidem stamus: Non efferamur animo, sed timeamus. Si enim Deus non pepercit Ecclesiis à tanto Apostolo plantatis, fundatis & confirmatis, metuendum est ne Nobis quoque tam horrendæ securitati deditis, non parcat.
units.tr: To whom this epistle was sent is shown in chapter 1, verse 1, for it says there that it was written to the saints and faithful in Christ Jesus, dwelling at Ephesus. They were first idolaters, worshippers of Diana (Acts 19:26-27), and devoted to magic (Acts 19:19). Through Paul, God converted them (ibid.), and for three years he strengthened them in the faith (Acts 20:31), though many enemies struggled against him (1 Cor. 15:31). Ephesus was a most famous city of Ionia, the metropolis of Asia Minor, founded by the Amazons in the reign of David over Judah, and very renowned for the temple built in honour of Diana. This city is now under Turkish rule, given over to the abomination of Mahomet and deprived of the gospel, in accordance with that threat of God in Revelation 2:5: The branches were broken off through unbelief. We stand through faith. Do not be proud in mind, but fear. For if God did not spare the churches planted, founded and confirmed by so great an apostle, we must fear that he will not spare us either, who are given over to such a dreadful security.

units.la: Occasionem quod attinet, duplex ea occurrit. Nam primò, (etsi Ephesij non dum defecerant, nec vllos in doctrina errores quemadmodum Corinthij & Galatæ, admiserant:) ex instinctu diuino nouerat, graues lupos non parcentes gregi, post suum discessum ingressuros esse in eam Ecclesiam, & ex illa ipsa exorituros esse viros peruersa loquentes, & discipulos quærentes, Act.20.v.29.30. Ne itaque Ecclesia illa aut lace-raretur, aut dispergeretur ex insidiis, scripto etiam, ut antea viua voce, de Satanæ conatibus eam docere voluit. Secundò, vbi Apostolus Euangelij causa in vincula coniectus esset, quærebant falsi doctores ex illis occasionem, auctoritatem & doctrinam ipsius elevandi & contemnendi. Ut ergo etiam hisce Satanæ insidiis obviaret, voluit Apostolus tempestiuè causam & utilitatem captiuitatis suæ ostendere, ut liquet ex v.1. cap.3. Discant hinc fide doctores, quanta solicitudine grex Domini sit obseruandus: quanta fidelitate pascendus, & quanta constantia, contra lupos & Satanæ molimina, protegendus.
units.tr: As for the occasion, it is twofold. First, although the Ephesians had not yet fallen away, nor admitted any errors in doctrine as the Corinthians and Galatians had, Paul knew by divine prompting that grievous wolves, sparing not the flock, would enter that church after his departure, and that men speaking perverse things would arise from among themselves to draw away disciples (Acts 20:29-30). So that the church would be neither torn apart nor scattered by these snares, he wished to teach it in writing, as he had before by the living voice, about the attempts of Satan. Second, since the apostle had been cast into chains for the sake of the gospel, false teachers sought from this an occasion to belittle and despise his authority and doctrine. So, to meet also these snares of Satan, the apostle wished to set forth in good time the cause and usefulness of his captivity, as is clear from chapter 3, verse 1. Let teachers learn from this with what care the flock of the Lord is to be watched over, with what faithfulness it is to be fed, and with what steadfastness it is to be protected against wolves and the schemes of Satan.

units.la: Scopus & summa Epistolæ. Hortatur Ephesios vt in doctrina cælesti à se tradita, & in vita Christiana constanter permaneant, nec patiantur se ab eo abduci vlla ratione; non vinculis suis moti, non à falsis doctoribus persuasi ac decepti; quin potius quotidie in doctrina & pietate proficiant. Ita primùm fidem, deinde vitam Christianam informat. Scopus hic liquet ex v. 13. cap. 3.
units.tr: The aim and sum of the Epistle. He urges the Ephesians to remain steadfast in the heavenly doctrine delivered by him and in the Christian life, and not to allow themselves to be drawn away from it by any means: not moved by his chains, nor persuaded and deceived by false teachers; but rather to make daily progress in doctrine and piety. Thus he shapes first their faith and then their Christian life. This aim is clear from chapter 3, verse 13.

units.la: PARTES
units.tr: PARTS

units.la: Epistolæ, præter vsitatam salutationem, in qua Ephesiis fauorem Dei & conscientiæ pacem & tranquillitatem precatur, (cap.1. v.1. 2.) & conclusionem; (cap.6. v. 21) duæ sunt. 1 Didascalica. i. institutio fidei: 11 Paranetica. i. vita Christiana informatio.
units.tr: Apart from the customary greeting, in which he prays for the Ephesians the favour of God and peace and tranquillity of conscience (chapter 1, verses 1-2), and the conclusion (chapter 6, verse 21), the epistle has two parts: (1) the didactic, that is, the instruction in faith; (2) the paraenetic, that is, the guidance of Christian life.

units.la: I. PARS.
units.tr: I. PART.

units.la: PRIMÆ partis propositio hæc est: Vos Ephesij non tantum debetis constanter perseuerare in doctrina, fide & vita Christiana, sed etiam in ea proficere. Est ea manifesta ex peroratione prioris partis, v. 13 cap. 3. inchoatâ.
units.tr: The proposition of the first part is this: You Ephesians ought not only to persevere steadfastly in doctrine, faith and Christian life, but also to make progress in them. It is clear from the peroration of the earlier part, begun at chapter 3, verse 13.

units.la: Argumentum & Methodus.
units.tr: Argument and Method.

units.la: Paulus salutatis primum Ephesiis, incipit deinde concionari de benedictionibus Dei spiritualibus in Christo, quas propositâ primùm ge-nerali nerali propositione, deinde factâ particulari be-nedictionum inductione, hoc est methodo & ordine plane naturali persequitur: nisi quòd semel atque iterum, non oblitus se pastorem esse, generalis benedictionis partes aliquot applicet ad Iudaeos & Ephesios, nominatim vocationem & viuificationem: semel etiam inserat motus animorum & beneuolentiae quendam locum. Post generalem illam doctrinam de benedictionibus spiritualibus, descendit ad speciem, & vocationem illam Ephesiorum quam attigit duntaxat at in generali doctrina, fusius iam pertractat comparatè primùm propositam, deinde argumentis aliquot confirmatam, hoc est, methodo etiam naturali explicatam. Postquam autem sic in genere primùm, deinde in specie docuit Ephesios, ne offendat praesens conditio personae docentis & aedificationis illud opus impediat, causa vinculorum suorum priùs expositâ, hortatur, ne ob afflictiones suas segnescant. Quòque magis afficiat eos conclu-sio hortationis, digreditur in locum motus & beneuolentiae.
units.tr: Having first greeted the Ephesians, Paul begins to preach about the spiritual blessings of God in Christ. He first states a general proposition and then makes a particular induction of the blessings, following a method and order that is entirely natural. Only once or twice, not forgetting that he is a pastor, does he apply some parts of the general blessing to the Jews and the Ephesians, namely calling and quickening. Once he also inserts a passage on the emotions and goodwill. After that general teaching about spiritual blessings, he descends to the particular and now treats more fully the calling of the Ephesians, which he had touched on only in the general doctrine. He first sets out the proposition in comparison and then confirms it by several arguments, so that it is explained by a natural method as well. Having thus taught the Ephesians first in general and then in particular, he does not want the present condition of the teacher to give offence or hinder the work of edification. So, after first explaining the cause of his chains, he exhorts them not to grow slack because of their afflictions. And so that the conclusion of the exhortation may move them more, he digresses into a passage of emotion and goodwill.

units.la: Cap.I.(post salutationem v.1. & 2.)est, 1. propositio generalis, de spirituali benedictione Dei Patris in Christo. v. 3. 11 Declaratio propositionis per particularem inductionem benedictionum, usque ad v. 15. 111 Digressio in locum beneuolentiae de Apostoli gaudio ob fidem & charitatem Ephesiorum, usque ad v.19. 1v Regressio ad declarationem propositionis & inductionem particularium benedictionum: a v. 19. usque ad finem capitis.
units.tr: Chapter 1 (after the greeting, vv. 1 and 2) contains: I. the general proposition, on the spiritual blessing of God the Father in Christ, v. 3. II. The declaration of the proposition by a particular induction of blessings, down to v. 15. III. A digression into a passage of goodwill, on the Apostle's joy over the faith and love of the Ephesians, down to v. 19. IV. A return to the declaration of the proposition and the induction of particular blessings, from v. 19 to the end of the chapter.

units.la: Hactenus beneficia Dei absolutè considerata: nunc ea amplificat per comparationem miseriae generis humani, & nominatim Ephesiorum: ut inde liberationis magnitudo melius conspiciatur.
units.tr: Hitherto the benefits of God have been considered absolutely. Now he amplifies them by comparing them with the misery of the human race, and of the Ephesians in particular, so that the greatness of the deliverance may be seen more clearly.

units.la: Postquam Apostolus in genere excellentem illam magnitudinem potentiae Dei, (quam hoc capite viuificationem nominat) substrato illi fundamento suo, nempe Christi resurrectione, & glorificatione, exposuit; iam cap. II. id ipsum applicat in specie ad Ephesios & Iudaeos vsque ad v. II. Deinde adhuc specialius ponit Ephesios ante oculos utramque conditionem suam, & illam praecedentem in Gentilismo, & hanc praesentem in Christianismo, vsque ad v. 14. Postremò confirmat ad finem vsque capitis praesentem illam ipsorum conditionem ac vocationem, nempe propinquos factos esse in Christo, per sanguinem ipsius.
units.tr: Having set out in general the excellent greatness of God's power (which in this chapter he calls quickening), and having laid as its foundation Christ's resurrection and glorification, the Apostle now, in chapter 2, applies the same in particular to the Ephesians and the Jews, down to v. 11. Then, still more specifically, he sets before the Ephesians' eyes both of their conditions, the earlier one in Gentilism and the present one in Christianity, down to v. 14. Finally, to the end of the chapter, he confirms their present condition and calling, namely that they have been made near in Christ through his blood.

units.la: Cap. III, arrepta occasione ex proximis verbis antecedentis capitis, occurrit offendiculo crucis suae, hortaturque Ephesios ne segnescant ob afflictiones suas pro ipsis. Cum enim hanc Epistolam scriberet Apostolus, Romae in vinculis erat: vsque ad v. 14. Deinde egreditur in locum beneuolentiae, quam significat ex seriis admodum pro ipsis precibus, quibus precatur Ephesios verae fidei & donorum spiritualium incrementum.
units.tr: Chapter 3, seizing the occasion from the last words of the preceding chapter, meets the stumbling block of his own cross and exhorts the Ephesians not to grow slack because of his afflictions on their behalf. For when the Apostle wrote this letter he was in chains at Rome, down to v. 14. Then he digresses into a passage of goodwill, which he signals by the very earnest prayers he offers for them, praying that the Ephesians may grow in true faith and in spiritual gifts.

units.la: II PARS EPISTOLAE.
units.tr: II PART OF THE EPISTLE.

units.la: ABSOLVIT hactenus Apostolus partem epistolae principalem, nimirum aidascalicam de beneficiis Dei Patris, quae in Filio suo nobis exhibuit, eaque longa expositione enumerauit, & ea ad Ephesios pertinere docuit, quos inde ad constantiam in hac doctrina est exhortatus. Nunc subiicit
units.tr: Hitherto the Apostle has completed the principal part of the epistle, namely the dogmatic part, concerning the benefits of God the Father, which he has bestowed on us in his Son. He has listed these in a long exposition and taught that they belong to the Ephesians, whom he has therefore exhorted to remain steadfast in this doctrine. Now he adds

units.la: cis doctrinæ de fide, locum de operibus renati hominis, ne fidei quodam inani spectro decipiamur.
units.tr: to the doctrine of faith a passage on the works of the regenerate man, lest we be deceived by some empty phantom of faith.

units.la: Argumentum & methodus huius partis.
units.tr: The argument and method of this part.

units.la: In hac huius epistolæ parte secundâ, paraene-tica nimirum, hortatur Apostolus ad fructus fi-dei, bona nimirum opera, seruata methodo pla-nè naturali, & propositâ primùm generalissima paraenesi ad officium omne Christiani hominis vocatione dignum: deinde inductis particulari-bus præceptionibus & officiis, primo loco iis, quæ ad quamcunque sine discrimine, hominum conditionem pertinent. Secundo loco iis quæ respiciunt certas quasdam hominum conditio-nes, vt mariti & vxoris, parentum & libero-rum, &c. Postremò & conclusionis quasi loco, subiecta generali & communi omnibus superio-ribus officiis paraenesi, de se corroborandis, vel induenda spirituali illa Panoplia. In his autem particularibus admonitionibus inducendis quis exactum & præcisum ordinem requirat?
units.tr: In this second part of the epistle, which is paraenetic, the Apostle exhorts to the fruits of faith, namely good works, following a method that is entirely natural. He first sets out a most general exhortation to every duty worthy of the calling of a Christian man. Then he introduces particular precepts and duties: first those that pertain to the condition of all men without distinction; second, those that concern certain specific conditions of men, such as those of husband and wife, parents and children, and so on; and lastly, by way of a kind of conclusion, an exhortation general and common to all the preceding duties, on strengthening oneself, or on putting on that spiritual panoply. But who would require an exact and precise order in introducing these particular admonitions?

units.la: Absolutis autem duabus illis præcipuis Epi-stolæ partibus, occupationis quadam specie, vt videtur, significat se credidisse res suas priuatas, de quibus etiam certiores fieri volebant Ephe-siis, Tychico fratri ac ministro, coram exponen-das. Postremò sic præcisa narratione rerum suarum priuatarum, quid reliquum fuit, nisi vt eadem salutatione, aut certè non valde dissimili, qua Epistolam incepit, eam etiam clauderet, optaretque gratiam Dei in Christo, non Ephesiis modo, sed omnibus etiam diligentibus Do-minum nostrum Christum?
units.tr: Having finished those two principal parts of the epistle, he signifies, as it seems, with a certain appearance of business, that he has entrusted his private affairs, about which he wished the Ephesians also to be informed, to his brother and minister Tychicus, who was to explain them in person. Finally, having thus concluded the account of his private affairs, what remained but to close the epistle with the same salutation, or at least one not very different from that with which he began it, and to wish the grace of God in Christ, not only to the Ephesians but to all who love our Lord Jesus Christ?

units.la: Cap: iv. Primùm hortatus in genere ad omne officium vocatione Christiani hominis dignum, descendit ad duo specialia officia, & inprimis ad concordiæ studium grauissimis rationibus exhortatur Ephesios: vsque ad v.7. Deinde arreptâ occasione ex loco proximè præcedenti, digreditur ad ostendendam donorum spiritualium diuersitatem, commemorans beneficia Christi ad dextram Patris collocati: vsque ad v.17. Postremò reuertitur ad præceptionem specialium officiorum, & ab Ethnica morum dissolutione dehortatur.
units.tr: Chapter 4. First, having exhorted in general to every duty worthy of the calling of a Christian man, he comes down to two special duties, and above all with the weightiest reasons exhorts the Ephesians to zeal for concord, up to verse 7. Then, taking occasion from the immediately preceding passage, he digresses to show the diversity of spiritual gifts, recounting the benefits of Christ seated at the right hand of the Father, up to verse 17. Lastly, he returns to the precepts of particular duties, and dissuades from the dissolute morals of the heathen.

units.la: Cap. v. persequitur præcepta officiorum specialia, quæ ad quamcunque hominum conditionem pertinent, ad versum vsque 22. Deinde aggreditur præcepta quæ respiciunt certas quasdam hominum conditiones, & primò eorum qui matrimonio sunt coniuncti; vsque ad finem capitis.
units.tr: Chapter 5. He pursues the special precepts of duties, which pertain to every condition of men, up to verse 22. Then he takes up the precepts which concern certain specific conditions of men, and first of those who are joined in marriage, up to the end of the chapter.

units.la: Cap. vi. primò pergit in specialibus præceptis quæ ad certas hominum conditiones pertinent, nempe eas quæ sunt in eadem familia, parentum & liberorum, dominorum & seruorum, vsque ad v. ix. Deinde concludens vniuersum hunc locum præceptionum, omnibus communiter subiicit generale quoddam præceptum de induenda illa tota armatura Dei, ad versum vsque 21. Tertiò accedit
units.tr: Chapter 6. First he proceeds with the special precepts that pertain to certain conditions of men, namely those who belong to the same household: parents and children, masters and servants, up to verse 9. Then, concluding this whole section of precepts, he sets down for all in common a general precept concerning putting on that entire armour of God, up to verse 21. Thirdly, he comes to

units.la: CONCLUSIO
units.tr: CONCLUSION

units.la: Epistola, in qua primò significat se credidisse Tychico tabellario res suas priuatas coram exponendas, vsque ad v. 23. Deinde claudit epistolam salutatione quadam, quâ bene precatur non tantùm Ephesijs, sed toti Dei Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: The epistle, in which he first states that he has entrusted his private affairs to Tychicus the messenger, to be explained in person, up to verse 23. Then he closes the epistle with a certain salutation, by which he sincerely blesses not only the Ephesians but the whole Church of God.

units.la: Synopsis totius Epistolæ talis est:
units.tr: The synopsis of the whole epistle is as follows:

units.la: Exordium complectens Apostolicam Salutationem. v.1.2. Tractationē principalem, in Doctrinalis fidei: in qua confirmat Ephesios: idque ex parte Christi: commemorans eius beneficia: quorum Pauli Apostoli: ubi recedet sua propositio generalis est, v.3. Tractatio ineorum tum particulari enumeratione à v.4 ad finem Speciali applicatione ad Ephesios, & amplificatione per comparationem miserrimi status prioris. cap.2. Pathemata & afflictiones: didicit: locuit: Mathemata, quae Adhortatione ad sanctitatem vitae: ubi est huius partis Generalis propositio: cap. 4. v.1. Tractatio: in enumeratione officium per tinentiùm ad Omnes homines, cap.4. à v.2. vsq; ad finem capitis, & c.5. vsque ad v.22. Certas quasdam hominum conditiones ut mariti & uxoris, àv 22. c. 5. ad finem; reliquorum in œconomia, cap.6. vsque ad v.10. Conclusio: de Panoplia Dei induenda, à v.10.vsque ad 21.
units.tr: The exordium, comprising the apostolic salutation, verses 1 and 2. The principal treatment, of doctrinal faith, in which he confirms the Ephesians, and does so on the part of Christ, recounting his benefits, of which the Apostle Paul's general proposition is given, verse 3. The treatment of these, first by particular enumeration from verse 4 to the end, and by special application to the Ephesians, and amplification through comparison with their most wretched former state, chapter 2. Sufferings and afflictions; he learned; he spoke; lessons, which contain exhortation to holiness of life, where the general proposition of this part is found, chapter 4, verse 1. The treatment, in the enumeration of duties pertaining to all men, chapter 4 from verse 2 to the end of the chapter, and chapter 5 to verse 22. Certain specific conditions of men, such as husband and wife, from verse 22 of chapter 5 to the end; of the rest, in the household, chapter 6 to verse 10. The conclusion: on putting on the panoply of God, from verse 10 to 21.

units.la: Conclusionem, in Apostolica & pia salutatione. à v. 21. ad finem epistolæ.
units.tr: The conclusion, in the apostolic and devout salutation, from verse 21 to the end of the epistle.

units.la: CAP.
units.tr: CAP.

units.la: Condidit vt teretem divina potentia mundum, Illius hoc placitum consiliumque fuit, Vt miseros solo saluaret munere CHRISTI, Quisolus nostri fons & origo boni est.
units.tr: Divine power formed the round world as it is. This was God's purpose and counsel: that he would save wretched people by the gift of Christ alone, who alone is the fountain and origin of our good.

units.la: Immunis nemo peccati a crimine viuit, Omnibus a CHRISTO prouenit almasalus. Hic etenim veteris tollens diuortia legis, E populis vnam fecit vtrisque domum.
units.tr: No one lives free from the guilt of sin, but almighty salvation comes to all from Christ. For he, removing the divorce of the old law, has made one house of both peoples.

units.la: Ferrea pro vobis gestamus vincula, fratres, Nam Deus hoc vestri munus haberededit. Ne tamen haec timidos offendant vincula, semper Pro vobis soleo sollicitare Deum.
units.tr: Brothers, we bear iron chains for your sake, for God has granted this as your gift. Yet lest these chains offend the fearful, I always pray to God on your behalf.

units.la: Conciliet vestras felix concordia mentes, Et castam vitam sit pia cura sequi. Ira, dolus, fraudes, turpis dicteria linguae Cedant, sit purae religionis amor.
units.tr: May happy harmony unite your minds, and may a careful concern to follow a chaste life take hold of you. Let anger, deceit, fraud and shameful words of the tongue give way, and let love of pure religion prevail.

units.la: Sit fraternus amor vobis, sit lingua pudica, Ingluuies, foeda & sit procul ebrietas. Coniugij casto seruentur pectore leges: Vt propriam Sponsam CHRISTVS amare solet.
units.tr: Let there be brotherly love among you, let the tongue be modest, and let gluttony and foul drunkenness be far away. Let the laws of marriage be kept in a chaste heart, as Christ is accustomed to love his own bride.

units.la: Officium quod sit natorum quodque parentum, Quid deceat seruos, quid dominosque, docet. Et multis Satanae describit prelia fani[?], Et quae illum possint vincere tela, docet. Catera narrabit Tychicus: vos sedulo pro me Fundite non falso pectore vota Deo.
units.tr: He teaches what duty belongs to children and what to parents, what becomes servants and what masters. He describes the battles of Satan and teaches the weapons by which he can be overcome. Tychicus will tell the rest. You, meanwhile, pour out your prayers to God diligently, with a sincere heart on my behalf.

units.la: ALITER.
units.tr: OTHERWISE.

units.la: CAP. I
units.tr: CHAP. I

units.la: Ante caput mundi selegit nos Deus, ob quod Flecto genu. Christo gloria magna datur. Blasphemos, irae natos, mera gratia seruat: Nunc vnum populum sanguis vtrumque facit. Conflictus rogo, cognosco mysteria Christi, Prædico diuitias membraque flecto Patri. 4 Digne viue.colas pacem.sunt plurima dona: Prisc us homo valeat.nil mali ab ore fluat.
units.tr: Before the foundation of the world God chose us, on account of which I bend the knee. Great glory is given to Christ. Grace alone preserves the blasphemers, born of wrath; now his blood makes both one people. I ask for conflict; I know the mysteries of Christ; I proclaim the riches and bend my limbs before the Father. 4 Live worthily, cultivate peace; there are very many gifts. May Priscus the man fare well; let nothing evil flow from his mouth.

units.la: 5 Ethica deformis[?],lingua vitiis & auaris. Occultis,vino,coniugibusque docet.
units.tr: 5 Deformed ethics, a tongue given over to vices and to the greedy. He teaches about secret matters, wine, and spouses.

units.la: 6 Filioli patribus,dominis vos subdite serui. Induite arma Dei: nam ferus hostis adest.
units.tr: 6 Children, obey your parents; servants, be subject to your masters. Put on the armour of God, for a fierce enemy is at hand.

units.la: NOTÆ CAPITUM CHA-racteristicæ.
units.tr: Characteristic notes of the chapters

units.la: 1 3 4 2 5 Exundans,Imus,Confortes,Omnia,& Offa: 6 Armatura Dei pectora nostra tegat.
units.tr: 1 3 4 2 5 Overflowing, Imus, Partners, All things, and Bones: 6 May the armour of God cover our breasts.

units.la: Declaratio.
units.tr: Explanation.

units.la: Exundans Dei gratia in nos. v. 8. Imus augularis lapis etiam Christus. v. 20. Confortes promissionis gentes in Christo per Euangelium, v. 6. Omnia vt implerer Christus donis suis,ascendit longe supra omnes coelos, v. 10. & Offa ex ossibus Christi sumus: v. 30.
units.tr: Exundans: God's grace poured out upon us. v. 8. Imus: the chief cornerstone, which is also Christ. v. 20. Confortes: the nations, partakers of the promise in Christ through the Gospel. v. 6. Omnia: that he might fill all things with his gifts, Christ ascended far above all the heavens. v. 10. And Offa: we are of the bones of Christ. v. 30.

units.la: Armatura Dei pectora nostra tegat: v, 11.
units.tr: Armatura Dei pectora nostra tegat: v. 11.

units.la: ANALYSIS EPISTO-LÆ AD PHILIP-pensēs[?].
units.tr: ANALYSIS OF THE EPISTLE TO THE PHILIPPIANS.

units.la: PHILIPPI fuit urbs,sita in prima parte Macedoniæ, quam olim Κρηνίδας[?] vocabant,à fontibus, quibus abundabat collis ille in quo condita fuit: cùm autem Philippus Rex Macedonum eam multis ciuibus auxisset, eandem postea suo nomine Philippos denominauit. Ad hos Philippos peruenit S. Apostolus vnà cum Syla,Spiritu S/[?] monitore, vt est Act: R. iiij. 16. & multis diebus ibidem docuit, hospitio vsus Lydiæ purpurissæ, mox vterque ibi cæsus & in carcerem coniectus est propter spiritum Pytho-nis à puella eiectum, sed mox mirabili Dei con-silio gloriosè iterum emittitur. Hos igitur recte à se antea institutos, nunc absens confirmat in suscepta doctrina, hortaturque vt constanter in fide persistentes, professionem hanc vitæ inno-centia ornent.
units.tr: Philippi was a city in the first part of Macedonia. Formerly it was called Krēnídes [Κρηνίδες], from the springs with which the hill on which it was built abounded. But when Philip, King of the Macedonians, had enlarged it with many citizens, he afterwards named it Philippi after himself. The holy Apostle came to these Philippi together with Silas, under the guidance of the Holy Spirit, as is related in Acts 16.16, and taught there for many days, lodging with Lydia, a seller of purple. Soon afterwards both of them were beaten and thrown into prison on account of a spirit of Python cast out of a slave girl, but by the wonderful counsel of God they were soon set free again with honour. Now, being absent, he confirms these people, whom he had previously and rightly instructed, in the doctrine they had accepted, and urges them to persevere constantly in the faith, and to adorn this profession with innocence of life.

units.la: Occasio scribendi oblata est ex domesticis dissidiis, quæ gliscebant, vt est videre cap.1.v.18. & cap. 2. v. 3. & 4. vbi hortatur ne quid per contentionem & æmulationem agant. Præterea imminebant ipsis, vt & aliis Ecclesiis pericula & persecutiones, in quibus ignominia crucis, & præsens Apostoli captiuitas multos percellebat, quæ omnia hac epistola diluit ipsosque contra hæc pericula & offendicula confirmat. Insuper sollicitabantur à falsis doctoribus, vt circumcisionem & alia onera legis admitterent, vt est videre capite tertio: ne igitur his eueniret quod Galatis acciderat, præmonet ne hos doctores admittant, imo tanquam canes & hostes crucis Christi diligenter caueant. Denique in ipsum Apostolum multa contulerant beneficia, pro quibus voluit illis agere gratias, vt est cap. 4.
units.tr: The occasion for writing was offered by the domestic dissensions which were growing among them, as can be seen in chapter 1, verse 18, and chapter 2, verses 3 and 4, where he exhorts them not to act out of strife and rivalry. Besides, dangers and persecutions threatened them, as they did other churches; the shame of the cross and the Apostle's present captivity troubled many. He deals with all these things in this letter and strengthens them against these dangers and stumbling-blocks. Moreover, they were being pressed by false teachers to admit circumcision and other burdens of the law, as can be seen in chapter 3. So, lest they should suffer what had happened to the Galatians, he warns them not to admit these teachers, but rather to beware of them carefully as dogs and enemies of the cross of Christ. Finally, they had conferred many benefits upon the Apostle himself, for which he wished to thank them, as in chapter 4.

units.la: Propositio & Argumentum Epistolæ ex his quæ dicta sunt, facile colligitur. Principalis pro-positio est, in hac ipsa doctrina Christianæ Religionis, quam acceperunt à Paulo, constanter Philippensibus perdurandum est, solum vitæ innocentia eandem strenuè ornent, vsque ad aduentum Domini Christi. Hoc totum Apostolus [?]us appellat, digne ambulare Euangelio, cap.1. vers. 27.
units.tr: Proposition and Argument of the Epistle are easily gathered from what has been said. The principal proposition is that the Philippians must persevere constantly in this very doctrine of the Christian religion which they received from Paul, and that they must vigorously adorn it by innocence of life alone, until the coming of the Lord Christ. The Apostle calls all this "to walk worthily of the gospel," chapter 1, verse 27.

units.la: Argumentum. Paulus Philippenses in fide Christi confirmatos (cap.1. v.3. usque ad v.27.) primo hortatur ad studium pietatis (inde à v.27. cap.1. usque ad finem cap.2.) Deinde monet eosdem ut sibi caveant à falsa Pseudoapostolorum doctrina, qui iustitiam legis cum iustitia fidei, perniciosò errore miscebant: (cap.3.) Tum iterum admonet eos in specie & in genere, ipsorumque erga se beneficentiam dilaudat, & postremò epistolam salutationibus concludit.
units.tr: Argument. Paul, having confirmed the Philippians in the faith of Christ (chapter 1, verse 3 to verse 27), first urges them to the pursuit of godliness (from chapter 1, verse 27 to the end of chapter 2). Then he warns them to beware of the false doctrine of the pseudo-apostles, who mixed the righteousness of the law with the righteousness of faith in a pernicious error (chapter 3). Then again he admonishes them, both individually and collectively, and praises their kindness towards him, and finally he concludes the epistle with greetings.

units.la: PARTIVM HÆC EST
units.tr: PARTIVM HÆC EST

units.la: Coherentia.
units.tr: Coherence.

units.la: [Hujus epistola] Salutationem : v. 1 & 2. Tractationem principalem, in qua est Constantiam in fide Christiàn[?] v. 12. cap. 1. usque ad v. 27. Exhortatio ad Sanctitatem vitae ad quam hortatur Comparatio, obtendens quos Simpliciter & absolutè, admonitiones ad pietatem tum speciales tum generales, cap. 4. usque ad v. 10. Imitentur nempe Se suamque in suis vinculis Constantiam & patientiam: reliquo capite primo. Alios: Christum nimirum humillimum & gloriosissimum: & eius discipulos Timoth:& Epaphrod:cap. 2. Fugiant, nempe circūcisionis non profuturæ, sed potius concisionis ministros: cap. 3. Gratiarum actio pro Philippensiū beneficiis: à v. 10. cap. 4. usque ad v. 20. Conclusionem, constantem ἀξιολογία[?], salutationibus, & valedictione.
units.tr: [The structure of this epistle is:] the greeting, v. 1 and 2. The main discourse, in which he exhorts them to constancy in the faith of Christ, cap. 1, v. 12 to v. 27. An exhortation to holiness of life, to which he urges by comparison, setting before them those whom he simply and absolutely commends, with admonitions to godliness both particular and general, cap. 4, v. 1 to v. 10. Namely, that they imitate himself and his constancy and patience in his chains (in the rest of chapter 1); others, namely Christ, most humble and most glorious, and his disciples Timothy and Epaphroditus (chap. 2); they should flee those who are ministers not of circumcision, which profits nothing, but rather of mutilation (chap. 3). Thanksgiving for the kindnesses of the Philippians, from v. 10 of chap. 4 to v. 20. The conclusion: a weighty closing [ἀξιολογία], with greetings and a farewell.

units.la: Dispositio capitis primi hæc est: Post salutationem, (v. 1. 2.) Primam principalis tractationis partem, partem, Exhortationem nimirum ad constantiam in fide Christi, his argumentis absoluit: 1 gratiarum actione erga Deum, propter ipsorum communionem in Euangelio, (v. 3. 4. 5.) 2 significatione spei suae de ipsorum in eadem perseuerantia, (v 6.) 3 testificatione sui erga ipsos amoris, (v. 7. 8.) praecando pro ipsorum in charitate, cognitione omnibusque spiritualibus donis progressu: (v.9.10.11.) 4 anticipando seu auertendo scandalum suorum vinculorum, ubi & de animi sui affectu, tum ad moriendum, tum ad viuendum diutius, testatur: usque ad versum 27.
units.tr: The arrangement of the first chapter is this. After the greeting (v. 1, 2), he completes the first part of the main discourse, namely the exhortation to constancy in the faith of Christ, by these arguments: (1) thanksgiving to God for their fellowship in the gospel (v. 3, 4, 5); (2) an expression of his hope concerning their perseverance in the same (v. 6); (3) a declaration of his love toward them (v. 7, 8), praying for their growth in love, knowledge and all spiritual gifts (v. 9, 10, 11); (4) anticipating and turning aside the scandal of his bonds, where he also bears witness to the disposition of his mind, both towards dying and towards living longer, up to verse 27.

units.la: Deinde hortari eos incipit ad studium pietatis, seu ad vitam Euangelio dignam, ac nominatim ad concordiam & tolerantiam: v. 27. usque ad capitis finem.
units.tr: Then he begins to exhort them to the pursuit of godliness, that is, to a life worthy of the gospel, and especially to concord and forbearance: from v. 27 to the end of the chapter.

units.la: Cap. II. Primo coeptam in superiori capite exhortationem de sectanda & fouenda concordia & humilitate persequitur, exemplum Christi in medium adducens, eiusque glorificati maiestatem commendans: usque ad v. 12. Deinde pergit eos hortari ad vitam inculpatam, usque ad v. 25. Poltremo commendat eis Epaphroditum.
units.tr: Chap. II. He pursues, at the beginning of the chapter above, the exhortation to cultivate and maintain concord and humility, bringing forward the example of Christ and commending the majesty of his glorified state, up to v. 12. Then he goes on to exhort them to a blameless life, up to v. 25. Finally he commends Epaphroditus to them.

units.la: Cap. III. Monet ut sibi caueant a falsa doctrina Pseudoapostolorum, qui iustitiam legis cum iustitia fidei pernicioso errore miscebant: quibus suum ipsius exemplum, tanquam veri & syncèri Apostoli, opponit; & ad illud imitandum hortatur. Initium versus primi videtur esse conclusio capitis secundi. Initium vero proprie capitis huius 3. eiusque prima pars est excusatio repetitionum salutarium, & cautio de vitandis canibus & malis operarijs: cuius cautionis ratio subiicitur, habens prolepsin; item definitionem verae circumcisionis, & exemplar verae iustificationis in Apostolo, usque ad v. 15. Deinde hortatur Philippenses, ut illud suum exemplum imitentur, & ita sint affecti, ut in solo Christo glorientur.
units.tr: Chap. III. He warns them to beware of the false teaching of the false apostles, who mixed the righteousness of the law with the righteousness of faith in a pernicious error. Against these he sets his own example, as a true and sincere apostle, and urges them to imitate it. The beginning of the first verse seems to be the conclusion of chapter 2. The true beginning of this third chapter, and its first part, is an apology for repeating salutary things, and a caution to avoid dogs and evil workers; the reason for this caution is then added, containing an anticipation; likewise a definition of true circumcision and an example of true justification in the Apostle, up to v. 15. Then he exhorts the Philippians to imitate that example of his, and to be so disposed that they glory in Christ alone.

units.la: Cap. I v. verso 1. est conclusio superiorum plena affectuum, ut fit in conclusionibus. Reliqui versus usque ad Conclusionem Epistolae, duo potissimum continent, admonitiones, easque duplices, privatas ad quasdam praecipuas foeminas, inter quas discordia aliquid exortum videtur, (usque ad v. 4.) & generales, ad gaudium spirituale, ad [illegible, ~12 letters], ad preces & virtutes alias, usque ad v.10.11. Gratiarum actionem pro liberalitate Philippensium, usque ad v. 21. ubi est Epistola huius.
units.tr: Chap. I, v. 1 (verso) is a conclusion to what precedes, full of feeling, as is usual in conclusions. The remaining verses up to the conclusion of the epistle contain chiefly two things: admonitions, and these twofold: private ones to certain prominent women, among whom some discord seems to have arisen (up to v. 4), and general ones, to spiritual joy, to [illegible, ~12 letters], to prayer and other virtues, up to v. 10, 11. Thanksgiving for the generosity of the Philippians, up to v. 21, where the epistle ends.

units.la: Conclusio, in qua petit alios suis verbis salutari: v. 21. salutat eos verbis aliorum: (v.22.) & tandem usitato voto concludit: v. ultimo.
units.tr: Conclusion, in which he asks that others be greeted in his words: v. 21 he greets them in the words of others (v. 22), and at last concludes with the customary wish: the last verse.

units.la: ARGVMENTA CAPITVM CAP. I
units.tr: THE ARGUMENTS OF THE CHAPTERS, CHAPTER I

units.la: Audeo quod sancti teneatis dogmata Christi, Nec vos, quae patior, damna movere queant. Plus etiam fidei fructus incommoda portant, Sed sanctam referat vita pudica fidem.
units.tr: I am bold to say that you holy ones hold fast the doctrines of Christ, and that the losses I suffer cannot move you. Indeed, these hardships bring forth even more fruit of faith, and a chaste life commends the holy faith.

units.la: Concordes animi celsos compescite fastus, Hoc etenim Christi vos pia vita docet. Qui quondam vilis, summo nunc fulget honore: Doctores verbi vos coluisse decet.
units.tr: Agree in mind and restrain your lofty pride, for a devout life teaches you this of Christ. He who was once lowly now shines with the highest honour; it is fitting that you honour the teachers of the Word.

units.la: Doctores falsos vigilanti mente cavete, Qui cum lege fidem composuisse solent.
units.tr: Beware with a watchful mind of false teachers, who are wont to mix faith with the law.

units.la: Iustitiam humanam summi rex spernit Olympi,Sed spem coelestem nos decet usque sequi.
units.tr: The King of the highest heaven scorns human righteousness, but it becomes us always to follow the heavenly hope.

units.la: Pergite constantes, concordi pergite sensu,Et vos commendet vita modesta simul.
units.tr: Press on steadfast, press on with one mind, and let a modest life commend you both.

units.la: Gratia sit, fratres, largo pro munere vobis.Dicatur sanctis fratribus alma salus.
units.tr: Grace be upon you, brothers, as a generous gift; let saving health be spoken to the holy brothers.

units.la: ALITER.
units.tr: OTHERWISE.

units.la: CAP. I
units.tr: CHAPTER I

units.la: Acito pro vobis grates, mea vincula crescant,Gaudent, mors lucrum est, vos quoq; damna iuvent.
units.tr: I give thanks for you; let my chains grow longer. They rejoice; death is gain; may your losses also help you.

units.la: Bis ter magnus honor Christum decet ista ferentem,Discipulos laudas optime Paule, tuos.
units.tr: Twice three great honours befit Christ, who bears these things. You praise your disciples, best of Paul.

units.la: Cæsa lucra cum sperno, quo lucrer Iesum.Quæ sunt a tergo mitto, cauete malos.
units.tr: Since I count gains as loss, that I may gain Jesus. I let go of what lies behind; beware of evil men.

units.la: Dilecti, state. & gaudete, & honesta patrate.Sperno quidem esuriem, sed tamen ista placent.
units.tr: Beloved, stand firm, rejoice, and do what is honourable. I indeed despise hunger, yet these things please me.

units.la: MONOSTICHON συμβολικόν.
units.tr: Symbolic Monostich [συμβολικόν]

units.la: Dissolui, Flectatur, ad Anteriora, Corona.
units.tr: I am loosed; let it bow; to the things before; crown.

units.la: Declaratio.
units.tr: Explanation.

units.la: Dissolui cupio & esse cum Christo: v. 23 Flectatur omne genu ad mentionem Iesu: v. 10. ad anteriora contendo, scopum versus, ad palmam supernæ vocationis, v. 14. Corona mea vos estis: v. 1.
units.tr: I desire to depart and be with Christ: v. 23. Let every knee bow at the mention of Jesus: v. 10. I press on to the things before, toward the goal, for the prize of the high calling: v. 14. My crown is you: v. 1.

units.la: ANALYSIS EPISTO-LAE AD COLOSSEN-SES.
units.tr: ANALYSIS OF THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS.

units.la: COLOSSÆ fuit civitas in minori Asia ad confluentem Lyci & Meandri sita, vicina Laodiceæ: idcirco cap. 4. vult Apostolus hanc epistolam Colossensibus communem esse cum Laodicensibus. Hanc Plinius lib. 5. cap. 32. inter celeberrimas Phrygiæ ciuitates numerat, & eius quoque meminit Herodotus, lib. 7. & Strabo lib. 12. Etsi autem ibi non docuerat Apostolus; cùm tamen apud eos per prædicationem Euangelij Ecclesia collecta esset, de eius statu certior factus, (cap. 2. v. 5.) procul dubio per Epaphram illius Ecclesiæ ministrum, qui S. Paulo Romæ aderat, dum hæc scriberet, noluit Apostolus Gentium committere, quin eos etiam de nonnullis necessariis commonefaceret.
units.tr: Colossae was a city in Asia Minor, situated at the confluence of the Lycus and the Meander, near Laodicea; for this reason in chapter 4 the Apostle wishes this epistle to be shared between the Colossians and the Laodiceans. Pliny, book 5, chapter 32, counts it among the most celebrated cities of Phrygia, and Herodotus, book 7, and Strabo, book 12, also mention it. Although the Apostle had not taught there himself, yet since the Church had been gathered among them through the preaching of the Gospel, and having been informed of their condition (chapter 2, verse 5), no doubt through Epaphras, minister of that Church, who was with St Paul at Rome while he was writing these things, the Apostle did not wish to leave the Gentiles without also reminding them of some necessary matters.

units.la: Occasio igitur hæc fuisse videtur, quòd intellexerat Apostolus, fermenti aliquid Pharisaici & humanarum traditionum à nonnullis admisceri doctrinæ Euangelij, quorum alij nimis Judaizantes, ritus & ceremonias Legis urgebant: alij ex gentibus conversi, nescio quæ philosophica dogmata, subtilia potius quàm utilia, invehebant: quibus nimis remisse occurrebatur, saltem à pastore illius loci, Archippo, cuius segnities notari videtur cap. 4.
units.tr: The occasion, then, seems to have been this: the Apostle had learned that some leaven of Pharisaism and of human traditions was being mixed into the doctrine of the Gospel. Of these men, some, being overly Judaizing, pressed the rites and ceremonies of the Law; others, converts from the Gentiles, introduced I know not what philosophical doctrines, subtle rather than useful. These errors were met too leniently, at least by the minister of that place, Archippus, whose sluggishness seems to be noted in chapter 4.

units.la: Hoc autem ordine in hac epistola progreditur Apostolus, ut ante omnia revocet eos ad doctrinam ipsis fideliter ab Epaphra traditam, & inprimis ad fundamentum & caput Ecclesiæ, Christum, & ad revelationem ingentis illius mysterij & beneficiorum Christi, in quo omnes salutis[?] nostræ partes sitas esse, luculenter docet Apostolus cap.1. ut merito immotum & incon-cussum manere debeat illud fundamentum, verf.23. Capite secundo, infert ex precedenti doctrina, non satis esse, accepisse tam excellentem cognitionem, sed illud σχῆμα[?] retinendum, & ab illis cavendum, qui deprædari illos volebant, id est, eripere ipsis thesaurum omnis scientiæ Christum, & pro thesauro carbones ipsis obtrudere, videlicet traditiones superstitiosas partim Iudaicas, partim Ethnicas. Postea suo more à doctrina fidei ad vitam Christianam transit, & ad præcepta tum generalia, tum speciala pertinentia ad œconomiam & familias Christianas: ac tandem cap. 4. piis votis, obtestationibus & salutationibus epistolam concludit.
units.tr: The Apostle proceeds in this epistle in the following order: first of all he recalls them to the doctrine faithfully delivered to them by Epaphras, and above all to the foundation and head of the Church, Christ, and to the revelation of that great mystery and of the benefits of Christ, in which all parts of our salvation are contained; the Apostle sets this out clearly in chapter 1, so that the foundation should rightly remain fixed and unshaken (verse 23). In chapter 2 he infers from the preceding doctrine that it is not enough to have received so excellent a knowledge; that form must be kept, and they must beware of those who wished to plunder them, that is, to snatch from them Christ, the treasure of all knowledge, and to thrust upon them in place of the treasure mere coals, namely superstitious traditions, partly Jewish, partly heathen. Afterwards, in his manner, he passes from the doctrine of faith to the Christian life, and to precepts both general and special, pertaining to the economy and households of Christians; and finally, in chapter 4, he concludes the epistle with pious wishes, appeals and greetings.

units.la: Cap. 1. post salutationem (v. 1. 2.) & proœmium accommodatum ad benevolentiam conciliandam (à v. 3. usque ad 12.) Primò, est expositio doctrinæ Christianæ, usque ad v. 23. Deinde, exhortatio ad constantiam in doctrinæ Christianæ fide: à v. 23. usque ad finem.
units.tr: Chapter 1: after the salutation (verses 1–2) and a proem fitted to win goodwill (from verse 3 to 12): first, there is the exposition of Christian doctrine, down to verse 23; then, an exhortation to constancy in the faith of Christian doctrine, from verse 23 to the end.

units.la: Cap. 11. Pergit Apostolus hortari colossenses ad constantiam in fide doctrinæ Christianæ quam ex Epaphra didicerant, & cuius summam ipse iam in hac epistola expósuerat: usque ad v. 8. Deinde in reliqua capitis parte monet eos, ut sibi à doctrinæ Christianæ corruptelis caveant.
units.tr: Chapter 2: the Apostle goes on to exhort the Colossians to constancy in the faith of Christian doctrine, which they had learned from Epaphras and whose sum he had already set out in this epistle, down to verse 8. Then, in the rest of the chapter, he warns them to beware of corruptions of Christian doctrine.

units.la: Hactenus prima epistolæ pars, quæ fuit de doctrina Christiana: sequitur secunda quæ est de vita Christiana.
units.tr: So far the first part of the epistle, which concerns Christian doctrine; there follows the second, which concerns the Christian life.

units.la: Ex doctrina igitur tradita deducit deinceps exhortationes ad Christianam vitam varias: quarum aliæ sunt generales, id est, ad singulos fideles communiter pertinentes; aliæ verò speciales, pertinentes nimirum ad certos ordines; nempe vxores, maritos; liberos, parentes; ser-vos, dominos.
units.tr: From the doctrine delivered, he then draws various exhortations to the Christian life; some are general, that is, pertaining in common to all the faithful; others are special, pertaining namely to certain orders: wives and husbands; children and parents; servants and masters.

units.la: In capite iii, praecedunt exhortationes generales seu communes, usque ad v. 18. deinde sequuntur speciales, usque ad v. 2. capitis quarti: unde perspicitur, primum illius capitis versiculum non recte ab hoc capite avulsum esse.
units.tr: In chapter 3 the general or common exhortations come first, down to verse 18; then the special ones follow, down to verse 2 of chapter 4; whence it is clear that the first verse of that chapter has not rightly been torn away from this chapter.

units.la: Capite igitur iv. v. 2. redit ad exhortationes generales, usque ad v. 7. inde commendat eis Tychicum & Onesimum, & alios nonnullos: ex quibus duos illos tunc ad ipsos mittebat, caeterorum autem verbis eos salutat, usque ad v. 15. Deinde iu-bet certos quosdam verbis suis salutari, epistolam hanc cum Laodicensibus communicari, & aliam quandam ex Laodicea scriptam, ab ipsis legi, tum Archippum officij studiose faciendi admoneri: usque ad v. 18. Postremo salutatione sua ad-scripta, vincula sua precibus ipsorum commendat.
units.tr: In chapter 4, verse 2, he returns to the general exhortations, down to verse 7; from there he commends to them Tychicus and Onesimus, and some others: of whom he was sending those two to them at that time, while he greets them on behalf of the rest, down to verse 15. Then he bids certain persons be greeted in his words, that this epistle be shared with the Laodiceans, and that another letter written from Laodicea be read by them; then Archippus is admonished to carry out his office diligently, down to verse 18. Finally, with his greeting added in his own hand, he commends his chains to their prayers.

units.la: SYNOPSIS
units.tr: SYNOPSIS

units.la: SYNOPSIS TYPICA.
units.tr: A Typical Synopsis

units.la: Continet hæc epistola (post salutationem) Rei ipsius Tractationem partim Didascalicam, ubi Docet Soli Christo fidendum & nitedum. cap. 1. Refellit & Pseudapostolos, & quæ illi cum Christo coniungunt, cap. 2. Hortatoriam, ubi Generatim de pietatis Fonte, mortificatione & regeneratione: cap. 3. Rivulis, variisque officiis: ibid. Speciatim, de officiis quorundam propriis. cap. 4. Conclusionem, quæ hortatur, laudat, præcipit, salutat.
units.tr: This epistle contains, after the salutation, a treatment of its subject. The first part is didactic: it teaches that Christ alone is to be trusted and relied upon (chap. 1). It refutes the false apostles and the things they join with Christ (chap. 2). The hortatory part speaks, in general, of the fountain of piety, mortification and regeneration (chap. 3), and of its streams and various duties (ibid.), and, in particular, of the special duties of certain persons (chap. 4). The conclusion exhorts, commends, instructs and sends greetings.

units.la: ARGUMENTA CAPITUM.
units.tr: THE ARGUMENTS OF THE CHAPTERS.

units.la: ἐμμελῆα[?]
units.tr: [ἐμμελῆα] (well-tuned, in harmonious measure)

units.la: Cap. I.
units.tr: Chap. I.

units.la: Gratulor ab fidei vobis praeconia vestræ, Quæ vos non falsa laude beare potest. Et merito: in Christo quoniam Pater omnia nobis Tradidit: hic omnis fons & origo boni est.
units.tr: I congratulate you on the report of your faith, which can make you blessed with no false praise. And rightly so, for since the Father has delivered all things to us in Christ, he is the whole fount and origin of good.

units.la: Callida multorum caveatis dogmata cauti, Queis doctos miscet subdola lingua dolos. Cur etenim libeat falso seducier astu, In Christo vobis cum bona cuncta sient?
units.tr: Be wary, cautious, of the crafty doctrines of many, to which a deceitful tongue mixes its learned tricks. For why should you be willing to be led astray by false cunning, when all good things are yours in Christ?

units.la: Deserite has terras, iam sint cælestia curæ, Nec libeat vitiis invigilare malis. Sit fraternus amor, sint & connubia sancta, Officium faciat filius atque pater.
units.tr: Leave these lands behind; let heavenly things now be your care, and do not be willing to keep watch over evil vices. Let there be brotherly love, and let there be holy marriages; let the son and the father each do their duty.

units.la: Hoc pariter serui faciant dominique tenaces. Personas nec enim respicit ipse Deus:
units.tr: In the same way, let servants and stern masters do likewise, for God himself does not regard persons.

units.la: Orandi studium sit vobis, sermoque prudens, Et sapiens pariter castaque vita sit[?], Vos etiam fratres fraterno corde salutant. Officium Archippo praecipit inde suum.
units.tr: Let prayer be your zeal, and let your speech be prudent, and let your life be likewise wise and chaste. The brethren also greet you with a brotherly heart. Hence he charges Archippus with his duty.

units.la: ALITER.
units.tr: OTHERWISE.

units.la: CAP. I
units.tr: CAP. I

units.la: Æstulit à tenebris Christus prior omnibus illa Impleo quae desunt iusta minister ago.
units.tr: Christ first of all has snatched us from darkness; I, the minister, fulfil what is lacking and do what is just.

units.la: Belle[?] suadet eis, legis, mundique, hominumque Præcepta, à Christi morte, valere nihil.
units.tr: He persuades them that the precepts of the law, of the world, and of men are worth nothing since the death of Christ.

units.la: Cælum quisque petat, terrestria mortificate. Hoc uxor, fili, serue, sequaris iter.
units.tr: Let each seek heaven and mortify what is earthly. Wife, child, and servant, follow this way.

units.la: De Dominis, precibus, peregrinis, & sale verbi Scribit, quod superest, verba salutis habet.
units.tr: He writes of lords, prayers, strangers, and the salt of the word; what remains holds the words of salvation.

units.la: VOCES CHARACTERISTICÆ memor:
units.tr: CHARACTERISTIC WORDS, for memory:

units.la: 1 2 3 4 Conciliat, Sophiæ, Vetere exuti, Dominorum.
units.tr: 1 2 3 4 Reconciles, of Wisdom, Having put off the old, Of the lords.

units.la: Declaratio.
units.tr: Explanation.

units.la: Conciliat Pater sibi omnia per Filium: v. 20. Sophiæ specie ne quis vos seducat: v. 8. Vetere exuti homine, nouum induite: v. 9. 10. Dominorum ergo seruos officium: v. 1.
units.tr: Reconciles: the Father reconciles all things to himself through the Son: v. 20. Of Wisdom: lest anyone deceive you by the appearance of wisdom: v. 8. Having put off the old man, put on the new: v. 9, 10. Of the lords, therefore the duty of servants: v. 1.

units.la: ANALYSIS EPISTOLÆ I AD THES-salonicenses.
units.tr: Analysis of the First Epistle to the Thessalonians.

units.la: THESSALONICA olim metropolis totius Macedoniæ, & in ora maritima loco ad-
units.tr: Thessalonica, once the metropolis of all Macedonia, and founded on the seacoast in a place ad-

units.la: [?] Reading of the italic word in the first verse line is uncertain. modum opportuno condita fuit, non procul à Berrœâ ad radices montis Citharij posita, quò sese Apostolus recepit seditione subortâ Thessalonicæ, vnde mox Athenas profectus, ad eos rescripsit hanc epistolam. Olim dicta fuit Therma, vnde sinus ille maris Thermaicus dictus est, vt est apud Herodotum lib. 7. Mutati nominis hæc videtur ratio: Philippus Amyntæ filius in his locis memorabili prælio Thessalos vicerat, in cuius rei memoriam vicinam vrbem Thermam appellauit Thessalonicam. De Pauli & comitum eius Silæ & Timothei in illam vrbem aduentu, & Thessalonicensium conuersione, vide Act.17.
units.tr: Thessalonica, formerly the metropolis of all Macedonia, was founded in a convenient place on the seacoast, not far from Berea, at the foot of Mount Citharius. The Apostle withdrew there when a sedition broke out at Thessalonica, and from there, having soon set out for Athens, he wrote this letter to them. It was formerly called Therma, and that gulf of the sea is therefore called the Thermaic Gulf, as in Herodotus, book 7. The reason for the change of name seems to be this: Philip, son of Amyntas, had defeated the Thessalians in a famous battle in these parts, and in memory of that event he named the neighbouring city Therma Thessalonica. For the arrival of Paul and his companions Silas and Timothy in that city, and the conversion of the Thessalonians, see Acts 17.

units.la: Ac magnam quidem eorum in fide constantiam fuisse, testatur ipse Apostolus cap. 1. & 2. Ideo non putauit, sibi faciendum, vt multum de doctrina ipsa repeteret, aut didascalicam epistolam ad eos scriberet, sed paraeneticam; laudans eorum constantiam, & hortans ad vitæ sanctitatem & sedulitatem in vocatione.
units.tr: That the Thessalonians were very steadfast in faith the Apostle himself testifies in chapters 1 and 2. For this reason he did not think it necessary to repeat much of the doctrine itself, or to write them a didactic letter. Instead he wrote a hortatory one, commending their steadfastness and exhorting them to holiness of life and diligence in their calling.

units.la: Prior epistola in duas partes præcipuas diuidi potest: Tria enim prima capita habent continuam fere narrationem, quâ eorum fidem & patientiam commendat, & suam in docendo fidelitatem, σοφίᾳ[?] & sollicitudinem erga eos ostendit. Altera pars cap. 4. & 5. est tota paraenetica, & ad genus deliberatiuum spectans, in qua suadet vitæ sanctitatem & charitatem Christianam: dissuadet luctum immodicum & gentilicium circa mortuorum funera, differens hac occasione de resurrectione mortuorum & vita æterna. Dehortatur etiam à curiosa vltimæ dici[?] inquisitione, monens, vt potius sese quotidie ad Christi aduentum religiosè comparent. Tandem etiam breuissimas de variis reb. admonitiones attexit.
units.tr: The former epistle can be divided into two main parts. The first three chapters contain an almost continuous narrative, in which he commends their faith and patience and shows his own faithfulness and care for them in teaching. The second part, chapters 4 and 5, is wholly hortatory and belongs to the deliberative kind. In it he urges holiness of life and Christian love, and dissuades them from excessive grief and the heathen mourning at funerals, using this occasion to discuss the resurrection of the dead and eternal life. He also warns them against curious inquiry into the last day, urging them rather to prepare themselves daily, in a godly way, for the coming of Christ. Finally, he adds some very brief admonitions on various matters.

units.la: Σύνοψις τυπικὴ[?]
units.tr: Typical synopsis [Σύνοψις τυπικὴ]

units.la: Paulus in Epistola ad Thessal: prima, post salutationem, Thessalonicenses tum Laudat quòd in tribulatione Euangelij Susceperint: cap. 1. Retinuerint, c.2. vbi etiam de ipsorum Suo ad illos introitu & conuersatione: couersione per ipsum: c.3. Confirmatio nem per Timot: Monet de Fugiendis: cap. 4. Faciendis: cap. 5.
units.tr: Paul, in the first Epistle to the Thessalonians, after the salutation: praises them because they received the Gospel in tribulation, chapter 1; they kept it, chapter 2, where he also speaks of his own coming to them and of their conversion through him; he confirms them through Timothy, chapter 3; he warns them what to flee from, chapter 4, and what to do, chapter 5.

units.la: Cap. I. Habet 1. Salutationem v.1. 11 Narrationem trimembrem: primò enim narrat quid quotidie propter Thessalonicenses agat, nempe quod Deo agat gratias pro donis spiritualibus in ipsos collatis: quorum etiam fontem indicat, videlicet electionem Dei: v. 2. 3.4. Deinde eâ occasione suum apud eos functum ministerium commendat ab ad-iuncta efficacia, v.5. Postremò, quomodo Thessalonicenses se gesserint, quum Paulus apud ipsos Euangelium praedicaret: nempe quod doctrinâ illam coelestem promte & alacriter amplexi sint fide: v.6. quod ipsum postea amplificat ex euentis, videlicet imitatione aliorum qui scilicet ipsos sint imitati, v.7. & fama fidei ipsorum apud complures diffusâ, v.8. )10. vbi etiam conuersionem ipsorum e suis parti-tus[?] plene describit, nimirum v. 9. & 10.
units.tr: Chapter 1. It contains: (1) a salutation, verse 1; (2) a narrative in three parts. First, he tells what he does daily on account of the Thessalonians, namely that he gives thanks to God for the spiritual gifts bestowed on them, and he indicates the source of these gifts, namely God's election, verses 2–4. Then, on that occasion, he commends the ministry he had performed among them, by the efficacy that accompanied it, verse 5. Lastly, he describes how the Thessalonians conducted themselves when Paul preached the Gospel among them: they embraced that heavenly doctrine promptly and eagerly with faith, verse 6. He then enlarges on this from the results, namely that they imitated others, or rather were imitated by others, verse 7, and that the report of their faith was spread among many, verse 8; where he also fully describes their conversion from idols, verses 9 and 10.

units.la: Cap. ii, In principio redit ad commendatio-nem sui apud Thessalonicenses functi ministerij: quam capite superiore v. 5. paucis attigerat. Atque in hac commendatione partim sibi tribuit boni Pastoris virtutes, partim à se remouet vitia quæ á Pastore debent esse aliena: vsque ad v. 13. Deinde rursum Thessalonicensium alacritatem sua in docendo diligentia respondentem, & eorundem infractam patientiam commendat, ipsosque contra scandalum incredulitatis Iudæorum confirmat, á v. 13. vsque ad 17. Postremò incipit se excusare, quòd ad ipsos non venerit, coram consolandi causa.
units.tr: Chapter 2. At the beginning he returns to commending the ministry he performed among the Thessalonians, which he had touched on briefly in verse 5 of the previous chapter. In this commendation he partly ascribes to himself the virtues of a good minister, and partly rejects from himself the vices that ought to be foreign to a minister, down to verse 13. Then again he commends the eagerness of the Thessalonians, which answered to his diligence in teaching, and their unbroken patience, and he confirms them against the scandal of the Jews' unbelief, from verse 13 to verse 17. Lastly, he begins to excuse himself for not having come to them, though he wished to come and console them.

units.la: Cap. iii. Pergit in institutâ sui excusatione cur ad ipsos non venerit, simulque argumen-ta quæ-dam affert quibus eos ad persecutionis tolerantiam & in fide perseuerantiam hortatur, ac tandem de suo ad ipsos veniendi proposito vehementer testatur. Sub finem huius capitis versu scil: penultimo in-cipit.
units.tr: Chapter 3. He goes on with the excuse he had begun, explaining why he did not come to them. At the same time he brings forward certain arguments by which he exhorts them to endure persecution and to persevere in faith, and at last he solemnly testifies to his purpose of coming to them. Near the end of this chapter, at the penultimate verse, he begins.

units.la: ALTERA EPISTOLÆ PARS,
units.tr: THE SECOND PART OF THE EPISTLE,

units.la: Ubi eos hortatur ad vitam Christianam; cuius duo capita generalia hic proponit, videlicet charitatem erga proximum, & cordis puritatem.
units.tr: Where he exhorts them to the Christian life; here he sets forth two general heads of it, namely love toward one's neighbour and purity of heart.

units.la: Cap. iv. Pergit in institûta paraenesi ad-studium pietatis, & varia vitæ Christianæ præcepta tradens, à variis contrariis vitiis dehortatur, vsque ad v. 13. vbi nominatim nimium defunctorum luctum vetans, hac occasione de resurrectione mortuorum & aduentu Domini ad iudicium docet.
units.tr: Chap. iv. Continuing his exhortation in the sphere of piety, he delivers various precepts of the Christian life and dissuades from various contrary vices, down to verse 13, where, expressly forbidding excessive mourning for the dead, on this occasion he teaches about the resurrection of the dead and the coming of the Lord to judgement.

units.la: Cap. v. in principio pergit in institutâ descriscriptione adventus Domini ad iudicium. Deinde redit ad exhortationes: quas pertexit usque ad v. 23. ubi concludit epistolam voto & privatis quibusdam admonitionibus & consueta salutatione.
units.tr: Chap. v. At the beginning he continues the description of the coming of the Lord to judgement. Then he returns to exhortations, which he carries on as far as verse 23, where he concludes the epistle with a prayer, certain private admonitions and the customary salutation.

units.la: SUMMÆ CAPITUM.
units.tr: SUMMARIES OF THE CHAPTERS.

units.la: Cap. I
units.tr: Chapter I

units.la: Gratulor ob vestram vobis nunc spemque fidemque, / Quam vos syncero corde tenere iuuat. / Nempe graues inter constanti corde tumultus / Exemplum fidei natio vestra fuit.
units.tr: I congratulate you now on your hope and faith, which it delights you to hold with a sincere heart. Indeed, amid grave tumults, with a steadfast heart, your nation has been an example of faith.

units.la: Doctrinae narrat propriae praeconia Paulus, / Vt fidei cernant fortia signa suæ. / Cognoscis fratres, vitae pia signa fidelis, / Nonigitur moneat impia turba, precor.
units.tr: Paul recounts the praises of his own teaching, so that they may discern the brave signs of their faith. You know, brothers, the pious signs of a faithful life; therefore, I pray, let not the impious crowd admonish you.

units.la: Timotheum misi, verbis qui subleuet almis / Vestram, cum vera religione fidem. / Quæ tamen haud unquam cum se submittat inanis, / Altisonum dignis laudibus usque veho.
units.tr: I have sent Timothy, to lift up your faith, together with true religion, with gracious words. Yet this faith, which never submits to empty things, I always carry on high with worthy praises.

units.la: Pergite constanti pietatem corde tenere, / Nec vitam immundâ polluat arte Satan. / Otia sint procul hinc: moderatum funera luctum / Posiunt[?], de terra surgere quippe solent.
units.tr: Persevere in holding piety with a steadfast heart, and let Satan not pollute your life with his impure arts. Let idleness be far from here; lay aside moderate mourning for the dead, for they are wont to rise again from the earth.

units.la: Incertum est Domini tempus, quo iudicet orbem, / Nos igitur curis invigilare decet. / Pastores doctos, sanctum & commendat amorem, / Cuncta probate: piis fausta venire precor.
units.tr: The time of the Lord, when he will judge the world, is uncertain, so we ought to keep watch over our cares. Commend learned ministers and holy love; test all things; I pray that good fortune comes to the pious.

units.la: ALITER
units.tr: Otherwise

units.la: Cap. I.
units.tr: Chapter I.

units.la: Astruit esse fidem veram, quam tradidit ante, / Cui quod crediderant, tollit ad astra viros.
units.tr: He asserts that the faith is true, which he handed down before; / to what they had believed, he lifts the men up to the stars.

units.la: Blandè se laudat, nec non sua facta sequentes. / Ne veniam Satanas pessimus ille vetat.
units.tr: He praises himself graciously, and likewise those who follow his deeds. / Lest that most wicked Satan forbid the pardon.

units.la: Confirmabit vos hic Palladis urbe profectus. / Usque videre iuuat gaudia magna datis.
units.tr: Having set out from the city of Pallas, he will strengthen you here. / It delights one to see, even to the end, the great joys given.

units.la: 4 Dat praecepta suis, & eorum laudat amorem, Quodque caro ad vitam sit reditura docet.
units.tr: 4 He gives precepts to his people and praises their love, / and teaches that the flesh is to return to life.

units.la: 5 Est ventura dies vt fur, vigilate, diei Nos sumus, haec moneo, verba notate mea.
units.tr: 5 The day will come like a thief: watch, we are the day. / I warn you; mark these words of mine.

units.la: SYMBOLA MEMOR:
units.tr: MNEMONIC SYMBOLS:

units.la: 1 2 3 4 5 Exemplar, Nutrix, Afflictio, in Aera, Charos.
units.tr: 1 2 3 4 5 Example, Nurse, Affliction, In the air, Dear.

units.la: Declaratio.
units.tr: Explanation.

units.la: Exemplar fidei sunt Thessalonicenses: v. 7. Nutrix fouens liberos suos.v.7.Afflictio neminem debet commouere: v. 3. in Aera rapientur viui in occursum domino: v. 17. charos quam maximè habeatis praesides vestros; v. 12. & 13.
units.tr: The examples of faith are the Thessalonians: v. 7. A nurse cherishing her children: v. 7. Affliction ought to move no one: v. 3. In the air: the living will be caught up to meet the Lord: v. 17. Dear: that you should hold your leaders most dear: vv. 12 and 13.

units.la: II EPISTOLA AD THESSALONI-censes.
units.tr: The Second Epistle to the Thessalonians.

units.la: OCCASIO epistolae huius posterioris ad Thessalonicenses scriptae petenda est ex priore. Nam cap. 2. v. 17. promiserat suum adventum: & cap. 3. v. 10. causam eius subindicauerat, quòd nimirum vellet supplere apud eos quaedam quae fidei ipsorum deessent, & quae data opera ad aduentum suum differebat. Capite 4 & 5. disseruerat de Domini Christi aduentu, seque his connumerauerat, quos Christus in hac vita esset deprehensurus, ex quo statim fluxit sinistra quaedam apud imperitos opinio, Christum nimirum venturum ad iudicium isto seculo, quo adhuc viuebat Apostolus: hinc illi ansam ad turpe otium arripientes, asserebant parum referre laborarent, nec ne, sine rerum omnium imminente, & ad hanc sententiam tuendam Apostoli autoritate abutebantur. Qua-re hanc secundam scripsit Epistolam ne Thes-salonicenses viderentur ab ipso negligi,cum vi-deret perpetuò occasiones conueniendi eos, si-bi eripi : item vt sententiam de aduentu Christi plenius explicaret, & otiosos ac curiosarum quæ-stionum amatores diligentius cauendos do-ceret.
units.tr: The occasion of this second letter to the Thessalonians is to be sought in the first. For in chapter 2, verse 17, he had promised his coming, and in chapter 3, verse 10, he had hinted at his reason: he wished to supply among them certain things that were lacking in their faith, and which he was deliberately deferring until his coming. In chapters 4 and 5 he had discussed the coming of the Lord Christ, and had counted himself among those whom Christ would find alive in this life. From this there arose a dangerous opinion among the unlearned, that Christ would come to judgment in this age, while the Apostle was still alive. Seizing on this as an excuse for shameful idleness, they asserted that it made little difference whether they worked or not, since all things were at hand, and they abused the Apostle's authority to defend this view. For this reason he wrote this second letter: so that the Thessalonians would not seem to be neglected by him, since he saw that his opportunities of meeting them were constantly being taken from him; also to explain more fully his teaching about the coming of Christ, and to teach that the idle and the lovers of curious questions must be guarded against more carefully.

units.la: Propositio totius epistolæ est: Constantia san-ctorum non solum ad crucis tolerantiam per-tinet, sed etiam ad opinionum veritatem, & tra-ditionum quæ verè sunt Apostolicæ conservationem, contra quascunque corruptelas, quæ vel nomine revelationum, vel spirituum, vel e-tiam autoritate Apostolica sanctis falsò obtru-di possunt. Partes epistolæ effen-[?]tiales, pro numero capitum, tres sunt:
units.tr: The proposition of the whole epistle is this: the steadfastness of the saints pertains not only to bearing the cross, but also to the truth of doctrines and to the preservation of traditions that are truly apostolic, against all corruptions which may be falsely thrust upon the saints, whether under the name of revelations, or of spirits, or even under apostolic authority. The essential parts of the epistle, according to the number of chapters, are three:

units.la: 1 Consolatoria contra persecutio-nes : cap. 1.
units.tr: 1. Consolatory, against persecutions: chapter 1.

units.la: 2. Prophetica, de aduentu Christi, & de Antichristo:cap.2.
units.tr: 2. Prophetic, concerning the coming of Christ and concerning the Antichrist: chapter 2.

units.la: 3. Paraenetica, ad varia pietatis of-ficia: cap. 3.
units.tr: 3. Paraenetic, concerning various duties of piety: chapter 3.

units.la: Cap. 1. (post inscriptionem, quæ continetur versu 1. & 2.) consolaturus eos, primum eis gratulatur ipsorum fidem & charitatem & tolerantiam: v. 3. & 4. Deinde cum persecutionum mentionem fecisset, consolationem subiungit: atque ita eos ad constantiam in persecutionibus tolerandis hortatur.
units.tr: Chapter 1 (after the inscription, which is contained in verses 1 and 2): intending to console them, he first congratulates them on their faith, their love and their endurance, verses 3 and 4. Then, having made mention of the persecutions, he adds consolation, and so exhorts them to constancy in enduring persecutions.

units.la: Cap. 11. Continetur secunda eaque præcipua huius epistolæ pars: vbi Paulus Thessalonicenses primum monet,ne patiantur se seduci falsâ doctrinâ,quasi instet dies extremi iudicij: v. 1. 2. & principio tertij. Deinde prædicit euenturam ante Christi aduentum apostasiam molto maximæ partis eorum qui Euangelium fuerint professi, itemque tyrannidem Antichristi, seu regni Antichristiani, nempe Papatus Romani; à v. 3. vsque ad v. 13. Postremo consolatur eos contra metum defectionis ac seductionis: simulque eos hortatur ad constantiam in doctrina ab ipso acceptâ; nec non veram consolationem atque constantiam à Deo eis exoptat: à v. 13. vsque ad finem capitis.
units.tr: Chapter 2 contains the second and chief part of this epistle, where Paul first warns the Thessalonians not to allow themselves to be led astray by false teaching, as though the day of the last judgment were at hand: verses 1 and 2, and the beginning of the third chapter. Then he foretells that before the coming of Christ there will be an apostasy of the greater part of those who have professed the gospel, and likewise the tyranny of the Antichrist, or the kingdom of Antichrist, namely the Roman papacy; from verse 3 to verse 13. Lastly, he consoles them against the fear of defection and seduction, and at the same time exhorts them to constancy in the doctrine they have received from him; and he also wishes for them from God true consolation and constancy: from verse 13 to the end of the chapter.

units.la: Cap. iii. Continetur tertia epistolæ pars, vbi varias admonitiones de Christiani hominis officio proponit: inter quas duæ præcipuæ sunt: vna de ignauo otio vitando, altera de disciplina ecclesiastica in inobedientes exercenda: vsque ad v. 16.
units.tr: Chapter 3 contains the third part of the epistle, where he sets forth various admonitions concerning the duty of a Christian man; among them two are chief: one, that idle inactivity must be avoided; the other, that church discipline must be exercised against the disobedient. This extends to verse 16.

units.la: Tribus vltimis versibus optatione & salutatione consuetâ epistolam concludit: simulque monet, se illam salutationem suâ manu subscribere solere in epistolis suis: ne scilicet falsæ pro veris supponerentur.
units.tr: In the last three verses he concludes the epistle with the customary wish and greeting; and at the same time he notes that he is accustomed to write that greeting with his own hand in his letters, so that false letters might not be passed off as genuine.

units.la: SVMMÆ CAPITVM. CAP. I.
units.tr: SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTER. CHAPTER I.

units.la: Gratia summa Deo, fidei quæ robora vestræ Adiuuat, ac hostes reprimit indeferos. Adueniet siquidem præscripto tempore Christus, Quem nos continua voce rogare decet.
units.tr: Grace, the highest gift from God, supports the strength of your faith and restrains the unbelieving enemies. For Christ will surely come at the appointed time, whom we ought to call upon with a constant voice.

units.la: Non tamen adueniet magni præsentia Christi, Ni prius adueniat ille prophanus homo. Qui specie falsa Christi pia nomina finget. Vos autem firmo pectore stare decet.
units.tr: Yet the presence of great Christ will not come unless first that profane man comes, who will feign the holy name of Christ under a false appearance. But you ought to stand with a firm breast.

units.la: Supremum sanctis precibus compellite Patrem, Vt verbi crescant semina sancta sui. Otia fugientes dignis compescite pœnis. Crescat & in sancto pectore sancta fidei [?]
units.tr: Beseech the Father at the last with holy prayers, that the holy seeds of his word may grow. Restrain those who flee from work with fitting punishments. And may holy faith grow also in the holy breast [?]

units.la: CAP. I
units.tr: CAP. I

units.la: Afflictos requies, Domino veniente, malosque Poena manet, dignos vos velit esse vocans. Ben Sathanæ veniet, quando? post talia, sed vos Elegit Dominus, iussa tenete mea. Consumant segnes proprio quæsita labore. Nam sic nos facimus, scribite cuncta mihi.
units.tr: Rest is for the afflicted when the Lord comes, and punishment remains for the wicked, while he calls you to be worthy. When will the son of Satan come? After such things. But the Lord has chosen you, so hold fast to my commands. Let the idle be consumed by what they have sought through their own labour. For thus we act; write all these things to me.

units.la: Breuissimè.
units.tr: Breuissimè.

units.la: Poenam, Antichristum, Vescatur pane laborans.
units.tr: Punishment; Antichrist; he who labours eats bread.

units.la: Declaratio.
units.tr: Declaratio.

units.la: Poenam pendent æterni exitij impij: v. 9. Antichristum describit, v.3. & seq. Vescatur pane laborans, non laborans non vescatur: v. 10.
units.tr: Punishment: the wicked suffer eternal destruction, v. 9. He describes Antichrist, v. 3 and following. "He who labours eats bread; he who does not labour does not eat," v. 10.

units.la: HACTENUS fuerunt Epistolæ, quæ à S. Paulo totis Ecclesiis particularibus inscriptæ sunt: sequuntur quæ scripta ab eodem & inscriptæ personis par-ticularibus: nimirum vel Euangelistis: vel aliis piis.
units.tr: Hitherto there have been the epistles which Saint Paul addressed to whole particular churches. There follow those written by the same author and addressed to particular persons, namely either to evangelists or to other pious men.

units.la: Euangelistis scriptæ sunt de Politia Ecclesiasti-ca, qualis constitui debet: ad Timotheum duæ, ad Titum una.
units.tr: Those written to evangelists concern ecclesiastical polity, as it ought to be constituted: two to Timothy, and one to Titus.

units.la: PRIOR AD TIMOTHEUM.
units.tr: THE FIRST EPISTLE TO TIMOTHY.

units.la: TIMOTHEUS natus patre Ethnico & matre Iudæa, Act. 16. à pueris tum à matre, tum ab avia in doctrina Ecclesiæ institutus fuit, 2 Tim: 1 Quia patre Græco progenitus, in prima infantia quoque circumcisus non est. Infra in 2. Epistola, cap. 1. maternum genus diffusius decladeclaratur. Hic Timotheus initio discipulus Apostolorum, postea propter alacritatem & fidem eximiam, in comitem multarum peregrinationum à Paulo adhibitus fuit.
