Tandem etiā cùm eum Apostolus videret in annis quidem nouellum, sed in virtutis & fidei laude proue-ctum, συνεργον[?] in prædicatione Euangelij esse passus est, & ad varias Ecclesias confirmandas eum non raro ablegauit. Eius honestissima fit mentio Rom. 16. 1. Cor. 16. 2 Thess. 3. Et vt communem habuit cum eo Ecclesiarum curam: sic communes voluit esse aliquot epistolas, vt ad Philippenses, Colossenses, Thessalonicenses. Ephesi autem fuisse Timotheum relictum, cùm haec epistola scriberetur, apparet ex cap. 1. v. 3. sed non est verisimile, eum ibi diu episcopatus munere functum, vt Eusebius & alij quidam putarunt. Nam multa loca ostendunt, eum plerumque Apostolo, etiam cum Romae captiuus esset, adfuisse.
units.tr: Timothy was born of a Gentile father and a Jewish mother (Acts 16). From boyhood he was taught the doctrine of the Church by both his mother and his grandmother (2 Tim. 1). Because his father was a Greek, he was not circumcised even in early infancy. Below, in the second Epistle, ch. 1, his mother's side of the family is set out more fully. Timothy was at first a disciple of the Apostles. Later, on account of his eagerness and outstanding faith, Paul took him as a companion on many journeys. Finally, when the Apostle saw that he was young in years but advanced in virtue and faith, he allowed him to be a fellow-worker [συνεργός] in preaching the Gospel, and often sent him to strengthen various churches. His very honourable mention is at Rom. 16, 1 Cor. 16 and 1 Thess. 3. And just as he shared with Timothy the care of the churches, so he wished some letters to be common to them, such as those to the Philippians, Colossians and Thessalonians. That Timothy was left at Ephesus when this epistle was written appears from ch. 1, v. 3. But it is not likely that he held the office of bishop there for long, as Eusebius and some others thought, for many passages show that he was mostly with the Apostle, even when Paul was a prisoner at Rome.

units.la: Occasio colligi debet ex primo capite huius epistolae, & ex 20. cap. Actorum. Nam Apostolus Paulus profecturus in Macedoniam, Timotheum reliquit Ephesi, vt scilicet ibi subsistens resisteret Nomodidascalis, aliisque corruptoribus sanae doctrinae, quos praevidebat illam Ecclesiam infestaturos. Deinde in illa Ecclesia nondum erat constitutus numerus ministrorum in docendo Euangelio necessarius, quem quidē[?] nemo rectius constituere poterat, quam is qui eligendi autoritatem diuinitus accepisset, qualis tum erat Apostoli, & inter eos Paulu[?], qui hanc curam Timotheo demandauit, atque ob id in electione quid debeat spectare, inpri-mis monet,ne cuiuis manus cito imponat, & ostendit qui ad ministerium admittendi,aut re-pudiandi sint. Hanc itaque Epistolam,non tam propter Timotheum, quàm vniuersam Eccle-siam scripsit, vt ea haberet ideam gubernationis ecclesiasticæ, & totius ministerij, quam dein-ceps tanquam regulam omnes sequerentur: no-minatim vero, vt suo calculo comprobaret Ti-mothei doctrinam, & sua autoritate iuuentuti eius præsidium afferret. Ne autem recordatio anteactæ vitæ in Iudaismo, Apostolo aliquid detraheret,non vult attendi , quid olim fuerit, quod non diffitetur,sed qualis per Dei gratiam sit factus.
units.tr: The occasion must be gathered from the first chapter of this epistle and from ch. 20 of Acts. The Apostle Paul, about to set out for Macedonia, left Timothy at Ephesus, so that by staying there he might resist the would-be teachers of the law and the other corrupters of sound doctrine, whom he foresaw would attack that church. Moreover, in that church the number of ministers necessary for teaching the Gospel had not yet been appointed. No one could appoint them more rightly than the man who had received from God the authority to choose, as the Apostles had, and among them Paul, who entrusted this care to Timothy. For this reason he warns above all about the choice: that hands should not be laid quickly on anyone, and he shows who are to be admitted to the ministry and who are to be rejected. He wrote this Epistle, then, not so much for Timothy's sake as for the whole Church, so that it might have a model of ecclesiastical government and of the whole ministry, which everyone would follow thereafter as a rule. He wrote it especially so that it might confirm Timothy's teaching by its own weight, and give young Timothy protection by his own authority. But lest the memory of his former life in Judaism should detract anything from the Apostle, Paul does not want attention paid to what he once was (which he does not deny), but to what he became through the grace of God.

units.la: Propositionem & scopum in hanc sententiam contrahimus. Timotheo summâ curâ anniten-dum est,vt in Ecclesia Ephesina quàm rectissi-mè omnia administret, tum in tuenda sana do-ctrina contra quasuis corruptelas, tum in ordi-nandis ministris Ecclesiarum , & in exequendo officio docendi & admonendi omnium ordi-num & ætatum homines. Hinc statuatur the-sis,seu generalis propositio: Omnes qui Eccle-siis præesse vtiliter volent, ad exemplum Ti-mothei, & ad præscriptum S. Pauli, ista quàm diligentissimè curare debent.
units.tr: We reduce the proposition and purpose to this sense: Timothy must take the greatest care to manage everything in the church of Ephesus as correctly as possible, both in defending sound doctrine against any corruptions, and in ordaining the ministers of the churches, and in carrying out the duty of teaching and admonishing men of every rank and age. Hence let this thesis, or general proposition, be laid down: All who wish to govern churches usefully ought to take the greatest care to do these things, after the example of Timothy and according to the precept of St Paul.

units.la: Genus principale est διδασκαλικόν, docens cap. 2. [?] quænam sit summa doctrinæ Christianæ, & eos reprehendens,qui relictâ Euangelij medul-lâ,inanibus disputationibus vacant: cap. 2. de necessitate ratione ac publicarum precum, & de persona ac officio Mediatoris, nec non de vero mulierum Christianarum ornatu: cap. 3. canones tradit & typos pastoris Euangelici, item de vita & morib. Diaconorum: cap. 4. Prophetiam subiicit de Apostasia vltimorum temporum, in qua graphicè admodum papatum nobis describit: cap.5. reliqua pertexit ad politiam Ecclesiae & bonos mores pertinentia: cap.6. de variis officiis regulas tradit: Item de recto vsu diuitiarum:&c: Pars Epistolae ad Tim. Inscriptio vice exordij v. 1. & 2. Propositio est v. 3. & 4. quae etiam repetitur v. 18. & 19. duobus versibus vltimis cap. sexto. Institutio cuius Primò de muneribus Praedicandi, per antithesin pseudoapostolorum & ipsius Pauli: cap. 1. Precandi in coetu publico cap. 2. Tractatio bipartitam [?] personis, vbi tradit praecepta Ecclesiastica de eligendis: vbi ostendit promouendos idoneos episcopos & diaconos. cap. 3. submouendos falsos doctores: c. 4. electis presbyteris & viduis: cap. 5. Ethica de seruis & diuitibus: cap. 6. Conclusio repetens principalem huius Epistolae propositionem: duobus versibus vltimis cap. 6.
units.tr: The principal kind is didactic [διδασκαλικόν], teaching (ch. 2) what is the sum of Christian doctrine, and rebuking those who, having abandoned the marrow of the Gospel, busy themselves with empty disputations. Ch. 2 deals with the necessity of public prayers, and with the person and office of the Mediator, and also with the true adornment of Christian women. Ch. 3 gives the rules and the types of the Gospel minister, and likewise the life and morals of deacons. Ch. 4 adds a prophecy about the apostasy of the last times, in which it describes the papacy to us very vividly. Ch. 5 continues with the rest, which pertain to the government of the Church and good morals. Ch. 6 gives rules concerning various offices, and likewise concerning the right use of riches, etc. The parts of the Epistle to Timothy are these. The inscription, serving as an introduction, is vv. 1 and 2. The proposition is vv. 3 and 4, which is also repeated at vv. 18 and 19 of the last chapter, ch. 6. The instruction has as its first part the duties of preaching, set out by contrast between the false apostles and Paul himself (ch. 1). The second part is prayer in the public assembly (ch. 2). The third part is the treatment of the persons, where he gives the ecclesiastical precepts concerning those to be chosen, and shows which bishops and deacons are fit to be promoted (ch. 3); which false teachers are to be removed (ch. 4); and concerning elders and widows who have been chosen (ch. 5). The fourth part is ethics, concerning slaves and the rich (ch. 6). The conclusion repeats the principal proposition of this Epistle, in the last two verses of ch. 6.

units.la: Cap. 1. praeter inscriptionem, quae continetur duobus primis versibus, duae sunt huius capitis partes: 1 Propositio summa de officio Timothei in coercendis per versis quibusdam legis doctoribus & in edificatione Dei quae est per fidem, id est, incremento cognitionis Dei, quae posita est in vera fide, procurando & promouendo: v.3. & 4. quae repetitur in fine cap. v. 18. & 19. 11. Tractatio propositionis per antithesin peruersi Nomodidascalorum studij (usque ad v.12). & commendationis sui (S. Pauli) ministerij seu Apostolatus.
units.tr: Ch. 1, apart from the inscription, which is contained in the first two verses, has two parts. (1) The chief proposition concerning Timothy's office: to restrain certain teachers of the law (vv. 3 and 4) and to promote and advance, by procuring it, the building up of God which is by faith, that is, the growth of the knowledge of God founded in true faith. This is repeated at the end of the chapter, vv. 18 and 19. (2) The treatment of the proposition by contrast: the perverse pursuits of the law-teachers (up to v. 12), and the commendation of Paul's own ministry or apostleship.

units.la: Cap. 11. in duas partes distingui potest. In prima parte hortatur ad publicas preces; & ostendit orandum pro quibusvis, ac nominatim pro regibus, & quibusvis magistratibus, usque ad vers. 8. In altera parte praecipit, quomodo se in publicis illis precibus & sacris conuentibus gerere debeant tum viri tum mulieres.
units.tr: Ch. 2 can be divided into two parts. In the first part he urges public prayers, and shows that prayer must be made for everyone, and especially for kings and all magistrates, up to v. 8. In the second part he instructs how men and women ought to conduct themselves in those public prayers and sacred assemblies.

units.la: Cap. 111. partes sunt duae. In prima docet, quales esse oporteat Episcopos, id est, pastores Ecclesiarum, itemque Diaconos, & utrorumque uxores, usque ad v. 14. In altera exponit, quo consilio ista ad Timotheum scribat, eaque occasione praecipua doctrina Christiana capita summatim commemorat.
units.tr: Ch. 3 has two parts. In the first he teaches what bishops, that is, the pastors of the churches, ought to be, and likewise deacons, and the wives of both, up to v. 14. In the second he sets out for what purpose he writes these things to Timothy, and on that occasion briefly recalls the chief heads of Christian doctrine.

units.la: Cap. 1V. primo praedicit Apostasiam euentu- ram posterioribus temporibus per quosdam falsos doctores, vbi in primis Antichristi doctrinam fugiendam admonet. usque ad v' 6. Deinde Timotheum ad varias officij sui partes cohortatur.
units.tr: Ch. 4 first foretells that apostasy will come in later times through certain false teachers, and there he warns above all to flee the doctrine of Antichrist, up to v. 6. Then he exhorts Timothy to the various parts of his office.

units.la: Cap. v. partes sunt tres: Nam primo monet, quomodo se gerere debeat Timotheus in reprehensionibus priuatis: v. 1. & 2. deinde quam curam debeat gerere viduarum, quarum aliquot recensetur genera: usque ad v. 17. postremo quomodo Ecclesia Ministri tractandi sint, edocet.
units.tr: Ch. 5 has three parts. First he advises how Timothy should conduct himself in private reproofs (vv. 1 and 2). Then what care he should take of widows, of whom several kinds are listed, up to v. 17. Last, he teaches how the ministers of the Church are to be treated.

units.la: Cap. VI. variae admonitiones continentur: ut de officio seruorum: (v. 1. & 2.) de vitandis per- uersis doctoribus; (v. 3. 4. 5.) de seruanda æquani- mitate, & fugienda auaritia, (usque ad v. 11.) de sectandis omnis generis virtutibus Christianis, ac inprimis fortitudine in defendenda doctrina Chri- stiana: (usque ad v. 17.) de officio diuitum; (v. 17. 18. 19.) & denique de inani Sophistices garrulita- te fugienda, v. 20. & 21. in quibus est Conclusio Epistolæ.
units.tr: Ch. 6 contains various admonitions: concerning the duty of slaves (vv. 1 and 2); concerning avoiding perverse teachers (vv. 3, 4 and 5); concerning maintaining equanimity and fleeing avarice (up to v. 11); concerning pursuing every kind of Christian virtue, and above all courage in defending Christian doctrine (up to v. 17); concerning the duty of the rich (vv. 17, 18 and 19); and finally concerning avoiding the empty chatter of sophistry (vv. 20 and 21), in which is the conclusion of the Epistle.

units.la: ARGVMENTA CAPITVM
units.tr: ARGUMENTS OF THE CHAPTERS

units.la: CAP. I.
units.tr: CHAP. I.

units.la: Inclyta describit Pastoris munera veri,
units.tr: The famous (letter) describes the duties of the true minister,

units.la: Et quæ doctrina forma tenenda fiet.
units.tr: And what doctrine and what form of teaching is to be held.

units.la: Vt doceat fidei synceri & munus amoris.
units.tr: That he may teach sincere faith and the duty of love.

units.la: Continet hoc totum religionis opus.
units.tr: This whole matter contains the work of religion.

units.la: 7 Summa Deo pietas, precibus se dedere sanctis,
units.tr: 7 The highest piety toward God lies in devoting oneself to holy prayers,

units.la: Et votis summum sollicitare patrem,
units.tr: And in earnestly petitioning the highest Father with vows.

units.la: Sit pia cura viris puras attollere dextras.
units.tr: Let it be a devout care to lift up pure hands.

units.la: Ornet fœmineum vita pudica genus.
units.tr: Let a chaste life adorn the female sex.

units.la: 3 Doctoris vitam tractat sanctique ministri,
units.tr: 3 He treats the life of the teacher and of the holy minister,

units.la: Cui sancti a Domino est tradita cura gregis.
units.tr: To whom the care of the holy flock has been committed by the Lord.

units.la: Coniugibusque horum quæ nam sit vita tenenda,
units.tr: He also says what life is to be kept by their wives,

units.la: Ne offendant Domini scandala cæca domum.
units.tr: Lest blind stumbling-blocks offend the house of the Lord.

units.la: 4 Doctrinam possint melius quo agnoscere falsam,
units.tr: So that they may better recognize false doctrine,

units.la: Illius quæ sint dogmata vana monet.
units.tr: He warns of the vain dogmas of it.

units.la: Instituit viduas pariter sanctosque ministros.
units.tr: He instructs widows likewise and holy ministers.

units.la: Fac stomachi infirmi sit tibi cura frequens.
units.tr: Let frequent care for the weak stomach be yours.

units.la: 5 Quo deceat monuisse modo iuuenesque senesque
units.tr: 5 In what manner it is fitting to admonish young men and old men

units.la: Fœmineumque genus, præcipit atque monet.
units.tr: And the female sex, he instructs and advises.

units.la: Instituit viduas pariter sanctosque ministros.
units.tr: He instructs widows likewise and holy ministers.

units.la: Fac stomachi infirmi sit ubi cura frequens.
units.tr: Let there be frequent care where the stomach is weak.

units.la: 6 Instituit seruos: doctrinæ dogmata sanctæ
units.tr: 6 He instructs servants: he hands down the holy dogmas of doctrine

units.la: Tradit, & hæc vigili mente docere iubet.
units.tr: And bids them teach these with a watchful mind.

units.la: Quanta timenda monet pestiferis incommoda auaris.
units.tr: He warns of how greatly to be feared are the troubles that come from pestilent covetous men.

units.la: Fac cautius vocum injuria vana cave.
units.tr: Be more cautious, and avoid the vain injury of words.

units.la: CAP. I
units.tr: CHAPTER I

units.la: Aufer legales scrupulos. lex nulla bonis est. Fers mihi in exemplar, Christe redemtor, opem.
units.tr: Take away lawful scruples; no law is for the good. Bring me help, Christ the Redeemer, as an example.

units.la: Belle pro cunctis orandum. unus mediator. Vir mulierque rogent, sit tamen illa silens.
units.tr: Pray well for all; there is one mediator. Let man and woman pray, yet let her be silent.

units.la: Curet Episcopus hæc, curent hæc iussa ministri. Si tarde veniam, sic rege tecta Dei.
units.tr: Let the bishop attend to these things, let the ministers carry out these commands. If I come late, so govern the house of God.

units.la: Dæmonibus credent supremo tempore multi. Ficta valere sinas, quæque iubemus age.
units.tr: In the last times many will believe demons. Allow false things to lose their force, and do what we command.

units.la: Elige sic viduas duplici digneris honore. Presbyteros, palam corripe, vina bibe.
units.tr: So choose widows; deign to honour them with double honour. Rebuke the elders openly; drink wine.

units.la: Falsi loquos vita, laqueos fuge divitiarum. Serua depositum, præcipe divitibus.
units.tr: Avoid false and idle talk; flee the snares of riches. Keep the deposit; charge the rich.

units.la: Breuissimè.
units.tr: In Brief.

units.la: Fabulæ, Adam, Domui, Pietas, Viduas, Oriuntur.
units.tr: Fables, Adam, House, Godliness, Widows, Arise.

units.la: Declaratio.
units.tr: Explanation.

units.la: Fabulæ non sectandæ: v. 4. Adam prior formatus est, deinde Eua: v. 13. Domui suæ qui bene præsit eligendus est Episcopus: v. 4. Pietas ad omnia utilis est: v. 8. Viduas honora quæ verè viduæ sunt: v. 3. Oriuntur ex verborum pugna lites, suspiciones malæ &c: v. 4.
units.tr: Fables are not to be pursued: v. 4. Adam was formed first, then Eve: v. 13. The bishop is to be chosen as one who rules his house well: v. 4. Godliness is useful for all things: v. 8. Honour widows who are truly widows: v. 3. Strife, evil suspicions, etc. arise from wrangling over words: v. 4.

units.la: II EPISTOLA AD TIMOTHEUM.
units.tr: The Second Epistle to Timothy.

units.la: OCCASIO huius secundæ ad Timotheum Epistolæ commodè sumi potest ex i-plo exordio, ex quo constat quod Timotheus Apostolum Paulum in vltimo digressu dimiserit multis lacrymis. Hunc dolorem in discipulo vt leniret, promisit illi in 1. Epist.; cap. 3. v. 14. suum reditum. Interea ut res humanæ incertæ sunt, Apostolus in vincula coniectus est, & ca-ptiuus Romam pertractus. Et res ita proce-dunt, ut tantum absit se redire posse Ephesum, ut potius præsentissima mors illi indies sit ex-pectanda, sicuti patet infra cap. 4. Itaque & fi-dem liberare voluit, apud Timotheum, & do-lorem lenire, & ipsum ad se Romam euocare certo consilio, ut scilicet ipsum contra molem persecutionum confirmaret, & de tota causa Religionis uberius cum illo conferret
units.tr: The occasion of this second Epistle to Timothy can conveniently be drawn from the opening itself, from which it is clear that Timothy had parted from the Apostle Paul at his last departure with many tears. To ease this grief in his disciple, Paul had promised him his return in the first Epistle, chapter 3, verse 14. Meanwhile, as human affairs are uncertain, the Apostle was thrown into chains and dragged to Rome as a captive. Events turned out so that he could not possibly return to Ephesus; rather, an imminent death was to be expected from day to day, as appears below in chapter 4. Therefore he wished, with a settled purpose, both to set his faith free before Timothy, to ease his grief, and to summon him to Rome, so that he might strengthen him against the mass of persecutions and confer with him more fully about the whole cause of religion.

units.la: Hæc igitur Epistola Romæ ex vinculis scripta miros habet affectus fidei, charitatis & animi ad martyrium ferendum præparati. Genus principale est προτρεπτικὸν [?] seu suasorium. Con-sumitur enim in adhortationibus ad constan-tiam in confessione, & ad synceritatem doctri-næ incorruptæ retinendam, ne propter vincula Pauli & imminens eius martyrium, vel propter Asiaticorum defectionem, aliorum animi la-bascerent. Non enim omnibus datum est credere & pati, Phil. 1. Et accedebat aliud malum quod plus Apostolum vexabat, quàm ipsa vincula, tædium scilicet Euangelicæ veritatis & simplicitatis, quod in multis videbat, & aures prurientes ad quæstiones inutiles & tales doctores audiendos, qui nec in doctrina synceri, nec in moribus integri erant.
units.tr: This Epistle, therefore, written from prison in Rome, has remarkable expressions of faith, love, and a mind prepared to endure martyrdom. Its principal kind is protreptic [προτρεπτικὸν] or persuasive. It is occupied with exhortations to constancy in confession and to keeping the doctrine uncorrupted in its sincerity, lest the hearts of others should waver because of Paul's chains and his impending martyrdom, or because of the defection of those in Asia. For it has not been given to everyone to believe and also to suffer (Phil. 1). And there was another evil that troubled the Apostle more than the chains themselves: the weariness with the simplicity and sincerity of the Gospel truth, which he saw in many, and their itching ears for useless questions and for hearing such teachers as were neither sound in doctrine nor blameless in morals.

units.la: Est ergo etiam hisce temporibus, huius Epi-stolæ doctrina utilissima, quibus multos pudet Euangelij propter crucem, multos eiusdem tædet propter eius simplicitatem, & doctrinâ de ve-tere homine abiiciendo, quæ plerisq; est odiosa.
units.tr: Therefore the teaching of this Epistle is also most useful in our own times, when many are ashamed of the Gospel because of the cross, many grow weary of its simplicity, and of the doctrine of putting off the old man, which is hateful to most people.

units.la: T. j. Salutationem, v. 1. & 2. Exordium: v. 3. 4. 5. Confirmatio-nem quæ primitus accommodatur ad tolerantiam præstandam sub cruce: cap. 1. deinde applicatur ad alteram partem de sana doctrinâ defendenda & propaganda, cap. 2. usque ad v. 14. Digressionem in ea vitia quæ sanam doctrinam ut plurimum euertunt; ac commodè distinguuntur in duos ordines: Alia enim in ipsis doctoribus ut plurimum resident, ut sunt λογομαχίαι, κενοφωνίαι [?], iuuenilis cupiditas, stultæ & incrudite quæstiones: usque ad finem capitis. 2. Alia communia sunt doctoribus cum auditoribus qualia recensetur cap. 3. usque ad v. 10. Reditum ad cœptam exhortationem vbi principales duos locos repetit, seruato ordine, scil: constantiam sub cruce, & de sana doctrinâ defendenda, ac propaganda: usque ad finem capitis. 3. Concludit: cap. 4. usque ad v. 9. Conclusionem continentem res priuatas: a v. 9. usque ad finem.
units.tr: Outline. Chapter 1. Salutation: verses 1 and 2. Opening: verses 3, 4 and 5. Confirmation, which is first adapted to the endurance to be shown under the cross, chapter 1; then it is applied to the other part, the defence and propagation of sound doctrine, chapter 2 up to verse 14. Digression into the vices that for the most part overturn sound doctrine; these are conveniently divided into two orders. The first, for the most part, reside in the teachers themselves, such as the λογομαχίαι and κενοφωνίαι [verbal battles and empty chatter], youthful desire, and foolish and uninstructed questions; this runs to the end of the chapter. The second, common vices, belong to teachers together with their hearers, of the kind listed in chapter 3 up to verse 10. A return to the exhortation begun, where he repeats the two principal points in their order, namely constancy under the cross, and the defence and propagation of sound doctrine; this runs to the end of the chapter. Chapter 3. He concludes: chapter 4 up to verse 9. A conclusion containing private matters, from verse 9 to the end.

units.la: Cap : 1. præmissâ salutatione (v. 1. & 2.)ordi-tur à commemoratione earum rerum quæ pertinebant ad testandum ipsius erga Timotheum amorem : ( v.3. 4. 5. ) Deinde illum hortatur ad studium studium proficiendi in cognitione Evangelii, & fa-cultate illius prædicandi, item ad fortitudinem & prudentiam in illo prædicando, nec non ad constan-tem Evangelii confessionem; & ad tolerantiam afflictionum illius causa: vbi exponit per occasionem beneficium Dei erga electos in conferenda ipsis sa-lute seu vita æterna: item annectit consolationem qua & seipsum & Timotheum contra sua vincula consolatur: (vsque ad v. 13. Tum ad exhortationes redit, & Timotheum ad sinceritatem hortatur ac prudentiam in doctrina Evangelii proponenda: (v. 13. & 14.) Postremò occurrit offendiculo quod ex sui a quibusdam defectione poterat exoriri: cui defectioni constantiam cuiusdam Onesiphori opponit.
units.tr: Chapter 1. After the salutation (verses 1 and 2), he begins by recalling those things that bore witness to his love for Timothy (verses 3, 4 and 5). Then he urges him to zeal in advancing in the knowledge of the Gospel and the ability to preach it, likewise to courage and prudence in preaching it, and also to constant confession of the Gospel and to endurance of afflictions for its sake. Here, in passing, he sets forth the benefit of God toward the elect in bestowing on them salvation, that is, eternal life. He also adds a consolation by which he comforts both himself and Timothy regarding his chains (up to verse 13). Then he returns to exhortations and urges Timothy to sincerity and prudence in setting forth the doctrine of the Gospel (verses 13 and 14). Finally, he meets a stumbling block that might arise from the defection of some; against this defection he sets the constancy of a certain Onesiphorus.

units.la: Cap. II. Ad exhortationes redit, ac Timotheum hortatur primùm ad alacritatem & tolerantiam in Evangelio docendo: (vsque ad v. 8.) deinde eum consolatur contra sua vincula & imminens supplicium: (vsque ad v. 14.) tertiò per digressionem quandam monet vt cohibeat contentiosos & vanos doctores: (vsque ad v. 22.) postremò ab aliis vitiis doctrinâ Evangelii deformantibus dehortatur, & commendat ei studium pacis & lenitatis in ignaris erudiendis.
units.tr: Chapter 2. He returns to exhortations and urges Timothy first to cheerfulness and endurance in teaching the Gospel (up to verse 8). Then he comforts him against his chains and the impending punishment (up to verse 14). Thirdly, by a certain digression he warns him to restrain contentious and vain teachers (up to verse 22). Lastly, he dissuades him from other vices that deform the doctrine of the Gospel, and commends to him the pursuit of peace and gentleness in instructing the ignorant.

units.la: Cap. III. Monet primò de hypocritis iam tum exorientibus in Ecclesiæ sinu, & postea amplius exorituris: (vsque ad v. 8.) quos vult vt Timotheus auersetur: & contra eosdem illum consolatur à turpi illorum exitu: (v. 8. 9.) Deinde ad cœptam exhortationem rediens suum ipsius exemplum Timotheo ad imitandum proponit tanquam fidelis doctoris: ac proinde Timotheum hortatur ad doctrinam à se acceptam constanter retinendam, simulque sa-cram Scripturam ei commendat.
units.tr: Chapter 3. He first warns about hypocrites who were already arising in the bosom of the Church and would arise more and more later (up to verse 8), whom he wants Timothy to avoid; and against them he consoles him with the shameful end of those men (verses 8 and 9). Then, returning to the exhortation begun, he sets before Timothy his own example to imitate, as that of a faithful teacher; and accordingly he urges Timothy to hold constantly to the doctrine received from him, and at the same time he commends the Holy Scripture to him.

units.la: Cap. IV. Redit ad exhortationes, & initio gravissima obtestatione adhibita Timotheum hortatur, vt omnibus boni doctoris atque pastoris partibus assiduè ac fideliter fungatur, à suo ipsius exemplo; vs-que ad v. 9. vbi incipit epistolæ huius
units.tr: Chapter 4. He returns to exhortations, and at the beginning, with a most solemn adjuration, urges Timothy to discharge all the duties of a good teacher and pastor faithfully and diligently, taking his own example; up to verse 9, where the conclusion of this epistle begins.

units.la: Conclusio
units.tr: Conclusion

units.la: Continens res priuatas, i aduentum eius esse accelerandum, quando præter mortem nihil amplius sperare potest: 2. admonet quibus rebus instructus venire debeat, (v. 11. 12. 13.) 3. querelas instituit de duplici hostium genere; (vsque ad v. 19.) 4. sequuntur salutationes, quibus interposita est ἐπεμβολὴ[?] de Erasto, Trophimo aliisque, & iterum monet de suo aduentu: postremo gemina comprecatione epistolam totam concludit: v. 21. 22.
units.tr: Containing the private matters: first, that his coming must be hastened, since beyond death he can hope for nothing more; second, he advises with what things he ought to come equipped (v. 11, 12, 13); third, he sets out complaints about a twofold kind of enemies (up to v. 19); there follow greetings, in which an insertion [epembole] is placed concerning Erastus, Trophimus and others, and he again warns about his coming; lastly, he concludes the whole epistle with a twofold prayer: v. 21, 22.

units.la: ARGVMENTA CAPITVM
units.tr: Arguments of the Chapters

units.la: ἐμμέτρα.
units.tr: ἐμμέτρα [in verse]

units.la: CAP. I.
units.tr: CHAPTER I.

units.la: GRatulor ob fidei tibi munera sancta fidelis: Qua te, qua matrem cerno valere tuam. Tu modo fac pergas constanti pectore semper. Ne moueat CHRISTI crux inimica piu.
units.tr: I congratulate you, faithful one, on the holy gifts of faith, by which I see that you and your mother are well. Only see to it that you press on always with a steadfast heart, lest the hostile cross move you, pious as you are.

units.la: Fac fortis Christi depugnes prælia miles, Nam Christum fortem vincula nulla ligant: Deficiunt multi: monuerat non dogmata sancta Fac tene, & errantes vt reuocare queas.
units.tr: Fight as a brave soldier the battles of Christ, for no chains bind the strong Christian. Many fall away, and holy doctrine has warned of this. Hold fast, so that you may also be able to call back those who err.

units.la: Vltima producent doctores tempora falsos, Qui toto cupiant perdere corde fidem. Tu tamen asbterea[?] Scriptura verba sequaris: Continet hæc totum religionis opus.
units.tr: The teachers will bring the last times, and false men will arise who desire with their whole heart to destroy the faith. Yet you, for your part, follow the words of Scripture: this contains the whole work of religion.

units.la: Diuini semper sac cures munera verbi: Hæc omnes puro corde docere velis. Tempus enim veniet, quo dogmata vera negabunt, Omnia sed felix vincere cura potest. Iustitiæ quoniam mihi iam datur alta corona, Quæ sibi postremò sint facienda monet.
units.tr: Always take care of the gifts of the divine word; you should wish to teach all these with a pure heart. For a time will come when men will deny the true doctrines, but care can happily overcome all things. Since the high crown of righteousness is now given to me, it advises what must be done for themselves at the last.

units.la: BREVIVS. CAP. I
units.tr: Brevius. Chapter I

units.la: AVge dona quæ habes, ante hac celata patefiunt. Depositum serua, viuat Onesiphorus. Bellator, pugil, agricola, Christusque resurgens, Cancer, vasa fides, sermoque recta docens. Consurgent lambri similes, hæc sum mala passus, Tradita conserues, omnia scripta iuuant. Doctrinam sanam sperneunt expectò coronam, Nunc absunt alij, nec mihi tunc aderant.
units.tr: Stir up the gift you have, which was once hidden and is now revealed. Guard the deposit; may Onesiphorus live. The soldier, the athlete, the farmer, and Christ risen, the crab-like canker, the vessels, faith, and the word teaching what is right. Like Jambres, they will rise up; these things I have suffered. Keep what has been handed down; all Scripture profits. They despise sound doctrine; I await the crown. Now others are absent, and they were not with me then.

units.la: Breuissimè.
units.tr: Very briefly.

units.la: Depositum, Tolerans, Ingrati, Penula Pauli,
units.tr: Deposit, Endure, Ungrateful, Paul's cloak,

units.la: Declaratio.
units.tr: Explanation.

units.la: Depositum illud præclarum serua: v. 14. Tolerans esto laborum: v. 3. Ingrati erunt homines extremis diebus: v. 2. Penula Pauli afferatur à Timotheo: v. 13.
units.tr: Guard that noble deposit: v. 14. Be enduring in hardships: v. 3. Ungrateful people will appear in the last days: v. 2. Timothy is to bring Paul's cloak: v. 13.

units.la: ANALYSIS EPISTOLÆ S. PAULI AD Titum.
units.tr: ANALYSIS OF THE EPISTLE OF ST PAUL TO TITUS.

units.la: TITUS natione Græcus, adeòque parentibus Ethnicis progenitus, & incircumcisus, (Gal. 2.) præceptorem habuit Apostolum Paulum, cuius etiam fuit in multis peregrinationibus comes, & non modo studiosissimus doctrinæ Euangelicæ, verùm etiam eiusdem præco,& Pauli in Ministerio collega, missus ab eo ad diuersas Ecclesias,tanquam legatus Christi. Sic ad Corinthios missus est ad colligendas Eleemosynas pro pauperibus qui erant in Iudæa; vt est in 2 ad Cor. 8. v. 6 & 16. Ex qui-bus constat eum Apostolo fuisse charissimum; quò facit etiam quòd passim illius facit honorificam mentionem,vt in 2.ad Cor. cap. 2. v.12. fratrem vocat,& 8. cap. v. 23. κοινωνὸν[?] & συνερ-γὸν[?]. In præsenti epistola, filium , In 2 ad Cor. cap. 7. v. 6. dicit se singularem consolationem accepisse ex reditu Titi.In 2. ad Timoth:cap.4. v. 10. scribit,illum abiuisse in Dalmatiam,haud dubie eò missus ab Apostolo ad docendum. Et in hac Epistola scribitur quod ab eodem in Creta,amplissima insula, vt quæ centum habitata fit vrbibus,fit relictus[?],non solùm ad docen-dum, sed etiam ad constituendum alios mi-nistros.
units.tr: Titus was a Greek by birth, and so born of Gentile parents and uncircumcised (Gal. 2). He had the apostle Paul as his teacher, and was his companion on many journeys. He was not only a most diligent student of the Evangelical doctrine but also its herald, and Paul's colleague in the ministry, sent by him to various churches as Christ's envoy. Thus he was sent to the Corinthians to collect alms for the poor who were in Judea, as is found in 2 Cor. 8, vv. 6 and 16. From this it is clear that he was most dear to the apostle. This is also shown by the fact that Paul makes honourable mention of him everywhere: in 2 Cor. ch. 2 v. 12 he calls him brother, and in ch. 8 v. 23 he calls him partner [κοινωνόν] and fellow-worker [συνεργόν]. In the present letter he calls him son. In 2 Cor. ch. 7 v. 6 he says he received singular comfort from Titus's return. In 2 Tim. ch. 4 v. 10 he writes that Titus had departed for Dalmatia, undoubtedly sent there by the apostle to teach. And in this letter it is written that he was left by the same apostle in Crete, a very large island, which is said to have a hundred inhabited cities, not only to teach but also to appoint other ministers.

units.la: Occasio scriptæ Epistolæ sumatur ex ipso Ex-ordio,in quo significat, Titum hoc consilio in Creta maris Mediterranei insula, ideò Episco-pum esse constitutum,vt oppidatim constitue-ret ministros, & docendo populi corrigeret mores. Nam cùm Satanas sua Zizania semper spargere conetur in agrum Domini, & loci illius incolæ præ aliis Græcis vani & ignaui essent,præmaturè exorti sunt in illa Ecclesia,vt ex hac epistola colligere non est difficile,duo ho-minum genera, qui veritatem doctrinæ Euan-gelicæ labefactarent. Prius ex circumcisione siue Iudaeis superstitiosi homines, qui disputationibus curiosis de cibis, gerealogiis, & aliis Iudaicis fabulis plus quàm doctrinae fidei & pietatis dediti erant, & se apud vulgus venditabant, quos cap. 1. perstringit, v. 10. & 14. Alij praetextu Evangelij, ordinem politicum & studium bonorum operum negligebant, quos notat cap. 2. v. 12. & cap. 3. v. 18. Apostolus igitur ut illis occurreret, & sua autoritate ministerium Titi, quem ordinauerat, muniret, hanc Epistolam scripsit in gratiam totius Ecclesiæ, ut Titi ministerium omnes reuererentur, & sibi cauerent ab illis sycophantis, ne Cretensibus competeret nota illa infamis, quâ jam olim ab Epimenide erant notati,
units.tr: The occasion of the letter is taken from its very beginning, where he indicates that Titus was set in Crete, an island of the Mediterranean Sea, as bishop for this purpose: that he might appoint ministers town by town and, by teaching, correct the morals of the people. For since Satan always tries to scatter his tares in the Lord's field, and the inhabitants of that place were more empty and idle than other Greeks, there arose prematurely in that church, as is not difficult to gather from this letter, two kinds of men who would undermine the truth of the Evangelical doctrine. The first were superstitious men from the circumcision, that is, Jews, who devoted themselves to curious disputes about foods, genealogies and other Jewish fables, more than to the doctrine of faith and godliness, and who put on a show before the common people; he rebukes them in ch. 1 vv. 10 and 14. Others, under the pretext of the Gospel, neglected civil order and the pursuit of good works; he notes them in ch. 2 v. 12 and ch. 3 v. 18. The apostle therefore, in order to meet them, and to strengthen with his authority the ministry of Titus whom he had ordained, wrote this letter for the good of the whole Church, so that all would revere Titus's ministry and beware of those sycophants, and so that that infamous mark, with which the Cretans had long before been branded by Epimenides, might not fit them.

units.la: Argumentum quod attinet: primò cur apud Cretenses reliquerit Titum, & quae sint veri Episcopi partes, praesertim erga refractarios & sycophantas, quorum multi apud Cretenses erant, describit Apostolus. Deinde certarum personarum & aetatum edocet officia, monens ut omnes suo loco doctrinam Evangelij honestâ vitâ exornent, argumento à fine redemptio-nis ducto, cuius modum & summam cap. 2. assignat. Inde ad ordinem politicum transit, ne quis putet Evangelium tollere politias, hoc praetextu, quòd magistratus tunc erant alieni à religione: ideò reuocat eis in memoriam vitam priorem in errorum tenebris transactam, & totam rationem nostrae iustificationis, quae vere & mere est gratuita, & tamen non abigit, sed exigit studium bonorum operum, atque ea quae honesta sunt & sociatati humanae utilia, cap. 3. Et ibi repetit iterum in fine admonitionem de inutilibus quæstionibus vitandis, & præcepta dat quomodo cum præfractis hæreticis sit agendum.
units.tr: As to the argument: first, Paul describes why he left Titus in Crete and what the duties of a true bishop are, especially toward the stubborn and the sycophants, of whom there were many among the Cretans. Then he teaches the duties of particular persons and ages, warning that all should adorn the doctrine of the Gospel with an honourable life in their own place, using an argument drawn from the purpose of redemption, whose manner and sum he sets out in ch. 2. Then he passes to civil order, lest anyone think the Gospel abolishes civil government on the pretext that the magistrates at that time were hostile to religion. He therefore recalls to them their former life, spent in the darkness of error, and the whole reason of our justification, which is truly and purely gratuitous, and yet does not drive out but demands zeal for good works, and for things that are honourable and useful to human society, ch. 3. And there he repeats again, at the end, the warning to avoid useless questions, and gives precepts on how to deal with obstinate heretics.

units.la: PARTES
units.tr: PARTS

units.la: Sunt Procemium, in quo Paulus suum commendat Apostolatum & Titum salutat, à v. 1. cap. 1. usque ad v. 5. Tractatio principalis, à v. 5. cap. 1. usque ad v. 12. cap. tertij, & Conclusio de quibusdam rebus priuatis, cap. 3. à verf. 12. usque ad finem. In principali Tractatione informat Titum quo-ad Disciplinam Ecclesiasticam, quid Tito in eligendis & ordinandis Pastoribus sequendum, quid fugiendum: cap. 1. Admonitionem spectantem speciatim ad certas personas & ætates in œconomia & Ecclesia, cap. 2. generatim ad Christianos omnes quales se exhibere debeant erga Magistratus politicum. Proximum. Hæreticos cap. 3.
units.tr: There is an Introduction, in which Paul commends his apostleship and greets Titus, from ch. 1 v. 1 to v. 5. The principal treatment runs from ch. 1 v. 5 to ch. 3 v. 12. And there is a Conclusion on certain private matters, ch. 3 from v. 12 to the end. In the principal treatment he instructs Titus on church discipline: what he must follow and what he must avoid in choosing and ordaining ministers (ch. 1); an admonition directed specifically to certain persons and ages in the household and the Church (ch. 2); and, in general, how all Christians ought to conduct themselves toward the civil magistrate and their neighbours; the heretics (ch. 3).

units.la: Obseruandum est artificium Spiritus S. in breui hac Epistola, qui in 1 cap. Ecclesiastica, in 2. Oeconomica, in 3 politica officia tradit.
units.tr: The artifice of the Holy Spirit is to be observed in this short letter, who in ch. 1 delivers the ecclesiastical duties, in ch. 2 the household duties, and in ch. 3 the civil duties.

units.la: Cap. 1. Post procemium 4. primis versibus comprehensum, monet Titum, ut in Ecclesiarum Cretensium constitutione pergat, ac primum ut oppidatim constituat Pastores, (v. 5.) Deinde describit, quales pastores deligendi sint, seu quibus virtutibus præditos esse oportet: (usque ad v. 10.) postremò, occasione virtutis quam postremam commemorauit, transit ad reprehensionem vanovanorum doctorum, quibus os obturari debeat.
units.tr: Ch. 1. After the introduction, comprised in the first four verses, he advises Titus to proceed in the constitution of the Cretan churches, and first to appoint ministers town by town (v. 5). Then he describes what kind of ministers are to be chosen, or what virtues they ought to possess (down to v. 10). Finally, on the occasion of the last virtue he mentioned, he passes to the rebuke of empty talkers, whose mouths must be stopped.

units.la: Cap. ii. Singulorum statuum in œconomia vi-tam informat, ac Titum admonet, vt in omnibus se præbeat exemplum bonorum operum, vsque ad v. 11. Deinde rationes enumerat grauissimas, quibus singulı ad officia sua studiose obeunda debeant monerı; a v. 11. vsque ad vltimum, in quo hanc exhortationem Epiphonemate concludit.
units.tr: Ch. 2. He sets out the way of life for each order in the household, and admonishes Titus to show himself in all things as a pattern of good works, down to v. 11. Then he lists the most weighty reasons by which each should be urged to discharge his duties diligently, from v. 11 to the end, where he concludes this exhortation with an epiphonema.

units.la: Cap. iii. Monet Titum de officiis quibus-dam communibus quæ auditoribus suis debeat suggerere: vt de subditorum erga Magistratum obedientia, ac præcipuè de humanitate erga extra-neos seu alienos à fide Christiana; cuius admonitio-nis rationes grauissimas adfert, partim à veteri natu-ra statu, partim à præsenti statu gratiæ deductæ: vsque ad v. 8. Deinde repetit admonitionem generalem de vrgendo studio bonorum operum: & contra hortatur eum ad cohibendum doctrinas inutiles, & contentiones; vsque ad v. 12. ad extre-mum concludens Epistolam de rebus priuatis quaedam addit.
units.tr: Ch. 3. He advises Titus about certain common duties which he ought to impress upon his hearers: chiefly obedience of subjects toward the magistrate, and courtesy toward strangers, that is, those outside the Christian faith. He brings very weighty reasons for this admonition, drawn partly from our former natural state and partly from our present state of grace, down to v. 8. Then he repeats the general admonition to press zeal for good works, and on the other hand urges him to restrain useless doctrines and contentions, down to v. 12. Concluding the letter, he adds certain matters concerning private affairs.

units.la: ARGVMENTA CAPITVM CAP. I.
units.tr: ARGUMENTS OF THE CHAPTERS. CHAP. I.

units.la: Inclyta qui doceas posui te mænia Creta. Fac animo officium nunc vigilante tuum, Presbyteros statues edoctos dogmata sancta. Non deerunt etenim dogmata falsa tibi.
units.tr: I placed you, who teach, on the famous walls of Crete. Now with a watchful mind perform your duty: appoint elders instructed in holy doctrines. For false doctrines will not be lacking to you.

units.la: 2 Instituit iuuenes fortes seruosque senesque, Cumque viris pariter fœmineumque genus. Vera etenim nobis apparuit ansa salutis. Præcipit hæc vitæ munera digna pie.
units.tr: 2 He instructs young men, strong men, servants and old men, along with men and the female sex. For the true handle of salvation has appeared to us. He prescribes these duties of life, fitting for piety.

units.la: 3 Principibus iubeat semper parere supremis, Quæ vitæ fuerit pristina forma, docet.
units.tr: 3 He bids them always obey the supreme rulers; he teaches what was their former form of life.

units.la: Divini ut videant non frivola signa favoris. / Quaeque sit haereticis forma tenenda, monet.
units.tr: That they may see that the signs of divine favour are not trifling. And he warns what form is to be kept against heretics.

units.la: BREVIVS. CAP. I
units.tr: BREVIVS. CAP. I

units.la: Abste pontifices hi [?] siant argue Cretae. / Sunt bona concta bonis, sunt mala cuncta malis. / Bis duplicem memorat sexum, piagratia [?] Christi / Nunc tandem apparens, omnia iusta petit. / Consule parendum, gratis nos Christe vocasti. / Bis monitum fugito, Nicopolimque veni.
units.tr: Away with these [?] high priests of Crete. All things are good to the good, and all things are bad to the bad. He recalls the twofold sex twice; Christ's grace, now at last appearing, seeks all things just. Be obedient, as it is to be obeyed: Christ, you called us freely. Shun the man once and again warned, and come to Nicopolis.

units.la: Breuissimè.
units.tr: Breuissimè.

units.la: Vaniloquis,& Anus, Haereticumque fuge.
units.tr: Vaniloquis, & Anus, Haereticumque fuge.

units.la: Declaratio.
units.tr: Declaratio.

units.la: Vaniloquis obturandum os:v.10. & Anus sint habi-tu qui sanctimoniam deceat: v.3. Haereticumque fuge post unam & alteram admonitionem:v.10.
units.tr: Vaniloquis: the mouth is to be stopped, v.10. & Anus: they should have the bearing that befits holiness, v.3. Haereticumque fuge: after one or two admonitions, v.10.

units.la: ANALYSIS EPISTO-LÆ AD PHILE-monem.
units.tr: ANALYSIS OF THE EPISTLE TO PHILEMON.

units.la: IN paulo-pleniore breuissimæ huius inter Paulinas Epistolæ Analysi, gustum seu specimen extraordinariæ nostræ, in cœtu studiosorum. S. Scripturæ lectionis & considerationis, præbiturus;primo de persona ad quam scribitur, deinde de scripti occasione, tertio de eiusdem pro-positione & summa, quarto de partibus eius quædam delibanda sunt: postea illa quæ ad spe-cialem Analysin Logicam & Theologicam pertinent, breuiter expediam.
units.tr: In this rather fuller analysis of the very short Pauline epistle, I shall offer a sample, as it were, of our extraordinary method of studying and considering Holy Scripture for the gathering of students. Some preliminary matters must be touched on: first, the person to whom it is written; second, the occasion of the writing; third, its proposition and summary; fourth, its parts. After that I shall briefly deal with those matters that belong to the special analysis, both logical and theological.

units.la: Philemon cui scribitur & inscribitur præsens S. Pauli Epistolium, Colossensis fuit, vt placet S. Hieronymo. Archippi enim Paulus in Epistola ad Colos: cap. 4. versu penultimo mentionem facit, quem in huius Epistolæ inscriptione cum Philemone coniungit. Porrò ex præsenti scripto colligi potest hominem fuisse diu-tem, magnisque inter suos conciues nominis, ad Christum ex Pauli prædicatione conuersum, & de Ecclesia Christi bene meritum: in cuius domo, tanquam priuata in Ecclesia, multi fuerunt peregrini, in quos liberalis & hospitalis fuit, vt constat ex v. 7. vbi habetur, quòd consolatus pauperes & viscera sanctorum refocillatus sit. Ad hunc igitur tanquam hominem notum & iure hospitij familiarem, imò & cooperarium suum, in Euangelij cursu suis opibus & liberalitate promouendo, Paulus præsentem scripsit Epistolam.
units.tr: Philemon, to whom the present epistle of St Paul is written and addressed, was of Colossae, as St Jerome thinks. For Paul, in his Epistle to the Colossians, chapter 4, verse 17 (the penultimate verse), mentions Archippus, whom he joins with Philemon in the address of this letter. Moreover, from the letter itself it can be gathered that the man was wealthy and held in great repute among his fellow citizens, that he had been converted to Christ through Paul's preaching, and that he had deserved well of the Church of Christ. In his house, as in a private church, many strangers were received, and he was generous and hospitable towards them, as is clear from verse 7, where it is said that he had refreshed the poor and the bowels of the saints. Paul therefore wrote the present epistle to him as a man known to him and familiar by the right of hospitality, and indeed as his fellow worker, whom he wished to promote the course of the gospel by his means and generosity.

units.la: Occasio:Philemon servum habuit Onesimum, qui (vt hoc genus hominum tum solebat) furto commisso aufugerat ab hero suo. Romam autem cùm venisset, audiuit Paulum docentem Euangelium, cuius doctrina in seruo fugitiuo fuit efficax, adeò vt conuersus ad fidem Christianam, seruiret Apostolo in vinculis: qui fuga & culpa eius intellecta, iussit ad herum redire, vtque illi facilius reconciliaretur, hac epistola aditum ei fecit.
units.tr: Occasion: Philemon had a slave, Onesimus, who, as slaves of that sort then commonly did, had run away from his master after committing a theft. When he had come to Rome, he heard Paul preaching the gospel, and the doctrine was effective in this fugitive slave, so that, converted to the Christian faith, he served the Apostle in his chains. Paul, understanding both the flight and the fault, sent him back to his master, and, so that he might be reconciled to him more easily, he opened the way for him by this letter.

units.la: Summa:Paulus Onesimum seruum furem & fugitiuum, à se in vinculis conuersum, Philemoni tanta humanitate, modestia, & suauitate commendat, vt maiore non potuerit. Et hac intercessione tam sollicita docet: Christum ve-nisse in hunc mundum, vt peccatores saluos faciat: &, lapsos, vbi resipuerint, recipiendos, & cum iis, quos offenderunt, reconciliandos esse. Propositio igitur est: Philemon condonato delicto, Onesimum in gratia debet recipere. v. 10.
units.tr: Summary: Paul commends Onesimus, a slave, thief and fugitive, who had been converted by him while in chains, to Philemon with such humanity, modesty and gentleness that he could not have done so more warmly. And by this earnest intercession he teaches that Christ came into this world to save sinners, and that those who have fallen, once they have repented, are to be received back and reconciled with those whom they have offended. The proposition, therefore, is this: Philemon, having pardoned the offence, ought to receive Onesimus into favour (v. 10).

units.la: Partes. Breuis quidem est Epistola: attamen partes Epistolae (quas orationis partes appellant Rhetores) omnes attingit. Habet enim, post Epigraphen & salutationem, Exordium, Propositionem, Petitionem, Confirmationem, Confutationem, & Conclusionem.
units.tr: Parts. The epistle is indeed brief, yet it touches on all the parts of a speech (which the rhetoricians call the parts of oratory). For after the epigraph and the salutation it contains the exordium, the proposition, the petition, the confirmation, the refutation and the conclusion.

units.la: Epigraphe seu titulus iustae magnitudinis ex suis integris constituitur partibus, nimirum subscriptione, inscriptione & salutatione, in quibus omnia ad conciliandam benevolentiam, & ad eo facilius quod postea petiturus est, impetrandum, diriguntur.
units.tr: The epigraph or title, of fair size, is made up of its complete parts, namely the subscription, the inscription and the salutation, all of which are directed to winning goodwill and to making it easier to obtain what he is afterwards going to ask.

units.la: Post Epigraphen sequitur ipsa πραγματεία[?] seu tractatio, sex illas orationis partes, vt iam annotatum, complexa.
units.tr: After the epigraph follows the discourse itself, the treatment [πραγματεία], or tractatio, which embraces those six parts of the speech, as has already been noted.

units.la: Primo est Exordium, (v. 4. 5.[?] 6. 7.) ad benevolentiam conciliandam & fouendam accommodatum. Namtestatur de suo erga Philemonem amore a suis effectis, nempe quod 1. & Deo gratias pro illo agat(v. 4.) cuius gratiarum actionis obiectum exponit, atque eadem opera Philemonis virtutes collaudat,(v. 5.) 2 & eundem pro ipso precetur, cuius precationis obiectum exponit, videlicet vt Philemonis fides & charitas per communicationem beneficiorum atque officiorum augescat atque innotescat(v. 6.) eandem charitatem & beneficentiam amplificat ex effectis, videlicet gaudio suo & conso-
units.tr: First comes the exordium (vv. 4, 5, 6, 7), suited to winning and fostering goodwill. For he attests his love towards Philemon from its effects, namely that (1) he gives thanks to God for him (v. 4), the object of which thanksgiving he sets out, and at the same time he praises Philemon's virtues (v. 5); (2) and he prays for him likewise, the object of which prayer he sets out, namely that Philemon's faith and love, through the sharing of benefits and services, may grow and become known (v. 6). He magnifies this same love and beneficence by its effects, namely his own joy and consolation which he derives from it (v. 7).

units.la: 2 Hierarchie Der schmuck (s) der Arbeitsleiter consolatione quam inde percipiat: (v. 7.)
units.tr: consolation which he derives from it (v. 7).

units.la: 2. Propositio generalis est v. 8. & 9. Ubi significat se Philemonem pro re quapiam precaturum: & hanc generalem sententiam amplificat antithesi diversorum, per enunciatum discretū: Quanquam habeo potestatem mandandi tibi, (v. 8.) tamen precabor (v. 9.) Huius discreti utramque partem illustrat ex causis.
units.tr: (2) The general proposition is in vv. 8 and 9. There he signifies that he will ask Philemon for something, and he amplifies this general statement by an antithesis of opposites, through a distinct sentence: although I have the authority to command you (v. 8), yet I will rather beg (v. 9). He illustrates each part of this distinction by its reasons.

units.la: Tertiò, est Petitio ipsa, ubi ostendit, 1.pro quo roget, nempe pro Onesimo (v. 10. & 11.) ubi & descriptio quaedam Onesimi est, ab eius adiunctis duobus, quae totidem sunt huius petitionis argumenta. 2 quid petat, nempe ut illum recipiat, (v. 12.)
units.tr: Third is the petition itself, where he shows (1) for whom he asks, namely for Onesimus (vv. 10, 11), where there is also a certain description of Onesimus from two of his attributes, which are two arguments for this petition; and (2) what he asks, namely that Philemon receive him (v. 12).

units.la: 4. Est Confirmatio, in qua propositae petitio-nis rationes plures adiungit. Plures dico, quia jam in exordio, propositione & petitione hinc inde spar-sa sunt semina argumentorum, quae ad flectendum Philemonem valebant. Prima igitur (praeter su-periores) petitionis ratio est, quòd Paulus tanti faciat fidem Onesimi in ministrando, ut eum cupi ve-rit apud se retinere, (v. 13.) cur autem id non fecerit, sed eum remiserit, exponit v. 14. Secunda ratio continetur v. 15. Videlicet consideratio providentia Dei, qua fugam istam Onesimi ita gubernauit, ut per illius occasionem ita immutaretur, ut in po-sterum non amplius fugitivus sit futurus, sed perpe-tuò cum suo Domino mansurus, eique fideliter serviturus. Tertia ratio continetur v. 16. Quia Onesimus ex servo factus sit frater, nempe frater in Christo, ac proinde jam duplici nomine diligendus Philemoni: videlicet tum secundum carnem, ut servus, tum secundum spiritum, ut Christianus. Quartū ar-gumentū est v. 17. ab amore Philemonis erga Pau-lum, tanquam socium: summaq; ipsa petitio renovatur.
units.tr: (4) There is the confirmation, in which he adds several reasons for the petition he has put forward. I say several, because already in the exordium, the proposition and the petition, seeds of arguments fit for moving Philemon have been scattered here and there. The first reason for the petition (besides those already given) is that Paul values so highly Onesimus's faithfulness in serving that he wished to keep him with himself; and why he did not do so, but sent him back, he explains in v. 14. The second reason is contained in v. 15, namely the consideration of God's providence, which so directed this flight of Onesimus that through it he was so changed that in future he would no longer be a fugitive, but would remain with his master for ever and serve him faithfully. The third reason is in v. 16: Onesimus, from a slave, has become a brother, that is, a brother in Christ, and therefore is now to be loved by Philemon under a double title: on the one hand according to the flesh, as a slave, and on the other according to the spirit, as a Christian. The fourth argument is in v. 17, drawn from Philemon's love towards Paul as his partner; and the petition itself is renewed in this same sentence.

units.la: 5. Confutatio,in qua per prolepsin crimen furti,quod reconciliationi obstare poterat, diluit, dum spondet, se pro Onesimo satisfacturum Philemoni (v. 18. & 19. ) veruntamen addit correctionem, qua significat, aequum non esse vt Philemon hoc debitum exigat: quippe qui ipsi longe plus debeat, nempe seipsum. Quibus verbis significat,Philemonem a se in fide Christiana quam fidelissime institutum esse. Ex his omnibus conclusionis loco infert, Philemonem petitioni sua locum concessurum. v. 20.
units.tr: (5) The refutation, in which, by prolepsis, he removes the charge of theft, which could have stood in the way of reconciliation, while promising that he will make satisfaction to Philemon for Onesimus (vv. 18, 19). Yet he adds a correction, by which he signifies that it is not fair for Philemon to demand this debt, since he himself owes far more, namely himself. By these words he signifies that Philemon had been most faithfully instructed by him in the Christian faith. From all these things, as the conclusion, he infers that Philemon will grant his petition (v. 20).

units.la: 6. Epilogus:vbi primum significat suam spem de Philemonis gratificatione, v. 21. Deinde petit sibi parari hospitium, atque ita significat suam spem de sui e vniculis liberatione, cuius causas exponit duas, videlicet preces fratrum & gratiam Dei, v. 22. Tertio, verbis quorundam Philemonem salutat, v. 23. 24. Postremo epistolam concludit voto consueto. v. vlt.
units.tr: (6) The epilogue: where first he expresses his hope of Philemon's compliance (v. 21). Then he asks that a lodging be prepared for him, and so expresses his hope of being freed from his chains, the causes of which he sets out as two, namely the prayers of the brothers and the grace of God (v. 22). Third, he greets Philemon with the names of certain people (vv. 23, 24). Finally he concludes the epistle with the customary wish (last verse).

units.la: Sic fuit explicatio logica, sequitur applicatio theologica, in vsu tum theoretico, tum practico.
units.tr: Thus the logical explanation is complete; there follows the theological application, in both its theoretical and its practical use.

units.la: Vsus theoreticus 1. in didascalia seu doctrina fidei, ex v. 4. Fidei ingenium est, Deum statuere esse Deum suum: item, promissionem gratiae omnibus credentibus factam, sibi priuatim applicare. Hinc Paulus ex fide dicit, Gratias ago Deo meo. Sic Gal. 2. v. 20. de Christo loquens ait, Qui dilexit me, & tradidit semetipsum pro me. Item ex v. 5. & 6. Praecipua Dei dona sunt, Fides & charitas, pro his enim Philemoni collatis Paulus nominatim gratias Deo egit; & vt illi augerentur, orauit. ii[?] in ἐλέγχῳ[?] seu refutatione falsi dogmatis ex v. 18:contra Anabaptistas: Communio illa fidelium siue sanctorum, non tollit rerum dominia; secus enim nemo posset alteri quicquam debere. At Paulus significat, Onesimum aliquid debere Philemoni, nempe idipsum quod furto abstulerat. Deinde Paulus restituit fugitivum utroque Christiano existen-te : & seruitutem non tollit. 111[?] in ἐκδικήσει[?] seu vindicatione loci à falsa interpretatione, seu abusu in structura falsæ consequentiæ ex eo : ut
units.tr: The theoretical use: (1) in teaching, or doctrine of faith, from v. 4. It belongs to faith to hold God to be one's own God, and to apply to oneself privately the promise of grace made to all believers. Hence Paul, out of faith, says: "I thank my God." So in Gal. 2. v. 20, speaking of Christ, he says: "who loved me and gave himself for me." Likewise from v. 5 and 6: the chief gifts of God are faith and love, since Paul thanked God by name for these gifts bestowed on Philemon, and prayed that they might be increased in him. (2) In refutation of a false doctrine, [Greek: elenchō], from v. 18, against the Anabaptists: that communion of the faithful or saints does not abolish the ownership of goods; otherwise no one could owe anything to another. But Paul signifies that Onesimus owes something to Philemon, namely the very thing he had taken by theft. Then Paul sends back the runaway, both being Christians, and does not abolish slavery. (3) In vindication of a passage [Greek: ekdikēsei], that is, in defence against a false interpretation, or misuse, in the form of a false consequence from it, as follows:

units.la: Si furibus resipiscentibus condonandum est, nunquam sunt occidendi [idem de latronibus, incendiariis &c : inferri posset]
units.tr: If thieves who repent must be forgiven, they must never be put to death [the same could be inferred about robbers, arsonists, etc.]

units.la: Sed verum est prius, ut patet ex Onesimi exem-plo:
units.tr: But the first is true, as is clear from the example of Onesimus:

units.la: Ergo & posterius. Resp: ad propositionem, negando eius connexionem, & distinguendo: Resipiscentibus furibus,latronibus &c: est condonandum, scilicet ex fraterna & Christiana charitate, quæ est depositio cupiditatis vindictæ privatæ. Condonatio est duplex: Condonatio fraterna, & condonatio pœnæ: ad priorem obligamur omnes. Posterior in arbitrio politici magistratus est sita: Vide Probl: Areti de Supplicis. i v in ἀπορίας λύσει[?], seu solutione dubitationis: v. 22. Sperauit Paulus se ex carcere liberatum iri: sed spes hac ipsum fefellit: quomodo igitur consistit illud Rom. 5. Spes non confundit? Resp: Apostolus non est confusus: quia sperauit liberationem é vinculis cum conditione seu exceptione voluntatis & gloriæ diuinæ, & ædificationis Ecclesiæ &c: qualiter omnia bona corporalia speranda sunt. Vide Probl: Areti de Spe.
units.tr: Therefore the second also. Answer: deny the connection of the proposition, and distinguish: thieves, robbers, etc., who repent, are to be forgiven, namely out of brotherly and Christian love, which is the laying aside of the desire for private revenge. Forgiveness is twofold: fraternal forgiveness and forgiveness of punishment. We are all bound to the former. The latter lies in the discretion of the civil magistrate. See the Problems of Areteus, on Punishment. (4) In the solution of a doubt [Greek: aporias lysei], v. 22: Paul hoped that he would be freed from prison, but this hope deceived him. How then does that saying in Rom. 5 stand, "hope does not disappoint"? Answer: the Apostle was not disappointed, because he hoped for release from his chains with the condition or proviso of the will and glory of God, and of the building up of the Church, and so on; in this way all bodily goods are to be hoped for. See the Problems of Areteus, on Hope.

units.la: Vsus practicus est 1. in pædia seu institutione vitæ: vt ex v.4. Officium fidelium est, pro fratribus, (id est, aliis fidelibus) precari, ac nominatim pro iis quorum pietas nobis nota est. Item, Ex v.7. Vera dilectio per opera misericordiæ, maximè erga sanctos (id est, fideles) egenos, & propter Christum persecutionem patientes, sese ostendat. Confer locum 1. Ioh.3. v.17. & 18. [Nota hic elegantem & Emphaticam metaphoram in voce viscera i. cor, animum: sic v. 12. & v. 20. refocilla mea viscera in domino: i. recrea cor meum in tali re quæ Deo ipsi grata est.] Item ex v.10. Pastores Ecclesiæ vt patres spirituales coledi sunt: quippe per quorum ministerium Deus vi spiritus sui, filios sibi gignit. Confer 1.Cor. 4. v. 15. Sic fidi præceptores tanquam animorum parentes suspiciendi, quibus non solum nostra, sed etiam nos ipsos debemus: v.16. [Sed quid fit? tam sunt, proh pudor! etiam in nostro grege, non nulli corde tam obdurato, vt non solum nullis quantumuis exquisitis exhortationibus ad pietatis & honestatis decus capessendum possint excitari, vt etiam contrà, præceptoribus bene meritis occasionem præbeant de ipsis merito conquerendi idipsum, quod Dauid de Achitophele, (psal.14.) Christus de Iscariotâ (Ioh.13. v.18.) conquestus est; qui edit mecum panem i. domesticus meus & alumnus mensæ ac disciplinæ meæ, sustulit aduersum me calcaneum suum, instar scilicet equi indomiti & ferocis calce ferientis dominum suum, &c:] 11 in Epanorthosi (seu admonitione de corrigendis vitiis, ex v. 10. & 11. Non debet nos cuiusquam, quantumuis tumultuis infimæ fortis,pudere, cui Deus gratiam dedit vt in Christum credeat. Sic Paulus Onesimum seruum & fugitiuum & furem ad Christum conuersum, filium suum, & sua viscera appellat: quibus verbis amorem erga illum paternum, eumque tenerrimum indicat. Eundem affectum declarat infra v. 16. & 17. III In παρακλήσει seu consolatione; Versus 16. seruit iis, qui in oculis mundi abiecti sunt, ad consolationem, ne humili sua conditione contristentur, quasi idcirco minus Deo accepti sint. Item Onesimus fur & fugitiuus gratiam inuenit & conuersus est ad Dominum: ergo etiam huic vel illi furi & malefico, non desperandum Christo duce & auspice Christo, &c:
units.tr: The practical use is (1) in paideia, or the training of life: as from v. 4: it is the duty of believers to pray for brothers (that is, other believers), and especially for those whose piety is known to us. Likewise, from v. 7: true love should show itself through works of mercy, above all towards the saints (that is, believers) who are poor and who suffer persecution for Christ. Compare 1 John 3, v. 17 and 18. [Note here the elegant and emphatic metaphor in the word viscera, that is, heart, mind: so in v. 12 and v. 20, "refresh my bowels in the Lord," that is, refresh my heart in such a matter as is itself pleasing to God.] Likewise from v. 10: the ministers of the Church are to be honoured as spiritual fathers, since through their ministry God, by the power of his Spirit, begets children for himself. Compare 1 Cor. 4, v. 15. So faithful teachers are to be esteemed as the parents of our souls, to whom we owe not only our possessions but even ourselves: v. 16. [But what happens? Alas for shame! There are some even in our own flock with hearts so hardened that they cannot be roused to take up the honour of piety and decency by any however exquisite exhortations, and on the contrary they give their well-deserving teachers occasion to complain of them with good reason, just as David complained of Ahithophel (Ps. 14), and Christ of Judas Iscariot (John 13, v. 18): "he who eats bread with me, that is, my domestic and pupil of my table and discipline, has lifted his heel against me," like an unbroken and fierce horse that kicks its master, and so on.] (2) In epanorthosis [Greek: correction], that is, admonition about correcting faults, from v. 10 and 11: no one should be ashamed, however humble his lot, if God has given him grace to believe in Christ. So Paul calls Onesimus, a slave, a runaway and a thief, converted to Christ, his son and his own bowels; by these words he shows his fatherly and very tender love towards him. He declares the same feeling below, in v. 16 and 17. (3) In paraklēsei [Greek: consolation]: v. 16 serves to console those who are despised in the eyes of the world, so that they should not be saddened by their humble condition, as if for that reason they were less acceptable to God. Likewise Onesimus, a thief and runaway, found grace and was converted to the Lord: therefore one should not despair even of this or that thief and evildoer, with Christ as leader and patron.

units.la: Argumentum ἀμέτρον.
units.tr: Argument [ἀμέτρον]

units.la: Affatur blando sermone Philemona, seruum (Fugerat is)domino conciliare studens.
units.tr: He addresses Philemon in a gentle speech, eager to win back his slave (who had run away) to his master.

units.la: ANALYSIS EPISTOLÆ AD HEBRÆOS.
units.tr: ANALYSIS OF THE EPISTLE TO THE HEBREWS

units.la: HACTENUS de illis S.Pauli Apostoli Epistolis, de quarum autore & autoritate nunquam fuit dubitatum; sequitur Epistola ad Hebræos, quam nonnulli nec Canonicam nec Paulinam quondam agnoscere volebant: alij Canonicam quidem, sed Pauli esse negant: sed doctiores & Canonicam & Paulinam affirmant & demonstrant. Quod sit Canonica seu authen-tica, dubitare amplius non possumus nec debemus, quia id probatur ipsâ doctrinâ Prophetis-cis & Apostolicis scriptis in omnibus consentiente. Paulinam verò esse hanc Epistolam, plurimis argumentis ostendi potest.
units.tr: Hitherto we have discussed those Epistles of the Apostle Paul about whose author and authority there was never any doubt. There follows the Epistle to the Hebrews, which some once refused to acknowledge either as canonical or as Pauline, and others, while granting that it is canonical, deny that it is Paul's. But the more learned affirm and demonstrate that it is both canonical and Pauline. That it is canonical or authentic, we can and ought no longer to doubt, since its doctrine agrees in all things with the prophetic and apostolic writings. That this Epistle is Pauline, however, can be shown by many arguments.

units.la: Quotiescunque enim Timothei mentio fit in N. Testamento, Pauli nomen aut praecessit aut subsequitur: at in hac Epistola fit mentio Timothei, v. 26. cap.ult. Cur itaque minister & Achates hic à Paulo seiungeretur? Propositio confirmatur ex Act. 17.v.14.cap. 18.v. 5.cap. 19. v.21.& cap. 20.v. 4. Quin etiam in omnibus epistolis, exceptis eâ quae ad Galatas & Ephe-sios est scripta, Paulus huius Timothei meminit: In reliquorum Apostolorum monumen-tis nulla omninò eius fit mentio. Hisce accedit, quòd sub finem narratur, epistolam hanc ex Italia,& quidem ex vinculis, ut ex 11. cap. v.34. videre est, ad Hebraeos esse missam. Annon Paulus Romae in vinculis detentus fuit, & in his Timotheus ei ministravit? Phil. 1. v. 13. Heb. ult. v.23. Quin etiam ipse Petrus Apostolus testatur, Epist. 2.cap. 3. quòd Paulus ad Hebraeos Epistolam miserit: cùm verò nulla alia appareat, quàm haec, cur dubitaremus Paulum eius esse organicum authorem? Sed & phrases, sententiae & voces Paulo familiarissimae in hac epistola inveniuntur, quibus, dum latere cupit, seipsum prodit. Conferantur itaque inter se haec loca, 1. Cor. 3. v. 1. 2. & Hebr. 5. v. 13. 14. Col. 1. v. 15. Hebr. 1. 3. Eph. 4. v. 14. Hebr. 13. v. 9. Philip. 4. v. 9. Rom. 15. v. 13. 1. Theff. 5. v. 23. Deus pacis. Hebr. 13. 20. 1. Cor. 9. v. 24. Hebr. 12. v. 1. Rom. 12. v. 1. 2. Hebr. 13. v. 15. 16. 21. &c: Ex his itaque apparet,organicam,instrumentalem vel ministrantem huius epistolæ causam esse Apostolum Paulum.
units.tr: For whenever Timothy is mentioned in the New Testament, Paul's name either precedes or follows. Yet in this Epistle Timothy is mentioned (chap. 13, verse 23, the last chapter). Why, then, should this minister and companion be separated from Paul? The proposition is confirmed from Acts 16:1, Acts 18:5, Acts 19:22 and Acts 20:4. Indeed, in all the epistles except the one to the Galatians and the one to the Ephesians, Paul mentions this Timothy, whereas in the writings of the other Apostles there is no mention of him at all. To this is added that at the end the Epistle is said to have been sent to the Hebrews from Italy, and indeed from prison, as may be seen from chapter 11, verse 34. Was not Paul detained in prison at Rome, and was not Timothy ministering to him there? Phil. 1:13; Heb. 13:23. Moreover, the Apostle Peter himself testifies (2 Pet. 3) that Paul sent an Epistle to the Hebrews. Since no other such Epistle appears, why should we doubt that Paul is its organic author? Furthermore, phrases, sentiments and expressions most familiar to Paul are found in this Epistle, by which he betrays himself even while wishing to remain hidden. Let these passages therefore be compared with one another: 1 Cor. 3:1-2 and Heb. 5:13-14; Col. 1:15 and Heb. 1:3; Eph. 4:14 and Heb. 13:9; Phil. 4:9 and Rom. 15:13; 1 Thess. 5:23, "the God of peace," and Heb. 13:20; 1 Cor. 9:24 and Heb. 12:1; Rom. 12:1-2 and Heb. 13:15-16, 21, etc. From these things it therefore appears that the organic, instrumental or ministering cause of this Epistle is the Apostle Paul.

units.la: Materiam huius epistolæ ostendet argumen-tum,cuius summa hæc est: Hortatur Apostolus Judæos Euangelij doctrinam amplexos, ne, propter persecutiones à contribulibus sufferen-das deficiant à Christo,nec in contribulium gratiam Ceremonias Mosaicas retineant,sed fide constanti,eaque bonis operibus vestita, missis umbris legalibus, Christo adhereant: eo quòd grauis pœna eos maneat,qui (cùm omnia ad salutem necessaria in Christo habeamus) eo non contenti,salutem contra ipsius mandatum, in externis quoque ceremoniis quærunt.Hortatur itaque ad constantiam in fide & bonis ope-ribus.
units.tr: The matter of this Epistle is shown by the argument, whose sum is this: the Apostle exhorts the Jews who have embraced the doctrine of the Gospel not, on account of persecutions suffered from their fellow countrymen, to fall away from Christ, nor to retain the Mosaic ceremonies in order to win the favour of their countrymen; but, with a constant faith, clothed with good works, and with the legal shadows laid aside, to cleave to Christ. The reason is that a grave punishment awaits those who, although they have in Christ all things necessary for salvation, are not content with this, but seek salvation also in external ceremonies, against his own command. He therefore exhorts them to constancy in faith and good works.

units.la: Formalis causa in Methodo consistit: de qua sequetur.
units.tr: The formal cause consists in the method, which will follow.

units.la: Finis quem sibi Paulus in hac epistola propositum habuit, ex jam dictis colligi potest: nempe ut hortetur Judæos à contribulibus vexatos ad constantiam in fide, & ad bona opera fidei veræ fructus. Hunc finem in omnibus Epi-stolis Paulus spectauit:primò enim informat in fide lectores, deinde in vita. Lex enim non est abrogata quoad obedientiâ, sed tantum quoad condemnationem.
units.tr: The end which Paul proposed to himself in this Epistle can be gathered from what has already been said: namely, that he might exhort the Jews, troubled by their fellow countrymen, to constancy in faith and to good works, the fruits of true faith. Paul aimed at this end in all his Epistles, for he first instructs his readers in faith and then in life. For the law has not been abrogated as regards obedience, but only as regards condemnation.

units.la: PARTES EPISTOLÆ
units.tr: THE PARTS OF THE EPISTLE

units.la: Fermè perpetuâ disputatione coherent. Nam Exordiū statim ab ipsa re sumitur. Ostendit enim doctrinam Christi unum esse ex mo-
units.tr: It holds together in an almost unbroken line of argument. The exordium is taken straight from the subject itself. For it shows that the doctrine of Christ is one of the modes of divine revelation,

units.la: [illegible, ~20 letters] dis diuinæ reuelationis, eumque præstantissi-mum,cùm sit per Filium factus, reliqui soluta per prophetas. Hinc statim ingreditur arcem causæ,docens Hebræos tum de persona, tum de officio ac beneficiis Christi; eosdemque passim ad fidei constantiam & fructus exhortans, vsque ad v.20.capitis vltimi: vbi Epistolam concludit voto Apostolico.
units.tr: and the most excellent of them, since it was made through the Son, whereas the others were given piecemeal through the prophets. From there it at once enters the heart of the case, teaching the Hebrews about the person, the office and the benefits of Christ. It exhorts them throughout to constancy in faith and to its fruits, right up to verse 20 of the last chapter, where the Epistle closes with an apostolic prayer.

units.la: COHERENTIA PARTIVM & capitum talis esse potest:
units.tr: THE COHERENCE OF THE PARTS AND CHAPTERS MAY BE AS FOLLOWS:

units.la: Agit Epistola ad Hebræos Christi ipsius Persona, respectu naturæ diuinæ: cap.1. humanæ: cap.2. officio prophetico: cap.3. & 4. Sacerdotali, quod præfert Leuitico, ratione Ordinis Melchizedec quod proponit: cap.5. exponit: cap.6.&7. Obiecti circa quod, vt offendtur generaliter: cap.8. Specialiter, cap. 9. Effecti collati cum defectu veterum. cap.10. Christianorum officiis, Fidei: cap. 11. Spe & tolerantia crucis: cap.12. Charitate: cap. 13.
units.tr: The Epistle to the Hebrews treats of the person of Christ himself: in respect of his divine nature, chapter 1; of his human nature, chapter 2; of his prophetic office, chapters 3 and 4; of his priestly office, which it sets above the Levitical priesthood with respect to the order of Melchizedek, which it proposes, chapter 5, and expounds, chapters 6 and 7. It then treats of the object with which that office is concerned, first in general, chapter 8, and specifically, chapter 9; of the effect, compared with the defects of the old covenant, chapter 10; and of the duties of Christians: of faith, chapter 11; of hope and endurance of the cross, chapter 12; and of love, chapter 13.

units.la: PRIMVM MEMBRVM DE persona Christi.
units.tr: THE FIRST PART, CONCERNING THE PERSON OF CHRIST

units.la: APOSTOLVS exhortaturus Hebræos ad perseuerantiam in fide Euangelij(id quod facere in-re inre incipit in principio capitis sequentis) præ-mittit illius exhortationis primum argumen-tum, quod sumtum est à causis efficientibus Euangelij: videlicet ab autore Deo, & administro præcipuo Iesu Christo: cuius propterea excellentiam in hoc capite variis rationibus declarat & confirmat; vt ostendat, eum talem esse, cui merito fides sit habenda. Ac excellentiam Christi primò simpliciter declarat vsque ad v. 4. Deinde eandem declarat per comparationem cum S. angelis, quibus longè præstantiorem esse Christum, variis argumentis confirmat: quæ ipsa testimoniis Scripturæ approbat.
units.tr: The Apostle, about to exhort the Hebrews to perseverance in the faith of the Gospel (which he begins to do at the start of the following chapter), first sets out the first argument of that exhortation, which is taken from the efficient causes of the Gospel: namely, from God as its author and from Jesus Christ as its chief minister. He therefore declares and confirms the excellence of Christ in this chapter by various reasons, so as to show that he is one in whom faith may rightly be placed. He first declares the excellence of Christ in a general way down to verse 4. Then he declares the same by comparison with the holy angels, to whom Christ is far superior, confirming this by various arguments, which the testimonies of Scripture themselves approve.

units.la: Cap. 11.
