Ex doctrina superiore capite exposita de excellentia personæ Christi, deducit nunc exhortationem ad attentam & assiduam meditationem Euangelij, eamque exhortationem pluribus argumentis confirmat. Deinde ad deprædicandam Christi Maiestatem redit, demonstrans Christum etiam secundum humanam naturam Angelis superiorem esse, quod inter cætera etiam Davidis testimonio probat: vsque ad v. 10. Tertiò, demonstrat variis argumentis, Christum verè humanam naturam assumpsisse; ac simul scandalo medetur quod ex humilitate & passione Christi nasci poterat: a v. 10. vsque ad finem capitis.
units.tr: Chapter 2. From the doctrine on the excellence of the person of Christ set out in the previous chapter, he now draws an exhortation to attentive and constant meditation on the Gospel, and confirms this exhortation by many arguments. Then he returns to proclaiming the majesty of Christ, demonstrating that Christ, even according to his human nature, is superior to the angels, which he proves among other things by the testimony of David, down to verse 10. Thirdly, he demonstrates by various arguments that Christ truly assumed human nature, and at the same time he meets the scandal that might arise from the humility and passion of Christ, from verse 10 to the end of the chapter.

units.la: Hactenus de Christi persona potissimùm egit: sequitur porrò.
units.tr: Hitherto he has treated chiefly of the person of Christ; there follows next.

units.la: DE OFFICIO CHRISTI.
units.tr: ON THE OFFICE OF CHRIST.

units.la: De officio Christi disserit triplici: videlicet Prophetico, Sacerdotali, ac Regio. Ac de duobus quidem prioribus disserit ex professo & copiosè. De Regio gio autem officio Christi agit breuiter & incidenter: vt cap.1.v.2.3.8.13.cap.2.v.9. cap.7.v.2.cap.8.v.1
units.tr: He treats Christ's office under three heads: the Prophetic, the Priestly, and the Royal. Of the first two he treats expressly and at length. Of Christ's royal office he treats briefly and incidentally, as at chapter 1 verses 2, 3, 8, 13; chapter 2 verse 9; chapter 7 verse 2; chapter 8 verse 1.

units.la: De prophetico Christi officio.
units.tr: On Christ's Prophetic Office.

units.la: Cap. 111. De prophetico Christi munere potissimum differens, rursus ex doctrina superioribus duobus capitibus tradita de Christo, deducit exhortationem, ad ipsum summum nostrum Apostolum seu Prophetam attente audiendum & doctrinæ eius credendum atque obediendum: & hanc exhortationem pluribus deinceps argumentis confirmat; quæ per totum hoc caput affert numero sex. Primum sumtum est à fidelitate Christi in officio suo Prophetico administrando, v.2. Secundum est ab exemplo Mosis, cui Hebrai prompte credebant, quem Christus multis modis antecellit, v. 2.3.4. 5. & 6. Tertium ab vtili effectu videlicet inhabitatione Dei in credentibus tanquam in domo sua, v.6. vbi simul renouatur ipsa exhortatio. Quartum ab autoritate spiritus sancti, qui suo testimonio doctrinam Christi tanquam veram & salutarem approbat, dum populum Dei ad vocem illius audiendam exhortatur, vbi simul femina [?] sparguntur caeterorum argumentorum, v.7.8.9.10.& 11. Postea v. 12.& 13, iterum renouatur ipsa exhortatio. Quintum ab alio effectu vtili, videlicet societate cum Christo in hæreditate illa caelesti, vbi rursus renouatur exhortatio, & accommodatur testimonium illud Spiritus sancti antea citatum; v.14.& 15. Tum v. 16. per prolepsin inseritur declaratio exempli patrum, cuius in illo testimonio facta est mentio. Sextum ab effectu pernicioso, videlicet poenis Dei temporalibus & aeternis, quæ contemptotemptorib. Euangelij ventura sunt; quod argumen-tum exemplo patrum confirmatur, tribus ultimis versibus.
units.tr: Chapter 3. Treating chiefly of Christ's prophetic office, he draws from the doctrine of the two preceding chapters concerning Christ an exhortation to listen attentively to our highest Apostle and Prophet, and to believe and obey his teaching. He confirms this exhortation by several arguments, six in number, which he sets out throughout this chapter. The first is taken from the faithfulness of Christ in administering his prophetic office, v. 2. The second is from the example of Moses, whom the Hebrews readily believed, and whom Christ surpasses in many ways, vv. 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. The third is from a useful effect, namely God's dwelling in believers as in his own house, v. 6; here the exhortation itself is renewed. The fourth is from the authority of the Holy Spirit, who by his testimony approves the teaching of Christ as true and saving, while he exhorts the people of God to hear his voice; here the remaining arguments are briefly touched on, vv. 7, 8, 9, 10, 11. Afterwards, at vv. 12 and 13, the exhortation is renewed again. The fifth is from another useful effect, namely fellowship with Christ in that heavenly inheritance; here the exhortation is renewed once more and the testimony of the Holy Spirit cited earlier is applied, vv. 14, 15. Then at v. 16, by way of prolepsis, an explanation is inserted of the example of the fathers, which was mentioned in that testimony. The sixth is from a destructive effect, namely God's temporal and eternal punishments, which are to fall upon those who despise the Gospel; this argument is confirmed by the example of the fathers in the last three verses.

units.la: Cap. I v. Duo postrema institutae exhorta-tionis argumenta superiore capite exposita, ex-polit & amplius declarat: differens de illa requie Dei à qua Patres Hebraorum propter incredulita-tem atque inobedientiam exclusi sunt; vsque ad v. 12. Deinde alia duo institutae exhortationis argu-menta adiunxit: vnum ab efficacia sermonis Euan-gelij, v. 12. alterum ab omni scientia Christi, v. 13. Postremò addit adhuc aliud institutae exhortatio-nis argumentum, à dignitate Christi pontificia seu sacerdotali, v. 14. eaque occasione transit ad doctri-nam de Sacerdotio Christi.
units.tr: Chapter 4, verse 1. He explains and further develops the last two arguments of the exhortation set out in the previous chapter, treating of that rest of God from which the fathers of the Hebrews were excluded because of their unbelief and disobedience, down to v. 12. Then he adds two other arguments for the exhortation: one from the efficacy of the Word of the Gospel, v. 12, and the other from the complete knowledge of Christ, v. 13. Last of all, he adds yet another argument for the exhortation, from the dignity of Christ's high-priestly or sacerdotal office, v. 14, and on that occasion passes to the doctrine of Christ's priesthood.

units.la: De officio Sacerdotali Christi.
units.tr: On Christ's Priestly Office.

units.la: Ad finem praecedentis capitis argumenta προτρεπτικὰ ex Pontificatu Christi producens, hunc ingressus est locum seu doctrinam de Sacerdotio Christi, quam per sex capita sequentia fusè exponit.
units.tr: At the end of the preceding chapter, having brought forward the protreptic [προτρεπτικὰ] arguments from Christ's high priesthood, he entered upon this place, or doctrine, of Christ's priesthood, which he expounds at length through the six following chapters.

units.la: Cap. igitur v. Aggreditur doctrinam de Sacerdotio Christi: ac primùm Christum Pontificem comparat cum Pontifice Leuitico vsq; ad v. 11. Deinde transitu facto ad comparationem alteram qua Christum comparabit cum pontifice Melchisedeco, prius digreditur in obiurgationem segnitiei Hebraeorum, vt eos ad attentam considerationem futurae illius diuinissimae comparationis excitet ac praeparet, reliqua parte capitis.
units.tr: Chapter 5. He therefore begins the doctrine of Christ's priesthood. First he compares Christ the High Priest with the Levitical high priest, down to v. 11. Then, making the transition to the second comparison, in which he will set Christ beside the priest Melchizedek, he first digresses, through the rest of the chapter, into a rebuke of the sluggishness of the Hebrews, so as to stir them up and prepare them for attentive consideration of that most divine comparison to come.

units.la: Cap. v I. adhuc pertinet ad locum praecedentem, scilicet ad exhortationem illam cuius sco-
units.tr: Chapter 6. This still belongs to the preceding passage, namely to that exhortation whose aim is that in faith we should always strive toward a greater knowledge of the truth.

units.la: V. iiij. pus est; in fide semper ad maiorem veritatis cognitionem esse annitendum. Primum renouat promissionem doctrina de sacerdotio Christi iam antea propositam (superioris capitis versu undecimo) usque ad v. 4. Deinde significat, doctrina illius fructum non peruenturum ad apostatas; quippe quos iusto Dei iudicio certum maneat exitium, usque ad v.9. Postea asperam suam admonitionem lenit, significatione bonae suaespei de perseuerantia ipsorum: qua occasione ipsos tum contra apostasiae metum consolatur, tum ad perseuerantiam in fide exhortatur: idque partim ab exemplo sanctorum Patrum, ac nominatim Abrahae, partim vero a promissione Dei iureiurando confirmata, usque ad v.19. vbi artificiose regressionem ad propositum instituit, usque ad finem cap.
units.tr: v. 4. First he renews the doctrine of Christ's priesthood already set forth earlier (in the eleventh verse of the previous chapter), down to v. 4. Then he shows that the fruit of this teaching will not reach apostates, for it remains certain that they face destruction by the just judgment of God, down to v. 9. Afterwards he softens his harsh warning by expressing a good hope of their perseverance. On this occasion he consoles them against the fear of apostasy and exhorts them to perseverance in faith, and does so partly from the example of the holy fathers, and especially Abraham, and partly from God's promise confirmed by an oath, down to v. 19. There he skilfully returns to his subject and carries on to the end of the chapter.

units.la: Cap. VII. Deinceps amplius ac fusius disputaturus de sacerdotio Christi, in hoc capite primum eum comparat cum Melchisedeco, ostendens per typum illius, qualis & quantus sit usque ad v. 4. eaque occasione redit ad comparationem ipsius cum pontifice Leuitico, quam instituit supra in principio capitis 5. Ostendit autem sex argumentis, Christum Pontificem, pontifice Leuitico longe praestantiorem, itemque sacerdotium ipsius, sacerdotio istius multo praestantius esse: primum sumtum est a pari: usque ad v. 11. Secundum ex effectis: usque ad v. 20. Tertium ab obiecto, nempe foedere in quo sanciendo tum Christus tum Leuitici sacerdotes occupantur: v.20.21.22. Quartum ab adiunctis, videlicet mortalitate & immortalitate: usque ad v.26. Quintum & Sextum coniunctim proponuntur, reliquis versibus.
units.tr: Chapter 7. Going on to dispute more fully and at greater length concerning Christ's priesthood, in this chapter he first compares him with Melchizedek, showing through that type what and how great he is, down to v. 4. On that occasion he returns to comparing Christ with the Levitical high priest, which he had begun at the start of chapter 5. He shows by six arguments that Christ the High Priest is far superior to the Levitical high priest, and that his priesthood is far superior to theirs. The first is taken from a parallel case, down to v. 11. The second is from the effects, down to v. 20. The third is from the object, namely the covenant in whose ratification both Christ and the Levitical priests are engaged, vv. 20, 21, 22. The fourth is from the attendant circumstances, namely mortality and immortality, down to v. 26. The fifth and sixth are proposed together in the remaining verses.

units.la: Cap. VIII. Pergit in demonstranda præstantia Sacerdotij Christi supra Leuiticum, primum repetens ac plenius exponens argumentum præstantiæ sextum, superiore cap.v.26.uno verbo propositum de gloria regia. Deinde adiungens alia argumenta tria: septimum quidem a gloria San-ctuarij,v.1.& 2. Octauum vero a præstantia victi-mæ,v.2.3. Nonum denique a præstantia fœderis: quod respectu sacerdotis habet rationem subiecti oc-cupantis siue obiecti, quippe cum sacerdos in illo sanciendo & confirmando occupetur.
units.tr: Chapter 8. He continues to demonstrate the superiority of Christ's priesthood over the Levitical. First he repeats and more fully explains the sixth argument of superiority, which he had proposed in a single word in the preceding chapter, v. 26, concerning royal glory. Then he adds three further arguments: the seventh from the glory of the sanctuary, vv. 1, 2; the eighth from the excellence of the sacrifice, vv. 2, 3; and the ninth from the excellence of the covenant, which, with respect to the priest, has the character of the matter occupying him, since the priest is engaged in ratifying and confirming it.

units.la: Cap. IX. Pergit Apostolus in exponenda comparatione sacerdotij Christi cum Leuitico, ac in ostendenda præstantia illius supra istud:& primùm commemorat tum structuram tabernaculi in quo sacerdotes Leuitici ministerium suum obi-bant,tum ipsius ministerij præcipuas partes,vsque ad v.8. Deinde ministerij illius infirmitatem seu im-potentiam & ( vt ita dicam ) inesficaciam ostendit, vsque ad v.11. Postea è regione comparat atque opponit efficaciam sacerdotij Christi,atque eo nomi-ne illud sacerdotio Leuitico tanquam præstantius anteponit;simul exponens causas cur Christum opor-tuerit sacrificare seipsum, seu offerre seipsum morte cruenta,vsque ad finem capitis.
units.tr: Chapter 9. The Apostle continues to set out the comparison of Christ's priesthood with the Levitical, and to show its superiority over it. First he recalls both the structure of the tabernacle in which the Levitical priests performed their ministry and the chief parts of that ministry itself, down to v. 8. Then he shows the weakness, or impotence, and, so to speak, the inefficacy of that ministry, down to v. 11. Afterwards he sets over against it the efficacy of Christ's priesthood, and on that account places it before the Levitical priesthood as more excellent. At the same time he explains why Christ had to sacrifice himself, that is, offer himself in a bloody death, down to the end of the chapter.

units.la: Cap: x. partes duæ sunt. 1 Quod superiore ca-pite docuit de infirmitate sacerdotij Leuitici,& con-tra de sacerdotij Christi efficacia : idipsum hic con-firmat vsque ad v.19. 11 Ex tota Doctrina in su-perioribus tradita deducit exhortationem ad con-stantiam in fide, vsque ad finem capitis.
units.tr: Chapter 10 has two parts. (1) What he taught in the preceding chapter about the weakness of the Levitical priesthood, and on the contrary about the efficacy of Christ's priesthood, he here confirms again, down to v. 19. (2) From the whole doctrine set out above he draws an exhortation to constancy in faith, down to the end of the chapter.

units.la: Hactenus de persona & officio Christi sequitur de officio Christianorum.
units.tr: So far concerning the person and office of Christ; there follows the office of Christians.

units.la: Quoniam superiore capite exhortatus fuit ad perseuerantiam in fide Christi, qua solâ iustificamur; nunc, cap. xi. fidei naturam declarat, primum quidem a certitudine doctrinae fidei, usque ad v. 4. Deinde exempla enumerat eorum, qui promissam in coelis hereditatem patienter fide expectarunt, & ex ea fide multa praeclare & heroicè gesserunt. Classes exemplorum quinque sunt. Prima est Abelis, Enochi & Noachi, ante diluvium: usque ad v. 8. Secunda est sanctorum Patrum qui vixerunt inde a diluvio usque ad exitum filiorum Israel ex Ægypto: ut sunt Abraham, Isac, Iacob & Iosephi usque ad v. 23. Tertia, ab exitu ex Ægypto, usque ad tempora Iudicum: usque ad v. 32. Quarta a temporibus Iudicum, usque ad tempora Maccabaeorum: usque ad v. 35. Quinta est eorum quae fidelibus acciderunt temporibus Maccabaeorum, quum Antiochus Epiphanes & aliy vicini reges in populum Dei saeuierunt.
units.tr: Since in the preceding chapter he exhorted us to perseverance in faith in Christ, by which alone we are justified, now, in chapter 11, he declares the nature of faith, first from the certainty of the doctrine of faith, down to v. 4. Then he enumerates examples of those who patiently awaited in faith the inheritance promised in heaven, and who by that faith did many things nobly and heroically. There are five classes of examples. The first is of Abel, Enoch and Noah, before the flood, down to v. 8. The second is of the holy fathers who lived from the flood until the exodus of the sons of Israel from Egypt, such as Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Joseph, down to v. 23. The third is from the exodus from Egypt down to the times of the Judges, down to v. 32. The fourth is from the times of the Judges down to the times of the Maccabees, down to v. 35. The fifth is of what befell the faithful in the times of the Maccabees, when Antiochus Epiphanes and other neighbouring kings raged against the people of God.

units.la: Cap. xii. Posteaquam superiore capite per digressionem quandam, fidei naturam ab effectis declarauit? Redit nunc ad exhortationem institutam capite 10. qua videlicet hortatur ad constantiam in fide, fidei confessione, & saepe sub cruce, usque ad v. 12. Deinde addit exhortationem ad studium aedificandi fratres, item ad castitatem & pietatem.
units.tr: Chapter 12. Having in the previous chapter, by a certain digression, declared the nature of faith from its effects, he now returns to the exhortation set out in chapter 10, which urges constancy in faith, the confession of faith, and this often under the cross, down to v. 12. Then he adds an exhortation to the duty of building up the brothers, and likewise to chastity and godliness.

units.la: Cap. xiii. Exhortatur eos ad omnis generis bona opera, maximè ea quae praecipiuntur in secunda Legis tabula, & ad dilectionem proximi pertinent: usque ad v. 20. Inde sequitur Epistolae huius
units.tr: Chapter 13. He exhorts them to every kind of good work, especially those things which are commanded in the second table of the Law and pertain to love of neighbour: as far as verse 20. Here follows the conclusion of this Epistle.

units.la: CONCLUSIO:
units.tr: CONCLUSION:

units.la: Ubi primum eis exoptat à Deo vires ad prae-standum Standum ea, ad quae hactenus per totam epistolam fuit exhortatus: v. 20. 21. Deinde rogat vt hanc suam exhortationem aequo animo ferant, v. 22. Tertio facit eos certiores de Timotheo soluto, suumque vna cum illo aduentum pollicetur, v. 23. Postremo annectit salutationes & votum Apostolicum.
units.tr: Here, first, he wishes them strength from God to perform those things which he has hitherto exhorted them to throughout the whole Epistle: verses 20 and 21. Second, he asks that they bear this his exhortation with an even mind, verse 22. Third, he informs them that Timothy has been set free, and promises his own coming along with him, verse 23. Lastly, he adds greetings and an apostolic wish.

units.la: ARGUMENTA CAPITUM
units.tr: ARGUMENTS OF THE CHAPTERS

units.la: Cap. I
units.tr: Chapter I

units.la: Ante Deus vatum fuerat sermonibus usu, Nunc proprij nati verba colenda dedit. Omnibus hic maior coelestis imago parentis, Angelicas vires exuperare solet.
units.tr: Formerly God spoke through the words of the prophets; now he has given the words of his own Son to be cherished. Of all these, the heavenly image of the Father is the greatest, and he is wont to surpass the powers of the angels.

units.la: 2 Ergò decet CHRISTI nos semper verba tenere, Quae Deus ipse pater signaque multa probant. Hic quoque verus homo miserae succurrere carni Assolet & sumum conciliare patrem.
units.tr: 2 Therefore it is fitting that we always hold to the words of Christ, which God the Father himself and many signs confirm. Here too the true man is accustomed to help wretched flesh and to win over the supreme Father.

units.la: 3 Vt Dominus vilem praecellit honore ministrum, Sic Christus Mosem vincit honore pium. Non igitur lubeat CHRISTI contemnere verba, Vt Mosem spreuit turba prophana patrum.
units.tr: 3 As the Lord surpasses his lowly minister in honour, so Christ surpasses the faithful Moses in honour. Therefore let it not please us to despise the words of Christ, as the profane crowd of our forefathers despised Moses.

units.la: 4 Non voluere patres requiem subiisse paratam, Nutarent falsa cum male corda fide. Sancta fides vobis sit cordi: verba Tonantis Non fallunt, seuo quae magis ense secant.
units.tr: 4 The fathers would not enter the rest prepared for them, since their hearts wavered in false faith. Let holy faith be dear to you: the words of the Thunderer do not deceive, and they cut more keenly than a cruel sword.

units.la: 5 Quem modo ritè Deum mortalis e corpore natum Sed non humano diximus esse modo. Idem etiam celebrat non friuola sacra sacerdos, Quae nobis possunt conciliare Deum.
units.tr: 5 He whom we have just said was rightly God, born of a mortal body, yet not in a human manner. The same priest also celebrates rites that are not trivial, rites which can win God over to us.

units.la: 6 Culpat Iudaeae socordia pectora gentis, Quae poenas magnas supplicium que ferant, Non etenim fallent supremi verba Tonantis, Quae iurans proprio comprobat ore Deus.
units.tr: 6 He rebukes the sluggish hearts of the Jewish race, which would bear great penalties and punishment. For the words of the supreme Thunderer will not deceive, the words which God confirms with his own mouth by an oath.

units.la: 7 Rex idem Salem fuerat Dominique sacerdos, Cuius nemo genus exposuisse potest. Talis enim CHRISTVS Rex maximus atque sacerdos, Cui par officium nemo Leuita gerit.
units.tr: 7 The same man was king of Salem and priest of the Lord, and no one can set forth his lineage. For Christ is such a great King and priest, and no Levite performs a like office.

units.la: Unicus & summus non falso est, more sacerdos
units.tr: The only and supreme priest is truly, after the order (of Melchizedek),

units.la: CHRISTVS, in æternum permanet huius honor.
units.tr: Christ; his honour endures for ever.

units.la: Pristina nam summus Aaronis munera magni
units.tr: For God has taken away the former gifts of great Aaron,

units.la: Per CHRISTVM è toto sustulit orbe Deus[?].
units.tr: Through Christ, from the whole world[?].

units.la: Quæ cecidit toties Aaronica victima nuper,
units.tr: The Aaronic victim, which has so often fallen of late,

units.la: Amplius haud nullum pondus habere solet.
units.tr: Is wont to have no weight any longer.

units.la: Unica nempe hominum est, quæ purgat crimina, Christi
units.tr: For Christ is the only one of men who cleanses sins,

units.la: Victima quæ patrem conciliare potest.
units.tr: The victim who can win the Father over.

units.la: Exponit veteris non vanas fœderis umbras,
units.tr: He sets forth the shadows of the old covenant, not empty,

units.la: Quæ morte implesti, CHRISTE supreme, tua.
units.tr: Which you, supreme Christ, have fulfilled by your death.

units.la: Pergite concordes transfire in tramite CHRISTI,
units.tr: Go on in harmony, passing along the path of Christ,

units.la: Nam fidei dantur munera digna piæ.
units.tr: For worthy gifts are given to pious faith.

units.la: Quid sit sancta fides, Domino quæ sola placere
units.tr: What holy faith is, which alone is wont to please the Lord,

units.la: Assolet, huius opes officiumque docet.
units.tr: He teaches, with its riches and its office.

units.la: Quotquot enim veram sancti meruere salutem,
units.tr: For as many as have deserved true salvation as saints,

units.la: Hanc retinent sola iustificante fide.
units.tr: Hold it by faith alone, which justifies.

units.la: Sit constans semper fortis in patientia corde,
units.tr: Let the reader be constant, always strong in patience of heart,

units.la: Quæ CHRISTVM nostram spemque ducemque videt.
units.tr: Who looks to Christ as our hope and leader.

units.la: Hinc Evangelij præstantia dogmata ponit,
units.tr: Hence he sets forth the outstanding doctrines of the gospel,

units.la: Quæ CHRISTO forti fidere corde iubent.
units.tr: Which bid us trust in Christ with a strong heart.

units.la: Sit facile hospitium, sint & connubia sancta:
units.tr: Let hospitality be easy, and let marriages be holy;

units.la: Nec nimias quærat dives avarus opes.
units.tr: Let not the rich, greedy man seek excessive riches.

units.la: Hinc fidei veræ constantia munera tractat,
units.tr: Hence he treats of the constancy of true faith and its gifts,

units.la: Et quod sit sanctæ religionis opus.
units.tr: And of what is the work of holy religion.

units.la: ALITER.
units.tr: IN ANOTHER WAY.

units.la: CAP. I.
units.tr: CHAPTER I.

units.la: AD patres loquitur per vates, nosque per ipsum
units.tr: God spoke to the fathers through the prophets, and to us through his Son, whom he teaches to surpass all things by far.

units.la: Natum, quem longè vincere cuncta docet.
units.tr: He who spurns these twice perishes; greater things are taught than to the ancients.

units.la: Bis perit hæc spernens, prisci maiora docentur.
units.tr: Christ was made man, dying to atone for men.

units.la: Factus homo est Christus, morte pians homines.
units.tr: Christ is preferred to Moses. Who did not enter rest?

units.la: Christus præfertur Mosi, qui non requierunt?
units.tr: Those who did not believe the word of the Lord.

units.la: Qui Domini verbu non habuere fidem.
units.tr: He discourses again on rest, and on the sword

units.la: De requie rursum dissertat, de gladioque,
units.tr: which penetrates the mind, and also on the power of the High Priest.

units.la: Qui mentem penetrat, vi quoque Pontificis.
units.tr: Christ is set forth through Melchizedek. God heard him crying out; there is need of joy again.

units.la: Exprimitur Christus per Melchisedech. Deus illum
units.tr: He will sit more excellently by faith, if I may so put it.

units.la: Clamantem audiuit, laetæ opus est iterum.
units.tr: By an oath the Lord bids that hope be made sure.

units.la: Fido sessurum melius, quamuis ita dicam.
units.tr: 7 Melchizedek was once greater than our father Abraham, and the new law gave things more advantageous than the old.

units.la: Iurando Dominus spem iubet esse ratam.
units.tr: 8 Moses looks to the pattern; the law is a shadow of what is to come. The new law is promised; therefore the old perishes.

units.la: 7 Grandior Abrahamo patre Melchisedech fuit olim, Et noua lex veteri commodiora dedit.
units.tr: 9 He compares the legal rites with the blood of Christ, showing the new things to be better than the old.

units.la: 8 Inspicit exemplar Moises lex umbra futuri est, Lex noua promissa est, ergo vetusta perit.
units.tr: 10 Christ accomplishes great things which the law denied it could provide; for sinners a dreadful punishment remains.

units.la: 9 Legales ritus cum Christi sanguine confert, Ostendens priscis villiora nova.
units.tr: 11 He recounts the many famous stratagems of the holy fathers, all of which were carried out through steadfast faith.

units.la: 10 Magna facit Christus, quae lex praestare negabat, Vitro[?] peccantes horrida poena manet.
units.tr: 12 Correction is altogether profitable; let no one fall away. He shows all things made gentle in place of harsh.

units.la: 11 Narrat multa patrum stratagemata clara piorum, Quae sunt per firmam cuncta patrata fidem.
units.tr: 13 Obey your rulers, lest new doctrines deceive you. Praise of marriage, and hospitality given.

units.la: 12 Omnino prodest correptio, nemo recedat. Mitia pro duris omnia facta docet.
units.tr: Briefly.

units.la: 13 Praepositis pare, ne te noua dogmata fallant. Connubij laudes, hospitibusque data.
units.tr: 1 2 3 4 5 Created, Subjected, Moses, Penetrating, Pity; 6 7 8 9 10 Taste, Melchizedek, Fixed, Veil, Shadow of the law; 11 12 13 What is holy Faith, the Lord chastises, Avarice.

units.la: Breuissimè.
units.tr: Explanation.

units.la: 1 2 3 4 5 Condita, Subiecit, Moses, Penetrans, Miserari: 6 7 8 9 10 Gustum, Melchisedech, Fixit, Velum, legis Vmbra 11 12 13 Quid sit sancta Fides, dominus Castigat, Anari.
units.tr: 1 2 3 4 5 Founded, Subjected, Moses, Penetrating, Pitied: 6 7 8 9 10 Tasted, Melchisedec, Fixed, Veil, Shadow of the law 11 12 13 What is holy faith, the Lord chastens, Anari.

units.la: Declaratio.
units.tr: Explanation.

units.la: Condita per Filium omnia: v. 2. Subiecit mundum futurum non angelis: v. 5. Moses fidus fuit in tota domo v. 5. Penetrans gladius est Dei verbum: v. 12. Miserari potest vicem ignorantium: v. 2.
units.tr: All things founded through the Son: v. 2. The world to come subjected not to angels: v. 5. Moses was faithful in all the house: v. 5. The word of God is a sword that penetrates: v. 12. He can have pity on the ignorant: v. 2.

units.la: Gustum qui habent doni coelestis: v. 4. Melchisedech rex Salem: v. 1. Fixit Dominus tabernaculum: v. 2. Velum post secundum erat tabernaculum: v. 3. legis Vmbra futurorum bonorum: v. 1.
units.tr: Those who have tasted the heavenly gift: v. 4. Melchisedec, king of Salem: v. 1. The Lord fixed the tabernacle: v. 2. The veil was the second tabernacle after the second: v. 3. The shadow of the law of good things to come: v. 1.

units.la: Quid sit sancta Fides docet ex Patrum exemplis. Dominus Castigat cum quem diligit: v. 6. Anari ne sitis: v. 5.
units.tr: What holy faith is, he teaches from the examples of the Fathers. The Lord chastens whom he loves: v. 6. Anari, be not: v. 5.

units.la: HACTENUS fuerunt Epistola Paulinae sequuntur reliquorum Apostolorum Epistolæ, quæ Catholicæ nuncupantur, vt quæ multis Ecclesiis ad communem ipsarum & posterarum vtilitatem scriptæ sunt.
units.tr: Hitherto the Epistles of Paul; there follow the Epistles of the remaining Apostles, which are called Catholic, as having been written to many churches for their common benefit and that of their successors.

units.la: ANALYSIS EPISTO-LÆ S. IACOBI.
units.tr: ANALYSIS OF THE EPISTLE OF ST JAMES.

units.la: Scriptor huius Epistolæ videtur omnino fuisse Iacobus Cognomento Alphæi. Nam Iacobus Zebedæi, frater Iohannis, statim sub initia prædicati Euangelij é medio sublatus fuit per Herodem, vt legimus Act.12. Hæc autem epistola aliquanto post tempore videtur scripta esse, quum Euangelium iam inter Græcos quoque prædicatum esset, inter hos enim Hebræi isti Christiani ad quos hæc epistola directa est, erant dispersi: vt liquet ex principio. Quò minus autem tribuenda videatur hæc epistola Iacobo illi cui cognomen erat Obliæ, quique vnus fuit ex discipulis Domini, & postea Episcopus Ecclesiæ Hierosolymitanæ: id obstat, quod Catholicam Epistolam scribere, id est, pluribus simul Ecclesiis communem, non autem vni certæ propriâ, videtur Apostolici muneris proprium fuisse.
units.tr: The author of this epistle seems to have been James, surnamed the son of Alphaeus. For James the son of Zebedee, brother of John, was put to death by Herod early in the preaching of the gospel, as we read in Acts 12. This epistle, however, seems to have been written some time later, when the gospel had already been preached among the Greeks as well, for the Hebrew Christians to whom this epistle is addressed were scattered among them, as is clear from the opening. What makes it less likely that this epistle should be ascribed to that James who was surnamed Oblias, one of the disciples of the Lord and afterwards bishop of the Church at Jerusalem, is that writing a catholic epistle, that is, one common to several churches at once and not to one particular church, seems to have been a proper task of the apostolic office.

units.la: Occasionem huic Epistolæ præbuerunt Christianorum mores, qui malè doctrinam Christi vitâ exprimebant. Nam præmaturè hoc malum Ecclesiam inuasit, quod dixit Dominus Christus de Iudæis aput Matth:23. In cathedra Moisis sedent, quæ vos docuerint facite, secundùm autem opera ipsorum nolite facere, significans Iudæos non rectè philosophari in legè Mosis. Sic Christi Ecclesia multos habuit quidem professores fidei: pauci tamen erant, qui Christianum esse putarent nihil aliud esse, quàm vitâ & moribus testari innocentiam. Horum ergo præposteros mores corrigit.
units.tr: The occasion for this epistle was given by the conduct of Christians, who expressed the teaching of Christ badly in their lives. For this evil had invaded the Church too early, the evil that the Lord Christ spoke of the Jews in Matthew 23: "They sit in Moses' seat; do whatever they teach you, but do not do what they do," signifying that the Jews did not philosophise rightly about the law of Moses. So the Church of Christ had indeed many professors of the faith, yet there were few who thought that being a Christian was nothing more than bearing witness to one's innocence by life and conduct. He therefore corrects the perverse conduct of these people.

units.la: Scopus Apostoli est, instituere & exhortari pios ad professionem fidei suæ ornandam omni bonorum operum studio. Ideò passim urget virtutes renati hominis: vt patet ex cap. 1. v. 22. & cap. 2 v. 14. & v. 20. item v.26: Fides sine operibus mortua est: significans ipsam professionem fidei sine studio bonorum operum esse inerum[?] simulachrum. Et cap. 3. v. 13. Siquis sapiens est inter vos, ostendat ex honesta conuer-satione opera sua; & cap. 4. ad finem: scienti bonorum facere & non facienti, hoc ipsi pecca-tum est: &c.
units.tr: The aim of the Apostle is to instruct and exhort the godly to adorn their profession of faith with every zeal for good works. Therefore he everywhere presses the virtues of the regenerate man, as is evident from chapter 1 verse 22, chapter 2 verses 14 and 20, and also verse 26: "Faith without works is dead," signifying that a profession of faith without zeal for good works is an empty image. And chapter 3 verse 13: "If anyone among you is wise, let him show his works by a good conversation"; and at the end of chapter 4: "To one who knows how to do good and does not do it, it is sin to him," etc.

units.la: Loci præcipui admonitionum hac epistolâ contentarum, sunt isti octodecim: 1. de patientia præstanda sub cruce, & de patientiæ dono petendo à Deo: 2. de cauenda blasphemia in constituendo Deo authore peccati: 3. de verbo Dei reuerenter audiendo ac meditando: 4. de religiositatis vana specie cauenda: 5. de iustitia adhibenda in honorandis proximis: 6. de cauenda inani iactantia fidei, & fide ex operibus demonstranda: 7. de cauenda arrogantia in corripiendis fratribus: 8. de lingua frenanda: 9. de cauenda inuidia & rixis: 10. de cauenda auaritia, intemperantia & superbia: 11. de cauendis obtrectationibus: 12. de cauenda inani confidentia in negotiis instituendis: 13. de cauendo abusu diuitiarum: 14. rursus de patientia præstandâ sub cruce : 15. de cauenda temeritate iudicandi: 16. de suscipiendis exercitiis pietatis in utroque rerum statu : 17. de orando pro ægrotis : 18. de fratre errante in viam reducendo.
units.tr: The principal topics of the admonitions contained in this epistle are these eighteen: (1) on bearing patience under the cross, and on asking God for the gift of patience; (2) on avoiding blasphemy, in making God the author of sin; (3) on hearing and meditating on the word of God with reverence; (4) on avoiding the empty show of religiosity; (5) on showing justice in honouring our neighbours; (6) on avoiding the vain boasting of faith, and on demonstrating faith by works; (7) on avoiding arrogance in rebuking brothers; (8) on bridling the tongue; (9) on avoiding envy and quarrels; (10) on avoiding avarice, intemperance and pride; (11) on avoiding slander; (12) on avoiding vain confidence in undertaking business; (13) on avoiding the abuse of riches; (14) again, on bearing patience under the cross; (15) on avoiding rashness in judging; (16) on taking up the exercises of piety in either condition of life; (17) on praying for the sick; (18) on bringing back an erring brother into the way.

units.la: CAPITVM HAEC QVALISCVNQUE Connexio est.
units.tr: WHAT THE CONNECTION OF THE CHAPTERS IS, SUCH AS IT IS.

units.la: Docet Iacobus fideles, quo modo se gerant erga Deum, in tentationibus externis & internis &c. cap. 1. Homines: vbi ostendit quam potissimum [?] quantur in [?] Facit, quoad diuites & pauperes: &c. cap. 2. Dicit is sermone publico & priuato &c: cap. 3. Fugiant vel Vniuersim omnes cap. 4. Speciatim diuites & pauperes: cap. 5.
units.tr: James teaches the faithful how they should conduct themselves towards God in outward and inward temptations, etc. Chapter 1: Let men [...] where he shows [...] as regards rich and poor, etc. Chapter 2: He teaches in public and in private speech, etc. Chapter 3: Let them avoid [...] universally all. Chapter 4: Specially the rich and the poor. Chapter 5.

units.la: Primo capite post salutationem (v. 1.) quatuor præcipuè loci admonitionum continentur. Primum enim consolatur eos sub cruce & ad illam patienter ferendam exhortatur: ac simul monet, patientiam tanquam singulare Dei donum, a Deo cum fide esse postulandum, vsque ad v. 13. Deinde dehortatur eos à blasphemia, qua nonnulli peccata sua transscribunt Deo, vsque ad v. 19. Tertiò, hortatur ad reverentiam in audiendo verbo Dei, & ad studium in eo meditando, facilisque exprimendo, vsque ad v. 26. Postremò monet, ne quis se decipiat vana opinione religiositatis: sed potius vt moderatione linguæ, beneficentia erga afflictos, & studio sanctitatis sese vere religiosos ostendant.
units.tr: In the first chapter, after the salutation (verse 1), four principal topics of admonition are contained. First, he comforts them under the cross and exhorts them to bear it patiently; and at the same time he warns that patience, as a unique gift of God, must be asked of God in faith, up to verse 13. Then he dissuades them from blasphemy, by which some transfer their sins to God, up to verse 19. Thirdly, he urges reverence in hearing the word of God, and diligence in meditating on it and expressing it readily, up to verse 26. Lastly, he warns that no one should deceive himself with the empty opinion of religiosity, but rather that they should show themselves truly religious by restraint of the tongue, by kindness towards the afflicted, and by zeal for holiness.

units.la: Cap. II Duos admonitionum locos tractat; quintum nimirum, de iustitia in honorandis proxi-mis adhibenda, usque ad v. 14. & sextum de cavenda inani fidei iactantia, & fide ex operibus o-stendenda.
units.tr: Chapter II deals with two topics of admonition: the fifth, namely, on showing justice in honouring neighbours, up to verse 14, and the sixth, on avoiding the vain boasting of faith, & on demonstrating faith by works.

units.la: Capite III. continentur tres admonitionum loci videlicet septimus, octavus & nonus. Quorum primus est de cavenda arrogantia in corripiendis fratribus, v. 1. & primo membro secundi. Secundus, de lingua frenanda v. 2. ibi: si quis in sermone: usque ad v. 13. Tertius de mansuetudine praestanda & cavenda invidia ac rixis.
units.tr: In chapter III are contained three topics of admonition, namely the seventh, eighth and ninth. The first of these is on avoiding arrogance in rebuking brothers, verse 1, and the first member of the second topic. The second, on bridling the tongue, verse 2, beginning "if anyone in speech," up to verse 13. The third, on showing gentleness and avoiding envy and quarrels.

units.la: Cap. IV. Tres admonitionum loci continen-tur: decimus, undecimus & duodecimus. Quorum primus est de cavenda avaritiâ, intemperantiâ & superbiâ, usque ad v. 11. Secundus de cavendis obtrectationibus v. 11. & 12 Tertius de cavenda inani confidentia in negotiis.
units.tr: Chapter IV contains three topics of admonition: the tenth, eleventh and twelfth. The first is on avoiding avarice, intemperance and pride, up to verse 11. The second is on avoiding slander, verses 11 and 12. The third is on avoiding vain confidence in business.

units.la: Cap. V. continentur sex reliqui admonitio-num loci: videlicet 13. 14. 15. 16. 17. & 18. Quorum primus est de cavendo abusu divitiarum, us-que ad v. 7. Secundus de patienter ferendis iniu-riis quæ inferuntur à fratribus seu domesticis fidei, à v. 7. usque ad v. 12. Tertius de cavenda teme-ritate iurandi v. 12. Quartus de suscipiendis e-xercitiis pietatis in utroque rerum statu, v. 13. Quin-tus de orando pro ægrotis, usque ad v. 19. Sextus de fratre errante in viam reducendo, duobus versi-bus ultimis.
units.tr: Chapter V contains the remaining six topics of admonition, namely 13, 14, 15, 16, 17 and 18. The first is on avoiding the abuse of riches, up to verse 7. The second is on patiently bearing injuries inflicted by brothers or members of the household of faith, from verse 7 up to verse 12. The third is on avoiding rashness in judging, verse 12. The fourth is on taking up the exercises of piety in either condition of life, verse 13. The fifth is on praying for the sick, up to verse 19. The sixth is on bringing back an erring brother into the way, in the last two verses.

units.la: CAPITUM SUMMÆ.
units.tr: Summaries of the Chapters.

units.la: Cap. I.
units.tr: Chapter I.

units.la: ADomino Cœli sapientia sola petatur, Quæ tristem[?] doceat sustinuisse crucem. Non tentat dominus : factis ostendefidele Pectus, id est verae religionis opus.
units.tr: Let wisdom from heaven alone be sought from the Lord, which teaches one to bear the sorrowful cross. The Lord tempts no one. Let the faithful heart show itself by its deeds, that is, the work of true religion.

units.la: 1 Non tibi sit potior flauo qui splendet in auro, Aequalis sancto pectore flagret amor. Quidque fidem iactas omni tu crimine plenus? Haec tua nempe fides mortua tota iacet. 3 Affectant multi doctorum nomina, qui non, Quod doceant, possunt sustinuisse modum, Labilis instituit quare moderamina linguae, Et quae prudentem corda modesta decent. 4 Taxat auaritiae studium nummique tenaces, Et quorum multis lingua nocere solet Magnanimo elatos reprehendit corde superbos, Qui spernunt vires consiliumque Dei. 5 Turgida diuitiis reprehendit pectora magnis, Et docet afflicto corde pericla pati. Iuramenta vetat, infirmos edocet inde, Et sanctae teneant pondera quanta preces.
units.tr: 1 Let the one who gleams in yellow gold not be more highly prized by you; let love, equal in a holy breast, burn. And why do you boast of faith, when you are full of every crime? Your faith, indeed, lies wholly dead. 3 Many aspire to the names of teachers, yet cannot keep the measure of what they teach; therefore the wavering one is taught the restraints of the tongue, and modest hearts become the prudent. 4 He censures the zeal for avarice and the tight-fisted hoarders of money, and those by whose tongues many are wont to be harmed; he rebukes the proud, lifted up in a magnanimous heart, who despise the strength and counsel of God. 5 He rebukes hearts swollen with great riches, and teaches them to endure dangers with a afflicted heart. He forbids oaths, and from this instructs the weak, and shows how great is the weight that holy prayers carry.

units.la: ALITER CAP. I
units.tr: ANOTHER, CHAPTER I

units.la: Afflictus gaude: pete fidens, te tua tendant. Fac legem faciasque, haec pia religio est.
units.tr: Rejoice in affliction; ask in faith, and let your own things stretch you. Do the law and do it; this is true religion.

units.la: 1 Bulla placet, vilescit inops, facit vnica summe Culpa reum, numquid sufficit vna fides? 3 Compescas linguam, qua nil violentibus vna. Terrea caelesti dissimilis sophia est. 4 Damnate has lites, petis male sitque fugentur. Reddite vos humiles, vita repente fugit. 5 Erugo, merces, patientia certa futuri. Ne iures, aegros vnctio sacra beat.
units.tr: A bubble pleases, the poor man is despised; one sin alone makes a man guilty. Is one faith enough? Bridle your tongue, which is nothing if not violent. Earthly wisdom is unlike heavenly wisdom. Condemn these quarrels; you seek badly, so let them be put to flight. Make yourselves humble; life quickly flees. Rust, reward, and the sure patience of the future. Do not swear; holy anointing blesses the sick.

units.la: Breuissimè.
units.tr: Very briefly.

units.la: Tardus, & Effectus, Flamma, Mercabitur, Est, non
units.tr: Slow, and effectual, flame, will be bought, is, not

units.la: Daclaratio.
units.tr: Explanation.

units.la: Tardus ad loquendum v. 19. & Effectus si dei, id est
units.tr: Slow to speak, v. 19, and effectual, if of God, that is

units.la: bona opera requiruntur: v. 18. Flamme instar lingua, non efferendam: v 5 Mercabimur hodie vel cras: v. 13. Est, non sit vester sermo: v. 12.
units.tr: good works are required, v. 18. Flame like the tongue, not to be lifted up, v. 5. We will be bought today or tomorrow, v. 13. Yes, not: let your speech be, v. 12.

units.la: EPISTOLA PETRI
units.tr: THE EPISTLE OF PETER

units.la: Prior.
units.tr: The First.

units.la: Auctor epistolae omnium consensu est Apostolus Petrus, qui natione fuit Galilaeus, ex vico Bethzaida oriundus, patrem habuit Iohannem piscatorem, fratrem Andream, eiusdem professionis hominem, cum quo adscitus est ad Apostolatum dum piscarentur ad mare Galilea: Math. cap. 4. Nomen illi fuit ex circumcisione Simeon, quod ei mutauit Dominus, vt est, Marc: 3. Iohan: 1. Tu es Simeon filius Ionae, vocaberis Cepha, quae Syra dictio significat petram. Graeci more Attico πέτρον[?] verterunt. In inscriptione huius Epistolae omnia tria nomina coniunguntur, vt intelligamus indubitanter Epistolam hanc Petri Apostoli esse. Porro Petrus videtur dictus propter fidei constantiam & robur. praeterea quod singulari audacia esset praeditus interrogandi Dominum & respondendi pro aliis: vt est videre Matth. 16. & 18. cap.
units.tr: The author of the epistle is, by universal agreement, the Apostle Peter. He was a Galilean by birth, from the village of Bethsaida, and his father was John, a fisherman. His brother Andrew, of the same trade, was with him when he was called to the apostolate while they were fishing on the Sea of Galilee (Matt. 4). His circumcised name was Simon, which the Lord changed to Cephas, as in Mark 3 and John 1: "You are Simon, son of Jonah; you shall be called Cephas," a Syriac word meaning rock. The Greeks translated it in the Attic manner as Peter [Πέτρος]. In the inscription of this epistle all three names are joined, so that we may understand beyond doubt that this epistle is that of the Apostle Peter. Moreover, Peter seems to have been so called because of his constancy and strength of faith, and also because he had a singular boldness in questioning the Lord and answering on behalf of the others, as can be seen in Matthew 16 and 18.

units.la: Quibus scribatur constat ex titulo: nimirum aduenis & peregrinis, non Iudeis modo, qui tum proprie dicti sunt aduenae & dispersi in toto imperio Romano: sed etiam Gentibus, vt constat ex cap. 1. v. 10. Sic cap. 4. v. 3. loquitur cum fidelibus tanquam ex Gentibus conuersis. Itaque sic statuendum est: Petrum in primarium. Apostolum non tam Iudæorum quàm omnium conuersorum habuisse rationem, quandoquidem sancti omnes sunt aduenæ & peregrini in hoc mundo.
units.tr: To whom it is written is clear from the title: namely, to sojourners and strangers, not only Jews, who were properly called sojourners and dispersed throughout the Roman empire, but also Gentiles, as is clear from chapter 1, verse 10. Likewise in chapter 4, verse 3, he speaks to the faithful as to converts from among the Gentiles. So we must conclude that the chief Apostle Peter had in view not so much the Jews as all converts, since all the saints are sojourners and strangers in this world.

units.la: Occasio, vt apparet, oblata est ex aduentu Syluani, qui prius cum Paulo in diuersis locis docuerat & instituerat ecclesias, ad quas nunc rediturus Babylonem transfuit, & isthic vt videtur, conuenit Petrum à quo hanc epistolam ad omnes electos accepit, vt partim armarentur contra aperta pericula, partim instruerentur contra falsos fratres, qui passim sanam doctrinam variis modis corrumpebant.
units.tr: The occasion, as appears, was offered by the coming of Silvanus, who had earlier taught with Paul in various places and founded churches. He was about to return to them, but he went over to Babylon, and there, it seems, he met Peter, from whom he received this epistle addressed to all the elect. It was meant partly to arm them against open dangers, and partly to instruct them against false brothers, who everywhere corrupted sound doctrine in various ways.

units.la: Scopum & argumentum huius epistolæ Petrus ipse indicat sub finem, vbi ait: Per Syluanum vobis fidelem fratrem (vt existimo) paucis scripsi, adhortans vos, & testificans hanc esse veram gratiam Dei in qua statis. Duo igitur potissimum in hac epistola Petrus agit: partim enim testificatur Christianis ad quos scribit, doctrinam de gratia Dei per Christum, quam doctrinam ipsi erant amplexi, & in cuius fide ac professione persistebant, esse veram illam atque unicam æternæ salutis doctrinam; partim vero adhortatur eos, vt nimirum & in hac fide eiusque professione perseverent, & vitam illa professione dignam Deoque placentem agant.
units.tr: Peter himself indicates the aim and subject of this epistle near the end, where he says: "By Silvanus, a faithful brother (as I suppose), I have written to you briefly, exhorting you and testifying that this is the true grace of God in which you stand." Peter therefore deals chiefly with two things in this epistle. On the one hand he bears witness to the Christians to whom he writes that the doctrine of God's grace through Christ, which they had embraced and in whose faith and profession they persisted, is that true and sole doctrine of eternal salvation. On the other hand he exhorts them to persevere in this faith and its profession, and to live a life worthy of that profession and pleasing to God.

units.la: Potest autem tota epistola, exceptâ inscriptione, distribui in octo partes. Primùm[?] enim vt eis de veritate doctrinæ Christianæ testificetur, eosque in illius fide confirmet; commemorat beneficia Dei spiritualia in ipsos collata & etiam-num conferenda. à Secundo ex illa beneficio-rum rum cōmemoratione deducit adhortationem ad studium pietatis: à vers. 13. capitis primi vsque ad versum 13. capitis secundi. Tertio à generali illa adhortatione transit ad speciales, præcipiens de subditorum erga præfectos sibi magistratus, famulorum erga suos dominos, vxorum erga suos viros, & vicissim virorū erga suas vxores,à v. 13. cap. 2. vsque ad v. 8. capitis tertij. Quarto redit ad exhortationes generales; ac vniuersos hortatur ad dilectionem fratrum,ad tollerantiam iniuriarum,ad temperantiam, & rursus ad dilectionem fratrum sollicitamque functionis impositæ administrationem à v. 8. cap. 3. vsque ad v. 12. Quinto peculiariter hortatur ad tollerantiam persecutionis propter confessionem Christi: à v. 12. capitis tertij vsque ad illius finem. Sexto redit ad exhortationes speciales: ac primum presbyteros hortatur ad curam grégis sibi commissi, deinde iuniores ad modestiam : à principio capitis quinti vsque ad v. 8. Septimo iterum redit ad exhortationes generales: & paucis verbis hortatur ad sobrietatem, vigilantiam, constantiam in fide & tolerantia persecutionum. v. 8. & 9. Octavo epistolam concludit.
units.tr: The whole epistle, apart from the inscription, may be divided into eight parts. First, to bear witness to them concerning the truth of Christian doctrine and to confirm them in its faith, he recalls the spiritual benefits of God bestowed on them and still to be bestowed (to verse 13 of chapter 1). Second, from this recollection of benefits he draws an exhortation to the pursuit of godliness (from verse 13 of chapter 1 to verse 13 of chapter 2). Third, from that general exhortation he passes to particular ones, commanding subjects to be obedient to the magistrates set over them, servants to their masters, wives to their husbands, and, in turn, husbands to their wives (from verse 13 of chapter 2 to verse 8 of chapter 3). Fourth, he returns to general exhortations, and urges all to love of the brethren, to endurance of injuries, to self-control, and again to love of the brethren and to diligent discharge of the office laid upon them (from verse 8 of chapter 3 to verse 12). Fifth, he exhorts in particular to endurance of persecution for the confession of Christ (from verse 12 of chapter 3 to its end). Sixth, he returns to particular exhortations: first he urges the elders to care for the flock committed to them, then the younger men to modesty (from the beginning of chapter 5 to verse 8). Seventh, he returns once more to general exhortations, and in a few words urges sobriety, watchfulness, steadfastness in the faith, and endurance of persecutions (verses 8 and 9). Eighth, he concludes the epistle.

units.la: Cap. 1. præmissi inscriptione ( v. 1. 2.) commemorat primum spiritualia Dei in eos ad quos scribit, collata & adhuc conferenda beneficia, videlicet, fidem, spem, dilectionem Christi, gaudium ex fide, & denique salutem seu vitam æternam: vsque ad v. 13. Deinde ex illa commemoratione deducit exhortationem ad studium pietatis.
units.tr: Chapter 1, after the inscription (verses 1 and 2), first recalls the spiritual benefits of God bestowed on those to whom he writes and still to be bestowed, namely faith, hope, love toward Christ, joy from faith, and finally salvation or eternal life, down to verse 13. Then from that recollection he draws an exhortation to the pursuit of godliness.

units.la: Cap.11. primum pergit in instituta exhortatione generali seu communi & ad omnes credentes pertinente, ad studium scilicet sanctè vivendi, usque ad v. 13. Deinde subiungit exhortationes speciales ad obedientiam erga superiores, reliqua parte capitis.
units.tr: Chapter 2 first proceeds with the general exhortation, given and belonging to all believers, namely to the pursuit of living holily, as far as verse 13. Then he adds particular exhortations to obedience toward superiors in the rest of the chapter.

units.la: Cap. III. continet adhuc duas exhortationes speciales: quarum prior pertinet ad uxores, posterior ad maritos: usque ad v. 8. Deinde redit ad exhortationes generales & omnibus communes: quas varias proponit usque ad v. 19. ubi digreditur in doctrinam de beneficiis Christi erga Ecclesiam tum veterem, tum novam, usque ad finem capitis.
units.tr: Chapter 3 contains two further particular exhortations: the first concerns wives, the second husbands, as far as verse 8. Then he returns to general exhortations common to all, which he sets out in various forms as far as verse 19, where he digresses into the doctrine of Christ's benefits toward the Church, both the old and the new, to the end of the chapter.

units.la: Cap. IV. primùm redit ad intermissam exhortationem, qua hortatur ad studium sanctè vivendi, usque ad v. 12. Deinde consolatur eos contra persecutiones quas patiebantur propter confessionem fidei Christianæ.
units.tr: Chapter 4 first returns to the exhortation interrupted before, by which he urges the pursuit of living holily, as far as verse 12. Then he comforts them against the persecutions they suffered for the confession of the Christian faith.

units.la: Cap. V. Redit primùm ad exhortationes speciales, ac efficii admonet tum presbyteros, tum juniores, usque ad v. 8. Deinde adiungit exhortationem generalem seu communem: v. 8. & 9. Postremò epistolam.
units.tr: Chapter 5 first returns to particular exhortations, and reminds both the elders and the younger men of their duties, as far as verse 8. Then he adds a general or common exhortation (verses 8 and 9). Lastly, the epistle ends.

units.la: CONCLUDIT
units.tr: CONCLUSION

units.la: Primùm voto, deinde doxologiâ seu celebratione nominis Dei, tum brevi praecipuorum capitum in epistola tractatorum indicatione, postremo salutationibus.
units.tr: First with a wish, then with a doxology, that is, a celebration of the name of God; then with a brief indication of the chief topics treated in the epistle; and lastly with greetings.

units.la: ARGUMENTA CAPITUM
units.tr: THE ARGUMENTS OF THE CHAPTERS

units.la: Cap. I
units.tr: Chapter I

units.la: FOrtia non mouebit mordax afflictio corda, Multaque pro Christi nomine ferre juvet. Hic etenim aeternae fons est & origo salutis, Hic manet: humana at [?] cuncta perire solent.
units.tr: Biting affliction will not move brave hearts; it is good to bear many things for the name of Christ. For this is the fount and origin of eternal salvation; this alone remains, while all human things are wont to perish.

units.la: Denuo, qui Christi fuerint per dogmata nati, Insontes mores obtinuisse decet. Fac colito proceres, populi qui sceptra gubernant. Nec pigeat forti pectore ferre crucem.
units.tr: Again, those born of Christ's teaching ought to keep blameless conduct. See that you honour the rulers who hold the sceptres of the people. Nor should it grieve you to bear the cross with a brave heart.

units.la: Coniungi leges diuino dogmate pandit. Sit tibi vita insons, sit pietatis amor. Nec moueat, si quae pro Christi nomine damna Eueniant: hic est vnica nempe salus.
units.tr: He shows that the laws are joined to the divine doctrine. Let your life be blameless and let there be love of godliness. Nor should it trouble you if any losses befall you for the name of Christ: this is indeed the only salvation.

units.la: Tollite uæsanæ fœdissima crimina vitæ, Quæ læthō Christus sustulit ante suo. Dispensēs digne diuini dona fauoris. Tristia constanti corde pericla feras.
units.tr: Cast off the most foul crimes of a frenzied life, which Christ before took away by his death. Dispense worthily the gifts of divine favour. Bear dreadful dangers with a steadfast heart.

units.la: Dogmata proponit sanctis seruanda ministris, Et iuuenum leges officiumque docet. Sint humiles animi & vigiles, sit sobria vita, Vt satanae possint tela nocere nihil.
units.tr: He sets forth doctrines to be kept by the holy ministers and teaches the laws and duties of the young. Let the minds be humble and watchful, let life be sober, so that the darts of Satan may harm nothing.

units.la: BREVIVS.
units.tr: IN BRIEF.

units.la: CAPVT I.
units.tr: CHAPTER I.

units.la: Audi quid credas, quid speres, cingite lumbos, Sanguine, non auro suspisat agnus oues. Bilis pellatur, lædit. nam vos genus estis Electum, cunctis detur honestus honos. Commonet vxores pia Sara, pericula ferte. Ima petit Christus. Noe lauacra noua. Defunctus vitiis benefac, si hospes amorem Serua, pro Christo vis tollerata beat. Este sacerdotes tales, parete minores. Sobrietas vigiles, nam leo quaerit oues.
units.tr: Hear what you should believe and what you should hope; gird up your loins. The Lamb has redeemed his sheep with blood, not gold. Anger is driven out and wounds. For you are a chosen race; let honest honour be given to all. Holy Sarah admonishes wives; bear dangers. Christ seeks the lowest things. Noah's washing is new. Dead to sins, do good; if you keep love as a guest, the endurance borne for Christ makes you blessed. Be such priests; obey as the younger ones. Be watchful in sobriety, for the lion seeks the sheep.

units.la: Breuissimè.
units.tr: Very briefly.

units.la: Vt Gramen, Alapis, Castam, Sobrij, Rugientis.{1}{2}{3}{4}{5}
units.tr: Grass, Buffets, Chaste, Sober, Roaring.{1}{2}{3}{4}{5}

units.la: Declaratio.
units.tr: Explanation.

units.la: {1} Vt Garmen est omnis caro: v. 24. {2} Alapis cùm cæ-dimini toleratis. {3} Castam vestram conuersationem: v. 2. {4} Sobrii estote: v. 7. {5} Rugientis instar Leonis obambulat Satan v. 8.
units.tr: {1} As "all flesh is grass": v. 24. {2} Buffeted when you endure being beaten. {3} Your chaste conversation: v. 2. {4} Be sober: v. 7. {5} "As a roaring lion, Satan walks about": v. 8.

units.la: POSTERIOR EPISLOLA S. PETRI.
units.tr: THE SECOND EPISTLE OF ST PETER.

units.la: APostolus Petrus in priori epistola magis voluit reddere constantes in professione Christiana, ne scilicet pij metu periculorum, aut molestia persecutionum deficerent à veritate. In hac autem posteriore magis hoc urget, ut pij crescant indies in renati hominis virtutibus, quibus professio ipsa est ornanda: disserit interea de aliis quoque locis, ut de çavendis falsis doctoribus, de consensu doctrinæ propheticæ & Apostolicæ, de statu nouissimi temporis, de præstantia Paulinæ doctrinæ, quæ omnia magno ardore piis inculcat.
units.tr: The Apostle Peter, in his first epistle, wished chiefly to make his readers steadfast in their profession of the Christian faith, so that the godly would not, through fear of dangers or the trouble of persecutions, fall away from the truth. In this second letter, however, he presses more strongly that the godly should grow daily in the virtues of the reborn person, with which their profession ought to be adorned. Meanwhile he also discusses other matters: the avoidance of false teachers, the agreement of prophetic and apostolic doctrine, the state of the last times, and the excellence of Paul's teaching. He urges all of these on the godly with great earnestness.

units.la: Quibus scribatur. In scribendo Apostolus omnium sanctorum habuit rationem, quod inde colligimus, quia in inscriptione huius epistolæ v.1. inquit; iis qui æquè pretiosam fidem nobiscum sortiti sunt. Nam hac phrasi æquat Iudæis Gentes in Christo,& Apostolorum fidem ut ut fuerit excellens gradu, submittit ad omnium credentium in Christum infirmitatem. Itaque & nobis & toti posteritati scripta est.
units.tr: To whom it is written. In writing, the Apostle had regard for all the saints. We gather this because in the address of this epistle, at verse 1, he says: to those who have obtained a faith as precious as ours. For by this phrase he makes Jews and Gentiles equal in Christ, and however excellent the Apostles' faith may be in rank, he lowers it to the weakness of all who believe in Christ. Therefore it has been written both for us and for all posterity.

units.la: Propositionem sumo ex cap. 1. v. 5. & 6. & cap. 3. v. 18. ex quibus locis hæc sententia eruitur: Pij confitentes Christum semper cauti esse debent contra seductores, & in cursu Christianarum virtutum indies magis magisque crescere.
units.tr: The proposition. I take it from chapter 1, verses 5 and 6, and chapter 3, verse 18. From these passages this statement is drawn: those who confess Christ must always be cautious against seducers, and must grow daily more and more in the course of the Christian virtues.

units.la: Partium ordo.
units.tr: The order of the parts.

units.la: Epistola 2. Petri notetur Inscriptio: v. 1. 2. Exordium: v. 3. & 4. Tractatio principalisio[?] Admonitione quid Faciendum: progrediendum & persistendum in fide cap. 1. Fugiendum: nempe Pseudodoctores, quos praedixit & describit. cap. 2. Irrisores adventum Christi negantes: cap. 3. Conclusio: v. 17. 18.
units.tr: In the Second Epistle of Peter note: the inscription, verses 1 and 2; the exordium, verses 3 and 4; the principal treatment, in which he admonishes what must be done: one must advance and persevere in the faith, chapter 1. One must flee from the false teachers whom he foretold and describes, chapter 2. The mockers who deny the coming of Christ, chapter 3. The conclusion, verses 17 and 18.

units.la: Cap. I. praemissâ in scriptione (v. 1. & 2.)
units.tr: Chapter 1, with the preface in the salutation (verses 1 and 2).

units.la: 1. Exodiens confirmat fideles in spe augmenti donorum spiritualium, v. 3. & 4. 11. Hortatur eos ad studium proficiendi in fide aliisque virtutibus Christianis, a v. 5. usque ad 12. Inde enim causas exponit huiusce suae commonefactionis; usque ad v. 16. 111. Hortatur ad constantiam in fide & confessione doctrina ipsis ab Apostolis traditae.
units.tr: 1. In the exordium he strengthens the faithful in the hope of an increase of spiritual gifts, verses 3, 4 and 11. He exhorts them to zeal for progress in faith and the other Christian virtues, from verse 5 to verse 12. For from there he sets out the reasons for this his admonition; down to verse 16. 111. He exhorts them to constancy in faith and in confessing the doctrine handed down to them by the Apostles.

units.la: Cap. II. Posteaquam hortatus est ut constâter[?] retineant doctrinam veram ac salutarem Apostolorum, nunc contra monet ut sibi caveat a doctoribus falsis in Ecclesia exoriturus & iam tum exorientibus, ne ab illis in haereses exitiales sedu-tantur: simulque more sipsorum describit, unde veluti ex notis quibusdam queant agnosci ac proinde caveri.
units.tr: Chapter 2. After he has urged them to hold firmly to the true and saving doctrine of the Apostles, he now warns them against false teachers who will arise in the Church and who already are arising, lest they be seduced by them into destructive heresies. At the same time he describes them by their manner, so that from certain marks they may be recognized and therefore guarded against.

units.la: Cap. III. Transit ad aliam commonefactio-nem, qua monet ut sibi caveant a seductione[?] irrisorum seu illusorum, qui negant adventum Christi ad iudicium universale & mundi huius interitum. Itaque Apostolus primo adventum illum certò[?] asseuerat atque confirmat: vsque ad v. 8. Deinde for-mam interitus mundi graphicè describit.
units.tr: Chapter 3. He turns to another admonition, warning them to beware of the seduction of mockers or deceivers, who deny the coming of Christ to the universal judgment and the destruction of this world. Thus the Apostle first asserts and confirms that coming with certainty, down to verse 8. Then he describes graphically the manner of the world's destruction.

units.la: SVMMÆ CAPITVM.
units.tr: Summaries of the chapters.

units.la: Cap. I.
units.tr: Chapter I.

units.la: Omnia per Christum supremi rectoris olympi Tradidit, illius nec dubitata fides. Hancque probant sancti, simul hac pater ipse probauit, Cuncta igitur fidei nomine ferre decet.
units.tr: All things were handed down through Christ, the supreme ruler of heaven, and his faith is not to be doubted. The saints approve this, and the Father himself approved it at the same time, so it is fitting that everything be borne in the name of faith.

units.la: Nec frustra hac moneo: doctores nempe futuros Aspicio falsos, qui mala multa ferant. Qui fastu turgent, queis cordi est sola voluptas, Sed perdet fortis pectore falsa Deus.
units.tr: Nor do I give this warning in vain. For I see that there will be false teachers who bear many evils. They swell with pride and hold only pleasure dear, but God will destroy their falsehoods with a steadfast heart.

units.la: Condatis memori, quæ dixi pectore verba: Nam patient homines vltima secla malos, Vltima qui sperant venturæ tempora lucis, Sed vobis veræ sit pietatis amor.
units.tr: Store in your memory the words I have spoken in your heart. For men will endure evil until the last age, those who hope for the final times of the coming light. But may the love of true piety be yours.

units.la: BREVIVS.
units.tr: IN BRIEF.

units.la: Cap. I.
units.tr: Chapter I.

units.la: Admonet ista Petrus morti vicinus, amicos, Quam sit certa fides, scriptaque voxque probant.
units.tr: Peter, near death, warns his friends how certain the faith is, as both his writing and his voice attest.

units.la: Blasphemos terret, immorans Loth, Noa, Gomorrham, Illos qui redeunt si fuge canisque nonant.
units.tr: He terrifies the blasphemers, dwelling on Lot, Noah and Gomorrah, and on those who turn back, as the dog returns to its vomit.

units.la: Christe licet tarde, venient elementa liquescent, Expectate diem, Paulus vt ille iubet.
units.tr: Christ comes, though slowly; the elements will melt. Await the day, as Paul bids.

units.la: Breuissimè.
units.tr: Very briefly.

units.la: Lucifer, vtque Volutabris, Elementa liquescent
units.tr: The morning star, and as the sow wallows in the mire; the elements will melt.

units.la: Declaratio.
units.tr: Explanation.

units.la: Lucifer donec oriatur in cordibus vestris. v. 19. vtque Volutabris sus tota voluitur: v. 22. Elementa liquescent in fine mundi. v. 10.
units.tr: The morning star, until the day dawns in your hearts. v. 19. As the sow wallows in the mire, so it is rolled. v. 22. The elements will melt at the end of the world. v. 10.

units.la: EVANGELISTAE IOHANNIS EPISTOLA prima
units.tr: The First Epistle of the Evangelist John

units.la: IOHANNES Euangelista & Apostolus (de quo dictum supra in Analysi Euangelij secundum Ioh:) informat praesenti Epistola vitam & mores hominis Christiani, offendens non satis esse quòd dicamur filij Dei, aut quòd habeamus communionem cum Deo, ipsum nouerimus, in ipso simus & maneamus, aut in luce Euangelij ambulemus: (sic enim in hypo-critarum quoque persona interdum loquitur Apostolus) nisi auerferit vitae innocentia, & mandatorum eius obseruantia,
units.tr: John the Evangelist and Apostle (of whom I spoke above, in the Analysis of the Gospel according to John) sets forth in this Epistle the life and conduct of the Christian. He shows that it is not enough to be called sons of God, or to have communion with God, to know him, to be in him and abide in him, or to walk in the light of the Gospel (for the Apostle sometimes speaks in the person of hypocrites in this way), unless the innocence of life and the observance of his commandments follow.

units.la: Vt igitur ad scribendum Euangelium exei-tatus est Cerinti & Hebionis haereticorum prauitate: sic ad scribendam hanc epistolam provocatus est licentia viuendi, inprimis eorum, qui speciosa nomina Christianae libeatatis perpetuo habebant in ore, interim his nominibus non respondebat vita. Propositio igitur totius Epistolae haec est: Filij Dei reuera isti sunt, qui sana de Christo doctrina imbuti fidem integritate vitae exprimunt. Nam vult Apostolus detrahere hypocritis larvam & speciosos titulos, quibus vtebantur sine fructu, quemadmodum hodie in Ecclesia passim speciosa nomina circunferuntur, sine re, sine veritate.
units.tr: Just as the Gospel was provoked by the wickedness of the heretics Cerinthus and Ebion, so this Epistle was provoked by licentious living, especially by those who always had the specious names of Christian liberty on their lips, while their lives did not match these names. The proposition of the whole Epistle is therefore this: those are truly sons of God who, steeped in sound teaching about Christ, express their faith in the integrity of their lives. For the Apostle wishes to strip the hypocrites of their mask and their showy titles, which they used to no profit, just as today in the Church such specious names are carried about everywhere, without substance and without truth.

units.la: Argumentum. Etsi varius est pro more ac libertate Spiritus Apostolici Iohannes: tamen tota ipsius Epistola ad haec tria potissimum capita subsequentia commodè redigi potest. Primò[?] quidem extollit inenarrabile beneficium filij Dei per incarnationem & passionem ipsius nobis partum. Deinde monet, quid Deus pro hoc immenso dono vicissim à nobis postulet, nempe dilectionem proximi synceram. Denique sollicitè exhortatur, ne tantum thesaurum Christi salutari adventu ad nos allatum, eripi nobis Pseudodoctorum versutiâ patiamur. Haec autem non sigillatim aut seorsim tractat singula, sed grata quadam variatione sic miscet, sic temperat, ut & à doctrinâ de beneficio Christi ad charitatem commendandam excurrat, & rursum à commendatione ad doctrinam de Christo nobis inculcandam redeat.
units.tr: Argument. Although John is varied, according to the custom and freedom of the Apostolic Spirit, the whole of his Epistle can nonetheless conveniently be reduced to the following three main heads. First[?] indeed, he extols the inexpressible benefit of the Son of God, brought to us through his incarnation and passion. Next, he admonishes what God, in return for this immense gift, requires of us, namely sincere love of neighbour. Finally, he earnestly exhorts us not to allow so great a treasure, brought to us by Christ's saving coming, to be snatched from us by the cunning of false teachers. He does not treat these matters one by one or separately, but mixes and tempers them with a pleasing variety, so that he passes from the teaching about the benefit of Christ to the commending of love, and then returns again from the commendation to the teaching about Christ, which is to be impressed upon us.

units.la: Capitum tamen connexio, doctrinae & memoriae causa haec notetur: Epistola Io-hannis pr. ma est tum Hortatoria ad Fidem Christi unde communio & unio: cap. 1. Charitatem, ubi Materia, quid diligendum, quid non: cap. 2. Forma dilectionis divinae & humanae: cap. 3. Didascalica de Fugienda seductione, cui opponitur dilectio: cap. 4. Amplectenda fide & charitate: cap. 5.
units.tr: For the sake of teaching and memory, the connection of the chapters is noted here: The First Epistle of John is at once exhortatory, to faith in Christ, whence communion and union (chap. 1); about love, where the matter is what is to be loved and what is not (chap. 2); the form of divine and human love (chap. 3); didactic, on avoiding seduction, to which love is opposed (chap. 4); and on embracing faith and love (chap. 5).

units.la: Cap. I. Orditur à Doctrina fidei, describens personam Christi & indicans praecipuum illius in fideles collatum beneficium, videlicet vitam aeternam: quam definit communione cum Deo & solido gaudio:
units.tr: Chapter I. Begins from the doctrine of faith, describing the person of Christ and pointing out the chief benefit conferred by him on the faithful, namely eternal life, which he defines as communion with God and solid joy:

units.la: gaudio: vsque ad v. 5. Deinde annectit præceptum sanctitatis, in eoque exponendo ad doctrinam fidei redit, exponens aliud Christi erga fideles bene-ficium, videlicet remissionem peccatorum: vbi simul reprehendit eos qui se peccati expertes profiten-tur.
units.tr: joy: as far as verse 5. Then he attaches a precept of holiness, and in expounding this he returns to the doctrine of faith, expounding another benefit of Christ toward the faithful, namely the forgiveness of sins; where at the same time he rebukes those who profess themselves free from sin.

units.la: Cap. 11. Exhortaturus Apostolus Christianos ad pietatem, principio paucis meritum bene-ficiumque Christi antecedente cap. explicatum, hic repetit: vsque ad v. 3. Deinde nouam obedientiam in genere, & dilectionem proximi tanquam obedientiæ huius nouæ partem in specie inculcat, vsque ad v. 12. Tertio commonefactionem eam ad statum gradus distributione quadam accommodat. vsque ad v. 18. Quarto de cauendis Antichristis seu Pseudodoctoribus monet. Tandem, ad constantiam in agnita semel veritate Euangelij exuscitat: a v. 24. vsque ad finem.
units.tr: Chapter II. The Apostle, about to exhort Christians to godliness, first briefly repeats the merit and benefit of Christ explained in the preceding chapter: as far as verse 3. Then he impresses upon them new obedience in general, and love of neighbour in particular as a part of this new obedience, as far as verse 12. Thirdly, he adapts this admonition to the stages of life by a certain distribution, as far as verse 18. Fourthly, he warns about guarding against the Antichrists, or false teachers. Finally, he rouses them to constancy in the truth of the Gospel once known: from verse 24 to the end.

units.la: Capite 111. Apostolus suum institutum persequens, principio dignitatem filiorum Dei proponit & extollit. Deinde hinc exhortationem extruit, variis rationibus & argumentis vitæ sanctitatem, nouam obedientiam & Christianæ charitatis studium vrgens, & fidelibus inculcans. Sic ergo duabus partibus principalioribus hoc vniuersum caput absol-vitur, quarum prior, de dilectione Dei & dignitate Christianorum, posterioris (v. 3.) quasi basis & fundamentum est, & posterior a priore connectitur & dependet.
units.tr: Chapter III. The Apostle, pursuing his plan, first sets forth and extols the dignity of the sons of God. Then from this he builds an exhortation, urging and impressing upon the faithful the holiness of life, new obedience and zeal for Christian love by various reasons and arguments. Thus this whole chapter is completed in two principal parts, of which the first, concerning the love of God and the dignity of Christians, is as it were the basis and foundation of the second (verse 3), and the second is connected with and depends upon the first.

units.la: Cap. 1v. Primùm monet vt sibi caveant à seductoribus: vsque ad v. 7. Deinde iterum horta-tur ad dilectionem fraternam.
units.tr: Chapter IV. First he warns them to be on their guard against seducers, as far as verse 7. Then again he exhorts them to brotherly love.

units.la: Cap. v. Fidei ac regenerationis insignes qui-dam effectus commemorantur. 1. monet dile-ctionem proximi fidelis indiuiduo nexu coherere cum dilectione Dei: 2. docet unde habeamus vires ad seruandum mandata Dei: à v. 3. usque ad v. 6. Tertiò testimoniis diuinis confirmat, Iesum esse Christum, authorem vitæ æternæ omnibus in eum credentibus: usque ad v. 9. Quartò hortatur ad fidem testimonii illis habendam, usque ad 14. versum. Commendat fidelibus preces concipiendas tum pro seipsis, tum pro fratre peccante non ad mortem; & contra eius peccati periculum seu metum fideles consolatur, eaque occasione amplissimum Do-mino Iesu testimonium reddit: usque ad v. 21. ubi eos monet ut sibi caveant ab idolis.
units.tr: Chapter V. Certain distinguished effects of faith and regeneration are recorded. (1) He teaches that love of the faithful neighbour is bound by an inseparable tie to love of God; (2) he teaches whence we have the strength to keep the commandments of God: from verse 3 to verse 6. (3) Thirdly, by divine testimonies he confirms that Jesus is the Christ, the author of eternal life to all who believe in him: as far as verse 9. (4) Fourthly, he exhorts them to hold the testimony of these things in faith, as far as verse 14. He commends to the faithful prayers to be offered both for themselves and for a brother who sins not unto death; and against the danger or fear of that sin he comforts the faithful, and on that occasion renders the most ample testimony to the Lord Jesus: as far as verse 21, where he warns them to beware of idols.

units.la: CAPITUM ARGUMENTA.
units.tr: ARGUMENTS OF THE CHAPTERS.

units.la: CAPUT I.
units.tr: CHAPTER I.

units.la: Non ego vilsa[?] scribo vobis, sed dogmata certa, Et quæ præsentes vidimus ante simul. Christus enim est solus nobis peccata remittens. Si peccatorem te fateare modo.
units.tr: I do not write to you of trifles, but of certain doctrines, and of things we saw with our own eyes before us. For Christ alone forgives us our sins. If you now confess yourself a sinner.

units.la: Sit pietatis amor, vigileris [?]pectore cauto. Nam falsos Christos ultima secla ferent. Quorum artes solos poterit vitare dolosque, Doctrinæ sanctæ qui pia iusta tenet.
units.tr: Let there be love of godliness, and watch with a cautious heart. For the last ages will bring forth false Christs. Only one who holds fast the pious and just teaching of holy doctrine will be able to avoid their arts and deceits.

units.la: Cernite quantum amor Christi, qui morte redemit Vos propria, & natos vos dedit, esse Dei. Non igitur vitam liceat tractare profanam. Fraternus casto pectore flagret amor.
units.tr: See how great is the love of Christ, who redeemed you by his death as his own, and made you sons of God. Therefore let no one allow himself to live a profane life. Let brotherly love burn in a chaste heart.

units.la: Edocet ut possint alienæ scita probare Doctrinæ, & sanctam continuare fidem. Denuo fraternum post hæc commendat amorem, Qui sancto similes, nos facit esse Deo.
units.tr: He teaches you to be able to test the decrees of foreign doctrine and to keep the holy faith. After this he again commends brotherly love, which makes us like holy God.

units.la: Quæ fidei virtus sit sancto disseris ore, Quæ firma in Christum credere mente, docet.
units.tr: You set out with a holy mouth what the virtue of faith is; he teaches what it is to believe in Christ with a steadfast mind.
