units.la: Totius hic etenim solus vita vnica mundi est,Quo sine (crede mihi) non venit vlla salus.
units.tr: For he alone is the one life of the whole world, and without him (believe me) no salvation comes.

units.la: BREVIVS. CAPVT I.
units.tr: BRIEFLY. CHAPTER I.

units.la: Auditum refero. Deus est lux: huic sociemur.Se patrasse negans crimina, vera negat.
units.tr: I report what we heard. God is light; let us have fellowship with him. Whoever denies that he has committed sins, denies the truth.

units.la: 2 Belle quid quis amet, quid non, advertite, erunt, moxAntichristi. vos unctio sacra docet.
units.tr: Mark well what each man loves and what he does not love; soon there will be Antichrists. The holy anointing teaches you.

units.la: 3 Christum cernemus, qui tollit Dæmonis artes.Vitemus Cainum. cor neget esse reos.
units.tr: We shall see Christ, who destroys the arts of the devil. Let us avoid Cain. Let the heart deny that it is guilty.

units.la: 4 Dico spiritibus non credendum esse quibusuis.Sit perfectus amor; cogit abire metum.
units.tr: I say that one should not believe every spirit. Let love be perfect; it drives out fear.

units.la: 5 Est invicta fides. tres sunt unum. bene credensAccipit. haud rogites pro graviore malo.
units.tr: Faith is unconquered. Three are one. The one who believes rightly receives. Do not ask for a greater evil in exchange.

units.la: Breuissimè.
units.tr: Very briefly.

units.la: 1 2 3 4 5 Vt Plenum, Mendax, Similes, ne Credite, Vincit.
units.tr: 1 2 3 4 5: That (Ut) Full, Liar, Like, Do not believe, Overcomes.

units.la: Declaratio.
units.tr: Explanation.

units.la: Vt Plenum sit gaudium vestrum, hæc scribimus: v. 4. Mendax est qui dicit se nosse Dominum, & mandata eius non seruat: v. 4. Similes Deo erimus: v. 2. ne Cre-dite cuiuis spiritui. v. 1. Vincit mundum quicquid ge-nitum est ex Deo: v. 4.
units.tr: So that your joy may be full, we write these things: 1 John 1.4. A liar is the one who says he knows the Lord and does not keep his commandments: 2.4. We shall be like God: 3.2. Do not believe every spirit: 4.1. Whatever is born of God overcomes the world: 5.4.

units.la: SECUNDA IOHANNIS EPISTOLA.
units.tr: THE SECOND EPISTLE OF JOHN.

units.la: Tractat locum de mutua dilectione in Christo. Nam ad eius exercitium hortatur Apostolo-lus hoc epistolio quandam viduam, quæ cum liberis suis veram de Christo hauserat doctrinam, qui & hanc cognitionem vitae & moribus apprimè ornabat. Et simul praemonet de cavendis seductoribus, qui passim circuibant & insinuabant se familiis, praesertim viduarum, ut eas seducerent: suggerit etiam regulam cognoscendi tales ex discrepantia morum, & ignorantia doctrinae Christi, cum quibus nulla debet esse piis communio, ut pote quae contagiosa est.
units.tr: It treats of the place concerning mutual love in Christ. For in this short letter the Apostle urges a certain widow to practise it. She, together with her children, had received the true doctrine about Christ, and she adorned this knowledge of the life of faith especially well by her conduct. At the same time he warns her to beware of seducers, who went about everywhere and insinuated themselves into households, especially those of widows, in order to lead them astray. He also gives a rule for recognising such people: their conduct disagrees with their profession, and they are ignorant of the doctrine of Christ. Godly people ought to have no fellowship with them, since such fellowship is contagious.

units.la: Partes epistolae sunt ita connexae: 1. est Titulus exprimens personam salutantem & salutatas, & comprecationem: v. 1. 2. 3. 11. Exordium ad benevolentiam accommodatum: v. 4. 111. Propositio, cuius duo sunt membra: prius est; Vidua haec cum sua familia in exercitio Christianae dilectionis quam constantissimè perseuerare debet: v. 5. [?] huius propositionis est v. 6. ostendens quam dilectionem suadeat. Altera pars propositionis de falsis doctoribus diligenter cavendis a v. 7. continuatur usque ad v. 12. Vbi est Epilogus in excusatione brevitatis, promissione sui adventus, & salutationibus.
units.tr: The parts of the epistle are so connected: 1. It is the title, expressing the person greeting and those greeted, and the wish of blessing: vv. 1, 2, 3, 11. The exordium, fitted to win goodwill: v. 4, 111. The proposition, which has two members. The first is: this widow, with her household, must persevere as steadfastly as possible in the practice of Christian love: v. 5. [?] Of this proposition v. 6 is the substance, showing what love it recommends. The second part of the proposition, on diligently avoiding false teachers, runs from v. 7 to v. 12. There is the epilogue, containing an apology for the brevity, a promise of his coming, and greetings.

units.la: Summa.
units.tr: Summary.

units.la: Adsit amor. seductor erit, quisquis negat ista, Hunc fuge, non scribam plura, sed ore loquar.
units.tr: Let love be present. Whoever denies these things will be a seducer; shun him. I will not write more, but will speak in person.

units.la: EPISTOLA IOHANNIS APOSTOLI tertia.
units.tr: The Third Epistle of the Apostle John.

units.la: APostolus Gaium, haud dubè non paruae in Ecclesia authoritatis virum, laudat propter studium syncerae doctrinae coelestis & verae pietatis, quam officiis charitatis erga fratres, imprimis verò fideles Ecclesiæ ministros declarabat. Et hortatur eum, vt in tam bene coeptis pergat, vsque ad v. 9. Deinde accusat Diotrephen, qui sibi imperium in Ecclesiam illam sumebat, eratque homo inflatus, nec syncera doctrina, nec charitatis studiosus : v. 9. 10. 11. Tertiò commendat alium Ecclesiæ ministrum Demetrium, à fidelitate, ob quam Ecclesiæ merito erat charus : idque ideo facit, vt doceat, arrogantes & insynceros Ministros esse fugiendos, bonos verò & fideles diligendos, & honore prosequendos: v.12. Postremò promissione sui aduentus, pio voto acsa-lutationibus Epistolam terminat.
units.tr: The Apostle commends Gaius, a man certainly of no small authority in the Church, for his zeal for sound heavenly doctrine and true godliness, which he declares is shown in the duties of love towards the brothers, and above all towards the faithful ministers of the Church. And he exhorts him to persevere in such a good beginning, as far as verse 9. Then he accuses Diotrephes, who was claiming power for himself in that Church, and was a puffed-up man, neither sound in doctrine nor devoted to love: verses 9, 10, 11. Thirdly, he commends another minister of the Church, Demetrius, for his faithfulness, on account of which he was rightly dear to the Church; and he does this in order to teach that arrogant and insincere ministers are to be avoided, but good and faithful ones are to be loved and shown honour: verse 12. Lastly, he ends the Epistle with a promise of his coming, a pious wish, and greetings.

units.la: Summa :
units.tr: Summary:

units.la: Macte animo, Gai, coeptum persoluito cursum, Sit fortis Veri : sit pietatis amor. Diotrephem taxat, laudat Demetrion inde: Etse venturum praedicat esse cito.
units.tr: Take heart, Gaius; finish the course you have begun. Let there be strength for the truth and love for godliness. He rebukes Diotrephes, praises Demetrius in turn, and declares that he himself will soon be coming.

units.la: EPISTOLA S. IUDÆ.
units.tr: THE EPISTLE OF ST. JUDE.

units.la: APOSTOLUS Iudas qui appellatus est Lebbæus & Thaddæus, qui fuit Alphæi filius & (vt in Epigraphe dicit) frater Iacobi Iusti, & per consequens Simonis Cananæi, cuius vocatio habetur apud Matth:10. Luc.6.Marc.9. & repetitur Act.1. qui docuit Euangeleum in diuersis nationibus Mesophotamia, Ponto, Ægypto & Perside: Hic (inquam) Iudas in hac sua ad omnes qui Christi nomen profitentur, epi-stolâ idem vrget argumentum, quod superiores Canonicæ epistolæ, nimirum pios oportere vocationi suæ quàm diligentissimè insistere. Nam Deus etiam punit vocatos, si non respondeant vocatione suæ vitæ innocentia. Hinc colligit varia exēpla iræ divinæ, ut in populo Dei, in Angelis lapsis, in Sodomitis, Gomorræis, quæ exempla accommodat ad statum Ecclesiæ, quæ similia portenta semper aluit, & adhuc alit, inprimis etiam inter doctores quosdam tales suis coloribus depingit.
units.tr: The Apostle Jude, who was called Lebbaeus and Thaddaeus, was the son of Alphaeus and (as he says in his superscription) brother of James the Just, and so also of Simon the Canaanite. His calling is recorded in Matthew 10, Luke 6 and Mark 9, and repeated in Acts 1. He taught the Gospel among various nations: Mesopotamia, Pontus, Egypt and Persia. In this letter, addressed to all who profess the name of Christ, Jude (I say) presses the same argument as the earlier catholic epistles, namely that the godly must give the most diligent attention to their calling. For God also punishes those who are called if the innocence of their life does not correspond to their calling. From this he draws various examples of divine wrath: among the people of God, among the fallen angels, and among the Sodomites and Gomorrhites. He applies these examples to the state of the Church, which has always nourished, and still nourishes, similar monsters, and especially he paints certain such teachers in their true colours.

units.la: Partes post titulum qui personas & comprecationem complectitur, (v. 1. 2.) quatuor sunt. 1. Exordium ad benevolentiam & attentionem accommodatum: v. 3. II. Propositio, pro fide diligenter esse vigilandum: eodem v. Confirmatio, in qua à seductorum turba, exemplis poenarum, ac etiam eventu diligenter pios excitat ad vigilantiam: usque ad v. 24. III. Concludit epistolam celebratione nominis Dei: & eâ occasione simul eis promittit Dei opem ad præstandum ea ad quæ fuerat hortatus.
units.tr: The parts of the letter after the title, which embraces the persons and the greeting (vv. 1, 2), are four. (1) An exordium, suited to win goodwill and attention: v. 3. (2) The proposition, that we must diligently watch over the faith: the same verse. The confirmation, in which, by the crowd of seducers, by examples of punishments, and also by the outcome, he diligently stirs the godly to vigilance, down to v. 24. (3) He concludes the letter by celebrating the name of God, and on that occasion at the same time promises them God's help in carrying out what he had urged them to do.

units.la: ARGVMENTVM
units.tr: ARGUMENT

units.la: Crescat sanctæ fides, aliosque juvate fideles, Conveniens fidei vitaque sancta fiet. Doctores pingit digno sermone dolosos, Illorum mores interitumque docens. Monostichon Notas memoriales, trium antecedentium Epistolarum complexum. Non Charta, & Calamo, Certans de corpore Mosis Declaratio.
units.tr: Let the faith of the saints grow, and help the other faithful; a faith fitting to them and a holy life will come. He depicts the teachers as deceivers with a worthy speech, teaching their manners and their ruin. A monostich, memorial notes summing up the three preceding epistles. Not with paper and pen, contending over the body of Moses: a declaration.

units.la: Non Charta mandabo ea quæ vobis scribenda erant. 2. Ioh. v. 12. Et Calamo non scribam scribenda. 3. Ioh. v. 13.
units.tr: I will not entrust to paper the things that were to be written to you. 2 John 12. And I will not write with pen the things that are to be written. 3 John 13.

units.la: v. 13. Certans de corpore Mosis Angelus Michael contra Diabolum. Iudæ v. 9.
units.tr: v. 13. Contending over the body of Moses: the angel Michael against the Devil. Jude v. 9.

units.la: Hactenus fuit Analysis Epistolarum Apostolicarum : sequitur
units.tr: Hitherto has been the analysis of the Apostolic Epistles; what follows is

units.la: DE LIBRO N. T. PROPHETICO, QUI DICTUR ET EST Apocalypsis Iohannis Theologi.
units.tr: THE BOOK OF THE NEW TESTAMENT THAT IS PROPHETIC, WHICH IS CALLED THE Apocalypse of John the Theologian.

units.la: EPIGRAPHE seu inscriptio & ipsum Exor-dium huius libri, sicut etiam nostra in primariis scriptorum N. Testrmenti analysibus, hucusque observata methodus requirit, ut προ-λεγομένων[?] loco nonnulla annotemus. de autore eiusque nomine. 2. de genere scripti & stylo. 3. de hypothesi, occasione & usu. 4. de partibus & earum ordine.
units.tr: The epigraph, or inscription, and the opening of this book itself, as our method hitherto observed in the main analyses of the books of the New Testament requires, calls for us to note some things in place of prolegomena [προλεγομένων]: (1) concerning the author and his name; (2) concerning the kind of writing and its style; (3) concerning the hypothesis, occasion and use; (4) concerning the parts and their order.

units.la: De primo. Rationes ab eruditis adferuntur validæ, quæ piis persuadere possunt & debent Iohannem potius Apostolum & Euangelistam, quàm ullum alium huius libri esse Scriptorem: qua etiam in sententia fuerunt Iustinus Martyr, Irenæus, Tertullianus, Athanasius, Augustinus & tertium Concilium Carthaginense. Prima ratio: Uero consentaneum est hæc magna mysteria illi potissimum discipulo à Christo fuisse revelata, qui ei semper præ aliis intimus & omnium arcanorum conscius fuit, qualem fuisse Iohannē, constat ex historia eius Euangelica cap. 1; & 21. Et id innui videtur cap. 1. Apoc.v.1. Ubi hæc à Christo per angelum Iohanni servo eius (procul dubio κατ' ἐξοχὴν[?]) significata dicuntur.
units.tr: Concerning the first. Sound reasons are brought forward by learned men which can and should persuade the pious that John the Apostle and Evangelist, rather than anyone else, is the author of this book. Justin Martyr, Irenaeus, Tertullian, Athanasius, Augustine and the Third Council of Carthage also held this view. The first reason: it is fitting that these great mysteries were revealed by Christ above all to that disciple who was always closest to him beyond the others and aware of all his secrets, which John clearly was, as his Gospel history shows in chapters 1 and 21. This seems also to be hinted at in Rev. 1:1, where these things are said to have been signified by Christ through an angel to John his servant (beyond doubt [kat' exochēn], the servant par excellence).

units.la: 2. Ratio: Quòd eodem capite scribit Iohannes, se tunc fuisse in insula Pathmo propter testimonium Christi, eò scil: relegatum à Domitiano, quod de hoc solo Iohanne Apostolo commemorat Irenæus libro quinto, cap 5. Hieronymus in vita Iohannis. Et Eusebius lib. 3. historiæ, cap. 16. sub finem imperij Domitiani, anno à Christo nato 96.3 Ratio: à peculiaribus quibusdam phrasibus Iohannis Apostoli, quæ in Apocalypsi reperiuntur: Veluti de teste fideli, & de testimonio: quæ non solum in ipsius Euan-gelica historia, verùm etiam in epistola 1. cap. 3. & 5. & alibi sæpe occurrunt. Sic & Apoc: 1. 12. 19. 20. sed imprimis illa appellatio τοῦ λόγου, quæ Iohannis est propria, cum agitur de persona Filij Dei, cap 1. Euangelij, & Apocal: 19. Nec ob-stat, quòd in multis variat stylus, & alius videtur in Apocalypsi, quàm in Euangelica historia: quia solenne est autoribus, ut pro diuersitate argu-menti stylum varient, præsertim in prophe-tiis, ut Genes. 49. & Deut: 33. videre est.
units.tr: The second reason: in the same chapter John writes that he was then on the island of Patmos on account of the testimony of Christ, namely that he had been banished there by Domitian. Irenaeus records this of John the Apostle alone in book 5, chapter 5; Jerome does so in the life of John; and Eusebius in book 3 of his History, chapter 16, at the end of Domitian's reign, in the year 96 after the birth of Christ. The third reason: from certain peculiar phrases of John the Apostle found in the Apocalypse, such as "faithful witness" and "testimony," which occur not only in his Gospel history but also in his first epistle, chapters 3 and 5, and often elsewhere. So also in Rev. 1:2, 12, 19, 20. But especially the appellation "the Word" [tou logou], which is proper to John, when the person of the Son of God is in view: Gospel chapter 1, and Rev. 19. Nor does it count against this that the style varies in many places and seems different in the Apocalypse from the Gospel history, because it is customary for authors to vary their style according to the diversity of their subject, especially in prophecies, as may be seen in Gen. 49 and Deut. 33.

units.la: Quòd nominum varietatem attinet, qua Iohannem hunc alij Theologum, alij Apostolum, alij Presbyterum, alij Euangelistam appellant, nihil detrahit nostræ sententiæ: cum hæ omnes appellationes de vna eàdemque persona hîc accipi debeant: quia ex vetustis autoribus colligitur, Iohannem Apostolum propter eximiam doctrinam de λόγῳ, Dei Filio, Theologum vocatum. Sicut & Basilio & Nazianzeno Theologia sæpe dicitur doctrina de Filio Dei. Sic & Presbyteri siue senioris nomen sortitus videtur, quod diutissimè inter Apostolos vixerit. Ideò in Complutensi editione talis est titulus, qui illas appellationes omnes complectitur: Apocalypsis S. Apostoli & Euangelistæ Iohannis Theologi.
units.tr: As to the variety of names by which some call this John the Theologian, others the Apostle, others the Elder, others the Evangelist, this takes nothing away from our opinion, since all these titles must be understood as applying to one and the same person. For from ancient authors it is gathered that John the Apostle was called "the Theologian" on account of his outstanding teaching about the Word [logos], the Son of God. So too Basil and Gregory Nazianzen often call the doctrine of the Son of God "theology." Likewise he seems to have received the name of Presbyter or Elder because he lived for a very long time among the Apostles. Therefore in the Complutensian edition the title runs thus, embracing all these appellations: "The Apocalypse of the Holy Apostle and Evangelist John the Theologian."

units.la: De secundo, hoc est de genere scripti, quod Apocalypsis vocatur, cap. 1. v. 1. non solum, quia immediatè per Christum hæc ei revelata fuerunt: quo sensu S. Paulus ad Gal: 1. ad Eph. 3. scribit, se Euangelium didicisse κατ' ἀποκάλυψιν: verum etiam, quia per speciales visiones, non quidem nova doctrina, sed novi ac varij euentus, typis repræsentati fuêre. Idcirco & Prophetia dicitur, vt sciamus genus doctrinæ esse propheticum, id est prædicti res futuras per certam & extraordinariam revelationem, qualis olim Prophetis iam vigilantibus, iam dormientibus offerabatur. Non ergo hic liber dicitur Apocalypsis, quasi omnia in eo sint clara, cùm potiùs sit κρυπτικὸν scriptum: sed quia res arcanas, quæ ab hominibus præuideri non poterant, Deus per revelationem in certis typis & figuris spectandas proposuit. Inueniuntur quidem prædictiones nonnullæ de rebus futuris, & de conditione Ecclesiæ apud Euangelistas quoque, veluti Matth. 24. Luc. 21. Ioh. 16. 2. ad Thess: 2. sed non ita copiosè nec cum talibus typis, quales totus hic libet habet, pingens nobis vtrumque statum Ecclesiæ, militantis scilicet & triumphantis.
units.tr: Concerning the second, that is, the kind of writing, which is called Apocalypse (Rev. 1:1): not only because these things were revealed to him immediately by Christ, in which sense St. Paul writes to the Galatians (1) and the Ephesians (3) that he learned the Gospel by revelation [kat' apokalypsin]; but also because they were set before him through special visions, not indeed as new doctrine, but as new and varied events presented in types. For this reason it is also called Prophecy, so that we may know that the kind of teaching is prophetic, that is, that it foretells future things by a certain and extraordinary revelation, such as was once offered to the Prophets, whether awake or asleep. Therefore this book is not called Apocalypse as if everything in it were clear, since it is rather a hidden writing [kryptikon]; rather, because God, by revelation, has set before us arcane matters, which could not be foreseen by men, to be contemplated in certain types and figures. Some predictions about future events and about the condition of the Church are indeed found in the Evangelists as well, for example Matt. 24, Luke 21, John 16, and 2 Thess. 2. But not so copiously, nor with such types as this whole book has, depicting for us both states of the Church, namely the militant and the triumphant.

units.la: De tertio: hoc est, occasione & hypothesi atque visu Apocalypseos. Erat proculdubio tunc Iohannes, vt ex v. 9. cap. 1. colligi potest, in insula Patmo variè afflictus, tũ propter persecutiones, tum inprimis propter corruptissimos multorum Christianorum mores, qui pertæsi iam ve-ritatis Euangelicæ veterem Zelum abiiciebant, & à Pseudoprophetis ac Antichristis, qui illis temporibus irrumpebant in Ecclesiam, se seduci patiebantur, vide cap. 2. v. 95. & 20. Voluit ita-que, Dominus ne vilesceret doctrina Euagelij, per hanc prophetiam & hos typos expergefa-cere & terrere securos & impios, eosque ad de-nunciatis propositisq. tot horrendis typis futu-rorum iudiciorum, ad pœnitentiam reuocare: partim Iohannem & alios pios erigere, ne animum desponderent, aut regnum carnale & mū-danum in terris sibi pollicerentur, sed intellige-rent imminere adhuc varia certamina. Mun-dum enim daturum pœnas suæ incredulita-tis, & Deum purgaturum suam aream. Denique, futura tempora tentationis, vt dicitur cap. 3. & complendum numerum interficiendorum propter testimonium veritatis: attamen illum Agnum Dei olim occisum, nunc viuentem in gloria Patris de omnibus suis hostibus triumphaturum, & suos electos, licet communibus plagis & miseriis involuantur, signaturum, vt dicitur cap. 7. ne eorum saluti quicquam noce-ant, & tandem Ecclesiam cum suo sponso in cœlesti illa & augustissima Ierusalem trium-phet.
units.tr: Concerning the third: that is, the occasion, the hypothesis and the aim of the Apocalypse. Without doubt John was then, as can be gathered from Rev. 1:9, variously afflicted on the island of Patmos: partly on account of persecutions, but chiefly on account of the thoroughly corrupt morals of many Christians, who, already weary of the Gospel truth, were casting off their former zeal and allowing themselves to be seduced by false prophets and Antichrists, who at that time were breaking into the Church (see Rev. 2:9, 5 and 20). Therefore the Lord, so that the doctrine of the Gospel might not be held in contempt, wished through this prophecy and these types to rouse and terrify the secure and the impious, and by setting forth so many dreadful types of future judgments to call them back to repentance. He wished in part to raise up John and the other pious, so that they would not lose heart or promise themselves a carnal and worldly kingdom on earth, but would understand that various conflicts were still impending: that the world would pay the penalty of its unbelief, and that God would purge his threshing floor. Finally, that there would be future times of temptation, as is said in Rev. 3, and that the number of those to be killed for the testimony of the truth would be completed. Yet he wished them to know that the Lamb of God, once slain and now living in the glory of the Father, will triumph over all his enemies and will seal his elect, though they are entangled in common plagues and miseries, as is said in Rev. 7, so that these do no harm to their salvation; and that at last the Church, with her bridegroom, will triumph in that heavenly and most august Jerusalem.

units.la: De quarto: Communis partitio libri talis est, vt diuidatur in quatuor partes: 1 in parascuen totius operis, quæ eius velut summam adum-brat in Epistolis scriptis ad septem Ecclesias, tribus prioribus capitibus. II.in pulcherrimam hypotypôsin Dei accingentis se ad iudicia sua exexsequenda, & Filij enarrantis illa iudicia, quæ aliàs sigillorum instar clausa essent, nisi ille aperiret: & hæc quidem cap. 4. 5. & 6. iii. in apertionem sigillorum signatis prius electis. cap. 7. 8. 9. 10. II. I V à cap. 12. ad finem continet novas & insignes visiones, quarum aliæ confirmant præcedentia: aliæ proprie ad regnum Antichristi pertinent & ad vltima tempora: aliæ duobus vltimis capitibus proponunt nobis hypotypôsin iucundissimam triumphi Christi & eius Ecclesiæ triumphantis in cœlis.
units.tr: Concerning the fourth: The common division of the book is this, that it is divided into four parts. (I) The preface to the whole work, which in a sense summarises it, in the epistles written to the seven Churches, in the first three chapters. (II) A most beautiful sketch of God preparing himself to carry out his judgments, and of the Son recounting those judgments, which would otherwise have been closed like sealed things unless he opened them; these are in chapters 4, 5 and 6. (III) The opening of the seals, after the elect have first been sealed, in chapters 7, 8, 9 and 10. (IV) From chapter 12 to the end, it contains new and remarkable visions, some of which confirm what precedes, others pertain properly to the kingdom of Antichrist and to the last times, and others in the last two chapters set before us a most delightful sketch of the triumph of Christ and of his Church triumphant in heaven.

units.la: Verum nos in capitum coherentia & dispositione indi-canda, lineamenta, à clariss. Theologo, D. Frn: Iunio dudta[?], potissimum sequemur.
units.tr: But in indicating the coherence and arrangement of the chapters we shall follow mainly the outlines drawn up by the most distinguished theologian, Mr. Francis Junius.

units.la: Partes itaque Apocalypseos sunt tres: eorumque duæ sunt & dicuntur ἀκρωτήρια[?] i. extremita-tes, partes accessoriæ, minusque principales. Principa-lis pars appellatur πραγματεία[?] seu Tractatio essentialis.
units.tr: The parts of the Apocalypse are therefore three, and of these two are called the extremities [akrōtēria], that is, accessory and less principal parts. The principal part is called the treatise [pragmateia], or essential discourse.

units.la: De Prima Parte,
units.tr: On the First Part,

units.la: Quæ est primum ἀκρωτήριον, vsitatè proœ-mium seu exordium vocitata i. Capite primo, à v. 1. vsque ad v. penultimum. Huius ἀ[illegible, ~6 letters] membra duo sunt Inscriptio duplex, vice exordij, Generalis, complectitur genus, autorem, finem, materiâ, instrumen-ta, modumque communicationis (v. 1.) fidem religiosissimam Apo-stoli ut testis publici, (v. 2.) usum communicationis illius:(v. 3.) Particularis, quâ salutantur certæ Ecclesiæ Catholicam Ecclesiam figurantes: ad v. 8. usque. Narratio præuia ad autoritatem & vocationem Apostoli Iohannis, in singulari hac revelatione exponendam, fidemque faciendâ huic Prophetiæ: usque ad v. penult. capitis I.
units.tr: Which is the first ἀκρωτήριον [akrōtērion, extremity], commonly called the proem or exordium: that is, chapter 1, from verse 1 to the penultimate verse. Its two members are: first, a double inscription serving as the exordium. The General inscription covers the kind of writing, the author, the purpose, the subject matter, the means, and the manner of communication. It sets out (v. 1) the most faithful witness of the Apostle as a public witness, (v. 2) the use of that communication, and (v. 3) the same. The Particular inscription, in which certain churches are greeted as figures of the Catholic Church, runs up to verse 8. Second, the preliminary narrative, which establishes the authority and calling of the Apostle John for this unique revelation, and makes this prophecy credible. It runs up to the penultimate verse of chapter 1.

units.la: DE SECVNDA PARTE, QVÆ est Tractatio principalis seu essentialis huius libri.
units.tr: THE SECOND PART, WHICH IS the principal or essential treatment of this book.

units.la: Principalis Tractatio habet Propositionem argumenti bipartitam, in ea quæ sunt præsentia cap. 1. duobus versibus vltimis. futura Enarrationem partium quæ est eorum quæ sunt præsentia, enarratio didascalica secundum septem Ecclesias. ca .2.&3. Futura: enarratio prophetica: quæ est Communis de mundo universi[?] eius partes duæ Præparatoria quæ narratur Iohannis vocatio, Revelationis auctoritas à persona[?] vocātis[?] Dei Patris c. 4. Filij: c. 5. Malorum quæ mundo eventura sunt divinæ prænunciationes, & præsignificationes: c.6. Electorum vindicatorū ab omni malo obsignatio divina, ante prænunciatorum malorum complementum: c. 7. Ipsa opera Dei iudicia Executio iudiciorū Dei in alia, c. 8. in homines vexationib. & cædibus cap. 9. Singularis de Ecclesia Christi: vide infra ad cap. 10. & sequentia.
units.tr: The principal treatment has a bipartite statement of its subject. The first part concerns the things present, in chapter 1 and the last two verses; the second concerns the things future. The explanation of the parts of the present things is a didactic narration according to the seven churches, in chapters 2 and 3. The things future are set out in a prophetic narration, which is common to the whole world and has two parts. The preparatory part narrates John's calling and the authority of the revelation, from the person of God the Father who calls (chapter 4) and the Son (chapter 5). The second part contains the divine predictions and foreshadowings of the evils that are to befall the world: the divine sealing of the elect, who are to be preserved from all evil, before the predicted evils are completed (chapter 6); the works of God themselves, the judgments (chapter 7); the execution of God's judgments on others (chapter 8); and the afflictions and slaughters of men (chapter 9). A particular account of the Church of Christ follows, which see below at chapter 10 and those that follow.

units.la: Post visionem, quâ admonitus fuit Iohannes de autore revelationis, & in quorum gratiam talis revelatio fieret, dictantur iam Iohanni cap. 11. & 111. septem Epistolae, pro numero & conditione earum Ecclesiarum, quae nominatae fuerunt supra cap. 1. v. 11. figuratae vero v. 12. & distributae conuenientissime in pastores & greges, v. 20. qui versus ad hanc partem fuit μεταβατικός[?]. Capite secundo sunt 4. Epistolae: 1. ad pastorem Ecclesiae Ephesinae. 11. Ecclesiae Smyrnensis: v. 8. 111. Ecclesiae Pergamensis: v. 12. 1 v.[?] Ecclesiae Thyatirensis: v. 18. Capite tertio tres 1. Ecclesiae Sardium. 11. Ecclesiae Philadelphiae: v. 7. 111. Ecclesiae Laodiceae: v. 14.
units.tr: After the vision by which John was admonished about the author of the revelation, and for whose sake such a revelation was made, seven letters are now dictated to John in chapters 2 and 3. They correspond to the number and condition of those churches which were named above in chapter 1, verse 11, and figured in verse 12, and are most suitably distributed into ministers and flocks, verse 20; that verse serves as a transition to this part. In chapter 2 there are four letters: (1) to the minister of the church of Ephesus; (2) to the church of Smyrna, verse 8; (3) to the church of Pergamum, verse 12; (4) to the church of Thyatira, verse 18. In chapter 3 there are three: (5) to the church of Sardis; (6) to the church of Philadelphia, verse 7; (7) to the church of Laodicea, verse 14.

units.la: Sunt autem hae epistolae partim νουθετικαί[?]: partim ἐλεγκτικαί[?]: partim παρακλητικαί[?]. Et septem illae Ecclesiae, vna cum his septem Epistolis videntur nobis repraesentare tres Ecclesiarum conditiones, quae omnibus fere temporibus occurrunt. Nam aliae sunt bene constitutae, in quibus vix aliquid desideratur. Tales fuere secunda & sexta Smyrnensis & Philadelphensis. Aliae habent non pauca laudabilia, sed tamen naevus non caret: tales fuere prima, tertia & quarta, Ephesina, Pergamena, Thyatirana. Aliae plenae sunt hypocritis, & multos habent defectus, quales fuere quinta & septima, Sardicensis & Laodicensis.
units.tr: These letters are partly admonitory, partly reproving, and partly consoling. Those seven churches, together with these seven letters, seem to us to represent three conditions of the churches, which occur at almost every time. For some are well established, and in them hardly anything is wanting. Such were the second and sixth, those of Smyrna and Philadelphia. Others have not a few commendable things, yet a blemish is not lacking; such were the first, third and fourth, Ephesus, Pergamum and Thyatira. Others are full of hypocrites and have many defects; such were the fifth and seventh, Sardis and Laodicea.

units.la: Sic fuit principalis Tractationis pars prima in narratione eorum quae iam tum erant, sequitur deinceps
units.tr: Thus the first part of the principal treatment, the narration of those things which already then existed, is complete; what follows next

units.la: PARS SECUNDA
units.tr: PART TWO

units.la: Quae tota argumento est prophetica eorum quæ futura erant, vt dictum est supra: cap.1.v.19. & hic diserte pronunciatur, in v. 1. cap. 4.
units.tr: This whole part is prophetic in its subject matter, concerning the things that were to come to pass, as was said above at chapter 1, verse 19, and as is plainly declared here, at chapter 4, verse 1.

units.la: Hæc autem in duas historias distinguitur; [?]nam communem totius mundi, ad caput 9. vsque: alteram singularem Ecclesiæ Dei, ad cap. 21. vsque. atque hæ historiæ singulis libris descriptæ fuisse dicuntur, cap. 5. & 10.
units.tr: This history is divided into two. The first, the general history of the whole world, runs up to chapter 9; the second, the particular history of the Church of God, runs to chapter 21. These histories are said to have been described in separate books, at chapters 5 and 10.

units.la: Rursum prioris prophetiæ quæ communis est totius mundi, membra duo sunt: quorum unum est de causis factorum & totius reuelationis, capite quarto & quinto: alterum de factis, capitibus quatuor sequentibus.
units.tr: Again, the first prophecy, which concerns the whole world, has two members. One concerns the causes of the events and of the whole revelation, in chapters 4 and 5; the other concerns the events themselves, in the four chapters that follow.

units.la: Causarum autem principalium secundum distinctionem personarum in unitate essentiæ Dei, & secundum ὁμοουσίαν seu dispensationem eius, duo sunt loci: unus de principio, quod est inaccessu Deus pater, de quo capite 4. alter de Filio ut causâ mediante, & ad accessum facili, quâ est θεάνθρωπις: capite quinto.
units.tr: There are two places concerning the principal causes, according to the distinction of persons in the unity of the essence of God, and according to his homoousia or dispensation. The first concerns the principle, which is God the Father, unapproachable, treated in chapter 4. The second concerns the Son as the mediating cause, and as the easy access, which is the God-man, treated in chapter 5.

units.la: Capite igitur iv. Secunda est visio diuinæ maiestatis gloriam continens: quæ (v. 8.9. ) à quatuor animalibus, & viginti quatuor senioribus (v. 10. & 11.) celebratur.
units.tr: Thus in chapter 4 there is a second vision, containing the glory of the divine majesty, which is celebrated by the four living creatures (vv. 8-9) and by the twenty-four elders (vv. 10-11).

units.la: Cap. v. est v. 1. transitio ad causam principalem secundam ordine, Filium Dei, Mediatorem omnium, Sermonem æternum Dei Patris in carne patefactum. Partes capitis sunt duæ: vna, parasceuastica ad reuelationem, ex historia occasionum quæ se obtulerunt: vsque ad v. 5. de libro
units.tr: Chapter 5, verse 1, is a transition to the second principal cause in order, the Son of God, Mediator of all, the eternal Word of the Father made manifest in the flesh. The chapter has two parts. The first, preparatory to the revelation, arises from the history of the occasions that presented themselves, and runs up to verse 5, concerning the book.

units.la: V. 1. cap. 4. à præcedente ad secundam partem est μετά-βασιν[?] siue transitiuus: vbi apertum cœlum, id est, res cœlestes reseratæ dicuntur, & vox tanquam tubæ clanxisse[?] è cœlo quæ Apostolum excitaret, & ad rerum futurarum comprehensionem aduocaret.
units.tr: Verse 1 of chapter 4 is a transition from the preceding part to the second part, a metabasis or transition. There the open heaven, that is, the heavenly things, are said to be unsealed, and a voice like a trumpet sounds from heaven to rouse the Apostle and to call him to the understanding of things to come.

units.la: septem sigillis obsignato, quem nemo aperire poterat. Altera in historia reuelationis Christi, vsque ad finem capitis: nam Agnus ille Dei, dignus qui librum obsignatum aperiat, omnium coelestium voce decantatur.
units.tr: ...sealed with seven seals, which no one could open. The second part, in the history of the revelation of Christ, runs to the end of the chapter, for that Lamb of God, worthy to open the sealed book, is sung by the voice of all the heavenly beings.

units.la: Sequentibus 4. capitibus prioris historiæ (quam totius mundi communem esse diximus) est secunda pars, de factis Dei in mundi huius gubernatione, cuius partis membra universa sunt: præsignificatio: cap 6. cautio, cap. 7. Exequntio, cap. 8. & 9.
units.tr: After the four chapters of the first history (which we said is common to the whole world) comes the second part, concerning the works of God in the governing of this world. Its members are all of these: the presignification, in chapter 6; the warning, in chapter 7; and the execution, in chapters 8 and 9.

units.la: Cap: VI. præsignificantur mala mundo imit-tenda per aperitionem septem sigillorum. Summa: Aperit Agnus primum libri sigillum, secun-dum (v. 3.) tertium, (v. 5.) quartum, (v. 7.) quin-tum, (v. 9.) & sextum, (v. 12.) Quibus apertis, cædes, fames, pestis, sanctorum quærela, terræmotus, & varia cœli prodigia oriuntur.
units.tr: Chapter 6: evils to be inflicted on the world are presignified by the opening of the seven seals. In summary: the Lamb opens the first seal of the book, then the second (v. 3), the third (v. 5), the fourth (v. 7), the fifth (v. 9), and the sixth (v. 12). With these opened, slaughter, famine, pestilence, the complaint of the saints, earthquakes and various portents in heaven arise.

units.la: Cap. VII, de cautione agit qua piis suis præ-cauit & prospexit Deus; vt exemplo Israëlita-rum olim Exod. 8. 23. è flagellis mundi istius im-pij, fideles eximerentur. Est autem vniuersus hic locus interductus cuiusdam, toto hoc capi-te, sumpta occasione ex prædictione & argu-mento sigilli sexti. Nam primum cauetur electis ab illo malo, vsque ad v. 9. Deinde gratia ab electis eo nomine, v. 10. & duobus seq. Postremo rei complementum exponitur, ad finem vsque ca-pitis.
units.tr: Chapter 7 deals with the warning, by which God foresaw and provided for his own faithful, as he once did for the Israelites by example (Exod. 8.23), so that the faithful might be spared from the scourges of this impious world. This whole place is an interpolated passage, drawn throughout this chapter, taking its occasion from the prediction and the subject of the sixth seal. First, the elect are warned against that evil, up to verse 9. Then grace is given to the elect on that account, at verse 10 and the two that follow. Lastly, the completion of the matter is set out, to the end of the chapter.

units.la: Cap. VIII. (vbi tertia Visio) Regressio ad hi-storiam sigillorum libri, quæ Agnus aperit. Est autem sigillum septimum proxima præsignifi-catio, præcisumque mandatum de executione summorum iudiciorum Dei in mundum hunc impium: qua præsignificatione ex sigillo visa, silent & horrescunt omnia in cœlo præ admiratione, donec mandata executionis à Deo sigillatim dantur administris eius. Sic transitur ad tertium membrum, de malorum quibus Deus mundum iustissimè statuit affligere, executione.
units.tr: Chapter 8 (where is the third vision) returns to the history of the seals of the book that the Lamb opens. The seventh seal is an immediate presignification, and a precise command concerning the execution of God's supreme judgments upon this impious world. When this presignification is seen from the seal, all things in heaven fall silent and shudder in wonder, until the commands of execution are given by God, one by one, to his ministers. Thus the account passes to the third member, the execution of the evils with which God has most justly determined to afflict the world.

units.la: Hæc autè executio primùm generatim præparatur ad v. vsque 6. huius capitis. Deinde minutatim, secundùm administrorum ordinem exponitur in seqq.
units.tr: This execution is first prepared in general, up to verse 6 of this chapter. Then it is set out in detail, according to the order of the ministers, in what follows.

units.la: Ad præparandam executionem narrantur ista: primum qui administri ac instrumenta illius: v. 2. Deinde quod opus tum principis Angelorum hac executionem informantis, (v. 3.4, 5.)tum administrorum eius. v. 6.
units.tr: To prepare the execution, the following things are narrated: first, who the ministers and instruments of it are (v. 2); then the work of the chief of the angels, who directs this execution (vv. 3-5); and then the work of his ministers (v. 6).

units.la: Narratio rerum singularium, quas Angeli sex numero operati sunt duo ordine, exponuntur deinceps, ad v. 20. vsque capitis sequentis: Concluditur verò indicatione euentus, qui ex his rebus gestis apud mundum consecutus est: duobus vltimis. A v. igitur 7. capitis octaui narratur quomodo quatuor primis Angelis clangentibus ignis decidat, mare turbetur, aquæ amarescant, & stellæ obtenebrentur.
units.tr: The narrative of the particular things which the six angels performed, in two groups, is then set out, up to verse 20 of the following chapter. It concludes with an indication of the outcome which followed in the world from these deeds, in the last two verses. From verse 7 of chapter 8 it is narrated how, at the sounding of the first four angels, fire falls, the sea is troubled, the waters become bitter, and the stars are darkened.

units.la: Cap. IX.
units.tr: Chapter 9.

units.la: Quinto Angelo clangente, locusta vastatrices prodeunt: vsque ad v. 13. Sextus autem clangens equites educit humanum genus deuastantes: vsque ad v. 20. Postremò communis euentus, in mundo ex antegressis excutitionibus inemendabili, exponitur v. 20. & 21.
units.tr: When the fifth angel sounds, locusts that lay waste come forth, up to verse 13. The sixth angel, sounding, brings forth horsemen who destroy the human race, up to verse 20. Finally, the common outcome in the world, from the preceding shakings which cannot be amended, is set out in verses 20 and 21.

units.la: Hactenus historia prophetica communis: sequitur
units.tr: Thus far the common prophetic history; there follows

units.la: PROPHETIA SINGVLARIS ET Ecclesiæ propria.
units.tr: Singular prophecy, proper to the Church.

units.la: Singularis historia Ecclesiæ propria habet Transitionem præparatoriam, quis, cui reuelauerit: cap. 10. Rem ipsâ, de statu Ecclesiæ qualis est In hoc mundo: vbi de scriptio Ecclesiæ Certantis Summatim cap. 11. distinctè, iuxta duo tempora, quorum prius de Ecclesiæ ortu cap. 12. progressu cap. 13. posterius cap. 14. 15. 16. Vincentis per Christum metrice: c. 17. 18. utraque bestiam, cap. 19. draconem cap. 20. Post huius mundi finem, de Ecclesia triumphante, cap. 21. & 22.
units.tr: The singular history proper to the Church has a preparatory transition: who it was revealed to, chapter 10; the matter itself, the state of the Church as it is in this world. Here the Church's fighting state is described in summary in chapter 11, and then distinctly, according to two times. The first concerns the origin of the Church (chapter 12), its progress (chapter 13), and the latter time (chapters 14, 15, 16). The Church conquering through Christ is set out in verse (chapters 17, 18). Both beasts are treated in chapter 19, and the dragon in chapter 20. After the end of this world, the triumphant Church is described in chapters 21 and 22.

units.la: Cap. x. Duo sunt parasceuastica seu præparatoria in Transitione: vnum, Christi reuelantis mysteria sua & seruum suum vocantis authoritas: vsque ad v. 8. alterum, singularis ad hunc locum repetita, queque Iohannis vocatio ad perceptionem sequentis prophetiæ: quæ mandatur ipsi primum signo, v. 8. 9. 10. Deinde apertis verbis, versu vltimo.
units.tr: Chapter 10. There are two preparatory parts in the transition. One is the authority of Christ revealing his mysteries and calling his servant, up to verse 8. The other is John's calling, singular and repeated for this place, to receive the prophecy that follows. This is first enjoined by the sign, in verses 8, 9 and 10, and then in plain words in the last verse.

units.la: Expositâ authoritate reuelationis institutæ, & necessitate vocationis illius quæ Iohanni singulariter fuit imperata, deinceps historia subiicitur de statu Ecclesiæ Christi, tum certantis siue militantis, tum vincentis in Christo: Nam & Ecclesia Christi certare edicitur contra Pseudochristianam Ecclesiam cui Antichristus imperat, Christo Iesu confundente Antichristum spiritu oris sui: & Christus vincere gloriosissimè, donec interueniet Antichristum reuelatione aduentus sui, vt, quemadmodum[?] docet Apostolus 2. Thessal. 2.
units.tr: Having set out the authority of the revelation instituted, and the necessity of that calling which was singularly enjoined on John, the history next turns to the state of the Church of Christ, both fighting or militant and conquering in Christ. The Church of Christ is bidden to fight against the pseudo-Christian Church, which is commanded by Antichrist, while Christ Jesus destroys Antichrist with the spirit of his mouth. Christ conquers most gloriously until Antichrist is revealed at his coming, as the Apostle teaches in 2 Thess. 2.

units.la: Prophetiæ historicæ, seu historiæ propheti-cæ de statu Ecclesiæ in hoc mundo partes sunt duæ: vna, de statu Ecclesiæ cum tentationibus conflictantis, ad cap. 17. vsque: altera, de statu eiusdem Ecclesiæ vincentis, inde vsque ad cap.21.
units.tr: The parts of the prophetic, or prophetic-historical, history of the state of the Church in this world are two. One is concerning the state of the Church struggling with temptations, up to chapter 17. The other is concerning the state of the same Church conquering, from there to chapter 21.

units.la: Prioris partis membra duo sunt, suis temporibus commodissimè distributa, quorum prius historiam Christianæ Ecclesiæ continet ad annos 1260. quum Euangelium Christi in cœlum quasi receptum est è medio hominum, Posterius eiusdem historiam ad consummationem vsque victoriæ continet.
units.tr: The former part has two members, most conveniently distributed in their own times. The first contains the history of the Christian Church down to the year 1260, when the Gospel of Christ was, as it were, taken up into heaven from the midst of men. The latter contains the history of the Church down to the completion of victory.

units.la: Capite autem xi. duo hæc membra summatim, quamuis distinctè, proponuntur: sed copiosius vtrumque posteà suo ordine enarratur. Ideò autem Iohannes vtriusque temporis historiam in hoc capite copulauit: quia de Prophetia hic agitur; quam vnicam esse iustam & immutabilem in Ecclesia agnoscunt omnes, & continuam esse præcepit Christus. Prioris temporis historia ad v. vsque 14. pertinet: in qua narratur 1. vocatio seruorum Dei, uersibus quatuor. 2. certamina à fidelibus pie in uocatione pro Christo & Ecclesia eius, obeunda, inde ad v. 10. & resurrectio eorum atque in cœlum receptio, ad v. 14. vsque. Posterior pars huius capitis summam complectitur Ecclesiæ Christianæ, inde à Bonifacy VIII. seculo ad consummationem vsque victoriæ, cœlestibus vocibus enunciatam: Huius autem summa historicæ tres sunt loci: 1. præparatio per clangorem Angeli, (v. 15.) 2. narrritio per cœlestium Angelorum & Seniorum voces, (v. 16. 17. 18.) 3. confirmatio per signum, v. 19. Deinceps prophetiæ summatim antecedente cap. propositæ locus prior cap. 12. & 13. posterior vero cap. 14. 15. & 16. exponetur.
units.tr: In chapter 11 these two members are set out in summary, though distinctly. Each is narrated more fully afterwards in its own order. John joined the history of both times in this chapter because prophecy is the subject here. All acknowledge that prophecy to be one, just and unchanging in the Church, and Christ commanded it to be continuous. The history of the former time extends to verse 14, in which are narrated: (1) the calling of God's servants, in four verses; (2) the struggles which the faithful must undergo piously in their calling for Christ and his Church, up to verse 10; (3) their resurrection and reception into heaven, up to verse 14. The latter part of this chapter embraces a summary of the Christian Church from the age of Boniface VIII to the completion of victory, proclaimed by heavenly voices. The historical parts of this summary are three: (1) preparation by the trumpet of an angel (v. 15); (2) narration by the voices of the heavenly angels and elders (vv. 16, 17, 18); (3) confirmation by a sign (v. 19). Next, the former part of the prophecy, proposed in summary above, will be explained in chapters 12 and 13, and the latter in chapters 14, 15 and 16.

units.la: Ad priorem locum duo pertinent, ortus, qui cap. 12. & progressus illius in certaminibus & Christiana luctæ: cap. 13.
units.tr: Two things belong to the former part: its origin, which is chapter 12, and its progress through conflicts and Christian struggle, which is chapter 13.

units.la: Capite igitur xii. de ortu Ecclesiæ agitur, quem definimus inde à momento conceptionis Christi, ad illud usque tempus quo Ecclesia hæc tanquam à lacte matris depulsa est: quum videlicet Ecclesia Iudæorum cum urbe & templo subuersa est iudicio Dei. Sic habetur in hoc capite historia annorum amplius sexaginta novem. Partes huius capitis sunt tres: prima historia conceptus & gestationis, versibus 4. Secunda, historia partus, a v. 5. ad 12. usque: tertia denique, historia puerperæ, inde ad finem cap. atque hæ partes singulæ suis certaminibus coniunctæ sunt.
units.tr: Chapter 12 therefore deals with the origin of the Church. We define this origin from the moment of Christ's conception up to the time when this Church was, as it were, weaned from its mother's milk, namely when the Church of the Jews was overthrown along with the city and temple by the judgment of God. Thus this chapter contains a history of more than sixty-nine years. It has three parts: the first, the history of conception and gestation, verses 1 to 4; the second, the history of the birth, from verse 5 to 12; the third, the history of the lying-in, from there to the end of the chapter. Each of these parts is joined with its own conflicts.

units.la: Expositio Ecclesiæ Christianæ ortu & conditione Ecclesiæ illius unde ortum ducit nostra, iam ad historiam Progressus transit Apostolus, qui hoc cap. xiii. distincte duobus membris exponitur: quorum unum est de imperio civili Romano, ad v. 10. usque: in quo narrantur 1. status illius imperii, quatuor versibus: 2. res gestæ, 3. versibus: 3. effectus, gloria amplissima, v. 8. postremo versus, & piorum militantio aduersus mala ab eo superuentura denuntiantur v. 9. & 10. Alterum visionis membrum est de imperio Ecclesiastico, quod Romæ successit politico, & est penes corpus Pseudoprophetarum: hinc eadem bestia idemque corpus à Iohanne Pseudoprophetæ appellatione donatur infra cap. 16. 13. & 19. v. 20. Huius autem Bestiæ primùm[?] species describitur, v. 11. deinde res gesta il-lius sequentibus, & sermo totus concluditur, vers. ultimo.
units.tr: Having set out the origin of the Christian Church and the condition of that Church from which our own takes its origin, the Apostle now passes to the history of its progress. In this 13th chapter it is set out distinctly in two members. One concerns the civil Roman empire, up to verse 10, in which are narrated: (1) the state of that empire, in four verses; (2) its deeds, in three verses; (3) its effect, its most ample glory, in the last verse of verse 8. The struggle of the pious militant people against the evils to come from it is announced in verses 9 and 10. The other member of the vision concerns the ecclesiastical empire, which succeeded the political empire at Rome and rests with the body of false prophets. Hence the same beast and the same body are called by John the false prophet, below in chapters 16:13 and 19:20. Of this beast, first its appearance is described, v. 11; then its deeds in what follows; and the whole discourse is concluded in the last verse.

units.la: Absoluta historia Ecclesiæ Christi ad annos amplius mille trecentos: reliqua demum historia sequitur certantis seu militantis Ecclesiæ inde ad tempora usque victoriæ ultimæ, tribus capitibus.
units.tr: Having finished the history of the Church of Christ down to about the year 1300, the remaining history follows, that of the fighting or militant Church, from there to the time of the final victory, in three chapters.

units.la: Capite igitur xiiii Primò quasi fundamentum totius historiæ, Agni illius constitutio cum copiis & comitatu eius describitur, quinque primis versibus. In qua descriptione ponuntur situs locus, & comitatus ipsius, quia cætera exposita sunt visis antecedentibus, præsertim verò in cap. v. Deinde à v. 6. huius capitis usque ad finem 16. capitis, Res gesta Agni seu Christi, quas fecit & facit adhuc potentissimè in fundendo Antichristo Ecclesiæque illius spiritu oris divini eius. Sermonum, usque ad v. 13. Rerum gestarum modus duplex est Factorum quorum genus 1. commune, bellorum calamitas in tota terra: reliquo cap. 4. 2. singulare, in terra & adoratores eius: cuius præparatio est cap. 15. Executio, cap. 16.
units.tr: Therefore in chapter 14, first, as it were the foundation of the whole history, the establishment of that Lamb with his forces and retinue is described in the first five verses. In this description his place and retinue are set out, because the other things were explained in the preceding visions, especially in chapter 5. Then from verse 6 of this chapter to the end of chapter 16 come the deeds of the Lamb or Christ, which he has done and still does most mightily in pouring out Antichrist with the spirit of his divine mouth. His words extend to verse 13. The manner of the deeds is twofold. The first kind, common, is the calamity of wars throughout the whole earth, which is the rest of chapter 14. The second, singular, falls on the earth and its worshippers. Its preparation is chapter 15 and its execution chapter 16.

units.la: Narratur ergo deinceps singulare opus iudi-ciorum Dei, ad fundendum Antichristum cum eius copiis pertinens: cuius operis diuini præparatio hoc cap. xv primùm quidem universè, & summatim v. 11. exponitur, deinde minutatim enar-ratur ratur, reliquo capite; cuius enarrationis partes duæ sunt: una sanctorum confessio glorificantium Deum, visa illa iudiciorum præparatione, ad v. 5. usque; altera instrumentorum quæ Deus ordinauit vocatio, instructio & confirmatio ad exsecutionem iudiciorum eius.
units.tr: Next is narrated the singular work of God's judgments, pertaining to the overthrow of Antichrist with his forces. The preparation of this divine work is set out in this chapter 15: first in general and in summary at verse 1, then it is narrated in detail in the rest of the chapter. The parts of this narration are two. One is the confession of the saints glorifying God, seeing that preparation of judgments, up to verse 5. The other is the calling, instruction and confirmation of the instruments which God has ordained for executing his judgments.

units.la: Cap. xvi. traditur exsecutio diuini operis. Ac primùm quidem hic de executione locus habet mandatum commune, in v. 1. Deinde verò singulare executionis ab unoquoque Angelo facta historia suo ordine, reliquo capite: Summa est; Effunduntur Angeli septem commissas sibi furoris diuini phialas: quibus effusis varia plagæ in orbe terrarum exoriuntur, ad terrendos improbos, & magna urbis incolas.
units.tr: Chapter 16 delivers the execution of the divine work. First, the execution has a common command, in verse 1. Then comes the singular history of the execution, done by each angel in its order, in the rest of the chapter. The summary is this: the seven angels pour out the seven vials of divine wrath committed to them. When these are poured out, various plagues arise over the earth, to terrify the wicked and the inhabitants of the great city.

units.la: Statu Ecclesiæ certantis expositio, sequitur status vincentis, qui 4. capitibus deinceps exponitur. Primò autem traditur historia Babylonis perditæ, cap. 17. & 18. secundò utriusque bestiæ, cap. 19. Postremò autem draconis, cap. 20.
units.tr: After the exposition of the state of the fighting Church follows the state of the conquering Church, which is set out in the next four chapters. First the history of fallen Babylon is delivered, in chapters 17 and 18; second, that of both beasts, in chapter 19; last, that of the dragon, in chapter 20.

units.la: Capite igitur xvii. post transitionem (v. 1. & 2.) Primò proponitur typus Babylonis & status illius, ubi describuntur duo: nimirum bestia illa, (de qua supra 13.) in v. 3. & mulier insidens bestiæ, usque ad v. 7. Deinde additur typi declaratio, ubi primò traditur enarratio bestiæ & historiæ eius, ad versum 14. postea verò meretricis, usque ad finem capitis.
units.tr: Therefore in chapter 17, after the transition (vv. 1, 2), the type of Babylon and its state is first set forth, where two things are described: that beast (of which above, at 13) in verse 3, and the woman sitting on the beast, up to verse 7. Then an explanation of the type is added. First the description of the beast and its history is delivered, up to verse 14; afterwards that of the harlot, to the end of the chapter.

units.la: Cap. xix. Secundus est locus historiæ Babylonicæ, qui est de funesto casu & ruina meretricis illius Babyloniæ. Triplex autem est historica de ea prædictio: una ruina illius aperta & simplex prædictio, tribus versibus: secunda figurata prædictio ex adiunctis, inde ad v. 21. usque, tertio, signo confirmata, ad finem usque capitis.
units.tr: Chapter 19. The second section of the Babylonian history concerns the fatal fall and ruin of that harlot Babylon. There is a threefold historical prediction of it: first, a plain and open prediction of her ruin, in three verses; second, a figurative prediction, confirmed by its circumstances, from there to verse 21; third, a prediction confirmed by a sign, to the end of the chapter.

units.la: Capitis xx. duae sunt omnino partes: Una μεταβατικὸν [?] seu transitiua, cuius duo loci: vnus laudatiuus, de ruina facta Babylonis, versibus 4. alter itidem laudatiuus atque propheticus, de aduentu Christi in regnum, & augustissimo eius coniugio cum Ecclesia sua, usque ad v. 11. Altera est historica victoria a Christo de bestia utraque parte: vbi primum describitur pugnaturus Christus, ad v. 17. tum ineunda pugna pronunciatur, vbi hostes sarcastice ad pugnam prouocantur, usque ad v. 19. Postremo autem victoria narratur ad finem usque capitis.
units.tr: Chapter 20 has two parts altogether. The first is transitional, and it has two passages: one laudatory, on the ruin of Babylon, in four verses; the other likewise laudatory and prophetic, on the coming of Christ into his kingdom and his most glorious marriage with his Church, to verse 11. The second is the historical victory of Christ over the beast on both sides. Here first Christ, about to fight, is described, to verse 17; then the beginning of the battle is announced, where the enemies are sarcastically challenged to battle, to verse 19. Lastly, the victory is narrated to the end of the chapter.

units.la: Cap. xxi. Tertius locus est, de victoria qua Draconem superauit Christus: quem locum necesse est cum historia cap. 12. sub finem coniungi, aptarique ad iustam intelligentiam illius. Sunt autem huius capitis partes duae: Una de Dracone victo, ad v. 11. usque. Altera de resurrectione iudicioque ultimo, inde ad cap. finem.
units.tr: Chapter 21. The third section concerns the victory by which Christ overcame the Dragon, which passage must necessarily be joined at the end with the history of chapter 12 and fitted to it for its correct understanding. There are two parts to this chapter. The first, concerning the Dragon overcome, runs to verse 11. The second, concerning the resurrection and the last judgment, runs from there to the end of the chapter.

units.la: Hactenus de statu Ecclesiae in hoc mundo; sequitur de statu futuro Ecclesiae coelestis post iudicium ultimum usque ad v. 6. capitis sequentis.
units.tr: Thus far concerning the state of the Church in this world; there follows concerning the future state of the heavenly Church after the last judgment, to verse 6 of the following chapter.

units.la: Cap. xxii. Primo summatim ante statum Ecclesiae status universitatis exponitur, coelum fore novum, terramque novam v. 1. atque hac sedes vel locus Ecclesiae, in quo iustitia habitat. Deinde status Ecclesiae illius describitur generatim idque in riso [?] eminus oblato, (v. 2.) & sermonibus e coelo enunciatis, usque ad v. 9. Secundo speciatim & minutatim, vbi est transitio complectens Iohannis singusingularem vocationem: (v.9.10. ii.) 2 Descriptio ipsa cœlestis Ecclesiæ, primum secundum partes essentiales ipsius, sub typo ciuitatis, ad v. 23. secundò ab exrernis accidentibus, ad finem capitis; tertiò ab effectis, principio cap. seq.
units.tr: Chapter 22. First, in summary, before the state of the Church, the state of the whole universe is set forth: the heaven will be new and the earth new (v. 1), and this is the seat or place of the Church, in which righteousness dwells. Then the state of that Church is described in general, and this in a vision seen from afar (v. 2) and in words spoken from heaven, to verse 9. Second, in particular and in detail, where there is a transition embracing John's singular calling (vv. 9, 10, 11). Second, the description of the heavenly Church itself: first, according to its essential parts, under the type of a city, to verse 23; second, from its external accidents, to the end of the chapter; third, from its effects, at the beginning of the next chapter.

units.la: Cap: igitur xxiii. absoluitur descriptio Ecclesiæ cœlestis ab effectis Dei habitantis in Ecclesia, quinque versibus. Reliquo capite est.
units.tr: Chapter 23, therefore, completes the description of the heavenly Church from the effects of God dwelling in the Church, in five verses. The rest of the chapter follows.

units.la: LIBRI HVIVS CONCLVSIO,
units.tr: THE CONCLUSION OF THIS BOOK

units.la: Quæ sit confirmatione & salutatione. (Confir-mationis loci sunt tres: 1. sermo Angeli, ad verf. 16. 2 sermo Christi, verf. 16. & 17. 3 obtestatio facta à Iohanne diuinitus vsque ad v. vltimum, in quo est salutatio Apostolica, omnium ferè Epistolarum clausula: quam Ecclesiæ, & piis omnibus illius membris, adeoque electis optamus in Domino Iesu Christo vsque in aduentum ipsius. Veni Domine Iesu, & fac. Amen iterum Amen.
units.tr: This consists of confirmation and salutation. There are three places of confirmation: (1) the speech of the Angel, to verse 16; (2) the speech of Christ, verses 16 and 17; (3) the solemn charge given by John from God, down to the last verse, in which is the apostolic salutation, the closing formula of almost all the Epistles, which we wish for the Church and for all the pious members of it, and therefore for the elect, in the Lord Jesus Christ until his coming: "Come, Lord Jesus, and so forth." Amen, again Amen.

units.la: ARGVMENTA CAPITVM.
units.tr: ARGUMENTS OF THE CHAPTERS.

units.la: CAPVT I.
units.tr: CHAPTER I.

units.la: Hic ventura canit venturo tempore fata, His scribens, Asiæ qui bona rura colunt. Apparens stellæ septem, candelabra septem, Mirifico ac anceps ensis ab ore micat.
units.tr: Here he sings of the fates that are to come in the coming time, writing to those who dwell in the good fields of Asia. The seven stars appear, the seven candlesticks, and from his mouth a wondrous two-edged sword flashes.

units.la: Admonet hic Ephesum famosæ & mænia Smyrnæ, Post illas pariter Pergama chara monet. Quæque Thiatiram victrix Ecclesia gentem Incolit, his quænam fata futura sient.
units.tr: He warns here Ephesus and the famous walls of Smyrna; after these he likewise warns dear Pergamum. And the victorious Church that dwells among the people of Thyatira: what fates are to come for these.

units.la: Fata canit Sardis, narrat Philadelphica fata, Fata canit dives Laodicæa tibi,
units.tr: He sings the fates of Sardis, he tells the fates of Philadelphia; the rich Laodicea, the fates she is to suffer, sing for you.

units.la: En Deus altisonans folio sedet altus eburno, Huncque senum turba bis duodena canit. Quatuor hunc etiam clamant animalia Sanctum, Sic Domino soli traditur omnis honor.
units.tr: Behold God on high, thundering, sits aloft on an ivory throne, and the crowd of twice twelve elders sings to him. Four living creatures also cry out to the Holy One; thus all honour is given to the Lord alone.

units.la: Cum clausum nemo posset aperire volumen Oblatum sumis[?], agne supreme, librum. Te quoniam dignum clamant, coelestia verba, ut Fatalis referes sancta sigilla libri.
units.tr: Since no one could open the closed volume, you take the book offered, O supreme Lamb. Since they cry out that you alone are worthy, heavenly words, that you may unfold the sacred seals of the book of fates.

units.la: Bella, famem, pestem, sacriqueincommoda verbi Admonitus certa voce propheta canit. Accipiunt niveas vestes, qui fata queruntur, Tristia sanctorum, saevaque damna simul. Concutitur tristis vasto volumine tellus, Territat & reges ira cruenta Dei.
units.tr: Wars, famine, pestilence, and the troubles of the sacred word: the prophet, admonished, sings in a sure voice. They receive white robes, who lament the fates, the sorrows of the saints and their cruel losses together. The sad earth is shaken by the vast volume, and the bloody wrath of God terrifies kings.

units.la: Ne noceat Domini veniens afflictio sanctis[?] Signatur forti in fronte[?] professa cruce. Tristia quaeque prius mundi sentire pericla, Astricolam celebrans pectora laeta Deum.
units.tr: Lest the coming affliction of the Lord harm the saints, the cross they profess is marked upon their brave foreheads. Having first to feel all the sad perils of the world, they celebrate God who dwells among the stars with joyful hearts.

units.la: Angelus ecce Deo nunc offert vota piorum, Quae summum possint conciliare patrem. Quatuor inde tubae crudeli murmure clangunt[?] Cum mare flamma ruit, sydera caeca latent.
units.tr: Behold, the angel now offers to God the prayers of the pious, which can reconcile the supreme Father. Then four trumpets clang with a cruel murmur, when the sea rushes on with fire and the blind stars lie hidden.

units.la: Ascendunt Stygio fortes de fonte locustae, Quae miseris nocent per mala multa viris. Angelus hinc clangit[?] non tanto[?] murmure, sextus, Armataque cadunt millia multa manu.
units.tr: From the Stygian fountain rise the strong locusts, which harm wretched men with many evils. Then the sixth angel sounds, not with so great a murmur, and many thousands fall by an armed hand.

units.la: Angelus en fortis coelestis venit ab arce, Qui terram calcat, qui pede calcat aquas. Infrendens quae ferox sinuosa volumina profert, Oblatum iussus devoratile librum.
units.tr: Behold, the strong heavenly angel comes from the citadel, who treads the earth and treads the waters with his foot. Fiercely muttering, he brings forth winding coils, ordered to devour the book offered to him.

units.la: Corrupti Vates metuunt limina Templi, Et Dominus testes proferet inde duos. Bestia quos laniat, laniatos excitat ipse Omnipotens, coeli & scandere summa iubet. Terrentur proceres: iam moenia magna ruuntur. Angelus ac inflat septimus inde tubam.
units.tr: The corrupt prophets fear the threshold of the Temple, and the Lord will bring forth from there two witnesses. The beast tears them; the Almighty himself raises up the torn ones and bids them climb to the highest heaven. The nobles are terrified; now the great walls are thrown down. Then the seventh angel sounds the trumpet.

units.la: Parturiens metuit serpentem foemina saevum, Angelica immanem perdidit huncce cohors. In coelo pax est, terras discordia vexat, Exitias[?] in sanctos proelia saeva draco.
units.tr: The pregnant woman fears the cruel serpent; a host of angels destroyed that monstrous one. There is peace in heaven, discord vexes the lands, and the dragon in fierce battles rages against the saints.

units.la: 13 [?] Romanum signans ascendit bestia regnum, Quod simul & terras oceanumque regit. Altera consurgit blasphemo bestia vultu, Quam si Pontificem dixeris esse, licet.
units.tr: 13 [?] The beast rising up marks the Roman kingdom, which rules both lands and ocean at once. Another beast rises with a blasphemous face, whom, if you call him the Pope, you may do so without fault.

units.la: 14 Agnum deducunt cultores agmine casto. Angelicos audit aure patente sonos. Ille fidem tradit: Babylonia fata minatur, Alter, & immanis dira periclaferæ [?]. Iam natura cadit feruenti tempore messis, Et spumant musto squalida praela novo.
units.tr: 14 The worshippers lead the Lamb in a chaste band and hear angelic sounds with open ear. He hands over the faith and threatens the fate of Babylon; and another, and the dire peril of a monstrous one. Now the harvest falls in the fervent season, and the filthy presses foam with new must.

units.la: 15 Apparent septem non læto corde ministri. Tradidit his septem verbera dira Deus. Iamque Deum celebrans resonanti voce supremum, Vicerunt tristis qui mala monstra ferae.
units.tr: 15 The seven ministers appear, not with a joyful heart. God handed them seven dire plagues. And now, celebrating God the Supreme with resounding voice, those have conquered who fought against the evil monsters of the sad beast.

units.la: 16 Cœlesti septem venientes arce ministri Septem pœnarum pocula plana gerunt. Hæc simul effundunt, his bestia tangitur ingens, Quæ turpes ranas ore patente vomit.
units.tr: 16 The seven ministers coming from the heavenly citadel carry seven flat cups of punishments. These they pour out together, and the huge beast is struck by them, the beast that vomits foul frogs from its open mouth.

units.la: 17 Immani vehitur meretrix obscœna dracone, Aurato calice mixta venena ferens. Cuius in immensum trepidanda potentia surgit, Hanc cupiunt reges, hanc cupiuntque duces.
units.tr: 17 The obscene harlot is carried on a monstrous dragon, bearing poisons mingled in a golden cup. Her dreaded power rises to an immense height; kings desire her, and dukes desire her.

units.la: 18 Vasta ruunt magnæ Babylonis mœnia, clamat Angelus, hei nimium mœnia tanta iacent. Mercantes lugent, summi lugentque Monarchæ, Quos duxit nimium tam lupa fœda diu.
units.tr: 18 The vast walls of great Babylon fall; the angel cries, "Alas, walls so great lie in ruins!" The merchants mourn, and the highest monarchs mourn, whom so foul a she-wolf has long led astray.

units.la: 19 Ultima narrantur cœlestis prælia pugnæ, Quæ ferus æthereo concidit ense draco. Iam pereunt quotquot Dominum impugnare parabant, Mergitur ardenti bestia sæva lacu.
units.tr: 19 The last battles of the heavenly fight are told, in which the fierce dragon fell by the ethereal sword. Now all perish who prepared to attack the Lord; the savage beast is plunged into the burning lake.

units.la: 20 Clauditur in tristem Satanas crudelis auernum, Qui redeat, cum sunt sæcula lapsa decem. Panduntur summi sinuosa volumina cœli, Defunctos fortis iudicat ipse Deus.
units.tr: 20 Cruel Satan is shut up in the sad abyss, to return when ten ages have passed. The winding volumes of the highest heaven are opened; the strong God himself judges the dead.

units.la: 21 Ecce novum cœlum, pariter nova & omnia vidi, Et nova de summo mœnia lapsa polo. Pingitur hac nobis victrix Ecclesia forma, Quæ fortis iuncta est sponsa pudica Deo.
units.tr: 21 Behold a new heaven, and likewise I saw all things new, and new walls fallen from the highest pole. Here the victorious Church is painted for us in this form, joined as a chaste bride to the strong God.

units.la: 22 Viventis cernit manantes fluminis undas, Ac urbis pingit iura celanda nova [?].
units.tr: 22 He sees the waters of the flowing river of life, and paints the laws of the new city, which are to be kept hidden.

units.la: Et monet hæc quam sint non falsa oracula Vates, Quæ summa decet nos coluisse fide.
units.tr: And he warns that the oracles of this prophet are not false, and that we ought to embrace them with the highest faith.

units.la: BREVIUS. CAP. I.
units.tr: A Briefer Account. Chapter I.

units.la: AD septem scribit, laudat Christum, venit alpha In Pathmo visi[?] quid sibi forma velit.
units.tr: He writes to the seven, praises Christ, and the Alpha comes; he sees in Patmos what the form means.

units.la: Bis geminas urbes, Ephesum, Smyrnam, Thiatiram, Pergamon, aut iustas, aut secus esse docet.
units.tr: He teaches that the four cities, Ephesus, Smyrna, Thyatira and Pergamum, are either righteous or otherwise.

units.la: Condemnat Sardes, Philadelphi facta probatur. Euomeris merito Laodicæa tepens.
units.tr: He condemns Sardis, and the deeds of Philadelphia are approved. Lukewarm Laodicea is rightly spewed out.

units.la: Describit sedes, seniores, Lampades, æquor, Et quadruplex animal, perpetuosque sonos.
units.tr: He describes the thrones, the elders, the lamps, the sea, the fourfold living creature, and the perpetual sounds.

units.la: Explicat hic librum, leo victor. & integer agnus, Dignus es unanimi millia voce canunt.
units.tr: Here he explains the book: the lion, victor, and the unblemished lamb; thousands sing with one voice, "Worthy art thou."

units.la: Fundit equos varios, animas de cæde querentes, Cum nigro Phæbo, syderibusque liber.
units.tr: He pours out the various horses, and the souls complaining of slaughter, with the black sun and the stars set free.

units.la: Grandesonat, signate pios, mox plurima turba, Laudat voce Deum. sanguine tincta stola est.
units.tr: He thunders loudly; the faithful are sealed; soon a great crowd praises God with one voice; the robe is stained with blood.

units.la: Incensum pia vota notat, volat ecce quadruplex Angelus, atque tuba mira sonante facit.
units.tr: He signifies the incense of pious prayers; behold, the fourfold angel flies and makes the wondrous trumpet sound.

units.la: Lux solis nigricat, fundit tuba quinta locustas, Tertia pars, sexta flante, necatur aquis.
units.tr: The light of the sun grows black; the fifth trumpet pours out locusts; a third part is destroyed by the waters when the sixth sounds.

units.la: Magna boans inquit, faciet tuba septima finem, Et torquet ventrem dulcis in ore cibus.
units.tr: The great seventh trumpet, roaring, says it will bring an end, and the sweet food twists the belly in the mouth.

units.la: Nemensuretur, testes duo vivificantur, Septimus examen clangor adesse docet.
units.tr: The temple is not measured; the two witnesses are made alive; the seventh clang teaches that the judgment is at hand.

units.la: Ornatæ partium cupiens draco præcipitatur; Nec tamen ornatæ definit esse gravis.
units.tr: The dragon, desiring the adorned parts, is cast down; yet it does not cease to be grievous to those who are adorned.

units.la: Prælia diragerit, colitur quoque bellua victrix, Altera succedit, facta prioris amans.
units.tr: Battles are fought; the victorious beast is also worshipped; another succeeds, a lover of the deeds of the former one.

units.la: Qui sunt qui cantant, Babylon cadit, ecce beata est, Mors iusti, segetem falx metit atque botrum.
units.tr: Who are they who sing? Babylon falls; behold, she is blessed; the death of the just; the sickle reaps the grain and the cluster of grapes.

units.la: Res mirae, vitreum mare, carmina, apertio templi, Et phialæ septem, quas repletæ gravis.
units.tr: Wondrous things: the glassy sea, songs, the opening of the temple, and the seven bowls, which when filled are heavy.

units.la: Sentit eas tellus, mare, fontes, flumina, Phæbus, Euphrates, sedes bestiæ & antra levis.
units.tr: The earth, the sea, the fountains and rivers feel them; the Phoebus, the Euphrates, the seat of the beast and the caves are light.

units.la: Tradit quid meretrix, quid eandem portans, Septenumque caput, quidque sit unda fluens.
units.tr: He tells what the harlot is, what she carries, the seven heads, and what the flowing water is.

units.la: 18 Vista[?] iacens Babylon, pateris te digna ruentem Culmide de tanto, vir mulierque stupent.
units.tr: 18 Babylon lies fallen, worthy of the cups, falling from such a height; man and woman are astonished.

units.la: 19 Agni laus, equitans, rex regum, carne volucres, Alta in sulphureum bestia missa lacum.
units.tr: 19 Praise of the Lamb; riding, King of kings; birds fed on flesh; the beast cast into the sulphurous lake.

units.la: 20 Bestia soluetur, nunc vi&a est, deinde peribit, Bis multi perient iudicio ante thronum.
units.tr: 20 The beast will be loosed, now it is alive, then it will perish; twice as many will perish by judgment before the throne.

units.la: 21 Cœlum aliud, tellus alia est pulsaque dolore, Conditur vrbs mirae nobilitatis opus.
units.tr: 21 Another heaven and another earth, and the earth struck with grief; the city is built, a work of wondrous nobility.

units.la: 22 Dat sanctis lignum vitae viuusque salutem. Define, mox adero, fac nihil adiicias.
units.tr: 22 He gives the saints the tree of life and living salvation. Make an end; soon I shall be there; add nothing.

units.la: Breuissimè.
units.tr: In Brief.

units.la: 1 2 3 4 5 Septè, Album, Tepidusq; , Throni, Signacula septè: 6 7 8 9 10 Rufus, Pulmaq; , Thuribulū, Caudasque, Tonitru, 11 12 13 14 15 Testes, Pugnaq; , Bestia, & Agnus, fundite Plagas: 16 17 18 19 20 Tu Phialas, Meretrix, Luxus, Stagnatis, in Orcu: 21 22 Sponsa pudica Dei: Iura colenda noua.
units.tr: 1 2 3 4 5 Seven, White, and Lukewarm, Thrones, Seven seals: 6 7 8 9 10 Red, Palm, Censer, Tails, Thunder, 11 12 13 14 15 Witnesses, Battle, Beast, and Lamb, pour out the plagues: 16 17 18 19 20 You, bowls, harlot, luxury, stagnant ones, into Orcus: 21 22 Chaste bride of God: new laws to be observed.

units.la: Declaratio.
units.tr: Explanation.

units.la: Septem candelabra, v. 12. Album calculum illi dabo: v. 17. Tepidusque quia es, euomam te, v. 16. Throni in circuitu erant throni 14. Signacula septem quibus liber obsignatus, v. 1.
units.tr: Seven candlesticks, v. 12. White: I will give him a white counter, v. 17. Lukewarm: because you are lukewarm, I will spew you out, v. 16. Thrones: there were thrones round about, 14. Seven seals with which the book is sealed, v. 1.

units.la: Rufus equus cui insidet gladiatus: v. 4. Palmaque gestatur in manibus populi, v. 9. Thuribulum aureum gestatur ab Angelo, v. 3. Caudasque habent similes serpentibus: v. 9. Tonitru locutum voces suas: v. 3.
units.tr: Red horse, on which sits one who bears a sword: v. 4. Palm carried in the hands of the people, v. 9. Censer of gold carried by an angel, v. 3. Tails they have, like serpents: v. 9. Thunder, its voices speaking: v. 3.

units.la: Testes amicti saccis, v. 3. Pugnaque Angeli cum Dracone, v. 7. Bestia utraque describitur, cap. 13. & Agnus stans super montem Sion: v. 1. fundite Plagas: v. 1. & vlt.
units.tr: Witnesses clothed in sackcloth, v. 3. Battle of the angel with the dragon, v. 7. Beast, both of them described, ch. 13. and the Lamb standing on Mount Zion: v. 1. Pour out the plagues: v. 1 and the last verse.

units.la: {tum}Tum Phialas. iræ Dei fundunt. cap. 16. Meretrix cuius damnatio Iohanni ostenditur: v. 1. Luxus Baby-lonis, v. 3. Stagnantis in lacum igne coniiciuntur ado-ratores Bestiæ: v. 20. in Orcum coniicitur Draco v. 3.
